                                  Dedication

We are deeply grateful to William (Willie) Will, one of the initiators of this
book. It was his foresight to collect and preserve the early history of Irvine
and area that we may relive the experiences of our forefathers and recall their
hardships, joys and accomplishments.

We therefore dedicate this book to William (Willie) Will of Irvine. Without his
dedication to the preservation of our heritage, A New Beginning would not have
become a reality.

We are saddened that Willie passed away at such a young age and did not live to
see his wish fulfilled.

                                   Foreword

Irvine was incorporated as a town over 80 years ago. Leading up to that time,
and in the years between then and now, there have been many people contributing
to what Irvine has become today. By recounting the histories of some of these
early pioneers, we hope to bring alive the past and feel some of the pride that
these people must have felt as they watched Irvine and its surrounding area take
shape during their building of a new life in an unknown land. The trials,
hardships, and rewards; the disappointments and triumphs of the past, are part
of our heritage. By getting to know our ancestors better we are getting to know
ourselves. It is our aim to pay tribute to these people who have come and gone
and we thank them for our new beginnings.


                                 Introduction

The compiling and publishing of this history book was intended to preserve
information of the early settlers, our forefathers and their families up to the
present time, most of whom came here at the turn of the century. We regret that
this was not undertaken at least ten years earlier when more of the homesteaders
were still alive and first hand information would have been more readily
available. Unfortunately we were not able to trace every one and we apologize to
any that we have missed. This was unintentional. Some had relocated and we were
not aware of where or how to contact them. Others, whom we did contact, did not
choose to contribute.

The contributions are presented in the most natural form of the writer wherever
possible. There may be some errors but we have attempted to present the writings
with the information as was supplied to us. The histories are those of the
writers and not necessarily the views of the Historical Committee.

If you get some enjoyment, as you leaf through the pages and read the histories,
that will be our reward.

WHEN WE WERE HOMESTEADING
We came to the prairies wild and wide
With a walking plow and some horses to ride,
We had helpful neighbors by our side
When we were homesteading.

We plowed the ground with heavy toil
And planted seeds in the fertile soil,
Often ate our lunch by a water hole
When we were homesteading.

Our house was just a soddy shack
There was a little garden out in back,
We had a few hens and some ducks to quack
When we were homesteading.

We took the good times with the bad
And did the best with what we had,
And raised some sturdy girls and lads
When we were homesteading.
- Dorothy Stange

                                A New Beginning

Geography

Geography has likely influenced the immigrants to settle in this area. Strangers
approaching the extreme southeast corner of the Province, from any direction,
will be impressed by three dominating features - its bareness, rolling contour
and its vastness. Approximately 25 miles south of the Town of Irvine, the
beautiful Cypress Hills rise to an altitude of 4,534 feet. The gigantic sheets
of moving, grinding ice gouged out many depressions, some of which eventually
became deep, cold lakes.

Irvine Badlands at a distance south of town (pic)

The Badlands and Bull Trail south of Irvine (pic)

Flood in Irvine flats (pic)

Spring flood in Irvine flats - 1939 (pic)

Garden plots in Irvine flats after spring flood (pic)

The rolling grassed approach from the Cypress Hills region was the beginning of
the ranching industry in the area. The light brown, moderately fertile soil
which ranges from two to five feet in depth was probably formed from the prairie
grasses on top of the glacial till through the thousands of years.

The emergence of the Russian-German settlers, about one century ago, and the
semi-arid nature of many areas, influenced the growth and development of
ranching and grain farming, with several large ranches found around the Irvine
area. Long hours of sunshine and many frost free days help the crops to mature
rapidly. Moisture conditions - over a 60 year period - average an annual
approximate 12 inches in the area and encourage the farmers. On the other hand,
the often hot dry month of July often causes the grain to wither and fade away.

Ben Schorr (on tractor) pulling out George Jeske gas truck, Ross Creek flood
(pic)

The Irvine dam (pic)

The warm Chinook winds, from across the Divide, made the area, especially in
certain regions, very adaptable to cattle and sheep raising. These winds often
bring spring-like days, in winter, to the whole of this southeastern area. The
rapid removal of the snow by the Chinook winds provides winter grazing for the
ranchers. Conversely, in summer, these winds become hot winds and may be a bane
to grain farmers. These winds, at times, blow from five to 75 miles per hour and
cause the scanty moisture in the soil to dry out rapidly and crops may ripen
prematurely and may be ruined. In the winter temperatures may drop as low as 40
degrees below zero, for several days, usually in January the coldest month. Wind
chill often causes much discomfort during the periods of these strong winds,
causing extremely low temperatures. Severe blizzards can sweep in without too
much warning and can pose a constant problem to stockmen.

Snow drifts between chicken house and barn. Jim, Diane and Norman Deering -
1951 (pic)

Snow drifts after snow storm - May 30, 1982 (pic)

The usual sunny and long summer conditions, the general one inch plus of
precipitation from April to June, although a hot and drier July sometimes
reaching as high as 95 to 105 degrees, has still left the settlers feeling
generally secure in the area and they have chosen to stay and continue in
agriculture and ranching. The lower prices of land in this immediate area was
likely also a contributing factor in settlers locating here.

The drought conditions that existed during the early thirties would lead one to
understand the perplexing problems the early settlers had to contend with and
very hard times that befell the people.  Some farms were abandoned and residents
relocated. Prices for agricultural products fell to a very low level and
unemployment figures rose, however by 1939 conditions improved slowly and
steadily and those that had stayed on realized the wheels of prosperity again
and consequently the Town of Irvine also began to prosper and expand once more.

The following article was published in the Medicine Hat News:

Dinosaur bones. Thirty years ago, on August 19, 1958, scientists of the National
Museum of Ottawa were digging up bones near Irvine.

The site was on the Bill Yanke farm about ten miles south of Irvine. The
skeleton of a Chasmosaurus was recovered The small dinosaur was, in life, about
15 feet long, 5 feet high and weighed about 3,000 pounds. It had a turtle-like
beak and an armored shield around its shoulders.

It was an exciting find for the scientists, since the skeleton was almost
complete. It would be shipped to the museum in Ottawa when fully excavated.

The hills immediately south of Irvine, known as "the bad lands" would contain
more of these artifacts.

Points of Interest
by William Glock

The Pointy Hill. (pic)

Irvine from the north, Spy Hill in background. (pic)

This is a bit of history about two points of interest on the outskirts of the
Town of Irvine.

One is about a quarter mile southeast of town and is called THE POINTY HILL,
also known as KAISER HILL. It got its name "Pointy Hill" because it looks like
an ice cream cone turned upside down, very large at the bottom and tapered to
the top. The hill is about 200 feet high, and anyone going to the top will find
it is about 20 feet in diameter, with a 2-3 foot depression that makes it look
as though it may have been a small volcano at some time. The entire hill is
covered with rocks (mostly small ones) and plenty of cactuses.

It was given the name "Kaiser Hill" during the First World War (1914-1918) when
Kaiser Wilhelm, the king of Germany, was burned in effigy on the top of this
hill.

The other hill is about 400 yards south of the town. This hill is about 250 feet
high, with the top about 100 feet wide and 400-500 feet long and very flat on
top.

The following story about this hill was told to me in 1938 by a gentleman who
was then 83 years old. This tale was passed on to him by his grandparents and
his mother, who were full-blood Cree Indians.

The area where the Town of Irvine now is was in the territory of the Cree. At
that time there were no white men here, and there was very good hunting in the
area, as this was Buffalo country (plus plenty of deer, elk, and antelope). The
buffalo migrated up here from the south, as this was their summer grazing range,
and therefor other Indian bands would also come here to hunt. Many of them were
enemies of the Cree. In order to protect themselves from attacks by these bands,
and also to locate the buffalo, deer, elk, and antelope, the Cree used this hill
as a lookout point, as you can see for miles around. The Cree name for the hill
I cannot remember as I did not write it down when I was told, but the gentleman
told me translated it meant "SEE FAR". The name was later changed when the white
man came. They called it "SPY HILL". by which name it is known today.

Surveying

Surveying was begun in 1872. The 49th Parallel forming the border between the
Western Provinces of Canada and the United States is known as the International
Boundary Line. Surveying of the west began at Fort Gary. Here the 1st Meridian
was established and, for the purpose of surveying, every fourth major meridian
west of the 98 degrees west major meridian became a survey meridian, so 102
degrees west became the 2nd Meridian, 106 degrees became the 3rd Meridian, 110
degrees west became the 4th Meridian, which forms the Saskatchewan-Alberta
border.

The area between these meridians is divided into six mile increments. These
divisions are called Ranges. There are 30 ranges between meridians, and they are
numbered east to west.

The land is again divided into six mile increments from south to north, which
are called Townships. They are numbered south to north. These six mile tracts of
land were divided into 36 equal portions of one square mile, called Sections.
The sections were numbered 1 to 36 starting with the SE corner and finishing at
the NE corner. Each full section was then subdivided into four equal

Quarter Sections.

While the surveying was being done each section was clearly marked at the
northeast corner with an iron stake. The land location was clearly marked on the
stake, eg: XVIII-X-II-WIV was Section 18, Township 10, Range 2, West of the 4th
Meridian.

Allowance was also made for the construction of roads, and these Road Allowances
were 66 feet wide. North to south road allowances were every mile while east to
west were every two miles apart. This system of division is called the Township
System.

Section 8 and three quarters of section 26, and all of section 26 in every fifth
township, were reserved for the Hudson's Bay Company as required by its contract
with the British Government in 1869. All uneven sections were Crown Land from
which the C.P.R. could select as required by the agreement in 1883. The
remaining even numbered sections were Free Homestead Land.

Immigration and Early Settlers

The story of immigration to the "West" begins with Confederation. This is when
Canadians first had the power to make their own decisions regarding immigration
to this country. Earlier it had been the responsibility of the French and
British governments.

In 1867 the Dominion of Canada consisted of only four provinces, Ontario,
Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. British Columbia was owned by the
British. The immense span of land, known as Rupert's Land, which drained into
the Hudson Bay was owned and governed by the Hudson's Bay Company.

After Confederation the eyes of the Canadian statesman turned toward the West.
There was apprehension that the United States might devise means for securing
territory in the West, which would prevent the linking of the older provinces
with British Columbia. In 1869, an agreement was reached by which the Hudson's
Bay Company, for $1,500,000, surrendered its rights of government and its
exclusive trading privileges to the British government. The British in turn
arranged for the transfer to Canada for all of its territory except the land
surrounding the trading posts and two sections in each township. This new
country became known as the North West Territories. In 1882 the portion of this
territory to which settlement was flowing was divided into four provincial
districts, Assiniboia, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Athabaska.

In 1870, the province of Manitoba was formed and in 1871 the province of British
Columbia confederated with Canada. The future of Canada was seen as lying to the
West and the government concentrated its efforts on the development of the
prairies. In order to make it attractive to settlers preparations involved (1)
marking of the international border at the 49th parallel and surveying the
agricultural area (This was begun in 1872); (2) bringing law and order to a
region that was becoming lawless. A large number of American free booters
(smugglers) conducting illegal trade aroused the hostility of the Indians. The
massacre near Battle Creek in the Cypress Hills hastened the establishment of
the North West Mounted Police in 1873. This force gradually took the entire
Western Plains under its protection. (3) Preparations involved securing title to
lands from the Indians. This was done by a series of treaties by which the
Indians agreed to settle on "reservations". (4) They involved the building of a
railway. McDonald's dream of connecting Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific
and keeping the promise to British Columbia, in the terms of union when British
Columbia joined Confederation, was realized with the completion of the Canadian
Pacific Railway in 1885. In an agreement between the C.P.R. and the government
of Canada, the C.P.R. received a grant of 25,000,000 acres of land in a belt 24
miles deep on each side of the railway, plus a subsidy of $25,000,000. This land
was known as C.P.R. land.

The building of the C.P.R. did not bring the expected influx of immigration and
it was not until 1896 that Clifford Sifton, Minister of the Interior, started an
aggressive campaign. He set to work setting up agencies throughout the United
States, Britain and Europe promoting immigration to Canada. Captain John
Palliser's concern about the aridity of the southern plains was forgotten in the
desire to settle the West. The Dominion Lands Act of 1872, which offered any
sole head of the family who had attained the age of 18 the right to obtain for
$10 a 160 acre homestead, was indeed an attraction. Offers of good land, a new
start, independence and adventure soon bore fruit.

Immigration to Canada between 1890 and 1914 has been described as "the mightiest
movement of people in modern history". The total immigration into Canada in 1897
was slightly over 21,000; in 1902 it had increased to 67,000; in the following
year to 128,000, and in 1913 it reached nearly 400,000. World War I brought a
halt to the influx of immigrants but it continued on a smaller scale by 1919.

In the years prior to 1874, the area around Irvine was inhabited by the
Assiniboin, Sioux, Cree and Piegan Indians. The first white men to come were the
explorers, traders and free booters.

Some of the early settlers before the "Great Migration" were ranchers who
settled mostly to the south of the C.P.R. Some of these pioneer ranchers were
the Porters, Goods, McLeays, Fawcett Bros., Rutherfords, Smiberts, Warwicks,
Browns, Benwells, and Grays. It is reported that the first livestock in Southern
Alberta were trailed in from Montana.

The majority of immigrants who settled in the Irvine district came from Russia
and were of German descent. Note: See "Our Bessarabian Ancestors". Many who came
from North and South Dakota, U.S.A. were also Bessarabian German. The stories of
good productive land in Canada inspired them to pull up stakes and move to the
north. They came by train and the more adventurous came by horse and wagon
bringing along their family and possessions.

A settlement known as Josephsburg was established south of Irvine. It was
comprised of Townships 9 and 10, Range 2 to 5. Some of the early settlers in the
area prior to and in 1900 were: Gottlieb Kaiser, John and Fred Bohnet, John
Vogel, Fred Weiss (1889), Ludwig Stelter (1896), Carl Weiss, Gottlieb Zaiser,
Alg Mort, Christian Heck, Alois Good, C. Wendland, Jacob Tschritter (1898) and
Christian Schorr (1898). The largest influx of immigrants. to this area arrived
during the early 1900's. These families dealt with a professional manager,
Joseph Edinger, whose homestead was SW 18-10-2-W4. He handled all land purchases
and homestead entries, as well as operating a store and the Josephsburg post
office. In 1905 Newburg became a post office, close to the original location of
the Josephsburg one. Another enterprising settler, James Robinson, became well
known. He provided board for the Mounted Police in 1896, was postmaster and mail
contractor in about 1900. In 1907 he was appointed Justice of Peace. That year
the first long distance telephone line, linking Medicine Hat, Dunmore, Norton,
Josephsburg, and Elkwater, was installed at the Robinson ranch. In 1928 a post
office was named after this man.

These pioneers were the heroes of the prairie agricultural epic. These newcomers
faced the problems of adaptation to a difficult environment with little help
from outside sources. Their tasks called for initiative, independence and
ingenuity.

The existing government of the North West Territories proved incapable of
meeting the more complicated needs of a large population. In 1905, the
government of Canada conceded to the wishes of the people for self-government
and the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were formed.

Alberta was named after Princess Louise Caroline Alberta, fourth daughter of
Queen Victoria and wife of the Marquis of Lorne, Canada's fourth Governor
General.

To some of these early settlers the struggle for survival in this district
seemed too great and they moved on to establish themselves elsewhere. For many
of those who did survive, we can see third and fourth generations reaping the
benefits of the labour and dreams of their grandparents and great grandparents.
The survival of the family farms depends on this new generation. May the hopes
and dreams of their forefathers never die.

Our Bessarabian Ancestors
by Dwayne Janke

Glance at many of the family surnames in this community history book. Notice a
certain similarity to them? Many of the families are descendants of
German-Russian immigrants from the province of Bessarabia near the Black Sea.
They were a people with a unique and fascinating history.

In 1804, Alexander I, Tsar of Russia, invited foreigners, especially Germans,
to settle large areas his armies captured near the Black Sea, including
Bessarabia. Like Catherine II before him, Alexander was eager to colonize
undeveloped but fertile black-soiled areas of his huge country. Alexander aimed
his efforts in the early 1800s at attracting immigrants that could serve as
models for agricultural occupations and crafts.

Generous promises were made to the foreign settlers and their descendants. They
were given free land for farms, interest-free loans for ten years, freedom from
taxes for various time periods, local self-government in their villages,
freedom to practice their own religion and freedom from military service.

The situation was exactly opposite to what many Germans experienced in Germany:
frequent military service in foreign wars, suppression by their own governing
leaders, crop failures, famine, land shortages, high taxes, religious
persecution and many other personal problems. Some had already left Germany and
settled in Poland, but destructive Napoleonic wars there left them eager to
listen to promises of a more peaceful life in south Russia.

From 1814 to 1842, about 25, mostly-German, settlements were formed in
Bessarabia. Most of the settlers came from Wurttemberg in south Germany,
Prussia, Bavaria and Poland. Bessarabia was then an untilled country of rich
rolling plains, with natural boundaries - the Danube, the Dniester and the
Pruth Rivers as well as the Black Sea. It would become a rich farming and
grazing country, in large part through the efforts of the new German-speaking
colonists.

Although there were exceptions, the new settlers to Bessarabia tended to band
together to form villages that were solidly Swabian and Platt dialect
German-speaking. Virtually all were Lutheran Protestants, although some were
Separatists, at odds with the established church and looking to Russia as a
sort of "promised land."

A typical colony consisted of long streets with farm yards on either side that
included a house and barns, a threshing place, straw stacks and orchards.
Farmland (every family received land as personal and hereditary property when
they came to Bessarabia) was located near the colony.

Life in the beginning was difficult, as the first settlers had little to start
their new lives and needed to learn to farm in the different climate of this
treeless steppe. But soon the Prairie-like grass was replaced by fields of
wheat, barley, oats, rye and maize. The production of grapes for wine was also
an important part of agriculture in Bessarabia. Garden produce and fruit was
plentifully grown. Horse, cattle, sheep, and hog breeding was also an important
industry.

In the Black Sea area, usually the colonists were not permitted to divide the
homestead land given to each family. It had to be handed down to an heir,
usually the youngest son. Fathers often had to buy land for their other sons,
so a great deal of property gradually was bought by the colonists. Large-sized
families and a growing need for land led to the establishment of daughter
colonies and further settlement. The population among German Bessarabian
settlements climbed to more than 33,000 by 1861.

Home life, church and school were closely linked among the Germans of Russia.
The church supervised instruction in religion and the study of German. Because
of this influence, the church helped to preserve the original German language,
culture and religion, even though the colonists quickly lost all contact with
the German fatherland. The villages, like German islands in a Russian sea, took
on only minor characteristics and a bit of the cultural life of the larger
Russian population.

The Bessarabia colonists prospered and progressed considerably. By 1871, the
German minority was seen as a prospering threat by some in Russian political
circles. They succeeded in having many of the rights ended which had been
promised to the colonists and their descendants at the time of settlement. The
Russian government, under Tsar Alexander III largely ended independent
self-government in the colonies and freedom from military service. As well, the
government moved to make Russian the language of instruction in schools in the
German villages. The government was determined to make Russians out of all
"foreigners." Land shortages also became a problem.

In North America, however, things looked much better. Just as the Russian
government had attracted Germans with free land and special rights in the early
1800s, the governments of the New World made similar offers. According to the

Dominion Lands Act of 1872, every immigrant to Canada could obtain for $10 a
160-acre homestead in the West, which became his property after three years.
Tens of thousands of German-Russians, including Bessarabians, were attracted by
Canada's land agents and recruitment advertising. They took up the offer to
come to Canada, especially between 1900-1913 when expanding railway branch
lines made the Prairies readily accessible to new settlers. (Those
German-Russians that stayed behind suffered many difficulties as time went by:
a campaign of hate in the first World War, the Russian Revolution, and
increased Russification.)

The emigrating German-Russians traveled by train across Europe to northern
shipping ports. There they boarded huge ships as third-class passengers for up
to two-week trips across the Atlantic, fighting sea sickness and occasionally
death. Many landed at Canadian points of entry at Halifax or Quebec before
another long train ride to the Canadian Prairies, including many to the
Medicine Hat area. They found conditions much like the steppes of the Black Sea
and adapted rather quickly. Today we enjoy many of the fruits of their hard
work and determination.

Dwayne Janke, a former journalist at the Lethbridge Herald, is currently
Publicity Manager of Wycliffe Bible Translators of Canada, Inc. A native of
Medicine Hat, Dwayne has traced some of his ancestors back 400 years through
Bessarabia to South Germany.

RECOMMENDED READINGS:

From Catherine to Khrushchev - The Story of Russia's Germans, by Adam
Giesinger. Marian Press, Winnipeg, 1974.

The Emigration from Germany to Russia in the years 1793 to 1862, by Karl
Stumpp. American Historical Society of Germans from Russia, Lincoln, NE, 1978.

Homesteaders on the Steppe, by Joseph S. Height. North Dakota Historical
Society of Germans from Russia, Bismarck, N.D., 1975.

The German Colonies in South Russia 1804 to 1904, by Rev. P. Conrad Keller,
Odessa, Russia, 1905.

The German Russians - Two Centuries of Pioneering, by Dr. Karl Stumpp. Atlantic
Forum, Bonn-Brussels-New York, 1967.


                                      Homesteaders

Clover Hill Homesteaders 1910 1915
from the Provincial Archives in Edmonton

Clover Hill homesteader map - 1910-15 (pic)

A few of the early homesteaders, who settled in the Clover Hill area, chose not
to submit any history and others we were not able to trace either because they
left the area and whereabouts unknown or no known surviving members.

We were able to locate some information on the following people from the
Provincial Archives in Edmonton:

NE 18-12-1-W4: George J. Coulhard applied but he soon abandoned the place and
said it was not fit for farming.

SW 30-12-1-W4: Bjoern Olson Tveten age 49, Norwegian and single, applied but
later decided to leave because he said it was too stony. He sold this parcel to
his nephews, Harold and Gunwold Tveten. Gunwold was a bachelor and died during
the 1918 flu epidemic. Harold later sold the land to Adam Roll Jr. and moved
slightly to the east.

SE 2-12-2-W4: George Cook Brotherton, age 19, applied for entry for a homestead
in 1910 and for land title in 1913. He had cultivated 30 acres, built a 14' x
16' house, barn and two miles of fence.

NW 12-12-2-W4: Theodore Kriegler, age 34 of Hienna, South Dakota, originally
from Germany, applied for entry May 10, 1910 and canceled in 1911. Frederick
James Appleyard, a clerk, age 28 of England, was married with two children. He
applied for entry on this same location on April 19, 1911, cultivated 25 acres
and had three cows and four horses. He apparently also canceled.

SE 12-12-2-W4: Michael Essar, age 50, a labourer from Russia, had a wife and
five children. He applied for entry on April 10, 1911. He cultivated 55 acres
and had four horses and a cow.

SW 13-12-2-W4: Simon Kuyath, citizen of Russia, age 56 and wife age 55 with one
child, applied in June 1911. By 1914 they had three children, had cultivated 43
acres, built a sod house, barn and granary from lumber and constructed two and
a half miles of fence.

NW 13-12-2-W4: Daniel Reichenberg, a farmer born in South Russia, age 38, had a
wife and eight children. He applied for entry on June 7, 1911. He cultivated 40
acres, had cattle, horses and hogs. He built a 24' x 26' frame house and barn
and two and a half miles of fence. By June 1914 he was a naturalized citizen.
Daniel's wife, Minnie, died May 1913 at age 34 and is buried in St. George's
Cemetery at Irvine.

SW 14-12-2-W4: Jacob Zwick, age 50, had a wife, age 45, a son, age 19, and
three daughters, ages 20, 14 and 12. Jacob was born in Germany and applied for
entry on April 15, 1912. He had 15 horses, cattle and hogs, constructed a 16' x
32' frame house, barn, granary and hen house. One of their daughters, Annie
(Zwick) Armstrong died at Bassano in July 1987.

SE 15-12-2-W4: John Frank Courad, a U.S.A. citizen, applied for entry April 6,
1910 and canceled August 25, 1915. Horace Holden Wood, age 23, single, and
British, then applied for entry on June 21, 1916. He built a frame house, barn
and granary and cultivated 58 acres.

Others that applied and apparently canceled follow:

NE 10-12-2-W4: Walter William Abbott of U.S.A., age 22, applied on July 6, 1912
and canceled July 18, 1913.

SW 12-12-2-W4: Nelson Simon Shunk, age 28, single, and a machinist, applied for
a homestead and abandoned on October 14, 1908. He went into the mercantile
business and was unable to go on the homestead. On June 27, 1911 Sidney
Appleyard of England applied for the same parcel of land and apparently also
abandoned. Later, Harry Jacobson, age 24 and born in U.S.A. and married,
applied for entry on June 26, 1913. He dug a well, cultivated 110 acres, built
a house, barn, granary, and one and a half miles of fence. He also had cattle
and horses. His history appears elsewhere.

Berry Centre Homesteaders
from the Provincial Archives in Edmonton

Berry Centre Homestead Map #79 (pic)

In 1903 John Crawford gained entry to homestead on SE 12-11-3-W4. By 1907 he
had broken 15 acres. By 1912 he had 100 cattle and 25 horses, a frame house 16'
x 24', a shed, stable, and hen house. He and his wife had eight children. He
was granted homestead November 23, 1907.

On November 29, 1902 James W. Crookes, age 33, gained entry to NW 10-11-3-W4.
He had a wife and four children. By 1906 he broke and cropped six acres, had
150 cattle, 25 horses, and four pigs. He had built one and a half miles fence,
18' x 38' frame house, sheds, stable, and corrals. He was granted homestead on
October 10, 1906.

George Drevend was 36 years old when he applied entry to homestead SW 2-11-3-W4
in 1902. He had a wife and five children. He built a 18' x 22' frame house, a
stable, a shed, two granaries, and one and a half miles of fence. He had 25
cattle, three horses, and was cropping 25 acres of cultivated land.

Jacob Genert was 29 years old, married with seven children, when he applied
entry June 13, 1904 to homestead NE 30-10-2-W4. By 1907 he had broke and seeded
50 acres, had four cows and five horses, a sod house 20' x 10', a well, and two
and a half miles fence. Homestead was granted June 18, 1908.

Zakarias Hollstein, age 54, married with eight children, applied for entry on
homestead SE 10-11-3-W4. In 1903 he built a house, had two horses, six cattle,
four hogs, and broke 30 acres.

August Hollstein, 22 years of age, gained entry April 30, 1903 to homestead
SW 10-11-3-W4. He broke 15 acres, had a granary and a fence.

Peter Hollstein, age 21 years, gained entry April 30, 1903 to homestead
NE 10-11-3-W4. He had a frame house, stable, granary, and two miles of fence. He
broke 20 acres and had two horses.

Helen Pauline Hurdman, age 60 years, applied for homestead on SW 22-11-3-W4 in
1903. She was a British subject with no family. In 1907 she had a house,
stable, corrals, a well, and broke 21 acres. In 1908 she had 30 horses, 45
cattle, and two mules.

William M. Keffer received entry for homestead NE 14-11-3-W4 and on October 18,
1901 abandoned. Through the Declaration of Abandonment Act he claimed a mistake
was made whereby he was granted the NE of 14 instead of the SW of 14. His entry
was transferred to SW 14-11-3-W4 free of charge.

In 1903 Gottfried Maier of German descent, age 45, married with two children,
applied for entry to homestead SE 18-11-2-W4. By 1905 he cropped 75 acres, had
15 cattle, seven horses, and two pigs. He built a 18' x 12' home, a stable, and
granary. Gottfried passed away in 1906 and his wife Christina Maier took over
the estate.

On July 28, 1902 Stewart McNutt, age 38, a Canadian born British subject,
applied for homestead SE 22-11-3-W4. He received patent on January 2, 1908. By
this time he had built a house, stable, hen house, corral, and had dug a well.
This land was suitable only for grazing. He had 100 cattle and 25 horses.

In 1910 when Frederick Schubert applied for entry to homestead NW 2-11-3-W4 he
had a wife and two children. He built a 22' x 36' house, a stable, shed, and
dug two wells. When he received title to his homestead in 1915, he was cropping
75 acres, had 23 cattle, and 17 horses.

Coal Centre Homesteaders
from the Provincial Archives in Edmonton

Coal Centre Homestead Map #1033 (pic)

On March 25, 1909 Fred William Becker, born in New York, son of Karl P. Becker,
applied for homestead SE 28-11-3-W4. He was 18 years old and single. He
canceled in 1910.

On September 14, 1910 Cornelius Cheret, age 45, applied for homestead
NW 20-11-3-W4. He took up residence May 8, 1911 with wife Louise and six
children. Cornelius, a miller, was born in Leige, Belgium. By 1913 they had
built a house, barn, hen house, granary, and well. He had four cattle, three
horses, and broke 25 acres. To earn a living for his large family he worked in
a mill in Medicine Hat. On April 21, 1915 he left for work and never returned
home. He had disappeared.

Edward Desmet, born in Belgium, age 30, single, and a carpenter, applied for
SE 30-11-3-W4. By 1913 he cropped 30 acres, had four cattle, six horses, two
hogs, a 20' x 20' frame house, granary, stable, pig pen, and two and a half
miles of fence. Homestead was granted April 27, 1914.

On July 26, 1910, William Fredrick Furber, a missionary, age 32, and his wife,
age 23, applied for homestead NW 22-11-3-W4. He came from Maine, Washington,
U.S.A. He had a house built by August 1910. By 1913 he had broken 42 acres, had
a frame house, stone barn, hen house, a well, four horses, and two cows. He
received patent March 10, 1914.

On June 24, 1902 Lenard Grossman, age 43, rancher, with wife and two children,
applied for homestead on NW 4-11-3-W4. He received title to homestead on June
25, 1925. He had built a frame house, stable, granary, and two miles of fence.

On January 27, 1917, Lughten Chas Dore Hagger, age 37, with wife and child,
gained entry on SW 30-11-3-W4. He had a 26' x 14' house, a stable and a
granary. By 1920 he seeded 10 acres, had one head of cattle, and four horses.
Homestead was granted November 25, 1920.

On May 13, 1913 Charles Gaudias Lachanel, age 42, single, applied for
NE 20-11-3-W4. He wag born in Quebec and had lived in Saskatchewan and had
worked as a salesman. He canceled November 24, 1915.

On August 24, 1912 Jean Baptiste Martle, born in Belgium, age 24, with wife and
four children, gained entry on NE 30-11-3-W4. They lived in Pashley. By 1912 he
had cropped 35 acres, had 16 cattle, a frame house 16' x 18', granary, pig pen,
and one and a half miles fence. Patent granted September 1917. He died around
1931.

On September 8, 1916 John Johnston Miller, age 51, with wife, age 40, and one
child applied for homestead NE 20-11-3-W4. He worked at Elkwater. By 1920 he
had 40 acres broken and 20 cattle. Patent was issued June 25, 1920.

Eugene Newberger, born in Germany, age 34, had a wife, age 32, and two
children. He applied for homestead SE 28-11-3-W4 on May 5, 1910 and abandoned
soon after.

On February 20, 1911, Marie Rabe, age 30, of German descent gained entry on
NW 30-11-3-W4. By 1912 she had 30 acres in crop, a 12' x 20' frame house, log
horse barn, and two miles of fence. Homestead was granted July 2, 1914.

On December 13, 1916 William Arthur Thompson, age 33, with wife, age 27, and
three children applied for homestead SE 28-11-3-W4. He was a farmer born in
Ontario. He also worked for Medicine Hat News. By 1919 he had built a frame
house, stable, hen house, and two miles of fence. He was issued title January
1, 1920.

On June 25, 1902 August Thurn, a rancher living with his father, applied for
homestead NE 4-11-3-W4. By 1905 he had built a house, stable, hen house,
granary and two miles of fence. He had 22 cattle, eight horses, and ten pigs.

Irvine Homesteaders
from the Provincial Archives in Edmonton

On September 10, 1900 William James Corbett, age 40, a married rancher, applied
for homestead NE 36-11-3-W4. By 1904 he had broken seven acres, had 60 cattle,
five horses, and two pigs. He built a frame house, shed, corrals, well, stable,
and hen house. On February 16, 1905, he received patent for homestead.

On March 7, 1903 Fredrich Cowan, a 24 year old rancher who lived with his
brother on NW 34-11-3-W4, applied for homestead NE 6-12-3-W4. In 1906 he built
a frame house. By 1909 he broke 35 acres, had 17 cattle, four horses, two miles
of fence, two corrals, hen house, and well. He received homestead patent in
1909.

On May 7, 1903 Fredrick John Crewe, a British subject by birth and a 33 year
old rancher with a wife and two children, applied for homestead NE 26-11-3-W4.
When absent from homestead, he was riding the range for Porter Bros. He
received his homestead patent in 1910 at which time he had broken 10 acres, had
150 cattle, and 48 horses. His land was used mainly for grazing.

In 1908 Thomas Andrew Foulton from Ontario, with a wife and one child, applied
for entry on the NW 32-11-2-W4. By 1910 he cropped 50 acres, had 12 cattle, and
six horses. He built a 20' x 24' house, a stable, one and a half miles of
fence, and dug a well.

In 1907 William Boyd Foulton, age 39 with a wife and four children, obtained
entry for homestead on the NE 32-11-2-W4. From 1908 to 1911 he broke 50 acres,
had seven cows, and four horses. He built a 24' x 28' home, a stable, one and a
half miles of fence, and dug a well.

Irvine Homestead Map #892 (pic)

On April 17, 1914 David Gilchrist, a farmer born in South Russia and who
previously lived in Manitoba, applied for homestead SW 34-11-2-W4. He had a
wife and one child. By 1918 he had broken 35 acres, built a 15' x 30' frame
house, dug a well and had four head of cattle. He received patent on December
16, 1918.

On February 5, 1904 Neil McMullin, 36 years old with a wife and two children,
applied for homestead SW 36-11-3-W4. In 1907, when he received patent for this

On August 23, 1902 Milbard Edwin Price, age 26 with a wife and six children,

On July 9, 1901 John Toll applied for homestead NW 36-11-3-W4. He was 25 years

On April 4, 1907 Angus A. Gray applied for homestead on SE 32-11-3-W4. On June

On February 14, 1903 L. E. Harris, age 23 gained entry on SE 34-11-3-W4. By

a log house 20' x 16', a stable, and corrals. He was cropping 46 acres, had six
cattle, and ten horses.

In 1907 Gottfreid Zieffle immigrated from South Russia with wife and four
children and applied for entry to homestead NW 24-10-2-W4. This homestead was
canceled.

Sentinel Homesteaders
from the Provincial Archives in Edmonton

Sentinel Homestead Map #1516 (pic)

In 1907 John Hoff applied for homestead SE 2-10-2-W4. It had a log barn and
granary. John broke 35 acres, and had one cow and five horses. He canceled and
applied for another homestead NE 12-11-3-W4 in 1907. No further records.

On May 20, 1904 John Koenig, an Irvine shoemaker, age 34 and married, gained
entry on homestead SW 10-10-2-W4. By 1907 he had broken and cropped 60 acres,
had a 20' x 16' frame house, stable, shed, chicken house, well, two miles of
fence, two horses and 12 cattle.

On September 11, 1902 Christian Pahl, with wife and four children, applied for
homestead NE 10-10-2-W4. He became a British subject by naturalization in 1907
at age 31. He had broken 50 acres, built a frame house and other buildings. He
had 13 cattle, six horses and four pigs.

In 1903 at the age of 68, Frederick Sailer applied for entry to homestead
SE 10-10-2-W4. By 1906 he had built a 16' x 20' frame house, cropped 30 acres,
had 12 cattle, two horses, built a barn, two miles of fence, and dug two wells.

On October 13, 1913 Thomas Scott, a British subject born in Scotland, 38 years
old with wife, 39 years old, and four children, applied for homestead
NE 12-10-2-W4. By 1916 he had broken and cropped 45 acres, had a 20' x 32' frame
house, barn and chicken house. He was a Canadian soldier who served overseas.
Title granted December 1, 1922.

On March 16, 1903 Christian Sturm, age 31, married with a family of two, gained
entry on SE 4-10-2-W4. By 1906 he had broken and cropped 60 acres, had a house,
stable, shed, three horses, nine cattle, and five pigs. Homestead was granted
May 8, 1907.

On June 25, 1903, application for homestead for John Weisharr, age 23, on SE
2-10-2-W4 was made by his father. He built a log barn and granary but later
abandoned stating "not suitable for farming".

Everett Stelter's Story of Irvine

At the age of 92, Everett describes life on the homestead in the Newburg-Irvine
area. His family moved from Dunmore to Newburg in 1896, about a year before he
was born.

It was spring when my parents moved into a bude, a dugout home which Dad had
prepared for the family to live in. While Dad was away the water came down the
creek, flooded over the banks, and came into the bude, caving it in. They had
one half bag of flour on a box which also caved in, but Mother saved enough of
it for pancakes. That's all the family had to eat, and Medicine Hat was 30
miles away.

There was an old log shack on the place and they put a sod roof on it. Those
days it rained and rained. The sod soaked up with water and when the rain was
over it still rained for a day inside. I was two and a half years old when we
moved into the house Dad built from logs which were brought from the Cypress
Hills. He was so particular every log had to be squared on all four sides,
fitted and then secured with hand made wooden staples. This building is still
being used today.

There was a section of C.P.R. land for sale adjoining our homestead, which my
dad needed for an access to our homestead in the creek, but he didn't have the
money to buy it. He took off for Medicine Hat worried about how he would manage
to purchase this land before someone else buys it. He had never dealt with the
banks so he decided to see Mr. James Rae, a merchant he had dealt with many
times. Mr. Rae, who had confidence in my dad, said "It's almost closing time
for the bank, but I'll go over and see." The bank manager was already outside
set to leave. After Mr. Rae's conversation with him, the manager motioned to
the teller, who was still by his desk, to open up and asked him to let him have
the 500 bucks. This was lent on Mr. Rae's word with no other backing.

After he had the land he needed money for wire to fence it in. Those days grass
grew high and thick, you could take the mower and cut hay anyplace. Since there
were no fences the ranchers' cattle roamed freely, up to 1000 head in one herd.
They cleaned up a lot of grass. To raise money Dad mortgaged the homestead to
the life insurance company for another $500. He also sheared sheep for Mr.
McKelvin, a sheep rancher, for 100 a head. He averaged 100 sheep a day. That
amounted to $10 a day and those days $1 was a lot of money. Dad then fenced in
the C.P.R. section. We put up 75 loads of hay that year, a load for each
critter.

We also had two small stacks of grain to thresh. Those days one neighbour
helped the other or you couldn't have existed. The cut grain was spread out on
the grass and with two horses going round and round over it, knocked out the
grain. The straw was forked off and the grain was swept up into a heap. To
clean out the grass and dirt, the grain was then fired against the wind onto a
screen.

The following year our neighbour, Mr. Bohnet, had an eight horse-powered
thresher with no elevator. We bushelled the grain into half bushels so we had
an idea how much grain we threshed.

In 1909 we had a 14 horse-powered 28 inch self fed thresher, but still no straw
blower. It was fed slowly so the horses could pull it. This thresher could put
out 800-1000 bushels of grain a day.

To secure a title to the homestead, we had to break up 30 acres in three years.
We had ten acres of land broken up but needed another 20. First Dad had a two
horse long handled plow but got a short hand one which was easier to handle.
The sod was heavily rooted with grass, it was hard to break up.

Dad bought an old high wheeled disc for a song but the wooden boxes were worn
out on it so he relined them with thick bacon rind which lasted longer than the
original liners.

A neighbour, Fred Derheim, who came from North Dakota, brought along the idea
on how to make a homemade schlep (drag) which was made up with green hawthorne
branches nailed between two planks about 14 feet wide. Rocks were placed on top
for weight. This drag pulverized the soil and smoothed out the sod for seeding.
When one side became worn he turned it over.

We kids did not get many presents. The only present I got was an engine with a
string on it. When I made a little money for myself from weasel and coyote
skins, I bought a train set which had a track, a wind up engine with a brake,
two cars, and a caboose, all for 50 cents.

The children in our district attended the Newburg school. During the busy
season my older brothers had to stay home and help along. Their teacher, Mr.
Sibley, felt it a shame for them to stop school so he gave them homework to do
at night. I started school at seven years old. My first teacher was Mr. Martin.
In those days we all came to school barefoot during the warmer weather.

I liked my teacher Miss Sterrit. She was the one we played a joke on. Emanuel
Lehr and I took the lead out of B B caps so they wouldn't go off and we put
them on the big heater. Later in the afternoon a cold wind blew up from the
north so Miss Sterrit opened the big heater door and stirred the fire with the
poker. The fire flared up and the one cap went off. "Oh!", she said, "Who did
that?" and Boom another one went off. She got so nervous she sat down at her
desk, holding her head in her hands. She looked up at me and said, "You tend to
the fire." She knew who had done it because to have B B caps you had to be
older and we were the oldest in the class. She was smart though, boy! I knew we
were not allowed to chew gum or candy during school hours. I had this candy and
was so careful not to suck it or let it show in my mouth. I was working along,
when the candy was finished I sort of licked my lips. She noticed this and
said, "Wasn't that sweet." She knew all the time I had this candy! How the
dickens she knew I don't know.

Our first school book was the Ontario Reader which had this verse "Apple,
apple, fine red apple, if you'd like one please take one." Then the Queen
ordered the Alexander Reader, which they said was free. I brought it home and
Mom said, "Take it back, there's going to be taxes on that. The old Ontario
Reader is good enough." The teacher said, "You have to keep it, that's what I
have to teach you from."

We had no exams or grades those days. I asked the last teacher I had, Mr.
Jeconette, a French man, to teach me how to figure. He sat down beside me and
said, "I'll teach you how to do the decimal if it takes me all week!" That came
in very handy to read measurements for reboring engines in the mechanic
business which I happened to be in for 40 years.

Mr. Martin, who lived on a farm and taught in the Newburg School, was also the
J.P. He opened a post office because the distance between Irvine and
Josephsburg was too far. He himself operated the post office until he sold this
land and moved to Irvine. That's when my sister, Lydia, took it over until she
got married in 1905. Then my mother was sworn in as postmistress. Mom didn't
have time so she had my brother, Fred, sworn in as deputy postmaster. However,
when anything official had to be signed, Mother had to sign it. They were very
strict about things like that those days.

The mailman, Mr. Frisch, who delivered the mail to Newburg, Josephsburg, and
Thelma, had to record arrival time and sign for every delivery. He used a
democrat or sleigh and often kept a second team at Elkwater to change off
because roads were rough.

To keep our milk and vegetables, we built a sod covered root cellar, but we had
problems with cave ins and flooding when snow melted in the trees above it. Our
second cellar we cemented the sides and roof, then covered with dirt for
insulation. For really cold weather, 40 below or so, Dad tied a bundle of straw
with the rope from binder twine sacks and pushed this into the entrance to keep
out the frost.

Our clothes were washed on a scrub board, and wrung out by hand. I was going to
school by the time we got our first cradle washing machine about 1907.

When our pants needed patching we had to go to bed till the job was done
because we had nothing else to put on. It was customary to pinch (pennies) in
those days. My older brother, Charlie, and I were reminiscing about that one
day and thought it was not necessary for Dad to pinch quite so much because we
had accumulated close to 100 head of cattle by that time. My mother maintained
that flour had to be a year old before it made good bread so we always bought
eight to ten bags at a time. Her bread always turned out so we couldn't argue
with her method.

In 1917 we sold our farm to Gottfried Schorr and our family moved to a farm in
Bruederheim.

In 1919 I came back to Irvine and along with my brother, Albert, built a
garage, 50' x 50', next to Koenig's store and went into business. Soon Albert
decided to leave the business and go into the ministry but I carried on. Albert
needed money and left me with little to operate with. We still owed money here
and there. One fellow I owed wanted me to pay up which would have closed me
down. Mr. Boschee had just brought in a car that needed a lot of repair. He
persuaded the fellow to have patience, that I would pay him once I got back on
my feet again. I had the car apart and needed $40 to lift the repairs which
came C.O.D. from Central Motors in Medicine Hat. I then went down the street to
see Mah Goung, a restaurant operator, and asked if he would lend me $50. I was
thankful for he saved my business from going under. After repairing the Boschee
car, I paid off some of my debts.

Dad needed help to seed the Bruederheim farm so I rented the business to Jack
DeBolt for a year. I married my wife at Bruederheim. We bought Albert's old car
and came back to Irvine in the fall of 1921.

Jack DeBolt and I decided to go into partnership. He had a lot of garage
equipment and we agreed I was to buy my share when I received a clear title to
our property. However the garage burnt down before the deal was made. In 1921,
Jack and I bought the livery barn and set up a garage again.

During these years business in Irvine went haywire when Hilda and Schuler built
their own shops. The taxes on our business were raised from $65 to $380. We
could not afford to pay that much, so we stayed for another three years, after
which we left our business and Irvine and moved to Claresholm.

Ranching in the Irvine District

During the last of his three journeys exploring and surveying the Canadian
West, Captain John Palliser left Fort Edmonton in 1859 and headed south. He
crossed the forks of the Red Deer and South Saskatchewan Rivers near Empress.
On his journey to the "Mountains of Jackpine" (Cypress Hills) or Montagne de
Cypre, as the French trappers had named them, he came across a large lake on
what was later to become the Walsh Flats.

According to Palliser's report, a large herd of buffalo were traveling around
the west end of the lake and into the hills to the south of where the town of
Irvine would later be located. The trails left by the buffalo are still visible
in the surrounding coulees today. Indian arrowheads can be found at the buffalo
jump south of Irvine.

While the large herds were gone by the time the railroad arrived, Senator
Gershaw in his history of the Medicine Hat area notes that "one of the last
buffalo shot in this area was killed on the prairie where the present town of
Irvine is located by the late Bob McCutcheon of Medicine Hat".

The cattle industry was not established in the Northwest Territories (Alberta
became a province in 1905) until the arrival of the railroad. A Montreal
businessman by the name of Cochrane brought a trail herd of 6,000 head from
Montana along the base of the Rockies to the area west of Calgary where the
town was named after him.

In the spring of 1883 the Canadian Pacific Railway continued construction at a
point 12 miles east of Maple Creek where it had stopped the previous fall. The
railway line followed the flats through the future sites of Walsh, Irvine,
Pashley, and Dunmore to the river crossing at Medicine Hat. A wooden trestle
bridge was constructed to cross the South Saskatchewan, and by November of 1883
the C.P.R. reached the summit of the Rockies west of Banff.

With the West opened, settlers arrived and began to file homestead claims at
which time the cattle industry in Southern Alberta was born.

From 1883 until the early 1900's the range was open. Cattle drifted from the
river at Medicine Hat northeast to the Many Island Lake district, east to Maple
Creek, and south to the Cypress Hills. In the fall of the year, ranchers sent
out roundup crews to gather and separate the herds.

Many of the earliest ranches in the Irvine area were established near suitable
shelter and water. The Cypress Hills, and the creeks such as the Ross, Box
Elder, the Bulls Head, McKay and others became the home locations of many of
the early ranches.

A number of horse ranches were established and flourished until the 1920's.
Their markets were the settlers who required horses to begin their homesteads
and the U.S. Cavalry who sent buyers to Alberta to purchase remounts for the
army. Horses were available to buy or rent from the livery stable located at
the east end of Irvine.

Porter Ranch (pic)

The town of Irvine had a stockyard operated by the C.P.R. and located at the
east end of town. Cattle were trailed in from local ranches and shipped out by
rail for markets in the east. During the late 1920's and early 1930's, a number
of ranchers shipped carloads of cattle from Irvine directly to the stockyards
in Chicago. Prices ranged from 2 to 3(r a pound for three year old steers, in
many cases not enough to pay the freight bill. Weaned calves sold for around $5
a head at the time.

Cattle buyers from Winnipeg and Toronto would come west in the fall of the year
and deal directly with the ranchers. Some of the old-timers will recall Sam
Wiener and Zeb Merkle of Winnipeg who bought and shipped thousands of cattle
from Irvine and Walsh. In later years Auggie Sauer, Earl Ligget, and others
purchased cattle that were shipped out of the Irvine stockyards.

With the establishment of the Walsh Cattle Marketing Association, many of the
local ranchers became members and marketed their livestock through the Walsh
sales. The quality of cattle from this short grass area of Southern Alberta and
Saskatchewan became well known throughout Canada and for years the Walsh Market
established the price of feeder cattle in the West.

Most of the grain and livestock raised in the area were sent to market through
Irvine. There are still people around old enough to recall grain wagons lined
up at the elevators and saddle horses waiting at the stockyards while the
ranchers and farmers had dinner and "refreshments" at the Great West Hotel.

During the 1920's, Irvine hosted an annual stampede and horse race. The grounds
were located on the northwest side of town. Many of the local cowboys and
ranchers took part in the events. The Irvine stampede corrals were sold to a
group of ranchers in the Cypress Hills who held a July 1st stampede at Grayburn
Gap during the early 1930's and 40's.

Branding a calf (pic)

Cattle ranching has been part of the history of Irvine and will no doubt
continue to be. The grass that attracted the buffalo to this area, with proper
management, will remain a renewable resource that will continue to produce the
best beef in the world. People who are willing to work hard, take risks, deal
with a fickle climate, and use sound judgment will raise cattle in the Irvine
area for years to come. Irvine and district still raises this kind of people.

Ed. Note: Some of the pioneer ranchers were Porters, Goods, Fawcett Bros., and
Smiberts. For information on sheep ranching see Engel and McLeay stories.

Joe and Jim Thomson and McLeay's sheep (pic)

Irvine Sheep Rancher Passes Through
Thrilling Experience

Mr. J.J. Wills, the well known Irvine rancher had a most miraculous escape from
being fatally injured on Monday last. It seems that a number of sheepmen in
that district were shipping wool on the siding there when an engine and several
cars backed down and shunted into their car without warning. Mr. Wills was
thrown between the rails and several cars passed above him before he was
rescued from his extremely perilous position. Fortunately he met with no worse
mishap than the fracture of one of his legs. He was brought up to the Medicine
Hat General Hospital where he is at present. Mr. Robt. Rutherford's team got
all tangled up in the moving car (Medicine Hat News, July 19, 1906)

Farming

The immense span of cultivated fields we view today was wide open space with
miles and miles of unfenced rolling prairie at the dawn of the 20th century.
The immigrant arriving at his homestead immediately began to plan how he was
going to break the sod. He required a plow and a strong team of horses or oxen.
The number of horses required depended on how many shares were on the plow. Two
horses could pull a one bottom plow.

Plowing with a hand plow - drawing by Elsie Heller (pic)

The horse became an essential asset to the farmer and as he prospered, his herd
of horses increased, often amounting up to 20. These mighty steeds received a
great deal of attention and care for they were the farmer's only "horsepower".
In early March they were brought into the barns once a day and fed grain to
condition them for the impending spring work. After the field work was done
they were put out to pasture and brought in again whenever they were needed.

Seeding was usually done with a disc drill and implements used to prepare the
land for seeding were plows, discs and cultivators. These implements had a
raised steel seat which often proved to be very unstable, especially when the
plow struck a big rock. The driver was catapulted into the air landing most
anywhere. On such an occasion a team of gentle horses was appreciated.

Cutting of the grain was done with a header when the crops were short and with
a binder when there was a heavier crop.

The header was an intriguing machine in that it was not drawn, but rather
pushed by a team of four horses. The steering was done by the driver who reined
the horses and manipulated with his legs a lever which was attached to the
seat. The lever guided the swivel wheel below, in reality it was a steering
wheel. The pushing of the horses activated the gears which moved the sickle
that cut the grain. The reels brought the grain onto the canvas on the platform
and the canvas elevated it up into the header box. Two people were needed on
the header box, one to fork the grain and one to drive the horses. Driving the
header box was often done by a youngster barely tall enough to see over the top
of the box. If this was the case, a small step was installed to accommodate him
or her. Usually two header boxes were used; while one was being loaded the
other was unloaded. The grain was unloaded by one man and the stack set by
another. Stacks were in rows and the space between them had to be wide enough
for the separator of the threshing machine.

A shower would have been a luxury after a hot day's work of "headering"!

The binder was usually drawn by four horses and operated by the driver. The
grain was cut by the sickle, brought up on a canvas and automatically tied into
sheaves or "bundles". These sheaves were accumulated, usually five to a dump,
and were manually dumped with a foot pedal, making sure that all the dumps were
in a row. This made it easier for "stooking". The tedious, back breaking job of
gathering three dumps and piling them together with the grain heads on top was
called "stooking". It involved the family and any able-bodied child was
recruited for this job. When you tired you could sit in the shade of a stook
and have a piece of mother's kuchen and a drink of water from a water jug
wrapped in a water soaked gunny sack.

Threshing was done with a threshing machine, driven by a big steam engine. The
threshing machine was owned by one farmer and the size of his crew depended on
how many farmers he threshed for.

The method of threshing depended on whether the grain had been headered or
bindered. If it had been headered the threshing machine was moved close to the
header stacks and forked onto the feeders. If bindered, the stooks had to be
hauled to the machine with wagons known as "bundle racks". Usually six to eight
racks were used, depending on the size of the threshing machine. The bundles
were forked or "pitched" onto the feeders which fed them into the separator
where the grain was threshed. The straw and chaff were blown onto straw stacks;
a change in the wind direction could also change the position of the new straw
stack. The grain was augered out onto horse drawn grain wagons. Unloading the
grain required a great deal of shoveling, not only from the wagon into the
granary but also inside where the grain had to be distributed.

In spite of the hard work, threshing time was actually a time of socializing
with your neighbors.

The young boys looked forward to the time when the threshing crew came to their
farm and they could sleep in the barn loft with the older boys, often taking
part in the pranks they played on each other. At daybreak everyone was roused
to tend to their horses and come for breakfast. A table big enough to
accommodate 20 men was waiting for them, laden with stacks of sliced fresh
baked bread, fried bacon and eggs, and the favorite Corn Flakes boxes. This was
just the beginning! After a few hours of work lunch would be brought out and
again a feast of coffee, milk and kuchen. Two more full course meals and one
more lunch break in mid afternoon, kept the women just as busy as the men.
After supper the men could rest but the women had yet to clean up, do dishes
and prepare for the next day. They were the last to go to bed and the first to
get up in the morning. This could go on for several days or weeks depending on
weather conditions.

Hay was mowed with a horse drawn mower and raked with a dump rake. This rake
dumped the hay into piles which were later loaded onto the hayrack with a pitch
fork and again unloaded by hand, stacking it into a neat sloped stack.
Throughout the years methods were devised to make the work of unloading easier,
e.g. slings and derricks.

These methods of farming gradually changed with the introduction of the tractor
and combine.

Ross Creek Irrigation District

First meeting of the Board of directors was held September 17, 1949, at the
residence of Henry Cavan.

In 1952 the storage reservoir created by runoff water from Gros Ventre Creek
was officially named and registered by the owners of the reservoir as "Cavan
Lake". It is so named in honor of Henry Cavan, district rancher of Dunmore, who
devoted years of study and work to bring the scheme to fruition. He was
responsible for the original survey of the water course.

Some fish fingerlings were planted in this reservoir in 1952 by Medicine Hat
Fish and Game Association.

Water levies were set per acre for all lands within the area designated as
irrigable, to help cover costs incurred, not covered by the Provincial
Government.

Ross Creek Irrigation District covers 1150 acres and is one of the smallest
irrigation districts in Alberta. Irrigation in this area has certainly helped
improve the growing of hay and corn crops, and has made Pashley Flats green.

                                    Schools

The School System

With special thanks to Glen Gebhard for his kind permission to use portions of
his writings of the School Division #4. Mr. Gebhard was a former principal of
the Irvine School.

In 1884 the government created a department of education and an educational
system where-by schools within each school district were controlled locally by
a board of trustees and schools were maintained through local powers of
taxation. During the first four decades of the twentieth century the
continuation of small school districts as a basic unit of school administration
stood out. In accordance with the regulations in the school act passed in 1905
(and amended almost every year since), in order to propose boundaries for a new
school district it was required that there be a minimum of four resident
ratepayers and eight children aged 5 to 16 years. A petition to the minister
was required for his approval of the proposed boundaries and finally, a vote of
the resident ratepayers determined the establishment of a new district. The
name and number was later announced in the Alberta Gazette by a declaration of
the minister of education. This district usually supported a one-room school
and a board of three elected trustees.

The inception of the large school unit took place in the fall of 1936 known as
Cypress School Division #4. The central section of the Cypress Division
included school districts close to Irvine. The area was sparsely settled and
had been subjected to a succession of very dry years. This diminished tax
collection of a number of school districts. A trend to special assistance from
the department to aid in education was established in 1940. A special grant of
$6,080.67 was received by Cypress Division. This resulted in lower rate of
school taxation which helped to offset tax collection problems.

With the outbreak of World War II in 1939, teachers were in short supply. This
created the need of new developments and generated a trend towards reorganizing
the school districts into larger unit areas. With the move toward
centralization, favorable acceptance by the general public seemed vital to
future development and there still remained perplexing and challenging problems
to develop these administration units.

On the 18th of January 1937 five determined, dedicated rural farmers (one from
each subdivision) had been elected as divisional trustees and met for the first
time. The first member elected in the Irvine and surrounding area (Sub-division
#3) was Ted Roll of the Clover Hill District. Mr. Fred McLaughlin, of Irvine,
became the first secretary-treasurer for the Cypress School Division #4 in
about 1939 and contributed in a very substantial measure to the early
development and success of the centralized school system. His popularity with
the rural and town people stood out as he knew them well and understood the
local school situations. His interest and services, both as a supporter and
official was valued by all. He continued to serve in this capacity until April
1, 1949 when he retired.

Since the year 1937 the divisional trustees took steps needed to improve
existing facilities for the education of the rural children. A few measures
included moving schools to centralized sites and thus the school bus system was
born. Eventually newer and larger schools were built and on September 1, 1939
the third room (for High School grades) was opened in Irvine. By December 1942
more rural schools were closed and children were conveyed to Irvine. Still
later, by the late 1950's a new modern school had been built. As the years
progressed more alterations and additions were made. Grades at all levels were
and still are taught in the Irvine school with children being conveyed from
areas such as Graburn from the east, Elkwater from south, Many Island from
north and Dunmore from the west, to name only a few.

In the fall of 1942 the Cypress School Division was renamed the Medicine Hat
School Division #4 and in the year 1986 it was again changed to Cypress School
Division #4 and remains the same to date.

Memories of a One-Room School
by Mary Deering

To someone who had spent her years of schooling in city schools, a one-room
school was an eye opener! Pupils of all ages six to fourteen, grades one to
nine. The first few days were nerve wracking! At night preparing lessons for
next day, my knees were knocking together under the table.

A teacher had to be a little of everything. I remember being janitor in my
first school. Summer and fall were fine but winter meant lighting the fire in a
huge heater and I knew nothing about coal and wood stoves. One morning I lit
the kindling and thought all was O.K. I went back to check and the door blew
open and flames shot out. I was wearing a leather helmet so some of my hair was
left. Eyebrows, eyelashes, and hair not covered by the helmet were gone! After
the excitement died down one little girl said, "Oh teacher, you forgot to open
the damper! " What did I know about dampers - but I soon learned.

Another time one of the bigger boys was limping - he didn't want to say why. It
finally came out that he had a long gash in the calf of one leg from jumping a
barbed wire fence. It was festering and looked terrible but teacher had to play
nurse and dress it every day!

At my next school a lot of the children spoke German at home, and at school
too, when I couldn't hear them. One day as I was watching them play, I heard
one boy call another a dumb ass in German (the only two words I knew). When
they came in I asked who was calling who a dumb donkey? No reply. Later I heard
one say to another "We can't get away with anything. This teacher understands."
Little did they know!

Dust storms were frequent in the thirties - after they were over we would spend
a whole day cleaning up. Books had to be shaken out one by one to get rid of
the dust. One day it was so bad I decided to drive instead of walk. We had to
turn back - we couldn't even see the radiator cap on my old Model A Ford. No
one else went that day either!

Halloween was a great time to play tricks on the teacher. One morning after
Halloween I arrived at school to find desks piled on my desk up front and a
potted Geranium on top of all almost touching the ceiling.

Christmas was another special time. We would spend a month getting ready for
our Christmas Concert. Everyone had a part to play. We would finish up with
treats for everyone from Jolly Old Saint Nick.

One day that I remember well was the day the boys were swinging from the
rafters to the manger in the barn - which they weren't supposed to be doing.
One boy fell and broke his leg. Teacher to the rescue again! We made a splint
from some boards we found and used hand towels for padding. It was Friday and
most parents were in town - I had my car at school so we loaded him into it and
off I went. I found his father and turned boy, car and all over to him. All
turned out well. One of the nurses at the clinic even gave us a compliment on
our splint.

I could go on and on but this will give some idea of what a teacher in a
one-room school had to cope with, besides lessons.

Berry Centre School District #796

The Berry Centre School District #796 was organized in February 1903 but a
school was not built until 1906.

Berry Centre School students - 1910: Back: Emil Otto, ?, ?, Jack Rath, Jack
Schneider, Henry Otto; Middle: Lydia Otto, ?, Emma Schneider, Bertha Eiffert,
Regina Shubbert, Annie Eiffert; Front: Ben Otto (pic)

Mrs. Vockeroth, Schubert and Bohnet named this area Berry Centre because it was
situated in an area surrounded by trees and shrubs bearing fruits such as
chokecherries, saskatoons, gooseberries, bullberries and possibly others not
named and likely unknown.

There is very little record of the operation of the school other than a list of
teachers commencing at 1907.

Berry Centre School students - 1919; Back: Martha Otto, Lizzie Patzer, Emil
Lehr, Ethel Wallace (Teacher), Leah Schneider, Pauline Rath, Gideon Lehr, Lydia

By the year 1942 it became apparent that some of the older buildings, such as
the barn and coal shed, had to be rebuilt unless the school was moved from its
present site. In 1943 a proposal was made to move a portable school from Walsh.
In 1944 the original school was moved from the NW 1-11-3-W4 site and situated
approximately four miles south of Irvine on NE 31-10-2-W4. It was renovated and
operated here until 1954. At this time the school closed its doors and the
buildings and site were sold. Christian Wirsch, who had been transporting the
high school students to Irvine since 1952, then began vanning all the children
to the Irvine School where they are still attending at the time of this writing.

Clover Hill School District #2584
by Ida L. (Roll) Gill

Prior to the arrival of settlers in general and possibly in the latter part of
the 1800's there is evidence that Indians inhabited and buffalo roamed the area
that was later to become the Clover Hill School District. Clusters of teepee
rings (circles of stones), arrowheads, tomahawks and deep rutted buffalo trails
were found in the surrounding hills and valleys. Then came the white man at the
turn of the century, taking up homesteads and it soon became apparent that a
school district needed to be organized so the children of immigrants, settlers
and ranchers would receive a proper education. With the help of several
residents in the area a petition was presented in 1912 to the Department of
Education applying to form a school district. There was some opposition by the
ranchers and it was not until the following year that the petition was granted
and a school district was formed.

According to the records, on January 22, 1913, a parcel of land on the SW
24-12-2-4 was purchased from Albert Glock for the sum of $8. On the 29th of May
1913 the district received a loan from the Alberta School Supply Co. in the
amount of $1000. Mr. Jacob Zwick was appointed the main carpenter and was paid
$205 to erect the building. Other costs were as follows: Lumber $487.75, school
supplies $194, plastering, Michael Essar $43.90, painting, Douglas Staniforth
$10, foundation and cellar, Adam Roll Jr. $70, and hauling lumber, Phillip
Neubauer $26.

In June of 1913 the school was completed and thus came into being the Clover
Hill School District No. 2584. I don't know about the clover but there
certainly are hills in abundance.

The first teacher was Mr. B.F. Beaton and he was paid a total salary of $150
from June to the end of December of that year. Teacher's salaries fluctuated
from $490 to $700 per annum up to 1934. Further records were not available.

Throughout the years the school house was also a place for church services,
socials, Christmas concerts, wedding dances and school picnics.
