My Year at Clover Hill
by Ruth (Colwell) Armstrong

I taught at Clover Hill S.D., in the year 1934-35, after graduating from
Calgary Normal School. I was very inexperienced as it was my first school and
my first experience at country living. It was during the Depression. I boarded
a month at a time with families in the community. My board expenses were taken
off their taxes, and I received the balance of my monthly stipend. The school
closed for the month of January, because of lack of funds. The total salary for
the year was $600 (including the value of the board, at $25 a month.) Even then
I received one N.S.F. cheque.

Ruth (Colwell) Armstrong  - Teacher 1934-35 (pic)

I walked to and from the school each day, except when I stayed with the Adam
Rolls. Rubin, Ida and myself drove to school with horse and buggy. What a treat
that was! I recall one winter day when I wanted to stay after school. The
weather changed suddenly, with snow developing into a blizzard. However, I left
the school and walked, and walked until I came to a fence. I climbed through,
and found myself back at the school. The Rolls came for me with horse and buggy.

One of the Brandt boys was not working as he should. I remember telling him
that if he didn't want to work he might just as well go home. To my surprise he
immediately packed up his books and left the school. I expected the worst, but
Carl came to the school, after closing time. We talked over the situation, and
I encountered no further trouble. Indeed, when I left at the end of the school
year, the Brandt family organized a dance, and Carl was one who helped provide
the music. Happy memory!

The beginners that year were Roy Neubauer and Victoria Maser. I also recall
that we had a heavy snowfall on the 24th of May weekend and overshoes had to be
worn again.

There was to be a dance in a neighbouring school district. I was invited by one
of the local young men. On the way back the horse came down with a condition
called "jiggers", and we were forced to spend the night with friends. The next
morning, when we were enroute back to Clover Hill, the local farmers were on
their way to the market at Irvine. Were we ever razzed!

The school children were co-operative and well-behaved, and it was a learning
experience for me. I shall always be grateful to the kind-hearted friendly folk
of Clover Hill, for their patience and understanding, when I blundered. It was
for me a rewarding year. Blest be the memory of Clover Hill!

Some Memories from Clover Hill
by Mrs. Evelyn (Glock) Hausauer

The Clover Hill School was closed in June 1945 and the pupils were bussed to
Irvine. Emmanuel Franz was the first bus driver from Clover Hill. He used his
half ton truck, with the back closed in and a couple of wooden planks for
benches to sit on. We had very little heat, great for summer, but we nearly
froze in the winter, however, much better than horse and buggy. I remember how
we used to. try to help push the truck when we got stuck, but we weren't much
help. Our lunch was frozen by the time we got to school in Irvine.

The first pupils to be bussed into Irvine were Alice and Roy Neubauer, Alvin,
Kenneth, Audrey and Wayne Wood, Charmaine and Carol Wood, Frieda and Ella Veil
and Evelyn Glock.

I remember when Roy Neubauer, Alvin and Kenneth Wood and Bruce Brandt built a
submarine out of the old stove that had been replaced in the school by a new
one. The stove had a metal enclosure around it, so it was put to use as a
submarine.

Roy Neubauer was the janitor and several times, when we came to school, Roy had
his jacket laying over the coal pail. He had forgotten to take the eggs out of
his pockets after gathering them and as a result they were broken. So Roy was
drying the pockets.

The old catalogues were used in the biffies. I guess those were the good old
days. When my parents spoke of 40 years ago it seemed like an eternity. Now we
speak of that "long ago" and it doesn't seem so long ago.

Clover Hill Reflections
by Roy Neubauer

As I walk up the hill to the north of the farm, I can feel the soft wind
blowing through the grass. Off in a coulee there are deer grazing, a coyote
howls in the distance, and a cow is mooing for her calf. The countryside seems
so peaceful and serene.

I am on top of the hill now. As I look to the south I see the Rolls, Edwin,
Ralph, and Emil, walking along the ridge of the hills toward the Clover Hill
School.

Coming down the hill from the south of Woods' farm is Horace with his tractor.
It's tea time, a trip he has made many times.

It's Sunday now, and look who is coming across the field to our house. It's old
Harry Hamilton, walking with his hands clasped behind his back. He is coming to
hear Aberhart on the radio. Mother is getting a glass of soda water to put by
his plate because he always gets indigestion when he eats.

There is Mr. Brandt, down from the school, working in his beautiful garden. And
there's Willie Glock - he just killed another gopher by throwing a rock at it.

To the west, Ted Roll is sitting in his International one ton truck watching
his sheep grazing the hillsides.

It's fall and to the south Harry Jacobson and Ed Glock are harvesting their
crop with a header. Harry does set such a straight stack.

A cloud of dust - and a wagon with two horses is coming from Irvine at full
gallop. Gust Maser and Ed Glock are scampering to open their gates. It's a
local character heading home, lying on the bottom of the wagon, dead drunk.
Over the many years, he always made it home safely - truly a miracle.

To the north, Adam Roll is sitting on a binder, driving four beautiful black
high-spirited horses and there is Rubin, setting up the sheaves. Here comes Ida
walking over the hill. As she is going over to the Clover Hill School she
cautiously watches a Government Short Horn Bull dragging a chain in its nose.

Below me is Tom Wood, with the Woods' threshing machine, harvesting our crops.
There is my dad hauling wheat to the granary with a wagon and horses.

What's this? It's my sister, Alice. She is riding on our old horse Tillie. It's
a runaway. You can see her red toque bouncing up and down as they travel over
the hills. My dad gets off his wagon and with long strides takes off after
them, soon to return with nobody the worse for wear. It's getting toward winter
now. I can hear laughter and music down the valley. It's another surprise party
at the neighbor's home. They have a hardwood floor and the family knows the
young people are coming - the Rolls, the Neubauers, Glocks, Masers,  Hamiltons,
Brandts, and Andy Lambie - all to enjoy the dancing and get-together.

The weather is cold now, as I look across the valley to Clover Hill School. You
can hear the kids playing fox and geese. The teacher is getting the school
ready for the Christmas Concert tonight. There are many happy days and many
happy events held at our school.

As I am looking around from the top of my hill, the scene starts to fade. It is
dark now. There is no one left but me. The good old days are gone forever.

Coal Centre School

Coal Centre School was built in 1904-1905 on two acres of land, located on the
NW 17-11-3-W4.

Some of the first persons on the tax roll for the Coal Centre School District
were Carl Beny, K.P. Becker, J.W. Crooks, Theodore Marks, D. Dawson, G.P.
White, Fred Trekofski, Leonard Grossman, George Mayberry, James Keating, George
P. Schneider, E. Sturm, John Sackman, Carl Meier, Karl Otto, and John Will.

Persons on the tax roll in the 1930's were Wm. Trekofski, Phillip Schneider,
Jacob Gust, Louie Grossman, Otto Deering, Fred Stuber, Emanuel Retelback, Jacob
Krauss, Clarence Sailer, and Jim Deering.

Coal Centre School was a one-room school house where grades from one to eight
were taught. There was a big pot belly stove in the back corner and the wood
floors were oiled. There was a janitor who went to school early in the morning
to get a fire going in the big stove so the school would be warm when the other
children came to school. The janitor was usually someone living close to the
school; the wages were about $5 per month.

Concordia School District #1004
by Edwin Gill

The earliest available records that I found were of a meeting June 15, 1904 by
a board of trustees, namely Jacob J. Dais, Ludwig Bischke and John Trekofski.
This board passed a bylaw to borrow $1,000 for the erection of a frame school
house on the land that was donated by Jacob Will. Other business included
borrowing $25 from the Union Bank of Medicine Hat for insurance, and also a
contract, for fire guards and one cord of stone, awarded to Michael Gill for
the sum of $6. Later a bid from W. Kearns was accepted for $695, authorizing
him to build the school. A contract for the foundation was given to Mr. Yess at
$22.75.

Chairman for these earliest meetings was John Trekofski and secretary was W.
Gingell at $40 a year. On August 22, 1904 Jacob J. Dais resigned as trustee and
Mr. T. Atkinson was duly elected to fill his place. He was later elected as
secretary-treasurer in 1905 at $30 a year, along with new trustees, J. Baumback
and J. Lehr. Back-tracking a little, to September 29, 1904, the board
advertised for a school teacher with a First Class Certificate and Simon
Heather was elected as trustee.

Further meetings show Jacob Will supplied three tons of coal at $2 a ton; John
Mayer cut and piled one cord of wood; William Olhausen delivered seats from
Irvine for the sum of $3.25; Simon Heather put up steps for the school house;
W. Gingell would supply blackboards guaranteed not to be broken on delivery.
Tenders for a shed were advertised and later awarded to Joseph Trekofski for
$124.85.

The school house passed building inspection and part payment of $125 was made
to Mr. Kearns, balance to be paid when board received the cheque for
debentures. The secretary was instructed to communicate with Territory
Teacher's Association for a teacher to commence school March 1, 1905. School
opened March 13, 1905 with the first teacher Mr. Wm. Miller and seven pupils
present. A school tax rate of 4 cents an acre or $6.40 per quarter section was
levied.

Records show teacher salaries as low as $46 a month in 1906 plus $2.50 a month
for caretaker duties, fire to be lighted one-half hour before opening. Not
enough money was coming in from taxes to pay teacher's salary and also poor
attendance resulted in the school closing April 30, 1909.

School re-opened again in 1910 with short periods anywhere from one to three
and four month sessions. Secretary-treasurer in the period was W. Dakin,
succeeded by J. F. Barschel; and in 1917 S. Wiedeman took over at $50 a year
for some six years. Attendance rose to forty pupils in 1922, and in 1923, Wm.
Hillenberg was declared secretary. It was also moved that same year that the
school house may be used for dancing and parties at the rate of $25 dollars a
night, in advance, and including liability for all damages to the property.

Newburg School

When the early settlers came to this area there were no schools and realizing
the need for education, T.B. Huddlestone obtained a contract to build a school
in 1898 or 1899 but the school was not built until about 1906. School taxes
were paid to the school board. Teachers and janitors salaries were paid by the
board, as well as repairs and upkeep of the buildings. A government grant was
received every year.

Newburg School - 1936

The janitor's duties included building the fires in the winter, sweeping the
floors, dusting desks, cleaning the outhouses, and whenever necessary, cleaning
the stove pipes and oiling the floor. The wages paid for one month were $4.75.
By 1950 $12 per month was paid for these same chores, and $6 for cleaning the
barn for one year. Half a gross of chalk cost $1.50, war taxes were 20 cents,
3000 pounds of coal cost $5.50, two blinds and two brushes, $2.55, one broom,
65 cents, and insurance was $10 for three years.

Newburg teachers from 1915 on include the following: Anne Thomes, Miss M.F.
Smith, J.W. Jones, E. Dollman, Mrs. A.L. Roy Sommers, Hazel E. Laurie, Alice
Buchian, Mrs. Hattie Sommers, Mrs. Roy Sommers, Mrs. Katie Tothill, Mrs. Grace
M.C. Lewiss, Carl Martin, Esther Johnson, Gladys M.C. Waine, Helen Nash, Harold
Delkon, Elizabeth Welsh, W.R. Morris, D.A. Becker, M. Wenzel, A.E. Ruff, E.W.
Schneider, Leona Bader, Clara Teel, Miss E. Checknitea, Frank Friesen, Jim
Kendle, Eva Bamber, Frank Pivat, J.F. Hughes, and Dorothy Ambrose.

"Spare the rod and spoil the child" was the rule, so the use of the strap and
standing in the corner was not uncommon. One teacher tried a new method. He
swept one child off his feet and hoisted him in the air, misjudged a bit, and
brought the stove pipes down. Good news, school was let out for the day!

Annie Lehr was the fastest runner and her brother, Arthur, the favorite to pick
for the wood pile game. Annie Vossler had to run for her life when she
accidentally spilled water into somebody's face as he came around the corner.
Everyone at the school joined in to catch her, and she finally ran into the
outhouse where she sat down and braced the door shut with her feet, but had to
surrender when they started to tip the thing.

The School Christmas Concerts were good and well attended. Most schools had a
concert and people from surrounding districts would attend them. Schools were
used for church services and Sunday-school until later, when churches were
built.

The school was closed in 1954, which ended that era of children going home on a
white horse, the rattling of buggies or sleighs cracking over the frozen snow
bringing the children from school or the snowball fights on the way home.
Instead, along comes a bright, shining, orange bus to pick up its passengers
with their fancy lunch buckets to a new centralized school.

The children from the Newburg, Sentinel, Robinson, and Evergreen School
Districts attended the Newburg School until the opening of the new Cypress View
School in December 1954. The teachers were Alex Predy and Marie Bischke.

A Year at Newburg
by Frank Friesen

It was September in the year of 1950.

A young, unmarried Saskatchewan school teacher, driving a blue 1936 Chev,
arrived at his boarding place at the home of Ed and Emma Tschritter. This was
really handy, since the one-roomed school was less than one quarter mile just
north of the farm.

The school still had some double desks, and had only two ordinary windows on
each side. There were about twenty students from grade one to eight with
Frances Lehr the biggest and oldest and probably Joey Schorr the smallest.

This was my first year of teaching in Alberta, and I was unfamiliar with their
"Enterprise System", so Mr. Walker, Superintendent, told me to teach Social
Studies, Health and Science as separate subjects. Another thing about school
that sticks in my mind is the day the kids taught me a new song, B.I.N.G.O. the
Dog, an excellent song for monotones, as I recall.

More vivid in my memory are the week-ends I spent in Medicine Hat along with my
one-legged friend Jim Kendal, who taught in a neighboring school "Evergreen"
and boarded at Johnny Lehr's. Jim owned a '34 Packard, which I usually drove
home when it was his turn to take his car, because he had a tendency to spend
too much of his week-end in the Assiniboia.

I also recall a shy, eligible young bachelor who informed me that Krausses to
the west had a young school marm boarding at their place and that we should go
over there for a visit. Although I was already spoken for by my present wife
Ruth, I eagerly accepted Beny's invitation and probably did most of the talking
that night. I think her name was Erna.

Most vivid in my mind is Monday, March 17, 1951. A beautiful week-end in
Medicine Hat with Chinook conditions had temperatures dropping suddenly. I
stayed over-night with Jim on Saturday night and left for home from Lehr's
Sunday night. My car's anti-freeze was too weak so when I got to Otto
Tschritter's farm it was near boiling, so I pulled in for a visit. After the
car had cooled off, I drove home and parked beside Ed's truck with the radiator
still frozen. Next morning there was a blizzard such as this Saskatchewan lad
had never seen before or after. In one day the snow drift was four feet above
my car and Ed's truck. We could step from the snow drift onto the roof of the
house. The temperature was -20 to -30 degrees F for the next week. The coal
shed was filled with snow to the very peak, and the wet Ajax coal wouldn't keep
the house warm using both stoves to capacity. Numerous cattle suffocated and
luckily it only lasted one day or many more would have died.

Jim and I enjoyed visiting with Albert and Irene Schorr. Since they had no kids
at this time, it was a place where we could let our hair down and didn't have
to maintain our teacher image. I remember one night about 2 am going out into
the garden to get some onion greens. Irene had baked some fresh brown bread and
those onion greens, along with some good farm sour cream, made a most delicious
dish.

After 35 years of teaching, I retired in 1983, but the year of 1950-51 will
always remain vivid in my memory.

Two divergent viewpoints about history:

History repeats itself. That's one of the things wrong with history.

History doesn't repeat itself, historians merely do.

Robinson School District #3779

Only the northern section of the Robinson district is included in this history
and the earliest records date back to 1900 and thereafter. Records from the
Provincial Archives in Edmonton show the following in this area of the district:

Jacob Zeske applied for homestead in July 1900, SE 10-10-3-W4.

Sam Kalmbach had applied for homestead in February 1901 and received title in
November 1905, SW 10-10-3-W4.

Adam Sackman applied in February 1903, NW 4-10-3-W4.

Robinson Homestead Map #3779 (pic)

School records show that Fred Schwabe and Adolph Brost were residents by 1928.
By 1931 such names as Jacob Gwinner, Gustav Herman, Fred Doerheim, Jacob
Herman, Daniel Wirsch, C. Wirsch, Karl Koening, Jacob Sulz, Nathaniel -Doering,
Sam Wutzke, Henry Wutzke and William and Henry Ohlhousen were listed as
residing in the area. Histories of some of the above were received and appear
elsewhere in the book and for others further information was not received.

Just when the Robinson School District was organized as such has not been
determined but the Robinson School was located on the SE 5-10-3-W4 site.

From 1920 through 1932 Sam Wutzke and Andrew C. Aman were secretary-treasurer
and John Frisch and Emanuel Deering were chairmen.

To compare with present day costs or salaries this is what was established:
Teacher's salaries ranged from $925 (1929) to $650 (1937) per annum. Emilia
Deering cleaned floors for $1.50. John Koening cleaned stables for $1.75. A
cord of wood, sawed and split, would cost $15. Gust Herman started fires one
half hour before school opening for 20 cents per day.

The ratepayers had difficulty collecting enough funds so the school would have
to close down for periods of time. In 1923 the school closed on April 13 and
did not re-open again until November 17, 1924. In 1925 the school again closed
on June 30 and remained closed for three months. The lack of teachers, right
after World War II, was also a major factor and the school would be shut down
for short periods. When the school was operating it also provided Christmas
concerts and the occasional dances for either fund raising or merely pleasure.

With the coming of centralization the Robinson district was not to be missed
and in 1954 plans were drawn up to build a new two room school approximately
four or five miles to the east and when this was completed Robinson School
closed its doors for the last time in June of 1954. In September of the same
year the children were vanned to the new school named Cypress View.

In September of 1955 the Robinson school was moved west to the Goose Lake
School District #1818 and by 1959 all remaining buildings, fence and the two
acre site were sold.

Teachers who taught in Robinson School, close as could be determined, were as
follows:

A Smile

A smile doesn't cost anything, but it's worth a lot. It enriches the one who
receives it without making the one giving it any poorer. It only takes a moment
to flash a smile, but its memory is sometimes unforgettable.

No one is so rich or so powerful that he or she can do without a smile and no
one is so poor that he or she can't become richer for making a gift of one.

A smile creates happiness, encourages goodwill and seals friendships. It brings
peace to those who are tired, joy to those who are discouraged, a ray of
sunshine to those who are sad. It is the best antidote nature has to fight
life's worries.

Schlaht School District #1293

On doing research for the Schlaht School District, although apparently
established about 1905, we were unable to find any records prior to 1914.
During that year and until 1920 we noted that families living in the area were
James Lindsay, George Schneider, William Krausz, Jack Aman, Gottlieb Banek,
John Bollinger, Henry Cook, A. Calkins, R.D. Porter, John Arnold, William Begg,
Fred W. Weiss, A.C. Aman, John Ehrman, Fred Leicht, P. Bauer, Henry Christman,
Alex Lindsay, John Schlaht, S. Wiedeman, Laidlaw Blanchard, Edward Noble and
Gottlieb Stadel. From some of the aforementioned we have received additional
history in the family section but there are numerous others on whom we have not
been able to find any further information.

The earliest records of any school activities were in 1914 showing Mr. Wm.
Krausz as secretary from 1914 to 1924, at a salary of $30 per year and books
were audited by Miss Schroder for $5. First record of building accounts was in
the same year with John Ehrman receiving $15, Christian Schlaht, $105 and Phil
Silver, $43. All this was indicated as construction expense.

Records of teachers serving in the area dated back to 1919 and names of these
were Margaret E. Kerr, Miss Ferne Stacey, Margaret Cruckshank, Bessie Shanks,
Mrs. Ida Jones, Miss Robina Scargie, Miss Bella Barmen, Vera Ansley, Miss
Frances E. McCandie, Esther C. Elford, Miss E.M. Thurn, Lee Leavitt, L.E.
Hawthorn, Doris Hawthorne, Murray Robison, Fred Fisher, Hazel Toole, Mrs. A.H.
Murphy, and finally Miss Helen Kosior, who taught in 1939 at a salary of $640 a
year. There appears to be no record of teachers after 1939. After the school
was closed students were transported to Irvine.

Teachers were deducted $20 a month for board and room which was applied against
the ratepayers taxes.

When the school districts were amalgamated with Cypress School Division #4, in
January of 1937, it was noted that the bank balance of the Schlaht School was
$50.

In July of 1938 a request was submitted to the Deputy Minister, Department of
Education, to have the Schlaht School site relocated 330 feet east and 396 feet
north of the original site. The new site was the property of Emil Pahl and he
gave his consent to use this land. No reason was stated for this requested
move, however, in a letter dated August 3, 1938 and signed by William Aberhart,
the then Minister of Education, this request was granted. The original site was
then canceled and a further request, also approved, was that a low-frame school
be re-constructed.

Mr. Charles H. Mooney was successful in his tender to reconstruct the 18' by
24' frame with an 8' by 10' porch for $350. He was instructed to use the
salvage lumber and was given permission to buy some new material where
necessary. He was granted a further $40 for a new floor.

In 1939 some of the work tendered was cleaning school and oiling floor once
every term at $2.50 a term to F.W. Weiss. Win. Krausz plowed a fire guard,
three sides, at $6. The fence was to be kept in good repair for the year at
$1.50 and the barn cleaned three times a year at 75 cents per cleaning. This
work was done by Emil Pahl. Harry Weiss did the janitor work at $4 a month for
seven months, sweeping the floor and starting the fire. The remaining three
months he was to receive only $2 a month because he was not required to heat
the school during the summer months.

There were notes suggesting the school be closed down as early as August of
1940 but we found no record of an actual closing date. Emil Pahl did request,
in February 1942, to rent the school house for $8 a month to be used as living
quarters while he and his family built a new house. This was approved.

In 1943 August Ehrman was employed as a van driver, at $3 per day, for the
Schlaht-Irvine school route.

In August of 1948 it was recommended to sell all the Schlaht buildings but
final approval was not granted until December 1, 1954 when the school board
approved the sale of site and buildings. Tenders were then received for $76.25
for the barn, $126.25 for the school and $16 for the land but there is no
record if this bid was accepted.

In our research we were unable to locate anything which would indicate that
other functions or activities took place in this school.

Sentinel School District #1516

Very little information could be found about the Sentinel School District other
than that it was established on June 25, 1906.

The teachers that have been recorded, though the list is incomplete, were from
1929 and thereafter as follows:

Kathleen Ingraham, 1929; W.R. Pilling, 1930-31; D.C. Pickard, 1931-32; Ruth
Sallons, 1933-34; Ruth Noble, 1934; Ida Atzinger, 1936; Geraldine Walker,

available for the last eight but it is fact that they taught there in the late
1930's, early and mid 1940's. Continuing on, there was Inga L. Schneider,
1947-50; and Eleanor (Peggy) MacKinlay (Mrs. Emil Neubauer), 1950-51; after
which time the school closed and the children were transported to the Newburg
School until the new two-room school, known as Cypress View, was opened in
1954. At that time there were only five children that were of school age from
the Sentinel School.

Irvine School District #892 Established 1903
by Shirley Belyea

memories of several old timers to thank for what information we have.

Irvine Schools - 1904 to 1920's (8 pic)

The first school was built on the corner of Railway Avenue and Dunmore Street.
It remains standing and is our present museum. The first teacher may have been
a Miss Mary Mitchell with a class of 50 pupils. It was used as a school from
about 1900-1903. During these years when an immigrant train stopped at Irvine,
the students would be dismissed and the immigrants given the use of the
building. The building was then used as Town Hall and Immigration Building.
Records indicate that it was rented by the school board to the Immigration
Department in 1910 for $15 a month for one year.

The next school erected in 1904 was on Railway Avenue between Forres and
Christie Streets. It is marked on a survey map dated September 1912 as Public
School.

As reported in the Medicine Hat News, Dec. 17, 1907, the school was too small
and an addition was needed for about 80 students (Irvine's population was about
500). At a special meeting, on May 11, 1909, it was moved by John Hausauer that
the amount to be extended on the building of the complete concrete block school
house be $6,000.

By-law #7 was passed on July 19, 1909, stating that the sum of $5,000 be
borrowed by debenture for the purchasing of a site (lots 19-24, block 12) and
the building of a concrete block school house and furnishing of same.

Plans of Mr. J. Trimble, Architect of Medicine Hat were accepted. Malcolm
Esplen of Medicine Hat was contractor. The school was completed by November
1909.

Sandstone school (pic)

In February of 1912, the tender of G. Ziffle was accepted in the sum of $65 for
the work on the proposed addition to the concrete block school.

During these years the town population grew to approximately 1,100 so on
December 13 of 1913, the school board decided to lease the lower floor of David
Roloff's store for a term of six months at the rate of $25 per month, the owner
to agree not to interfere with the school by putting noisy tenants upstairs!

Sandstone school and May pole (pic)

At the February 20, 1914 board meeting, Mr. F.G. McLaughlin was appointed
secretary-treasurer at $120 per year.

To ease the crowded conditions, more classrooms were needed. On May 6, 1914 a
motion was passed by Phil McLeay that a new brick school be built on the site
of lots 1-18, block 17 (Alberta Avenue between Durham and Elgin Street). This
was to be a two story, two classroom brick school on a cement foundation.

Architect W.T. Williams drew up the plans. The tender of Nels Dalstrom was
chosen. The building was to be completed by August 29, 1914

Brick School built in 1914 (pic)

Mr. R.S. Shaw was principal at this time. As he had taken on teaching grade 9
he was given $1,000 a year. He resigned in January 1916 to "join the colors" .
He was told his position would be open for him on his return.

In January of 1917, the School Board informed the Board of Health that they
desired the children be vaccinated before attending school. This was done in
September.

Two hundred Russian Poplars were ordered for school yard planting in 1918.

Upon the advice of the school inspector, arrangements were made with the
principal, Miss H.C. Brown, to teach grade 9 in 1919.

On December 8, 1919 the brick school was gutted by fire. An excerpt from the
Medicine Hat News, December 13, 1919 carried this description:

The fully up to date $1,000 brick school house built in 1914 was totally
destroyed by fire on Monday afternoon. The fire was first in the upstairs room,
where the principal, Miss Brown, was teaching. Great praise is due to the
teachers, Miss Brown and Miss Tinney, in the expeditious way in which the
children left the building. Miss Brown, showing great presence of mind in the
use she made of the patent fire extinguisher kept in the building; she
completely smothered the flames issuing from one of the radiators in her room
but unfortunately the flames had such a hold on the upper part of the building
that her heroic efforts proved fruitless and in a few minutes the flames were
bursting from the roof. In the meantime, she had sent two students, Roy Beny
and Clarence Weiss, to give the alarm and ring the fire bell. Constable Rhyce
was the first of the citizens to arrive on the scene of the disaster. Within an
incredibly short time the fire brigade were on the spot and assisted by a
number of citizens did all in their power to save the building but to no avail
and all that is left of the Irvine Public School are four brick walls.

Mr. Ted Aman was in class in the brick school at the time of the fire. He
recalls that the pupils did not panic as they had practiced fire drills. Reuben
Weiss remembers being taken by the hand and led to safety by Sophia Thiede.
Mrs. Emma McLaughlin was attending class in the cement block school at the
time. She remembers the teacher, Miss Crockford, pulling the blinds so her
pupils could not watch the fire.

At a special meeting on Tuesday, the school board decided to have the senior
room in the town hall and the vacant room (addition) in the cement school for
the intermediate grades.

Bricks from this school were still available in 1927 at 1 cent each.

On September 15, 1921, the school inspector requested the board to hire a third
teacher. This was refused. This was again requested September 29, 1921 and
again refused. The Irvine School continued with two classrooms and two teachers
until the end of the 30's.

Through the years one method the school board had of handling overcrowding was
to restrict enrollment age to seven. A motion passed on August 2, 1920 allowed
children five years and over to be accepted in the primary room, provided there
was accommodation and that they start at the beginning of the term,
accommodation limited to 45.

In August of 1929 a request by Mr. Cook and Mr. F. Schneider to have their
boys, Eugene and Emil, take grade XI at Irvine School was granted - provided
the principal could handle this grade without interferences to the other
scholars.

In 1934 the Irvine Women's Institute, with the help of a grant of $27.80 from
the school board, purchased a piano for the school. A teacher to be hired that
year was accepted provided she was musical enough to instruct the children for
festival work. Records show that Crewe's Transport took the children to the
festival May 5, 1939 and also took them to see the King and Queen, May 24, 1939.

In 1935 the trustees agreed to have the secretary order the Neilson map for
schools - free.

One hundred Coronation buttons were ordered in May of 1939. Those not used for
gifts were to be sold to the children for 10 cents each.

These early years saw epidemics of communicable diseases occur.

Records show a measles epidemic in January of 1917 and again in February 1937.
A diphtheria epidemic struck in February of 1926. School records show the
school was closed for disinfection on February 8. The records indicated too,
that one grade nine pupil, Johnny Schwabe, died of diphtheria at that time.

Infantile paralysis struck in the fall of 1937. The board responded by
arranging with the Cypress Division and Nurse Hagerman to take care of the
preventive treatment during the epidemic.

Teachers salaries followed the norm of the times, ranging from $500 to $1,000 a
year. At the teachers' request for an increase in salary, several times the
records show the reply to be "that if satisfactory progress be made in all
grades at the examination, the board will consider a bonus at the end of the
term".

The board has also been supportive of the School Christmas Tree. Each year,
along with the W.I., a contribution was made. The Annual Christmas Concert is
still a strong tradition at Irvine School and is the highlight of the season to
the elementary students.

Mr. F.G. McLaughlin left the school board both as trustee and secretary
treasurer on February 22, 1939, after serving for 20 years. He took the
position of secretary-treasurer for Cypress Division #4. The board expressed
their "sincere thanks for his untiring labors and success in his new chosen
field".

August of 1939 saw the culmination of a year of negotiations by Irvine School
District #892 with Cypress Division #4. This mutual agreement would provide
grade 10, 11 and 12 to the high school students from the Irvine District and
the surrounding nearby part of the Division. Irvine was to supply the room and
pay for heat and janitor. Cypress was to hire and pay the teacher, also to
supply blackboards and some classroom supplies. The senior room opened in our
present museum.

Due to a teacher shortage in 1942, the Cypress Division moved the following
schools to Irvine: Wilkinson, Abelein, Waddington and Fifteen Mile. Students
from these schools were vanned to Irvine. Students from Many Island Lake and
Coal Center were about to be conveyed to Irvine by the end of 1942. Long Valley
and Clover Hill were attending Irvine in September of 1945.

In the late forties, Irvine School consisted of one concrete building built in
1909 and four rural schools built about 1912. As they were scattered about the
school yard, supervision was difficult. These buildings were in a poor state of
repair as a report from the Irvine W.I. to the Department of Education pointed
out and this was verified by reports from the fire inspector and superintendent.

One hundred seventy pupils were expected to attend school in the fall of 1949.
The time was definitely ripe for a new school.

in March, 1949, by-law #3 was passed by the board. It was to enable the board
to borrow $80,000 to build a six-room school with full basement at Irvine. The
plebiscite held six months later rejected the proposal by a vote of 3 to 1. The
town of Irvine was almost 100 percent in favor.

A special meeting attended by 45 Irvine ratepayers on August 6, 1949 indicated
their disapproval of the school issue. There were comments put forward about
Irvine being discriminated against and possibly withdrawing from the Division.

At annual meetings held throughout the Division at the end of 1949, ratepayers
expressed their agreement of a four-room school for Irvine.

On May 15, 1950, by-law #4 was approved for the borrowing of $41,000 by
debenture. The rest was financed from current revenue, the total cost of the
school being $85,000.

Construction of the new school began in 1951. It was to consist of four
classrooms upstairs, two smaller classrooms and a gymnasium in the basement.
The school had a new well and a diesel lighting plant. (Calgary power reached
Irvine in 1953) The official opening of the new school was held on December 21,
1951 in the new gymnasium.

A primary wing was added to the south of the new school. It consisted of four
classrooms, principal's office, staff-room, washrooms and auditorium. One
basement classroom was converted into a Home Economics room. It was in use by
September of 1955.

Since then three other wings have been added, a junior high wing, which houses
the Home Economics department, a senior high wing of two classrooms and
gymnasium, and in 1981 the shop area was given a permanent location. Cypress
View School is still in use at Irvine - its two classrooms used for business
education and computer technology.

With the closing of Cypress View School in the 1960's all possible school
districts, some 35 of them, were closed and the students vanned to Irvine.

The Irvine School has a high educational standard. It is an attractive building
and is well maintained. There are at present 22.5 teachers on staff as well as
three aids and one secretary.

Come September, 1989, nine school buses will roll up and stop. The 300 children
gathered there will be starting another year at Irvine School.

Irvine School - 1988 (pic)

A Tribute

Irvine S.D. #892 has through the years been voluntarily served by caring
trustees. Descendants of many of them are still in the area.

I would like to pay a special tribute to one of them: Mr. Ted Roll. Beginning
in 1937, Ted served as Divisional or local trustee for 23 and a half years.

These were years of change and challenge for Irvine School. Those of us who
taught at Irvine during this time very quickly became aware that Irvine School
was Ted's pride and joy. We also found that what Irvine School needed - Irvine
School got. As far as the school was concerned, Ted was the right man in the
right place at the right time.

Note: If you have any recollections of the early Irvine School years you would
like to share, I would like to have them for an expanded history of the school.

Shirley Belyea, Retired teacher 1955-1988.
Irvine, Alberta, July 15, 1989.

Footnote: The night of September 22, 1989 saw a devastating fire sweep through
the Irvine School completely destroying it.

We hope that like the phoenix rising from the ashes so will a new Irvine School.

Editor's Note: Irvine School Fire

On the night of Friday, September 22, 1989 at about 11 o'clock, R.C.M.P.
Constable Raymond Duquette, while on patrol, discovered smoke and flames inside
the Irvine School. Despite an all night battle by 13 Irvine firefighters, the
Medicine Hat and Walsh fire departments, and Irvine residents who volunteered
by moving hoses and bringing food, they were unable to save the building. By
Saturday morning the school had burned to the ground.

The blaze started in the southeast corner and only a few clumps of bricks,
warped and distorted steel beams and some of the north end of the walls were
left as a grim reminder of what had once been a 19 classroom school.

The building was first constructed in 1951 with additions in 1955, 1959, 1964,
1980 and lastly in September of 1989 when the Cypress School Division had just
finished installing a $350,000 new air conditioning and ventilation system,
which was to have been tried for the first time on the Monday.

The building was covered by insurance in the amount of $4.8 million, the
contents of $460,000, demolition and site clean-up for $75,000 and other
expenses for $500,000.

The immediate reaction was that the fire originated from an electrical short
but on further investigation Provincial fire investigator Fred Westerson
indicated that the school was burned too severely to determine what sparked the
flame.

Education
by Ben Otto Sr.

Education plays a part,
To our life it gives a start.
Without it, what could we all do,
Life for us would soon be through.

When we were young and all so free,
One and One was always three.
Addition always was a chore,
Two and Two did not make four.

When the time had come to spell,
I know we didn't do so well.
The letters always looked so strange,
And they were always disarranged.

Then came the time to draw a map,
That for sure would be a snap.
We searched the books until we found,
That our world was really round.

If we would have our test today,
I'm sure we'd almost pass away.
For one and one I'm sure it's three,
And two and two is too hard for me.

                                   Churches

St. George's Anglican Church

In November 1896 Mr. Sam Cooper and Mr. A. Mort built the Church of England
Mission Church at Josephsburg (Medicine Hat News, November 5, 1896). Church of
England services were held in Josephsburg Mission on Sunday, July 22, 1906; at
the Mill, Cypress Hills at 11 am; at St. Ann's Church, Josephsburg at 3:30 pm;
and at St. Albert's Church, Gros Ventre at 7 pm (Medicine Hat News, July 19,
1906).

In 1907 St. George's Parish was established in Irvine, when the church and
vicarage were built. Four lots on the north side of the track were donated in
1907 and a contract was let to Patzer Bros. for $12.50 to be completed in seven
weeks. "This church would have a chime of tubular bells. Bishop Grisdale will
consecrate the church and preside at the opening ceremony." (Medicine Hat News,
June 20, 1907) According to the Medicine Hat News this consecration took place
November 5, 1907. A later report by the news lists Rev. Percy C. Jerrold as the
presiding minister in the year 1908; and in 1911 and 1914 as listed in the
Henderson's Directories.

Mrs. Percy Jerrold - wife of Rev. Jerrold (pic)

Confirmation was held at St. George's Parish and seven young people were
confirmed: John Francis Thomas, Joseph Henry Crookes, Thomas Arthur Barrigan,
James Henry Barrigan, Mary Ellen Crookes, Elizabeth May Price, and Florence
Henrietta Barrigan. (Medicine Hat News, December 3, 1914).

Certificate of Baptism: Elizabeth Crewe - 1909. Signed by Percy C. Jerrold (pic)

Certificate of Baptism: Viola Crewe - 1921. Signed by P.C. Jerrold (pic)

In the Irvine Insight of 1978 Thomas Wood reports Rev. Jerrold was the minister
all the years the church was active. He reports the attendance became less and
less and it was finally closed. According to Wood the church was moved to the
Clearwater district north of Irvine in 1944.

Baptist Church

The Baptist Church in Irvine was built about 1914. Emma McLaughlin's
"Grandfather Schneider" laid the cornerstone. The church was across the street
from the school and just north of where Lynn McLaughlin's home now stands. The
McLaughlin house was built in 1916 as the church manse. People moving away
caused the membership to dwindle to a very few and services were discontinued.
Several years ago the church was sold and moved to Medicine Hat.

Baptist Church group - 1920's (pic)

Records show that there was a German Baptist Church in Irvine before the
Baptist Church was built in 1914.

In 1909 Rev. D.B. Harkness served the Baptist Church. January 20, 1910 Mr. O.
Mayberry and Miss Madiss were married at the German Baptist Church. In 1911,
Rev. W.A. Mueller was the minister at the German Baptist Church. In 1914 Rev.
Fred Mindrop was minister. The wedding of Emma Schaller, daughter of George
Schaller, to Mr. E. Weiss of Cypress Hills took place at the German Baptist
Church. Rev. Mindrop performed the ceremony (Medicine Hat News, November 24,
1914).

Christ Lutheran Church

The Lutheran Church congregation in Irvine was formed in October 1909 with
Pastor G. Spohr presiding. The members present on the day of organization were
Jacob Bollinger, John Koenig, Christian Schlaht, Albert Glock, Gottlieb
Zieffle, John Pudwell, and Fredrick Meske. They apparently met in private homes
until the church was built in the town of Irvine in 1912, under the name of
"Evangelical Lutheran Christusgemeinde".

Offering at the first church service October 10, 1909 was $1.35 for the church
and $6.55 for mission work. The first Christmas program was in 1914 and the
first record of confirmation in 1915. The first mission festival was November
3, 1918  with Pastor G.H. Senft from Medicine Hat as guest speaker.

Service and all church records were in German the first years but the German
language was gradually phased out during the 1950's with all English by 1960.

(pic)

On July 12, 1921, the church was damaged by lightening. The interior of the
church was renovated in 1965. After renovations were completed, the church was
rededicated and the name was changed to "Christ Lutheran Church" on November
14, 1965. Bathrooms and a furnace room were added to the church during the
winter of 1979-80.

Christ Lutheran Church (pic)

Services in the church were discontinued in June of 1986. A final church
service, led by Pastor Phil Hink of Edmonton, was held May 26, 1988 to
officially close the church. Pastor M. Rude was also in attendance at this
service.

The pastors who served the congregation were Pastors G. Spohr, J. Oberhammer,

Schaefer, E.K. Rostad, K. Spoonheim, L. Arndt and M. Rude.

John Oberhammer

John Oberhammer was born in Austria and traveled to St. Paul, Minnesota and
then on to Drake, North Dakota. He came to Alberta in the spring of 1909,
disembarking at Lethbridge. He eventually took out a homestead in the Coaldale
area. In 1910 he and his wife, Minnie, traded this land for a homestead
northwest of Irvine in the Clearwater District, SE 30-12-3-W4. Born to the
couple were Harold, Herbert, Frieda, Martha and Victoria.

John, being an ordained minister of the Lutheran Church as early as 1911,
stayed on his homestead and traveled in a two-wheel cart pulled by his horse,
Sam, and ministered in homes since churches were not built at that time. He
served in surrounding areas, including Medicine Hat, and at Christ Lutheran
Church in Irvine. Some of the places he attended required as much as two to
four days traveling time. While he was away serving the congregations, his
family remained on the homestead and tended the farm.

In 1920 Harold took charge of the farm and eventually Pastor John and the rest
of the family moved to Prelate, Saskatchewan where he continued to minister
until he retired.

John Oberhammer passed away in Calgary in 1947.

History of Peace United Church
by Ted Aman as he remembers it

The Congregational Friedens Gemeinde was organized on August 19th, 1918.

Services were held in the home of Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Aman until the new church
building was erected.

Rev. Henry Treise was the first minister. Sam Kalmbach was first
secretary-treasurer, Jacob Maser as elder, and Andrew Rieger and Jacob Aman as
trustees, Fred Knoblick as Sunday School Superintendent, Ida Kalmbach as
organist and Mrs. Margaret Aman as choir leader.

The pastoral charge was made up of Irvine, North Irvine, Schuler, Graburn and
North Foris. The minister was resident in Irvine and was transported by
whatever means available by the members of the outlying congregations.

In 1920, Rev. G.J. Ricker became our minister and the pastoral charge consisted
of Irvine, North Irvine, Graburn, Gros Ventre, and Kincorth, Saskatchewan. The
minister had the use of horse and buggy for visitation and was otherwise
transported by the members. During the ministers absence the laymen took the
service. Rev. Saul did visit in between as he traveled from one congregation to
the other.

In 1925 when the Methodist, Presbyterian and Congregational churches united we
became known as Peace United Church.

During the second term of G.J. Ricker's ministry we became a part of the
Medicine Hat Pastoral charge, consisting of Irvine, North Irvine, Graburn, Gros
Ventre, Seven Persons and North Foris in Alberta, and Surprise, Leader,
Westerheim in Saskatchewan. The minister traveled by car and had three services
per Sunday. Even though there were no roads. he always got there. He used to
shovel quite frequently. He held confirmation whenever called for and held
special services in the fall in the various congregations. These lasted from
one to two weeks and many were brought into the church by profession of faith.

One of the highlights of those days were the lay conferences, held annually at
different congregations. These were organized by a committee of laymen, and
they were responsible for choosing the various speakers. These meetings lasted
from Friday till Sunday evening. The ministers took the Sunday Services and
served communion with the Sunday service. People came from all over and were
provided with free meals and lodging for the duration. Meetings were held in a
big tent and the church was used for serving meals. A house was moved from the
Aman farm and was used for a kitchen. The young people waited on tables.

Friedens Congregational (United) Church, Irvine confirmation class - March 25,
1923: Back: Art Aman, Rudolph Stehr, Jacob Weiss, Gus Pheifer; Front: Rev. Ed
Hildebrand, Linda Streich, Maggie Fischer, Lizzie Wallewein, Linda Kalmbach
(pic)

Another highlight of those early days was confirmation. This lasted for four
weeks and ended on Palm Sunday. Classes were held from 9 o'clock till 4
o'clock, five days a week. You memorized the catechism and most of the New
Testament scriptures relating to the fundamentals of our Christian faith.
Besides Bible history, there was some instruction in writing German. Palm
Sunday was the big day and we marched from the ministers residence in pairs,
and as we approached the church we sang, Jesu geh Voran - interpreted into
English, Jesus Lead the Way. We were put to the test and had to answer
questions as stated in the catechism. We received our first communion. The
young people attended from the different congregations in the area and stayed
with the people from the local congregation.

1959 United Church Confirmation class: Back: Ken Zeller, Norman Aman, Stanley
Ziegler, Rev. Allan Hunt, Harvey Aman, Terry Krauss, George Simmons: Front:
Sharon Ziegler. Shirley Zeller (pic)

Another highlight was our Christmas program. They were held each year and
preparation began at least a month before Christmas Eve. Attendance was high
and the church was usually filled. This was one time when the church was too
small. We had around 50 children taking part plus a choir and were packed in
very tight, with people standing right to the door.

Ministers who served the congregation in German were Rev. Henry Treise, Rev.
G.J. Ricker, Rev. Jacob Kesler, Rev. John Gebhard, Rev. Gross, Rev. Cypress,
Rev. Schulteiss, Rev. Reutermann, Rev. Paul Hediger and Rev. George Spady who
was bilingual.

Later when our old people were no longer with us, we held our services in
English and a number of English speaking families joined our church. Ministers
serving in English were Rev. Norman Levein, Rev. Marvin Fowler, Rev. Allan
Hunt, Deaconess Audrey Lawrence, Deaconess Marge Ashton, Rev. Godfrey, Rev.
Syer, Rev. Godley and Rev. Leroy Angle.

Irvine United Church - 1988 (pic)

Irvine United Church bell (pic)

In 1960 we decided to build a new church with facilities for Sunday School in
the basement and also kitchen facilities. We had a large Sunday School and
needed better accommodation.

We had good response from the community and volunteer labour was usually
available when needed. This helped to keep our costs down. Mr. Wahl was our
supervisor and he came when we needed him and let us do whatever we could on
our own, which also helped keep our costs down.

When Memorial and Salem congregations united with one minister serving both
congregations, it left one manse available. They kept the best one and the
other one was sold. Irvine got a small share of that money which went to the
building fund. The Home Mission Board gave us a loan plus a small grant. We
sold some bonds, most of which were later donated. As 1961 was the driest year
in our history, we did run into difficulty financing the project, but were
eventually able to pay out our mortgage in full.

We are now accommodating the E.C.S. in our basement.

I have taken part in most of the services down through these many years and
certainly have been blessed in many ways.

Newburg Evangelical Church

The work was started in 1907 with Rev. Domm as a missionary from Ontario. In
1908 a church was built on NE 16-10-2-W4 and dedicated July 5, 1908 with Rev.
J.S. Domm and Rev. Bell and Superintendent Wagner officiating.

It was a mission church served from the Medicine Hat Memorial Evangelical
Church. This Pastor would serve churches at Wisdom, Little Plume, Gros Ventre,
and Newburg. He would have a service every second week, and getting to church
was difficult due to no roads, so he would travel by car as far as he could and
farmers would take him by horseback or team to the various churches and then
take him to the next station to get to the other church. This carried on for
many years to bring the gospel to the farmers and ranchers in the area.

The work continued until 1945, when the church was closed down due to lack of
interest. A lot of the supporters had retired and moved to Medicine Hat.

In 1959, through the efforts of Hillcrest Christian College, work began in the
Cypress View School and an old school house from the Woolchester area was moved
to the site at SE 4-10-2-W4. The work continued till 1970 and again the church
was closed due to lack of interest and people moving away. The building and
equipment were sold and funds went to Wycliffe Bible Translators and Marion
Heaslip at La Paz, Bolivia, South America.

There are two cemeteries, one at SE 4-10-2-W4 and the other at NE 16-20-2-W4.

Newburg Evangelical Church and Congregation - 1963 (pic)

Newspaper Article Newburg E.U.B. Church - 1963 (pic)

Vol. 35 MEDICINE HAT, ALBERTA, NOVEMBER 1963
--JIMMIE KNODEL--

In the 26th Chapter of Genesis, we have an account of Isaac as he re-opened the
wells that his father had dug but later were closed up. Similar to this is the
story of the Newburg E.U.B. Church.

Approximately 35 to 40 years ago the church of Newburg was founded. It was
operated as such until about 1945 when it was closed down because most of the
elder people moved to the city, and there was no one to keep the work going.

Than about 4 years ago some students from H.C.C. began a work at the Cypress
View School. This was an encouragement to the people and with the help of Mr.
W. Ammon, the work kept going. However it wasn't until Jan. 1963, after a week
of revival services held at the school house with Rev. N.W. Heebner as
speaker, that we began to contemplate securing a different building, one that
we could call our own. After the close of these meetings Rev. Heebner come to
us and turned over honorarium which he had received for his services to us,
making the first donation to the building fund. This soon grew to several
hundred dollars as many of the farmers contributed liberally. Hillcrest and
Memorial churches also lifted an offering for us which was very gratefully
received. The building is now completed including a piano, pews, a stove, and
Calgary Power. All of this is paid for and we did not have to go one cent into
debt for which we praise the Lord.

Our church is not a new one, it is simply an old school house which we
remodeled and redecorated and now serves as the Newburg Church, located 36
miles South-East of Medicine Hot.

It was a real honor to have Rev. T.E. Jesske along with Rev. L.V. Myers, and
Rev. A.W. Riegel share in our dedication service on Sept. 29. A crowd of
approximately 150 people were in attendance. We had an afternoon and evening
service separated by on outdoor supper which was enjoyed by everyone. Special
music consisted of the Proclaimers Quartet, Miss Amy Enslen and Rev. A.W.
Maetche.

Please Pray for this little church that God may use it as a channel where-by
many of the people in this district will find Christ.

Newburg Church of God

Newburg Church of God was begun as a German speaking congregation. Minutes
available record the first meeting February 3, 1925. Meetings were held in
various homes.

On December 11, 1925, estimates for material for the church and barn were
obtained from Revelstoke Sawmill Co. Ltd. In May of 1926, materials were
purchased and the Church was erected on the SE 16-10-3-W4. The oil for the
floor was purchased June 22, 1926. This would seem that the church was in its
final stages if not complete. Mr. Jacob Deis was appointed as builder with
numerous volunteers helping.

Members of the Church Board that appear on the promisary note payable to
Revelstoke were August Jans, Dan Wirsch and Emanuel Doering.

The minutes of meetings are recorded in German 1925 to 1948. From 1951 to 1966
English was used. Last minute records were 1966 and the congregation faded.

The horse barn was sold in 1951 and moved off the site. Due to the fact that
the church was not being used, people began abusing the building and contents,
with the clock, organ, and stove being removed (stolen). The church was sold
and dismantled in 1973.

In 1975 the cemetery was fenced and a tombstone was erected on the cemetery
site with all known names of the loved ones put to rest there. The cemetery is
all that remains as a reminder of the church that once was.

Ministers and Evangelists as remembered were Reverends Butgereit, J. Weins, L.
Millensifer, M. Babel, J. Tjart, C. Arbeiter, A. Schneider, K. Krause, J.
Reimchen and R. Farmer.

Seventh Day Adventist Church

The Seventh Day Adventist Church was built in 1916, and was located about 12
miles south of Irvine. The church basement was used as a school until the
Robinson School was built in 1919. In the late 40's the church building was
sold to the congregation of the Irvine Church of God, and moved Irvine.

Irvine Church of God

The records of Irvine Church of God are limited. In the spring of 1946, the
congregation of the Church of God bought the Seventh Day Adventist Church
building, which was located about 12 miles south of Irvine, and moved it to
Irvine. It was located on the north side of the railway tracks on Pacific
Avenue.

It was officially opened in the summer of 1946. The first Pastor to serve the
congregation was Rev. Karl Krause. The services were in the German language.
From April 1950 to the fall of 1952, Pastor August Schneider served the
congregation. The Graburn Church of God, located about 25 miles south of Walsh,
and the Newburg Church of God were included in their parish. For 17 years the
church membership was very active. As years passed by, members moved away, and
the church was closed.

In 1963 the church building was sold to the Hatton Full Gospel Congregation and
moved to Hatton, Saskatchewan.

Pastor August Schneider

It was an eventful day, when the young couple, Rev. and Mrs. August Schneider,
moved into Irvine April 15, 1950 to Pastor the German Church of God located on
the north side of the railway track in Irvine. Two out of town points were
included in their parish, and were served alternate Sundays. The meetings at
both Graburn (south of Walsh) a distance of 25 miles, and Newburg (15 miles
south of Irvine) were held in the afternoon and were in the English language.

It was an exciting day July 8, 1950, when twin sons were born to Pastor and
Mrs. Schneider. They remember with deep gratitude those who offered help in
caring for and clothing given for little Reginald and Ronald.

In the fall of 1952 the Schneiders were called to Pastor the Silver Grove
Church of God in the Shellbrook, Saskatchewan area, and moved to that location
in October of that year. This again was both English and German services. In
March of 1954 another son, Douglas, was born completing the family of three
boys. In this year also the family moved to Creston, B.C. where they were asked
for help in establishing a new church. It was God's timing as the church was
well received there and continues to this day.

Other points the Schneiders served were Chilliwack, B.C., 1960-66, a new Church
opened at Barrhead, Alberta, retiring in Armstrong, B.C. They are presently
(1988) living in Vernon, B.C. Ron and his wife live at Armstrong, B.C. Reg and
family live at Armstrong, while Doug and his wife and family live in
Revelstoke, B.C.


                                    Irvine

Colonel A. G. Irvine

Acheson Gosford Irvine was a Canadian by birth, the son of Lieutenant Colonel
Irvine of Quebec who was principal A.D.C. to the Governor General of Canada. He
was born in Quebec on December 7, 1837. He was educated there and spent some
years in commercial life.

Colonel Irvine joined the North West Mounted Police and was appointed a
Superintendent on November 7, 1875 and Assistant Commissioner on January 1,
1876.

Colonel Irvine became Commissioner on November 1, 1880.

The important part played by the C.P.R. in the development of Western Canada
cannot be exaggerated. It is no wonder then that the Commissioner received
letters from prominent officials of the Railway, among them one from Mr. Van
Horne, the General Manager, expressing the Company's obligations to the
N.W.M.P. in generous terms.

In April 1886, Colonel Irvine retired, after having served in the Force for
approximately ten years and having been its Commissioner for over five years.

After retiring from the Force Colonel Irvine, who was unmarried, became Warden
of Manitoba Penitentiary on October 13, 1892, and was awarded the Imperial
Service Order in 1903.

Lieutenant-Colonel Acheson Grosford Irvine (pic)

It is quite clear that Colonel Irvine was a very fine type of gentleman. He
earned the affection and respect of all who served under him by his
consideration, tact and fairness and discharged a most difficult task with
great credit to himself in the face of extremely unfair criticism.

Taken from Biographical information supplied by R.C.M.P.

The Town of Irvine
Geographical Background

Irvine is situated in a glacial valley. On the southeast of town there is what
is known as the badlands. Another landmark is the pointy hill. The buffalo jump
is southwest of Irvine along Ross Creek. The last of these majestic buffalo
herds in this area was killed on the flat known as Irvine in 1882 by Mr. R.
McCutcheon. Ross Creek runs through the south side of Irvine. Water comes from
the Cypress Hills and runs through Irvine, then west to Medicine Hat eventually
connecting to the South Saskatchewan River. The "Bull Trail" originated in
Montana, U.S.A. and comes across the Cypress Hills and down into Irvine. Parts
of this trail are still visible in the Cypress Hills. It was used by traders to
bring supplies into the district before the railway's appearance in 1883 and by
immigrants. They came by cart pulled by four oxen to what was then known as 20
Mile Post.

North of Irvine is flat prairie with the exception of a few hills and rocks.
There is evidence that the Indians once had their camps there.

Wagon ruts of the old Bull Trail. (pic)

Native People

The first inhabitants of this area were said to be the Indians. A hundred years
ago this area was an immense open prairie. It was the home and hunting grounds
of the Piegan, Blackfoot, Assinaboin, Blood and Sioux Indians.

The first white men to come to this area in the years before 1874 were
explorers, traders and smugglers. The traders and smugglers traded whiskey,
rifles, trinkets, etc. to the Indians for furs.

A skeleton, believed to be that of an Indian was found along the Ross Creek in
1914. It was interred on September 8 of that year in St. George's Parish
Cemetery.

Exploration and Early Settlement

In the years prior to 1874 there were few settlers.

The village of Irvine started to materialize about 1876 and became the northern
terminus of the "Bull Trail". The trail's southern terminus was Fort Benton,
Montana, U.S.A. It wandered across the prairie and still goes by its old name.
It crosses the Trans Canada highway at the southeast corner of town.

The settlers started to arrive in larger numbers; first the ranchers, followed
by farmers and businessmen.

Irvine began as a shipping point for lumber from the sawmills in the Cypress
Hills. The original lumber yard, first owned by L. Sands, started operations
before 1887. The R.N.W.M.P. established themselves in 1883 and the C.P.R. laid
out the village plan in 1903.

Most of homes built in Irvine were of wood with rock foundations. Many
homesteaders built their first homes with sod, they called them "sod shacks".
Most immigrants came to this area by train. They would get off at the C.P.R.
station and spend the remainder of the day or night at the "Immigration Hall".
They would stay there until friends or relatives arrived in the horse and buggy
to take them to their homes. Some of these immigrants took up homesteads in the
area and some stayed to try their hand in a business venture in the village.

Permanent Settlement

Irvine was first known as 20 Mile Post. It came by that name because it was a
trading post at the end of the Bull Trail. It was 20 miles from Medicine Hat
and about half way between there and Fort Walsh. The town of Irvine was named
after Colonel A. Irvine, a commissioner of the North West Mounted Police.
Colonel Irvine was with General Middleton during the Northwest Rebellion.
(Alberta Inventory of Geographical Names)

The population of Irvine in 1903 was 250. The Weiss General Store and the
Golden West Hotel were built that year. The C.P.R. station followed in 1905,
the same year a sanitarium building was constructed and then quickly converted
to the Alberta Hotel. A grain elevator had just been completed and a major
business in the town was a meat packing and canning business operated by Fred
Schubert.

The first school was built in 1904 with a student population of 80. Larger
premises would soon be needed as the town's population in 1907 was 500.

Government and Political Development

Irvine was in the district of Assinaboia, North West Territories, and in 1905
became part of the Province of Alberta.

1907 - Before Irvine became incorporated as a town its governmental and
political affairs were looked after by a village overseer. In 1907 Mr. S.
Kalmbach was the overseer and Mr. H.S. Newby was the secretary.

1909 - The meeting of the first council of 1909 was held in the Lower Grade
School House on January 19 at 7:45 p.m. Those present were Oliver Mayberry,
Chairman, Fred Weiss Sr. and Geo. Schaller. A motion was passed appointing H.
S. Newby secretary-treasurer for the ensuing year and by the passing of another
motion he be paid a salary of $118 per year, this to include any rent he may
have. A special ratepayers meeting was held in the Higher Grade School on
January 30, 1909 with 23 ratepayers present. At that meeting the motion was
made by Carl Beny and seconded by Geo. Schaller "That we apply for
Incorporation as a Town and that Council take the necessary steps to act in the
matter and appoint a Censor to take the census and they act on same at once."

On February 4th the papers were taken to Medicine Hat and handed to D.G. White
for immediate attention.

Irvine was to consist of all of Section 31, Township 11, Range 2, W4M and all
of the Northeast quarter of Section 36, Township 11, Range 3, W4M all in the
Province of Alberta.

In March of 1909 the people were still asking to have the village incorporated
to town status. The Irvine addition lots were selling for $60 and up and the
lots on the townsite were selling for $75 to $500. By April H.S. Newby,
secretary of the village, predicted that by May 6th Irvine will have reached
town status.

Irvine was finally incorporated as a town on June 11, 1909.

Council met in Immigration Building early 1900's; now Irvine Museum (pic)

Immigration Building, Irvine, typical office furniture and equipment early
1900's (pic)

A meeting was held on July 27, 1909 for the purpose of nominating seven
candidates for the office of Mayor and Councillors. Carl Belly was nominated
for mayor and he consented. The nominations for council were William Corbett,
not consented, John Hausauer, consented, John Pollock, not consented, Joseph
Beitz, consented, Oliver Mayberry, not consented, Fred Brosz, consented, Gott.
Weiss Sr., consented, T.B. Augles, not consented, John Koenig, consented, and
Jacob Jeschki, consented.

Medicine Hat News ad - 1909 - Irvine Addition (pic)

Proclamation of Incorporation 1909 (pic)

Certificate of Incorporation 1909 (pic)

The first meeting of the mayor and councillors was held at the residence of the
mayor on August 17, 1909. They read their first eight by-laws at that meeting.

By-Law #1

"That if any member of the council does not appear at any advertised meeting
shall be fined the sum of $1 unless prevented by unavoidable circumstances."
Amended February 27, 1911.

By-Law #2

"That Councillor John Hausauer supervise the building of the town well and hire
help at the cheapest possible rate of wages."

By-Law #3

"That a license be imposed at $25 on any track grain buyer buying on the
streets of Irvine."

By-Law #4

"That a pole tax be collected from parties staying in town and not being in
possession of taxable property after such party has stayed in town for more
than three days at a rate of $2."

By-Law #5

"That a license of $2 be collected from any traveling show or concert
exhibiting in the town of Irvine."

By-Law #6

"That a license of $20 be collected from any peddler that offers for sale goods
of any kind whether such goods are sold by any tax payer in town or not."

By-Law #7

"That a license of $50 be collected from anyone not a tax payer of the town of
Irvine who deals or attempts to deal in real estate in what ever shape or form
in the town of Irvine."

By-Law #8

"A license of $15 to be collected from everyone who so ever does any work in
the line of livery or dray work in the town of Irvine whether such party is tax
payer or not."

Some of the problems facing this new council were that of repairing the town
well and sidewalk improvements. Sam Kalmbach, as foreman was to receive $2.50
per day, a man and team $4.50 per day, and a man alone 200 per hour for a ten
hour day for the building of plank sidewalks and the grading of South Railway
Avenue, Ross Street, Walsh Street, and the street by Hotel Alberta. Tenders
were called for the building of the town well. The well was to be built on the
north side of Pacific Avenue opposite the lumber yard.

Council's next meeting was held August 27 at the secretary's office. They read
By-Law #9 and #10.

By-Law #9

"That the estimate of the School Board of $1800 be accepted." This was the
requested recompense for the coming year.

By-Law #10

"That 10 mills be rated on school taxes and 6 mills on town taxes."

To begin with council meetings were held weekly. A building committee was
appointed for the supervision of the new school house. By-Law #11 was read.

By-Law #11

"That the mayor and secretary-treasurer be empowered to borrow from the Union
Bank of Canada the sum of $100 and that the mayor and secretary-treasurer sign
a note from the Union Bank of Canada for the amount of the loan together with
the amount of present overdraft on behalf of the town for the term of three
months with interest at a rate of eight percent per annum."

All the above mentioned by-laws were passed in September.

A special meeting was held on August 31, 1909 for the purpose of making
arrangements regarding a natural gas well.

The first court of Revision was held at the town office at 10:00 am on
September 25, 1909. They had nine appeal cases. Of these nine cases, six were
reduced, two were let stand, and the other one was sustained.

1910 - Geo. Schaller was appointed tax assessor for the year 1910. He received
a salary of $25 and an extra $10 for clerical work. Meetings were now held on a
monthly basis. The health committee and the improvement committee were
appointed by the council.

The A.B.C. of Irvine, Medicine Hat News - 1907 (pic)

On May 12, 1910 a motion in council "That the debenture debt of the Village of
Irvine of $1000 be accepted and the mayor and secretary-treasurer be empowered
to issued cheques in payment of same as the payments thereon became due."

A motion was passed by council on July 20, 1910 for the town to issue $5000 of
debentures for the term of 20 years at 6% interest for the purpose of
purchasing a Watrous fire engine and installing all the necessary appliances
belonging to it; fire engine and tank or cistern used in the Fire Hall. The
election on the by-law regarding the issue of $5000 debenture was accepted. The
fire engine and hose was purchased for $3165.

1911 - On January 27, 1911 the Irvine Board of Trade considered a proposition
by Sidney W. Arbuckle regarding the sinking of a gas well in the Irvine town
limits. Council accepted with amendments thereto, subject to the votes of the
ratepayers.

On February 3, Mr. T.D. Sissons, Mr. James Porter and Mr. R.D. Porter
personally presented a drafted agreement between them and the Town for the
purpose of sinking a gas well in this town

At the March 1 meeting council instructed the secretary-treasurer to inform
Sidney W. Arbuckle that his by-law has finally passed and ask him to get busy
as soon as possible.

An Early Closing By-Law was presented by the Irvine Board of Trade regarding
the closings of stores at 7:00 pm, presented in April and passed on June 7,
1911.

At a special meeting on June 24, 1911 a motion was passed in council "That
schools and churches and all public meetings be all closed and that parents be
instructed to keep their children under 15 years of age in their yards for one
week and that this order be enforced for a longer period if necessary. That a
proclamation be made for that effect."

Several quarantines were placed upon the residents of Irvine in those early
years. There were contagious and infectious diseases such as smallpox,
diphtheria, scarlet fever and measles. The town would obtain anti-toxins which
could be given to the people.

A fire station 16' x 24' x 8' was completed in December 1911. W. Bagshaw was
employed as "caretaker of the Engine House" at a salary of $15 per month.

1912 - The town council had been receiving complaints from time to time
concerning stock and dogs running at large and so becoming a public nuisance.
On July 20, 1912 Council drew up a bylaw creating a pound to house these stray
animals. One exception was made. The animals would not be impounded one hour
between 7:00 am and 8:00 am and one hour during the evening, the time the herd
is being delivered to its respective owners, places, yards, or stables. The
charges on these impounded animals were for cows, heifers and steers, 50 cents
for impounding and 25 cents for feed per head per day; bulls and horses were $1
for impounding and 50 cents per head per day for feed; and dogs were 50 cents
for impounding and 25 cents per head per day for feed. An amendment to this
by-law was made at the next meeting stating that the by-law referring to dogs
did not apply to farmers who may have left dogs in town for a day or two.

In October of 1912 a reservoir was completed and in November it was council's
decision to leave it up to the Fire Brigade to see to it that it was filled at
once.

A gratuitous cheque for $25 was paid to Corp. Wiedeman. He was asked by council
to go around the town and keep order in December of 1912. Corp. Wiedeman
returned the cheque to the town. In April of 1913 Frank Corby was appointed
town policeman for a salary of $80 per month.

1913 - In May of 1913 the town purchased the SW 5-12-2-W4 from the C.P.R. for a
nuisance grounds at $10 an acre.

At the September 29, 1913 council meeting a committee was appointed to took
into the matter of street lighting. At this time Sidney Arbuckle was to be
asked what arrangements were being made by him as to the completion of the gas
well.

The town purchased the "Old School House" to use as a town hall. In October
1913 laborers were employed to remove partitions, patch, kalsomine walls and
paint the woodwork. The mayor and secretary-treasurer were instructed to
purchase the necessary furniture. In November the secretary-treasurer was to
procure a daily newspaper and have a telephone installed in the town hall.

In December of 1913 a night watchman and policeman, Joe Angin, was hired at a
salary of $40 per month. The matter of his duties was to be left up to the Fire
Committee.

1914 - A report from the gas well committee was presented to council on January
27, 1914. They reported "that operations were started on the gas well on May
26th, 1911, continued to work until November 16th, 1911 - nothing done from that
date until on or about April 23rd, 1912 - from there until March 28th, 1913
worked about half the time - then worked from May 20th until July 30th, 1913 -
nothing done since that date."

In February of 1914 a motion was made in council that a cell be built in the
town hall at once and in March a motion was made to dispense with the night
watchman's services and that the street lights be discontinued after April 2.

A market by-law was passed in May of 1914. A sum of $20 was to be expended for
advertising the market sales.

1915 - In January of 1915 the town council made a motion to the effect that no
political meetings were allowed in the Town Hall. However at the January 26
meeting a motion was made that all political meetings would be charged $5 per
meeting. The Town Hall was rented for other meetings such as agricultural and
church meetings. School meetings were free.

In June of 1915 a committee was appointed to collect for the Polish people and
in August the town gave $10 to the overseas Aircraft Fund. The town also looked
after the returned wounded soldiers.

The Gas Franchise business was closed in October of 1915.

1916 - A special meeting was called on June 13, 1916 for the purpose of
proclaiming June 30 a holiday. The town council donated $50 to the sports
committee for their use.

1917 - The town of Irvine took out $2000 in Victory Bonds in November 1917.

1918 - In February of 1918 the town was looking into the matter of electric
lights for the lighting of Irvine.

The above touches lightly on some of the decisions the town council made in
order to govern this rapidly growing town. Many challenges were met and we
today have to commend their leadership and skill in carrying out this great
task.
