Conclusion - The town today and its future

The population of Irvine today is 301 compared to that of the very early years
when, it has been said, at one time the population was 1000.

As the small farms have vanished and are now combined into larger agricultural
operations and with the coming of paved highways and modern transportation, the
people were drawn to the larger centres. Industry, most businesses, and health
services have gone to the city.

Irvine is the smallest town in Alberta. The brave pioneers of the early 1900's
brought self government to our town and managed to build a good foundation for
future generations.

George Schlaht, John Diefenbaker and Glen Gebhard (Irvine principal) - 1963
(pic)

Flag raising ceremony - 75th Anniv. - 1984 (pic)

Cutting Ribbon opening Irvine Park: Art Zeller, Leslie Lutz, George Schlaht
(pic)

The town prospered for a time until the 1930's. The population remained low and
rather constant until late 1970 when it almost doubled and several new homes
were built. These were good times in Alberta and the town grew.

In 1988 the town experienced a water shortage crises, but with government aid
drilled two new water wells and upgraded the water treatment system.

Irvine boasts a rural lifestyle which may be envied by larger urban centres.
This seems to be the drawing card for families. Wage earners mostly commute to
Medicine Hat for employment. The children attend grades one to twelve in Irvine.

The future of the Town will depend on the economy of the land. Over the years
Irvine has prospered for a time and then leveled off. This seems to be a
pattern for the future.

IRVINE

An incorporated town on the main line of the C.P.R., 22 miles east of Medicine
Hat. Located on Sec 31, Tp 11, Rg 2, west of the 4th Mer. in the electoral
division of Medicine Hat. Irvine Addition is located on Sec 36, Tp 11, Rg 3,
west of the 4th Mer. This is a large stock shipping point and natural gas is
found in the neighborhood. The district consists of splendid farming land.
Mails daily.

Early Irvine Memories
by Evelyn Hausauer as told by Mrs. Ed Glock

The only building in Irvine in 1902 was the C.P. Rail station. Irvine (town)
was started in 1903. The late Emmanuel Strum was working for the town at that
time.

The first white child born in Irvine was Irvina Pahl, who was born in Ed
Glock's barn on Walsh St.

The Golden West Hotel was built by Dave and Jake Waldner prior to 1906. It was
owned by Mr. John Pollock (whom Eva (Hausauer) Glock worked for) and perhaps
Fred McLaughlin and George Haycock. (Mr. Haycock drowned while swimming in Ross
Creek or the big town dam.)

This hotel burnt in 1912, accidentally by Mr. Pollock himself, when lighting
the old fashioned lamps. This hotel was on the lot where George's Service now
stands on Railway Avenue. The Golden West Hotel #2 was owned by Mr. John
Pollock, perhaps financed by Harry Yuill Sr.

A livery stable owned by Adolf Brost was on the lot before this hotel was built.

The hotel was almost the full length of the lot. The back of the building was a
pool room and barber shop. Ed Glock worked for Mr. Charlie Clarkson, who had
rented the pool room from Mr. Pollock. That building burnt partly about 1918,
when the Chinese cook was arguing with a customer while making donuts, and the
lard he was using became too hot and caught fire.

The hotel was rebuilt and is now the present Great West Hotel.

The Cypress Hotel was started to be built prior to 1906 and was completed in
1906. Dr. Phillips had this built as a hospital. The upstairs was used as a
hospital and the main floor as a hotel, which included a bar, and living
quarters for the proprietors. It was used as a hospital during the 1918 'flu
epidemic. Mr. and Mrs. Phil McLeay helped during the epidemic.

Mr. Lou Rhodes was the cook in the hotel. Mr. Caulkins was in the hotel part of
the business. Later Dave and Gutfried Roloff (Dave Roloff was W. Roloff Beny's
Grandfather) owned the hotel.

This place was later (about 1927-1940) operated as a restaurant by Messers. Lou
Sing and Mah Gong. The bar part of the building was made into a post office and
operated by Fred Crewe. Earlier Lou Sing had a little place on the west side of
Sergius Nesdoly's Insurance building (which is a vacant lot now). He later
moved to The Great West Hotel and then to The Cypress Hotel.

The first store was built about 1903 and operated by the Weiss family,
Christian Sr., Fred Sr., and his son Christian and Mr. Andrew Brandt.

Mr. John Koenig built a store (about 1906) where the Alberta Wheat Pool house
stands, across from the Town Garage.

The first butcher shop was built by Fred Brost about 1904. It was a long narrow
building on the corner of Railway Avenue and Walsh Street and wasn't a butcher
shop very long.  It was moved away and Sam Kalmbach (he also had a laundry for
sometime) built the Kalmbach block in 1910 (which still stands). The Union Bank
was the part which in later years was the Post Office.

Mr. John Hausauer Sr. built a meat market in 1907 on Railway Avenue. This
building had the meat market in the front of the building and a pool room in
the back, with a dance hall the full size of the building upstairs. Mr. John
Hausauer Sr. was also an auctioneer.

When the Weiss Store burnt down about 1914, the meat market also burnt. Mr.
Hausauer Sr. rebuilt it to the size of the building where the Post Office is
presently located.

Mr. John Hausauer Sr. and Mr. Beitz also built a small elevator about 1907 or
1908 where the Alberta Wheat Pool #2 stands. They had it about two years then
sold it. Mr. Benwell built the first garage on Pacific Avenue about 1913 on a
lot between the Fred Stuber house and where the curling rink was, now a
playground.

This garage was used for an ammunition dump during the 1914-1918 war. Later it
was sold to Jack DeBolt (he later resided in Claresholm), and Mr. DeBolt opened
the first garage there. Mr. Jim Crookes Sr. bought this garage for his son
Harry, who operated the garage and named it Irvine Garage, later he moved over
on Railway Avenue.

Campbell and Griffin operated a creamery, built before 1917 where Geigle's Pool
Room was on Railway Avenue. Cream buyer was Mr. Merkley. George Dinkel operated
the Pioneer lumber yard on Pacific Avenue on the lot just west of Gordon
Woodward's residence, another lumber yard was just west of this location and a
little north of where the playground is now.

A lumber yard and a tinsmith shop was back of Geigle's Pool Room on Ross
Street. In later years Carl Beny built a large machine shed on part of that
property and the rest was used for a market square, having been moved up from
the market square which we know as the W.I. playground next to where the
Prairie Museum is located.

Memories of Irvine - 1929 to 1935
by Florence Hofer

Back in 1929, when we moved to Irvine, the school consisted of two large rooms
with swinging doors between the two classrooms, Miss Courtice teaching the
grades from one to five, the second room teacher teaching from grade six to
grade nine. Miss Lillian Hunt taught me in grade three, then Miss Courtice
returned and she was my teacher for grade four and grade five.

In grade six Mr. Joe Noviski was my teacher and he was quite strict. If he
caught you misbehaving, or not paying attention during class, he would punish
you by giving you a multiplication question that consisted of about 25 numbers
on top, multiplied by about 18 numbers below. The next person caught
misbehaving had to divide it to see if the first person had the correct answer.
It was my misfortune to receive one of these multiplication questions once. My
lips are sealed as to who got the division end of it, nor did I find out if my
answer was correct. No calculators in those days! Other times you had to write
out whatever you were caught doing a hundred times or more. Many of us got
quite good at handling a number of pencils at one time, so it wouldn't take so
long to write out the lines. We really weren't that disobedient in school, just
normal, healthy, energetic pupils.

Mr. Ham Byers was my grade seven and grade eight teacher. As I recollect he was
more easy going and I think there were times the students taxed his nerves.

I remember the school bell, atop the school, ringing twice before school
started: the first time, fifteen minutes before school started, to remind you
to be on your way, then the second time when school started. It was also rung
at noon and when school was let out at 4 pm. Many folks in town went by the
school bell, knowing what time of day it was. Usually the teacher, or one of
the pupils in the second classroom who was picked for a week, rang the bell.

Irvine, back in those years, was a small village as I recollect; perhaps two
hundred and fifty people, more or less, resided there. The town contained five
elevators; agents were Mr. Lionel Chell, Mr. Schmidt and Mr. William Bauer. I
can't recall the two others. Grocery stores were run by Mr. Eddie Hausauer, Mr.
Fred and Mr. Jake Schneider (brothers) and Mr. A. Wiedemann. When we first
arrived in Irvine, Mr. and Mrs. Stephen Wiedeman had a dry goods store. Mr.
Wiedeman had an office at the back. Later they moved into a different building
and added groceries. The local hotel was run by Mr. and Mrs. George Burchak.
There were three garages, operated by L. Bischke, Crewe brothers, Albert and
Buster, and Mr. Harry Crookes. A restaurant and confectionery was run by Mr.
Lou Singh. Mr. Fred Crewe was the postmaster. Mr. John Hausauer had the meat
market. Later Eddie Hausauer moved from the smaller store into this building
and combined both businesses. Mr. John Geiger ran the lumber yard and a Mr.
John Fyke was the local barber. The Glock brothers, Chuck and Andrew, did the
blacksmithing. Mr. Bob Davidson was the station agent and Mr. Naylor, the
R.C.M.P. constable. Mail in those days was moved by C.P.R. train and it cost 30
to mail a letter, which was delivered promptly. The passenger train stopped
each day, traveling east and west. Mr. Christ Maser was the dray man who
delivered any business freight that was dropped off these trains or any freight
train., His team of horses and wagon were recognizable by everyone.

We lived in a two story, C.P.R. company house on the north side of the tracks
on the east end of town. The house is no longer there. It was torn down due to
modernization of C.P.R. policy, I believe. Our home was not insulated as well
as many others in this period of time, nor was it heated by a furnace. We had
no electricity, running water or indoor bathroom. No telephone, radio or T.V.
back then either. Business places had telephones, but not many homes had them
then. A few families had a radio but we did not and those who did, and were
interested in sports, listened to Foster Hewitt on Saturday nights announcing
the hockey games. His familiar phrase, "He shoots, he scores," is well known
today. Amos and Andy was also a popular program on radio in the early thirties.
Not every family owned a car then, either. We were one of the fortunate few who
did. We walked, ran, jogged and skipped and no one referred to it as
participation in those days.

History of Irvine by Freda Glock - 1935 (17 pic)

Every morning my mother trimmed the oil lamp wicks and washed and polished the
lamp chimneys. Laundry then was no easy task for my mother. I recall my mother
using a large galvanized laundry tub and board. The board had a glass rippled
centre encased in a wooden, two legged frame with a lip at the top to hold the
bar of soap. This wash board, as it was known, was laid into the tub, a bit
slanted. My mother was bent over for many hours rubbing the clothes on this
board to get them clean. White clothes were boiled after this procedure, then
hung on a clothes line outside to flutter in the breeze and dry. Ironing was
done with flat irons, irons put on the top of a heating wood and coal stove, to
get them to the right temperature. Then a handle was connected to the flat iron
and clothes that had been previously dampened, were ironed. The irons had to be
the right temperature, if too hot, clothes were burnt, if not hot enough,
wrinkles stayed in. Ironing, though time consuming, was much nicer in the
winter time, 'cause you were kept warm, but on a very hot day with your stove
burning, handling hot irons became almost unbearable. In 1932, my father bought
a washing machine, a big advantage. This time you didn't bend over the tub, you
stood up straight and swung the tub from side to side by a handle in the middle
of the machine. No wonder wash days back then were known as Blue Mondays. Quite
different from todays method! Water was carried into the home by pail from a
cistern, by the railroad track, which was filled every week when a special
freight train with a water tank left water for all employees in that division.
Our home was heated by a wood and coal stove in the kitchen and heater in the
front room. On very cold days you didn't move too far away from the heat and
even then, sometimes, you found your back cold while your front was warm, just
standing beside the stove. Homes then had pantries where the dishes and food
were kept, not elaborate kitchen cupboards like one sees today. No fridge to
keep food from spoiling, but an odd family had a small ice box. Vegetables and
meat were canned and fruit as preserved in those days.

Two important days of the year, then, were the school picnic at the end of the
school term where, after all the races were completed, we were treated to lunch
and ice cream; and the annual Christmas concert, which seemed to always hit the
coldest night of the year, when we budding actors and actresses did our part to
impress the community with our talents. Be it good or bad, we always managed to
entertain the local people. Back then, this was the big social event of the
year for, after the concert, a dance was held. Sometimes our parents stayed for
a while so we could exercise our limbs across the dance floor for an hour or so
to the music of Johnny Glock at the piano, Frank McLeay on sax, Chuck Glock on
the violin, and Eddie Hausauer on drums. Then we went home happy, to warm up a
cold bed and to dream of next year's concert.

Spring time found the boys looking for the smallest patch of dry ground where
they could play marbles and they had a language all of their own. They spoke of
dibs, alleys, steelies, glassies and fudging, while mothers were kept busy
sewing patches on the knees of their sons' trousers.

Girls would play hop scotch and several would skip when two girls would hold
the ends of a long rope and turn it round and round to "one, two, button your
shoe; three, four, close the door."

Not every family could afford a bicycle during the thirties, the Babuk family
being one of them. Some children used their own imagination and enthusiasm to
construct their own methods of transportation. My brother, William, built a car
one summer from wood that came from apple and orange boxes. Today boxes are
made of cardboard. His car was big enough for him to sit in, and his motor was
anybody who had a strong back and good running legs to push him and his car. He
always carried a hammer, as it was a necessary tool to keep the wheels on
properly. Incidentally, his love of cars still haunts him today.

I remember boys running behind a moving tire that they kept in motion by
pushing it with a light slap of the hand periodically. Those who where brave
sat inside the tire while someone else moved it down the road.

Girls played house with their one and only doll and imagined they were fancy
ladies living in magnificent homes and traveling to exotic places. Red jelly
beans were specified when buying candy and hoarded to be used later as
lipstick. The candy itself became our gourmet meal afterwards.

Money was not plentiful then, in fact many people had barely enough to get by
on. I recall going to school and looking at the elevator that Mr. Chell worked
at and seeing 19 cents posted for a bushel of wheat. If you were lucky to be
given a five cent coin, you could buy yourself an ice cream cone, or a
chocolate bar, or a package of gum.

I remember my mother paying 15 cents for a pound of butter and 3 cents for a
dozen eggs. A dollar bought twelve quarts of milk. A lot of men were unemployed
and traveled on the freight trains looking for work. Many times some of these
men came knocking on our door asking for something to eat, when their train
stopped for one reason or another. Mother always made them a sandwich from
something she had in the house. I also recall in the summer of 1935, I believe,
a slow moving freight train loaded with unemployed men passing through Irvine
around eight o'clock on a bright sunny morning. They were on their way to
Ottawa to voice their complaints, and were stopped in Regina, where they had a
clash with police and a man was killed. Men who did have a job were very
fortunate to be making 25 to 30 cents an hour. A pair of shoes were taken care
of and polished frequently to keep them presentable. Clothes were handed down
and made over for younger family members. Yet everyone seemed happy.

Adults visited one another and attended local whist drives for amusement. On
long summer evenings, one could hear the young children playing run-sheep-run,
or anti-i-over. In the summer time, on a Sunday afternoon, one could attend a
local ball game, held west of town, where a silver collection was sometimes
taken. Ball games, even today, remind me of Mr. Joe Noviski, as he had the
habit of sucking a lemon before the game started. Haven't figured-out yet, if
this was done for the spectators benefit or if it improved his game of ball. He
also liked to steal bases and many a time we sat anxiously wondering if he'd
make it safely or not. While he ran back and forth between bases, the basemen
drew in closer and closer throwing the ball back and forth. Sometimes he was
safe; then we cheered. Other times he was put out and we'd boo the umpire. In
the winter we skated, or went sleigh riding, or attended the odd hockey game
for entertainment.

In 1934 a group of young girls got together and formed the junior W.I. Many of
our mothers belonged to the local W.I. We called ourselves the "Peppy Pals". We
held our meetings once a month and Mrs. Eva Chell was our supervisor. We raised
money during the year by having a tea and whist drive, and other small
projects. During the summer holidays we rented a cottage for two weeks at
Elkwater Lake and every one enjoyed the rewards of a year's work.

While living in Irvine, I remember one bad fire which happened during the
night. The first grain elevator on the west end of town burnt down. I think it
was around 1934. I also remember the Chautauqua coming to Irvine about 1931 or
1932.

People often refer to the thirties as the hard times, the dirty thirties, the
dust bowl, etc. My recollections of the days we lived in Irvine when we were
children were happy ones. I realize though, parents then must have had many
difficulties raising a family.

Post Offices
Irvine

Irvine was named after Col. A. Irvine, Commissioner of the Royal North West
Mounted Police.

The post office came into service January 1, 1900. In 1903 efforts were made to
get a post office moved into the village. In March of 1904 the first post
office was located in the C.P.R. section house. W. J. Harris was our first
postmaster. He resigned in 1907. The post office was then located in a general
store run by Henry Vockeroth. The stage left Irvine every Saturday and called
at Newburg, Josephsburg and Elkwater, at which point Strathmartin mail was
fetched.

The Irvine post office had something new added to its service by handling
parcel post. In 1914 not only could the people mail letters but parcels also.
H. Price was the postmaster at that time.

Frederich Meier hauled mail from Irvine to Thelma and points in between from
1912 to 1915.

F.J. Crewe and A.B. Crewe served as postmasters approximately 1918 to 1925.
Elizabeth and Florence Crewe also worked in the post office, which was located
in the Roloff Hotel. Fred Crewe hauled mail from Irvine to Hilda, Schuler,
Robinson, Elkwater, Fox and Thelma post offices in those early days, about 1927.

G. Sullivan was appointed the next postmaster. The post office was connected to
the former Wiedemann's store where the town hall is presently situated.

The next postmaster was Fred Schneider. His daughters, Rosie, Esther and Irene
also helped. In 1927 Fred had the mail route to Hilda and Schuler.

George and Mary Ambrose took over the post office, Mary later moving to the Ed
Glock store building which she owned. Mary remained postmaster until she
retired in 1975. Evelyn Woodward was then appointed postmaster and is presently
employed by Canada Post.

There have been many changes made in the transportation of mail: from horse
drawn carts, to trains, to trucks and airplanes. Many more services have been
added. Nowadays people can mail almost anything to all parts of the world in a
variety of ways. Another change made has been from hand sorting the mail to
automated machines.

An historic date for Canada's Postal Service was October 16, 1981 -
Proclamation Day, when Canada Post employees across Canada became a Crown
Corporation.

Today Canada Post Corporation delivers 34 million pieces of mail per day and
handles 8.3 billion pieces per year. The network consists of 10.6 million
points of call.

Down through the years the local post office has been one of the central points
of the town and surrounding areas. With today's trend towards automation and
the dwindling rural population we hope that it will remain so for a number of
years to come.

Josephsburg

Josephsburg was named after the town in Austria from which the first settlers
came. They were dried out in their first attempt so they moved, taking the name
with them. On January 16, 1890 the German Colony of Josephsburg petitioned the
Post Office department to have a post office established. They were driving 25
miles to get their mail at Dunmore, Alberta. The post office came into service
on June 1, 1890. It was located on 7-10-2-W4. Joseph Edinger was the first
postmaster. He resigned July 7, 1890. John Henry Kern was the next postmaster,
December 1, 1890 to April 4, 1893, when he too resigned. C.H. Fox became
postmaster on July 1, 1893 until his death in 1894. Walter Blackburn followed,
June 1, 1894, until his resignation on January 1, 1895. The next postmaster was
Joseph Dunn, May 1, 1895 until his death on March 20, 1899. James Robinson was
appointed postmaster on March 1, 1901. He resigned on March 25, 1911. August
Boschee became postmaster on July 29, 1911 until his resignation on May 10,
1916. John Lust was the last postmaster. He was appointed on June 26, 1916 and
resigned July 4, 1917. Josephsburg post office was closed on November 14, 1917.

Newburg

The Newburg post office came into service on September 1, 1904. It was located
on 12-10-3-W4.

W.E. Martin was appointed postmaster September 1, 1904. He resigned on June 17,
1905. Miss Lydia Stelter followed, October 1, 1905 until her resignation on
January 1, 1906. W. E. Martin became postmaster April 1, 1906 until September
1909. Mrs. Amelia Stelter was the next postmaster, January 23, 1909 to January
5, 1918 when she resigned. F.W. Weiss was the last postmaster, January 17, 1918
to March 16, 1918. The Newburg post was then closed.

Robinson

Robinson post office was named after James Robinson. It came into service on
May 1, 1923 and was located in a dwelling on 22-9-3-W4 and NE 34-9-3-W4. The
postmasters were A. C. Aman, appointed May 1, 1923 to January 2, 1925; Fred
Boschee, May 20, 1925 to August 28, 1931; Mrs, Martha Seitz, April 1, 1932 to
March 24, 1944; and Jacob Ziegenhagel, September 30, 1944 to August 27, 1954.
All the above postmasters resigned their positions. On July 28, 1954 Arthur
Ziegenhagel was appointed acting postmaster. He held that position until he was
appointed postmaster on December 6, 1954. The post office was permanently
closed on January 6, 1964.

The Tothill post office was named after Mrs. Tothill who operated the post
office for many years.

Many Island post office was established in 1910.

Police Royal North West Mounted Police

In 1896 S. Werner was the policeman for the Josephsburg district. In 1897 the
police detachment was manned by Constable Helm. W.E. Martin of Josephsburg was
appointed J.P. of the district.

Irvine Police

In 1904 Fred McLaughlin was Irvine's first Town Policeman. Others included
Frank Corby in April 1913, and Ted Roll in the forties.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police

The Irvine area in the very early days was policed by members at Medicine Hat.
The Irvine Detachment was opened some time in 1907 as part of the "K" Division
at Lethbridge. One Corporal was stationed at Irvine in 1907 and by 1909, the
number had risen to three with a Corporal, Constable and Special Constable
being stationed there. Stephen Wiedeman was RCMP corporal in Irvine in December
1912. The detachment remained open until late 1917 or early 1918 when many
detachments were closed after the Alberta Provincial Police took over the
responsibility for policing Alberta. The Irvine Detachment was opened again on
May 28, 1932 when the Force absorbed the Alberta Provincial Police and remained
open until April 28, 1934. Constable W.G. Naylor, Regimental Number 5097, was
in charge of the detachment between 1932 and 1934. In 1935, Constable Naylor
was transferred to Vulcan Detachment.

Canadian Pacific Railway

Irvine was known as Siding #13, which was 638.1 miles west of Winnipeg.

The track went through Irvine on May 21, 1883. They averaged three miles of
track per day. This was under the leadership of Mr. James Fisher, chief
construction engineer.

The first passenger train through Irvine came from Winnipeg to Medicine Hat on
June 11, 1883. From Medicine Hat it returned to Winnipeg.

On December 10, 1885 the C.P.R. struck a flowing water well. The section
foreman for the West was McNulty, and for the East was Carlson.

There were anywhere from five to seven wagons, loaded with lumber from the
Cypress Hills, brought in every day, as this was the shipping point for all
lumber from Louis Sands Mills.

Narrow gauge railway tracks are three feet apart and regular tracks are four
feet eight inches. A C.P.R. depot was constructed near the present site of
Irvine in 1882. The new, larger one was built in 1905 and demolished recently.

In August 1903, the C.P.R. built a dam across Ross Creek just south of the
townsite, creating a large body of water for use in train engines.

The interests of the C.P.R. were looked after by J. Christie, who came from
Toronto with high recommendation.

In 1904 the C.P.R. installed two new tool houses. The station and freight yards
were finally to be built. In June 1904 a railway crossing was requested for
Irvine to get from one side of town to the other.

On November 7, 1905 the C.P.R. received a license to direct water from Ross
Creek on NE 31-11-2-W4 for domestic purposes.

In 1907 there were three passenger trains operating with about 96 daily
passengers and two second class freight trains. It took four hours to come from
Maple Creek to Medicine Hat.

The following men were employed by the C.P.R., working in the Irvine area: In
1911 W.H.A. Auger was agent; F.J. Barber, night operator; and W.J. Corbett,
section foreman. H.S. Newby was C.P.R. land agent and Fulton Bros. (Wm. and
Thos.) were railway contractors.

In February 1914, Mr. William, was pumpman; Mr. Faureau, night operator; Mr.
M.A. Dickson, C.P.R. operator; and W.J. Corbett, section foreman. In September
1914 Win. McIntosh, C.P.R. agent at Irvine, left for Halifax to be wireless
operator on H.M.S. NIOBE.

In 1916 M.A. Yule was assistant C.P.R. agent and Mrs. S.F. Koen was night agent.

Bob Davidson was station agent 1923-1951. Bert Simmons took over as station
agent until the station was closed down.

Nick Babuk moved to Irvine in 1929 and worked as section foreman. Later the
foreman was Mr. Eichorn.

Frederich Linderman supervised bridge building prior to 1929, and was also
foreman of fireguard -plowing along the C.P.R.

Utilities

Gas

It was thought that there could be an abundance of gas in the town of Irvine so
on October 18, 1906, Superintendent Niblock was asked on behalf of the C.P.R.
to sink a gas well. In 1911 Sidney W. Arbuckle was given permission to drill a
well in the town. Town records state five Pitner gas lights were installed
before December 1913. One is visible on the 1913 picture of main street and a
family history places another on the corner of Pacific Avenue and Durham
Street. A council motion was made that the street lights be discontinued after
April 2, 1914.

Water

On December 19, 1907 Medicine Hat News article states the C.P.R. dam was built
in 1906. Water was supplied from Elkwater Lake which was a good source. A
Medicine Hat News article on November 26, 1908 states that the Alberta
Government at the suggestion of Hon. W.T. Finlay (local member) had placed a
well drilling outfit at Irvine for use among the settlers in the district. The
water supply came mostly from wells until 1975 when, according to Tom Wood,
water and sewer were made available through the town.

1939 Pontiac, Christina and Fred Weiss (pic)

Adam Roll in School Van (pic)

Telephone

An application for rural telephones was made in 1909 and according to the
Medicine Hat News the line was completed to Pashley by June 21, 1911. Mr. C.R.
Mitchell assured that Irvine would have long distance phone connections with
Medicine Hat and this was completed by July 27 that same year. One of the first
operators was Miss Price in 1918. Eva (McLaughlin) Chell worked as a telephone
operator until about 1930 in the telephone office which was run by the
McLaughlin family until it was transferred to Medicine Hat in 1968 for direct
dialing.

(Information from Medicine Hat News, Town Records, and family histories)

Alberta Government Telephones building (pic)

Garden in back of A.G.T. office (pic)

View of garden in back of A.GT office (pic)

Pashley Mutual Telephone

In March 1959 a meeting was called by acting chairman William Will to organize
a telephone mutual. Len Anderson was recording secretary. To get the ball
rolling, each member put in $100. The original members were Ed Miller, Sam
Roth, Anders Anderson, Anderson Dairy, William Will, John Zmurchyk, Jack
Jenkins, Ruben Franz, Bill Driscol, Harold Oberhammer.

The group got together and went to the Cypress Hills and got poles. The bark
was cleaned off these and used as posts. We could phone our local area at
Christmas time, then later we were hooked up to Medicine Hat. What a treat, but
you also had to wait your turn, with 15 subscribers on the line.

In 1972 we were hooked up to A.G.T. and got split lines with only three or four
on each line. After this the lines and material were taken down and disposed of.

Irvine Fire Department and Fires

The first record of organizing a fire brigade in Irvine was noted on June 4,
1908 at which time a chemical engine was purchased. On July 20, 1910 a motion
was passed by town council to buy a newer type engine from Waterous Engineering
Company of Winnipeg, and to build a fire hall and a cistern to store water for
fire fighting purposes. This holding reservoir was to be located on the
northeast corner of Ross St. and was to have a capacity of 20,000 gallons and
all this at a total cost of $3,160. The engine and all necessary appliances
arrived in December of 1910 and the building was completed by December of 1911.
A request was made that all stores and hotels each furnish one man to serve on
the brigade. In 1912 a fire bell was purchased. In September of 1912 a
suggestion was made that a new fire hall should be built and that money, to the
sum of $4,000 should be raised. No record was available whether this proposal
developed. The fire chief also requested that all lanterns be in good working
order and those not satisfactory should be replaced. Fire buckets were
purchased and painted red with I.F.D. painted on same.

Irvine's First Volunteer Fire Brigade, 1st left Emanuel, 2nd right John Zaiser
(pic)

Between the years 1913 and 1922 gymnasium equipment was purchased for use by
the Irvine fire brigade at a cost of $20. Fire hoses had to be inspected,
tested and repaired regularly. Slickers and fire masks were purchased and
citizens were requested to attend fire protection meetings. Fire equipment was
required to be kept in good condition, the fire hall was heated during the
winter months and the reservoir was to be full at all times. A windmill was
placed over the well and was used to pump water into the reservoir. The fire
engine had to be started once a week for the six colder months and once a month
during the summer.

Improvements and more up to date equipment were installed from year to year. A
500 gallon cistern was dug and fire hazards spots were checked. The chief
concern was the empty lots with high weeds. A portable pump and engine, on two
wheels, were purchased and still later a secondhand fire truck was acquired
from Lethbridge which is still used as a standby unit. The old horse drawn fire
engine (antique) was sold to Emerson Porter in 1956. In 1972 a well pump with a
larger hose and a motor was built by Jacob Bechtold and moved to the fire hall.
Several fire extinguishers were purchased and placed in the fire hall,
community hall and municipal garage. In 1975 boundaries were outlined where the
Irvine fire department would serve. By 1976 and from there on the fire chief
was required to attend provincial fire fighting courses. C.B. radios and a
secondhand fire truck were purchased. During 1979 fire phones were placed in
the homes of the fire men and the fire hall. The town, by this time, had two
fire trucks and 16 members, six of whom were women qualified to assist in
operating fire equipment. A recommendation was made that registration areas be
set up in case of a major disaster so whereabouts of individuals would be known
and an evacuation route could be followed. By 1984 a water storage tank was in
place with a capacity of 500,000 gallons. Smoke detectors were installed and
two way radios were installed in the fire trucks in 1987. In 1988 the town of
Irvine and its fire department experienced many problems when their well became
dry and water was not available should fires occur. Spray units were installed
in front of water trucks and Medicine Hat and Walsh Fire Departments provided
back up contingency plans if water was required. At the present time fire
drills are held once a month, the M.D. supplies the town with a fire truck, and
the town operates the fire equipment for the town and surrounding area.

Irvine Fire Department - 1907. Some of the people: Zaiser, Hausauer, Ihringer
and Roloff (pic)

Between the years 1912 up to the present time personnel in the fire department
were the following: Mr. W. Bagshaw was fire chief in 1912. In 1913 Henry
Blakeley applied for the position of fire chief at $10 a month. When he
resigned Otto Kuchn was promoted to this position, Emil Bietz was captain of
the fire department and John Zaiser was chief engineer the same year. In
January 1914 J. Barrigare became fire chief and new recruits for the fire
brigade were Fred McLaughlin, Frank Etter, C.D. Pols, Pete McLeish, J. and Gus
Heine, Alan Pollock, A. Teschner, J. Zaiser and F. Trautman. The bucket brigade
was Mayor Crawford, Frank Corby, H.S. Newby, Nick Ibley, Reverend Jerrold, Carl
Beny, Fred Crewe and Curley Rott. Between 1915 and 1920 Gottfried Ziffle, Ed
Aman and Jake Begon were fire engineers and the salary was indicated as $5 a
month. J.H. Iringer was chief engineer. Fire committee members in 1924 were
J.H. Diebold and Mr. Stelter. Mr. Trekofski was the janitor. Going on to 1925
some fire brigade members were J.H. Diebold, J. Salway, I. Cottrel, J. and Ed
Hausauer, A. Jacobson, and J. Schneider. Skipping a few years and listed is L.
Bischke Jr. as fire chief in 1937. There is another space of time where no
information is available but by 1973 Gordon Woodward was fire chief followed by
Dennis Douglas in 1975, Raymond Jans 1976, Garry Lentz 1981, and 1985 to the
present time Allan Sox.

Some of the major fires in and around Irvine were noted as follows:

April 17, 1902 there was a huge prairie fire between Irvine and Dunmore but no
mention made of how it was extinguished.

January 14, 1909 the insurance office of H.S. Newby was gutted by fire and
totally destroyed. The safe was damaged to such an extent it had to be sent to
Winnipeg to be opened.

July, 1912 the fire brigade was called out to put out a fire in the Golden West
Hotel but they were unable to stop it and the hotel burnt down.

October 31, 1913 there was a fire in the Ogilvie elevator and it burned to the
ground.

February 22, 1914 the town of Irvine had a devastating fire which gutted
Hausauer's butcher shop on Main Street and quickly spread to the general stores
next to it, consisting of Fred Weiss & Sons and Carl Beny, burning them and
everything in them to the ground. Only by the super human effort of Mayor
Crawford, the fire brigade and the entire population of the town was the fire
contained in the block. John Koenig's store was in flame several times and had
it spread to the lumber yard the whole town of Irvine would have been
obliterated. The total loss was estimated at $80,000.

December 18, 1914 prompt turnout of the fire brigade saved the Golden West
Hotel from burning down. (F.E. Etter, Proprietor).

December 1919 the brick school was gutted by fire and burnt down. Classes were
moved to the old sandstone building and the town hall.

In 1921 the fire department was called out four times to the Gus Heine grocery
store, the Fred Gwinner shoe and harness repair shop and the Fred Weiss and
Sons general store. The fire started in the Heine grocery store believed caused
by an overheated stove. It was in control when the fire department arrived.

May 3, 1922 the Fred Weiss block was completely destroyed by fire which started
in the Diebold and Stelter garage. The garage, Fred Weiss and Son store and
warehouse, and a private garage were destroyed.

November 1922 a fire started about 10:00 pm in the Cook and Porter livery
stable. The fire, fanned by a high south wind, spread rapidly and consumed the
entire contents including 47 head of horses and J. Bohnet's private garage.

Another fire of note was in 1958 when Wiedemann's General Store was broken
into, merchandise taken and subsequently a fire started inside. This caused
much damage and the store was closed for quite some time in order to clean up
the debris and restock merchandise.

A fire at the Hink residence, about 1979 caused considerable damage. The fire
chief checked out all rooms to be sure there were no children in any of them.
He was quite startled when he found a crib with a small body in it but, on
closer inspection, he was much relieved when he realized it was only a doll.

Irvine Fire Department - 1984 (pic)

There were probably many more fires, possibly worthy of mention, but no records
were available particularly from the late 1920's to the early 1970's. Fires
were attended in the Irvine community and to the outlying areas such as Walsh,
Maple Creek, Saskatchewan, Elkwater, the Hutterite Colony and vehicle fires on
the Trans Canada Highway. The year 1987 was a devastating year for Irvine when
Wanda Lee Woodward went missing and the Irvine fire department played a major
role in helping to locate her by organizing a search party.

Fires were always a concern to the residents of Irvine in the early days and
this holds true even now. This brief outline of the fire department and fires
from the earliest of the 20th Century up to the present, with some years in
between where no information was available, points out the devastating effects
of some of the fires and the importance of an adequate fire department and well
trained staff.

Doctors and Care of the Sick

The services of doctors in Irvine began in 1904 when Dr. Smith arrived. Later
in that same year Dr. Phillips from Black Creek, Wisconsin arrived and built
what was to be a sanitarium in 1905, but as soon as a license was obtained it
was run as a hotel. In 1908 Dr. Dawson, a dentist as well as a homesteader near
Irvine, set up shop one day a week in the Alberta Hotel to attend to dental
work for area residents.

In 1908, Dr. Ferguson arrived in Irvine and located his office in H.
Vockeroth's store. In 1909 Dr. Gallagher became his assistant. Town minutes of
1910 indicate S. Bolton M.D., a health officer, was paid $20 per month. He
practiced in Irvine until 1914 at which time Dr. E. Fischer from Winnipeg came
to take up duties as local physician. He cared for the sick during the "Flu
Epidemic" along with one registered nurse and many volunteer ladies. Some of
these volunteers were Mrs. George Armstrong, Mrs. Carl Beny, Eva Chell, Sophie
Thiede and Mrs. McLeay. A makeshift hospital was set up in the Cypress Hotel
formerly Hotel Alberta.

In 1925, the town records show F.W. Gershaw as a Medical Health Officer. They
also indicate that there was a Board of Health before 1913 and that in 1920
this board consisted of Dr. E.B. Fischer, J.H. Ihringer and F.G. McLaughlin.

Not only did Irvine have local doctors, they also had a drug store. The first
drug store was operated by Henry Vockeroth in 1908. Dr. Koesling, a druggist,
lived in Irvine in 1914 and owned a drug store on Railway Ave.

The "Rawleighs" wagon provided many households with non-prescription drugs. Was
there a household that didn't have a tin of Rawleighs Medicated Ointment or a
bottle of "Sloan's Liniment"?

Tribute must be paid to our pioneer doctors who often worked with
inadequate tools but with a lot of dedication, devotion, and above
all, caring for the sick.


                             Business and Industry

Irvine Village Progressive
Medicine Hat News, December 19, 1907
Eastern Suburb is Thriving

Over 20 years ago the village was started by Mr. L. Sands establishing lumber
yards here and making it the shipping points for his lumber camps in the
Cypress Hills. When the railway was completed to the coast it was found
advisable to close down and consequently all works at this point were abandoned.

Mr. W. Smibert purchased the sawmills in the Cypress Hills, but they finally
passed into the hands of the present owner, Mr. W. Rutherford, who has run them
now for a long time.

Mr. J. Peters has this fall started a sawmill at the east end of the Cypress
Hills which will soon be in full running order. None of this lumber is shipped
out, the local market being capable of consuming the total output.

The present village was laid out by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in
1903.

Weiss & Co. started a store here in that year and the Golden West Hotel was
built that summer by Waldner Brothers and Bohnet. After passing through various
hands it was finally bought by its present proprietor, Mr. John Pollock, who
intends to enlarge it in the near future. The foundations for the addition are
already built and when the structure is completed will form a nice addition to
our main street.

Another store was built the following year and is now run by Fred Weiss & Son,
who also run a well-stocked lumber yard in connection.

Mr. John Koenig has also recently started a general store.

The C.P.R. built a nice station here in the year 1905. Most of the trains stop
here for water, which the C.P.R. have at considerable expense brought from the
Cypress Hills to supply the large dam they built here last year. At the present
time there are two operators at this point.

In 1905 the Alberta Hotel was built by Dr. Phillips as a sanitarium, but as
soon as a license was obtained it was run as a hotel. The Alberta Hotel is now
owned by Chas. Calkins, who bought it from Dr. Phillips.

This summer the C.P.R. and C.N.W. laid out six blocks on the north side of the
track opposite the depot. A considerable number of lots have been bought and a
good start has been made toward building up the town on that side. Messrs
Cousins and Fatt of Medicine Hat purchased Mr. W. Corbett's farm adjoining the
town on the west and it was laid out by Mr. A.W. McVittie into town lots. This
property is also selling well. These gentlemen gave four lots to the English
Church of St. George which was completed this fall together with the Vicarage
and is situated on the north side of the track. Others have also built quite
close to the church, and as good water has been found at a depth of only
twenty-two feet there is no doubt that many others will now erect houses there
too.

There is an intention on the part of the German Baptists to erect a church in
the near future. This will probably also be constructed on the north side of
the railway but the exact site has not yet been decided on. Messrs Cousins and
Fatt have very kindly offered them land if they build on the Irvine Addition;
but until a meeting has been called this offer cannot be accepted. A
much-needed improvement was made this summer by Mr. Kalmbach when he erected a
building on the north side for the use of the R.N.W.M.P. The upper part of the
building forms a large room in which the trials are held.

A new lumberyard was started this fall by Mr. S. Kalmbach who is doing a good
business.

Fred Schubert has established a meat packing industry and enjoys a large
patronage in the district.

A barber is starting in business this week and intends carrying on a poolroom
in connection.

A school house was erected in 1904. The present accommodation is not sufficient
for the number of scholars attending. As soon as the necessary additions are
made another teacher will be required, the number of children being about 80.

The present population is estimated to be about five hundred.

The Irvine Elevator Company was formed this summer and an elevator was erected
of a capacity of thirty-five thousand bushels at a cost of about seven thousand
dollars.

The post office is run by Mr. Henry Vockeroth and a stage leaves here every
Saturday calling at Newburg, Josephburg, and Elkwater, from which the
Strathmartin mail is fetched. Mr. Vockeroth runs a general store in connection
with the post office.

A rifle association was formed this summer which has a membership of 58. The
Captain is Mr. Carl Beny, Treasurer, Mr. A. Deutchmann, and the Secretary, Mr.
H.S. Newby. A suitable range was found on the north side of the track.

There are also a barber shop, several blacksmiths, two livery and feed stables
and harness shop.

Amongst the contractors the largest are Mr. W. Dunn and Messrs Patzer Bros,
while Messrs Fulton Bros. are the largest railway contractors.

There are two real estate offices in town, namely Mr. Jake Waldner and Messrs
Newby & Co.

The Overseer of the village is Mr. S. Kalmbach and the Secretary in Mr. H.S.
Newby. The assessments for this year will amount to over two hundred thousand
dollars, an increase of about seventy thousand dollars.

Considerable improvements are contemplated for the coming year, amongst others
the extending of the sidewalks, more fire protection and a larger water supply.

Several gentlemen are about to bore for gas, as there is every indication that
it will be found here in large quantities and possibly oil as well.

The district has large deposits of coal which should make our town a
distributing point if only some capitalists would develop them.

In the past this district was noted for a fine ranching district, but at the
present time it is becoming more and more a farming country. A large section of
the land to the south is entirely cut up by the fences of the farmer, and as
they gain experience as to the best methods to adopt we have no doubt that this
will be one of the best districts in Alberta.

Amongst the largest and most successful farmers we may mention Messrs Peter
Hawk, H.H. Hassard, J. Robinson, G. Sneider, J. Crooks and George White.

Amongst the largest ranchers are Messrs Porter Bros., Fawcett Bros., R.O.
Warwick, L.C. Brown, H. Smibert, E.G. Benwell, McLeay, Gray, Rutherford and W.
Smibert.

It speaks well for the future of our town when such men as Messrs. Cousins and
Fatt and H. C. Yuill and J. McNeely of Medicine Hat, have large interests here.

Implement agents are represented by Mr. Jacob Bollinger and Weiss & Son.

Stores

Information pertaining to the operation of General Stores in Irvine was
obtained from weekly articles in the Medicine Hat News dating from 1903-1914.
Additional information was taken from family histories.

Before the influx of the immigrants at the turn of the twentieth century it is
believed a general store was built by John and Ken Koenig in 1892.

During the "boom years" Irvine became a thriving community. Farmers traveled to
Irvine to stock up on essentials from as far north as Schuler and south to the
U.S. border. To accommodate the needs of the settlers stores sprung up rapidly
during 1903-1914.

Carl Beny, Mr. Schaller, John Brandt, Henry Vockeroth, Fred Weiss Sr.,
Christian Weiss, Christ Weiss in front of store (pic)

In 1903, Weiss & Co. was formed by Christian and Fred Weiss, George Schaller,
H. Vockeroth, J. Brandt, and C. Weiss Jr. (son of Fred Weiss). In August of the
same year John Trekofski opened a store.

In 1904, a store was built by Fred Weiss & Son, who also ran a well stocked
lumberyard. Weiss & Co. doubled the size of their store. John Koenig bought a
house and lot on South Railway Street from John Trekofski and opened up a boot
and shoe store. Sam Mitchell, built a store stocking it with groceries, pottery
and ranching supplies, selling it later to Dave Rhodes.

Men's wear and furniture (pic)

Fred Weiss Sr. (pic)

Weiss harness and leather shop (pic)

In 1907 John Koenig expanded by opening a store in which he handled dry goods,
boots and shoes, and men's wear, etc. William Kearns built a butcher shop and
John Hausauer Sr. built a meat market. Henry Vockeroth owned a jewelry store,
which was refitted in 1908 to carry a good supply of drugs. In 1908 Weiss & Co.
sold their store to Fred Weiss & Son. Mr. Schaller remained with the business.

In 1909, the Medicine Hat News carried the following ad for business in Irvine:
"F. Roth & Co. a general merchant selling groceries, harness, machine oil,
patent medicine etc."

John Hausauer Sr. butcher shop (pic)

In 1914 a fire destroyed several stores including those of Carl Beny, Fred
Weiss & Son and John Hausauer. Carl Beny built a new brick store that same
year. John Hausauer rented the front part of the tin shop to continue his
butcher shop business until his new building was completed.

In 1918 a grocery business was operated by Gustav Heine.

In 1917 Carl Beny sold the stock in his store to Phil Silver but kept his
machinery business. In 1924 a store owned by Joseph McNae Thomson was destroyed
by fire.

Merchants tokens - good for trade (pic)

About 1922 another Weiss & Son store burned down along with the shoe store next
to it which was originally a saddle and harness shop owned by Fred Weiss Jr.

Some merchants bought local produce from area farmers with tokens which could
be used to buy merchandise in only their particular store.

Grocery, general stores and meat markets owned and operated by the following
people will be remembered by many who read this history book:

Eddie and Martha Hausauer, Schneider Bros. (Fred and Jake), John Hausauer, Ed
and Bill Glock, Alois, Victor and Herman Wiedemann, and Stephen and Marie
Wiedeman who operated the Golden Rule store.

A tribute should be paid to the Alois Wiedemann family who have served Irvine
and surrounding districts for the past 72 years, beginning with Mr. Alois
Wiedemann's Rawleighs store on wheels to the present day Wiedemann's General
Store operated by his son Herman Wiedemann.

Wiedemann's General Store - 1988 (pic)

Hotels and Restaurants

The Golden West Hotel was built during the summer of 1903 by Waldner Bro. and
Bohnet, and after passing through various hands it was bought by John Pollock
in 1905. "The hotel contains an office, dining room, kitchen and bar on the
main floor with 11 bedrooms upstairs. Mr Pollock intends to enlarge and when
completed it will form a nice addition to Irvine's main street." (Medicine Hat
News, December 1907) The addition was completed soon after that.

In 1912 the Golden West burned down and was rebuilt in 1912-13.

In 1909 a Medicine Hat newspaper ad read, "Golden West Hotel a good place to
stay." February 18, 1914 "Golden West Hotel is doing brisk business."

Golden West Hotel (pic)

In December 1914, prompt turnout of the fire brigade saved the Golden West
Hotel from burning down; F.E. Etter was the proprietor.

In 1918 the hotel was again partially gutted by fire. It was rebuilt and is now
the Great West Hotel. In 1921-22 Charlie Mayberry operated the hotel. A list of
known proprietors of the Great West Hotel are John Graff 1928-29, Burchak
29-40's, Henry Renner, Henry Otto, Earl Ligget, Gerald Wright operator, Roy
Ayling, Con Williams, Duff Couillard and presently Ernest Dattenburger.

Great West Hotel - 1960's or 70's (pic)

The Alberta Hotel was built in 1905 by Dr. Phillips as a sanitarium, but as
soon as a license could be obtained it was run as a hotel. This was the same
year Alberta became a province. In 1907, the hotel was bought by Charles
Calkins and he and David Roloff are listed as proprietors in 1911. In 1914,
Henry Weiss was the proprietor and it was then called the Cypress Hotel. 1928
Henderson Directory lists Mah Goung as hotel keeper. In 1945 this hotel was
torn down by Lou Bischke.

Golden West Hotel Bar - burnt down 1912 (pic)

Front entrance and registration counter, hotel (pic)

Golden West Hotel bar, Chris Weiss, Curley Rute (pic)

Golden West Hotel Bar - 1912, Bartender Les Cooley (pic)

Union Bank building, opening - 1910 (pic)

Same building - 1988 (pic)

The Lou Sing establishment was well known to the Irvine area. The Henderson
directory indicates Lou Sing operated the Canadian restaurant in 1911, 1914 and
in 1928 Mah Goung was Cypress Hotel keeper and Lou Sing operated the Elite Cafe
up to the early 40's.

Sante Devalter took over the Elite Cafe from Lou Sing and operated it for one
year, then made a move to the restaurant in the Great West Hotel and operated
it for one year. Mr. Devalter being a baker, had his own recipe for spudnuts
which his customers enjoyed.

In 1903, Mrs. Clark opened an Ice Cream Parlor.

In 1908 J.A. Strong opened a fruit and confectioners store.

On July 27, 1911, Mr. F.K. Baker opened a restaurant on Railway Avenue called
"Dine at the Princess Cafe".

Golden West Hotel - 1905 - lady upstairs window Mrs. Phillip Schlaht (pic)

Real Estate, Licenses and Banks

The settlers of the early 1900's were on the move, and that likely was the
reason a town like Irvine could support Real Estate and Finance offices. In
March of 1904 Waldner & Co. opened a Finance and Real Estate office going into
farm real estate in September. Land was selling at $1.50 per acre. That same
year Gottlieb Zaiser opened a land office. On March 23, 1907 Alberta Realty and
Brokerage Co. opened a branch office in Irvine with W.E. Martin in charge. That
year there were two Real Estate offices, Jake Waldner and Newby and Company. On
November 11, 1909 the Real Estate business of Newby and Barschell had dissolved
and was then continued by Barschell.

The April 21, 1910 edition of the Medicine Hat News reports the Eastern Alberta
Land and investment Co. Ltd. in Irvine with Leslie Mais secretary-treasurer,
selling land at $22 to $25 per acre. C.P.R. lease could be had for $11-$12 per
acre when paid by cash.

On February 18, 1914, F.J. Crewe took over the Insurance of L.R. Harris and
joined Gottlieb Zaiser in his real estate business.

On April 7, 1904, Zaiser and Co. opened up an employment office.

Marriage Licenses

On May 19, 1904, Zaiser and Pingle were allowed to sell marriage licenses. Mr.
Steve Wiedeman also sold marriage licenses.

Banks

In 1908 the Union Bank had offices next to the Alberta Hotel and on April 28,
1910 E.H. Bally was the sub-manager. In June 1910 a new building was
constructed which housed the Union Bank. On February 22, 1914, Mr. Vic Crawford
was ledger keeper and Mr. H. Steinecker severed his connection. On September
23, 1914, Mr. W. Orchard was manager and stayed with the Union Bank until it
closed in about the 1920's.

Information from the Medicine Hat News.

Livery Stables, Drays and Blacksmiths

The livery stables originated from the need of the many farmers who traveled to
Irvine with horse drawn vehicles. Records show the following people as
operators of livery and feed stables: Around 1899-1900 Adolph Brost; 1904 -
John Brandt; Lust and Kalmbach; McLaughlin, Haycock and Warwick; and George
Armstrong. 1907 - John Frisch, William Kearn and George Sept; 1908 - Oliver
Mayberry, who sold to his son Charles and Sam Kalmbach in 1910; 1910 - Crawford
and Unterscher. Crawford was still in the business in 1914.

Livery and Feed stables - early 1900's (pic)

According to family histories, Rudolf Deering had a livery business in 1915-16.
In 1916 Otto bought into the business and they ran it under the name of Deering
Bros. Livery until 1917.

The livery stable operated by Tony Jacobson and owned by Henry Cook was
destroyed by fire in 1922.

With the coming of the "horseless carriage" the need for livery stables
diminished and eventually became obsolete.

Many of us remember the "Dray Wagon", a flat deck wagon drawn by 2 horses.
Local businesses used the services of the dray business which delivered their
merchandise, shipped in by C.P.R., to their place of business. Their services
to local citizens included the delivery of coal and wood.

Otto Deering and John Becker operated dray businesses in 1910 and Emil Pretz
between 1911 and 1913. Christ Maser bought the dray business from Andrew Rieger
in the late 1920's, and we believe he sold to Pete Schaffer and Sons.

Exterior Harness shop and shoe repair - far right Christ Weiss (pic)

Interior harness shoe repair (pic)

Side view of harness shop, note buggy (pic)

Apparently there was a need for a harness shop and records from the Medicine
Hat News show that a harness shop was owned by Mr. Brandt and sold to D.M.
Boade in June 1904. In October of that same year Mr. Brandt and Mr. Weiss
started a harness shop. Mr. John Becker started a harness repair shop in 1910
and continued in this business for many years.

C.H. Adams Blacksmith shop - 1910-11, two soldiers and Martin Boees Sr. and
Martin Jr., Mr. Adams far right (pic)

Andrew Glock Jr. and Sr. blacksmith shop, possibly early 1920's (pic)

The ringing of the steel hammer on the anvil could be heard in the early
morning as the busy blacksmith began his task of sharpening and pointing
(verspitzen) plough and cultivator shares. Some of these early blacksmiths were
John Ore, Jacob Gast, C.H. Adams and Andrew Glock Sr. Two local boys, Chuck and
Andrew Glock Jr., operated a blacksmith shop in the 1930s until the mid 40's

Wittke machine shop - 1941 (pic)

In 1932 Otto Wittke began his blacksmith business in a converted granary on the
west side of town. See Otto Wittke family history.

Jacob Bechtold in his blacksmith shop - 1970's or 1980's (pic)

The last of these enterprising individuals was Jacob Bechtold. He began his
business in 1946. The term "Bechtold Pump" was a household word in many rural
homes. Jacob semi-retired in 1975 and the blacksmith era ended in Irvine when
he closed shop in 1983.

Farm Implement Dealers

According to the Medicine Hat News, Gottlieb Zaiser opened a farm implement
office in 1904.

Two implement dealers in Irvine, Jacob Bollinger and Fred Weiss & Son were
issued business licenses in 1907. Mr. Bollinger sold Massey-Harris machinery
and Fred Weiss & Son sold McCormick and International Harvester machinery.

Information from a 1908 map of the town of Irvine shows eight implement
locations, indicating that selling farm machinery was a good business.

According to the directory in 1911 Jacob Bollinger was still selling
Massey-Harris; Fred Weiss & Son was agent for McCormick Harvesting Machinery
Co.; Chris Weiss Jr., International Harvester agent; Gottlieb Weiss & Son,
Deering Harvester Co. agent; Zaiser and Kalmbach, implement agents; and Rath &
Co. sold implements in conjunction with their store.

Machine shed - 1916 (pic)

McCormick harvest and Oliver plow shop with Christ Weiss (pic)

Weiss & Co. Store and Deering Farm and Implement shop (pic)

Beny's machinery sales - tractors and threshing machines (pic)

In 1913 licenses to conduct an implement yard were issued to David Roloff, L.R.
Harris, George Schaller, McLaughlin and Weiss, and the Irvine Trading Co. and
in 1914 to Nick Ihly. The 1914 directory shows C. Beny, agent for Deering
Harvester Co.; Schaller (Geo.) and Mauch (Daniel), agents for Massey-Harris
Co.; Christ Weiss continuing as agent for International Harvester Co.; and Fred
Weiss for McCormick Harvesting.

Implement dealers from 1914 to the early 1950's include John Geiger, an
International Harvester agent; George Schaller and Daniel Mauch, Cockshutt
agents; K. P. Becker, a Cockshutt Plow Co. and Massey-Harris Co. agent; Ludwig
Bischke, a Massey-Harris agent; Buster and Albert Crewe, Minneapolis Molene
agents; Tony Jacobson, a John Deere agent; Harry Wilde & Sons, John Deere
agent; and Emil and Art Wittke, J.I. Case agents.

In 1941 Otto Wittke owned a shop called "Irvine Machine Shop". Here he
manufactured duck foot seeder attachments, grain augers and scrapers, selling
them to local farmers and as far away as Swift Current and Lethbridge.

Elevators

The earliest history of grain buying indicates that Gottlieb Zaiser was an
agent for the Medicine Hat Flour Mill in 1904. The first elevator in Irvine was
built in 1907 by the Irvine Elevator Co. of John Hausauer, Carl Beny, and Jacob
Bietz with a capacity of 35,000 bushels and at a cost of $7,000. Sam Kalmbach
was an agent for the Alberta Pacific Grain Elevator Co. in 1909 and worked
almost around the clock because there was so much grain coming in. Also in
1909, Mr. E.F. Kain was apparently a grain buyer but later in that same year
Mr. Schaller and Mr. Lehr took over. There must have been heavy yields of grain
that year because all elevators were handling grain to capacity.

Information was received that, two years after it was built, the Irvine
Elevator Co. elevator was sold to Ogilvie. Further information indicates a fire
broke out on October 31, 1913 in the Ogilvie Elevator which was completely
destroyed. This elevator was later rebuilt. Robert H. Brehmer was manager in
1928. Information was given that the elevator again burnt down in 1934 and was
rebuilt in 1935 with Cliff Lewis as agent. Ira R. Atkinson was the agent for
the Ogilvie Elevator from 1942 until he retired and at that time the elevator
was sold to the Alberta Wheat Pool. No other records could be found as to who
was in charge of the Ogilvie Elevator between the 1910's to 1928 and the early
1930's.

A license to sell flour and feed was obtained by Mr. Becker and Mr. Diemling in
1924.

By 1937 there was a Maple Leaf Elevator operated by Fred Nitschke until he
retired in the 1970's. Emanuel Franz took over from there until he retired in
the mid 1980's.

The Lake of the Woods also had an elevator in Irvine. In 1928, William Bauer
was agent. Others were Bill Bohnet and Serge Nesdoly. In 1960 it was also sold
to the Pool.

Inspection Certificate - Maple Leaf Milling Co., Irvine - 1921(pic)

Reverse of Inspection Certificate - 1921. Note: French also. (pic)

License to operate a country elevator Irvine, 1924 (pic)

The Alberta Wheat Pool had its beginnings in Irvine in 1929 when a 40,000
bushel capacity elevator was built by R.O. Benell Const. Co. and a balloon
annex was added in 1941 by Voss Brothers. This had a capacity of 45,000 bushels
and a further 31,000 bushel elevator, that had been built by the Ogilvie Flour
Mill in 1935, was purchased from them in 1960. Further construction took place
in 1970 when a 70,000 bushel elevator was built and the 31,000 bushel capacity
elevator was converted to a twin elevator. A 27,000 bushel annex, built in
1940, was sold in 1964 and the balloon annex was also sold. One of the other
elevators that had been acquired was dismantled and removed from the site.

Alberta Wheat Pool received grain in 1929-30 and deliveries amounted to 50,546
bushels. The lowest grain receipts were in 1936-37 (4,069 bushels) and the
highest were in 1983-84 with a total of 969,467 bushels.

Alberta Wheat Pool elevator agents were J.E. von Schmidt, 1929-36; closed from
1936-38; J.W. Dyer, 1938-51; A.T. Anderson, 1951-53; A. Boschman, 1953-54; R.A.
Popel, 1954-85; E. Kraemer, (No. 2) 1960-62; and J.J. Zahn, 1984 to the present
time.

For the Alberta Pacific Grain Co. the only records available show Sam Kalmbach
as agent in 1909 and 1911, and Lionel Chell in 1928 until 1939.

Contractors, Carpenters and Lumber

Articles from the Medicine Hat News gave us information on the following
contractors and carpenters.

1904: John Draudson was doing contract work, he built a store and some houses.
J. Jeske did some building for Fred Weiss and Rev. B. Schlepf.

1907: Mr. W. Dunn and Patzer Bros. were among the largest contractors. Fulton
Bros. were the largest railway contractors.

The Henderson Directory of 1911 provided the information for the following.
John Brandt, contractor; A. Frenberger, plasterer and stonemason; John Krauss,
contractor and builder; James A. Strong, contractor; and Chris Sturm,
contractor.

Family histories provided the names of Jacob Gwinner and Theodore Ziegler,
local farmers who built for area residents.

Lumber

Information for the following was obtained from the Medicine Hat News,
Henderson Directory and family histories.

The first lumber yards were established by Mr. L. Sands as early as 1887.

Businessmen who handled lumber in conjunction with their other business were
Mr. Schlipf in 1903, Fred Weiss & Co. in 1904, and F. Rath & Co. in 1911. In
1907, Sam Kalmbach started a new lumber yard.

Pioneer lumber yard - 1919: Mr. and Mrs. Ihringer and Mary (pic)

No information was available as to when the Citizen Lumber Co. and Pioneer
Lumber Co. opened in Irvine but by June 1911, Mr. Battson was an agent for
Citizen Lumber Co. followed by George W. Dinkel that same year, John Gieger
from 1925-1938, Nick Pohlman from the late 30's to early 40's and Emil
Schneider. Joseph Ihringer was an agent for Pioneer Lumber from 1911-24.

George and Harvey Maser started a lumber yard business in 1944.

Moving Citizens Lumber Co. building - 1966 (2 pic)

Garages

In 1913, Mr. E.G. Benwell owned an auto garage on Pacific Avenue (where the old
curling rink was located). During World War I it was used as an ammunition
dump. It is believed that this garage was sold to Jake Schuster, who in turn
sold it to Jim Crookes. Jim bought it for his son Harry and named it Irvine
Garage. When Mr. Crookes built a new garage on Railway Avenue, this old
building remained empty until Hausauers used it for their Cinder Block factory.
Later Ludwig Bischke purchased it and moved it onto Mike Bischke's farm where
it is now used as a storage shed by Theophil Heller.

In 1919, Everett and Albert Stelter owned and operated a garage south of the
Fred Weiss & Son Store. A fire which originated in their garage destroyed it
and several stores, including the Fred Weiss & Son Store. Everett and his
partner Jack DeBolt bought Roloff's livery barn and converted it into a garage.
They operated this garage for about three years, then due to high taxes they
moved their partnership to Claresholm.

Bischke Garage - 1930's (pic)

Ludwig Bischke built a garage on the location of the former Fred Weiss & Son
Store (where the present town garage is located) in about 1928. Along with his
son-in-law Frank Huddlestone and, later, his son Lou, they sold B.A. (British
American Oil Co.) products and Chrysler cars. This building was later
dismantled when Buster and Albert Crewe built a new shop, selling farm
implements.

Bischke Garage - 1945 (pic)

Ludwig's son Lou demolished the ruins of the former Alberta (Cypress) Hotel and
built a new garage selling B.A. gas. This garage was sold to Tony Jacobson in
1947. Tony had previously purchased the Irvine Garage from Harry Crookes and in
conjunction with the Bischke garage continued to sell Imperial and B.A. gas and
oil, delivering bulk fuel to outlying areas. In 1949 he sold his business to
Harry and Mabel Wilde and sons, Stan and Harold. It is believed Holger Nelson
had a share in their business as a mechanic. Later when the Wildes sold out
Holger bought their share and continued as a mechanic until he retired in 1972.
This building now houses Kitchen Plumbing and Kulpa Body Shop.

The Irvine Garage was sold to Peter Schaffer who dismantled it and used the
lumber to build a new Imperial Gas Service Station and garage. This was located
on the east end of Irvine adjacent to Highway #1. Other owners of this garage
were Leonard Gehring, Gust Schlaht, Mike Holyk, Gordon Chambers, Fred and Ida
Franz, Blair Arsenault, Dennis Lutz, Gil Austin and Harry Dietelback.

Kitchen's Plumbing and Kulpa Auto Body - 1988 - former Bischke Garage (pic)

Dave Bohnet, a mechanic, owned and operated a garage selling White Rose gas.

The garage known as George's Service located on Railway Avenue was built by
Buster Crewe in about 1930. Owners and operators selling North Star Oil and Gas
were Gus Nagel, Eddy Herman and Les McLeave, Norrie and Fawcett, Schlaht Bros.
(George and Gust from 1949-1959), and the present owner George Schlaht.

In 1954 Art and Emil Wittke built the Texaco Service Station on the west end of
Irvine adjacent to the Trans Canada Highway. They sold the business to Stan and
Eileen Wilde who sold it to William Leith. After purchasing the garage William
and Audrey expanded their business when they built motels on the same parcel of
land. Other owners were Paul Golwaski, George and Caroline Bohnet and present
owner of Irvine Truck and Car Stop is Nada Zvonko.

Garage on Trans Canada Highway - 1988 (pic)

Irvine Cinder Brick Plant

The Cinder Block Plant was established in Irvine in 1947-48, by Chuck Glock and
Eddy Hausauer. The machinery to make cinder blocks was built by Chuck Glock and
Eddy Hausauer in the old Glock Blacksmith Shop. It was a very interesting
machine, all hand made with old scrap iron, old pulleys and belts from old
machinery that blacksmiths used to have at their shops in those early days. The
cinder block plant was located a half block south of the present high school,
where the old curling rink was located in later years.

Cinder Brick Co. with George Maser - Irvine - 1947 (pic)

Ken Hausauer hauling cinder blocks (pic)

The plant required three men to operate the machine for manufacturing the
cinder blocks. Ken Hausauer, Donald Hausauer and George Maser worked at the
plant. The plant would manufacture about 1,000 cinder blocks per day. The
material used to make the cinder blocks was Portland Cement and cinders, which
came from the C.P.R., the waste from the old coal burning locomotives. The
finished product was a much lighter block than the present day cement block.

Cinder Block Co. 1947 Owners Chuck Glock and Eddie Hausauer (pic)

There was quite a market for these cinder blocks in those days, and they were
shipped to all parts of southern Alberta. The old cinder block building was
moved four miles east of Irvine, and is still being used by Theophil Heller
today.

Miscellaneous Businesses
The Market Square

May 3, 1906: F.S. Pingle spent Tuesday in Irvine attending the market, and in
an interview with The News, stated his astonishment at the large crowd of
farmers and buyers who assembled in the village. Main street was a scene of
bustling activity. The farmers brought in cattle, horses, pigs and all kinds of
farm produce. Mr. Gottleib Zaizer made the first sale in disposing of a pig at
10 cents a pound. Quite a number of heavyweight horses changed hands. Oats sold
at 40 cents a bushel, and wheat brought 66 cents. The farmer did not come to
market alone but brought his wife and family along. While he was disposing of
his produce, they were making purchases in the stores. The merchants are
satisfied that they made a good move in establishing their market, which will
be held the first and third Tuesday of each month. (Medicine Hat News, May 2,
1987)

Scene in Irvine (pic)

A council decision was made to have all teams of horses tied on the market
square behind the business section of town. "The town well has been cleaned and
a water trough has been erected for use by the farmers and their horses. It has
been decided to have market day opening on June 18, 1914 for the farmers and
their produce." (Town minutes)

Market Square (pic)

Coal Mine

Information from the Medicine Hat News and an early resident informed us that
in 1907 John Waldner and J. Fitzgerald opened up a coal mine. Apparently this
coal was of very poor quality and in spite of the belief that Irvine could
become a coal distributing point it closed down the same year it was opened.

Brick Factory

In 1904 a brick factory was in operation with Mr. Carleton as manager. Their
first order of 325,000 bricks was from Winnipeg. We don't know if they were
delivered because according to the Medicine Hat News, the brick yard became a
thing of the past that same year. There was too much alkali in the fire-clay.

Laundry and Cleaning

In 1911 Lou Sing operated a laundry and in 1914 Mr. Fred Walker had a cleaning
and pressing establishment. This business lasted for only a short time.

Barber Shops and Billiard Rooms

The names of the proprietors who established a barber shop and pool room in
1907 are not available.

In 1911 Hansom and Schlatt operated a billiard hall and A.S. Girrard owned a
barber shop and pool room. In 1912 there was a barber shop in what is now the
New Horizons kitchen area.

In 1914 Charles Clarkson operated a barber shop and pool room at the rear of
the Golden West Hotel which was owned by John Pollock.

Barber shop in Irvine, 1912, located where present recreation centre is (pic)

Other barbers in Irvine included Ross Fyke in the early thirties and Edwin
Schneider from 1932 to 1973.

John Hausauer had a pool room in the back of his butcher shop.

Other owners and operators of billiard rooms were F.G. McLaughlin, in 1919; T.
Rhodes, a manager in 1922; Henry Wolfe; Bill Schlaht; Rueben Giegle; and Les
Woodward.

Dairy

According to the Medicine Hat News, Irvine was hoping to have a creamery in the
summer of 1899. In 1910 F.J. Hansom operated the Irvine Creamery Company which
included butter-making. In 1928 Campbell and Griffin Ltd. had a cream station.
John Hausauer had a small dairy and was agent for Crystal Dairy. During the
1950's and 60's Mary Ambrose delivered milk to town residents.

Meat Packing Factory

1907: Fred Schubert established a meat packing industry.

December 20, 1906: Fredrich Schubert has started a meat packing factory and
hopes by only handling the best class of stock to build up a large business.
Irvine is the centre of the district where a great number of cattle are raised,
a new industry will doubtless be a flourishing one in the course of a short
time. (Medicine Hat News)

January 24, 1907: Fred Schubert of Irvine was in the city yesterday and stated
to the News that he had placed orders for his brand of canned meats with all
the leading grocers of Medicine Hat. In these days of startling revelations
concerning the packing house methods of the United States, it is a pleasure for
the News to personally endorse the product of Mr. Schubert's factory. A sample
can opened in the office surpassed even Mr Schubert's claim for it. Spiced and
jellied to a nicety, it makes a rare table delicacy and fills a long-felt want
in the West. The cleanliness of the methods adopted in the canning are a great
recommendation. Mr Schubert does all his own killing and Mrs. Schubert
superintends the curing and packing.(MHN)

The Homesteader

God gave all men all earth to live,
But since all hearts are small,
Ordained that each one spot should prove
Beloved over all.

Golden Rules for Easier Living

1. If you open it, close it.
2. If you turn it on, turn it off.
3. If you unlock it, lock it up.
4. If you break it, admit it.
5. If you can't fix it, call in someone who can.
6. If you borrow it, return it.
7. If you value it, take care of it.
8. If you make a mess, clean it up.
9. If you move it, put it back.
10. If it belongs to someone else and you want to use it, get permission.
11. If you don't know how to operate it, leave it alone.
12. If it's none of your business, don't ask questions.
13. If it ain't broke, don't fix it.
14. If it will brighten someone's day - Say it!


It's in your face

You don't have to tell how you live each day;
You don't have to say if you work or you play;
A tried, true barometer serves in the place,
However you live, it will show in your face.

The false, the deceit, that you bear in your heart
Will not stay inside where it first got a start;
For sinew and blood are a thin veil of lace -
What you wear in your heart, you wear in your face

If your life is unselfish, if for others you live,
For not what you get, but how much you can give,
If you live close to God in his infinite grace -
You don't have to tell it, it shows in your face.
