                                 Organizations

Irvine Agricultural Society

The Irvine Agricultural Society held their first meeting on April 11, 1908. At
one of their meetings of that year the speakers spoke German as the majority of
the audience was German.

On October 6, 1908 the Society held their first annual fair.

Elected to the Executive of the Ag. Society in December of 1909 were L.H.
Dawson, president, G.P. White, vice-president, Jas. Crawford, 2nd
vice-president, and L.R. Harris, secretary-treasurer.

The Irvine Seed Fair was held in the years 1909 and 1910, perhaps on an annual
basis. In 1909 there seemed to be some protest about the wheat grown by a
farmer who entered it in the fair. The fellow who protested claimed the wheat
was grown by another person. In 1910 the seed fair was not too well attended.
There was $180 in prize money but only $80 of that was handed out for prizes.

In 1914 the Ag. Society and the Poultry and Pet Stock Association held a
meeting pertaining to having a Fall Fair. New members were Gottlieb Weiss and
Jacob Maser bringing the membership up to 58 members.

In 1918, 125 members belonged to the Irvine Agricultural Society. The
membership fee was $1. Women belonging to the society were Mrs. Etter, Mrs.
Jerrold, Mrs. Solverson, Mrs. Yule, and Mrs. Pfaff. These women were noted
under occupation as "Married Woman". Requirements for being a member of the
Irvine Agricultural Society consisted of the following:

"1. Over 18 years of age.
 2. He is a resident of the province of Alberta.
 3. He is not a member of any other agricultural society.
 4. He has subscribed to the funds of the society the sum set opposite his name
    in the fourth column hereunder and that he has paid to the said funds the
    sum set opposite his name in the fourth column."

The Fall Fair of August 13, 1918 raised between $300 and $400 for the Red
Cross. They had to pay out $1000 dollars in prizes and the entries totaled
$717. Malcolm McIntosh was the secretary-treasurer.

Construction of the Irvine Sports Complex (6 pic)

On April 15, 1930, Mr. Fred McLaughlin was the secretary of the village, the
school board, etc. He was in close touch with the Agricultural Society for
years and he stated that it was impossible to foster any interest in the
society, and at that time the grounds owned by the society were being used by a
group of men known as the Sports Committee. The Agricultural Exhibition had
been replaced by an annual Stampede. Banking was done with the old Union Bank
at Irvine, which had now amalgamated with the Royal Bank, the office being in
Medicine Hat. The last Agricultural Exhibition was held in the year 1920 and
entry fees were paid to the secretary but no prize money was paid to the
winners.

The society was in the state of liquidation in 1927. P.W. Johnson was the
liquidator for the Agricultural Society.

Assets (of the Agric. Society):
Land - Blocks 6, 7, 8, and 37. Plan 2696 M Irvine Addition
1 Exhibit building, approximately 30 x 36
Rental by Sports Committee for use of ground $1 per year

Liabilities:
Unpaid 1920 prizes
Pioneer Lumber Company mechanics lien $236

Mr. J. Hausauer of Irvine, purchased the old agricultural society building for
$32 on March 22, 1934. The agricultural society building had a mechanics lien
filed against it by the Pioneer Lumber Company Limited, of Saskatoon.
Apparently the society of Irvine owed the lumber company $236.

The Agriculture Society of Irvine and District is active today.

Irvine A.W.I. Certificate of Incorporation 1921 (pic)

Irvine Women's Institute

The Irvine W.I. was organized in 1921 with Mrs. Phyl McLeay as first president.
Other charter names available were Mrs. Carl Beny, Mrs. F.G. McLaughlin, Mrs.
Steve Wiedeman and Mrs. Bill Corbett. For 62 continuous years this group
enthusiastically kept their branch functioning according to their motto, for
"Home and Country". For "Home" their aim was to learn, as was the original
intent of Adelaide Hoodless when she organized the first group at Stoney Creek,
Ontario in 1897. For "Country" meant reaching out to help others, but country
also meant the World.

The Irvine W.I. found innumerable ways to raise funds for many worthy causes,
be it within the community or across an ocean. Down through the years donations
were made for scholarships to local high school graduates, playground
equipment, skating rinks, flood and fire victims, George P. Vanier School,
Mental Health Hospitals, Red Cross, Heart and Cancer drives. Thousands of
pounds of clothing, powdered milk, and soap were sent through the U.S.C. for
the needy in the Third World. Among other projects, support was given to an
orphans' school in Korea, and for child adoption.

There have been many dedicated members throughout the years, among whom were
Sophia Thiede (33 year member), Freda Roll (31 years), Thelma Porter (23
years), president and constituency convener for a time, and Ruby Schlaht, who
was also president for a number of years.

It was always a learning and sharing experience, attending conferences on the
constituency, district and provincial levels, and knowing we had a voice in the
Federated W.I. Being affiliated with the Associated Country Women of the World
also opened many doors.

Members of the Irvine W.I. at the time of disbanding were Mrs. Lorna Phaff,
president; Frieda Will, secretary, who received a 30 years of service pin; Mary
McLeay, treasurer, was given a silver charm and received special recognition
for her work with the U.S.C.; Martha Hausauer, a 37 year member; Mary Deering;
Isla Jackson; Margaret Cavan; and Hazel Webber.

As one branch must fold it is hoped another is being organized somewhere, who
will carry on with new ideas for "Home and Country".

Farmers' Union

The Irvine Farmers' Union was in existence in the mid 1940's. At this time
conventions were held in Calgary.

The F.U.A. brought in lumber and fence posts and sold them to farmers at cost.

Money was raised by putting on socials and dances.

The F.U.A. helped out farmers in the area, who had suffered in fire losses on
their property. They contributed money to the Cancer Fund and gave gifts to the
Irvine School graduates.

An F.W.U.A. local was also formed. This was the ladies side of the Farmers'
Union of Alberta. They disbanded and joined with the men in 1958. In October
1969 the Irvine local joined with the Clearwater local.

In March 1970 a Founding Convention was held in the MacDonald Hotel in
Edmonton, with' the Farmers' Union of Alberta and the Alberta Federation of
Agriculture. As a result of this convention we have one farm organization named
Unifarm.

Frieda and Willie Will with Unifarm Float - 1975 (pic)

The Chinook Club of Irvine (1952-1988)
submitted by Art Zeller on behalf of all past and present members

The Chinook club of Irvine had its early beginnings in 1951. In this year,
Emerson Porter would bring his wife to Irvine to attend the monthly Women's
Institute meetings. (Emerson Porter is the late father of our present Member of
Parliament, Bob Porter.) Having nothing else to do while waiting for Mrs.
Porter, Emerson would go to the telephone office. Here he would visit with Mr.
Lynn McLaughlin, the telephone office Operator. At closing time, these two men
would then venture to the local tavern and meet with the company of Mr. Emil
Schneider.

It was these three men who decided that, because they had all this idle time
and nothing special to do when the Women's Institute meetings were scheduled,
they should form a men's club.

Horse and R. Porter advertising Chinook Club, 1955 (pic)

The following month, these three men decided that they would each bring another
man along to the monthly gathering, thus increasing their number to six. The
same was done the next month. Therefore, in December of 1951, they had a total
of twelve men - enough to form an official club.

These first twelve members of the newly organized club were Emerson Porter,
Lynn McLaughlin, Emil Schneider, George Ambrose, Bert Curran, Ted Maser,
Leonard Lien, Ted Roll, Stuart McAlpine, Victor Wiedemann, Walter Nelsen, and
Bert Simmons.

Their next meeting, January 24, 1952, went on record as the first official
meeting. But in order to be properly organized, the men's club needed a name.
The following is a list of names that were suggested for the club: Irvine Men's
Club, The Enterprise Club of Irvine, Community Club, Chinook Club of Irvine,
Irvine Goodwill Club, The Independent Man's Club, Men's Service Club of Irvine,
The Number Twelve Club, The Booster Club of Irvine.

All of these names were voted on by secret ballot and it was declared that the
name of the men's club shall be "The Chinook Club of Irvine". The purpose of
the club was unanimously decided to be "to support community projects and to
provide entertainment to its members".

A constitution was drawn up to form the guidelines under which the club would
operate. Two important clauses were built into the constitution. One dealt with
scheduling the meetings, and the other, with the election of new members to the
club. Both of these clauses have remained relatively the same for over 30 years.

Regarding the meetings, a constitutional clause stated that "The Chinook Club
of Irvine will meet every fourth Wednesday of each month". This scheduling was
originally intended to coincide with the meetings of the Women's Institute
Organization.

The second important clause dealt with the election of new members to the club.
The constitution was drawn up to read that "any member of the club could
propose a man's name as a prospective member, and all members of the club who
were present would vote on it. Three dissenting votes from any of the twelve
members automatically disqualified that person named from becoming a member. A
waiting period of one year had to be honoured before that person's name could
be proposed again".

This clause was put to use during the next meeting of the club. In February of
1952, The Chinook Club of Irvine brought forth its first elected members from
the community. These men were Fred Franz, Art Zeller, Holgar Nelson, Art
Schultz, James Irvine.

Over more than 30 years, The Chinook Club of Irvine has managed to grow in
number and in popularity. To date, there have been over 75 active members
having their names added to the club roster. However, the maximum membership
for each year of operation is held at 30. The only way that a new member can be
nominated to the club is if one of the present members either voluntarily
resigns his membership, or becomes deceased. The acceptance of new members is
still done in a similar fashion, requiring a 75 percent majority vote, as was
set down by the constitution initially.

With respect to the purpose of the club, (i.e. support community projects and
entertain members) both facets have been adequately served. By way of
entertainment, some of the annual events which The Chinook Club of Irvine
sponsors are summer picnics, Pancake Breakfasts, Hawaiian Night, Fall Turkey
Shoot and Curling Bonspiel. In addition, several social evenings are sponsored
through the year. Quite a number of these events are open to the members and
invited guests. Thus, many in the community have an opportunity to share in the
entertainment.

Hawaiian night feast - hostesses: Donna Lee Porter, Hanah Lor Lentz, Rachel
Zeller (pic)

Art Zeller - Chinook Club (pic)

Regarding the support of community projects, there have been a number of
matters undertaken. Most important of these is the Medicine Hat College
Scholarship Award which has been offered annually since 1965. Another annual
donation, started in 1962, has been that of the Social Studies Award given to a
worthy student at the Irvine High School Graduation. Other than these, The
Chinook Club of Irvine has also sponsored students going to Youth Seminars and
Drug and Alcohol Abuse Conferences. Through all of these, this men's club has
certainly portrayed support for the youth of the community. Above all this, the
records show that there were also a lot of community service jobs done over the
years. To mention a few, there were community Children's Christmas parties,
tree planting bees, clean up of cemeteries and fund raising projects for area
residents who met with misfortune in one way or another.

All in all, The Chinook Club of Irvine has made a significant contribution to
the betterment of the community. After 36 years the purpose of the club is
still being upheld, and its membership has passed into the third generation.
There is a lot to be said for the organization, and the men behind it, who have
made The Chinook Club of Irvine a historic success.

U.C.W. 25th Anniversary Report
information submitted by Bette Frisch

In 1962 the W.A. and W.M.S. united under the name U.C.W. (United Church Women).
The inaugural service held in Lethbridge was attended by Anna Aman, Lily Crewe,
Mary Simmons, Leona Neubauer and possibly Ruby Woodward.

Mary Simmons was the first president, Leona Neubauer was the first incoming
U.C.W. president, and Lily Crewe was the secretary. Meetings began with a hymn
and the Lord's Prayer, and now they begin by repeating Our Purpose. Bible
studies included "Jesus Christ and the Christian Life" in 1966, "The Gospel of
Mark" by William Barclay until 1987 and presently, "Two World's in One" by
James Taylor. We have sent flowers to the bereaved and sick in hospital, and
sympathy and get-well cards. Visits to the sick, and bereaved, and to newcomers
to the community are reported at each meeting.

The funds required for repair, renovations and other needs of the church were
raised by the members from bake sales, kuchen sales, fall suppers, catering to
weddings, anniversaries, and the Irvine graduation banquets, curling rink
concessions, funeral lunches, Nabob coupons, sale of cook books, and cash
donations.

Some of the major items we donated funds for are 110 chairs, pews, $607.90 for
central vacuum, $600 for plumbing repairs, $600 to the organ fund, $300 for the
lot beside the church, 20 hymn books, 30 service books, hot water tank, fans
for the Sanctuary, kitchen equipment, church building fund, the Elkwater camp,
M & S, $525 to Irvine Complex, $250 to New Horizons, $200 to the Hunger
Foundation, $700 to Medicine Hat Regional Hospital, $500 to the Women's
Shelter, and many other smaller donations. We have sponsored an Indonesian boy
since 1981. Our first project for this year was a donation to the Fifth Avenue
Church Food Bank with Herman Wiedemann's help.

To the ones who have made various donations and given volunteer time, we shall
acknowledge that we appreciate everything that was done for the U.C.W. We gave
engraved spoons to the women who left our congregation. We had farewell potluck
suppers for Mrs. Lizzie Hausauer in 1966, for Mr. and Mrs. Ted Aman when they
moved to Medicine Hat in 1972, and for Victor and Betty Wiedemann in 1982.

Life membership pins were given to Adeline Sackman and Betty Wiedemann in 1982.
I had the honor to receive one this year.

We have attended presbyterial meetings, the first one in 1968 and in 1979 I
became communications convener for the South Alberta Presbytery. A quilt patch
was made for a South Alberta Presbyterial banner which was on display at the
Banff Women's Conference. In 1985, we had the Spring Presbyterial meeting in
our church.

For several years we worked along with the Lutheran ladies of Irvine on
projects such as fall suppers and World Day of Prayer services. In 1982 we
catered to the Herman Wiedemann Appreciation Banquet at which time we presented
him with a lifetime ticket to our annual suppers.

U.C.W. presidents have been, in 1966-67, Betty Wiedemann; 1968-70, Leona
Neubauer; 1971-72, Betty Wiedemann; 103-75, Leona Neubauer; 1976-81, Betty
Sauter; 1982-85, Linda Woodward; and 1986-87, Betty Sauter.

Vice presidents were in 1966-69, Lolly Genert; 1970-71, Bette Frisch; 1971-72,
Leona Neubauer; and in 1976-87, Shirley Hagel.

Secretaries were 1966-67, Bette Frisch; 1968-71, Olga Bollinger; 1972-73, Betty
Wiedemann; and 1974-87, Bette Frisch.

Treasurers were 1966-67, Lily Crewe; 1967-75, Dorothy Smith; 1976-81, Betty
Wiedemann; 1982-84, Olga Weiss; and 1985-87, Eleanor Christie.

Present members are Betty Sauter, Shirley Hagel, Linda Woodward, Dorothy Smith,
Audrey Leith, Annie Schneider, and Bette Frisch.

C.G.I.T.
by Bette Frisch

I took over the leadership of the Irvine C.G.I.T. (Canadian Girls In Training)
in 1966. A highlight of that first year was a pajama party held in our hayloft.
I think I enjoyed it as much as the girls.

The next year Olga Bollinger became my assistant leader. That year we held a
sleepover at her farm where we went on a hike in their creek. We slept in tents
pitched in their yard.

C.G.I.T. girls: Betty and Bernice Ewaseschko, Carol Wood - 1958 (pic)

In 1969 through to 1972, Herb, myself, Edwin and Olga Bollinger along with the
girls went on long weekends, camping at Waterton Park, Alest Glacier Park,
U.S.A. and Fairmont Hot Springs. The girls usually slept in tents, with the
leaders and their husbands sleeping in a camper shell on the back of the truck.
One year Victor Wiedemann's tent trailer was borrowed for some of the girls and
a tent was used by the other girls.

Each family supplied some food for the meals and the girls helped with the
preparation and cleaning up. A camp kitchen was often taken over by us with all
our girls and supplies. Sometimes some of them would sleep in there; one
particularly stormy night at Waterton, I think they all slept in it.

In 1973 when Janice Bollinger broke her leg, Edwin and Olga weren't able to go
with us, so Leslie and Evelyn Woodward went instead. It rained all the time
that we were at Fairmont. We had a very small cabin into which we crowded. Most
of them slept in it, except for a few that slept in the trucks. Meal times were
especially hectic and you ate wherever you found room - on a bed, or if you
were fortunate, on one of the few chairs.

A Vesper Service was held each year at Christmas in the Peace United Church.
Meetings were held once a week in the church basement. Each meeting was begun
by repeating the C.G.I.T. Purpose. A Bible Study would be held and various
types of activities, and many varieties of crafts were done. One such project
would be a gift for the citizens of Irvine that lived alone (usually elderly
people).

C.G.I.T. Girls - Irvine: Judy Wiedemann, Darlene Jans, Betty Aman, Betty Anne
Bollinger, Christine Kundert, Sharon Heller, Darlene Frisch, Sandra Woodward,
Joyce Aman, Pat Crewe (pic)

Rallies were attended at Medicine Hat, Brooks and Ralston. An overnight one
held at Empress in about 1971 saw the girls and leaders sleeping in sleeping
bags on the floor of a large hall. No one got much sleep that night!

We slept in sleeping bags in the church basement in Irvine when just our group
held an overnight session.

Money was raised through bake sales in Wiedemann's Store. One sale consisted of
strictly kuchen. It was baked the day of the sale at Olga's and my house. We
each had several of the girls helping us to do the baking. The girls enjoyed
this and the kuchen turned out well.

Another fund raising project was running concessions at the curling rink for
the Ladies Bonspiel each year for several years. Each girl took a shift and
brought two pies to sell along with the hamburgers, coffee, chocolate bars,
etc. This was usually quite profitable and provided money for their camping
trips.

Membership began to drop until there weren't enough girls to continue a
purposeful program. Much to my disappointment we discontinued C.G.I.T. in 1973.
I really did enjoy working with these girls, who included Alice and Donna Skye,
Gloria Maser, Judy and Joan Wiedemann, Betty Anne and Karen Bollinger, Darlene
and Allison Jans, Marie Herrel, Kathy Booth, Esther and Dorothy Schorr, Cheryl
Raymond, Sandra Maser, Doris Nelsen, Judy Smith, Rennie Wangsness, Jo Ann
Schlaht, Barbara Smith, Bonnie Becker, Yvonne Heller, Sandra Woodward, Debbie
Jans, Shirley and Phyllis Chesney, Wanda Woodward, and Janice Bollinger.

Girl Guides of Canada

Girl Guides and Brownies of Irvine came into being with the forming of the
Local Association in September of 1976. The first members of this association
were chairperson, Lexy Zeigler; secretary, Madeleine Denis; treasurer, Sara
Kroft; badge secretary, Madeleine Denis; vice chairperson, Marilyn Barton; and
telephone convener, Betty Sauter. The purpose of the Local Association was to
aid in starting up the guide movement.

The guiders of the 1st Irvine Co. were Guide Captain, Shirley Maier; Guide
Lieutenant, Evelyn Woodward; Brown Owl, Barbara Majore; and Tawny Owl, Ruby
Brost of the 1st Irvine Brownie Pack.

Brownies and Guides held their first meetings in a classroom at the Irvine
School and then in the basement of the United Church. There were 10 guides and
15 brownies registered.

To get started, support was received from the Girl Guides of Canada
organization, the Town of Irvine, local clubs and organizations, and
individuals. The funds were used to purchase such things as camping gear, hats,
pins, scarves, and for other expenses. The guides and brownies also raised
money be selling cookies, calendars, cookbooks and by putting on bake sales and
teas.

The guides and brownies earned their badges by completing certain
qualifications in sewing, swimming, camping, canoeing, baking, skating, child
care, folklore, and fire safety, just to name a few.

Brownies and Guides participated in Baden Powell Week, dance festivals,
camping, fun days, sleepovers, swimming, Mother and Daughter Banquets,
delivering of Christmas boxes of goodies to senior citizens, and Easter Sunrise
Services followed by a pancake breakfast at the United Church.

The Local Association disbanded in 1979 and the Brownies and Guides continued
until the summer of 1981.

Boy Scouts

The Boy Scouts organization was started by Blanche Davidson in 1977-78 by
forming a group committee of interested parents of Irvine and District. Scout
masters were Wilfred Krushel and Mulvey Kroft, cub leader was Melvin Lineman,
and beaver leaders were Margot Krushel and Cheryl Gilsig.

The scouts participated in many activities such as overnight camping at Camp
Apistotoke in Elkwater, hay rides at Christmas time delivering Christmas gift
packages to senior citizens, and a C.P.R. Via Rail train ride from Maple Creek
to Medicine Hat. The group started Easter Sunday Sunrise Services held on
Irvine Hill and followed by a pancake breakfast.

New Horizons Club

In the fall of 1980 meetings were held to organize a senior citizen club. By
springtime of 1981 the club was incorporated as Irvine and District New
Horizons. To become a member you or your spouse needed to be fifty. The towns
new complex being under construction meant the community hall belonging to the
town would soon be vacant. It was decided that the town would use the east
portion for the town office and the west portion would be available to use as a
senior citizen centre with utilities shared with the town.

The first year the club booked the hall mainly for every Thursday night for
card games and meetings.

Gordon Woodward made two sets of floor curling discs for discing. In April 1982
the floor was marked for discing and all enjoyed the game. Now the club needed
the hall an additional night. Wednesday night was chosen, so the hall was
booked for every Wednesday night also.

In the spring of 1984 the recreation board began using the new complex so we
then had control of our hall.

Our monthly meeting night was changed from the first Thursday of the month to
the 2nd Tuesday of the month. In place of December and April meetings we have
potluck suppers and these are very much enjoyed by all.

In June of 1984 the club was given a set of floor curling rocks. This is
similar to the discing and uses the same floor markings only there are handles
on these rocks. We soon got to prefer this to the discing so we purchased a
second set. Now the discs are somewhat retired.

We have gone to Medicine Hat to social funday floor curling at the Veiner
Centre, Westminster Church and Strathcona Centre, also tournaments at the
Veiner Centre. In return these clubs have visited us. We've had annual
tournaments with clubs from Medicine Hat, Redcliff and Brooks.

New Horizons bus trip 1983 - to North Battleford: Standing: Bernice Jans,
Evelyn Woodward, Lydia Trekofski, Levern Weiss, Bill and Audrey Leith, Herb
Frisch, Brenda McLaughlin, Harry and Mary Dietelback, Annie Schneider, Shirly
Hagel, Edwin Schneider, Betty Frisch, Ted Aman, Linda Woodward, Art and Rachel
Zeller, Gordon Woodward; Sitting: Olga Weiss, Clarence Jans, Ida Franz, Ted
Kundert, Walter Jans, Florence Jans, Martha Kundert, Gary Lentz (bus driver);
Inset: Emma McLaughlin (pic)

On October 10, 1981 the club held its first Tea and Bake Sale including tables
of baked goodies, crafts, plants and white elephants, etc. In the summer of
1982 the club bought material and made a quilt for a raffle to be held at the
annual fall Tea and Bake Sale. This making of quilts and raffling has remained
an ongoing thing every year. For these quilts the blocks have been hand
embroidered, painted with liquid embroidery, or patch work.

The club also has an annual Strawberry Shortcake Mother's Day Tea and Bake
Sale. These Tea and Bake sales are our main fund raising functions.

The club has gone on outings for supper and bowling in Medicine Hat, bus trips
to Calgary's Heritage Park, "Them Were the Days" at North Battleford, Brooks
Horticulture Field Days, Drumheller Tyrrell and Pioneer Museums, and Rosebud
Supper-theatre.

Club membership has averaged about 50 annually. Club executives have been,
presidents, Art Zeller, Alvin Reimann, Harry Dietelback, Annie Schneider, Olga
Weiss; secretaries, Shirley Hagel, Ruby Schlaht, Jean Wangsness; and treasurer,
Gordon Woodward.

Irvine and District Lions Club

The club was formed in 1983. Charter night was held on June 4, in the Irvine
and District Community Hall. Thirty-six members were inducted into the
fellowship of Lions Clubs.

Some of the clubs programs include diabetes detection, drug awareness, and
working with the C.N.I.B.

During the past five years some of the members have moved on, leaving the
membership to stand at 16. Nevertheless, these members have worked diligently
for this community, by sending handicapped children to summer camp and
purchasing equipment for these children, through fund raising, by donating
equipment and building tables for the Irvine Complex, by volunteering their
services to the C.N.I.B. to help with their bingos, by buying a mile for the
Rick Hansen World Tour, and other community projects.

Lions clubs get together at different locations for zone meetings, ceremonies
and banquets. Here they get an opportunity to meet other Lion members from
different countries and neighbouring provinces to exchange ideas, pins and
fellowship.

As a member of an international organization this local Lions Club hopes to
remain active in this community.

Irvine Mercurys
by Bert Ehrman

In 1950, when I joined the Irvine Mercurys, Art Wittke and George Doktor were
our star pitchers. Chester Ambrose was our short stop and as I recall other
members included Harvey, Roy and Clarence Schaffer, Otto and Victor Wiedemann,
Jim and Cecil Hausauer, and Leslie Woodward.

The only competitor we had at this time was the Elkwater team which included
Harvey and Lawrence Good, Albert and Emil Neubauer, Jim Schneider, Dave Kusler
and John Beierbach.

I believe it was 1953 when we couldn't field a team in Irvine, so we moved to
Walsh to combine forces, which really turned out quite well. Ernie McKay was
appointed as our manager and Roy Ayling was our coach. At this time we almost
had enough players to field two teams. We had Jim Schlenker, Harry Heller,
Bruce Brandt and Norman Mock pitching. As far as I can remember, the rest of
the team consisted of Henry Ziegenhagel, Henry (Hank) Haag, Peter Rolick,
Harold Mock, Ed Nitschke, Jim Hausauer, Allister and Hugh MacArther, and
myself, Bert Ehrman. It was a fun year.

The following spring of 1954, Bob Lindsay moved into the district and called a
meeting for all interested ball players. Bob appointed himself as playing
coach. We had no equipment, not even a decent diamond to play on, so we decided
to put on a Mother's Day supper to raise money. We traveled around the district
and asked people to donate a chicken or two. The people were to be commended
for their co-operation. In fact we stole two chickens from Harvey Good. There
was no one home, so we picked out two big fat ones and when we saw him we told
him. He said "you should have taken more." Our supper was a great success. with
the help of our mothers and friends.

Irvine Mercury Ball Team: Pete Rollick, Norman Mock, Berl Ehrman, Harry Heller,
Art Wittke, Bob Lindsay, Ed Nitschke, Henry Haag, Henry Ziegenhagel; Kneeling:
Ernie McKay, Stanley Schlaht (pic)

We made enough money to buy all the equipment we needed, plus build a good
diamond and dugouts.

Later we joined the Sask-Alta League. As I recall, it consisted of two Medicine
Hat teams, Hilda, Schuler, Fox Valley, Burstal, Leader, Maple Creek, Richmound
and the Irvine-Walsh Mercurys.

At this point the work began for us players. Bob was a terrific coach and he
made us work hard to get into shape. Needless to say, he had his hands full
with all of us green farmers. It was a great success. We had more fans at our
games than any other team. The excitement was so great that on several
occasions Ernie McKay was seen with two cigarettes going at one time.

Art Wittke stayed our star pitcher, Henry (Hank) Haag was back catcher, Ed
Nitschke first base, Norman Mock second base, Bob Lindsay playing coach, Henry
Ziegenhagel short stop, and Harry Heller covered third; Jim Hausauer was our
star lead off batter and played left field; I played centre and first on
occasion; right field was covered by Ray Ehrman and Peter Rolick. When Ed
Nitschke quit, I played first base, and Ray Ehrman covered center. We also had
"strong arm" Dave Kusler who played most any position, including pitching.
George Doktor and Bruce Brandt also pitched. Stanley Schlaht was our bat boy
and did a marvelous job of it.

Bert and Ray Ehrman, 1958 (pic)

In 58 or 59, the League split up, and since we hardly had any Walsh players
left, we moved back to Irvine. At this time the Irvine Mercurys consisted of
Norman and Stan Gill, Paul Vaessen, Bruce Brandt, Maurice Engel, Leslie
Woodward, George Schlaht, Ray Ehrman, Jim Hausauer, and myself, Bert Ehrman. No
doubt there are others I can't recall at this time. We had a smaller league,
which to my knowledge consisted of Hilda, Schuler, Medicine Hat and Maple Creek.

Needless to say, it was good fellowship and left beautiful memories that will
never be forgotten.

First Irvine Band ready to play (pic)

Stage curtain in Magnet Theatre (pic)

Some dances of note were (1) New Year's Eve Masquerade in 1906, held at the
Irvine School. Admission was $1 for gentlemen and ladies free; (2) May 3, 1907,
Irvine Opera House opening dance hosted by Carl Beny with the Men of Hussars
supplying the music; (3) February 13, 1914, Mephistos Valentine Ball, with
music supplied by J. Barrigan, H. Steinecher, Vic Crawford and Clyde Polloch.
Dances listed in dance cards issued at Balls included Grand March, Waltz, Two
step, Three step, French Minuet, Schottische and Lancers.

An article from the Medicine Hat News in 1988 read as follows: Had there been a
Guinness Book of Records 83 years ago, a group of Irvine young people might
have been accused of trying for a record. The story, on March 9, 1905, was
titled DANCED AROUND THE CLOCK. IRVINE YOUNG PEOPLE ENJOY THEMSELVES FOR TWELVE
CONSECUTIVE HOURS.

"The Irvine Dance came off on Friday evening in the schoolhouse and was largely
patronized, those attending having a delightful time. Dancing began at eight
o'clock prompt and was kept up till eight o'clock next morning, which makes a
record for the Medicine Hat district. Music was furnished by Mr. Allan Irwin
and Mrs. Darling of Medicine Hat. The floor was in splendid shape. A luncheon
was served in the spacious dining room of the Golden West Hotel.

Our Pioneers
by Ben Otto Sr.

When our folks came to this land,
They got not a helping hand.
They had to labour every day,
But never did they get much pay.

Their house was built of sod alone,
And then this was their very own.
The pots and pans hung on the wall,
When needed, they could reach them all.

Tractors they had not at all,
Only oxen in the stall.
The farmer's work was never done
They laid the furrows one by one.

For many years the grass had grown,
I'm sure it only once was sown.
In summer they did mow the hay,
A colder day was on its way.

We always had enough to eat,
But candies were to us a treat.
We had not many clothes to wear,
But we were young and didn't care.

We thank our parents for what they've done,
We know they did not have much fun.
God had led them by the hand,
Into a better promised land.

By now our folks are laid to rest,
We know that they had stood the test.
Many days have gone by,
And it almost makes me cry.

The Model T
by Ben Otto Sr.

There was a time when we were bored,
Then went to town and bought a Ford.
It was a pretty thing to see,
Because it was a Model T.

This did make us feel so proud,
You could hear us think aloud.
That was quite a car you know,
For now no more would we go slow.

It had power we know of course,
Because we'd passed a running horse.
We were happy as can be,
For now we owned that Model T.

The car was nice so sleek and black,
Never would we give it back.
A better friend could never be,
Than that good old Model T.


                                    Family Histories

Jacob and Elizabeth (Schmidt) Aman
by Ted Aman

Jacob Aman was born in Russia, and at the age of ten years immigrated to South
Dakota with his parents, Philip and Rosina Aman.

Elizabeth Schmidt came to South Dakota with her parents in 1885 at the age of
five years.

In 1898 they were married and farmed in the area of Eureka, South Dakota until
1903 when they moved to Alberta, Canada and took up residence just cast of the
Bob Porter Ranch headquarters, where they farmed and ranched in horses and
cattle and also had a dairy herd. They sold butter and eggs to Kalmbach's store
and took chips. These you could use to buy goods from his store.

Eight children were born to this marriage, and no school operating nearby.

In 1914 the family moved to lots adjoining the town of Irvine where they built
a new home. There were about fifteen acres surveyed in lots and at one time
there were nine homes in what was known as the Holland addition to the Town of
Irvine. In the event of ten homes being built we would automatically become
part of the Town of Irvine. Most of the people had cows, pigs and chickens and
one flock of sheep plus some horses. While the town cows went east with the
town herdsman, the cows from our immediate neighborhood went west and were
brought home with our cows. There was still a lot of open range both east and
west of the town.

We all attended school at Irvine up to grade eight. I was required to go to
Medicine Hat for grade nine.

Dad bought the Loyd farm, one mile north of Irvine in 1917, and Jacob, Rosie,
Christina and 1, Ted, lived on that while the family were still home. Later we
farmed it from our residence bordering the town. We built some accommodation
for milk cows and horses and went to milking cows and making butter which we
sold to customers in Medicine Hat on Fridays. They were cold winters with lots
of snow. There were no roads to speak of, certainly no snow plows, just a big
shovel.

There were no heaters in the cars and no antifreeze in the radiators. We had
our regular customers and did get 350 a pound for butter and 300 a quart for
sweet cream. It was the milk cows that took us through the drought years of the
thirties. Russian thistle was our main feed supply.

I lived with the folks and did both their farming and my own as I had some land
of my own and had some rented. In 1929 Dad traded horses for a Hart Parr
tractor and plow and disc.

In 1945 Dad and Mother sold their house and their land, some to me and some to
Art Zeller, and bought a home in Medicine Hat, which they sold later and took
up residence in the Haven of Rest.

Dad was chairman of the Irvine School District 892 for many years, and an
original member of what is now the Peace United Church, where he served as
treasurer for many years. He was an avid horseman and had a good percheron
stallion on stud for many years, and traveled a route through the south country
annually, leaving many good horses. He knew the country well, and traveled with
the different cattle buyers who scoured the country in the fall. He was a good
judge of both horses and cattle and was able to assist buyers in determining
weight as cattle were bought on the hoof.

Bertha married Konstantine Maser and they farmed in the Clover Hill district.
They had six children.

Jacob Aman married Margaret Diedelbach and they farmed the Mason farm and later
the Kalmbach farm.

Rosie married Fred Hildebrand and they farmed in the Norton district and later
moved to Little Plume. In 1936 they moved to a farm in Wetaskiwin, Alberta.
They had ten children.

Christina married William Hehr and they moved to Sacramento, California and
worked for Libby, McNeil and Libby Canneries. They had no family.

Emma married Ira Wright in Alhambra, California. They had two children.

Ted married Anna Ebel and they farmed at Irvine. They had six children.

Mary worked in the Medicine Hat Potteries for many years and married Adam
Miller, and they ranched near Maple Creek, Saskatchewan. They had no family.

Edward never married, and is now residing in the Pleasant View Lodge in Bow
Island.

Ted and Anna (Ebel) Aman
by Ted Aman

Ted Aman was born on May 29th, 1907 in the Stony Creek area, adjacent to the
Bob Porter ranch headquarters, the son of Jacob and Elizabeth Aman.

In 1914, I moved with my family to lots bordering the Town of Irvine, known as
the Holland addition to the town.

I attended school in Irvine up to grade eight, and well remember the day when
the two room brick school burned down. It was a very cold day, thirty below,
and it was a real tragedy. Two classes moved to what is now the museum, and two
classes moved back to the old stone building. I took my grade nine in Medicine
Hat and quit school at sixteen.

I farmed for my dad till I was 23, and also ran a dray delivering coal around
town in the fall. My dad had bought the Loyd farm in 1917 and I lived there for
several years with my older brother and two sisters, walking to school one
mile. In 1930 I rented land from Henry Crooks and farmed that and my dad's land
in partnership till 1940. In the year 1934, I bought the Fischer farm,
adjoining the quarter I got from home. In the fall of 1940, I bought my first
combine and John Deere tractor, and did a lot of custom work, both combining
and making summer fallow.

On December 15, 1940 I was married to Anna Ebel, of Surprise, Saskatchewan and
we moved to the Fischer farm.

We milked some cows and delivered butter and eggs to Medicine Hat, as we had
for many years with Mother and Dad. I purchased a number of dairy cows from
Burnside Farms and we increased our herd to 17 cows. We also purchased a milk
machine which made milking easier. During that time we delivered cream to
Medicine Hat and also delivered milk daily to residents of Irvine.

Norman was born in 1942, Harvey in 1944, and Raymond in 1946.

We sold our dairy in 1946 to my brother-in-law, Fred Hildebrand, and bought the
old Aman home from Otto Wittke, and moved just as the cold weather set in. This
was an improvement over what we had.

In January, 1948 our first daughter Betty was born. In June, 1949 our second
daughter Joyce was born.

In 1950 we purchased the Fred Schneider home, so handy to the school, as Norman
and Harvey were already attending, and here we had 32 volt power.

That same year I was elected to the Board of School Division No. 4. We had
started vanning quite a number of school children from the country to Irvine.
We needed a new six room school in Irvine to accommodate grades one to twelve.
We had a plebiscite which would allow us to borrow the necessary funds, and it
was turned down. Conditions were such that something had to be done. I spoke to
the trustees' convention, and got a sympathetic response. The Provincial
Inspector called a meeting with the other members of the Board, and was
prepared to over-rule the plebiscite if they agreed. They did not agree, but
decided to borrow the $40,000 we were allowed and finance the balance from
current revenue. The board decided to build it at cost, rather than by
contract. They asked me to be in charge of hiring labour and buying material,
with a carpenter in charge of construction. I agreed to this and immediately
got busy getting a plan for four classrooms upstairs, and an auditorium and two
classrooms downstairs for Shop and Home Ec. There was no redi-mix at that time,
so we had to mix the cement on site, and haul it to where it was needed by
wheel barrow. We tried to use all the local help possible. At first everybody
wanted to work, but as soon as it rained, the farmers had other things to do,
and it took a lot of scouting around to get enough help. However, we built the
school with a new well and a diesel lighting plant, for $85,000 which was
$25,000 less than Foremost paid for the same plan by contract. My remuneration
was 100 per mile for all necessary travel.

In April 1951 our youngest son Wesley was born, right after a blizzard that
stopped all highway traffic.

In 1958 we built a new home on the farm, with all the modern facilities, as
power was now available on farms.

Throughout the years I have served as member of the Church board, and taught
Sunday School for all of 35 years. I served on the local school board for
District 892 until I was elected to No 4 Division and served also on the
Provincial Farm Purchase Board. I was Secretary of the local farm organization
and also of the Social Credit group.

We have had our good years, and our bad. In 1961, we had no rain and grass
didn't turn green. There was no water in dams or dugouts. We threshed 35
bushels from 500 acres of crop. We hauled our breeding stock to Suffield
Community Pasture, and rented a quarter of hay-land in the irrigation for feed.
We had to buy our seed and still, by the Grace of God, we can't say that we
suffered.

Our family all took part in 4-H and I was a leader for one year.

Ted Aman Family: Back: Wesley, Harvey, Norman, Raymond; Front: Joyce, Ted,
Annie, Betty (pic)

Norman took up accounting and moved to Calgary.

Harvey stayed on the farm and we bought the Oberhammer farm, which he farmed
for a number of years. He married Elaine Matuska. They have one boy.

Raymond took up teaching, and is now Principal at Riverside School. He married
Darlene Jans. They have one girl and two boys.

Betty married Ron Sauter and lives on a farm southwest of Irvine. They have
three boys.

Joyce took up secretarial work and teaching and taught at Calgary Tec. She
married Peter Camber and moved from Calgary to Toronto, where she attended
university, received her degree in Education and has been teaching. They have
no family.

Wesley married Peggy Coulard and lives in Medicine Hat. He was on the farm for
a few years, but sold out and moved to Medicine Hat. They have two girls and
two boys.

When we quit the home place, we moved to Medicine Hat for a year and a half.
Then we sold our home in Medicine Hat, moved back to Irvine, and bought the Vic
Sky place. Later we sold this home and built a new home in Aman View, right
across the road from were we farmed.

Anna had the misfortune of falling and breaking her leg. She was confined to
hospital for seven months and never got back on her feet. She was in the wheel
chair for four years. She became ill and was taken to hospital where she died
suddenly of a heart attack.

My family surprised me on my eightieth birthday, and it was a real surprise. My
sister Emma and her son Bob and his wife came from California and we had a very
nice evening together, with a lot of our friends. The whole family, including
our eleven grandchildren sang my favorite song (How Great Thou Art) and John
and Freda Ebel sang a duet. There were numerous readings and other
presentations. Reverend and Mrs. Angle were there and took part. Mrs. Angle
provided the music. We took a lot of pictures and it is certainly something to
look back to.

I have been on Town council for many years and now I serve as Mayor.

Ambrose Family
by Dorothy (Ambrose) Braham OZ

World War II began. Three small children watched the guns, the fire, and the
blood in the shimmering brilliance of the Northern Lights that winter. They
heard a lot about the war as they were shushed for every newscast on the radio.
Finally the father could stand it no longer; in June, 1940 when Jenny Lee was
born, he joined the Canadian Army. Three weeks later, the Ambrose family moved
from The Bench on top of the Cypress Hills to Irvine where there was a "good
school" and housing.

Our father, George Russell Ambrose, was born in Maple Creek in 1896 and passed
away in Medicine Hat in 1956 from injuries he sustained in a fall from a little
granary he was building. He served overseas for two years in the First World
War and for five years in the Second World War. In 1931 he married Mary
Wrobleski in Medicine Hat. He was a forest ranger in the Cypress Hills for 13
years and then postmaster in Irvine for six. Dad was filled with a love of life
and laughter.

Our mother, Mary Eva Wrobleski, was born in North Dakota in 1910 as the family
moved through northern United States to take up a homestead near Schuler. At a
very young age she became a "hired girl" for the Gorrell family in the
Willowbunch district of Southern Saskatchewan. She later cared for the Gorrells
in our home in Irvine for many years. Next she worked at the George Armstrong
ranch where she met our Dad. Mom devoted her life and her energy to her
children, stressing always the importance of an education, of honesty, and of a
respect for nature.

George and Mary Ambrose (pic)

At first, life in Irvine was traumatic as the new kids in town fought for their
place. Soon the family joined the rest with a strip of garden in the community
plot down by the creek and a cow in the back yard. We took our turn herding the
cows; this meant gathering the cows from each yard each morning, chasing them
to a community pasture and returning them at night - for $1 a cow a month. We
lived on $75 a month soldier's pay; rent was $15 and Dad had a hundred and
fifty dollars a year insurance policy that had to be kept up. All this meant
lots of home-made soup and headcheese. Gloria Jean was born in 1942 and somehow
our Mom managed alone to cope with five young kids in a cold, cold house,
mending and sewing clothes out of old ones by the light of a coal-oil lamp late
into the night. The sidewalks in Irvine were uneven wood planks. With the soles
of our shoes usually loose and flapping we often tripped and another knee in
the stocking had to be replaced.

School, piano lessons from Dorothy Davidson, violin lessons (and chocolate
bars) from Ira Atkinson, the elevator man, and chores kept the children busy.
Finally the war ended and our Dad came home. The Rehabilitation Years were
difficult as Dad tried unsuccessfully to get his old job back, tried forestry
at Bragg Creek, bought the Hausauer Store in Irvine which eventually failed
with competition from three others, picked rocks for the Trail Smelter, and
finally became Postmaster. In the meantime, Mom started a small dairy in 1949
that continued until pasteurized milk came to Irvine in the sixties. The
Ambrose kids, carrying milk in old army bags, became a familiar sight in Irvine
as did the hated job of washing bottles on the home front. In 1953 a car
slammed into the herd of milk cows crossing the highway at sunset. Our greatest
fear had happened.

The emphasis of school in our lives drew results as three of us became
teachers, one a nurse and one a Mountie.

Dorothy, Jean, Flora, Jenny. Inset: Chester Ambrose (pic)

George Chester was a member of the RCMP for twenty-three years, retiring as a
staff sergeant. He married Joan Jenkins of Pashley and they raised three
children. Randal, Ardella and Tannis. The family owns a clothing store in Peace
River.

Dorothy became a school teacher and married George Braham. Their family
includes Karen, Cindy and Andrew. They are retired in Trochu where George was
principal for eighteen years.

Flora also obtained a teaching degree and is the librarian in the high school
in Stettler, where she lives with her sons, Jason and Cameron.

Jenny taught school also. She is married to Robert King-Brown and had three
children -Michael Hinchcliffe of Vancouver, Stephen and Shannon of Lethbridge.

Jean nurses in the Red Dear Hospital. She married William Bell and they have
three sons -Warren, Daniel, and Aaron.

Jenny, Flora, Mary, George, Dorothy, Jean Ambrose - 1978 (pic)

As everyone left home, Bill Schneider and his horse, Copper came to live at our
place. Billy, then in grade seven, went to school and helped with chores until
he graduated.

Our Mother continued to run the Post Office in Irvine until 1975. She enjoyed
growing her flowers and garden, and raising cattle until she died in January of
1981. Her death ended forty years of our story and our lives in Irvine. But
Irvine will' always be part of our roots; its badlands, its chinook winds, the
smell of wolf willow along the creek, and its people are woven into our
memories.

Paul Ammann Family
by Paul Ammann

I, Paul Ammann was born in Winterthur, Switzerland on February 9, 1904, son of
Jacob Ammann, a steam engineer of a large factory in the city of Winterthur,
Switzerland with a family of eight children.

I was educated there including a machine apprenticeship. Realizing that there
was no future for advancement in Switzerland, I decided to immigrate to Canada
in the spring of 1927, after seeing an advertisement in the Swiss paper for
people to come to Canada to work on farms. My first job was on a farm near
Newburg, Saskatchewan but as my English wasn't up to par, I decided to attend
school in Regina to learn the language more thoroughly.

In 1929, I moved south of Irvine to a farm belonging to the uncle of Bertha
Sulz who eventually became my wife in the fall of 1931. We worked on Bertha's
home farm for a few years, then bought one of our own nearby. When it came time
for the children to go to high school, we moved to Medicine Hat, where I worked
part-time for an implement company, until I retired at the age of 69. I am the
only surviving member of my family, but I keep in touch with some nephews in
Switzerland and have visited my homeland twice since coming to Canada. Our farm
was southeast of Irvine with our neighbour, Emerson Porter, living only two
miles north of us. In the spring of 1943, we built our first house with the
help of William Sulz, my father-in-law who then lived in Medicine Hat. The only
outside worker was a plasterer from "the Hat" as we called it.

Paul Ammann Family: Back: Edwin, Paul Jr., Fred, Arthur, Werner; Front: Bertha,
Paul, Gladys (pic)

We raised a fairly good quality of milk cows that kept the family healthy and
strong. We never lacked eggs or bacon during those dry years. The last two
years (1936-1937) were the worst when everything blew out and we couldn't even
make any feed for our livestock. In order to get feed from the government, we
had to sell our milk cows down to four cows. This was the rule, "four children
and you get feed for four cows!" Some of our neighbours tried to get by with
stacks of thistles, but sad to say, they lost most of their stock in 1937-38,
as there was no grass, either. Land was getting cheap to buy and when we had
saved some money in the next few years we were able to buy good land around us
for $1,000 to $2,500 a quarter.

Our oldest son, Werner wanted to stay on the farm and in time purchased the
land before it really went up in price. The rest of the children "flew the
coop" so to say and are well-established now with their own families.

The dream I had 60 years ago to immigrate to Canada, a promised land by the
advertisers, became true in my case. Due to a good wife and helping
father-in-law, plus God's blessing, we reached our goal and now enjoy our old
age in the Medicine Hat Primrose Villa.

"Honor thy father and thy mother that thy days may be long upon the land which
the Lord, thy God giveth" has been my guide through life.

Werner P. Ammann Family
by Werner Ammann

I am the eldest son of Paul and Bertha (Sulz) Ammann. Our land location is NE
28-10-2-4. I lived there all my life until 1979, when we sold the farm and
moved to the Medicine Hat area. (A6) - RR is my brand. (PA) - RR was my dad,
Paul Ammann's. It was registered in the thirties and passed on to his grandson,
Lyle. LR is Brent's brand.

Werner Ammann Family: Back: Brent, Lyle, Gilda; Front: Werner, Ruth (pic)

I was married July 30, 1955 to Gilda Schock from Glenbain, Saskatchewan. God
blessed our home with three children.

Lyle Douglas, born July 13, 1958, farms and ranches south of Medicine Hat.

Ruth Gilda, born June 9, 1962, married Kenneth Sailer on June 11, 1983. They
farm and ranch in the Elkwater area. They have two sons, Jason, born June 19,
1984 and Blaine, born March 5, 1986.

Brent Werner, born October 13, 1964, is still at home with his parents, south
of Dunmore.

I have served on various committees and organizations. I worked on the Cypress
R.E.A. to get power to the farms in the late fifties and on the Irvine Mutual
Telephone Company in 1967, and this committee was able to get underground
telephone in the area. I also helped to organize several community pastures,
serving as secretary for the Cressday Grazing Association. I am also serving as
President of Southern Alberta Grazing Association, which gives the opportunity
to work with government people on pasture and grazing problems. I helped and am
presently serving on the 11-22 Co-op Seed Plant Board. It was started in 1959
with the Chamber of Commerce holding a meeting concerning the need for a seed
cleaning plant in the area. Due to drought conditions in 1960 and 1961 it was
held up and on October 13, 1964 the official opening of the plant was held. We
were at the banquet when I had to take my wife to the hospital for Brent to be
born. To this date a lot of joking and ribbing goes on at the board because of
this. Not very often is a son born to the secretary and his wife on the
official opening of a seed plant. It has been a neat experience and a pleasure
to serve on this board for 26 years.

We as a family have been involved in church work all our lives in the Newburg
area and the Elkwater area.

South Eastern Alberta is known as the forgotten corner. In serving on various
boards over the years, I am convinced that we are. We were the last to receive
power, telephone, and roads. Roads in the 50's and 60's were something out of
this world, especially to get children to school. Mud or blocked with snow,
we'd get the children with tractor or team of horses from the bus, which seemed
to be stuck all the time. I am glad to say things have improved except for the
wind and drifting snow. On our farm it was the first to start and the last
place to quit. As a family we enjoyed our stay there and work in the community.
God has truly blessed and we thank Him.

John and Albina Arnold
by George Linderman

John Arnold was born in South Russia. He and his wife Albina (Melham) and
family came to Canada in 1903 to a farm five miles south and two miles east of
Irvine. They had three girls and five boys.

John Arnold - 1918 (pic)

Albina died in 1905. John Arnold moved to Irvine in 1923 and his son, Henry,
took over the farm.

Henry was married to Pauline Leicht. They had four boys and two girls who
attended Berry Centre School.

Pauline married John Linderman. They had five children.

Henry and Pauline Arnold
by Howard Arnold

As most of you know we farmed south of Irvine. There were six of us children:
Eddie, Henry, Howard, Alvina, Alice and Clarence. We all went to Berry Centre
School, when it was still down along Ross Creek. I can still remember we had to
go barefooted, as there was no money to buy shoes. In 1936, our dad left us, so
Mother moved into Irvine and we went to school there in the spring of 1937. I
went out to work for Harry Faulkner, and in the summer Mother moved to Whitla,
and we boys worked around Whitla and Bow Island.

Henry Arnold Family - 1930: Back: Howard, Henry, Pauline, Henry Sr., Eddy;
Front: Alvina, Clarence, Alice (pic)

In February, 19411 joined the Army, and July 4th I went overseas. Henry joined
up in 1942. He was sent to France, where he was badly wounded, but he made it
o.k. Eddie and Alice (Robinson) went in the services in 1943. The same year I
went to Africa. From there I went to Sicily, then to Italy where I was in
hospital for five months. I was sent back to England after that, and that was
when I got married to my lovely wife Edith, in 1945. Clarence went in the Army
in 1945 and stayed for thirty years. He now lives in Victoria, B.C. The rest of
us all live in Medicine Hat, Alberta.

Nick and Mary Babuk 1929 to 1935
by Florence Hofer

In the spring of 1929 Nick and Mary Babuk and family, Florence, William, Helen
and Stanley, moved into Irvine from the small hamlet of Pashley, Alberta about
seven miles west of Irvine, now non existent. My father worked for the C.P.R.
as a section foreman. Schooling was his reason for moving as Florence had
already started school, and was boarding at the Colonel Jenkins home in Pashley
in order to attend a small country school, which I believe was called Abelene.
My first school report card in Irvine of April 1929 shows that Miss Jean
Courtice was my first teacher there. Actually my first teacher at Abelene was
Mrs. Drinnon. My two brothers and sister started school in Irvine and Miss
Courtice taught them also.

Nick, Mary Babuk and Florence (Babuk) Hofer (pic)

We lived in a two story, C.P.R. company house on the north side of the tracks
on the east end of town. The house is no longer there. It was torn down due to
modernization of C.P.R. policy, I believe. Our home was not insulated as well
as many others in this period of time, nor was it heated by a furnace. We had
no electricity, running water or indoor bathroom. No telephone, radio or T.V.
back then either.

Babuk Home (pic)

In November 1935, when I was in grade eight, my dad decided to leave Irvine
again because of schooling. He wanted his children to get all the education he
was able to give them, and this time we moved to Leader, Saskatchewan where we
received our high school.

Today our parents are no longer with us. Nick, our father, passed away on
February 3, 1959 and Mary, our mother, passed away on August 23, 1978.

Babuk Children: Back: Stanley, William; Front: Helen, Florence - 1934 (pic)

The years in between, found William following his father's footsteps, by
working for the C.P.R. as a station agent in several points in Alberta and
Saskatchewan. He married Margaret Lyster of Empress, Alberta in December, 1947.
They have two sons and a daughter, an adopted son, and four grandchildren. He
is presently retired and they live in Calgary.

Stanley attended University in Saskatoon and upon graduation went to Calgary to
work for Sun Oil Company, where he worked until 1984, when he had to take early
retirement because of his health. He married Thelma Corrigan of Ferme, B.C. in
September, 1959, and they have three daughters and four grandchildren. They
also live in Calgary.

After graduation from high school, Helen worked for a Leader newspaper. Her
marriage to Bill Kowatch of Estuary, Saskatchewan took place in September of
1947. They have two sons and a daughter, seven grandchildren and one great
grandchild. When Helen's family grew to be young teenagers, she went back into
the work force, working in a Nursing Home in Leader. She is presently widowed
and main cook in the Nursing Home. She lives in Leader.

Florence stayed home to help her mother upon graduation from high school. She
married Robert Hofer of Leader, Saskatchewan in May 1942 in Sudbury, Ontario.
They moved to Whitby, Ontario shortly after, where she helped win the war by
filling and reaming shells for a Shell Plant in Ajax, Ontario. In August, 1943,
she moved to Vancouver to buck rivets for Boeing Aircraft, assembling war
planes, in 1947 left the coast and followed her husband to several points in
Saskatchewan and Alberta, eventually landed in Medicine Hat in September, 1962
back to where she was born. They have a daughter. She is married and living in
the city also. They are presently retired and enjoy their Golden Years with
their three grandchildren living near by.

People often refer to the thirties as the hard time, the dirty thirties, the
dust bowl, etc. My recollections of the days we lived in Irvine when we were
children were happy ones. I realize though, parents then must have had many
difficulties raising a family.

Gottlieb and Christeana Banek
by Edna (Maser) Schau, granddaughter

Gottleib was born in Russia, May 30, 1868. Christeana (Kern) Banek was born in

little girl on the ocean when coming to North America. Four children were born
while they lived in South Dakota: Jacob, Lydia, Gottlieb, and Richard.

Gottlieb and Christeana Banek (pic)

Gottlieb and Christeana came to Canada about 1901 and got a homestead about
fifteen miles south of Irvine. Their first home was a sod house built by
themselves. They built a farm home later when their economy was better. Two
more children were born while they lived here, Katherina and Ida.

Their son Richard took over the farm around 1925 or 1926. Gottlieb and
Christeana moved to Irvine to live out their retirement years. Ida was still at
home and took her last years of school in Irvine.

Gottlieb died May 28, 1939 in his home at Irvine, the same day and time that
his first great grandchild was born - Donald Arthur Shau. Christeana died in
December, 1948, while she was a resident in the Baptist Haven of Rest in
Medicine Hat, Alberta. She was eighty years old.

Jacob was born July 11, 1891 at Campbell County, South Dakota. He was never
married and farmed in the Brooks area most of his life. He died in the spring
of 1974 at Brooks, Alberta.

Lydia, born August 27, 1895 at Campbell County, South Dakota, married Christian
Maser on April 7, 1916. They had four children.

Gottlieb, born November 22, 1897 at Campbell County, South Dakota, never
married. He died in Calgary before 1980 and is buried there.

Richard, born March 1, 1899 in Campbell County, South Dakota, married
Christianna Weiss March 27, 1923. They had seven children. Richard died
November 8, 1984 in Brooks, Alberta.
