Alexander and Katharina Bechtold
by George Bechtold, Oliver, B.C.

1870: Shouted curses of bullwhackers echoed from banks and bluffs along the
Bull trail as bulltrains from Montana brought firewater over the
Thunder-breeding Hills to the popular campsite where the Native People waited
to trade. Then, the gun was the only law, and killings sometimes resulted.

1884: The North West Mounted Police came to build Fort Walsh and Fort Macleod
and to patrol the hills and the short-grass plains.

1885: The Canadian Pacific Railway sprout towns along the way. Fort Walsh was
abandoned when Medicine Hat became Headquarters of wide Patrol Area. In time,
the Campsite became 20 Mile Post, a Supply Depot for the Red-coated Riders.

1905: A boom-town had grown up around 20 Mile Post and was named Irvine, after
a Superintendent of the North West Mounted Police. The prairie lands were
surveyed, and homesteads in the shadow of the Hills (now Cypress Hills on the
map) were being filed on daily as sod-busters came in from Latvia, Bessarabia,
the Ukraine, Britain, Scandinavia, and the U.S.A.

Enter the Bechtolds.

Alexander and Katherina Bechtold (pic)

1906: A pioneer living west of The Hills wrote of The New World to his
relatives in the Ukraine, the Volga Settlements, and the Caucasus in Russia. In
a wilderness area north of the sea of Azov, the stories about the Hills and
plains aroused a dream in the heart of one Alexander Bechtold, a Sergeant
locked for three years into the army of The Tsar of Russia. Alexander married
the petite Katharina Schaubert, so they dreamed together, of freedom and
independence, a place of their own, instead of the meager allotment of land in
the Caucasian village; and they saved and worked hard to lay by passage money
to the New World.

1910: At last there was enough money. Katharina's child was born four days
before the date of their excursion, but wild horses could not have kept her
back at that point. A week on the 4th Class Car (a boxcar made over) to
Bremerhaven in Germany, ten days on the stormy Atlantic in a huge passenger
liner to New York, then four days and nights on the CPR from Montreal to
Irvine, where their relatives, the Baumbacks and Dells, gave them shelter.

Bechtold Home (pic)

1911: Alexander and Katharina became Alex and Katie to their friends and
neighbors when they found work on larger farms and ranches. Alex found a
homestead beside The Spring, once a popular Indian campground, surrounded by
teepee rings and a web of converging buffalo trails - and a million bleaching
bones. He built a cabin on weekends, marked off his west half of Section
21-12-2, the beginning of the reality of his dream. In spring of 1912, Katie
and her infant son moved out onto the open prairie, five miles north and east
of Irvine. All around were the wild range cattle, the "broomtails" (wild
cayuses) and the ducks on the ponds and coyotes in the coulees. No more village
choir or daily visitors, only distance and silence and loneliness. The high
dark line of The Bench, the forest on the Cypress Hills, dominated the immense
landscape. No fences or buildings were in sight. The meadow lark which perched
on the hitching post and sang each day was the only visitor at first, till the
neighbors discovered her, neighbors who also came from far away to find a
homestead. Alex had secured a job as porter and bartender in the Golden West
Hotel in Irvine. He walked home late Saturday night, and back into town early
on Monday morning.

1915: Alex commenced full-time farming operations in the boom year of 1915,
with a granary full of wheat and a huge straw pile, which became a favorite
romping site for children in later years. Their neighbors were the Albert
Tohms, Albert Engels, Robert and Isaac Baumbacks, Ted Zieglers, Ed Wilcox, the
Levi Lutz family and Charlie Winberg. To the east lived the Thomas Woods, Otto
Brandts, and the Roll family with several sons taking up homesteads - and later
on came the Albert Woodwards, Zellers, and Trekofskis.

Wilkinson School stood on a windy plain nearly three miles westward, and was
attended by Bechtold children from 1916 until the larger School Units were set
up in the early 40's. Alexander and Katharina lived on their homestead for 40
years and raised ten children. George had been brought with them from the
Crimea. Emma, Ida, Anne, Sylvia, Elly, Ethel, Fred, Irvine, and Roy, all
absorbed their three R's in Wilkinson. The three boys finished in Irvine School.

Alex and Katie became well known, driving to market in Medicine Hat and Irvine
in their democrat drawn by a pair of gray broncos from the open range. There
were always steady customers for their table cream and dairy butter, eggs,
frying chicken, vegetables and berries.

1951: in 1951 a violent blizzard covered their house with four feet of snow for
three days. Fred was home and wielded a mighty shovel to help save the house,
and their lives. So Alex and Katie sold their old home and spent the rest of
their time growing great trees and beds of flowers near their eldest son and
daughter's families in the Okanagan Valley in B.C. Alex passed on in 1966 in
his 81st year. Katie lived on until she was 87. She and Lotta Schwarts, a
former schoolmate from the Crimea, were rooming together, and both passed on in
the same week.

Sylvia, Emma, Ida, Annie, Elly, Ethel and Katherina Bechtold (pic)

Now, like a ship sunk in the ocean, the old homestead has vanished from the
face of the earth. Only a few gnarled old elms and maples mark the spot where a
vigorous family had studied and played and earned a living for 40 eventful
years.

The Present Whereabouts of the Bechtold Family
by Ida Wood

Mom and Dad have both passed over the "Great Divide".

George and his wife, Helen, have recently retired to Oliver, B.C.

Emma and her husband, Albert Reimche, have an acreage on the outskirts of
Armstrong, B.C. with some of their family living nearby.

Ida, with her husband Tom Wood, of Irvine, live within five miles of the old
Bechtold homestead.

Back: Irvine, Fred, George; Front: Roy, Alexander Bechtold (pic)

Annie, who lost her husband a number of years ago, now lives in an apartment in
New Westminster, B.C.

Sylvia, who lost her husband about five years ago, is remarried and living in
Victoria, B.C.

Elly, and her husband, Jim MacKenzie, who has recently retired from work, are
now living in Surrey, B.C.

Ethel, and her husband, Bob Turner, live on an acreage near High River,
Alberta. Ethel works as a stenographer in the Agricultural office in High
River, while Bob works at many things, one of them being cattle.

Fred died in a fishing accident a number of years ago, after receiving the
Award for the biggest fish of the Derby.

Irvine, who was draughtsman for an oil company in Calgary for years, was laid
off and now owns a Bottle Depot. His wife, Elaine, works as a doctor's
receptionist in Calgary.

Roy is maintenance engineer in the Calgary University. His wife, Rosemarie,
works with the Calgary Herald.

During World War II, Sylvia was in the Canadian Women's Army Corps, and was
stationed in London, England. Elly was in the Canadian Air Force, also being
stationed in London, England. She had the experience of surviving a bombing
raid; some of the plaster of the ceiling of her room was blown off. George was
in the army stationed on Vancouver Island instructing personnel in
Identification of enemy aircraft. Irvine was in the Air Force as Driver Trainer
down east in various locations. Roy was also in the Air Force and after the war
worked as machinist at Suffield Research station for a number of years.

The Jacob Bechtold Family
by Chris Bechtold

Jacob was the oldest son of Henry and Margarete Bechtold, who emigrated from
Neu Doenhoff, Russia. Leaving their farm home on September 17, 1901, Henry, and
his wife Margarete, came as far as Winnipeg. There he worked as a tailor before
coming west to the homestead. Their first homestead was somewhere south of
Elkwater. That homestead was a bad piece of land so they relocated south of
Irvine where Jacob grew up.

Louise was born in Klichstahl, Russia on June 8, 1914 to Christian and Louise
Gust. She lost her family to the flu. Louise came to Irvine on August 21, 1926
with Mr. and Mrs. John Will. She was their adopted daughter and grew up with
her step sister, Katherine and step brother William.

Jacob was married to Lousie (Gust) Will, of Irvine, on October 15, 1936. After
getting married, Jacob and Louise farmed south of Irvine for seven years along
with operating the local threshing crew with a separator and Case tractor. He
also built barns in the surrounding area to make ends meet. Story has it that
Jacob came to town to buy a load of lumber to build a blacksmith shop on his
farm. Word of this got from Schneider's Lumber Yard to Andrew Glock, who was
one of the town blacksmiths. Andrew managed to convince Jacob to buy the
business. On October 15, 1943 Jacob and Louise moved into Irvine and they built
a new blacksmith and welding shop in 1946 to replace to old wooden "Glock"
building. He ran this business until semi-retiring in 1975 and finally closing
the doors completely in 1983.

Jacob also served on the town council from 1964 until retiring from civic
politics in 1983. Louise worked in Medicine Hat, Haven of Rest, until retiring
in 1979 and they are still happily retired in Irvine.

Born to the Jacob Bechtold family were three sons and one daughter: Christian
(Chris), born August 6, 1937; Wilbert David, May 25, 1942; Clarence Leonard,
January 4, 1947; and Louise Lorine, September 22, 1949. At the time of this
writing Jacob and Louise had ten grandchildren, with eight still living, and
two great-grandchildren.

Bechtold Family: Jacob, Wilbert, Louise Lorine, Louise, Clarence, Chris (pic)

Mother, Margarete Bechtold moved to Irvine in July 1948 and lived there until
she moved to Medicine Hat, Haven of Rest, in 1962, where she resided until her
passing in February 1965.

John and Rosina Becker

Like so many of the settlers that came to Canada, John Becker and his wife
Rosina (Moser) were Russian immigrants. Leaving their farm in Russia, they
started a new life in North Dakota, U.S.A. Here, five children were born,
Elizabeth, Albert, Lydia, Beata and Robert.

From Elgin, North Dakota, they traveled by train arriving in Irvine, Alberta,
in the late summer of 1910. Here John ran the dray service and made harnesses
for settlers. The three youngest children attended school. In the spring of
1911, the family moved to Hilda, Alberta, where they took up homesteads, until
1925. Then John, Rosina, Albert, Robert and his wife Lindina (Hoffman) moved to
the Stony Plain district.

Rosina passed away in 1942. John moved to Medicine Hat in 1947 and passed away
later that year.

Robert and Lindina moved back to Hilda in 1929 with two of their children and
later to the Schuler district. Their family grew to seven children and then
they retired to Medicine Hat, where Robert and Lindina passed away.

John and Rosina's three daughters married in the Hilda district.

Elizabeth married Ludwig Lippert, and they later moved to the Vermilion
district, and had nine children. Elizabeth and Ludwig are now deceased.

Lydia married William Heringer and they farmed in the Horsham, Saskatchewan
district, until they retired to Medicine Hat. Lydia and William had eleven
children and are now both deceased.

Beata married Karl Heringer (brother of William) and they moved to the Rocky
Mountain House district and later retired to Rimbey. Both are deceased. They
had nine children.

Albert married but had no children. Albert and his wife Dorothy are deceased.

Karl Philip Becker
by Don Weiss

Irvine history would not be complete without some mention of this prominent
man. Because he had no known descendants, details of his life are sketchy. He
was a harness-maker and shoe maker by trade and had a well stocked business
place where he supplied most of the settlers in the district. He farmed for a
time southwest of Irvine as well.

He applied for a homestead on NW 28-11-3-W4 on April 9, 1904. At that time he
had a wife and three children and had British naturalization papers. He applied
for the patent on July 30, 1908. By then he had built a frame house, a stable,
a mile and a half of fence, and had broken 100 acres.

Karl Becker, or K.P. as he was known, was a devout and active member of the
Lutheran Church. There was a certain chair in the church that was occupied at
the services by no one else but K.P. It was a known and standing tradition that
only he would sit in that particular chair and no other member dared to
challenge this fact.

Mrs. and K.P. Becker - 1928 (pic)

Mr. Becker married Louise Schaller, widow of the late George Schaller of Irvine
in 1922 and it was a happy and content union. Some of the Schaller children
were still living at home and K.P. became a second father to them. The
Schaller-Becker house was a location for many a church member's birthday party
and a good many happy occasions were celebrated there. Louise died suddenly in
1927 at the age of 55 and Karl was a widower. He later remarried to a lady from
Manitoba. He passed away in July 1941 at the age of 76 and is buried in the
Irvine cemetery.

Philip Becker Sr. Family
by Edwin Gill

Philip Becker Sr. came to Canada in 1902 and lived with John Mayer for a period
of time while he was establishing a residence of some sort on his homestead
three miles west located on the SE 20-10-3-W4, in the Concordia district.

All information was obtained through visits to the homes of Philip Jr. and
Reinhold who are both retired in Medicine Hat.

Of a family of eleven, six have passed away as follows: Katie was married to
Andrew Rieger; Jacob married Katie Daffy; Rosie was married to Valentine
Rieger; Henry was married to Christina Rieger; Robert married Martha Heather;
and Albert died as a young lad.

Still living are Philip married to Emma Jeske; Tillie who was married to Adam
Schneider; Reinhold who was married to Selma Schwab; Adam, married to Ida
(Edith) Jeske; and Eva who was married to Ben Buechler.

When asked about early school days Philip Jr. relates that arithmetic was his
favorite subject and when the teacher wanted to pass him into a higher grade he
questioned the teacher as to why he should have to memorize a whole new book
when he already knew the one he had.

A story had been circulated, by old-timers, about Concordia School days (where
the Beckers had attended) that, on a warm day, with the windows wide open, the
teacher was busy writing on the blackboard and when he or she turned around all
the boys had left the school via the windows. When I confronted Reinhold with
this story he told me he was a good boy but did not deny that it could have
happened.

I asked Philip Jr. about life in the early 1900's and he told me about
threshing grain with a horse driven thresher owned by a Mr. Rieger and Jacob
Boschee. All grain was sacked at the machine and put on a flat deck to haul to
the farm where it was emptied into the granary. He said that was one of the
easiest jobs as the threshing was very slow. Their family made their living the
hard way, like everybody else, milking cows, raising chickens etc. but managed
to buy a new car in 1915.

The farm was sold to Reinhold and Emanuel Gill in 1922 when the Becker family
moved to the Schuler district and continued their farming.

Shirley May Belyea

I was born in Herbert, Saskatchewan, the youngest daughter in a family of four.

My father's family came from France and arrived in Canada, via the United
States in 1783.  I found it to be of interest that the first Lieutenant
Governor of Alberta, G. H. U. Bulyea, who in 1909 signed the proclamation
pronouncing Irvine a town, was a cousin of my father.

My mother's family (Morgenstern) immigrated to Canada in 1909 and homesteaded
in the Kincorth, Saskatchewan area.

I came to Irvine in 1955 to teach at the Irvine School. I taught grade one for
the next 15 years. Class sizes varied from 13 to one memorable fall when 42
pupils enrolled. We were together for six weeks - finally 12 were moved to
another small room and I was left with 30. It was during these years I was
given the honorable title, MOM.

The opportunity to teach Home Economics opened, so for the next few years I
enjoyed cooking and sewing with the girls. Some of the girls were very talented
sewers and I am always pleased to find they have kept it up. I transferred to
the library and it was from here I retired in June of 1988.

Another path by which to trace the years is by the duplicating equipment we
used at school.

First was the hectograph - a gelatin like substance on a canvas back. A special
purple pencil was used to make the pattern. Once it was used, you waited a day
before you could use it again. I used to have six of these on the go!

Next came the Gestetner. This machine worked fine, if you remembered to put the
typewriter on "cut".  It could have you black to the elbows if you had to "ink"
it.

The spirit duplicator followed. It had a tank of "spirit" and woe betide if the
person before you had forgotten to reverse the tank. You found "spirits"
flowing - to wipe up!

The Xerox was next. You simply pressed the numbers two and five for the 25
copies you wanted. When you came back you'd find it jammed at copy 14!

The Apple is here now - and I wish the teachers following me the joy of it.

I have been a member of Peace United Church for 28 years. I have served on the
Board and have been treasurer for the last few years.

I took over the Explorer Group at Peace United Church in the late 50's from
Mrs. Eileen Wilde. This group met for about ten years. During this time we
contributed to the finishing (door, tile, and cupboards) of one of the
classrooms of the church.

I have always enjoyed curling and have long been a member of the curling club.
Sophie Thiede and I were the only lady contributors to the first artificial ice
plant.

Irvine remains my home, at least for now. Who knows what the years will bring?

Carl and Mamie (Hefner) Beny

We need to look back to appreciate the contributions of our forefathers, in
this great land, and due to the 20 Mile Post Historical Society of Irvine, we
will recall many of these pioneers and know that they are truly legends.

Carl Beny, a young man (pic)

Grandmother Becker - Carl Beny's mother (pic)

Carl Beny, son of Marc and Marguerite Beny was born on March 25, 1877 in Gow
Heppenheim, Germany. He was the youngest of four children, two boys and two
girls.

His father died at an early age leaving his mother with the responsibility of
rearing a very young family. After her marriage to Karl Becker the family
immigrated to the U.S.A. in 1891 and settled in Long Island, N.Y. Here Carl
obtained work at a small shop as a delivery boy. In his daily tour he used to
call at the Hefners, who had a daughter, Maria Bibiana, in whom he became
interested.

In 1898 Carl enlisted in the Spanish-American War. Typhoid fever and malaria
were the outcome for him of this venture. When Carl returned he and Maria
Hefner were married in 1900 in St. Joseph's Rectory in Long Island.

Carl Beny (pic)

Mamie Beny (pic)

Reverend Sillak was instrumental in Mr. Beny and his family immigrating to the
territory of Alberta. Rev. Sillak had a charge 12 miles south of Irvine. Carl,
his step-father Karl Becker, and his brother-in-law, lured by the prospect of
making two dollars a day, arrived in Medicine Hat on a colonist train March 26,
1904. From there they walked 22 miles to Irvine and hence to Rev. Sillaks,
through snow. On their way they were given hospitality by the Holsteins and
Vockeroths.

Fred Weiss and Sons, general merchants, hired Carl Beny as bookkeeper and
manager at one thousand dollars per-annum. He took extra jobs to assist with
the financial obligations of a homestead and to bring his mother, brother and
sister from New York in the fall of 1904. In 1905 he brought his wife Mamie,
son Charlie and daughter Helen.

Charlie and Helen Beny - 1904 or 05 (pic)

In 1907 he bought the store from John Weiss who had previously purchased the
Rath store. In 1914 fire destroyed the store; insurance had lapsed, and a years
supply of merchandise was lost.

Homes in Irvine occupied by the Beny family were a two room house, the Bischke
residence, the Hausauer house on Walsh Street, and in 1913 he built a large
home on Walsh Street.

In 1914 he built the brick store, a two-story building with a service elevator.
Many people have fond memories of the Christmas parties for customers, with
gifts for all given by Santa Claus who came down the stairway. At Easter the
Easter Bunny came with dozens of real Easter eggs. The large plate glass
windows always had an appropriate setting. One was a large doll house, at least
three by five and three feet tall, covered with corn on the cobs. Two dolls
represented a farmer and his wife, a windmill, truck, animals, etc. depicting a
farm. Many times live animals such as rabbits and calves were the central theme.

Carl Beny house (pic)

Backyard - Beny home (pic)

Pond in back yard - Beny home (pic)

The store dealt in groceries, hardware, boots, shoes, dry goods, clothing,
furniture (on the upper floor), flour, feed, and harvesting machinery, traction
engines and threshers as well as General Motors cars. In 1915 he sold Ford cars
for five hundred dollars each.

In 1907 Carl Beny, John Hausauer and Jacob Beitz built the first elevator in
Irvine. Two years later they sold it to Ogilvies. It burned down in 1913.

Roy and Marion were born in Irvine in 1906 and 1908.

Carl Beny coins (pic)

Coins - C.B. representing Carl Beny (pic)

Carl used merchandising coins from 1912 to 1917. They were in denominations of
5, 10, 25, 50 cent, and $1 coins. Produce was purchased from the farmers with
these coins which were only redeemable at Beny's store. Butter at that time was
5 cents: per pound, eggs 8 cents per dozen, and 25 cents per bushel for
potatoes.

Customers came from Empress, Hilda, Schuler and from as far south as the
border. They made one or two trips a year by wagon and spent a week in town
holidaying and making large purchases. Parents bought their daughters, about to
be married, furnishings for their new homes.

During the First World War Carl Beny personally sold $105,000 in war bonds, the
quota for Irvine was $50,000. Every $5,000 over that was awarded a "crown" -
thus winning eleven crowns on the flag.

His first car was an International Harvester with high wheels and no doors or
top. A Tudhope was another one of his first cars, still no doors or top.

In 1916 he acquired a General Motors sub-dealership at Irvine. In 1917 he sold
the stock of the store to Mr. Phil Silver and kept the machinery business,
which was adjacent to the large store.

In the late twenties Jacob and Fred Schneider rented the store for a number of
years. Alois Wiedemann bought the store in 1951.

The Beny house was later sold to Nina and Emanuel Franz.

Charlie served his apprenticeship at Irvine, selling machinery and cars under
his dad's guidance until they opened up a branch of business in Medicine Hat
selling Oldsmobiles. In 1925 an additional franchise was obtained to sell
Chevrolets, Pontiacs, and Buicks. In the 1930s Charlie expanded to-Lethbridge
and his son, Chuck, assumed command in Medicine Hat.

Diploma Mamie Beny (pic)

Elizabeth Hefner, Helen and Mamie Beny (pic)

Carl Beny Family: Back: Marion, Charles, Roy, Helen; Front: Mamie, Carl (pic)

Roy, as he grew older, became associated with his father in business
particularly in the implement business until Carl retired in 1937 due to ill
health. Roy then started Modern Service in Brooks. Roy's son, Bill, was an
associate with his father in the Brooks enterprise.

Carl retired to Medicine Hat in 1943 and passed away on August 7, 1970 at the
age of 93. He had four children, ten grandchildren, and 26 great-grandchildren.

Carl Beny will long be remembered as a great humanitarian.

Wilhelm and Magdalena Bischke
submitted by Marie Lust, Harvey Mayer and Florence Nelsen

Wilhelm Bischke was born December 19, 1850 in Neudorf, South Russia, son of
Michael and Katherine Bischke, both born in 1822 in South Russia, and grandson
of Christian and Anna Marie (Wert) Bischke who were born in 1783 in Poland.
Christian had moved his family from Warsaw, Poland to Neudorf, South Russia in
1814. At that time his name may have been Bieschke or Pischki.

Magdalena Will was born January 1, 1854 in Neudorf, South Russia, daughter of
Phillip and Margueretha (Krein) Will.

Wilhelm Bischke (1850-1922) (pic)

Certificate in German - Bischke family - 1885 (pic)

Wilhelm and Magdalena were married October 21, 1873. They emigrated from
Neudorf to Hosmer, South Dakota in April, 1885 with five children: Marguretha,
Ludwig, Johann, Catherine, and Magdalena. The oldest was eight and the youngest
was ten months. Four children, Phillip, Jacob, Martha and Gottlieb were born in
Hosmer.

Wilhelm and Magdalena came to the Irvine area in 1903, along with their
children, some young, some grown up. They took up a homestead on what is now
the Harvey Derheim place in Township 10, Range 4.

About 1917, they moved to the town of Irvine where their grandchildren visited
and stayed with them while taking confirmation classes. Magdalena died March
17, 1921 and Wilhelm on August 13, 1922. They are buried in Medicine Hat.

Of their nine children, eight grew up and had large families of their own. Some
of them or their descendants stayed or returned to the Irvine area and some of
their histories are included in this book.

Marguretha, born August 15, 1874, married Ludwig Heather and died in 1954. They
had eleven children and lived in Medicine Hat.

Ludwig was born October 10, 1877, and married Magdalena Heid. They had seven
children and lived in the Concordia district, in Irvine and in Medicine Hat.
Their story follows.

Johann, born May 23, 1880, married Katherine Forcher and died in 1959 in Olds,
Alberta. They had ten children.

Catherine was born January 12, 1882, married Frederick Jacober and died in
1953. They had ten children and lived in Medicine Hat.

Magdalena, born June 26, 1884, married William Krauss on February 24, 1903.
They lived in the Norton District and had eighteen children, two of whom died
in infancy. Magdalena died in 1949. Descendants living in the Irvine area
include Krausses, the Fred Stuber family and the Christ Yanke family.

Phillip, born in 1888i married Elizabeth Fischer. They had six children and
lived in the Concordia School District and Elkwater area. He died in 1968 in
Medicine Hat.

Jacob, twin of Phillip, born in 1888, died in 1899.

Martha, born in 1890, married Isaac Baumbach. They had ten children and lived
in Medicine Hat. She died there in 1966.

Gottlieb was born in 1896. He attended school in what was later the Krauss
School. In 1913, he took out a homestead in the Schuler area where he built a
home and farm which he vacated in 1917. Later he had a farm in the Woolchester
area. He married Amelia Franz and they had nine children. he died about 1982 in
Red Deer.

Ludwig and Magdalena Bischke

Ludwig Bischke, born October 10, 1877, son of Wilhelm and Magdalena Bischke,
was seven years old when his family came from Neudorf, South Russia to Hosmer,
South Dakota in April of 1885. On May 8, 1899 he married Magdalena Heid in
Eureka, South Dakota.

Magdalena Heid was born a twin, on July 22, 1880, to Michael and Rosina
(Elsasser) Heid. She grew up in the same village in Russia, and came from there
on the Kaiser Friedrich, in April, 1899, to Eureka, South Dakota.

Bischke Family: Back: Maggie, Bill, Tillie; Middle: Jake, Magdalena, Mike,
Ludwig, Lou; Front: Rose (pic)

Ludwig and Magdalena came to the Irvine district with their two small boys,
Jacob and William, in April 1903 where they set up a homestead on
SW 20-10-3-W4. They had five more children, three girls and two boys, Magdalena,
Matilda, Ludwig, Michael and Rosina. The children went to the-Concordia School,
two miles away.

When William (Bill) married in October 1923, he took over the farm and the
family moved to Irvine. Mike and Rose were still in school.

About 1928, Ludwig, Senior, built the garage in Irvine and dealt in Massey
Harris machinery and Chrysler cars. During that time he owned a very nice car
which was stolen and ruined.

Grandpa and Grandma made good chokecherry wine and had good parties. Grandma
knitted, crocheted and embroidered in addition to cooking, canning, cleaning,
and sewing. When he wasn't busy in the garage, Grandpa told tall stories with
friends and neighbors on the bench out front and in his spare time he fixed
watches. He was always so punctual you could set your clock by him.

In 1949, our grandparents celebrated their fiftieth wedding anniversary with
most of their family at their home in Irvine. In 1950, they moved to Medicine
Hat. In 1959, they celebrated sixty years of marriage with another family
gathering at their home on Braemer Street. Grandma did all the preparations for
forty-five family members. They were still doing all their gardening and still
had their hobbies. Grandpa was then making some upholstered furniture.

Ludwig and Magdalena Bischke - 60th Anniv., May 8,1959 (pic)

Grandpa died just before their sixty-second anniversary in 1961. Grandma lived
to be eighty-eight years of age and died in December of 1968.

Bischke Family: Back: Jake, Maggie, Bill, Tillie, Lou, Rose, Mike; Front:
Ludwig and Magdalena - 50th Anniv., 1949 (pic)

Jacob (Jake), born July 8, 1900, married Mathilda (Tillie) Gehring in January,
1926 and lived in Acme, Alberta where he was a mechanic. They later moved to
Calgary. They had three children, Edith (Paron), Norman, and Mylene (Smith),
who all live in Calgary.

William (Bill), born January 11, 1903, married Mary Sulz, and lived on the
family farm in the Concordia district until moving to Medicine Hat. They had
four children, Leah (Ginther), Reuben, Alice (Haas), and Edna (Kanewischer).
Reuben is still on the family farm.

Magdalena (Maggie), born March 20, 1905, married Adolph Mayer, and lived in the
Newburg and Pashley areas. They had four children, Harvey, Florence (Nelsen),
Gladys (Quast), and Elmer.

Matilda (Tillie) was born February 8, 1907, married Frank Huddlestone and had
four children, Leonard, Frances (Broadhead), Robert, and Ralph.

Ludwig Junior (Lou) was born May 9, 1908, married Violet Flood of Walsh and had
two children, Marie (Lust) and Jack. They lived in Irvine, Medicine Hat, Brooks
and Elkwater.

Michael (Mike) was born December 10, 1911, married Bertha Derheim and had two
children, Roy and Vivien (Rossetti). They lived in the Irvine area before
moving to other parts of Alberta.

Rosina (Rose), was born September 15, 1915, married Alfred Baumbach and had one
son, Clarence. They have lived in Medicine Hat for many years.

William and Mary (Sulz) Bischke

Lou and Violet (Flood) Bischke
by Marie (Bischke) Lust

Lou and Violet Bischke about 1939 (pic)

Ludwig (Lou) Bischke was born on May 9, 1908, to Ludwig and Magdalena Bischke.
He attended the Concordia School until his parents moved to Irvine in 1923,
after which he worked for his brother, Bill, who had taken over the family
farm. He worked in his father's garage in Irvine later, then operated Mrs.
Appleyard's garage in Walsh for several years. In 1931 he married Violet Flood.

Sarah "Violet" Flood was born on August 25, 1912 to John Joseph and Sarah
Elizabeth (Roberts) Flood of Walsh. Violet grew up in Walsh and attended school
there to grade nine. She was a pretty good soccer player.

John Joseph Flood was born in England in 1868. At the age of 15, he came to
Canada and went to work for the CPR in the Winnipeg area. By 1906 he was
section foreman at Walsh and had a small farm near the town. When he retired in
1933 he had been with the CPR for three months less than 50 years.

In 1910, a widower with six children, he married Sarah Elizabeth (Roberts)
Smith, a widow with two children. She and her two small girls, Ivy and Doris,
were all born in England and had come to Canada with her parents in 1905, to
the Winnipeg area. Her parents, John William and Mary Jane Roberts, also came
to Walsh where John Roberts was a Justice of the Peace and, at different times,
operated a drug store and a pool hall. Tom Wood remembers them as being "the
spark plugs for our great picnics and other social affairs" (Cypress Courier,
May 5, 1982). An early Cummins Rural Directory Map lists the names of both J.W.
Roberts and Mary Roberts on land in the Walsh area.

Lou Bischke and Violet Flood were married on November 9, 1931 and lived in
Walsh for a short time. About 1933, they moved to Irvine where Lou returned to
operate the Bischke garage, which his father had built by 1928. On July 9, 1933
their daughter, Luella "Marie", was born. For awhile they lived in a house on
Dunmore Street, but later moved to another on Walsh Street.

Marie's earliest memories are of the house on Walsh Street, between Benys and
Jake Schneiders, with McLaughlins next to that. Water was carried from
Schneider's well. That house was across the alley from Christ Maser's Dray
Service and his big, white, 30-year-old horses. It was down the alley from her
dad's garage and Sophia's store (in reality, Schneider's Store). Grandma and
Grandpa Bischke lived a couple of blocks down the alley and to the west of the
garage.

John William (Jack) was born October 14, 1936.

In 1940 the family moved to the old police house just north of the railway
crossing. It had a big basement with a furnace which held a lot of coal and
kept the house nice and cozy. There was a huge water tank that collected rain
water which could be pumped up to the kitchen above, and there was room for a
good-sized pool table where friends often gathered. It sometimes had electric
lights supplied by 32 volt wiring and batteries which could be recharged on the
Delco at the garage. There were three bedrooms and room to keep a teacher in
board. There was an upstairs that was unfinished and a great place to play. In
the dining room there was room for a piano - a dream come true.

Lou had an aptitude for mechanics and he eventually earned his mechanics papers
with very little formal training. He was always fixing or building something.
He also loved to hear and tell jokes and was never happier than when he was
making others laugh.

Violet became a member of the W.I. about 1937, was treasurer in the early
forties, handicraft convener in 1947, and constituency convener in 1949. She
took piano lessons from Dorothy Davidson when her children did. Other hobbies
included ladies softball, reading, sewing, embroidery and other handicrafts.
She and Marie enjoyed very much the exercise classes of Mary McLeay in the old
Magnet Theatre.

Lou and Vi learned to golf on the golf course that was constructed on the hills
to the northeast of town, a sport they enjoyed for years afterward. They also
enjoyed fishing and hunting and dancing.

About 1946, Lou tore down the old Alberta Hotel, with the help of some friends
and neighbors, and built a new garage on the site, with a residence attached at
the rear. He continued to sell B.A. gas and oil and obtained the Greyhound Bus
Depot franchise. This move did not create the hoped-for increase in business
and the garage was sold in 1947.

Lou and Vi and family Moved to Medicine Hat where Lou worked for Gardner Motors
and Vi worked for awhile at Medalta Potteries and then at Eaton's Department
Store. In 1949 they packed again and moved to Brooks where Lou worked for
Murray Gordon Motors and later for Beny's. Violet worked in the Newell Hotel as
a waitress, then for Carol's Fashions. They returned to Medicine Hat in 1956,
soon after their first grandchild was born. In 1964 they moved to Elkwater
where they lived for about nine years until returning to Medicine Hat to retire.

Lou died on April 17, 1981 and Violet, on September 1, 1988.

Marie and Jack attended school in Irvine and took music lessons from Dorothy
Davidson until the family moved to Medicine Hat in 1947. They finished their
schooling in Medicine Hat and Brooks.

Jack enjoyed painting, photography, and was usually busy designing something
new. He made enamel jewelry and experimented with several techniques for
printing greeting cards.

Marie and Jack Bischke (pic)

Marie graduated from the Brooks High School and took one year of teacher
training at the U. of A. in Calgary. She taught school in the County of Newell
for two years, then returned to the Irvine area to teach at the newly
established Cypress View School. She married Arthur Lust of the Robinson area
in 1955. They farmed in that area until selling out and moving to Medicine Hat
in 1975. Art drove for Lawrence Meier Trucking for nine years. Marie worked in
the College Bookstore for several years and took a number of courses at the
college.

Their three children, Frances, Wayne, and Patricia, attended Irvine School and
Medicine Hat College. Frances has two boys, David and Michael Munroe, who now
also attend school in Irvine. Wayne is a fireman in Medicine Hat. He and his
wife, Bogusia, have three boys, Derek, Andrew, and Joshua. Patty has been
attending Medicine Hat College.

Michael and Bertha (Derheim) Bischke

Michael Bischke was born December 10, 1911, son of Ludwig and Magdalena
Bischke. He went to the Concordia School until his parents moved to Irvine in
1923 when he was twelve years old. He continued his schooling in Irvine.

Bertha Derheim was born April 12, 1913 to Fredrick and Alvina (Lehr) Derheim.
She went to the Newburg School.

Mike and, Bertha were married June 17, 1933 and lived for several years in the
Concordia School District on SW 30-10-3-4. In the fall of 1938, Mike went to
work in his dad's garage in Irvine and in 1940, he began trucking. In 1943, the
family moved to a farm east of Irvine on section 34-11-2-4. Their two children,
Raymond "Roy" and Vivien Rose-Marie, were bussed to school in Irvine.

Michael Bischke Family: Roy, Phyllis, Mike, Bertha Bischke, Vivian and Denis
Rossetti; Front: Rocky and Roxanne Bischke, Tammy and Lee Rossetti (pic)

In May, 1954 Mike and Bertha moved to the Calgary area, and from there to
various places in Southern Alberta until arriving in Magrath where they are
now. They are in good health and have many interests.

Roy was born February 19, 1935 and married Phyllis Smith in 1959. They have two
children, Rocky and Roxanne.

Vivien was born March 14, 1942 and married Denis Rossetti in 1961. They have
two children, Tammy and Lee, and one grandchild.

Fred and Christina Bollinger

Fred Bollinger was born in 1888 in Bessarabia, Russia. In 1902 at the age of
fourteen years, he moved with his brother to South Dakota. He came to Canada in
1909 and worked on a pipeline between Cypress Hills and Walsh.

In 1910, Fred married Christina Hoff, daughter of Ludwig Hoff. They settled on
a homestead in the Hilda district where they lived in a two roomed house with
dirt floors. Three daughters were born. Mary, Martha and Rosie.

Times were very hard, so in 1917 they moved to the Robinson district to farm.
Two sons, Arthur and Edwin, were born. In 1929, they moved again, this time to
the Berry Centre area on the former John Lehr farm along the Ross Creek, where
they farmed and ranched. In 1936, another son, Freddie, was born. They lived in
a two-story home, part of which was moved there to make it large enough. The
original home was a log and mud house which they used as their summer kitchen
and later used to hold their neighborhood dances in. This house was later
pulled away needing six tractors to move it.

Fred was well known for his horse trading. They would never know when he'd come
home with a different one. They would go for miles by horse and sleigh for
visiting.

Moving log house - 1956 (pic)

The children attended school at Berry Centre, where they either walked or went
on horse back.

On June 16, 1941, Fred passed away suddenly of a heart attack. By this time
only the boys were home, and they continued farming.

In 1943, Arthur married and left home, and Edwin went to work shortly after,
which left Freddie at a very young age with his mother, Christina, to run the
family farm.

Christina Bollinger (pic)

Christina retired to Medicine Hat in October 1952. She lived in her own home on
9th St. SE where she had a large garden. She loved her garden and plants and
did all her own yard and house work. In the spring of 1985, she decided to sell
her home to the First Assembly of God Church, in which she was very active, and
she moved into the Maranatha Villa. Her house was later torn down and the lot
is now used for church parking. At ninety-six years of age, she is still in
fairly good health.

Fred and Christina had six children, three sons and three daughters.

Mary married John Zeller. They have three children, Harry, Darlene and Violet.

Martha married Ted Schneider. They have three children, Dorothy, Merle and
Vernon.

Bollinger Family: Freddie, Rosie, Arthur, Martha, Edwin, Mary, Christina
sitting Pic)

Kronberg (mother), Merle Hoffman (grandmother), Christina Bollinger (great
great grandmother), Dallas Kronberg (great great grandson) (pic)

Rosie married Dave Miller. They have two sons, Jim and Glen.

Arthur married Freida Gwinner. They have two children, Sharon and Garry.

Edwin married Olga Meier. They have four children, Betty Ann, Clifford, Karen
and Janice

Freddie married Beatrice Stuber. They have four children, Dennis, Rodney,
Darrell and Sherry

Edwin and Olga Bollinger

Edwin, son of Fredrick and Christina (Hoff) Bollinger, was born February 7,
1926 at Newburg, Alberta, grew up and was educated in the Berry Centre
District. In 1943, Edwin worked at the Redcliff Brick plant, staying with his
sister, Mary Zeller, saving enough money to buy his first car, a 1931 Chevrolet
Coupe. In 1946 he bought the Jacob Patzer farm, living a bachelor's life.

I, Olga, daughter of Reinhold and Magdelina (Sturm) Meier, was born August 30,
1931 at Fox, Alberta. My parents made several moves, so schools I attended were
Clearwater Lake, Feldman Lake, Jenny Lind at Scandia and Alcoma at Rainier. In
1947 we moved to Meadowview, Alberta, about eighty miles northwest of Edmonton.
I was working in Medicine Hat at the New Club Cafe when Edwin and I met. We
were married October 9, 1949 in the country church at Meadowview.

Edwin and Olga (Meier) Bollinger - October 9, 1949 (pic)

After applying new sidings, building new kitchen cupboards, wallpapering and
painting throughout the old house built by Edwin's Patzer grandparents, it was
nice and cozy. Our first girl Betty Anne was born May 15, 1952.

That was the last year that we bindered, stooked, and threshed part of our
crop. Threshing in the last field, a slender young man crawled into the machine
to make a minor repair or adjustment. While crawling in or out, he got caught
on a sharp edge, ripping his back pocket. Matches must have dropped out falling
into the fan. When the machine was started up the first thing to land on the
already made, big strawstack was a ball of fire. The machine was shut off and
quickly pulled back from the site, and a fireguard cultivated. No damage except
the loss of the strawstack. The machine was operated and owned by Arthur
Bollinger.

Fire hit us again in late summer of 1954 when it gutted our house. With the
help of many neighbors some things were saved, plus the other buildings.
Everyone was so good to us.

Our neighbors, Carl Vosslers had outgrown their little house, and had a new one
near ready to be moved into. We bought and moved the little house onto our
farm, onto a full basement and added a larger entrance.

On February 7, 1956, Wayne Edwin was born, but was with us only a short time
and passed away March 28, 1956. Karen Faye was born January 16, 1957 and
Clifford Ray on May 21, 1958. Now there was need for more room so two bedrooms
were developed in the basement.

1960 and 1961 were very dry. We had no water for the cattle, had a well
drilled, and were very lucky. We got a well with lots of very good water. This
well served us well for twenty years. It was the first well with usable water
on this farm.

Janice Lynn was born October 7, 1961. By now Betty Anne was a great help
especially outside for her dad.

Edwin Bollinger Family: Back: Betty Anne, Edwin, Olga; Front: Clifford, Karen,
Janice (pic)

We had no graded road to our farm. This made traveling in and out very
difficult especially when we had lots of snow, as we had in the winter of 1962.
Betty Anne spent several weeks in Irvine at Mrs. Adeline Sackman's to attend
school, coming home only for weekends. That summer we had a surveyed road
built. That made it nice.

Edwin and Olga Bollinger (pic)

In 1964 Edwin was very sick. Spring seeding and summerfallowing was done by his
brothers and friends while he was in hospital. He recovered well, but slowly.

The children rode their horses in the Medicine Hat Stampede Parade several
years, extra work but worth the effort.

In 1973 we sold the milk cows, so we had next to no yard chores, so I went to
work at the Texaco Coffee Shop for Bill and Audrey Leith. This gave us the
freedom to go places as a family.

Our happy family era ended January 16, 1977 when Edwin very suddenly died of a
heart attack. By this time Betty Anne and Karen were married, so we had three
grandchildren.

Janice (Bollinger) and Daniel (pic)

Betty Anne married Samuel Hauck of Thelma on November 1, 1969. They now live in
Irvine with their children, Chuck and Roxie.

Karen married Brian Waldbauer of Graburn on July 20, 1974. They now have two
children, Teresa and Dwayne and live in Bow Island.

Clifford took over the farm duties after his dad's death at the age of
eighteen. he bought the farm the following year, 1978. On October 7, 1981, he
married Wendy Phaff of Hatton, Saskatchewan. They now have two children, Brandy
and Dallas.

Janice married Daniel Wahl of Surrey, B.C. on June 11, 1988 at the home of her
sister Betty Anne and Sam Hauck. Janice and Daniel make their home in Surrey
where Janice is employed at Gilfords Creative Goldsmith Jewelry Store, while
Danny drives a transport truck in the city of Vancouver.

Clifford and Wendy Bollinger

I, Clifford, only son of Edwin and Olga (Meier) Bollinger, born May 21, 1958 in
Medicine Hat, spent all my school years at Irvine, and graduated there in June
of 1976. After school I started working at Canadian Pittsburg, which was a
glass company in Medicine Hat. I worked with this company till my dad passed
away. I then farmed on my own for four years and then got married October 7,
1981 to Wendy Phaff of Hatton, Saskatchewan.

Clifford Bollinger Family: Wendy, Clifford, Dallas, Brandy - 1988 (pic)

Wendy is the only daughter of Marvin and Elaine (Waldbauer) Phaff. She was born
in Medicine Hat on January 11, 1956 but was raised on her parents' farm at
Hatton and educated in Maple Creek, Saskatchewan.

On our second anniversary, October 7, 1983, we had a baby girl. We named her
Brandy Jill. Our second baby, a boy, was born on June 19, 1987, Dallas Clay.

I decided to break up all the land possible to be used for wheat. In the spring
of 1981, we sold all our livestock and just rented in cattle for fall grazing.
Over the past 7 years we did a lot of yard work planting trees, building a new
home and two new quonsets.

In January, 1988 my father-in-law, Marvin and I threw ourselves into a whole
new thing of seeding crested wheat grass on irrigation. Marvin has grown
crested wheat grass for many years on dry land but never irrigated. The land we
purchased is about one mile west of Redcliff which includes the river frontage.
For now driving back and forth to work trying to get all the kinks out of the
irrigation system has been quite hectic. In the meantime I have been renting
out my land to the Elkwater Hutterite Colony on a lease basis and this seems to
be working out real well.

Freddie and Beatrice Bollinger
by Beatrice Bollinger

Freddie, the son of Fred and Christina Bollinger, was born January 25, 1930.
Freddie received his education at Berry Centre School which was located about a
mile from their home place. He would walk or go on horse back. His first
teacher was Miss Bader. He had the misfortune of losing his dad when he was
only eleven years old. So after his two older brothers, Arthur and Edwin, left
home he was left with his mother, Christina, to run the family farm.

I, Beatrice, the daughter of Fred and Emilie Stuber, was born May 10, 1935, the
third youngest of eight children. We all attended school at Coal Centre. Our
home place was two and a half miles west of the 41 highway, known as the Coal
Centre District and the school was along the Gros Ventre Creek, two miles north
of where we lived. We quite often walked, but mostly went by horse and buggy or
sleigh. I remember many times in the spring we would cross the main creek to
get to the school and by home time the creek was so high that it almost took
the horse and buggy down stream with the heavy flow of water. Our teacher was
Mrs. Mary Deering. I attended school at Coal Centre for my first four years.
Then in Grade V, I started school at Irvine, having to catch the bus down along
the 41 highway, a two and a quarter mile walk every morning. The school bus,
driven by Christ Wirsch, was just a ton truck with a wooden shell. Our seats
were uncovered wooden benches and the only heat came through an opening made by
removing the back window. The 41 highway, known then as the 48, wasn't too good
in the winter. When there was a lot of snow we would have to circle around in
the fields to miss the large snow drifts. I finished only my grade eight, then
I had to stay home to help with other work. Those days they thought learning to
wash clothes, cook and bake bread were more important than finishing school.

In 1952, Freddie and I were married. We farmed and ranched on the home place
where Freddie grew up. The farm along the Ross Creek was ideal for cattle. The
roads we had to travel were only cow trails which made it very hard for travel
in the winter or in the mud. We finally had the roads built up and graveled
when our children started school and the school bus had to come in to pick them
up.

We began a pattern of life very similar to that of the neighborhood. We farmed,
raised cattle, hogs and chickens, milked cows and shipped cream.

On March 4, 1954, we had our first son, Dennis. Then on April 18, 1956, we were
blessed with another son, Rodney. That same year we got Calgary Power which was
quite a change. In 1963, seven years later our third son, Darrell arrived and
two years later in 1965 we finally had our baby girl, Sherry. The children
attended school in Irvine where all four graduated. They were all involved in
4H. They had their own club in the Irvine area, which is still going strong.

In October 1975, Dennis married Gwen Lentz, daughter of Bill and Lilly Lentz.
They live and work on a farm in the Dunmore district and during the summer
months, Dennis works for the MD of Cypress. They have two girls, Jody and Jane.
They both attend school in Irvine.

In July 1981, Rodney married Erna Sept, daughter of Bernie and Nora Sept. They
are farming and ranching in the Wisdom area on the former George Seitz farm.
They both enjoy curling. They have three girls, Carla, Karl, and Lindsey. Carla
attends school in Medicine Hat.

Freddie Bollinger Family: Rodney, Darrell, Beatrice, Freddie, Dennis, Sherry
(pic)

Darrell married Margaret Roth in June 1984. Margaret is the daughter of Ralph
and Grace Roth. Darrell drives truck for Hypoint Feeds in Medicine hat, hauling
to points in Saskatchewan and Montana as well as the immediate area. Margaret
is a school teacher. They both enjoy curling, slowpitch and golfing, keeping
them both very busy.

Sherry is still single and has been employed at Huttons in Medicine Hat for the
past two years, starting out delivering parts and now as secretary. She is an
active member of the Women of the Moose Lodge. She also enjoys slowpitch and
golfing.

In April 1985, we moved to Medicine Hat and are straight grain farming from the
city. We find time now to -golf in the summer, which we both enjoy, and we curl
in the winter.

The years have certainly had their ups and downs. The things we are most
thankful for are that we have a good and healthy family and a happy married
life.

The Brandt Family Back to 1865
by Robert Brandt

Records are in Prussia, which is Germany now.

Ferdnand Brandt married Tehia in 1868. Ferdnand was a Colonel in the German
army. It was at the time of the war between Germany and Denmark. When the war
became critical, Germany used gas and Ferdnand was caught in the gas and died.
Their son, Otto Ferdnand, was three years old.

Later, Tehia married Fred Trepton and they came to the U.S.A. when Otto Brandt
was seven years old. He was naturalized when he was eight years old. He had one
stepbrother and one stepsister.

Otto and Emelia (Tohm) Brandt

When Otto Ferdnand grew up, he married Emelia Tohm and homesteaded in Gardena,
North Dakota. They had eight children, Everett, Ben, Florence, Willard, Clara,
Carl, Ruth and Claudia. Florence passed away at the age of three, Willard and
Clara at the age of one.

Otto and Emelia Brandt moved to Canada in 1911 to Irvine, Alberta. They
homesteaded in the Clover Hill district where they had four more children,
Dora, Wilfred, Robert and Lorene.

Lorene passed away at the age of six. Everett had one step-son. His history
follows. Ben passed away at the age of 82. Carl had one daughter and one son.
He passed away at the age of 72. Ruth went back to the States. She had twelve
children. Claudia had one girl. Dora had one son and one daughter. She passed
away at the age of 46. Wilfred passed away at the age of 67. Robert had two
boys and one girl. His story follows.

Tony Jacobson, Clarence Tohm, Everett Brandt, Douglas Staniforth, Harry
Jacobson, John Conrad - sitting, Otto Brandt - lying down (pic)

Everett Brandt History from 1911-1924
by Everett Brandt

My dad and I arrived in Irvine October 17, 1911 from Gardena, North Dakota. We
came by boxcars composed of seven head of horses and four head of cattle, with
farm machinery and household furniture. My uncle Albert Tolim moved in the
spring of 1911 to Irvine. We unloaded the horses and one wagon and drove four
miles to my uncle's place. The next day we unloaded the cattle and the rest of
the things and hauled them out to my uncle's place.

It was snowing and cold the following day. Dad and Uncle Albert went to Irvine
and hauled two loads of lumber to our farm. There were no buildings as it was a
homestead. By November 19 we had the house and the barn partly built. Then Dad
wrote for Mom to come. She landed at Irvine on December 6, 1911 with the rest
of the family. There was Ben, Carl, Ruth and Claudia. So we were a family
again. Dora, Wilfred, Robert and Lorain were born at Irvine.

At that time the area around Irvine and Medicine Hat was changing from ranching
to farming. There were no schools in that area at that time. After New Year's
1912, Dad, Mr. Zwick, and Tom Wood, Sr. called a meeting to organize a school
district. The district was formed and it was named Clover Hill by Mrs. Zwick.
They applied to the Provincial Government for a school. It took over a year to
get that approved by the Government.

The Rancher Association fought against it. Finally the Government gave
approval. Mr. Zwick and his son Lester built the school. It was finished in
June, 1913. The school board hired a student teacher for July and August 1913.
The children did real good, as some could not speak English at all.

For the school year starting September 1st, 1913 they hired a regular teacher.
I attended for one year myself. I was fifteen years old. But the children lost
one year of school.

In the winter of 1914, 1915, and 1916 they had night school for three months,
two days a week. Adam Roll and I attended when we were not too busy. A lot of
older people attended. Every school district had a picnic in the summer. There
were sports of all kinds for the young and the old. All the school districts
had ball teams. Some were quite good. Some teams played against Irvine and
Walsh. I still have a cracked finger as I was the catcher sometimes. There were
some country stampedes. Irvine always had a stampede on July 1st every year. I
left Irvine in July, 1924. I did not return for a visit until 1949. I was a
stranger to most of the people I knew before. So that ends most of my memories
of Clover Hill School District.

The Robert Brandt Family from 1924-1987
by Robert Brandt

In 1924, I went to the U.S.A. with my mother. Her father passed away in the
spring of 1926. In the fall, I broke an ankle and I went to the hospital in
Medicine Hat in August, 1926. I spent my seventh, eighth and ninth birthdays in
the hospital. I came out in February, 1929, and again I went with my mother to
take care of her mother. I went to school in North Dakota until 1931. Her
mother passed away and we came home.

I walked on one crutch. I walked to school in the morning and at noon on one
crutch. We lived a quarter mile from school. That amounted to a mile a day. My
folks made me walk on one crutch so I would use my leg. They took off that
inside part of the ankle that broke off and scraped the bone to below the knee
to get the austes off the bone. It healed up and when the war broke out, I
joined the Lord Strathcona Royal Canadian Army, in April, 1940. I had an
accident on a motorcycle maneuver and injured that leg. I was discharged in
1941, May 1.

I farmed until 1944, when I sold out. I married Ellen Dorge on December 30,
1944. We moved to Wildwood where I worked at a planing mill. We had 60 German
prisoners there. In the summer months, the foreman and I were there with them.
I spoke German, so I could tell them what we wanted done.

We came back to Medicine Hat in 1948. We have three children: Ronald, a teacher
at Kamloops, B.C.; Louella, a legal secretary in Calgary; and Reginal, in
Engineering Graphics Technology (Diploma of Technology).

Ronald has three children, Robert, Robin and Kelly. Louella has two children,
Deby and Mark. Reg has two children, Paula and Michael.

I worked for Scott National for 18 and a half years and then I worked for the
Canadian Armed Forces. I was transferred to the British Army Training Unit as
Accountant and Bookkeeper for three years and then I transferred back to the
Canadian Armed Forces in Medicine Hat, where I retired in 1985. We sold our
third home and bought a mobile home. We travel about six months of the year. I
received a plaque from the Canadian Armed Forces signed by Prime Minister
Mulroney for service I gave them.

Adolph and Matilda (Doering) Brost
by Annie Brost

Adolph Brost was born March 20, 1883 in Dennvitz, Bessarabia and came to North
Dakota with his parents, Michial and Caroline (Issac) Brost as a very small
child.

In the year 1899 he came to Canada along with two of his brothers. He worked as
a laborer and for a few years operated a livery barn in Irvine with his
brother, and later ran a boarding house in Medicine Hat. On April 8, 1908 he
married his young bride, 16 year old Matilda Doering. They continued in the
boarding house business for a short time then took up a homestead in the Gros
Ventre area. They farmed there for several years then bought a section of land
from Mr. Harry Yuill (Sr.) just on the north side of the town of Irvine. He
also continued farming his homestead driving 18 miles or more by horse and
buggy to get there.

Adolph and Matilda Brost - about 1940 (pic)

Brost home at Irvine (pic)

Adolph Brost was a very hard worker and continued in mixed farming and raising
a large family of 14 children, seven boys and seven girls. Mr. Brost lived on
his farm until his sudden passing in April of 1958.

Alfred and Annie (Boschee) Brost
by Annie Brost

Alfred was born May 27, 1916, at Gros Ventre, son of Adolph and Matilda
(Doering) Brost. As a young boy, he moved with his parents to a farm on the
outskirts of the town of Irvine. He received his education at Irvine and helped
with the farming.

When the "dusty thirties" came along Alfred's father had a hard time feeding
his 14 children. So Alfred, along with some friends, set out to find work in
the central part of Alberta. Alfred landed a job a few miles out of Wetaskiwin,
putting up hay. In the winter he would work in the Wetaskiwin Hotel for a Mr.
Bannerman. Later, that summer, he worked for a dairy and hog farmer by the name
of Mr. Kaiser. The wages were seven to ten dollars a month, and meals at the
hotel could be bought for 35 cents for a steak and all the trimmings. He didn't
get rich but at least he had a place to eat and sleep.

He returned home in 1939 to help his father harvest, as crops had been a bit
better. He eventually settled on a farm one and a half miles north of Irvine
which his father had purchased from Mr. McLaughlin and here he batched for a
few years.

I, Annie, daughter of Fred and Emily Boschee was born November 23, 1921 at
Josephsburg and attended Cypress School, after which I worked at several farm
homes.

Alfred and I were married January 26, 1943, in Medicine Hat. We continued to
farm, milk cows, raise chickens, geese, ducks and turkeys and we had a big
garden and some fruit trees. This helped support our five children, three boys
and two girls.

Alfred Brost Family - 1973: Back: Darlene, Glen, Harlow; Front: Annie, Alfred,
Merle, Gaylene (pic)

Alfred passed away very suddenly in 1976 at the age of 59 years. I then moved
to Medicine Hat where I am presently residing.

Our children are all graduates of the Irvine School. The boys, Harlon, Merle,
and Glen are engaged in ranching and farming in the area. Harlon is on our home
place. Our oldest daughter, Darlene, after a nursing career for 11 years,
married Barry Litke, a farmer in the Crossfield, Alberta area. They have two
children, Erin and Dale. Gaylene was employed for several years with Canada
Manpower and Immigration. She married William Kendall, an R.C.M.P. Sergeant.
They are presently residing in the N.W.T., where her husband is stationed and
they have a daughter, Ashley.

The Burchak Family

Mary (Grandma) Burchak was born in 1854. Her son, George, born 1891 and his
wife, Annie, born 1896, were from Czechoslovakia and all are now deceased.

Mrs. Annie Burchak - 1934 (pic)

The family came to Irvine in 1928 from Wayne, Alberta. They owned and managed
the Great West Hotel during the years 1928 to 1944. In the dining room one of
their menus offered soup, steak, pie and coffee for 50 cents. If you wanted a
case of beer from the bar the going price was $2.20 a dozen for takeout. The
hotel paid $2.00 a dozen to the A.L.C.B. and sold it for a profit of 20 cents.

Four children were born to George and Annie. They were Thomas, Edward, Francis,
and Joseph Leonard.

Thomas was born in 1915. He married Martha Milialik in Lethbridge, Alberta.
After serving in the Royal Canadian Dental Corps, he worked as a steel
fabricator in the B.C. Sugar Refinery in Vancouver. Thomas is deceased.

Edward was born in 1921 in Wayne, Alberta. He married Katherine Mihalik who was
born in Lethbridge, Alberta. He received his B. Educ (B.C.) and his M.A.
(Washington). During the war he served in the Royal Winnipeg Rifles. Edward
became head librarian at Gladstone Secondary School in Vancouver. He retired
after 40 years of teaching. Their three children, Karen, Arthur and Mark, are
residing in Vancouver, B.C.

Francis, born in 1923, received his B.Ed. (Alta.) and M.Ed. (B.C.). He was
commissioned to the Canadian Cadet Corp. Francis married Nan Dunne who was from
Tilley, Alberta. He retired as Superintendent of the Wheatland School District
in Strathmore, Alberta. Francis and Nan have three children: Michael resides in
Sylvan Lake, Alberta; Frances (Bates) resides in Innisfail, Alberta; and Marla
(Greydanas) resides in Leduc, Alberta. Francis is now deceased.

Joseph Leonard was born in 1928. He served in the Royal Canadian Engineers. Joe
lived in Irvine and made his living as a trucker.

Ed. Note: Many of us will always remember Joe as part of this community up
until his death on February 5, 1976.

Lionel and Eva (McLaughlin) Chell
by Arthur Chell

Lionel Chell was born 16 December 1893 in Stourport, Worcester, England,
youngest child of Arthur Thomas Chell and Harriet (Hawkins) Chell of Stourport.
Lionel immigrated to Canada, as a Bank employee, in 1912 at the age of 19.
After a short period of banking in Eastern Canada, he moved west and found
employment with Alberta Pacific Grain Co. In the capacity of Elevator Agent, he
lived in several Alberta communities, one of which was Irvine. In this
southeast town, he met and married Eva Katherine McLaughlin.

Eva, the oldest child of Stanley McLaughlin and Katherine (Yeskie) McLaughlin
was born in Medicine Hat, Alberta on the 8th of May 1906. Eva's father, Stanley
died when she was 12 years old. Following this death Eva came to Irvine to live
with her uncle Fred and Auntie Katherine McLaughlin. She lived with Fred and
Katherine until her marriage to Lionel Chell. Eva completed her education in
Irvine and Raymond Agriculture School, then worked in the community of Irvine
as an employee of Thompson Store and then as a telephone operator.

Lionel and Eva were married the first of August 1930 in St. George's Church,
Irvine, Alberta, by Rev. M. Stewart. After a honeymoon to Banff the newlyweds
continued to reside in the community of their marriage, in a house owned by
Alberta Pacific Grain Co. on Pacific Ave.

Lionel and Eva (McLaughlin) Chell - August 1, 1930 (pic)

Chell children: Arthur, Thomas, Nora (pic)

This union produced three children: Arthur Stanley, born 2 June 1931 in
Medicine Hat, Thomas McLaughlin born 16 September 1936 in Medicine Hat, Nora
Isabella, born 28 May 1941 in Vulcan, Alberta. In 1939 the family of four moved
to Vulcan, Alberta where Lionel continued to buy grain.

In 1951 the family, now of five in total, moved to Monarch, Alberta where
Lionel still bought grain, until his death, at his elevator desk, in 1960 at
the age of 67 years. At this time Eva moved to Fort Macleod, Alberta where son
Arthur and family lived.

Arthur and Ruth Chell

Arthur, eldest child of Lionel and Eva, lived in Irvine until 1939 then, at the
age of eight years, moved to Vulcan with his parents. In this location he
completed his schooling. During the school years he learned the retail meat and
grocery business. This experience was gained by working part time for Con
Kettleston, Bob Symington, and Charles Northcott. Following schooling Arthur
obtained his Queens Commission (Reserve) at Dundurn, Saskatchewan. Following
this six week military course he spent the winter working as a meat cutter with
Safeway in Saskatoon. In 1953 he moved to Fort Macleod where he opened a retail
meat business in Reach and Company Store. In 1954 Arthur married Ruth Brett, a
long time friend from Vulcan.

Ruth, the oldest child of Albert and Mona Brett, was born in Champion, Alberta
on 21 December 1930. Her parents farmed in the Champion area until 1952 then
moved to Calgary. Ruth attended school at Champion, Carmangay, and Nobleford,
Alberta. She was employed at King's Drug Store, Vulcan and later by Alberta
Government Telephones as an operator.

Arthur and Ruth were married 30 June 1954 in the Vulcan United Church. This
union produced four children: Stanley Lionel, Allan Arthur, Colleen Ruth,
Cameron Brett.

This branch of the Chell family continued to live in Fort Macleod, Arthur
self-employed in the meat business until retirement in 1980. Ruth opened and
managed a retail flower business. A second florist business was opened in
Claresholm, then in due time sold to Mary K Flowers. The flower business in
Fort Macleod sold in 1984. At this time Arthur and Ruth and Cameron, youngest
child, moved to Lethbridge. Arthur and Ruth continue to reside in Lethbridge.
Arthur has accepted a position with Associated Grocers as a Meat Merchandiser,
Ruth works as a florist for Janco Jewelry and Flowers at Coaldale, Alberta.

Stanley, eldest son of Arthur and Ruth, born 22 May 1955 in Claresholm,
Alberta, completed his schooling at Fort Macleod, Trinity College, Port Hope,
Ontario and one year at University of Alberta. He is employed by Alberta
Government Telephones in Foremost, Alberta. Stanley married Sharon Wright of
Medicine Hat on 6 August 1977 in Holy Trinity Anglican Church, Medicine Hat.
Sharon is the only child of Harold and Anna Wright. Anna died when Sharon was
three years old; subsequently Sharon was raised by her aunt Lillian Wright of
Medicine Hat. Stanley and Sharon have two girls: Alexandra Lillian, born 6 June
1983 and Lauren Annett, born 3 July 1986.

Allan, second child of Arthur and Ruth, born 1 May 1957 in Fort Macleod,
Alberta, completed school at Fort Macleod, Trinity College, Port Hope, Ontario
and one year at University of Alberta. He is a partner in the firm of "Bond
Power" of Lethbridge. Allan married Lori Ully of Lethbridge in St. Augustine's
Church on I March 1980. Lori is the eldest daughter of Len and Romila Ully of
Lethbridge. Allan and Lori have two children: Brett Allan born 16 June 1981 and
Courtney Lane born 5 June 1983.

Colleen, third child and only daughter of Arthur and Ruth, was born in Fort
Macleod on 31 March 1959. She completed school at Fort Macleod, Prelate,
Saskatchewan, and one year at University of Alberta. Colleen owned and operated
a Deli in Claresholm for five years, then moved to Calgary to work as a sales
representative for Schneider's Meats for three years. Colleen and Walter
Rudolph were married 26 March 1988 in St. Augustine's Anglican Church in
Lethbridge. Walter is the youngest child of Henry and Anna Rudolph of
Lethbridge. Walter works as a welder. Walter and Colleen reside in Calgary.

Cameron, youngest child of Arthur and Ruth, was born 25 September 1968 in Fort
Macleod. He attended school at Fort Macleod, Immanual Christian in Lethbridge
and is now at Mount Royal College and the University of Calgary, in Calgary.
Cameron was very involved in track and field as a decathlon competitor.

Thomas, second child of Lionel and Eva, lived in Irvine until 1939 then, at age
three moved with parents to Vulcan. Tom completed school at Vulcan, Nobleford,
then graduated from Royal Military College with a degree in engineering. He
completed his tour of military duty in Calgary and at the Pentagon in U.S.A.
Transferring to civil servant, he served in Bonn, Germany, Buffalo, New York

Nora was born 28 May 1941 in Vulcan, Alberta, the only daughter of Lionel and

attended school at Vulcan and Nobleford, Alberta. Obtaining a teaching degree

Alberta. On 1 August 1966 she married Douglas Townsend, son of Ralph and

operates Townsend Drugs in Claresholm. Doug and Nora have three children:

Emil and Angela Chomistek and Family
by Angela Chomistek

The Emil Chomistek family came to the Irvine district, from Scandia, Alberta,
in the summer of 1974.

Emil is the second oldest son in a family of four, of Mr. and Mrs. Paul
Chomistek Sr., then of Scandia, now of Brooks, Alberta. He was born in October
1935. He mix farmed, potatoes, cattle and grain, with his Dad there on
irrigation. Emil started farming on his own in the Scandia area in 1960. The
same year he married former Angela Stauch, youngest daughter in a family of
five of the late Mr. and Mrs. Stanley Stauch of Yarbo, Saskatchewan, born
January, 1939. In July, 1961 twin boys, Daniel and Patrick, were born, a
daughter Kathleen in July 1962 and another son Guy in October 1963.

Our main crop was potatoes along with cattle and grain. Emil started competing
in Pro Rodeo while in Scandia. His favorite events were calf roping and steer
wrestling. In 1962 he won the calf roping trophy saddle for the Southern
Alberta Rodeo Circuit. He also enjoyed curling. I joined the local ladies
fastball club and curling club. I played ball until the family began playing
league ball. The children also joined the Judo Club in Rainier.

Chomistek Family: Back: Kathy, Dan, Guy; Front: Pat, Angie, Emil (pic)

Then in 1973 we decided to leave irrigation. We sold our farm and bought a
place in the Irvine district in spring of 1974. In Irvine we were mostly in
cattle along with breaking a few horses for others. Later Emil started breaking
up land and so grew a few acres of wheat. Emil still "pro rodeoed" for two more
years and then we got involved, with the family, in the Elkwater Roping Club
which held its ropings every Sunday all summer. Our family also joined 4-H Beef
and got involved in school curling and also very much into school league
volleyball. Emil and I joined the Irvine Curling Club and also belonged to the
Medicine Hat, Alberta Farmers Curling Club. While in Irvine, Pat and Dan
completed their grade twelve.

Then early in 1979 we decided to check out a larger ranch just north of
Tompkins, Saskatchewan and saw it was great cattle country. So we sold our
place in Irvine and bought it. We moved in the fall of 1979 to the Tompkins
district. Here again it was mostly cattle but we added a few more horses to the
ones we already had. Pat and Dan are on the ranch so they and Emil started
breaking horses for both ourselves and others. Kathy and Guy finished out their
education at Hazlet, Saskatchewan. We joined the local Hazlet curling club and
family curled until Emil and the boys started rodeoing steady in the C.C.A.
Rodeo Circuit. We also had our own family orchestra for about three years and
really had a lot of fun at it. Pat still plays occasionally now with another
orchestra. Dan and Pat have also joined the Swift Current Karate Club. Kathy
went on to Nurses Training in Saskatoon at the Kelsey Institute in 1980 and has
been nursing full time in Elrose, Saskatchewan since 1982. Guy, right now, is
competing in the Pro Rodeo Circuit both in Canada and U.S.A.

So, in all, we have left a super nice community and Irvine, to us, holds many
beautiful memories. We will always remember the many friends we made while
there. Our move again has taken us to yet another nice friendly community.
