The Cook Family
by Eugene T. Cook

John Henry Cook came to Irvine in 1901 from Orangeville, Ontario, to join his
sister Florence who had married a rancher, Robert Porter, in the 1890's. Two
Porter brothers, Robert and Jim, had begun ranching in the 1880's following a
stint of construction work in the building of the CPR with their father, Sam.
Henry Cook had been in Manitoba in 1899 on a harvester excursion but had
returned to the East after the harvest. James Cook, father of Florence and
Henry, joined his family in the West and homesteaded the NE 11-2-W4M on March
11, 1905. Henry developed this property. From a base in Irvine he worked on
ranching, railroading, surveying and logging throughout the West for several
years.

In January of 1913, Henry married Pearl Thompson in Medicine Hat. Pearl had
come West in 1911 from Shelburne, Ontario, to join her father, Joseph, and
brother, William, who had homesteaded north of Foremost. Pearl's forebearers
came from Northern Ireland in the 1840's to Canada. When Pearl came to Burdett,
the nearest railway point to the homestead at that time, a large sign on the
fence of the local lumber yard read "Burdett has a future, watch her grow".
Pearl, who was an accomplished seamstress, did not stay on the homestead but
moved to Lethbridge and later to Calgary where she met Henry.

In the fall of 1915 Henry and Mrs. Cook moved from the farm to Irvine where
Henry had purchased a livery, feed, and sales stable. A house was purchased on
North Railway Street from a Mr. Newby, a realtor and insurance agent. Mr.
Newby's advertisement was on a firewall curtain of the Magnet Theatre operated
by the Fred McLaughlins for many years. The Fred Crewes lived on one side of
the Cooks, the John Pollocks on the other, and down the street a short distance
away was the Pioneer Lumber operated by Joe Irhinger. It was a great playground
for the youngsters. On the corner, by the John Pollock's, was a lamp post
erected in anticipation of the use of natural gas for street lighting from gas
to be obtained from a gas well started but never completed on the west side of
town near the home of Bill Corbette, the section foreman. Dr. Fisher, MD, lived
down the street. A short distance away on a side street was an abandoned North
West Mounted Police barracks.

Back seat: Fred and Pearl Cook; At wheel: Henry and Eugene Cook; On running
board: Margaret Thomson (pic)

Henry's father, James Cook, at the age of 18, emigrated from Northern Ireland
to United States in 1846 during the time of the potato famine. Later he moved
to Ontario where he farmed and taught school. In his later years he came West
to live with his daughter Florence at the RP ranch and in Medicine Hat. Before
his health failed parts of some years were spent with Henry and Mrs. Cook in
Irvine. In 1910, despite his advanced years he had helped Henry with the
fencing of the homestead quarter. He was living in town at the time of the
burning of the two-story brick school in the school yard north of Jake Thiede's
house in Irvine. When the weather permitted he would take a daily walk with the
aid of his cane and usually return home with a bag of candy from Lou Sing's
which he shared with the four Cook children, Eugene, Fred, Burton, and Ruth,
who had rounded out the Cook family by 1920. James Cook passed away on January
24, 1927, in Medicine Hat, at the age of 99 years and one month.

Henry and Mrs. Cook were active in the life of the community. Henry served on
the town council and on the local school board and took part in the operation
of the local sports day usually held on the first of July. He was a Justice of
the Peace. In later years he helped during the winter season in the development
of a skating rink and hockey for the youngsters. Mrs. Cook was an active member
of the Anglican Church and was particularly supportive during the years when
the Rev. P.C. Jerrold was the resident minister. She was also a member of the
local branch of the Women's Institute.

Henry managed his farm, his livery and draying business, and bought and sold
horses and cattle. Horses were bought and sold in Alberta, Saskatchewan, and
Manitoba wherever demand existed. Cattle were purchased in the late summer and
fall and shipped to commission agents in Calgary, Moose Jaw, Winnipeg and
Chicago. In 1922 when Henry was away in Chicago with a shipment of cattle, the
Irvine barn burned with the loss of 49 horses, 100 tons of hay, two cars and
one chain drive truck. This was the time of year when grain was being hauled
and farmers were stabling their horses overnight.

Horses provided the power for hauling and for the farm operations of those
times. Grain was delivered to the railway in wagons from as far north as Hilda,
some forty-five miles away. The railroad to Hilda and Schuler was not built
until later. Mail was transported from Irvine to rural post offices such as
Thelma, Fox, Elkwater, Schuler and Hilda. Fred Crewe, the local postmaster, in
1927 won a contract to haul mail. to Schuler and Hilda. He used horses in the
winter when the roads were blocked with snow. Even the No. 1 highway from
Irvine to Medicine Hat - at that time over the hills north and west from Irvine
and down the flats to the east - was blocked with snow drifts for most of the
winter. The opening of the roads to motor travel in the spring was an eventful
occasion.

In the fall of 1929 the homestead farm property, which had been expanded to one
section, was sold along with a tract of pasture land near Elkwater Lake. The
town business had been given up with the advance of the machine age and
increased competition in draying. Farming operations were shifted to other
property northeast of Irvine.

Henry passed away in 1935 from equine encephalitis and was buried in Medicine
Hat. In 1937 Mrs. Cook with Fred, Burton, and Ruth moved to a farm near Rocky
Mountain House.

Mrs. Cook left the farm in 1941 and, after a brief period in Calgary,
established a home in Red Deer. She resumed her work as a seamstress until
retirement. She passed away in 1964 in Innisfail and is buried in Red Deer.

Fred farmed for a number of years at Rocky Mountain House, then left the farm
to follow business opportunities in Rocky. He married Anne Neilsen of Rocky and
raised five children, Jean, Donna, Marjorie, Ronald, and Alan. Anne passed away
and Fred, later, married Iola (Darby) Martz who also passed on. A widower, Fred
now lives in retirement in Rocky.

Ruth graduated from the Calgary Normal School in 1940, taught near Hanna, at
Knee Hill Valley, and at Bowden. She married Lloyd Saunders of Knee Hill
Valley, raised two children, Donald and Audrey, and is now retired in Innisfail
where she enjoys gardening, golf, and support of the local hospital.

Burt and his mother, Pearl Cook - 1942 (pic)

Burton left the farm to work in a wartime plant at Fort William, then served in
the Mounties for a time and later enlisted in the RCAF to see service in the
UK, India, and Ceylon. Discharged in 1946, he made his home in Red Deer
involving himself in the merchandise trade. For a time he was in partnership in
a grocery business. The last few years before retirement saw him in the Civil
Service. He married Cathie Hodge of Innisfail and raised two children, Gregory
and Bruce. He lives in Red Deer.

Eugene, after graduation from Calgary Normal School, began teaching in the fall
of 1933 near Foremost, where he spent four years followed by two years near
Winnifred and two years at Rocky Mountain House. Four years were spent in the
RCAF during which he instructed in Navigation and completed two tours in Bomber
Command in the UK with the RAF Pathfinder Force on Lancasters. He was awarded
the Distinguished Flying Cross. Following WWII he graduated in Engineering from
the University of Alberta in Edmonton and spent 30 years in the oil industry.
Married to Helen Carroll of Eckville, with no children, he is retired in
Calgary.

James and Catherine (McKay) Crawford
Information supplied by Ralph Crawford

James Crawford and Catherine Elizabeth McKay were married in Lethbridge,
Alberta. While living there two children were born: Bertha, born December 31,
1889, and Francis, born August 20, 1891. Irene, Victor, and Cecil were born in
Winnipeg, Manitoba: Irene on June 9, 1893, Victor, on March 9, 1895, and Cecil,
on February 15, 1897. Mary, Greg, John and Ralph were born in Irvine or
Medicine Hat, Alberta: Mary, on December 17, 1898, Greg, on September 2, 1900,
Johnny, on February 27, 1907, and Ralph, in Irvine on April 23, 1913.

Back: Francis (Ashe) Crawford, Irene Crawford; Front: Weldon Ashe, Ralph
Crawford, Frank Ashe - 1915 (pic)

Johnny Crawford (pic)

James Crawford managed R. C. Becker's ranch in the coulee. The brand was 9 half
diamond. Dick Becker was Ralph's uncle. James was captain of the roundup of the
ranches in the Cypress Hills area. Later James farmed about six miles south of
Irvine. His stable was burned down in 1912 or 1913. Arson is believed to be the
cause. Ralph's brothers and sisters all went to Berry Centre School down in the
coulee.

James built a large house opposite the C.P.R. station in Irvine on the north
side of the tracks. It is believed the Sommers family lived there after the
Crawford family moved to Medicine Hat, Alberta.

They moved to Medicine Hat about 1915 or 1916 but continued to farm about six
miles south of Irvine for another six or seven years. These were tough years.
There were no crops and there was a cyclone.

Ralph's memories of Irvine are the dances in the theatre with all the babies
lined up on the stage, attending the Anglican church as it was the only church
in town, swimming in the creek on the south side with the water coming up to
his chin as he was only six years old, riding in their Model T up the hill
south of Irvine, and Vic owning a motorcycle. A lot of summers were spent at
the cottage in Elkwater Lake. In those days there were very few cars and to get
to Medicine Hat you went north to the Hilda-Schuler road and then turned west.

Both Cecil and Victor worked in the bank. After James died Victor ran the farm
and also served in the R.C.A.F. in Canada. Cecil was in the army and served
overseas for two years. Ralph is the only surviving member of the original
family and is now residing in Vancouver, B.C.

Frederick and Margaret (Hausauer) Crewe
by Babs (Crewe) Rosvold and Judith Crewe

Frederick John Crewe was born in Malvern, England, of parents Henry and
Elizabeth Crewe. Fred wanted to be a cowboy and see the west, so at age 13, in
1889 he came to Canada and went to work for the RP Ranch of Robert Porter.

Margaret Hausauer was born in Odessa, Russia in 1889, and was seven weeks old
when her parents, John and Margaret Hausauer, sailed with her to the United
States and settled in Eureka, South Dakota. In 1902, they moved to the Irvine
area where her father homesteaded.

Margaret worked the land as a child, and when a teenager went to work for Mrs.
Robert Porter. There she met Fred Crewe. They were married May 12, 1906 and set
up housekeeping on a homestead just west and north of Irvine. There they had
two daughters, Mary Margaret, born March 31, 1907 and Elizabeth Edith, born
March 3, 1909.

Fred was seriously injured when a horse he was "breaking" fell on him. The
accident broke his shoulder blade and a number of ribs and one rib punctured a
valve in his heart. Doctors said he couldn't live, but he proved them wrong.
The accident ended his ranching days, though, and the family moved into Irvine,
where Fred went into the butcher shop business with his father-in-law John
Hausauer.

Crewe house, Lizzie, Buster, Maggie, Fred (pic)

Elizabeth (Lizzie) Crewe (pic)

John (Buster) Crewe (pic)

Crewe house, Buster on steps (pic)

Fred later left the meat market and became Irvine's second postmaster. In the
early days he also hauled the mail from Irvine to all the outlying towns:
Hilda, Schuler, Thelma, Fox, Robinson, and Elkwater. As the saying goes, in
cold, heat, rain or shine, the mail went through, and he made the long trips by
horse and sleigh or wagon. He also sold insurance.

Fred was a staunch Anglican and believer in Royalty, and always had a helping
hand for anyone in trouble, often doing without to help someone else. Although
Margaret Crewe was unable to read or write she was an accomplished seamstress
and cook. She took many prizes at fairs throughout her lifetime, for both her
sewing (quilts and rugs, etc.) and also for her baking and cooking. She worked
diligently for the Irvine Women's Institute and was always there when needed to
help someone giving birth, since there were no doctors in town.

Fred and Maggie had four more children, John Frederick (known as Buster), born
October 9, 1910, Albert Bromley, born October 29, 1912, Florence Mabelle, born
January 12, 1916, and Viola Victoria (known as Babs), born December 20, 1921.

Mary died at age four and is buried in Irvine. Elizabeth married David
Schneider and died in 1931 with her first child. Elizabeth (Lizzie) worked with
her father in the post office and was always active in sports and welfare work.
She too was a hard worker for the Irvine Women's Institute.

Fred Crewe died in 1944, and Margaret in 1971.

Buster, as he was always known, lived his life in Irvine with the exception of
a sojourn on the Alaska Highway during World War II. He always had trucks and a
trucking business. He also had a garage called Central Motors until the war,
when it was sold. After the war he went into the farm machinery business. In
1945 he married Lillian Linderman, and he died May 2, 1950. They had three
daughters, Sharon Joy, Clara Jane, and Patricia Naomi. Sharon became a nursing
aide and married Bob Shannon, who was killed in a car accident after a short
marriage. Sharon later married Ken Muir. They have their own business in
Calgary and have two children, David and Angela. Clara Jane, a real homemaker,
loved baking and sewing and keeping house. She met and married Beau Wallace,
and they now live in Blairmore where Beau teaches school. They have five
children, Rex, Dixie Ann, Tasha Rose, Tansy, -and Caley. Patricia was the
tomboy of the three, loving the outdoors and sports. She moved to Brooks to
work, and there met Ken Williamson of the R.C.M.P. They were married, and as
with all Mounties, moved around a lot. But they stopped long enough to have two
boys, Robert and Darcy.

Albert lived his younger years in Irvine and worked as a mechanic for Harry
Crooks in the Irvine Garage. Later, Albert and Buster joined in owning Central
Motors. When World War II broke out, they left the garage and Albert joined the
Navy, attaining the rank of chief petty officer. After the war he again joined
Buster in the farm machinery business, until Buster's death. He then moved to
Calgary and was a mechanic with General Supplies. In 1957 he met and married
Myrtle Brocklebank. They had no family. Albert died December 27, 1986.

Margaret (Maggie)-and Florence Crewe (pic)

Viola V. Crewe, Raymond Jacobson (pic)

Florence Crewe (pic)

Florence (Jo) grew up in Irvine and also worked in the post office with her
father. She also bought a horse and herded the townspeoples' cows. She left
Irvine about 1935 and went to Regina, and from there to Claresholm, where she
met and married Gordon Teters May 10, 1940. They moved to Calgary, and Jo
worked for W.H. Harper Company and Gordon worked for Universal Sales. In June
1948 they had a daughter, Judith Elaine, who attended University of Calgary,
University of Alberta, and Simon Fraser University, obtaining degrees in
English, a teaching certificate, and a certificate in Local Government
Administration. She now lives in Redwater.

Viola (Babs) worked at all sorts of jobs in Irvine during the Great Depression,
as jobs were hard to get. She met and ' married Haldor Rosvold who taught
school in Irvine. They went to California in 1941 where Haldor attended
Stanford University until called home to go into the army. She divorced him
after the war and went to work for Alberta Wood Products in Calgary for 18
years. When Florence divorced Gordon in 1965, she too worked for Alberta Wood
Products. In 1971, Babs and she, Jo, left that firm and moved to Edmonton where
they opened their own ready-to-finish furniture store called Color it Wood,
until 1986. They are both now retired pensioners in Edmonton.

Rev. G. and Johanna (Krompharf) Daechsel
by Mrs. Lillian M. (Daechsel) Assmus

Rev. G. Daechsel, his wife Johanna, and their daughter Magdalene came to Irvine
in the fall of 1930 from Radisson, Saskatchewan where he had pastored the
Lutheran Church. He then became the pastor of Christ Lutheran Church in Irvine
from 1930 to 1936. When they left Irvine they returned to Saskatchewan and
retired at Grenfell. Rev. Daechsel was 87 and Johanna was 83 when they passed
away at Grenfell.

Magdalene was a school teacher and taught at Clover Hill from 1933 to the
spring of 1934. She also taught in the town of Walsh. Magdalene was also active
in the Irvine W.I. At one of these meetings Mrs. Stephen Wiedeman, convenor for
Canadian Industries and Alberta Products, chose as her subject "Buy at Home"
and illustrated her subject with a very attractive display of products from
Alberta factories: woolen goods, cereals, canned goods, growing plants, cut
flowers, biscuits, crockery, etc. Magdalene was so inspired by this
presentation she composed the following song, "Alberta Industries" or "Buy at
Home", sung to the tune of "My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean".

Alberta Industries

To beautify happy occasions
Let flowers the Rosary send,
Carnations, forget-me-nots, tulips
And roses will "tell it" your friend.

Chorus

Help make Alberta prosperous
Give her gladly your helping hand;
Prosperous, prosperous;
Buy products of your own land.

The 'Hat grinds white and graham flour,
Try Maple Leaf or Robin Hood,
Gas City and Dederer's rollers
Provide bread and much breakfast food.

With bread you want butter and honey,
The melilot grows "Oh! So high!"
The tourists love scenting sweet clover,
Where millions of busy bees fly.

Eat vegetables, summer and winter,
We grow corn, peas, beans and so forth,
Where buffaloes roamed the wild prairies
Are gardens, look East, West, South, North.

For breakfast have oatmeal or creamlets,
Each morning a dish you should eat;
They give proteins, carbohydrates,
And vitamins too; they're a treat.

The sodas beloved by the children
From Calgary's I.B.C.O.,
With soups and at many occasions
Their crispness and whiteness can show.

The ditches of deep irrigation
Refresh the wide stretches of beet,
For sugar is now an essential -
It's needed for each ice cream treat.

For lard, bacon, ham, cheese and sausage,
Try Calgary's meat packer 'Burns';
The hogs that are fed on our prairie
He quickly to sausage-meat turns.

The lamp chimney's blown by machine now -
At Redcliff you'll find much glassware;
The housewife's beloved fruit sealer,
Glass vases and bottles they've there.

For pottery tea-pots and earthware,
For crocks, jars and pitchers of clay,
The Medicine Hat famous pottery
Will fill all your orders today.

There's many a plant that a farmer
Can raise with a profit today;
The house must be neat, clean and tidy
Hear Taber say: "Sweep thrice a day."

Mitts, socks, sweaters, stockings, wool garments,
Of beautiful color and shade;
Inquire for products from Caldwell,
From wool of our prairie sheep made.

In Calgary, our largest, clean city,
The dresses are sewn by Hatchivear;
The housewife's delight at her duties
Are dresses that don't quickly tear.

When boys and men dress up for Sunday,
For shirts from the Great West they call,
And each working-day they delight in
The ready to wear overall.

The children collect all the wrappers;
"We want Royal Crown Pearl," they say,
From naphtha is made the white product,
That gives joy on each working day.

With industry comes joy and gladness -
Help diligence where e'er you roam;
When shopping, remember your own land -
Do you share to aid "Buy at Home!"

-Miss M. Daeschel

Magdalene also made cluny lace and this art was called "klepling". The lace is
created on a fairly large sized pin cushion that is rotated and, with the aid
of color beaded pins, the yarn is wound around these pins, thus creating a very
nice delicate lace which is used to edge collars or hankies.

When her parents moved to Grenfell she went with them and also taught there.
Eventually she moved to Calgary where her sister, Lillian M. Assmus, also lived
in the Bethany Care Center. Magdalene died, in Calgary, on December 16, 1980.

Bob Davidson
by Mrs. Guy (Dorothy Davidson) Olmstead

My parents "Bob" and Florence Davidson moved to Irvine from Lethbridge in
January, 1923.  Dad was delighted with his new job as station agent for the
Canadian Pacific Railway. It had regular eight to five working hours and the
fabulous salary of $200 a month. Years later he confided in me that when he got
his first pay cheque he "had so much money he didn't know what to do with it".
For my mother the move was not so exciting. She came from a comfortable home in
the city to a CPR dwelling in a small town where their source of heat was the
coal stove, lights were kerosene lamps and water was drawn from an outdoor
pump. But after a period of adjustment she made the old station into a
comfortable home for the next 28 years.

Both my parents took an active part in the community. Mother was a member of
the Women's Institute and renewed her former school teaching profession as
substitute teacher on a few occasions when the regular teacher was ill. Dad
served on the local school board and on various Band Drive committees during
the war years, 1939- 1945. An ardent sportsman, he took great pride in his gun
collection and he and Nick Pohlman - Manager of the Citizens Lumber Company -
were instrumental in starting a nine hole golf course on the hills east of
Irvine. He, with many others - Hank Cook, Bill Naylor, to name only a couple,
spent long hours flooding the skating rink next to the town hall only to have
all the ice melt with every chinook wind. In 1951, they transferred to
Innisfail and three months later to Maple Creek, retiring to Medicine Hat in
1953.

Dorothy
My early school days began in the old two room sandstone school with teacher
Audrey Terry. Subsequent teachers in the primary room were Olga Tinney, Jean
Courtice and Lillian Hunt. In the senior room, grade six to nine we had Joe
Noviski and Hamilton Byers. On completing grade nine several of us wanted to go
on to High School so our parents agreed to pay the teacher, Tom Collinger, to
conduct our grade ten classes by lamplight after regular school hours. By the
time we were ready for grade eleven a third room had been established in the
town hall and a third teacher hired. It was from here that Irvine's first high
school class graduated with a grade twelve standing under the capable and
dedicated tutoring of Haldor Rosvold.

Shortly thereafter, having acquired my Associate Degree for piano from the
Royal Conservatory of Music, I went to Toronto to further my studies. Upon
returning west, I married Guy Olmstead, an employee of the Crystal Dairy, in
1948. We have continued to live here in Medicine Hat and are now enjoying
retirement. We have two married sons, Robert of Red Deer and Douglas currently
of Calgary, and three grandchildren.

Among my earliest close friends was Margaret "Binks" Cotteral whose father was
with the RCMP. Ruth Cook and I were inseparable for years until the family
moved away. Gertrude Wiedeman and I became close friends during our high school
days and still keep in touch. Florence Babuk, whose father was the CPR section
foreman, was one of the gang and now lives in Medicine Hat. We all enjoyed many
good times in McLaughlin's Magnet Theatre when Johnny Glock and his orchestra
played for community dances; and our school teachers provided parents and
friends with plenty of entertainment with the annual Christmas school concert
in which all local "kids" were obliged to take part.

Eli Dennis
Eli Dennis was born in Oxford Co. Ontario in 1847, the youngest of ten children
of Thomas and Mary (Palmer) Dennis who came to Canada from Devonshire, England
c. 1832.

Margaret Hansuld was born in Oxford Co. in 1854. Her Hansuld forebears
emigrated from Wallersdorf, Hessen, Germany to Ontario in 1842. Margaret was
the second oldest child in a family of nine.

Eli married Margaret Hansuld in Ontario c.1875 and they farmed on lot 33, con.8
of W. Zorra Tp. Oxford Co. Ontario until they sold their farm and moved to the
Irvine district with their nine children, seven sons and two daughters, in 1910.

Eli and Margaret Dennis homesteaded on the NE 6-14-1-W4 and they also owned the
adjoining NW 5. Their sons homesteaded nearby as follows: Reubin Ezra,
NE 12-14-2-W4; Harry Franklin, NW 12-14-2-W4; Norman Eli, NW 7-14-1-W4; Orwell
Palmer, NE 7-14-1-W4; Roy Havelock, SE 7-14-1-W4; Warren Ray, SE 6-14-1-W4.

Their other son Edwin Nelson did not file on a homestead and after a time
returned to Ontario. Harry also moved back to Ontario and lived in Sarnia. Roy
left his Many Island Lakes farm in April 1919 and moved to Boise, Idaho where
he was a building contractor until his death in 1955. Reubin, Norman, Orwell
and Warren left their farms about 1925 to relocate on farms near Orkney,
Saskatchewan where two of their cousins, Wilson and Lloyd Dennis, had been
farming for several years.

There were two other children in the family Mary Elizabeth (Mima), who was born
in 1876 and died in 1900, and Milton Conrad, a twin brother of Mildred, who
died in infancy in 1890.

Mildred Margaret Jane married Albert John Theodore Schmidt, the son of Ernst
and Bertha Schmidt, on April 16, 1919 in Medicine Hat, Alberta. Albert and
Mildred had two children, Harvey and Doris.

Alice Maude Deborah, the youngest child, married Robert Ayling in Medicine Hat
on September 12, 1921 and they had one child, Roy.

Eli and Margaret also left the farm about 1925 and moved to Medicine Hat. Eli
died in 1927 and is buried in Hillside cemetery in Medicine Hat. Margaret died
in 1930 at the hospital in Climax, Saskatchewan and is buried in the
Orkney-Masefield cemetery near Orkney, Saskatchewan.

Fredrick and Alvina (Lehr) Derheim

Fredrick Derheim was born October 7, 1867 in Neudorf, South Russia. He
immigrated to North Dakota where he married Alvina Lehr on November 23, 1895.
Alvina was born September 28, 1874 in Kassell, Russia. Their three oldest
children were born in North Dakota: Lydia, John and Fredrick.

Alvina and Fredrick Derheim (pic)

Hearing that great amounts of I and were available in Canada, they took their
family and belongings and came by train to the Irvine district in 1902. They
bought land and set up their homestead ten miles south of Irvine. A large
amount of work was done, building a log home and breaking land so that it could
be seeded and harvested. Fredrick brought along from the USA. a large breed of
heavy work horses, which were a great help working their land. They also raised
and sold horses to other pioneers.

As the years went on, the family grew larger. Seven more children were born:
Karl, Emma, Edward, Emil, Albert, Bertha, and Rueben. Fredrick and Alvina
purchased more land at this time. In 1934, Fredrick and Alvina retired in
Medicine Hat. Fredrick passed away May 8, 1936. Alvina remarried in later years
to Christ Vossler, who also passed away later. Alvina lived to be 84 years old
before she died on August 24, 1958.

Lydia was married to Manual Ulrick, Dan Herter, and Chris Walker. All are
deceased. She had three daughters: Elsie Ulrick was married to Ed Krauss and
Sam Mutschler, both of whom died; Annie Ulrick married August Schneider, both
deceased; Alice Herter married Pete Proll.

John married Annie Hoffman (deceased) and had ten children: Dave, deceased,
married to Rose; Inez, deceased; Henry, Irene, married to Roy Deering; Edward,
married to Ida; Ivy, was married to Louis Mardian and later to Steve
Karmoniski; Shirley, deceased; Joyce, married to Hans Rehm; Chesley, deceased;
and Marlene, married to Marvin Krauss.

Fred is deceased.

Karl married Mary Heller and had one daughter, Ruth.

Emma married Christ Vossler, deceased, and had eight children: Fred, married to
Lorna; Ralph, married to Ruth; Ralph's twin, Esther, deceased; Albert, married
to Yvonne, both deceased; Wallace, deceased, married to Shirley; Beny, married
to Rose; Roy, married to Faye; and Irene, married to Eddie Wiessgerber.

Edward was married to Martha March and had no children.

Emil married Lydia Scheffelmeier and had three children, Norman, Harvey and
Agnes.

Albert married Dorothy Vossler and had no children.

Bertha married Mike Bischke and had two children, Roy and Vivian.

Rueben, deceased, married Elma Schneider. Their daughter, Marge, was married to
Gordon Heather, deceased, and is remarried.

Carl Derheim Family
by Mary Derheim

On February 11, 1925, I, Mary Heller and Carl Derheim got married and made our
home on a farm 12 miles south of Irvine. Our parents gave us a bit of land, a
team of horses and a few household and personal things but we had no house to
live in. A two story house was purchased at Irvine but how to move it was the
problem. So with the help of some neighbors, the house was cut in half. Then
each half was loaded on wagons and transported through gullies and up hills,
with hope upon hope that the house would get to its destination intact. It did,
but putting the two halves together again was a real challenge. While Carl was
working in the field, I was handy with a hammer and saw. After months of hard
work and even though there was very little money, with wallpaper and paint we
finished the inside into an attractive home for three, as Ruth, our only
daughter, was born on August 4, 1928. We ended up farming four quarters in
grain, and one quarter pasture with about 55 head of cattle, until the fall of
1947.

Carl hadn't been well for some time as he had muscular dystrophy that disabled
him more and more. Now Ruth needed to be her dad's companion outside, working
with him most of the time, before and after school. In the later years of our
farming, Carl had been very ill and Ruth and I farmed. Finally in 1947 we had
to sell and auction all our belongings; it was sad to leave our home and
friends. We moved to Kelowna, B.C. Carl had several heart attacks but survived
them, but his muscular dystrophy got worse and he became bedridden in 1970. We
bought a battery operated wheelchair and Carl went down town in it almost every
day until his death on January 7, 1982.

Ruth married Cecil McConnell, a logging truck driver, on January 4, 1956. They
lived in Woss Lake on Vancouver Island till 1973 when they, too, moved to
Kelowna. They have three children, Sandy, Dan and Barry. I have six
great-grandchildren. Sandy lives in Kelowna. Dan, Barry and their families live
in Cranbrook, B.C.

I now live in an apartment and at 84, still enjoy good health and am quite
active.

Edward Derheim

Edward was born and raised south of Irvine. With the help of his father,
Fredrick, he purchased his own land to farm.

Edward married Martha March in May of 1935. They continued farming on this land
and worked hard building a new house, barn and other outside buildings.

Edward's life came to a tragic end on a rainy June morning in 1956. He was
killed while driving his car across a railway crossing west of Irvine.

Martha farmed two more years and then moved to Medicine Hat in 1958. She died
in 1974. Edward and Martha had no children.

Martha and Edward Derheim (pic)

Emil Derheim

Emil Derheim was born on the family farm in the Newburg the Newburg district.
He attended School and helped out with the farming. On February 11, 1930, Emil
married Lydia Scheffelmeier and they lived on the same farm as Emil's parents,
but in the original house. Emil's parents had built and had been living in a
new home by then.

In 1932, Emil and Lydia's first child, Norman, was born. Two years later,
another son, Harvey, was born. Both sons were born in the same house as their
father.

Emil's parents moved to Medicine Hat in 1934. That same year Emil's youngest
brother, Rueben, married and moved into the newest home on the homestead. Emil
and Rueben farmed together until the early spring of 1936, and then Emil and
Lydia bought and moved to a farm in the Norton district.

A year later a daughter, Agnes, was born to Emil and Lydia. Lydia's health was
poor and she passed away in July, 1938, leaving Emil with three small children.
Emil remarried in 1939 and sold his farm a few years later. He then moved to
Calgary with his new wife and daughter, leaving Norman and Harvey with
relatives in the district.

Emil and Agnes returned to Medicine Hat, after his divorce. Agnes then went to
live with her grandmother, Rosie Scheffelmeier.

Emil's life came to a tragic end in May 1950, in a train and car accident.

Norman, Emil's oldest son, moved to Medicine Hat in 1947. He started to work at
the Potteries and later at a billiard room, which he purchased and is still
running. He married Jean Becker in 1954. They had three children: a son, Barry,
a daughter Tannis, and a son Randy. Randy died in a car accident in 1983.

Harvey is still living and farming in the Robinson district. He bought the farm
from his uncle Albert and aunt Dorothy Derheim. In 1958, he married Martha
Geigle. They have two sons, Gary and Gerald. His two sons are in the farming
business, too.

Agnes joined the Air Force after completing her schooling. This is where she
met and married Gordon Minnes in 1960. They have two children, a son, Rodney,
and a daughter, Debbie. Gordon retired from the Air Force in 1975 and they
moved to Camrose, Alberta, where they are currently living.

Frederick and Magdaline Dietelback

Frederick and Magdaline Dietelback emigrated from Austria to Many Island Lake
district in 1912. They brought with them ten children, three of whom are still
living, Jack of, Ponoka, Joe of Medicine Hat and Christina (Johnson) of
Medicine Hat.

Christina married August Johnson in 1931. Of this union there were five
children: Evelyn and Ray Jans of Irvine, Herbert and Gloria of Drumheller,
Caroline of Lethbridge, Leonard and Ruth of Medicine Hat, and August Jr. and
Donna of Calgary.

George W. Dinkel

George W. Dinkel was agent for Citizen's Lumber Co. in 1911 and 1914 and
president of the Board of Trade in 1914. He was chairman of the Dominion Day
Sports Day during this time.

According to the Schuler History Book he moved to Schuler about 1920 and later
resided in Calgary.

Daniel and Louise (Roloff) Doering
by Clara Jane Larson

Daniel Doering was born January 19, 1856 and had one brother, Johan, and one
sister, Susan. He was a farmer.

Louise (Roloff) Doering was born in April 1857 and was a midwife.

Daniel and Louise had eight children, six boys and two girls. All of the family
migrated from Bessarabia, Russia to Canada in 1903 to take up homesteads in the
Robinson area.

Daniel and Louise Doering (pic)

Three sons, Nathaniel, John and David, were married before coming to Canada.

Daniel and Louise moved to Irvine in the early 20's. In July 1926 Daniel built
sidewalks there. He worked 28 hours for 30c, which came to $8.40.

Daniel died on June 15, 1927 and is buried in the Irvine cemetery. Louise lived
in Medicine Hat after Daniel passed away. She was still doing mid-wifery until
her passing on January 15, 1939 and is buried in Medicine Hat.

Nathaniel, born February 6, 1877, died June 19, 1962.

Minnie, born September 24, 1878, married Jacob Sulz and died October 16, 1941.

David, born August 26, 1880, died April 17, 1967.

Rudolf, born February 19, 1885, died about 1947.

Otto, born March 26, 1887, died March 24, 1947.

John, born May 10, 1889, died February 1, 1972.

Matilda was born November 17, 1891, married Adolf Brost and died July 19, 1985.

Emanuel, born July 13, 1895, died May 3, 1982.

have endeavored to use the preferred spelling of each but have arranged them in
our usual family grouping.

Nathaniel and Justina Doering

Nathaniel and Justina (Burkholz) Doering were both born in Kulm, Russia, and
came to Canada in 1903. They homesteaded in the Josephsburg, Alberta, area
until 1932, and then moved to a farm two miles north of Irvine. The family
consisted of 13 children, two of whom died in infancy, Thomas (1902-1904) and
Lydia (1914). The remaining 11 children, from oldest to youngest were: Ida,
Albert, Gordon, Emilia, Melitda, August, Emil, Karl, John, Leah and Rachel.
While living in the Josephsburg district, the children attended school in the
Robinson School District. After 1932, they attended the Irvine School.

Daniel Doering Family: Otto Deering, Matilda (Deering) Brost, Louise Doering,
Nathaniel (Dan) Doering, Dave Deering, Minnie (Deering) Sulz, Rudolph, John,
Emanuel Deering (pic)

Nathaniel and Justina moved into the town of Irvine upon their retirement.
Justina passed away in 1946, and Nathaniel passed away in 1962. They are both
resting in peace in the Irvine Cemetery. By the time of Nathaniel's passing,
his children had given him 43 grandchildren.

Ida (August 10, 1900 - March 14, 1985) married Reinhold Frisch and lived in Red
Deer. They had two boys and three girls.

Albert Doering (November 7, 1903 - October 18, 1984) married Violet Stuber;
their family consisted of three girls and one boy. Violet lived in Medicine Hat
until her passing on May 9, 1988.

Gordon Deering (June 1, 1905 - April 8, 1985) married Martha Krauss and raised
a family which consisted of four girls and three boys. One son, Raymond, died
in 1978. Now widowed, Martha lives in Claresholm.

Emilia (October 11, 1906) married Ludwig Hildebrand. They still live in
Medicine Hat. They had two sons and two daughters.

Melitda (September 11, 1908 - October 22, 1984) married Sam Koppenstein and
lived in Lethbridge. They had two daughters.

August Deering (February 26, 1910 - May 11, 1987) married Elizabeth Boschee.
Now widowed, "Lizzie" lives in Stettler. They raised four daughters and two
sons.

where they raised three sons and two daughters.

Rachel (August 6, 1920 - August 20, 1987) was the only Doering child who stayed
in Irvine all her life. She married Arthur Zeller in February of 1941. Their
family consisted of two boys and five daughters.

Over the years, few of these families have remained in the Irvine community,
and unfortunately, at the time of compiling this family history only four of
Nathaniel and Justina's children remain: Emelia, Karl, John and Leah.

August Deering
submitted by Lizzie Deering

August Deering was born on February 26, 1910 at Josephsburg, later called
Robinson, on the homestead of his parents, Nathaniel and Justina Deering. He
was the seventh of 13 children. August attended Robinson School for a few
years. At a young age, he went to Hilda to help his brother-in-law, Reinhold
Frisch. He also attended school there for awhile. Then when he went back home
he had to work. There was no more schooling for him. When his parents moved
away from there in the early thirties, Emil and August were left batching on
SW 6-10-3-4.

August and Lizzie Deering - 50th Anniv., March 2, 1983, Rumsey, AB. (pic)

August Deering Family: Back: Norman, Jim; Middle: Betty, August, Clara Jane;
Front: Brenda, Lizzie and Diane (pic)

August and I, Lizzie Boschee, met in 1932. On March 2, 1933 we were married.
Those were the hard times. We milked cows and raised chickens and geese. The
crops were poor for lack of rain. It was pretty tough going for awhile. Things
started to pick up later on. In 1951 crops were pretty good. We had four army
boys to help along with the harvest. They were on a harvest leave.

The Family of Karl Doering
submitted by Eileen Cicon

Karl was born on October 31, 1912, in the Gros Ventre District, later known as
the Robinson District. He was schooled in the Robinson District until grade
eight and part of grade nine. He moved to a farm north of Irvine, W 8-12-2-4 in
1932. The depression took its toll on Karl, consequently in 1937 he went by bus
to Wetaskiwin and worked for the Goodrichs, stooking, threshing, and other odd
jobs until the middle of November. of 1937. He and his brother, Johnny, who
also worked in Wetaskiwin, combined their earnings and bought feed for the
cattle on their farm in Irvine. Thank goodness for 1938; the crops improved
steadily, ceasing the need to work outside of their own farm.

Alice (Boschee) and Karl Doering - October 25, 1940 (pic)

Karl, Johnny, and their parents lived on the same farm until 1939, when their
parents moved to Irvine. On October 25, 1940, Karl married Alice Boschee of the
Robinson District.

Karl and Alice Doering had six children: Geraldine Faye, born August 5, 1945;
Clifford Dale, April 6, 1947; Eileen Rose, July 23, 1948; Audrey May, September
15, 1951; Warren Karl, November 24, 1954; and Sandra Alice, November 5, 1957.

Alice was an avid gardener and like many farm women, milked cows and raised
chickens. She had many customers in town who purchased her eggs and cream.
Karl's mixed farming proved to be successful and life was indeed pleasant.

In January of 1960, tragedy struck. While traveling home from Medicine Hat, the
vehicle in which Karl, Alice and Clifford were traveling was struck by an
oncoming car. Both Alice and Clifford were killed instantly and Karl was
seriously injured. In 1962, an attempt was made to re-establish the family, but
failed. The children were all placed in different homes.

After several years in Claresholm, Karl now resides in Medicine Hat, at the
Central Park Lodge.

Geraldine and Alvin Polanchek, and their two children, Michael and Lori, reside
in High River, Alberta.

Alvin Polenchek Family: Back: Alvin; Front: Michael, Geraldine (Doering), Lori
(pic)

Eileen and Jim Cicon, and their two children, Coralee and Colette, live in
Medicine Hat.

Audrey and Delmer Haggkvist have three children, Troy, Kerry, and Jason, and
have taken up residence in Bella Coola, B.C.

Warren and Marion live in Redcliff, Alberta.

Sandra and Tom Kelly live in Little Britain, Ontario with their son, Jordon.

John and Victoria Doering

I, Johnnie, son of Nathaniel and Justina Doering was the third youngest of 11
children. I was born January 11, 1917 in the Josephsburg district, now known as
the Robinson District. I received my education at the Robinson School until
grade eight, at which time I had to quit. I was quite upset about this, as I
enjoyed school and wanted to continue. However, my parents required my help on
the family farm.

In the late fall of 1932 our family left the Robinson District and moved to a
farm north of Irvine on W1/2 3-12-2-4.

The depression years were extremely tough With the drought, there were no
crops, resulting in a shortage of feed for the cattle. In 1937, due to another
crop failure, I left home and went out working. So, along with a few friends, I
hopped the freight train and headed for Wetaskiwin Alberta on July 5, in 105
degree weather. We worked there for various farmers and helped with the haying,
stooking of grain, and threshing. Upon completion of the fall work, I returned
home the end of November. Using my earnings I was able to purchase some feed
from Brooks to winter the stock.

In the spring of 1938, there was a terrible snow storm resulting in a lot of
cattle losses. However, from that time on conditions improved, resulting in
much better crops and feed for the livestock.

Tom Kelly Family: Sandra (Doering), Tom, Jordan (pic

John and Victoria Doering (pic)

On October 17, 1939 I married Victoria Trekofski, daughter of John and
Christina Trekofski. They lived about one mile north of our homestead. Victoria
was born on September 14, 1919 at Irvine, Alberta. Following our marriage my
parents retired to the town of Irvine.

My older brother Karl and I continued farming the home place together. At that
time we had to do all the land work with horses, until we bought a Model D John
Deere tractor and various other machinery to work with. During the next few
years, Victoria and I were able to purchase our first vehicle. It was a 1927
Chev car, which we later converted into a truck.

In 1947, Karl and I decided to set up our own farms. I moved one mile southeast
of the home place on the E 1/2 8-12-2-4 where Victoria and I continued to farm.
We also raised cattle, hogs and poultry. In those days milking cows was one of
the main tasks. In fact, at one time We milked 18 to 20 head by hand,
purchasing a milk machine later on. In addition to that we sold and delivered
eggs, cream, butter and poultry for extra income.

We were avid choir and church members of the Peace United Church in Irvine. Our
choir became well known and consequently traveled to different churches to sing.

Victoria and I were blessed with three children: Leona born in July, 1942,
Janet born in November, 1946, and Garry, born in May, 1949. They all attended
school in Irvine. Janet and Garry, however, finished their high school grades
in Medicine Hat, Alberta.

Because the farm wasn't large enough to be a self-supporting operation, we
moved to Medicine Hat in the fall of 1961, with hopes of finding a job while
continuing to farm. I started working for Oland Construction who had the
contract to build Webster Niblock School and add on an addition to both the
Crescent Heights High School and the Auxiliary Hospital. In 1962, I started
working for the Medicine Hat Exhibition and Stampede Company. Victoria worked
at various jobs until later devoting all her time to the household duties. In
1966, we sold the farm to Leslie Woodward and restricted ourselves to city
living. I carried on working for the Stampede Company until in the late 1970's
when I retired. Since then, we've enjoyed our retirement to the fullest. At
present, we're members of the Memorial Salem United Church in Medicine Hat.
Over the years we've been involved in many travels, especially to Whitehorse,
Yukon Territory to visit family.

Jim and Mary Deering
by Jim and Mary Deering

Jim was born in Irvine, December 20, 1910, to Otto and Caroline Deering. He
spent his early years in the Irvine district and attended school in Irvine.
Later he farmed in partnership with his father on a farm south of Pashley. Here
he worked a lot with riding and breaking horses, but he also liked playing
baseball in his spare time.

In 1939, he married Mary MacLeod in Medicine Hat. Mary was born in Medicine Hat
on March 30, 1912 to John and Annie MacLeod. She was raised in the city and
received her public and high school education there. In 1930, she attended
Calgary Normal School for her teacher's training, graduating in 1931. She
taught various schools until 1939 when she got married.

They moved into a home a quarter of a mile from the home place. Mary being a
city girl, Jim had to show her the ropes. It was very different than teaching
school. Baking bread became a great challenge. Her first efforts left much to
be desired, but she finally mastered it, and with Jim's help she also learned
to milk cows, raise chickens and help with the farming. Three children,
however, were soon to follow. The first, Mac, was born in 1940, followed
closely by Ronald in 1941, and finally a daughter, Lynne Anne, in 1943. During
this time Mary also taught at the Coal Centre School in 1942, and again in 1944
to 1950.  Obviously the Deerings had their hands full, but together, with the
occasional hired girl, they managed. Their children attended the Coal Centre
School until Mac was in grade nine, when they were bussed to Irvine. Jim and
Mary not only saw their children moving to another school, but his mother and
father retiring to Medicine Hat. Then they moved their family onto the home
place, and Jim took over the whole operation. They lived there until 1968 when
they sold and moved into Medicine Hat.

Ron, Mac and Lynne Anne Deering (pic)

Jim now keeps busy farming on a smaller scale. He grows a prosperous garden
every summer and gives most of the produce to the children and grandchildren.
He also plays cards every chance he gets. Mary is involved with the Co-op
Women's Guild and also enjoys bowling.

Back: Murray, Shannon, Lynne Anne and Chester Herman; Middle: Jim and Mary
Deering, Russell Herman; Front: Theresa and Suzette Herman (pic)

Mac is presently living in Redcliff. He has been working for Dome Glass for the
past 25 years. He has two daughters, Sheri Maki and Keli Deering.

Ron lived in Redcliff and worked for the Canadian Forces Base Suffield. He
married Judy Geisbrecht of Swift Current. He passed away in 1979. Their
youngest daughter Kristy lives with Judy in Redcliff. Their oldest daughter
Holly lives and works in Swift Current. Their son Robyn passed away in 1980
after struggling with Cystic Fibrosis.

Lynne Anne married Chester Herman and lives near Elkwater. They have four
children: Murray, who married Shannon Bitz and lives in Medicine Hat; Russell
who also lives and works in Medicine Hat; and the girls, Suzette and Theresa,
who are presently attending the Medicine Hat College. Lynne Anne's children are
the third Deering generation to attend Irvine School.

and Army Service Corp. He married Nellie Wilkinson and they live in

retired due to ill health. His son, Barlow, now operates the farm with his two

John Samuel Deering,

John (Jack) Deering, the fourth eldest son of Otto and Caroline Deering, was
born July 4, 1916 in the Irvine district. He attended school at Taylorville,
south of Cardston, and Coal Centre in the Pashley area. After working for Mr.
Bill Putman of the Tothill district for a couple of years, Jack moved to
Medicine Hat in 1941 where he was employed by the Dederer Puffed Wheat Plant.
Then in October of that same year he started his railroad career as a wiper. He
was promoted to fireman and then engineer for the Canadian Pacific Railway.

In 1942, he married Joyce Cannings and they made their home in Medicine Hat.
After 35 years of service with the C.P.R., Jack retired in May 1976. He has
many hobbies and interests which makes retirement most enjoyable.

Jack and Joyce have two daughters, a son, and seven grandchildren.

Jacqueline (Mrs. George Temple) lives in Calgary and has a son, Christopher.

Arlyne (Mrs. Robert Boswell) resides in Spring Bank and has a son, Jeffrey, and
a daughter, Allison.

Donald lives in Medicine Hat and has four daughters, Jasmine, Heather, Melanie,
and Angela.

Ruben Daniel Deering

Ruben Daniel Deering served in the Canadian Army from 1941 to 1943 and was
stationed in Petawawa, Ontario. He married Luella Peters and lives in Calgary.
His family consists of three sons and three daughters and they, all live close
by.

Herbert Peter Deering

Herbert Deering was born in Irvine in 1919. He spent most of his childhood in
the Irvine district except for four years when the family farmed in the
Cardston area.

Herb and I (Melba Yanke) were married in October 1941 and in 1942 he went into
the army. His training was at Penhold, and from there he was stationed at
Terrace and Prince Rupert, B.C. He was moved to Nanaimo for a short time before
they shipped out to the Aleutian Islands. After his term of duty at Kiska, he
came back to Camp Gordon at Victoria. He was discharged in September 1944, at
which time we moved to Medicine Hat. He worked for local hotels until 1953,
then worked for a local dairy.

In 1958 we purchased the Ed and Henry Herth farm and engaged in mixed farming
till 1962 when Herb had a farm accident. We sold the farm and moved back to
Medicine Hat while he spent four months in the hospital in Calgary. We spent
the remaining years in the 'Hat'. Herb retired in 1980.

We had three sons, Barry, Darrell, and Randall, who attended Irvine School from
1958 to 1962.

Jerry Dunn
submitted by George Maser

Jerry Dunn came to the Irvine area from Franklin Centre, Quebec (near Montreal)
in 1904, at the young age of about 20. He took out a homestead on the SE
4-12-2-4 about three and a half miles east of Irvine. He had learned the
grocery business around Montreal, but decided he didn't like it, so he went
West. On his way, he stopped and worked in Winnipeg for a short time and then
went further west and settled in the Irvine area. Jerry raised chickens and
sold eggs to people in Irvine. In the poor years this was his main source of
income. He also raised Short Horned cattle. They were probably one of the best
herds in the area. Jerry never had a car. He would go to town with a one-horse
buggy. I remember him ploughing his land with four horses and a two bottom
plough. He never had a tractor.

Jerry had five sisters and four brothers. He never got married but remained a
bachelor all his life.

Jerry left the Irvine area in the early forties, and went back to his home
town, Franklin Centre. Jerry's own words, before he left, were, "I just can't
take any more of this" (dry years and bad prices). Unfortunately, after he left
the good years came back. Prices of everything went up; especially the price of
cattle kept going up and up. This didn't help Jerry because he was back home in
Franklin Centre, Quebec.

Johann and Rosina (Schlaht) Ehrman
information submitted by the Ehrman family and Illene (Pahl) Schock

Johann Ehrman was born on December 1, 1873 in Hoffnungstahl, in Russia and
immigrated with his parents, Jacob and Johanna Ehrman, to South Dakota in 1885.

Rosina Schlaht was born July 15, 1875 in Odessa, Russia. She immigrated to
Eureka, South Dakota with her parents in 1888.

Johann Ehrman married Rosina Schlaht (sister of Mrs. Fred Weiss, Irvine) at age
19, on April 8, 1894 in Campbell County, South Dakota.

John and Rosina Ehrman with Christina and John - about 1898 (pic)

In 1903 Johann and Rosina left Eureka, South Dakota with their family for
Irvine. They had four children at that time. Their homestead, SE 14-11-2-4,
southeast of Irvine, was eventually taken over by Christian Ehrman (son) in
1928, then by Emil and Meta (daughter) Paul in 1933, and finally by Stan
(grandson) and Lillian Pahl.

In 1904 they built a log house on the homestead. Johann later bought a steam
engine and did custom work, breaking land. He also bought a threshing machine
for his own use and for custom threshing.

The Schlaht School was one quarter mile west of the homestead, which the Ehrman
children attended only six months a year. This school was also used for church
services, and the Ehrman children were all baptized there. The school was moved
east of the homestead in the mid 30's, and in the early 40's was closed down
and the children were bussed to Irvine.

There were many happy times and many hard working hours spent together to raise
a large family of nine children by this young couple.

Johann and Rosina moved to Medicine Hat in 1928 where for eight short years he
was retired and lived a comparatively "easy life". He prided himself in the
good time that his pocket watch kept and always checked it with the "Noon
Whistle" that sounded daily at 12 noon in Medicine Hat. One day he gave August
his precious watch saying, "Here, I won't need this anymore". Shortly afterward
he passed away at age 63 on December 22, 1936. August passed this watch on to
his son, Bert.

Rosina stayed at 939 Elm Street with their daughter, Irene. Eventually Irene
married Arnold Adams and the three lived together in harmony until Rosina's
death at age 72 on May 1, 1948.

Johann and Rosina will probably always be noted for their hospitality to anyone
who needed a bed and food in the days when travel was slow and few people had
friends and family in the city of Medicine Hat. As a result they hosted not
only family and distant relatives but friends of mere acquaintances. The spirit
of hospitality was always evident in that home.

Twelve children were born to Johann and Rosina; one daughter in the United
States and two sons in Canada died in infancy. Three sons and six daughters
lived to adulthood: Christina (Christman/Iback), born in 1895, John Jr., born
in 1897, Martha (Good), born 1900, August, born in 1902, Christian, born in
1904, Emma (Heinrich), born in 1906, Ida (Lutz), born in 1908, Meta (Pahl),
born in 1910, and Irene (Adams), born in 1914.

Irene and Arnold Adams lived in Cranbrook, then Calgary and eventually retired
in Medicine Hat. They have one daughter, Janice, Mrs. Don Adrian, and three
grandsons: Shawn, Ryan and Kelly, great grandsons of Johann and Rosina. After
Irene died Arnold remarried Lolita, a lady from the Phillipines, who has one
son, Nathan.

August and Christina Ehrman

August, born December 1, 1902, came to Irvine from Eureka, South Dakota with
his parents as an infant.

Christina Alber was born October 20, 1902 at Huffnungstall, South Russia and at
the age of ten arrived in Irvine with her parents and stayed briefly at the
home of Mr. and Mrs. Mose Felesky with her siblings until her parents had made
homesteading arrangements and then came for them for their trip to Hilda.

August and Christina met in 1925. She won his heart in that she was not only
beautiful but beautifully clad in red. They were married in 1926 and lived for
a short time with Johann and Rosina Ehrman, August's parents. They took up
homesteading two miles south where they lived for 26 years.

In 1927 the twins, Doris and Doreen, were born and two and a half years later,
in 1930, Bert was born.

Christina and August Ehrman (pic)

Doris and Doreen Ehrman (pic)

It was a loving, caring home and a strong sense of family love was instilled.
The home was built on a foundation of Christian principles. During the 1930's
the times were hard for everyone. In those days one had to rely on neighbours,
thus developing a community feeling of belonging to and caring for one another.

While August was busy with farm work and cattle raising, Christina spent any
leisure time she had knitting, crocheting, tatting, sewing the children's
clothes and beautifying the home.

Probably the most difficult time for August and Christina was when in 1937
August was forced to go to Winnipeg, hiring out as a farm labourer. He was a
good worker and was soon recognized for it as he was given a 50 cents a day
raise and was admonished not to let the other workers know. Shortly after that,
Bert (age seven) contracted polio and August took the first train home, spending
most of his earnings. But the family was together again and that is what
mattered.

Ehrman Homestead (pic)

The 1940's were good years and best of all was the arrival of a baby boy, Ray,
on July 5, 1941. He was a joy to every member of the family and also to all the
young friends who gathered at the farm on Sundays. The young people had fun
playing cards, singing with Doris and Doreen, accompanied on their guitars,
playing ping pong or exercising the art of conversation.

Bert, Doris, Doreen and Ray Ehrman - 1984 (pic)

August and Christina were socially active. They always kept in touch with
friends and neighbours. "Visiting" was a means of entertainment which may have
consisted of a short chat, or a glass of wine, or a game of cards, a midnight
lunch or even a full course dinner. They thoroughly enjoyed their friends.

They kept the family occupied in church functions and choir work, and as a
family they regularly attended Irvine dances.

Christina in Costume to serve tea (pic)

Christina was active in women's groups, such as the U.C.W., W.I., and F.W.U.
(Farm Women's Union) and served on the executive. They retired in Medicine Hat
in 1959 where they became active in the Senior Citizens' Club and again she
served on that executive as President and Vice-President.

August was a member of the Farmers' Union and the Chinook Club. He was a great
pool player. In his retirement years it was imperative that he left the house
for the pool room at 11:30 a.m. so that he was able to have access to a table.

In his later years he studied the Bible with Doris and under her direction
became a regular reader of his Bible.

Christina took up painting in 1967 and did 54 oil paintings. August watched her
and tried his hand at it too. He painted four paintings, one for each child. In
fact one of his paintings was a pool room scene. He had all his friends painted
into the picture. This painting hung in the pool room downtown for some time.
All these paintings are very beautiful and very precious.

August died on September 25, 1973, at the age of 71 due to a cerebral
hemorrhage. Christina was alone for six years until she died due to cancer at
the age of 77 on June 10, 1979.

Ben and Doris (Ehrman) Lust

Doris is the twin daughter of August and Christina Ehrman. She and her twin
sister, Doreen, were born on April 6, 1927 on the old homestead southeast of
Irvine.

On December 1, 1949, the same date as her father's birthday and one year to the
day of her twin sister's wedding, Doris married Ben Lust. They resided in
Medicine Hat, built their new home there in 1956 and resided there until 1967,
when they and their children moved to Calgary where Ben worked in various oil
and gas firms as a chief draftsman and manager of drafting services.

Doris, due to her upbringing, made the ministry her career. She has been one of
Jehovah's witnesses for the past 30 years and 20 of those years have been spent
as a pioneer (full time ministry). Ben and Doris took up residence in British
Columbia on Vancouver Island in 1982. Both are enjoying a life as active
Christian witnesses of Jehovah God. Ben and Doris had two children, Patricia
and Kirby.

Ben Lust Family: Ben, Doris (Ehrman), Patricia and Kiroy (pic)

Patricia was born on March 2, 1952 in Medicine Hat and after moving to Calgary
she completed her high school obtaining a Senior Matriculation Diploma. Shortly
thereafter, Pat and Pam, Doreen's daughter, toured Europe and both worked in
England for a short time. Upon returning, Patricia attended the University of
Calgary for a year and then moved to Vancouver to further her. education. In
1977 Patricia obtained a Bachelor of Arts Degree, majoring in English, at
U.B.C. She then worked at U.B.C. as a computer technician until 1983, when she
once again enrolled as a student, and in 1987 received her Bachelor of Laws
Degree. Patricia passed her Bar Exam and is presently articling with a law firm
in Vancouver.

Kirby was born November 14, 1953, in Ottawa, Ontario. Kirby received his Senior
Matriculation Diploma in Calgary. After completing high school he was employed
in the capacities of assistant and manager of major appliance department
stores, both in Calgary and in Vancouver. When Kirby returned to Calgary he
expanded his career to restaurant administration management and has been
employed with a number of well established restaurants in Calgary in this
capacity. At present he has branched out into the field of restaurant
consulting management. Recently, Kirby has become interested in languages and
has studied Spanish, French, and Russian. In 1987 he toured seven European
countries. His goal is to major in the field of interpreting languages.

Cecil Albert (Bert) Ehrman
by Bert Ehrman

I was born in Medicine Hat Hospital on January 10, 1930 and raised ten miles
southeast of Irvine. I was the first born son of August and Christina Ehrman. I
attended Schlaht School until grade four. I then went to the Irvine School when
the bussing system began. Dad was our bus driver.

During the Dirty Thirties, Dad tried to make some extra money, so he went to
Winnipeg to work on a farm. He earned $1 a day for his hard work. During this
time I contracted polio. Mom wired Dad that I was sick, so he came back by
train. It cost him everything that he had made to come home to his family. To
top it all off, Dad stuck his head out the window of the train and lost his
cap. I was hospitalized in a ward with 16 other polio victims. My whole left
side was paralyzed. I was very fortunate to regain all movement again in a
fairly short time and with no side effects.

I took over farming at the age of 14, with Dad's supervision. We had five
quarters at this time (1944). A few years later Dad bought two sections of
pasture land. In 1951 Dad bought the Schlaht place, along the Trans Canada
Highway five miles east of Irvine, which we moved to. It was exhausting work
for a boy of 13 to 14 years old with little sleep when we would custom combine.
But as the years went by I became accustomed to the hard work and long hours.
When I was 20, in my spare time, I started to play baseball. For winter
activities I curled.

In 1956 I met Mary Kozway. On February 19, 1957 we were married. We had a short
but happy time together as Mary passed away July 20, 1957, due to heart
failure. She was 21 years old.

In 1958 I met Shirl Holte. On January 31, 1959 we were married, and moved to
the old place. Our daughter, Andrea Charlane, was born August 19, 1959. In
December the folks moved to the Hat and Shirl and 1, with Andrea, moved down to
the highway. On July 31, 1960 our son, Eric Bert, was brought into the world.
Now we were blessed with two healthy children.

Shirl and Bert Ehrman - 1984 (pic)

In 1963 we looked for better farmland and ended up settling 20 miles southwest
of Beaverlodge, Alberta. We started out farming ten quarters of land, then sold
some and bought more closer to the home place. We farmed six quarters.

Baseball was still a part of my life as I coached 48 boys in a Junior League
for three years. Curling was still a favorite winter pastime which, when Andrea
and Eric got older, involved us all in a family team. The men's team that I
curled with in Beaverlodge in 1975 took the U.F.A. Alberta Championship
playdowns in Edmonton.

Eric and Andrea Ehrman - Christmas 1962 (pic)

Shirl began driving school bus, which she did for nine years. 1, in turn, would
spare drive occasionally. She was a great help on the farm as she knew how to
run all the machinery. She made a great wife and mother for the 25 years we
were married. After building up the farm, and nicely treeing it, we decided to
sell. In April of 1978 we moved to town. I then started Ehrman Construction. I
built 12 homes from 1978 to 1980.

In April of 1979 we acquired a good and prosperous son-in-law when Andrea
married Bob Zieglgansberger. They live in the Grande Prairie area. In October
of 1980 they had our grandchild, Vanessa Rose Zieglgansberger.

Andrea, Eric, Shirl, Bob, Vanessa and Bert - 1981 (pic)

Our son Eric was, and still is, very athletic. In the 1980 Alberta Winter
Games, Eric won three gold medals in boxing. He also held the Golden Gloves for
Alberta for a year. He now resides in California. He is following in his
father's footsteps as he works in the construction business. Eric also is
pursuing a modeling career.

In February of 1981 Shirl and I moved to Kelowna, B.C. In July of 1982 we moved
back to Beaverlodge. In 1983 I built six houses in Kelly Lake, B.C., during
which time we discovered that Shirl had cancer. She took her treatments at the
W. W. Cross Cancer Clinic in Edmonton. On July 22, 1984 Shirl passed away. She
has been missed greatly by all that knew and loved her.

In the fall of 1983 I went to Edmonton and got my Boiler's Ticket and have been
operating boilers on service rigs during the winter months ever since. In the
summer I do some finishing work in homes, enjoy golfing, fishing, water skiing
and traveling.

Ray Ehrman

Ray Ehrman, son of August and Christina Ehrman, was born July 5, 1941, and
graduated from Irvine High School in 1958. On June 2, 1962 he was married to
Marguerite (Peggy) Smith of Medicine Hat.

Ray started working for Northwest Nitro Fertilizer Limited in Medicine Hat in
the office and later as a plant operator. He moved to Calgary in March 1964 to
work for Western Co-op Fertilizer Limited as an operator and later as an
electrician and instrument technician. Over the next ten years he upgraded his
education by taking every electrical, instrumentation, electronics, computer
hardware and computer programming course SAIT (Southern Alberta Institute of
Technology) and the University of Calgary had to offer. Presently, he is a
senior electrical engineering technologist and still attending courses and
seminars to stay abreast of ever changing technology.

In May of 1969 he started working for Nova Corporation of Alberta, formerly
Alberta Gas Trunk Line Limited, as an electrical and instrumentation
technician, and in September 1975 moved to Edmonton in charge of all electrical
and computer maintenance in northwestern Alberta. Still with Nova, he moved to
Calgary in March 1977 to work in the Electrical Engineering Department. In
September 1985 he moved back to Edmonton, and is presently a supervisor in the
technical services department (Maintenance Planning Group) in charge of
preventive maintenance done by 130 technicians to control and computer
equipment on 90 compressors (up to 45,000 horse power jet engines, all
controlled remotely from Edmonton) and 715 Meter Stations measuring the amount
of natural gas going into the pipeline. One of these Meter Stations is called
"Irvine" and is located approximately three miles north of the Ehrman farm on
the Trans Canada Highway between Irvine and Walsh.

Ray and his wife, Peggy, and their three children live in Riverbend in
southwest Edmonton at 4122-147 Street.

Peggy works as a secretary at the University of Alberta in the Recreation and
Leisure Studies Department. She works from September to April every year and
has the summer off.

Their oldest daughter, Katherine Annette, born September 18, 1964, works as a
secretary in Edmonton. She is also enrolled, and taking courses through the
Athabasca University.

Laura Jane, born June 24, 1968, is in her second year at the University of
Alberta taking Education, majoring in Music and minoring in Social Studies. She
has been teaching organ lessons for five years.
