Albert Engel

Albert Engel moved with his wife, Linda, and two children from Glover, N.D. on
a railroad pass to Medicine Hat in the winter months of 1910-1911. They got
their homestead in 1911, but stayed living in Medicine Hat, the 900 block of
7th Avenue, now Kingsway. While living there, the other homesteaders that they
had gotten to know while proving their homestead would stop at their place to
water their horses in wash tubs filled from the water well that was in the
cellar of their house.

They moved out to the homestead, NW 28-12-2-4, to make improvements, erected a
two room sod house, and added on to it in 1926. They carried their drinking
water three quarters of a mile till they got their own well dug, but still had
to carry the drinking water a quarter of a mile up a hill.

Albert cycled to Irvine, working as a mortar mixer to supplement their farm
income. He also worked for the C.P.R. on the section for a period of time.
During the 20's and 30's they took produce to the market in Medicine Hat:
butter, cottage cheese, buttermilk, cream, milk, live and dressed chickens.
They also had regular customers that they delivered to on a weekly or
bi-monthly basis.

During the dirty 30's the Engels had the only source of water in the
neighborhood. The people who were close enough to trail their livestock over
for water did so, and others came with their wagons loaded with barrels and
hauled the water for their livestock. In the morning they would water their own
cattle and move them out to pasture away from the well, then someone else would
be there to fill their water or have livestock there to water. Everyone that
used the well had an appointed time; if it hadn't been that way there would
have been a real mix-up. There was a windmill on the well but if there was no
wind everyone had to pump their water by hand. The well could be used 24 hours
a day and not go dry; being a bored well there was enough reserve. There are
two wells in the same vicinity today that have yet to go dry. They are drilled
wells so the pumps have to be set to accommodate the incoming flow of water and
not remove the water faster than it comes in. Otherwise you could be short of
water for a while.

Albert passed away in 1939. Linda passed away in 1962. They had nine children:
Alfred and Edwin born in the States, Nettie, Violet, Walter, Junuis (June),
Allen, Percy and Nina.

Alfred never married.

Edwin married Verna Tohm, a neighbor girl.

Nettie had one daughter, Ruby, who is married to Joe Reeder and lives in
Medicine Hat.

Violet married Willard Tohm, a neighbor boy.

Walter married Ida Ulrich from Schuler while in the army, lived on the farm in
the Flemming house, and then moved to Medicine Hat where they still reside.
They had one son, Delbert, who owns Del Rossi men's clothing store.

June married Rueben Franz. They lived on his family farm four or five miles
southwest of the Engel farm until her passing in May of 1970. They had three
boys: Leroy, married and living in Didsbury; Brian, living at home; and Terry,
married and presently living at Brooks.

Allen married Gertrude Roll from Walsh and stayed on the farm, running it for
his mother, until the farm was split up. He then moved a house onto the SW half
of section 33 and farmed his own land until he sold out in 1962 to his nephew,
Maurice. They moved into Irvine and he worked for the Alberta Pacific Grain
Company. He was transferred to Monarch, Alberta when the elevator in Irvine was
sold and worked for the company until the elevator was closed down. He then
bought the general store in Monarch, which he operated until there wasn't
enough business to keep it open. They still live in Monarch. They had five
children: Blaine, married and living in Monarch; Lorna, married; Valarie,
married; Theresa (Terri), married; and Darrin, still at home.

Percy married Clara Cotton (Mund) and lived in Redcliff. They had four
children, Colleen, Bradley, Collen, and Orleen, all married.

Nina married Emanuel Franz. They also lived in the Flemming house for a short
time after their marriage, then moved into Irvine where they still reside. They
had four children, Ernie, Greg, Linda, and Holly.

Carl Engel

A bachelor brother of Albert, better known as Charlie, homesteaded on Section
31-12-2-4 in 1909 He lived in a cave which is still visible today. While living
in his cave, when he left and didn't expect to return home before dark, he
would light a lantern and raise it up a pole, so he would be able to find his
cave on his return.

In the winter if it snowed and drifted during the night, in the morning he
would have to shovel the snow back out. Some of the snow was melted for washing
and cooking. Later he built a bachelor shack.

He passed away in 1918 during the Flu Epidemic.

Charlie Winberg was another bachelor that lived in a cave or dugout on the NW
17-12-24.

Edwin Engel

Edwin Engel was born in Glover, N.D. and came to Canada with his parents as a
very young child of less than a year of age. In 1938 he married Verna Tohm, one
of the neighbor girls.

Both Edwin and Verna attended the Wilkinson School, two and three miles from
their homes. They walked to school except in the winter months when someone
would drive a team and sleigh. If it got too cold the school would close
because a great number of families never had enough money to buy all their
children winter shoes. They went to school until they finished grade eight,
then went out working to earn their own living.

During his teenage years Edwin played the saxophone and the guitar. He taught
himself to play these two instruments, sent away for lessons and then practiced
long hours during the winter to perfect his playing. He was better on the
saxophone than the guitar. When he wasn't Sure how to play some of the music,
he would ask someone who was more knowledgeable to find out how it was done. He
even transposed a lot of music from some other instrument to the saxophone
because there wasn't the money to buy the music for each instrument. He played
in a dance orchestra that included some of the Tohm boys and some of the Brandt
boys. They played for dances from Graburn Gap and Elkwater to north of Irvine
where he was raised, and all places in between, in homes, in barns, and in
school houses. He also played ball for various teams in the surrounding area as
catcher.

Edwin went working on threshing crews in the fall, eventually getting to the
Nanton and Didsbury districts, stooking and pitching bundles during the harvest
season. He also learned to be a separator operator.

Verna went working at the sugar beet factory at Raymond, Alberta and as a
domestic in various homes in Picture Butte, Claresholm, Vulcan, and on the
Minor Ranch. For one job the criteria was to be able to wash woolens without
matting or shrinking them, which she was able to do. That was a job within
itself because there was a whole year's supply of woolen blankets to wash. It
took a good many wash days to get them all washed. She did house work for a
living until she returned home and got married.

Edwin applied for a homestead in 1933, the SW 35-12-2-4, and paid $10 for it
just like all the other homesteaders did. He lived in a bunk house before he
moved George Mackie's log house about half a mile to the south and closer to a
source of water.

After their marriage, Edwin and Verna lived on the homestead every summer and
moved back up to the log house for the winter months. They moved between their
homestead and the log house every year until they bought the Tohm home place in
1949. They moved there permanently so they would be closer to the school bus
route. Verna would herd sheep during spring work and do the cooking during
harvesting when the children were small. They had three children, Maurice,
Estelle and Dorne.

I can remember going to school in Irvine in the winter Dad would take us up to
Grandma Engel's where Allen would be starting out with the bus route, the bus
being a team of horses hitched to a sleigh, called a jumper, that was closed in
and covered over with binder canvas and gunny sack to keep the wind and snow
out, but it never ever kept the cold from penetrating. Mom used to put bricks
in the oven and on top of the heater over night so that they would be hot, then
wrap them in burlap to help keep our feet warm on the way  to school. There
wasn't anything to warm our feet on the way home, though, because Allen stayed
in Irvine during the day as the double trip would have been too hard on the
horses. The cold and stormy days were the worst part of going to school in a
sleigh, but the warm sunny days were a delight, going for a sleigh ride two
times a day. The afternoons were the best because there was no time limit to
adhere to. Sometimes the older boys like Maurice, Dorne, and Ken Zeller would
get out and run alongside the jumper In the dead of winter he would leave home
in the dark and also return home in the dark. In the spring, we would move down
to our homestead or, as we were then calling it, the sheep camp. Mom or Dad
would drive us up to catch the bus in the morning but we would have to walk the
two and a half miles back home in the afternoon. When we first started school
we went to the one room school houses that had been moved in when they
centralized the schools. In the spring of 1952, when the oldest part of the
present school was finished, we moved into it. In the early 50's the government
improved the school bus roads. Dad got an hydraulically operated V-snowplow and
helped keep the roads open in the winter, so we were able to ride to school in
a heated bus, a big difference from the sleigh and a lot shorter ride in time,
if not in distance. All three of us attended the Irvine School and graduated
from Irvine School.

Edwin bought some sheep in the early 40's and took sheep on shares, with his
mother and Earl Ligget, eventually buying them. To save money he learned to
shear sheep, first with the hand shears. In later years he graduated to the
mechanical clippers after attending a one day shearing school at Swift Current,
Saskatchewan. When he was shearing all by himself and had a small flock, he
would shear some in the morning, take the sheep out to graze, bring them in a
little early and do some more shearing until it got too dark.

The mechanical clippers were run by gas engine until electricity was brought
into the area. It made the shearing go much faster. They started shearing early
in the morning, stopping for coffee break in the morning and in the afternoon,
with dinner at noon, and supper when they were finished late in the evening,
continuing in this vein until all the sheep were shorn. The shearing was
usually done around the middle of June, after lambing was finished. After the
shearing was completed the wool would be bagged in oversized gunny sacks 36
inches wide and 96 inches long. When there was more than one person bagging the
wool, there would be a competition to see who was able to pack the most in the
bags. One person would climb into the bag while it was hanging up and someone
else would drop fleeces in for him to pack. This was done with the feet,
rolling the fleece to the outsides of the bag and pushing it down along the
side till it was firm. Someone on the outside would tell the packer where there
were hollows, so that the packer would know where to do just a mite more
packing when the next fleece was dropped. If the packer was really energetic
and took his time, he could pack over 400 pounds in the bag. The difficulty
then would be to get enough men around to help move the bags after they were
sewn up.

After that came the dipping of the sheep for keds. A special vat was dug in the
ground and filled with a dip solution; one end was straight and the other was
slanted with cleats fastened on so the sheep were able to walk out. By that
time they would be pretty heavy as their wool would soak up the dip. They would
be held in an old wagon box so most of the dip would drain off them and run
back into the vat. This was a hard and dirty job. The sheep never liked to jump
into water, so they would have to be pushed in and then made to go completely
under. Then they would swim until their feet touched bottom and then walk out.
The people working the front end would always be drenched with the dip
solution, so they worked hard and fast to be able to get out of their soaked
clothes and have a bath.

Edwin and Verna had three children, Maurice, Estelle and Dorne.

Maurice married Estella Ulmer, helped on the farm for part of the year, and
then moved to Medicine Hat and worked at the Western Co-op Fertilizers, Good
Year for a short time, and then back to the fertilizer plant until its closing
in 1987. In 1962 he bought the farm from Uncle Allen and helped farm it on
weekends and on his holidays. They had three children, Cori, Dale, and Twila.
Since his early forced retirement, Maurice moved out to the farm and is helping
with the running of the farm with the rest of the family.

Estelle married Wallace Koenig and they lived on his farm in the Monitor,
Alberta district in the summer and moved to Consort, Alberta in the winter.
They bought the Engel home place in 1962 from Nina and Emanuel Franz, and moved
back to farm here. They lived on Maurice's farm for a couple of years until a
house was purchased and moved onto their own property in 1965. They had five
children, Clayton, Brent, Sherri-Lynn, Trevor and Derek.

Clayton graduated with honors from Irvine School and was accepted for Officer
Training in the Armed Forces, attending The Royal Military College at Kingston,
Ontario. He attended the University of Montreal on a three year scholarship
which he completed in two years and took all his subjects in French. He said he
had an advantage over the Francaphones because all the reference books were
printed in English. At the present time he is serving in the Armed Forces Naval
Division and studying for further advancement.

Brent also graduated from the Irvine School with honors, attended the Medicine
Hat College for two years and then transferred to the University of Calgary
where he's still attending besides trying to earn enough money during the
summer to keep him going.

Sherri-Lynn graduated from Irvine School, attended the Medicine Hat College for
one year and then transferred to the University of Alberta, attending the Saint
Jean Campus and taking most of her courses in French.

Trevor and Derek are the youngest and still attending the Irvine School.

Dorne married Anne Morris, formerly of Newfoundland. He attended the University
of Alberta, got his teaching certificate and taught school at Rush Lake and
Schuler, besides subbing at the Irvine School for a period of time. He then
took over the operating of the farm for quite a number of years. He bought the
Ed Herth farm in the mid sixties and does most of the mechanic work and welding
that needs to be done on the farm. Since his marriage he lives in Medicine Hat
and drives out to the farm.

John Fandrick
by Fred Sauter (Vauxhall) and Ida Gill - nephew and niece

John Fandrick was born in 1882 and Christina Rauser, daughter of Jacob and Anna
Maria (Dulker) Rauser, was born on January 6, 1888. They were married in 1907
and emigrated from Bessarabia, South Russia to Canada, in March of 1910.
Christina's sister Mary Rauser (Mrs. Karl Sauter) also came to Canada with them.

They settled in the Thelma District and farmed there for four years, then
eventually moved to the town of Irvine where Mr. Fandrick worked for a
merchant, Mr. Sam Kalmback. He later farmed north of town. He was known as a
great well digger and cistern maker. A cistern was used to store water for
household purposes. He was one of Irvine's (you might say) characters.

Christina and John had no family and Christina learned, early in her married
life, one step-saving method. She trained her dog to fetch the cows when it
came milking time. She trained several dogs in her lifetime and the only name
she ever gave these trained dogs was "Puppy". They were always ready and eager
when she commanded "go get them".

John and his wife moved to Medicine Hat in 1944 and he passed away in July
1950, age 68, and is buried in Hillside Cemetery at Medicine Hat. Christina
Fandrick passed away on December 18, 1966, age 78, and is also buried in
Hillside Cemetery.

George Adam and Elizabeth (Huber) Fischer

George Adam Fischer was born June 10, 1852 and married Elizabeth Huber on
November 11, 1880. They immigrated to the U.S.A. in 1884 with two small
children, Mary and Jacob. Four more children were born in South Dakota: Lydia,
Elizabeth, Barbara, and William. Elizabeth died, leaving George with four small
children to care for. Mary and Jacob were almost grown up.

In the fall of 1901 George was married to Elizabeth (Fischer) Freimark, who was
also widowed with six children, three of them between three years and 13 years
old, and three of them grown up. This created a family with seven children
between one year and 13 years old, and five young adults.

In 1902, George's daughter, Mary, born August 14, 1881, was married to
Elizabeth's son, Gottlieb Freimark, and Jacob Fischer, born July 27, 1882, was
married to Elizabeth Knodel. In the spring of 1903, these families and the
Knodel family moved to Canada, settling 15 miles southeast of Irvine in the
Newburg area.

Lydia, born July 16, 1890, married Emanuel Jeske on March 18, 1907; Elizabeth
(Lizzie) married Philip Bischke; Barbara married John Sackman; and William,
born in 1900, married Ida Vossler.

William Fischer Family

William Fischer, son of George Adam and Elizabeth (Huber) Fischer, was born in
1900 in South Dakota, U.S.A.

In 1921 he married Ida Vossler, daughter of Christian and Margaret (Sackman)
Vossler, and took over his dad's farm. To this marriage three children were
born: George, Margaret, and Albert. They lived on the farm at Newburg until
1944 when they sold it and bought a farm near Walsh. They lived there until
1954 when they moved to Medicine Hat to retire.

William, Albert, George, Margaret, Ida Fischer (pic)

The children received their education at Sentinel School while living at the
Newburg farm. The school was about three miles away. They have many memories of
how they went to school compared to the way they go to school nowadays. Another
memory they have is of their granddad and the way he taught them to count in
Russian. They could all count to ten in Russian. They recall him talking about
the years he was in the Russian War.

In 1954 George, the eldest son, was married to Frieda Hoffman, daughter of Mr.
and Mrs. Jacob Hoffman of Estuary, Saskatchewan. They took over the farm at
Walsh where they raised their two sons who attended school in Irvine. Donald
makes his home in Medicine Hat and is employed with the Department of Highways.
He has a daughter, Mandy. Dean took over the farm in 1980 when George and
Frieda moved to Medicine Hat in retirement.

Margaret married Werner Kempf in 1959 and moved to the Stettler area. They have
a son and a daughter.

Albert, the youngest, passed away in 1978.

John and Agnes Flaig
by Irene (Flaig) Kleckner

John Flaig was born April 28, 1910 in Altbota, Russia. He immigrated to Canada
in May of 1911, along with his parents, John and Margaret and older sister
Elsie. They settled in Medicine Hat where John Sr. was employed at the Medicine
Hat Foundry. Medicine Hat was also the birthplace of the younger brother
Richard.

Two years later John Sr., Margaret and sister Elsie all died in a matter of a
few months. The deaths were believed to have been caused by tuberculosis and
typhoid fever. John was then sent to live with Andrew and Rosena Sackman, who
homesteaded in the Sentinel district. The Sackmans later adopted John and he
was raised and educated there but was insistent on keeping the Flaig name.
Richard was taken to an uncle and aunt, John and Katherine Sackman, who lived
in the same area.

John Flaig Farm (pic)

John married the former Agnes Sturm in 1929. The Sackmans then moved to
Medicine Hat and John and Agnes took over the Sackman family farm. Here they
worked hard for many years, putting in long hours just to make a living. It was
during those difficult times that John would have to go away from home for
several months at a time, to find work in order to make ends meet, while Agnes
stayed on the farm raising the family and keeping things up. In later years
they were able to enlarge their farm and times were somewhat easier for them.
In 1948 they were able to buy a farm south of Piapot, Saskatchewan. They farmed
there for a few years and then moved back to the home farm at Sentinel. In 1955
they moved to Medicine Hat where John was employed with Little Chief
Construction until retiring in 1974. During the early years of city living they
still went out to the two farms to help out in the busy seasons.

Back: John, Agnes; Front: Elmer and Reuben Flaig (pic)

John enjoyed his carpentry, fishing, gardening and church activities during his
retirement, until his passing on September 1, 1986. Agnes still lives in her
own home and enjoys fairly good health. She keeps herself busy with
handicrafts, gardening and lawn work in the summer, and visiting her family.

They have four children. Reuben, the oldest son, took over the family farm in
Saskatchewan and still resides there. He has two children and four
grandchildren.

Elmer, who took over the farm at Sentinel, now resides in Medicine Hat and his
youngest son is now living on the farm. Elmer has four children and eight
grandchildren.

Agnes, Irene, John; Front: Adeline Flaig (pic)

Irene (Kleckner) lives in Medicine Hat and has three children and one
grandchild.

Adeline (Ressler) lives in Airdrie, Alberta and has three children.

Greg was born in Medicine Hat and took grades one to nine in Irvine and ten to

Ernst and Elizabeth (Fischer) Freimark
by Viola Kirschenman and Bev Eiserman

Records show that an Ernst Freimark moved from Konstantin, Poland, to
Friedenstahl, Bessarabia, Russia, in 1824. Likely he and his relatives were of
those Europeans who migrated into Russia during "The Great Migration", which
was promoted and begun years before by Catherine the Great. We have no
information about Ernst's wife, or any of the rest of their family, except that
they had a son, whose name was also Ernst, born on February 21, 1855. He
married Elizabeth Fischer, who was born in January, 1855. Both were born at
Friedenstahl, Bessarabia, Russia.

When Bolshevism began to take over Russia many people decided to migrate to
America. Ernst and Elizabeth, with their three small children, left Russia and
arrived in Mina, South Dakota in 1879. They settled here and probably farmed.
Their family increased and they had a total of 14 children which were as
follows: Frederick, born June, 1875; Daniel, July, 1876; Jacobina, June, 1878;
Margaret, December 11, 1879 in U.S.A.; Gottlieb, March 21, 1882; Magdaline,
December 2, 1883; Katherine, April 30, 1885; Bertha, November 14, 1886;
Christian, August 11, 1888; Katherine, June 26, 1890; Mathelda, April 13, 1892;
John, November 11, 1893; Emanuel, May 11, 1896; and Martha, October 25, 1898.

In the winter of 1895, six of their children died, three so close together that
they were all buried in one grave. They felt that someone must have put a curse
on them; likely it was a flu. One of the girls, Jacobina, passed away at the
age of 17.

Ernst died at the young age of 46 in the spring of 1901. Now Elizabeth was left
with six children: Daniel, Margaret, Gottlieb (our forefather), Christian,
Emanuel and Martha.

In the fall of 1901, Elizabeth married again to a widower named George Fischer.
His wife, Babel, had died earlier and he was left with six children to care
for. The Fischers had migrated also from Bessarabia, Russia, in 1884 when Mary,
their eldest, was three years old. The children of George Fisher were Mary,
Jacob, Lydia, Elizabeth, Barbara, and William.

Through this combined family, Mary and Gottlieb were actually stepbrother and
stepsister, but they were attracted to each other, and got married on March 11,
1902.

Gottlieb and Mary (Fischer) Freitnark
by Viola Kirschenman and Bev Eiserman

Gottlieb Freimark was born March 21, 1882 in Mina, South Dakota to Ernst and
Elizabeth (Fischer) Freimark. His father, Ernst, died in 1901.

Mary Fischer was born August 14, 1881 in Bessarabia. She came with her parents,
George and Elizabeth (Huber) Fischer to South Dakota when she was three years
old. Her mother, Elizabeth, died about 1901.

Gottlieb and Mary Freimark (pic)

Each widowed, and with six children apiece, George Fischer and Elizabeth
(Fischer) Freimark were married in the fall of 1901.

Gottlieb Freimark and Mary Fischer were married March 11, 1902.

A severe drought which began in 1889 in South Dakota, and lasted for ten years,
is probably what prompted Gottlieb and Mary and their parents, the George
Fischers, and others to move north to western Canada.

In the early spring of 1903, Gottlieb, who was about 21 years of age, along
with other young men came by train to Irvine, Alberta. His homestead was 15
miles southeast of Irvine. This land had belonged to Alfred Weiss and was
situated about two miles from the Cooper place, which later became the home
place. Gottlieb quickly built a shack, made with log walls and plastered with
mud. The roof was made with large pieces of sod butted tightly together. A
similar building was built to shelter the animals. The women and their children
would be arriving later on, by passenger train, and after that the older men
and boys arrived, by freight train, because they brought the horses and wagons,
and cows.

Mary, Elizabeth and the children, and some other women and children, arrived in
Irvine one afternoon. There was no one there to meet them, so they didn't know
what to do, because they knew absolutely no one. Luckily the women had lots of
warm feather quilts and pillows with them. They also had some food with them.
In those days every small town had a coal shed and that is where they decided
to bunk down for the night. They waited anxiously for Gottlieb to come,
hopefully the next morning. How forlorn and frightened they must have felt, but
they had each other, and soon the coal bin didn't seem so terrible. This was in
the month of May, but it was cold outside. One of the worst blizzards had swept
across the western prairie provinces, hundreds of cattle had been buried by the
snow. The women were happy for the shelter of the coal shed, and being so weary
they snuggled into their warm quilts, and were soon fast asleep. All except for
Mrs. Wahl, who was in labor. It was time for the baby to be born, and luckily
Elizabeth was an experienced midwife, so the delivery went fine. A healthy baby
girl was born, and was named Irvina, after the town of Irvine.

When Gottlieb came with a team of horses and wagon, the family all climbed in
and were on their way to their new home. The roads in those days were wagon
trails, and were very rough. It took them several hours until they reached the
last hill, where Gottlieb finally pointed out the shack. There it was waiting
for them. Soon they would enjoy the warmth of the coal stove, and before long
the aroma of fresh perked coffee would fill the air. They were so glad to be in
their new home. George and Elizabeth lived a short distance to the northeast
and it was a delight to visit back and forth in those days.

The days passed by and because Gottlieb was a hard worker, and was determined
to get ahead, he soon obtained cows to milk, hogs to feed, hens to lay eggs,
and of course a good line of horses. The days were long and hot, and by
nightfall both men and beast were weary.

It didn't take long for Gottlieb to realize that there wasn't enough water on
this place for them and the animals. They looked for a different place and were
able to find some land for sale about two miles to the northeast. Another shack
was built by the creek. They dug a well, but found that there was no water. For
the second time they had to look for a different location. This time they
bought a half of a quarter section, two miles south of the grandparents. This
was known as the Old Home Place. Here they had a well with plenty of water.

On June 18, 1903 Gottlieb and Mary had their first child, a daughter. They
named her Elizabeth after her grandmother. On November 29, 1904 their second
child, a boy, Emil, arrived. Now they had a helper for the farm work. On May
15, 1907, another daughter was born, who was named Margaret.

The Sturms lived on the other half of quarter that Gottlieb owned. One day Mrs.
Sturm asked Mary and the children over and treated them to some homemade ice
cream. This was the very first time they ever tasted ice cream. My how
delicious it was! The ice cream was made by placing a mixture of cream, eggs,
vanilla, sugar, and milk into a syrup pail. The lid was sealed and then the
pail was placed in a tub with a layer of ice covering the bottom of the tub.
More ice and salt were then packed around the syrup pail, then the pail was
twirled back and forth by hand until the ice cream became thick and frozen. The
ice came from the ice house, which a lot of people built in those days. The
main purpose for them was to store meat, cream, etcetera. The ice was collected
in chunks during the winter and lasted through the summer. Sometimes firmly
packed wet snow was used. Straw or sawdust would be placed over the ice to keep
it from melting. The meat was placed in crocks and the cream in a cream can,
syrup pails were used as containers too. These containers would be placed
directly on the ice. An ice house consisted of a hole about six feet deep (dug
by hand) and then a building over that with a roof and a door. Sometimes ice
could be found in early summer, under straw where the cattle had been fed in
the winter. This ice was also used sometimes to make ice cream.

Elizabeth Knodel remembers one day when their mother sent her, Emil, and
Margaret out to the north field to where their father was ploughing. He was to
take them down to the grandparents' place to stay for a few days. The girls
were wearing their new green dresses, made of heavy green material, which their
mother had just sewn for them. They were anxious to show the new dresses to
their grandparents. Little did they realize that this, was planned beforehand.
A little later that day Grandmother walked to their home to perform the duties
of midwife which she often did. When the children returned home they were
overjoyed to discover their new baby brother, Alfred. (Born March 3, 1910.)

In 1909 the Sturms decided to move and their land was for sale. Of course
Gottlieb was anxious to have this land, since it was the other half of his
quarter. He had no money, but he had bought a quarter of C.P.R. land a few
years earlier, which was three miles to the northeast. He hoped he could sell
that and buy the Sturms' land. A Mr. Brost wanted to trade some cattle for the
C.P.R. land, so if Mr. Sturm would accept cattle from Gottlieb instead of money
a deal could be made. Eventually after a bit of hassle the deal was made. The
Cooper place was now theirs and they moved into the larger two story wooden
house. It had an outside stairway to get to the bedrooms.

During the summer months, the children were required to bring the milk cows
home from the pastures. Since there were no fences, the cows would often roam
four or five miles away. With coyotes howling and imaginations running wild,
the young children would be terrified, but a good sturdy willow stick gave them
a good sense of security.

In the spring of 1910 Grandpa Fischer had some bad luck. He was burning some
pasture, and the fire got out of control and spread to the neighbor's land. He
was reported and fined heavily. This discouraged and angered Grandpa Fischer,
and he decided to leave this country. A sympathizing neighbor offered him a
deal. So Grandpa Fischer traded his two quarters of land, some milk cows, a
line of horses and enough equipment to make a living, to this man, for two
houses in Winnipeg which he hadn't seen. It sounded like a good deal. They
would live in one house and rent the other one out to make a living. They left
for Winnipeg with only their personal belongings. When they arrived, they
discovered they had been took. The two houses turned out to be two shacks, run
down, dirty and full of bugs. Sadly, they all pitched in and cleaned them up to
make them liveable. Two years later Grandpa Fischer was able to trade these two
shacks for 80 acres of bush country in the Pineridge area, about 35 miles north
of Winnipeg. This place had a wooden house for them to move into now.

In 1911, Mary decided to visit the grandparents, at Pineridge. She took her
four youngsters along: Lizzie 8, Emil 7, Margaret 4, and Alfred 1. This would
be the first train ride for the children. Oh, how exciting! The train left in
the evening and. soon it was dark. The children were fascinated with the lights
of Swift Current; they had never seen so many lights before. These four little
tykes were quite a handful, and getting them settled for the night was almost
impossible, especially with Emil wailing "I want to go home," ever since it had
become dark.

They got to Winnipeg the next day, at about two o'clock. There were people and
more people. They were pushed and shoved about. How lost they must have felt.
Mary had been on a train before, but could speak very little English. It was a
nerve wracking experience, with a baby in her arms and three little ones
clinging to her skirt. They found a place to sit, and they waited and waited
till at long last they saw their grandpa, pushing his way through the crowd,
coming toward them. He got them settled in the buggy and drove through the
crowded streets. There were buggies and wagons, ox carts, cars, and even street
cars. It was just-too much for Emil, and again he started to bawl. Grandpa
Fischer stopped in at a little Jewish store, but Emil refused the banana and
the chocolate bar that the friendly storekeeper offered him. Stubbornly he kept
on with his "I want to go home". By now it was getting dark. They climbed back
into the buggy and headed for Pineridge. They followed a rough trail lined on
both sides with pine trees, so thick you could barely see. Everyone fell asleep
except Grandpa Fischer, who kept the team under control. It took hours to
travel those 35 miles, but at long last Grandpa let out a whoa! It was four or
five in the morning. They climbed out of the buggy, and after happy greetings
the children were tucked into a fluffy bed of feather quilts, made up on the
floor. It was so quiet and peaceful and soon everyone was asleep.

Mary and the children enjoyed being with the grandparents again. It was a
delight for the children also, to be with their young aunts and uncles who
showed them around the place. It was especially great because it was strawberry
and raspberry time. They ate and ate. How big and luscious and plentiful the
berries were.

The days passed by, and soon it was time to go home for Mary and the children.
Emanuel would be going with them. Grandpa Fischer couldn't handle the rascal
and he was old enough to help his brother Gottlieb on the farm. Emanuel was
always trying to impress his younger nieces and nephews with his citified ways.
After all, he had lived in the big city of Winnipeg for two years and could
speak some English. On the way home he would enjoy terrifying the children by
immediately dashing off the train and just barely making it back on as the
train was already moving. They were sure he wouldn't make it. How he worried
them!

Finally the conductor called "Irvine!" Everyone scrambled to the door. How
happy they all were to pile into the buggy with their father and head for home.
Gottlieb was driving his prize team of horses that day. They were so tiny yet
so strong. It was unbelievable that they could pull a load of wheat those 15
miles to town. Just a quick whistle and away they flew. The children shrieked
with joy as their father showed off, passing everyone on the way.

The Newburg Evangelical Church was built in 1908 by the men in the community
and named after the Newburg community. The church was located about two miles
north and one mile west of Gottlieb and Mary's. Each morning Gottlieb would
walk across country to help with the building. Emil remembers those days well,
even though he was only four years old. He could hardly wait for his dad. Many
times during the day, he would run up the hill to see if his father was coming.
Finally there he was, away off in the distance. As his father came closer Emil
could see his hammer and saw. Emil would then run to meet him. A few years
later the church was moved two miles north, making it more central.

On Sundays the family climbed into the black two-seater buggy and were off to
church. The children were taught the German ABC's, usually by one of the women.
This prepared them to read and write, and to better understand the German
sermons and hymns.

In 1912 Sentinel School was built on the C.P.R. land which now belonged to Mr.
Brost. Now the children could go to school to learn and write and also to learn
English. By this time Elizabeth was nine years old and often had to stay home
to help with the farm work, as many other children had to do in those days.
There were no government rules as to school age or attendance and, therefore,
many children acquired only a grade three education. The teachers were always
men and were very strict. The children were really terrified of the teacher and
the classroom was deathly silent. In summertime the Freimark children walked
three miles to school. In winter they drove a horse and sleigh, which their
father had made. The lunches were usually sandwiches of homemade bread, with
chokecherry or gooseberry jam. Syrup pails made great lunch pails. In the
summer fresh lettuce sandwiches with salt and pepper were a real treat, or
perhaps just buttered bread with a handful of radishes. Their mother always had
a nice vegetable garden and grew a variety of flowers and berry bushes.

In 1912 the grandparents came from Pineridge to Irvine by train. They brought a
team of horses and all their personal belongings with them. They were able to
rent some land for one year. The following year, they bought land, which was
actually the north half of the land they had previously owned when they first
arrived in Canada. Gottlieb helped them out by trading some horses and a cow
for the Pineridge land title. Their herds increased and the crops in 1914 and
1915 were good. Later on Bill Fischer owned this land and today it belongs to
Jeff Freimark. Grandpa Fischer died while they were still living on this farm.
In later years Elizabeth lived with her son Emanuel, who took care of her.

Meanwhile Gottlieb and Mary's family increased. Bertha was born on November 12,
1912, William, on August 14, 1914, Albert, on November 27, 1916, Emma, on April
13, 1920, and Rose, on November 12, 1922.

The old house was now too small and was in need of repair, so Gottlieb decided
to pull part of it down, and put on an addition. First of all a cellar hole was
dug, for cold storage. In one corner of the cellar, a hole was dug, about three
feet deep and about 30 inches in diameter. Two large pottery tiles were then
placed end to end in the hole. Due to the high water table it filled with
water. The main floor included a kitchen, entrance hall, and two pantries. In
one of these pantries was the stairway that led up to a large bedroom for the
boys. The other pantry had homemade cabinets with a sink and a hand water pump,
which was just above the well. Fresh cold water could be pumped almost
instantly. Oh! what an improvement and work saver. There was plenty of water,
and no longer the need to carry it by the pailful.

On December 12, 1924 Edward, the youngest son, was born. Martha, the youngest
daughter, was born on June 20, 1927.

Gottlieb Freimark Family: Back: Alfred, Albert, William, Emil, Edward; Front:
Emma, Bertha, Gottlieb, Margaret, Mary, Elizabeth, Rosie; Sitting: Martha (pic)

Gottlieb never learned to read or write, but could sign his name. He was a
clean living person, and didn't drink or smoke. Mary loved to sit by the
kitchen window on Sunday afternoons and read her beloved hymnal, over and over.
Gottlieb and Mary retired to Irvine in 1946. Two sorrowful events happened
during these years: Martha died of Hodgkins disease, then in 1954, Albert, the
fourth son, was killed instantly when he collided with a train at an Irvine
railway crossing. This happened on May 6th and he was only 38 years old.

Mary Freimark died at the age of 69 on December 29, 1950. Gottlieb at a ripe
old age of 78, passed away on December 7, 1960. Bertha (Link) died of cancer on
November 28, 1962 at the age of 50.

On this day, July 12, 1987, eight members of the Gottlieb Freimark family
remain: Elizabeth (Knodel), Emil Freimark, Margaret (Lehr), Fred Freimark,
William Freimark, Emma (Mook), Rose (Stark), and Edward Freimark.

Emil and Martha (Sulz) Freimark

Emil Freimark, oldest son of Gottlieb and Mary (Fisher) Freimark, was born
November 29, 1904, in the Newburg area. Close family ties allowed Emil to
reside at home until his marriage to Martha Sulz, December 9, 1924. Martha was
born July 24, 1905, the oldest child of Wilhelm and Christina (Yanke) Sulz,
with one sister, Bertha, married to Paul Ammann, and two brothers, Wilhelm Jr.
(deceased 1984), who was married to Erna Krauss, and Fred, who was married to
Marj Nittle.

They started life together on a farm, one mile west of the Senior family, which
was formerly farmed by George Kuche. This property had a creek running through
it with native shrubs and willows growing freely. The creek was fed with water
from the Cypress Hills, making it an ideal area for the livestock that Dad
kept, including approximately 20 head of sheep. It was quite a stable source of
income and fresh meat for the growing family. Meat and other perishables were
often put in a crock with a lid and hung in the well. This provided a form of
refrigeration, at least for several days. The cows, pigs, chickens, and basic
vegetables that were raised on the farm provided a pretty healthy diet for the
family. Of course, there was the famous chokecherry jam, both now and then,
that was prepared by Mom each year and always a real treat. The drought years
brought many difficulties. For a six month period, $11 per month relief was of
great help to provide the needed groceries. Land taxes and relief monies could
be paid off by doing road work. Dad would take pick, shovel, team of horses,
plus a simple lunch and be gone for the day, repaying his debt. He never liked
debts and worked very hard to repay as quickly as possible. The Government
supplied equipment, such as fresnos, scrapers and plows. Community members were
very important to each other at this time. Neighbors exchanged food and helped
each other with the farm work, which kept expenses for all to a minimum. Waste,
of any kind, was not heard of. Everything and anything had value.

Sentinel School, one mile north and two miles east of our farm, had the
traditional pot-bellied stove. A hand rail around the center of it was
sometimes used to lay bottles of coffee on, which provided a warm drink for
lunch. One day a bottle got too warm, popped the cork, and drained onto the
dark, oiled wood floor. Cold weather put that old stove to good use. We'd bring
in the coats, boots and mitts from the frosty cold cloakroom and pile them all
around so they would be warm for "home-time". Home-time was always a race to
hook up your horse and get on the road first. One of these races brought about
our barely missing the gate post; however the wires got tangled in the wheel of
the buggy, causing the buggy and contents to tip.

Remember when you had to bring your own water to school? All that was changed
when a cistern was made and an earthenware water dispenser and wash basin were
supplied. A row of towels, one for each family, was hung at the back of the
room, on nails. Split peas were used to form pictures, the alphabet or numbers.
The pull down maps in the cabinet above the chalk board and the globe that
could be let down on a rope and pulley were considered to be some really
"high-tech" learning aides. We always feared a visit from the School Inspector,
for some reason.

The family was helped out with cattle feed from Grandpa Freimark, who had
property on the Bench where the drought was not quite as severe. It was an all
day job to bring home a big load of hay all that distance, but with everyone
pitching in, it was made a little easier. When a load tipped it really made our
day! A sight that was always welcome was five or six loads successfully
rumbling down the road towards home.

In the fall, a flat wagon would be used to bring home rails to make corrals, to
cut into fence posts or to provide firewood. Coal, for heating, could be
brought from either the Elkwater or Medicine Hat mine or purchased in Irvine,
having been brought in by rail. Over the years our family grew. Our parents
were kept busy providing for and teaching us. We are all thankful for the
Christian principles that they taught us. Mom had a full-time job sewing to
keep us clothed.

In 1949, Dad purchased the Sarnia Ranch at Walsh, Alberta, selling it three
years later. He kept the original farm until 1956 when he sold it to Walter
Jans. He then bought the McLeay Ranch at Irvine (now known as the Phaff Ranch).
The family at home was decreasing and retirement was approaching, which led to
the sale of the ranch in 1962. Farming, however, was still in Dad's blood and
he purchased a smaller farm near Medicine Hat, where they were now residing.
Len, our younger brother, bought this farm from Dad, after Dad decided to
retire completely. In October 1986, at the age of 81, Dad suffered a heart
attack which demanded that he lead a quieter life. Mom is still quite active
and has been able to keep a small garden of peppers, tomatoes, etcetera, and
beautiful flowers.

The family of 11 children made for some hard times earlier; however, the
closeness that has developed from the good and hard times is of great value to
us all. Mom and Dad celebrated their sixtieth Wedding Anniversary in December
1984. Dad's family had an exciting reunion in Irvine in July 1987, with
approximately 200 family members attending the two day occasion.

We, the family, wish to pay tribute to our Mother and Father for being great
parents and for all the hard work, tears and love that were given us.

Family members, oldest to youngest, as of February 27, 1988 are listed here.

Annie, married to Elmer Ebel, had two sons, two daughters, and nine
grandchildren.

Emma, married to Elmer Perrin, had one son and one daughter.

Leah, married to Harold Cash, had three sons, one daughter, and four
grandchildren.

Viola, married to Louie Kirschenman, had two sons, three daughters, and six
grandchildren.

Benjamin had two sons.

Clara, married to Mervin Heebner, had two sons, two daughters, and two
grandchildren.

Cora, married to Harvey Knoblich, had two sons, two daughters, and six
grandchildren.

Ella, married to Herbert Gueldner, had one son and one daughter.

Elkwater Reunion July 1984: Lenard, Julia, Annie, Betty, Clara, Leah, Ella,
Viola, Emma, Cora, Benjamin; Seated: Martha and Emil Freimark (pic)

Lenard had one daughter.

Julia (Serfas) had two daughters and two grandchildren.

Betty, married to Grayson Kramer, had one son and one daughter.

William and Edna (Lehr) Freimark
by Marion Freimark as told by Bill and Edna

William Freimark was born on the family farm at Irvine on August 14, 1914, the
sixth child of Gottlieb and Mary (Fischer) Freimark. He started public school
at the Sentinel School at the age of seven. From the time Bill was nine until
he finished his school years at age 15, his father would obtain a permit from
the school board which allowed Bill to stay home from school for two weeks each
spring to help with the work on the farm. Bill says he did learn a lot in
school, but the only way he got any sense in his head was by the teachers,
especially Alice Banks, knocking it in with willow sticks.

One interesting event Bill can recall from his childhood happened when he was
about 14. There was a circus in Irvine, and he got a free ticket to it by
leading a camel to drink at the creek a quarter of a mile away.

During their teen years, Bill and his brothers would load 60 bushels of wheat
by hand into a wagon and by lunch time they would have walked the team of
horses to Irvine. They would unload the wheat, then water the horses at the
creek and feed them the big sack of hay and pail of oats they had brought
along. The children would buy a loaf of bread for about 7 cents, a can of
sardines for about 3 cents, and a pound of grapes for about 15 cents, and have
lunch. They would leave Irvine in the early afternoon and be home in time for
supper.

On April 6, 1935, William was married to Edna Lehr, the daughter of John Lehr
Jr. and Lizzie (Schatz) Lehr. Edna was born on July 12, 1916 at Irvine, and
took nine years of schooling at Newburg School. When Bill and Edna were
married, they lived on N 33-9-2-4 with 27 head of cattle and six horses. Their
crop was poor, and the next year Bill harvested only 163 bushels of wheat from
125 acres. There was absolutely no crop in 1937 so the young couple was forced
to go on relief and sell all of their cattle, except for five cows, for about
$5 per cow and $3 per calf. That fall Bill walked to work around the
neighborhood, picking rocks, carpentering, and doing odd jobs for 25 cents a
day. Things began to gradually improve over the next years. Bill and Edna
milked six or seven cows and sold cream, which Bill, Andrew Knodel, and Emil
Freimark took turns hauling to Irvine by buggy once a week.

In 1944, Bill traded his two quarters of land for his brother-in-law Bill
Lehr's two quarters, and he also bought three quarters from his father.

Since the farm was snowbound in the late fall of 1946, Edna stayed in Medicine
Hat with her mother for two months. On December 1, their daughter Gloria Faith
was born. Emil Freimark drove Edna and the new baby home to the farm when
Gloria was two weeks old.

In 1946, Bill bought a quarter of land from his brother Emil, and bought
another quarter from Henry Bechtold in 1948, to make a total of seven quarters,
which they called the Karkland place. In 1950, Bill and Edna moved to the Beny
house in Irvine when they rented the land to Charlie Bechtold, and in 1954 all
the land was sold to Herb Klaudt.

Gloria (Freimark) Marran, Jeff, Bill and Edna Freimark, 50th Anniv. - April 6,
1985 (pic)

On June 26, 1956, their son William Jeffery, was born in Medicine Hat.

During the years when they lived in the town of Irvine, Bill worked in the
local lumber yard, did carpentry work all over, as well as working in the bar
in his spare time, and Edna had many boarders.

In 1958, Bill got three quarters of his land back, and also took over three
other quarters from Herb Klaudt, two of which (N 3-10-2-4) had been owned by
Bill's grandparents, George and Elizabeth Fischer, prior to being owned by
their son, William Fischer. In 1960, Bill rented the S 10-10-2-4 from Alfred
Vossler, and in 1963, he bought the NW 11-10-2-4 from John Schorr. After
renting the two Vossler quarters for 19 years, this land was finally purchased
in 1979.

Bill and Edna bought a house in Irvine from Ted Aman and moved there in June of
1981 so their newly married son, Jeff could live on the family farm.

Through the years, Bill has built numerous root cellars, barns, houses,
churches, quonsets, and many other buildings all over the area, including
Irvine's first curling rink.

William and Edna celebrated their fiftieth wedding anniversary on April 6, 1985.

William Jeffery and Marion Freimark

William Jeffery Freimark was born in Medicine Hat on June 26, 1956, the son of
William and Edna (Lehr) Freimark. He lived with his parents and sister, Gloria,
in the town of Irvine until the family moved to the farm when he was two years
old. Jeff should have started at Cypress View School in 1962, but since the bus
took Gloria to school in Irvine, Jeff was able to go along and start school
there instead, where all of his schooling was taken.

On June 13, 1981, Jeff was married to Marion Hansen, the youngest daughter of
Mr. and Mrs. Steen Hansen of Eckville. Marion was born in Eckville on June 15,
1955, and went to school there for 12 years before going to Olds College. She
worked at the Children's Service Centre in Calgary for six years prior to her
marriage.

When Jeff got married, his parents moved to Irvine to let him take over the
family farm. He and his family live on the N 3-10-2-4. This land was bought in
the very early 1900's by Jeff's great grandparents, George and Elizabeth
Fischer. It was later owned by their son, William Fischer, then by his nephew
William Freimark, and now by his son, Jeff Freimark.

A snowstorm in late May of 1982 dumped three feet of snow south of Irvine.
After three hours of constantly getting the 4x4 stuck in the middle of the road
and shoveling it out, Jeff finally got Marion to Irvine to stay with his
parents for a few days until the roads were passable. Two weeks later, on June
12, their son, Colin Jeffery, was born in Medicine Hat. Their daughter, Karen
Lynn, was born on June 4, 1985, also in Medicine Hat.

Albert Freimark
by Rosie (Freimark) Piea

Albert Freimark, son of Gottlieb and Mary Freimark, was born and raised in the
Newburg District.

Albert and I, Rosie, were married on September 13, 1943. We lived on a farm 20
miles southeast of Irvine, on the Old Bull Trail. We moved the house to a lot
at Elkwater Lake on May 7, 1949, as a cabin for the summer. A few days later we
moved to the Oswald place four miles south of Walsh and ranched there until
1954. I remember in November 1949 the lights of electricity were brought to
Walsh and Irvine areas. It was a very dry and dusty year and a very cold winter.

Albert and Rose Freimark (pic)

On May 5, 1954 Albert was killed in a car accident in Irvine, Alberta. After
Albert's death I stayed on the ranch with my daughter, Shirley, and her
husband, Edward Freimark. I moved to Medicine Hat in the fall of 1955.

I had two children from my first marriage.

Harold Weiss married Frances Perren. They have five children: Connie, Wade,
Randy, Barry and Louanne. Harold passed away in January 1977.

Shirley Ann (Weiss) Freimark has five children: Bev, Bob, Monty, Tony and
Marianne. They live at Buffalo, Alberta.

I have ten grandchildren and 16 great grandchildren. I enjoy bowling, outreach
program (visiting and taking people to the Veiner Centre), cooking, baking and
helping people. I work with the diabetic association and have done lots of
babysitting.

Edward Freimark Family

On a cold, December day in 1924, I was brought into this world about 17 miles
south of Irvine in the Newburg District. I don't remember much about the 1920's
but I can remember a lot about the "dirty thirties". At church one night when
Reverend Harry Gross was ministering, a dust storm came up very suddenly. We
left immediately with the horse and buggy. The visibility was so poor that
someone had to walk in front of the horses so we didn't go off the trail. 1936
was very dry and many people ran out of water. My brother Fred and his family
moved into our summer-house for the winter. They brought with them all their
livestock and belongings.

I remember the snow storm of 1938. It lasted three days. My sister, Martha, and
I managed to attend school all three days along with the teacher, Miss Gerry
Walker, Jim Schneider, and Herb Widmer. We were each awarded a Brownie camera
for being at school every day that year.

A yearly routine was going haying in the Cypress Hills. We had a quarter
section of hay land on "the Bench" about 20 miles south. I can remember cooking
tea on open fires in a syrup pail, that was left from one year to the next, and
frying home-cured bacon and eggs for our meals. Haying at that time involved
the whole family.

In 1945, I worked in Brooks and Tilley. I remember a letter I received from my
sister, Martha, that had a four cent stamp on it. My, times have changed!

By 1946, my folks had moved to Irvine leaving me to watch over the homestead.
That didn't work out for the best so we bought a place at Many Island. My
sister, Emma, and her husband, John Mook, moved to our new place with us.

The next move we made was to my brother Bill's place at Cypress Hills. I stayed
with them for a couple of years.

Next I moved to Medicine Hat to work at the foundry during the day and at night
I slung beer at the Cos Hotel. I visited Shirley Weiss a lot that winter. She
worked at the hospital. My youngest sister, Martha, died that winter from
cancer, at 21 years of age.

April 2, 1949, Shirley and I were married and moved back to the old Freimark
place. On December 20, I took Shirley to Medicine Hat and left her there in
case of a storm. On December 23, 1949, our eldest daughter, Beverley Anne was
born. About the 6th of January, I made my way back to Medicine Hat with a ton
truck and the road was terrible. In town I met Jack Kundert and he volunteered
to take Shirley and our daughter home in his car. Winter stayed for six weeks.

On December 29, 1950, our mother died at the age of 69.

In 1951, Fred Knodel and I formed a construction company and built two houses
on Riverside. While we lived there our first son, Robert Charles was born, July
14, 1951. I then worked for a bridge construction on the #1 Highway and then I
was the steel foreman at the Power House.

In the spring of 1954, we moved to the ranch south of Walsh. Our daughter,
Beverley Anne, was flower girl for Albert and Yvonne Vossler when she fell and
broke her arm. A few days later she came down with polio. She was in Calgary
Red Cross Hospital for nine months. Many trips were taken to Calgary that year.

On July 8, 1958, Monte Edward our second son, was born and on June 6, 1962,
Anthony Kelly was born.

On December 7, 1960, our dad passed away at the age of 78. On November 28, 1962
our sister Bertha died from cancer.

We moved to Walsh in 1967 and took over the Grand Cafe. After buying the Gulf
Station, we decided to build a new house.

Ed Freimark Family: Tony, Bev, Ed, Shirley, Bob, Monte; Front: Marianne (pic)

The last of our family was born on July 27, 1972, a girl named Marianne Rose.

Bev married Norm Eiserman in 1967. They have three children. Lorelie Anne was
born on August 28, 1968, Jason Michael was born on January 3, 1971, and Craig
Edward on April 12, 1972. They presently live 20 miles west of Maple Creek on a
farm. They have farmland and a small business in which they fix engines.

Robert married Sherry Houff on September 25, 1970. They have three children,
Shawn Edward, born September 24, 1971, a daughter Bobbi Joe, born August 14,
1973, and a daughter Dusty Lee, born on January 11, 1976. They live on a farm
near Scandia, Alberta.

Monte married Gina Osadczuk on May 13, 1978. Thomas Smokey was born December 3,
1980. Jaydee Edward, was born October 10, 1982. The only girl, Sally May, was
born March 27, 1984. Monte and Gina live next to us out at Buffalo. They run
several hundred head of cattle and have some irrigation.

Anthony (Tony) married Lorraine KuKura July 23, 1983. Kellee Anne was born
March 1, 1984 and twin girls Toni Dee and Joni Lee were born November 17, 1986.
Joni Lee passed away the next day. Tony is working out at Buffalo for the
Dynamar Gas Company. Later he will take over our farm.

Marianne Rose is presently living with her sister, Bev, and finishing her grade
ten in Maple Creek.

Herb and Bette Frisch Family
by Bette Frisch

We moved to the Dave Sulz farm in the Irvine district in 1959. We had three
children, Darlene, Lorne and Tim. Darlene and Lorne began to attend the Irvine
School. Darlene was in grade five and Lorne in grade two.

Herb did a lot of custom farm work in the area for several years. The children
and I milked cows, fed pigs and chickens and grew a fairsized garden.

We attended the Peace United Church where I taught Sunday School for several
years. I also was a C.G.I.T. leader for a few years. I have always belonged to
the UCW and have served as secretary for many years.

Lorne and Tim were 4-H members and Herb helped along with the 4-H organization
and was an assistant leader for awhile. Darlene was involved with Explorers and
later with CGIT. She was in the drama club at school, plus she and Lorne were
in the church choir. This kept us busy taking them to their various meetings.
In 1965 we had an addition to our family with the arrival of our son, Darcy. He
was born on his brother Tim's ninth birthday and Tim was delighted - for
awhile. Darcy enjoyed music and started taking guitar lessons at the age of
seven. He took seven years of lessons and plays in a band now.

Herb Frisch Family: Back: Darlene, Tim, Lorne, Bette; Front: Darcy and Herb
Frisch and Todd Glock (pic)

Darlene got married in 1966 and presented us with a grandson, Todd. He and

Darcy attended one year of college, then worked at various jobs for four years.

Back: Todd Glock, Darlene and Paul Foster, Darcy and Lorne Frisch; Front:

While I was a CGIT leader, Herb and 1, along with Edwin and Olga Bollinger,
took these girls on camping trips to several places like Waterton and Fairmont.

We and the Bollingers went to Creston for fruit each fall for a few years.

We have been going on trips each summer for several years. On one occasion we
went to Ramore, Ontario to visit my pen pal with whom I've been corresponding
for over 40 years. She and her husband have been to visit us a few times.

We are members of the Irvine New Horizons Club and when possible take part in
their floor curling each week. We are still farming and are not yet ready to
retire, although we will be celebrating our fortieth anniversary this fall,

Jacob and Ottilia Gast
by Lillian (Gast) Lang

Jacob Gast (Oct. 18, 1886 - Oct. 29, 1978) and Ottilia Gast (Feb. 9, 1890 -
Feb. 28, 1979) came to Canada in 1911 from Romania. They settled in the town of
Irvine, Alberta where Jacob Gast was the local blacksmith for a year or two.
Then they moved to the Newburg district, where they farmed till 1929 (I went to
school there till I was 15 years old). Then they moved to Magrath, Alberta
where they bought another farm which they farmed till their retirement. They
moved to Lethbridge, Alberta where they lived till they passed away.

Glenn and Elnora Gebhard
by Glenn Gebhard

Glenn Gebhard was born in January of 1924 in Liberty, Saskatchewan. He received
his education in the Liberty school. In 1942, he enlisted in the R.C.A.F. for
aircrew training, which ultimately led to his Bombardier Wings. From an
R.C.A.F. operational base, Squadron 44 at Dunholme, England, a tour of 35
missions on Lancaster bombers was completed. After three years of service, he
was discharged in 1945.

In 1940 Glenn received a Bachelor of Education degree at the University of
Saskatchewan, then went teaching for three years at Midale, Saskatchewan.
During the sixties, he took postgraduate work at the University of Alberta
which resulted in a total of six years training, as well as a Diploma in
Educational Administration.

Glenn Gebhard Family: Back: Dale; Front: Glenn, Laurie and Elnora - 1959 (pic)

On August 9, 1952, Glenn married Elnora Mayer of Moose Jaw. Elnora received her
education at the Moose Jaw Central Collegiate and became a medical
receptionist. They had two children, Dale and Laurie.

Dale, a video marketing manager, was born in December of 1954. He married
Valerie Burgess of Surrey, British Columbia in 1979. They have two daughters,
Krista, seven, and Becky, five, and reside in Surrey.

Their daughter, Laurie, was born in January of 1958. She married Jim Tamchy in
August of 1983, and lived in Edmonton, Alberta. Laurie lost her life in an auto
accident on June 21, 1986.

After serving as principal of the Schuler School for one year, Glenn then was
principal of the Irvine Centralized School for 14 years, 1953-1967. During this
period the school grew in both size and number. In 1951-52, the total pupil
enrollment was 180 students and six teachers; whereas, in 1962-63, the
enrollment was 355, and 16 teachers.

In 1967, they moved further west to Delta, B.C. where Glenn taught science for
six years in the Delta Senior Secondary School at Ladner. Then, in 1973, he was
transferred to the new Secondary School at Tsawwassen where he has been a
science department head, as well as a teacher. They presently reside in North
Delta, just across the Fraser River from New Westminster.

As I conclude my family history, I would like to add a personal note. Although
20 years have elapsed since we left Irvine, our 14 year stay there continues to
give us many endearing and lasting memories. If a significant number of
graduates has gone on to achieve success in their chosen fields of endeavor, I
believe their success is due in large part to the kind and quality of people in
the town and surrounding area. Dedicated board members, enthusiastic teachers,
caring parents and others, together provided the strong support needed to make
the Irvine Centralized School a successful one. The fact that the school
continues to carry on the fine tradition of effective teaching and learning
lends credence to this assertion.

John and Caroline Geiger
by Morley Geiger

John Geiger, born in Listowell, Ontario, came out west and settled in Irvine in
1913 working for International Harvester Machinery Company as collector of
accounts. He soon tired of that and turned to carpentry. He lived in the Irvine
Hotel where he liked the food so much that he married the cook, Caroline, in
1915. They had a son Morley born September 12, 1917.

In 1925, John Geiger was hired by Citizen's Lumber Company of Winnipeg to
manage the lumber yard in Irvine. The yard was located on the property now
called Woodward Park. John Geiger and son Morley planted the trees inside the
lumber yard fence and kept them thriving by carrying water to them from the
fire hall cistern during the drought of the 1930's.

John Geiger retired from the lumber yard in 1938 and remained in Irvine. Mrs.
Geiger passed away there in 1957 and soon after that John moved into a senior
citizens' home in Medicine Hat. He passed away there in 1963.

Morley Geiger
by Morley Geiger

Morley Geiger, son of John and Caroline, was born September 12, 1917, raised
and educated in Irvine. He took over management of the Citizens Lumber Company
yard when John Geiger retired from there. Morley enlisted in the Canadian Army
in 1941, trained in Regina and Camp Shilo, Manitoba, and was sent overseas in
1942. He went into battle in France in July of 1944. He was wounded September
14, 1944, hospitalized for two weeks, then returned to regiment at the battle
lines while still in protective bandages over the wound. He managed to stay in
battle until the war ended.

Morley Geiger (pic)

Lynne and Gary Geiger (pic)

Morley Geiger was married in Irvine in 1940 to a girl from Tilley, Alberta.
They had two children while in Irvine, a boy, Gary, and a daughter, Lynne. On
returning from Europe, Morley and Mrs. Geiger parted ways.

Morley returned from Europe in January 1946 and went back to work for the
lumber company in Lafleche, Saskatchewan. A year later he transferred to High
River, Alberta. He transferred again to Fort William, Ontario where he left the
lumber company to go to work for a general contractor as general superintendent
and chief estimator on industrial and commercial buildings only. After 21 years
there, he retired at age 65 and now lives in Kelowna, B.C. with his wife that
he married in 1958 in Fort William. They welcome any visitors from the Irvine
area to their home in the Okanogan Valley of B.C.

Gary and Lynne were educated in Irvine and later moved to British Columbia.
Gary has three children, two boys and one girl. The girl, Marla, Morley's
granddaughter, was on the curling team that won the first ever world junior
women's curling championship in Chamonix, France, defeating eight other teams
from Europe and U.S.A.

The Christian Gill Family
by Thomery Miller

My grandfather, Christian Gill, was born in Torutino, Bessarabia, Russia on May
31, 1853. He married the former Justina Klaudt to whom six children were born,
Michael, Daniel, Emanuel, Benjamin, Reinhold and Emelia.

Christian Gill Family, 50th Anniv. - 1926: Back: Ben and Helen (Mayer) Gill,
Reinhold and Eva (Sturm) Gill, Emanuel Mantz and Emilia (Gill) Mantz; Front:
Katherina (Jans) and Emanuel Gill, Magdelena (Olhausen) and Daniel Gill,
Christian and Justina (Klaudt) Gill, Michael and Magdalena (Dais) Gill - house

Christian and his wife, and four sons born in the old country, immigrated to
U.S.A. in 1894. They lived in Kulm, North Dakota for eight years before moving
to Canada in 1902 where he located on a homestead south of Irvine, Alberta.

The three older sons also took up homesteads in the same area, where they all
farmed for some years.

Michael, after a few years, moved to Leader, Saskatchewan.

Daniel moved to Olds, Alberta where some of his family still reside.

Emanuel moved to Indian Head, Saskatchewan in 1927 leaving his homestead for
his son, Arthur.

Benjamin, the fourth son, took over the homestead when Grandfather Christian
Gill retired to Medicine Hat in 1917.

Reinhold, the youngest son, farmed two miles west of the original homestead.

The only daughter, Emelia, married E. A. Mantz and she lived in the town of
Hilda, Alberta.

Grandfather passed away May 2, 1944 after a lengthy illness at age 90 years, 11
months and one day.

Emanuel and Katherina Gill

My father, Emanuel Gill, was 11 years old when my grandfather came to the

Jans of Martin, North Dakota, and to this union ten children were born, two who
