Ben Gill Family by Edwin Gill

Ben Gill, as many of the early settlers, came to Canada from the U.S.A. with
his parents Christian and Justina (Klaudt) in 1902. Born a farmer's son, his
heart was in farming till the day he died at the age of 92.

Ben and Helen (Mayer) Gill - January 27, 1917 (pic)

He married the former Helen Mayer, daughter of Ludwig Mayer, in 1917 and
together they farmed on the original homestead of his father for many years.
Their family included three sons, Harry, Edwin, and Norman, along with one
daughter, Isabelle, now married to George Phillips.

Helen, in her short life span of 59 years, was a devoted mother and enjoyed
singing and reading Bible stories to her grandchildren. She was a great
inspiration to her family in the field of music.

Ben can best be remembered as an untiring worker, always willing to give a
hand. His sons found it hard to understand how their dad could derive such
great satisfaction from the most tedious jobs such as picking rocks, fixing
fences and cleaning corrals. Much was sacrificed in the hungry years so the
children could have a better way of life such as education and music. One of
the first combines in this district, a rubber tired tractor, along with a grain
unloading elevator, were owned by Ben Gill. Many innovative ideas in farming
were introduced and practiced during the Second World War years to compensate
for the manpower shortage, such as cutting the grain with a header onto a barge
and then stacking it ready for the thresher to take over.

When his older sons returned after the war and the work load decreased the farm
was subdivided amongst the boys, although Ben kept one quarter which he farmed
on his own long after they moved to Medicine Hat in 1950.

Ben Bill Family: Back: Ben, Helen, Harry; Front: Edwin, Isabelle and Norman
(pic)

Harry and Ida (Roll) Gill
by Harry and Ida Gill

I, Harry Gill, was born November 25, 1917, the oldest child of Benjamin and
Helen (Mayer) Gill. I grew up on the farm with my parents, two brothers and one
sister, in the Concordia District where I also received my education.

I believe I was a relatively fine student but I am reminded (from time to time
by former school mates) of the time I misbehaved and the teacher tried to
punish me. I managed to slip out the classroom door and run around a democrat
with the teacher in hot pursuit but she wasn't able to get me until I came back
into the school.

After I finished school I helped with the farming operation. In the fall of the
year, on several occasions, I attended Youth Training courses in Medicine Hat
and did some woodwork there. In fact Ida is still using the ironing board I
made at one of these sessions and that was about 50 years ago.

After World War II broke out I took my basic training at Red Deer in the winter
of 1942 and I was called into the Services in December of 1942. I served with
several Regiments but lastly I was with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment and served
in areas in Alberta and British Columbia, such as Wainwright, Prince George,
Nanaimo, Terrace, Port Alberni and Vernon until 1944 when I went overseas
shortly after Christmas. Over there I served in Belgium, Holland and Germany,
seeing active duty in the front lines. I was very fortunate to come home
without any injuries. I returned from overseas in October of 1945 and was
stationed at the Prisoner of War Camp, in Medicine Hat, looking after the
German prisoners. In the spring of 1946 I received my discharge.

Ida (Roll) and Harry Gill - September 3, 1944 (pic)

I, Ida Louise (Roll) Gill was born on May 26, 1921 and am the only daughter of
Adam and Bertha (Rauser) Roll. I was raised and educated in the Clover Hill
District, north of Irvine. After elementary and junior high I took two years of
high school - one at Clover Hill by correspondence and one year at Irvine.
After that I took a year of secretarial training in Medicine Hat and from 1939
to 1944 I worked for School Division No. 4, under the very capable supervision
of the late Mr. E.G. McLaughlin. I will be eternally grateful to this gentleman
for his patience in training me in the business world that only practical
experience can teach one regardless of all the "book learning".

Prior to Harry's call into the Services I had met him and we courted - mostly
via Her Majesty's Mail (only then it was His Majesty's Mail) until 1944 when we
were married, on September 3, in the Washington Avenue Church of God by Rev.
Millensifer.

Gill farm yard, 1946 before house remodeled (pic)

In the spring of 1946 we purchased the Charlie Koenig place in the Robinson
District and began operating a mixed farm. A few years later we purchased a
parcel of the Henry Otto land, a few miles north of our place of residence and,
at that time, owned by E.A. Mantz. We operated on a small scale as did so many
residents. Some of the years it was "tough sledding" but other times it went
quite well. Improvements came slowly. We advanced from farming with horses to
tractor, from cutting grain with the binder to combine, and from putting up
loose hay with the pitch fork to baling feed. The farm home also improved, from
living in a two-roomed little home converted from a garage to a house, then to
a two bedroom house that was located on the place and built of logs but
required complete renovation. We also went from heating with coal and wood to
heating with oil and propane, from coal oil mantle lamp to electric lights and
other electrical conveniences, from no phone to rural party line phone. We were
not fortunate enough to have indoor plumbing because, after drilling several
wells, we were still unable to strike a good stream of water. So water for
household purposes was brought in with a tank and stored in a cistern, and the
well that was located on the farm supplied us with sufficient water for
drinking and cooking purposes.

Harry Gill Family: Back: Marilyne, Robert, Brent Greenstein, Harry Gill, Gwen
Schneider; Middle: Tammy Greenstein, Ida Gill, Joelene, Leanne Schneider;
Front: Amber Greenstein, Carla Schneider (pic)

We spent 20 years on this farm and recall many events while living there. We
were both active with the F.U.A. and F.W.U.A., the Elkwater and Irvine Curling
Clubs, and the Home and School Association at both Cypress View and Irvine.

In the fall of 1966 we sold our farm to Chris Vossler and in the spring of 1967
moved to Medicine Hat. Since coming to the city I (Harry) have helped farmers
during harvest time, did a bit of construction work, worked at the Husky Truck
Stop, was employed with A.G.T. and at the Medicine Hat Curling Club until I
retired a few years ago. I (Ida) have also had my turn at working away from the
kitchen. I was employed at Eaton's, at K Mart, and for eight years I was in
charge of the bookstore at the Medicine Hat College. I am also retired now. We
both bowl and/or curl, do some traveling and are fortunately still well enough
to enjoy social life in general.

Gill farm 1961 (pic)

Our family consists of two daughters.

Marilyne Faith was born August 26, 1946, which was also the birthdate of her
grandfather Roll and her great grandmother Roll. Marilyne received her
education at Robinson, Cypress View, and Irvine Schools. When she graduated she
took a year of University in Calgary and then returned to Medicine Hat and
worked for Avco Financial Services. She married Robert Greenstein and they
lived in Medicine Hat until 1983 when they bought a small irrigation farm eight
miles west of the city where they grow alfalfa and Robert operates R.
Greenstein Cat Service. They built a new home out there and live there with
their three children, Brent, Tammy, and Amber.

Gwen, Ida, Harry, Marilyne Gill - 1966 (pic)

Gwendolyne Hope was born March 2, 1948. She also attended Robinson, Cypress
View, and Irvine Schools. After her graduation she attended NAIT in Edmonton
and trained as a dental assistant. She has been employed with various dentists
in Medicine Hat and is presently working at Care Dental Centre. She had an
unsuccessful marriage and is a single parent with three daughters, Joelene,
Leanne, and Carla (Surname Schneider).

Edwin Gill Family

I, Edwin, grew up on the family farm south of Irvine, attended Concordia
School, and later Alexandra High in Medicine Hat. I enlisted in the R.C.A.M.C.
in 1941 and went overseas with the 13th Cdn. Gen. Hosp., returning in 1946 to
settle on a farm bought from Isaac Meier in 1947 (former Joe Trekofski place).

Dorothy (Mutschler) and Edwin Gill - July 1, 1949 (pic)

In the summer of 1948 I caught a ride with Reuben Schneider, my brother Norman
and his wife Edna; off to the Maple Creek Cowtown Rodeo where I met my future
bride Dorothy, daughter of Chris and Louise Mutschler of Fox Valley,
Saskatchewan. The transfer from town life in Saskatchewan to country life in
Alberta brought about a few changes such as buying groceries in bulk and baking
bread during our first winter of six weeks isolation on the prairie.

Our first son Reg was born in 1950, Darrell, in 1952, Wayne, in 1954, Robert,
in 1958. Later all attended school in Irvine. With a growing labour force I
added to my farm, part of the Henry Otto place, and also the farm of Ken and
Diane Krauss (formerly the Dan Meier farm), then later the Reinhold Gill farm
which was the original homestead of Philip Becker.

Gill-T-Feeling record cover: Back: Ed, Robert, Darrell; Front: Wayne, Reg, Stan
Gill (pic)

Reginald Gill Family: Back: Gail, Colin, Reg; Front: Sheldon, Devin (pic)

At early ages the boys started music lessons and were frequent contestants in
talent shows throughout the area. I remember one such event when Reg and
Darrell were determined not to allow Wayne to accompany them on his homemade
maraca. Dorothy's uncle and aunt from Saskatoon said, "Take him along and
you're going to win!" When they came home he was all smiles and said, "See I
got $5."

They lost interest in practicing until a teacher by the name of Brian Hiebert
lit their spark again with ukuleles and ballads which was the beginning of the
"Gill-T-Feeling" band, later joined by their father and cousin Stan Gill.

Reg married Gail Schmidek and they have a family of three boys, Colin, Sheldon,
and Devin.

Darrell married Sharon Heller and they live on a ranch south of Walsh. They
have a boy, Clayton, and a girl, Shelly.

Darrell Gill Family: Shelly, Darrell, Clayton, Sharon (pic)

Wayne married Debbie Eric, is now divorced, and lives in Spruce Grove. He has
one son, Michael.

Robert married Georgina (Kim) Hoffner and they have a boy, Jason, and a girl,
Candice.

Some of my earlier recollections consist of many interesting categories such as
working on threshing crews (Albert Wutzke, Gust Herman, Isaac Meier, etc.).
Each could be a story in its own. Bull Clubs; where a bull was supplied by the
Department of Agriculture for the use of several farmers with small herds to
improve their cattle. We also belonged to Junior Grain Clubs which influenced
farming techniques later on. As a youngster I recall what seemed as endless
wagon trains in the summer and sleighs in the winter hauling wheat to Irvine
day in and day out.

Wayne and Michael Gill (pic)

Robert Gill Family: Back: Robert, Kim; Front: Candice, Jason (pic)

Church services at Newburg Church of God were as routine as the sunrise and
sunset and I recall sitting as close to the windows as possible so we could see
the cars going by to Elkwater Lake while we were confined to our religious
teachings for three hours. In contrast, on the lighter side there were school
dances, barn dances, wrestling and boxing matches, Christmas concerts, etc. I
also remember my first silent movie, summer Bible Schools, picnics and ball
games. Those were the good old days and I do truly miss them.

Dorothy and Edwin Gill (pic)

The Norman Gill Family

I was born the third child of Benjamin and Helen (Mayer) Gill in the Concordia
district where I received my education.

My brothers, Harry and Edwin, and I used various ways of getting to school such
as horse and buggy in the summer, horse and sleigh in the winter, bicycle and
walking. I also had a younger sister, Isabelle, who later joined me in going to
school.

In my teen years, my father and I worked the farm, NW 15-10-4-W4, while my two
brothers were overseas in the army during World War II. We also operated a
ranch in the Elkwater area (the Bresnahan place) during this time where I spent
some time living by myself.

In 1944 I married Edna Irene Schneider who was raised in the same community as
I was and also went to the Concordia School. We took over my father's farm in
the fall of 1944. My father and mother built a house on another quarter of land
northwest of us where they lived until retiring to Medicine Hat.

Norman and Edna (Schneider) Gill - March 5, 1944

We operated this farm until 1963 when we sold it to Gottfried Schorr. Our
family then moved to Elkwater where, a year later, I began working for the
Provincial Parks Department. I worked at Elkwater until 1975 when I was
transferred to Rimby, Alberta. We lived there until 1977 when I retired to
Medicine Hat where we are presently residing.

We had one son, Stanley Donald, and one daughter, Arlene Jane, both receiving
their education at Irvine School. They were bussed to school in a makeshift bus
operated by Christian Wirsch.

Norman Gill Family: Edna, Arlene, Norman, Stanley (pic)

Stanley, after finishing Grade 12 at Irvine School, attended the University of
Calgary and after two years took a teaching position at Schuler, Alberta. After
teaching there for two years, he returned to university and received a Bachelor
of Education and a Bachelor of Science in Biology. He then took a teaching
position at McCoy High School in Medicine Hat where he is still teaching. Stan
married Carolyn Lehr in 1965 and they had three sons, Drew, Hugh and Kyle. This
marriage ended in divorce. He later married Leslie Blenner-Hassett and they now
live in the Eagle Butte district where they are raising registered quarter
horses.

Arlene, after finishing her Grade 12 at Irvine School, took a position with the
Provincial Health Administration in Edmonton. After a short time, Arlene moved
back to Medicine Hat and took a position with Trader's Finance. In 1965 she
married Harry Seitz and they began ranching in the Eagle Butte district where
they continue to do so. They have two daughters, Darla, who is presently in
dental assistant college in Regina, and Noella, who is joint owner of an
aesthetician business in Medicine Hat.

Memorable Reflections
by Florence Isabelle (Gill) Phillips

Family Histories are all much the same,
Someone begat someone to keep up the strain,
So down through the ages our fore-fathers came
Giving to each one their chosen name.

Ben Gill's history, by now, is nothing new,
I'm the only daughter and last of the crew,
So I'll not bore you with statistics of mine
But portray a few facts in prose and rhyme.

Altho' the youngest, I too was a Gill
But my youthful days were before the pill,
Before daycare, population explosion and the rest,
But our parents always gave us their best.

I was born before television, polio-shots or known aids,
Antibiotics, frisbies and the fast-food craze,
Nylons, dacron, electronic equipment and the rest,
But our parents always gave us their best.

Ball-point pens and credit cards never entered the scene
And fluorescent lights and radar were yet but a dream,
Family sharing for us meant a time of jest,
But our parents always gave us their best.

A chip always meant a piece of wood
And hardware meant hardware as we understood,
Software wasn't even a word as yet
But our parents always gave us their best.

I grew up before there were panty hose
Or even a sign of drip-dry clothes,
No thought of ice-makers, freezers or a toothpaste called Crest,
But our parents always gave us their best.

Air-conditioners, dishwashers and clothes dryers too
Were something of which we never knew,
It was a time before star-wars and also jets,
But our parents always gave us their best.

Food processors, kraft dinners and microwaves too
Would have fascinated us just through and through,
Electric blankets were never found in a chest,
But our parents always gave us their best.

Time has a way of slipping by
And cannot be stopped, however we try,
Through our growing years, we were very blessed
As our parents gave to us their best.

Through this changing world things remain not the same,
George Phillips decided to change my name,
So on August 25th in the year Sixty One
A new life for us had thus begun.

We were married a few years and then did agree
That perhaps we should start a family,
And what do you know it wasn't long
Until a wee daughter to us did belong.

We thought of Juanita for her given name
And then we decided to add Charmaine,
What a pretty name it turned out to be
For the first born in our family.

In two years or so, our family grew,
A gift from God, this we all knew,
"It's another girl", they said with glee,
So we named the little one, Dawn Marie.

As our children grew we did not rest
Until we gave to them our best,
There was music, baton and speech arts too
In which they excelled and loved to do.

Today our daughters have homes of their own,
So once again we are all alone,
Now looking ahead on our life's quest
As parents, we'll continue to give them our best.

My tribute to Nellie Mehrer, author and composer.

Andrew and Emilie (Bauer) Glock
by Evelyn (Glock) Hausauer

Andrew Glock Sr., born May 5, 1860, and Emilie (Bauer), born December 14, 1865,
came from Otar Krimea, Russia to Canada arriving at the port of Halifax in
November 1905. He was naturalized in Medicine Hat, Alberta, August 3, 1910.

While traveling west by train, the train was in a wreck, and their son, Edward,
was injured and hospitalized, making it necessary for the family to stay in
Winnipeg for some time. Then they came on to settle in Irvine in 1906, to build
and operate a blacksmith shop where the Jacob Bechtold residence is now at
Forres Street. At the same time Andrew took up his homestead in the Clover Hill
District, SE 24-12-2-W4, building a sod house and adding more buildings at a
later date. Here they resided until his death, November 4, 1926. After Andrew's
death, Emilie Glock took up residence in Irvine in the former Sam
Kalmback/Henry Wolff house on Walsh Street for a short time. (That house is no
longer there because of the highway. It was purchased in the early 50's by Emil
Ulrich and moved out of town.) She took up residence on Durham Street, living
there until her death May 13, 1932. This house was later occupied by Alexander
and Emilie (Glock) Page, then by Charles (Chuck) and Martha Glock. Later it was
occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Francis Clarke, and from 1957 to 1960, by Jim and
Evelyn (Glock) Hausauer, owners of the house until 1977.

Andrew and Emilie had three daughters and eight sons.

Ida (1884-1924) married Fred Sastovnik (deceased).

Albert Jacob (1887-1964) married Katharina Rosa Weiss (deceased 1962).

Edward (1889-1960) married Eva Hausauer (1890-1967).

Daniel - 1891-1926.

Andrew Jr., born in 1894 (deceased), married Selma Wernke (deceased).

Katharina (1896-1976) married Stanley Clarke (deceased). Stanley was with the
R.N.W.M.P. posted in Irvine at one time.

Jacob, born 1898, died when seven days old.

Jacob (Jack), born in 1900, married Dorothy Patterson. They are presently
residing in Lethbridge, Alberta.

Karl or Charles (Chuck) (1902-1981) married Martha Kirschenmann. Martha is
presently residing in Medicine Hat, Alberta.

Emilia (Millie), born in 1908, married Alexander Page who died in 1937, after
which she married Charles Nelson (deceased 1970). Millie is presently living at
Vauxhall, Alberta.

Albert and Katharina (Weiss) Glock
by Evelyn (Glock) Hausauer

Albert Glock, son of Andrew and Emilie Glock, homesteaded on the SW 24-12-2-W4
about 1906. He married Katharina Rosa Weiss at Irvine in 1908. In 1913 they
moved to Billings, Montana, U.S.A. accompanied by their two eldest children,
John and Erna. In Billings they were blessed with four more daughters and two
sons. Some of the family still reside in Billings. One daughter resides in St.
Louis, Missouri.

Rosa died in 1962 and Albert died in 1964.

Andrew and Selma Glock
by Harvey Glock

Andrew Glock Jr. (1894-1969) came to Canada with his parents in 1905, to the
Irvine area. He married Selma Wernke. Andrew was the blacksmith and served many
people in and around the Irvine area until the early 1940's when he and his

They have three children, Lynne, Melody and Ian, and they all live in B.C.

are Judy, who also lives in Rutland, and Gloria, who is living in eastern
Canada. Freda died in the spring of 1988.

I, Harvey, married Lila Christien from Lumby, B.C. We have three daughters:

and has three children and also lives in Nelson; Rae Anne manages the
hairdressing department in Zellers in Trail, B.C.

I retired from teaching school in 1984 and am enjoying my early retirement
doing all the things I didn't have time to do while working.

Mother died in 1984. While cleaning up the estate in Vernon, I came across a
little booklet that Freda must have compiled while she was in school. It is a
treasure to me so I am sending along a copy.

There is still a warmness in my heart for Irvine and the standing joke around
here is that "I'm going back to visit" every summer but I never seem to get
there. Maybe next summer.

The names Woodward, Weiss, Roll, Schneider, Hausauer, among others still ring a
bell. When we left Irvine electricity was not in the area, so there have been a
lot of changes.

I like the name "20 Mile Post".

Nils Gutterud Family
by Ruth (Gutterud) Lyons

Nils Gutterud was born in Adalen, Norway February 10, 1879. He was an
apprentice in cabinet making and also worked in a paper factory.

Gunhild Olava Hallingby was born in Hoenifoss, Norway, October 24, 1876, and
worked in the same factory as Nils. They were married in Hoenifoss in 1898
where they lived until 1907 when Nils immigrated to North Dakota, U.S.A. Olava
came later with their five girls, Ragna, Marie, Thora, Helga, and Roennaug. She
also came with her sister-in-law and a friend as far as Minneapolis, Minnesota.
It was quite an adventure for her as she had never been out of Norway before.
They settled in Union, North Dakota first.

On their way over, Father came on the ship called Virginian, and Mother on the
Victorian. They landed in Quebec, then went to Chicago, Minneapolis, and then
settled in Union.

In 1910, all the girls became sick with scarlet fever and the three youngest
died in one week. Marie and Ragna were very sad as it was close to Christmas.
Three more children, Olof, Thorvold, and Helga, were born in North Dakota. Olof
died at the age of two.

They moved to Walsh, Alberta in 1911, where Father took a homestead. They lived
in a dugout for two days until a shack was built and lived in the shack for two
years before Father could afford to build a house. He brought, by train from
North Dakota, two horses, seven head of cattle, and some chickens to Tvetens'
place. They stayed there until the well was dug and a yard fenced in for their
cattle. They also stayed at Tom Coulthards for a few days until the shack was
built. They had to pull all their water by hand to give to the cattle and
horses, and for their own use.

Father built a house in 1916 with a full basement, four rooms on the main
floor, and three bedrooms upstairs. This was nice for them as they had three
more children, twins Olga and Ole and myself, Ruth. Because they were music
lovers, Father bought a piano for which he traded six cattle and some cash. He
also brought a violin and auto harp with him from Norway, and their place
became a social gathering every weekend. I remember the folks mentioning
neighbors that came over quite often, the Woods being their closest, and the
Soderquists; Tvetens, Glocks, Brandts, Neubauers, George Hamilton,
Hendricksons. Olsons. and many more.

Gutterud Family: Back: Marie, Ragna, Nils, Olava, Helga-, Front: Thorvold, Ole,
Olga, Ruth (pic)

In 1918 the flu hit the neighborhood, and several neighbors passed away
including Father's friend Bjorn Tveten. All our family was very sick except
Mother and Ragna. They managed to look after the rest of us. The Woods were
very kind, and brought us our mail and groceries.

In 1924, after seven years of dry summers, they moved to the Red Deer district.
It was quite different from the Prairies as they now had lots of trees. I can
still remember our two boys, Thorvold and Ole climbing the trees with Elmer and
Ernest Soderquist. The Soderquists came with us from Walsh and lived in our
yard for a few months until they found a place of their own.

In 1925, tragedy struck again when we all got Black Diphtheria and it claimed
Thorvold, 15 years, Helga, 14 years, and Ole, 9 years, in four days. This was
very sad for Mother and Father, for they lost their last two boys. For some
reason, God spared us four girls.

They lived on this farm for 20 years and moved to Sylvan Lake in 1945 where
they bought five acres of land on the outskirts of the town. They lived there
until the passing on of the rest, Father in 1955 at the age of 76, Mother in
1965 at the age of 90, Olga in 1967 at the age of 51, and Ragna in 1970 at the
age of 70.

I moved to Vancouver in 1938, and Olga came in 1939. Olga married Rolf Holmgren
from Sylvan Lake in 1966.

Ruth (Gutterud) and Fred Lyons - 1985 (pic)

In 1942 I married Fredrick Lyons who spent three years in the Navy. I went with
him to Halifax in 1943, and lived there until the war was over. We both came
back to Vancouver and bought a home. Our four children, Freddie, Donald,
Patricia, and Tereasa, were all born there. We moved back to Sylvan Lake in
1965 as we had land here which I inherited from my father. Fred and I bought an
acreage here and have lived on it for 20 years, but we're selling again and
going back to Vancouver Island. Two of our children are living there. Donald
and his wife life in Kelowna. Our oldest daughter, Pat, and family live in
Sylvan Lake, but all plan to go back to Vancouver Island in the future. We have
five grandchildren. This place has been a fun place for us all as we all love
music, outdoor recreation, and the various arts.

The Jacob Gwinner History
by Hertha (Gwinner) Sulz

Jacob Gwinner was born in 1895, in Wittenburg, Romania, the son of Adam and
Dorothea (Miller) Gwinner. He had three brothers and two sisters, Frederick,
John, Andrew, Mary, and Dorothea. He was six years old when his father passed
away in 1901. His mother was poor and had to go to work. His cousin John
Gwinner took him in and he had to work for his keep. He was also sent to
school. His uncle taught him to do carpentry, saddling, and fixing harnesses
for horses. He had a hard life and had to work hard.

He came to Canada in March 1913 with his brother Frederick and family. They
came to the Schuler district where they had friends. He had to help Aunt Lydia
with the children to earn his keep. He also worked for Robert Trieber, drilling
water wells, and worked with the Traxels in Schuler. He worked in the Five
Roses Mill, and worked making streets and sidewalks in Medicine Hat. He then
took up a homestead in the Schuler area. Brother Frederick by now had made
several moves, living in Irvine and operating a harness and shoe repair shoo
that burned down.

Our dad then married Christina Schorr, born November 13, 1907, daughter of
Christian and Dora (Rath) Schorr, on February 13, 1921.

Jacob Gwinner Family: Back: Frieda, John, Hertha; Front: Jacob (80th birthday),
Christina (pic)

In 1922 their first daughter, Hertha, was born. In 1923 another daughter,
Christina, was born and passed away in infancy.

In March 1924 Jacob's brother, Frederick, left for Portland, Oregon to look for
work and his wife packed up her family and moved down there too. They lived
there until their passing.

Jacob and Christina moved to the Sommer place in the Newburg District where
their third daughter, Frieda, was born. Our brother, John, was born in Newburg
in 1926. In 1926 they bought and moved onto the Gustav Herman place.

We kids went to Newburg School. It was a one room school teaching from first to
twelfth grade. It was the school where our mother, her brothers and sisters,
neighbors and relations had gone.

We lived on Section 2-10-3-W4. We had cattle branded @V, on left ribs. We had
ranch cattle and milked ten to twelve cows every summer. We worked our summer
fallow and seeded with machinery drawn by horses. There were very few tractors
at that time, so everything was done with horses. Hay had to made by cutting
the grass or green feed with a mower drawn by horses. Then it had to be raked
into piles, loaded by hand with a hay fork, and then stacked into stacks; it
was quite a job to make hay.

Our dad did a lot of carpentry work for others. He built granaries, hip roofs
on barns, and put windows and door jambs in houses. He also built a hip roof
barn, granaries and a garage for himself. He helped to build the Church of God
in the Newburg area where they were members.

Christina and Jacob Gwinner (pic)

Our parents were great believers in the Bible. Every morning devotions were
held and every Saturday night our Sunday School lessons were read and studied.

In 1942 Dad bought another farm and ranch, the John Weiss place. He seeded
some, grazed our ranch cattle and fed cattle in the winter. In 1949 Jacob and
Christina moved to Medicine Hat, to 1205 Yuill St. They lived there for three
years, built a new house on Crescent View at 1946 15th Avenue SE and moved into
it in 1953. They then bought another farm, the Jacob Sulz place. They took
great pleasure in fishing and gardening. They raised more vegetables than they
or their children could use. Mom took great pleasure in her big tomatoes and
peppers she raised. Dad just loved his fruit trees and was very proud of his
products.

In later years poor health set in and Dad passed away on December 17, 1978 and
Mother on December 6, 1979. They will always remain in our memory as they are
sadly missed.

John and Edna (Tschritter) Gwinner

Edna Tschritter was born on a farm about 12 miles south of Irvine on May 21,
1932. John Gwinner was born in Medicine Hat on February 7, 1926. They both
attended Newburg School and we were married in Medicine Hat on October 26,
1950. Their only child, a son named Glen Wayne Gwinner, was born on September
14, 1951.

Glenn Gwinner (pic)

They lived on a farm south of Irvine about eight years, then moved to Medicine
Hat, and later to Grande Prairie, and to Lethbridge. In the fall of 1970 they
moved to Taber, Alberta. There they opened a western store named "Gwinner's
Rodeo Supplies". The enclosed photo is the grand opening of the store with John
and Edna Gwinner and Herman Linder of Cardston, Alberta, a well-known rodeo
performer, cutting the ribbon. They sold the western store in 1973 and moved to
Lethbridge where they are now residing.

John and Edna Gwinner, Herman Linder, Official Opening, Gwinner's Rodeo
Supplies, 1970 (pic)

Glen Wayne Gwinner married Maxine Ruth Hart on October 26, 1973. Maxine was
born in Taber on May 14, 1958. Their five children were all born in Lethbridge,
Alberta. Linann Jeannie was born January 25, 1974, John Wayne, November 6,
1976, Corrin Judy, February 28, 1981, Angela Cindy, December 6, 1983, and Kathy
Crystal, December 14, 1984.

Elmer and Shirley (Zeller) Hagel
by Shirley Hagel

I, Shirley, was born and raised in Irvine. I was the oldest daughter of Art and
Rachel Zeller, one of seven children. We lived on a farm three miles north of
Irvine. When I started school, I remember, most of us were very fluent in
German, but were not allowed to speak it even on the playground. Anyone using
that language was punished. What a change to now when we encourage people to be
bilingual!

John Wayne, Corrine, Kathy, Angie; Inset: Linann Jeannie Gwinner (pic)

The schools at the time were several small school houses just east of the
present centralize, school. Two grades were in each school with a hug pot belly
stove in each one. In grade three and four Mrs. Mary Nesdoly was our teacher
and everyday in winter at noon she had a pot of soup cooking That sure took the
winter chills away. In grade five we moved to the new school which is now the
upper elementary. Mrs. Bohnet was our teacher and there were still two grades
in each room. The school board kept adding to the structure ever few years
until now there is one grade per room and at times two rooms per grade.

My first bus driver was Walter Nelsen who drove a van in the summer and a
sleigh drawn by horses in winter. The roads were very poor then so when the
snow was too deep on the roads the sleigh would travel in the fields, picking
out the high spots. Then when spring came we converted back to the van again
and because of the road conditions, we sometimes got bogged down in the mud and
arrived late for school. Part of the fun of going to school then was getting
there and, quit, often, hoping to get stuck. The heater in the sleigh was a
large rock which had been heated overnight and tons of blankets.

As the years passed the roads improved an( so did the vans. My last bus driver
was Alan Engel and you could set your clock by him. We walked a quarter mile to
the gate where he picked us up The time never seemed to vary in summer or ii
winter and we never arrived late for school anymore.

Growing up on a farm was a lot of work and fun. Dad always said that busy
children are happy children and I think he saw to it that we were happy.

Every day we would get up and milk 13 cows (by hand) before breakfast. Then we
would get ready for school and get on the bus at 8:30 a.m. After school we
lunched and started with the evening chores which usually took till six o'clock
We had chickens to feed and eggs to gather, pig! to feed and feedlot cattle to
feed and cows to mill again. Everyone had their job to do plus help babysit the
young ones. Mom and Dad worked with us. There was always a radio playing in the
barn and time for a joke or a good laugh. At the supper table Dad would tell us
about the day! happenings, the meeting he attended, or some new jokes he had
heard. Mom always replied to his jokes or unbelievable stories by saying, "Oh
Art, you must be number one"; that was our clue that he had made it up and we'd
smile.

Apart from work on the farm we were active in church groups, school and 4-H
clubs.

Life on the farm was great and so are the memories. The lessons learned then
will carry through my life. I enjoy working in my community and good humor
occasionally, and I enjoy very much raising my family of five children with my
husband Elmer.

Elmer was born and raised in Golden Prairie, Saskatchewan, the youngest of four
children of Henry and Christina Hagel.

In September 1961 we married and bought a house in Medicine Hat. Elmer worked
for Sept Tire for eight years, then for Art Boschee Implement Dealer, Jack
Stephanson, Knight Schmidt Industries, and then, after receiving his journeyman
ticket, he became self employed in the carpentry business.

After my schooling at Irvine School I attended Garbutts Business College and
worked at the Treasury Branch until I decided to stay home and raise a family
in 1963.

In 1970 we lived in Calgary while Elmer went to college. We decided we didn't
like the big city and came back to Medicine Hat. When we got to the 'Hat we
couldn't find a house so we looked around Irvine. Mrs. Trekofski had a big
house at 50 Pacific Avenue. We bought that house and lived there until 1976
when we bought a lot on Amherst Street and built our own house. This is where
we live today.

When we first came to Irvine everyone had their own well and septic tank. In
1974 the town put in the water and sewer system. This was great because this
was the beginning of the small growth of the town. New houses appeared and also
nicer lawns. In 1987 the town undertook a road and street program which again
helped to clean up some of the muddy streets by the use of pavement and cold
mix. The town is progressing slowly but the changes in the last 15 years have
really changed the town's image.

Elmer and I have five children who attended Irvine School. The school is the
main reason we stayed in Irvine. Elmer always worked mainly in Medicine Hat and
area so he sometimes suggested that we move, but the kids protested because all
their friends were here and, believe it or not, they liked the school and
teachers. Someday we may move but we'll go with a lot of good memories.

Reg, born March 1963, lives in Medicine Hat and works with his dad doing
carpentry work. His main hobby is rebuilding trucks. He is a member of the
Medicine Hat 4 x 4 club and was a member of the 4-H Club for five years and had
the 4-H Club Champion calf for three years. He won the music festival vocal
solo award in grade six.

Elmer Hagel Family: Back: Reg, Tim; Front: Elmer, Chad, Valerie, Shawna,
Shirley (pic)

Valerie, born January 1965, lives in Lethbridge and graduates from Lethbridge
University in May 1989 with an Education Degree, majoring in Math. She received
volleyball scholarships from the Medicine Hat College and University of
Lethbridge and also M.V.P. awards. At the South Alberta Summer Games she won
several gold medals and the Irvine School Track and Field Crest, every year for
12 years, for top points in track and field events. She was the Irvine School
female athlete in 1983 and a 4-H Club member for six years. She has also won
curling and baseball awards.

Shawna, born March 1966, lives in Lethbridge and graduates from University of
Lethbridge in June 1989 with a degree in Physical Education. In the South
Alberta Games she won several gold and silver medals. She has also received
curling and baseball awards. She was a 4-H Club member for six years and the
Irvine School female athlete in 1984. In the Irvine School Track and Field she
was a bar winner (every other year) - six in total, and a crest winner - six
also.

Tim, born September 1972, lives at home and attends Irvine School. He was 4-H
Club member for three years, received the 4-H Showmanship award for two years,
and had the 4-H Reserve Champion calf for two years. He won ten track and field
awards, five crests and five bars, and awards in curling, baseball, boxing and
hockey. Tim's main hobby is fixing up an antique truck from a piece of junk
into a good looking vehicle.

Chad, born February 1975, was a 4-H Club member for one year. He won a curling
trophy, is a baseball and track and field participant, and a pigeon fancier.
Chad's main hobby is working on electronic equipment like V.C.R.'s and
camcorders, and making his own movies.

Elmer has been a Medicine Hat Elk's Club member for 20 years and is an Irvine
Ag Society Charter Member. He participated in curling and coached high school
baseball. Being self employed for many years he was able to use his work for a
hobby as well as for making a living. Lately his favorite hobby is working the
remote control for the T.V. With the new cable system we get 13 channels.

I (Shirley) was the 4-H assistant leader from 1978 to 1983, the
Secretary/Treasurer for the Irvine and District Recreation Board from 1972 to
1987, Irvine Curling Club Secretary from 1975 to 1986, U.C.W. Vice President
from 1976 to 1988, New Horizons Seniors Club Secretary from 1981 to 1985, Town
Councilor and Deputy Mayor from 1985 to 1988 (first term), and Cypress View
Foundation Board member from 1985 to 1988. My hobbies these days include
curling and going to meetings.

Harry Edward Hamilton

Harry Edward Hamilton was born in 1875. We have no record exactly where he was
born but when he came to the Irvine area he came from Blackhawk, Iowa, U.S.A.
He was a farmer with a wife and two children.

According to archives information he applied for a homestead on SE 13-12-2-W4,
in the Clover Hill district, on May 2, 1910. At the time of their entry he had
cultivated 52 acres, had built a 12' x 14' house and a 14' x 16' barn. He had
also constructed two miles of fence.

Harry Hamilton and (grandson) Harold Hamilton (pic)

The Hamiltons: George, Helen, Julia, Hazel(pic)

Further recollections are that later on Harry lived alone with the one son,
George. He also traveled to Medicine Hat on a bicycle and worked there making
clay sewer pipes. He would come home on weekends to see how George was doing as
he was tending the farm. Eventually he took on full time farming again. Harry
died on November 30, 1940 at age 65 and is buried in Hillside Cemetery.

George and Harry Hamilton (pic)

After George was grown he left the farm and pursued music in Saskatchewan and
this is where he met and married Julia - do not know her maiden name. After
George and Julia were married, they moved back to the farm. While here they had
three children, Harold, Hazel, and Helen. They pulled up roots again some time
in the later 1930's or early 1940's and moved to St. Albert, Alberta. George
died up there and as far as we know Julia and the rest of her family, who were
all married, still reside there.

Samuel and Betty Anne (Bollinger) Hauck

Samuel was born November 7, 1941, son of Joe and Mary (Helber) Hauck of Thelma,
Alberta where he was raised and educated. Besides helping his dad on the ranch
he worked for the park at Elkwater and for the Department of Highways. He was
also an active member of the Elkwater roping club.

I, Betty Anne, was born May 15, 1952, daughter of Edwin and Olga (Meier)
Bollinger of Irvine, received my education in Irvine School, was active in

Church and one year in 4-H.

Samuel Hauck Family: Back: Sam, Betty Anne; Front: Chuck, Roxie (pic)

In 1983 we sold at Walsh and bought an acreage with a house on it at Irvine. We
developed a large yard and renovated our house. Sam is still busy with his

John Hausauer Sr.
by Evelyn Hausauer

John Hausauer Sr., born October 20, 1862 at Glueckstal, South Russia, and
Margaretha Opp, born April 26, 1863 at Glueckstal, were married there on
October 6, 1882. They left Glueckstal, on March 21, 1889 and came to Eureka,
South Dakota the same year. They lived in Eureka until about 1898 or 1899, then
moved to Lehr, South Dakota, living there until July 1902, when they came to
Canada and settled in Irvine, Alberta on Walsh Street.

John Hausauer Sr. Family: Back: Maggie and Fred Crewe, Eva; Middle: Katie;
Front: John Jr., Mary Crewe, John Sr., Edward, Margaret, Lizzie Crewe - about
1910 (pic)

John Hausauer Sr. was an auctioneer, a cattle buyer and a butcher by trade. He
built a meat market in 1907 on Railway Avenue. This building had the meat
market in the front part of the building, a pool room in the back part, and a
dance hall upstairs, the full size of the upstairs.

When Weiss's store burnt down in 1914, the meat market also burnt. Mr. Hausauer
rebuilt it the size of the building where the Post Office is presently located.

John Hausauer and a Mr. Beitz built a small elevator about 1907 or 1908 where
the Alberta Wheat Pool Number 2 Elevator stands. They had this elevator only
about two years, then sold it. John Hausauer continued with the butcher
business along with his two sons, John Jr. and Edward, and his son-in-law,
Edward Glock, until his death on November 3, 1931.

Margaretha Hausauer resided in their residence on Walsh Street until about
1936, when she resided with her daughter and son-in-law Eva and Edward Glock on
the farm northeast of Irvine until her death, November 6, 1938.

John and Margaretha had three daughters and two sons: Margaretha (1889-1971)
married Fred Crewe (1876-1944), Eva (1890-1967) married Edward Glock
(1889-1960), Katherine (1896-1980) married Anthony (Tony) Jacobson (1890-1985),
Edward (1897-1976) married Martha Boees, who is residing in Medicine Hat, John
Jr. (1899-1964) married Elizabeth Patzer (1905-1977).

Edward and Martha (Boees) Hausauer
by Ruby (Hausauer) Schlaht

Edward Hausauer was born on September 11, 1897 in Eureka, South Dakota. He came
with his parents to Canada in about 1902, and settled on a farm south of
Irvine. Later the family moved into town and opened a meat market. They had a
slaughter house just west of town on the way to the cemetery. In 1921 Edward
married Martha Boees.

Martha Boees was born in Bessarabia on January 26, 1902 and came to Irvine with
her parents, Martin and Sarah Boees, from Carlock, South Dakota in about 1910
or 1911. Martha Boees worked for Mrs. Kusling in the drugstore for some years.

Edward and Martha ran a grocery store for 25 years, known as E & M Cash Store.
They also had a small farm about a mile north of Pashley which they farmed for
several years. They had a garden beside the dam and some years had so many
muskmelons they hauled them home by the trailer-full.

Ed Hausauer and Chuck Glock also started a cinder block factory which lasted
for several years. In 1957 they moved their house and themselves to Medicine
Hat.

Edward Hausauer Family: Edward, Ruby, Hugh, Donald, Kenneth, Martha (pic)

Edward and Martha had four children:

Ruby Delmaine, born in May 1922, was a school teacher for a few years. She
married William Schlaht of Walsh in 1947. Bill and Ruby operated a pool hall in
Irvine for several years, until Bill bought a backhoe and went into business
digging and trenching around the area. They had four children. Cheryl, born in
1948, is married and has two sons, William and Shane, and lives in Medicine
Hat. Gregory, born in 1953, died in 1953. Wayne, born in 1956, lives in
Calgary. Robin, born in 1961, is a photographer studying movie filming in
Regina, Saskatchewan.

Hugh Hugo Humphrey (Dad named him) was born in November 1923. He lives in
British Columbia, and he and his wife Mary have no children.

Kenneth Edward, born in 1926, died in 1958. He and his wife Mavis had three
children who are scattered all over Canada.

Donald Keith was born in February 1931. He was in the air force and retired
from there a few years ago, and is living in Ralston. Donald and his wife Pam
had five children. Keith is in the air force, Trudi is married to a service
man, and Karen is also in the air force. Ken is living in Suffield. Donna was
killed in an accident.

John Hausauer Jr. Family
by Frances Good

John Hausauer Jr. was born at Lehr, South Dakota on October 20, 1899 and
married Elizabeth Patzer at Irvine on July 7, 1924. Elizabeth was born July 1,
1905, the daughter of Gottlieb and Elizabeth Patzer. They had four children.

John and Lizzie Hausauer - 40th Anniv., July 7, 1964 (pic)

John Jr. worked in the butcher shop along with his brother Edward and
brother-in-law Ed Glock for a number of years.

In 1933 John Jr. moved the house they were living in one mile south of Irvine
(now Larson's Feedlot). They worked very hard to build up the farm. The crops
were poor so cows were milked and children would put cream cans on a wagon and
pull it to the C.P.R. Station. Lizzie made butter and took it to the store in
Irvine and exchanged it for groceries. Chokeeherries were also picked and sold.
At harvest time the farmers helped each other.

In 1939, the grain in the granaries was damaged when the nearby creek flooded.
John Jr. sold the farm to Earl Ligget, his brother-in-law, and moved back to
Irvine and worked for Earl Ligget. He later moved another house to the
outskirts of Irvine and started a small dairy and also operated the Great West
Hotel restaurant for one year. He then bought the Golden Rule Store from
Stephen Weidemann and operated that for several years. In 1958, he moved their
house back to Irvine onto the foundation on Emil Wittke's lot and then worked
with his brother-in-law Jacob Patzer for the Department of Highways.

Lizzie was very good at making clothes, among other things. Lizzie always made
her own patterns out of newspapers or brown paper, never wasting or having much
material left over. She made almost everything, including winter coats and hats
for her family. In the fall when the catalogues were received, she would decide
what and how much to get and when the catalogue order came she would start to
sew. The same procedure was followed for spring and summer clothes. She also
had a big garden and did lots of canning of vegetables, fruits and jams.

John Hausauer Jr. passed away November 11, 1964. Elizabeth Hausauer moved to
Medicine Hat in 1966. On December 7, 1967 she married George Ehrman. Elizabeth
passed away on September 23, 1977.

John Jr. and Elizabeth (Lizzie) had two sons and two daughters. Frances
Margaret was born on October 22, 1925 and married Harvey Good; Cecil John was
born on December 17, 1926, and his story follows; Sophie Elizabeth was born May
22, 1928 and married Art Wittke; James Allen was born May 27, 1931 and married
Evelyn Glock.

Cecil John Hausauer
by Cecil Hausauer

I was born in Irvine and received my education in Irvine. In my high school
years, my dad had a small dairy for which I delivered the milk by bike every
day, summer and winter. I made two trips in the morning and two at night.

In 1947 I went to High River to work for Citizens Lumber which was managed by
Morley Geiger, a former Irvine resident.

In 1951 I was transferred to Stirling, Alberta to manage the lumber yard there.
I met Guila Barton here and she became my wife in 1952. In 1953 I left the
lumber yard and went to work for Lethbridge Sash and Door Factory where I was a
salesman. Later this company dropped the millwork and changed their name to
Advance Glass and Aluminum.

Cecil Hausauer Family: Front: Cecil; Back: Terry Elliot, Guila and Teresa Gayl
(pic)

We have two daughters: Teresa Gay, who married Terry Elliot on August 22, 1981,
has three children; Judith Rae, who married John Molcak in 1975, has four
children.

James and Evelyn (Glock) Hausauer
by Evelyn Hausauer

James Hausauer, born May 27, 1931, and Evelyn Glock, born April 27, 1933, were
married in Irvine on August 1, 1954.

Jim Hausauer Family: Jim, Evelyn, Rodney, Jocelyn - 1976 (pic)

I, Evelyn, attended Clover Hill School until it closed in June 1945; then I
attended Irvine School. I was a Girl's Club member and W.I. member for several
years. I worked in my dad's store, and also for Robert and Ellen Brandt in The
Great West Hotel as a waitress, and for Mr. and Mrs. Dave Clapper in Pop's Cafe
as a waitress. Pop's Cafe was the former Golden Rule Store owned and operated
by Stephen Wiedemann, and later owned and operated by John Hausauer Jr. Later
it was owned and operated by Sergius Nesdoly as an Insurance Company.

Jim attended school in Irvine from grade one to twelve. He worked for his dad
in the Great West Hotel Restaurant about 1943-1944. While attending high school
he worked for his dad in The Golden Rule Store, and also for his uncle Edward
Hausauer and Charles Glock in their Cinder Brick Factory. After completing
grade 12, he worked for the Department of Highways as a surveyor, in 1950
surveying the Monalta Highway, now the #41. He also worked in Calgary and area
as a surveyor. In July 1951 he began working for the C.P.R. and remained with
the company for 35 and a half years, retiring on December 1, 1986.

We resided in Irvine until 1960 on Durham Street in the former Emilie Glock
residence, then in Field, B.C., and in Calgary. We moved to Medicine Hat in
1966, and still reside there.

Bruce Macauley Family: Back: Jocelyn, Bruce; Front: Craig, Chandra (pic)

Since our retirement we are keeping active square dancing (which we had started
while in Field, B.C.) with The Hat Swingers, being directed by Jo and Emil
Schlenker. We took part in a square dance tour in Germany in 1973. We danced at
many a homecoming celebration during Alberta's 75th birthday in 1980, and again
during the Centennial in 1983. We performed at the opening ceremonies for the
Universiade Games in Edmonton, July, 1983 for Prince Charles and Lady Diana.

We have one daughter, Jocelyn, and one son, Rodney.

Jocelyn, born October 15, 1957, married Bruce Macaulay on June 26, 1976. They
have one daughter, Chandra, born May 27, 1980, and one son, Craig, born March
16, 1983. Jocelyn started school in Field, B.C. in 1963, attended two years in
Calgary, and completed her schooling in Medicine Hat, graduating from Medicine
Hat High School. During her last year in high school she worked at The
Cinderella - Petite Shop. She took piano and was active in several sports. She
began figure skating in 1966; continuing with it, she became a professional
coach and taught skating for 12 years. Her husband Bruce is a cost analyst with
Good Year. They reside in Medicine Hat.

Rodney, born April 1, 1960, started school in Medicine Hat and graduated at
Medicine Hat High School. He also took one year at Medicine Hat College. While
attending his last year of high school and college, he was employed at Safeway.
He took piano, was active in sports and began figure skating in 1966 and
continued with it. He was a competitive skater, competing at many provincial
and western Canada divisional competitions, winning gold, silver and bronze
medals. At present he is a professional skating coach at Grande Prairie.

Fred Heather

Fred Heather was born on July 3, 1910 and is the son of Fred and Rose Heather.

Fred Heather Sr. was born March 28, 1884 in Eureka, South Dakota and died
October 3, 1939. Rosa Meckler was born September 17, 1884 in Sultz, Russia and
died February 13, 1985 at the age of 100 years and five months. Fred and Rosa
Heather were married October 7, 1907 and had nine children: Bill, Fred, Emil,
Edna, Irene, Otillia, Edwin, Tilly, and Reuben. The family lived north of
Irvine. After Fred Sr. died, Rosa lived in Irvine for three years, then moved
to Medicine Hat.

Fred Jr. attended school at Long Valley north of Irvine until age 15. He helped
on the home farm until 1943 when he moved to the town of Irvine where he bought
a little house. Freddie worked as a laborer in Irvine at different jobs such as
shoveling coal out of box cars, shoveling wheat, and at other jobs wherever he
was needed.

In 1976 the town of Irvine resurveyed an area for residential lots. This meant
that Freddie had to move from his home behind the Lutheran church in order for
an alley to go in. The town purchased a house for him setting it up on a lot
beside the church. The new area was named Heather Court.

At the age of 65 Fred retired and lived in his home until 1987 when he took ill
and had to be taken to the hospital. After recovering from an operation he
moved to the Central Park Nursing Home where he now makes his home.

The Simon Heather Family

Simon Heather was born January 22, 1856 in Petersthal, Russia to parents
Nicolaus and Katharina (Bibelheimer) Heather.

Friederika, Simon Sr., and Simon Heather (pic)

On June 15, 1882, Simon Heather married Friederika Siegle in Huffnungsthal,
Russia. Friederika was born on June 15, 1860 to parents Gottlieb (born 1833)
and Elizabeth (born 1837) (Lutz) Siegle.

In 1885, Simon and Friederika Heather moved to Eureka, South Dakota, U.S.A.
Born to them were eight children: Elizabeth, Friedrich, Simon, Rosina,
Johannes, Katharina, Lydia and Heinrich. All were born in South Dakota except
Lydia, who was born in Santa Rosa, California, in 1896.

In 1901, the family moved to Canada and settled south of Irvine, on what was
later the Henry Mayer farm. The Simon Heather farm was used as a NWMP stopover
for many years. Simon Heather passed away in 1922 and is buried in Irvine.
Friederika Heather later married George Sulz. She died in 1937.

Lydia Heather married George Gordon Schneider in 1917.

Michael and Rosina (Sulz) Hehr

Mike Hehr was married to Rosina Sulz, daughter of George Sulz. When he applied
for his homestead on the NE 32-10-2-W4 on April 19, 1903, he was 38 years old
and had five children. He built a 20 x 30 log house and a log stable and was
granted title to the land in May 1912.

He farmed for some time in the Irvine area and in the thirties he moved to
Medicine Hat where he worked at Alberta Clay Products until retirement.

The children of Mike and Rosina included Bill, Ole, Martha, Fred, and
Christina. Christina Rossi is living in Chilliwack, B.C.

The Gustav Heine Family
by Becky Weiss

Gustav Heine was born in Krem, North Dakota, September 13, 1893, the son of
Johan and Katherine (Schweigert) Heine. He came to Irvine with his parents as a
young man.

Mrs. Weiss, Gustav Heine, Martha Weiss (pic)

Gustav and Martha (Weiss) Heine - wedding October 5, 1913 (pic)

Martha Weiss was born on January 2, 1895 in Alt-Postal, Bessarabia in South
Russia, the daughter of Christian and Christina (Heller) Weiss. She came to
Canada to Josephsburg with her parents in 1898. In 1901 she moved to Irvine
with her parents and lived there until her marriage to Gustav Heine on October
5, 1913. In 1914 they took up a homestead in Surprise, Saskatchewan. Two years
later they bought a restaurant and rooming house in Forres (Hatton),
Saskatchewan. In 1918 they sold out in Forres and moved back to Irvine where
they went into the grocery business. In 1920 part of a block of businesses
burnt down including their grocery store. In 1922 they moved to Lodi,
California where Gust managed Tobins Grocery Store for the next seven years. In
1929 they moved back to Canada and after living in several places in Alberta
and B.C. they settled in Calgary in 1947, where Gust was employed by Alberta
Poultry Packers as a grader and packer until ill health forced him to retire.
On October 5, 1963 Gust and Martha celebrated 50 years of marriage. Gust had
been in ill health for some time and he passed away on March 5, 1964 at the age
of 70 years.

Martha and Gustav Heine 50th Anniv., October 5, 1963 (pic)

Martha stayed on in Calgary until 1970 when she moved to Medicine Hat to make
her home with her sister and brother-in-law, Gusta and Walter Good. Martha
spent six months of every year visiting her family and at the time of her death
on July 7, 1982 at the age of 88, she was visiting her daughter and son-in-law,
Freda and "Tex" Hemphill in Wenatchee, Washington. She was buried beside Gust
in Queens Park Cemetery in Calgary.

Gustav and Martha Heine had six children and also raised a granddaughter.

Freda married Robert "Tex" Hemphill and they make their home in Wenatchee,
Washington. They have one daughter Sherry and one grandson Shane.

Earl married Esther Koch and they make their home in Burnaby, B.C. They have
one son Douglas.

Elmer lived in Vancouver after his discharge from the army. He moved to
Craigmont, Idaho where he owned and operated a bowling alley. He died on
November 16, 1984 in Lewistown, Idaho.

Viola married Don Ringer now deceased. She lives in Seattle, Washington. She
has one son Kenneth.

Percy makes his home in San Francisco and has one daughter Sandra and one
granddaughter Rachel.

Grace married Sterling Orgain and they live in Billings, Montana. They have one
son Bart and two grandchildren.

Arthur Hennes Family
by Beatrice Hennes

Arthur and Beatrice moved from Eatonia, Saskatchewan in 1965. They bought the
"Old Andrew Knodel Farm" in the Newburg district. With their young family of
four, Deborha, Grant, Blair and Scott, they enjoyed mixed farming. All the
children attended Irvine School. The family were involved in Cottage Prayer
Meetings, Stoney Hill Grazing Co-op, neighborhood brandings and friends. These
were some of the highlights over the years.

Arthur Hennes Family: Back: Deborha, Arthur; Front: Blair, Beatrice, Grant and
Scott (pic)

Arthur and Beatrice moved to the city in 1978, and are presently farming eight
miles south-west of Medicine Hat.

Grant, living in Langley, B.C. for the past eight years, is a Dairy Inspector
for the B.C. Government for the Vancouver Area. He married Joanne Samarin and
they have two children, Ian and Kirsten.

Deborha, presently living in Calgary, Alberta is married to Milton Makus. Deb
is working for MacLeod and Dixon Law Firm. Milton is employed by Carter Chev
Motors.

Blair, presently farming south-west of Medicine Hat, married Carol Knodel. They
have one son Trevor. Carol is employed as secretary in Medicine Hat Utilities.

Scott graduated as a medical doctor in 1987, is a Family Practice Resident at
the Misacordia Hospital, Edmonton, Alberta. He married Margeret Moss who is
teaching in the School of Nursing at the University Hospital.

Beatrice's roots go back to 1911, when her father, Albert Gehring, emigrated
from Bessarabia, Russia with his parents, Emanuel and Caroline, and family as a
young lad of 13 years. He lived in Irvine for three weeks, till moving on to
Medicine Hat. Her father tells this story. While living in Irvine, he was sent
out to work for a farmer south of town. He became so homesick, he went as far
back as the bridge and sat and cried, too homesick to go back and too scared to
go home.

Frederick and Khristina Herman
by Mrs. Alfred Lust

Fred and Khristina Herman immigrated to Canada from Bessarabia, Russia in 1898,
and homesteaded in the Robinson District. They had seven children, Sam, Marie,
Bertha, Amielia, Gustav, Johannes, and David. David died at birth and Johannes
passed away at the age of 23 when he got kicked by a horse. Sam, Bertha, and
Gustav stayed in the Robinson district and the others moved elsewhere, all
staying in Alberta.

Sam married Bertha Schneider, daughter of George and Louise (Bachman)
Schneider, and they had five children, Martha (Yanke), Emil, Ed, Art, and Erna.
They lived in the Newburg area.

Bertha married Phillip Schneider, son of George Phillip and Elizabeth (Schmidt)
Schneider. They had nine children and farmed about six miles south of Irvine.

Gustav married Lydia Pahl, daughter of Christian and Justina Pahl.

Gustav and Lydia (Pahl) Herman
by Mrs. Alfred Lust

Gustav Herman and Lydia Pahl were married in 1917, and stayed with Gustav's
parents until a house was built. They had ten children, Clara, Edith (Ida),
Wilbert, Edwin, Vila, Alice, Isabel, Doreen, Gordon, and Adeline (Jackie).

In 1925 Gustav and Lydia bought and moved to the Rub place which was only one
mile west of the Herman homestead. Lydia made many pounds of butter, selling it
to the stores for groceries and to house customers to make a few extra dollars
in the hard times. She also had lots of eggs and chickens for her customers.

The next year they decided to go to the States (California) for a year and they
rented the land out. When they came back they settled on the same farm until
1944. In 1928 Gustav bought a threshing machine and threshed for neighbors for
some years.

Mr. and Mrs. Gustav Herman - 1917 wedding (pic)

The youngsters' main transportation to Robinson School was by buggy or sleigh,
or on foot.

In 1944, Gustave and Lydia moved to the city of Medicine Hat with the four
youngest of the family. They operated a grocery store for a few years, then
they semi-retired, doing some traveling to other parts of the country. Gustav
raised purebred Hereford cattle, which he was proud of, in partnership with his
son Gordon. When fully retired, Gustav and Lydia enjoyed fairly good health
until their passing, Lydia in 1970, and Gustav in 1974.

Clara (Lust), Edith (Ida) (Lust), Wilbert, Vila (Boschee), and Doreen
(DesHarnais) live in the city of Medicine Hat. Isabel (Banner) and Adeline
(Jackie) (Attrill) moved to British Columbia. Alice (Raithey) passed away while
living in Brandford, Ontario in 1971. Edwin was living in Calgary at the time
of his passing in 1972. Gordon passed away in 1985 while staying in the Calgary
Nursing Home.

Gustav Herman and purebred bull (pic)

Gustav Herman Family: Back: Doreen, Edith, Vila, Clara, Alice, Isabel; Middle:
Edwin, Gustav, Adeline, Lydia, Wilbert; Front Gordon (pic)

Marilyn and Bryan Hiebert and Family

Marilyn Roll, the youngest daughter of Freda and Ted Roll, completed high
school in Irvine and then attended university in Edmonton. After receiving her
teaching certificate, she returned to Medicine Hat School Division #4 to teach
at Seven Persons. She met her husband Bryan Hiebert while he was teaching in
Irvine. They were married in 1968, moved to Schuler to teach for a year, then
from 1969-71 they taught school for the Department of National Defense in Lahr,
Germany. They returned to the Medicine Hat area to teach for a year in Jenner,
then moved to Edmonton where they completed graduate degrees at the University
of Alberta.

Marilyn, Matthew, Ted and Bryan Hiebert - 1986 (pic)

Their first son Theodor was born in 1973, and their second son Matthew was born
in 1976. In 1978 the family moved to Jasper, Bryan as a School Psychologist,
Marilyn as a Reading Consultant, and both as dedicated parents. The following
year in Coquitlam, B.C., Bryan joined the Faculty of Education at Simon Fraser
University as an Educational Psychologist. Ted started grade one. Marilyn and
Matthew worked at home. Sometimes Marilyn taught at Simon Fraser. A small
business which they developed provided Marilyn and Bryan with work to occupy
their spare time. The seven years in Coquitlam were also filled with soccer
games, piano practice, Beavers, Cub Scouts and an emerging dedication to
swimming and schooling as Ted and Matthew grew from babies into very individual
people. Returning to Alberta in 1986 was exciting for the family.

Ted, who is in grade nine, is studying French, thinks that swimming three
kilometers a day is easy and spends his spare time drawing and reading.
Matthew, in grade six, is excited about cross-country running, competitive
swimming and spends his spare time drawing and making things. No boxers yet,
but ... perhaps the next generation? Bryan is a professor at the University of
Calgary and Marilyn continues to teach university courses in her spare time.

Ludwig Hoff

Ludwig Hoff was born in South Dakota. He married the former Elizabeth Weiss,
who was born July 18, 1863 in Bagdorf, South Russia. They had a family of three
sons, John, Peter, and Edward, and one daughter, Christina.

In 1894, they moved to North Dakota where they farmed. Ludwig Hoff passed away
in 1896.

In 1899, Elizabeth married Gottlieb Patzer. Peter and Edward Hoff passed away
before 1906 when the Patzers immigrated to Canada with Christina and John Hoff,
Elizabeth and Gottlieb's four small children, and Gottlieb's grown sons from a
previous marriage. They homesteaded on a farm four miles south of Irvine. In
the winter months they drilled wells and made dugouts.

John married Barbara Weishaar. They lived south of Irvine for sometime then
moved to the Many Island district. John was a horse and cattle buyer while
farming and after he retired to Medicine Hat. The home farm quarter was in the
family for 50 years. Barbara was born January 1, 1885 and passed away September
5, 1961. John was born July 17, 1888 and passed away on May 10, 1964. Their
children included Dan, born March 11, 1911; John, August 9, 1912; Emil, January
30, 1914; Agnes, November 13, 1915; Linda, April 23, 1917; Martha, November 13,
1918; Irvina, February 19, 1920; Albert, February 16, 1924; Frieda, January 2,
1927.

Christina married Frederick Bollinger in 1910. Fred and Christina had six
children, three sons and three daughters. (See Frederick Bollinger story.)

The Hollstein Family
by Hardy Hollstein

Zachairus VonHollstein, with his wife Dorthea (Ulrich), left Germany around
1885-1887. They operated a family business in Liege, Belgium, Feed and City
Drag Business. They did this until 1902 when they returned to Germany only to
voyage to Canada in 1903.

My grandfather, Zachairus VonHollstein, with his wife, Dorthea VonHollstein,
and their eight children left in March of 1903. They all were venturing into a
distant and strange land. Eventually, however, they reached the land of
Halifax, Nova Scotia. The large family continued their strenuous journey until
reaching Irvine, Alberta. At the time of their arrival there was a terrible
blizzard. This was when the voices of doom rang out and they began to question
why they came. They asked, "Why are we in a country that is wild?" Zachairus
responded, "There will be a time when in Germany there will be not a stone left
upon a stone. That is why we are here." The family stayed with the people by
the name of Vockeroth for the rest of the storm.

Time passed and the VonHollstein family set up a homestead. Zachairus took
SE 10-11-3-W4 and his two sons took up a homestead as well. Ernest took
SW 1O-11-3-W4 and Peter took NE 10-11-3-W4 (where the Hollstein farm now
resides).

The family worked together to develop their newly acquired homesteads. Ernest
August Hollstein and his brother Peter Hollstein worked for the Lethbridge
Sheep Co. My father, Ernest Hollstein, also worked for the Rutherford Sawmill
in the Cypress Hills. He also assisted in building the CPR station in Medicine
Hat. His brother, Peter Hollstein, hauled water for Medicine Hat for many years
by horse and wagon.

Ernest Hollstein

In 1912-13, my father, Ernest Hollstein, built a log home with logs hauled from
the Cypress Hills. The cabin remains even though many years have passed since
its creation. During this time Zacharius and his son, Peter, went to
Manyberries to acquire a second homestead, leaving my father to look after the
present farm.

During 1915-16, there was a severe drought in the area. My father bought cattle
in the southern part of Alberta for Adam Wood & Weiler of Calgary so the farm
could make it through these hardships.

In 1922 my mother, Wilhelmina (Abe), came from Bochum, Germany to marry my
father, Ernest Hollstein. When she arrived in Canada it was a bit of a
disappointment. In Germany she had been an assistant bank manager in the German
Bank of Commerce. There she had all the luxuries and here there were none. She
had to learn to carry water and chop wood, tasks which were unusual to her.
Many times she longed for Germany. My mother learned how to survive and how to
endure through hardships.

In 1926 I, Hardy Ernest Hollstein, was born. In the following year my sister
Wally was born.

The years of 1928 and 1929 were good crops years. In the fall of 1929 my father
took the family to Germany for the winter. I still remember the voyage on the
Bremen and the Europa on the maiden voyage and how seasick I was. I can still
see my grandmother's house and all my aunts and cousins who I played with in
Germany.

It was while over there that the stock market crashed in 1929. Dad received a
telegram that he had lost stock in the New York grain exchange. That year wheat
dropped to 19 cents a bushel.

However, the family came back in the spring of 1930. Dad bought the George
White quarter (NE 3-11-3-W4). Then he hired help and they broke up the quarter.
Dad also bought 200 pure bred hogs shipped from Calgary. There were hogs and
piglets all over the place. The market for hogs dropped and Dad sold the hogs
for 5 cents a pound dressed. There have been no pigs on the place since. After
that father went into sheep for about 15 years.

In 1932 the farm was completely destroyed by fire just before thrashing time,
followed by years of severe drought.

My sister Wally and I went to the Berry Centre one-room school. Teachers were
Miss Otto, Mr. Schneider, Miss Jesse Rielly, Miss Mark, Mrs. MacDonald and, my
last teacher, Miss Bader. They were all very fine teachers. Due to labour
shortages I left school after completing grade eight. I then worked on the farm
for my father.

My youngest sister Yvonne, who was 10 years younger than I, went to Irvine
School. This was when they started to centralize the school systems. Yvonne
graduated from Irvine School in 1954. In 1955 she married Albert Vossler. In
1967 she died.

My sister Wally married Jack Rinke in 1954 and farmed south of Dunmore until
her passing in 1975 .

In 1940 my father bought 10 quarters of what is known as the Cavan Lake area.
He donated the land in. which Cavan Lake is now located. This development has
been a great asset to the Pashley flats.

In 1963 I, Hardy, married Gloria Spielman and continued farming. We have three
sons and three daughters, James born in 1964, Charles born in 1965, Bryan born
in 1970, Carol born in 1972, Lynda born in 1975 and Sylvia born in 1979.

Our three sons have since graduated from Irvine School. At the present time our
three daughters are attending Irvine School looking forward to graduating in
the future.

While farming techniques have changed along with agriculture itself, we look
forward with confidence to the future. We look forward not only for ourselves
and for our neighbours, but also to a whole new world system, when all the
difficulties that mankind has experienced will be passed. It will be when
people will live and farm in complete security.

Albert and Freda Houff

Albert Houff was born in the Josephsburg area, which was later called the
Robinson area. At the age of two he moved with his parents to the Valleyview
School District south of Seven Persons where he was raised and went to school.
He later worked for various farms and ranches in the area. In 1941 he became a
member of the Canadian Army in World War II where he served for some four
years. In 1944 he married the former Freda Mayer from the Norton District where
she was educated at Feldman Lake School, southeast of Dunmore. Later in 1944,
Albert Houff was discharged from the army for medical reasons. In 1945 he
started farming and late in 1947, moved to the Concordia area where he farmed
for 20 years. In 1973 he sold the farm and moved to Medicine Hat. The Houffs
had two children, Florence and Sherry.
