Freda Houff and 1927 Allis-Chalmer (pic)

Florence married John Schock Jr. in 1962, and they and their two sons operate a
ranch in the Maple Creek, Saskatchewan area.

Sherry married Robert (Bob) Freimark in 1970. They, with one son and two
daughters, operate a cattle and irrigation farm at Scandia, Alberta.

Thomas Berchmans Huddlestone

Thomas Huddlestone was born in Manchester, England in 1867. As a young man he
was educated in music, and was training for the Catholic Priesthood when he
left England before taking his vows, and sailed for Canada in 1887 at the age
of 20. As he worked his way west across Canada, he worked as a farmer and as a
Canadian Pacific Railway section hand. He joined the Northwest Mounted Police
in 1891 and served his five year term at Fort Walsh. In 1896 he took a
voluntary discharge and was awarded a discharge rating of "very good". He was
described on the records as a good sound man. He took up a homestead at the
foot of the Cypress Hills on the Bull Trail and there met another family who
had also come to Canada from England years earlier and who were farming there.
They were Algernon and Sarah Ellen Mort. He married their oldest daughter Mae
Dorothy Mort in 1899 at Robinson, Alberta.

Thomas and Mae homesteaded at Newburg, Alberta and lived in the Irvine district
for about 20 years. They had four living children born to them there: Francis
Orsby in 1901, Oswald Harold in 1902, Sheila Dorothy in 1905, and Robert
Charles in 1910. Thomas, Mae, Robert and Dorothy moved to Vancouver, B.C. in
later years.

Francis, known as Frank, married Mathilda Bischke of Irvine in 1927, and he
operated a garage in Irvine. They have four children and in the early 30's they
moved to Medicine Hat, where Frank worked as a salesman for Massey Harris
Company.

Oswald married Buelah Lehr from Irvine and they moved to northern Alberta.

The Joseph Ihringer Family
by Margaret Gill

My parents, Mary and Joseph Ihringer, lived in Irvine from 1911 until 1924. My
mother was born in Ohio, U.S.A. and my father was born in Michigan, U.S.A. They
were married in North Dakota in 1911 and moved to Lethbridge, then to Irvine,
where my father managed the Pioneer Lumber Yard until it closed in 1924. We
then moved to Leader, Saskatchewan, where my father managed the Ford Garage and
then the Revelstoke Lumber Yard. My two sisters, Sister Gertrude (Helen) and
Sister Louise (Mary) and I were born in Irvine. Sister Gertrude and I attended
school there for several years in the little grey school house.

Ihringer Family - 1928: Front: Margaret, Mary, Helen; Back: Mary and Joseph
(pic)

While running the lumber yard my father also attempted to farm. He took out a
homestead a few miles northeast of Irvine. He built a home there where my
parents lived during the spring and summer during which time my father
"commuted" to town by horse and buggy. He also built a home in town where we
lived until we moved to Leader.

Ihringer residence built in 1917, later Lutheran Parsonage (pic)

My father was very active in the Irvine community. He served on the village
council for many years and was also the fire chief. The Women's Institute, to
which my mother belonged, was a very popular ladies' organization during the
1920's.

My sisters and I finished our high school education at St. Angela's Academy at
Prelate, Saskatchewan and then went on to Teachers' College. We taught in many
schools in Saskatchewan, Alberta and B.C.

Sister Gertrude and my mother passed away in 1978 and my father in 1965. Sister
Louise is retired and living in Medicine Hat. 1, Margaret, married Albert Gill
and continue to live in Leader where Albert farmed and ranched. He passed away
in 1973. Our son Bill, after graduating from university, returned home to look
after his father's interest in farming and ranching. He is married, lives in
Leader and has two daughters.

These are some of the people, events and places I remember about Irvine: the
big school fairs in the early 1920's, the little town hall where Catholic
Church services were held, the day in 1922 or 1923 when the big red brick
school burnt, Mrs. Kusling's Ice Cream Parlour, Helen (Beny) Gibson who taught
us religion, Edna (Price) Benjamin who ran the telephone office, Mr. Thiede who
worked for my father, Florence Singh whose parents owned the local hotel, and
Mr. Wiedeman, the Rawleigh man.

Charlie Ismond

Charlie Ismond was born on the section of land where the Hon. W. R. Motherwell
Museum now stands at Abernethy, Saskatchewan on July 28, 1908. Part of his
grade school and high school was taken in Medicine Hat, Alberta. George Henchel
of that city was his foster father. Prior to his marriage Charlie was a member
of the United States Prohibition Squad.

Charles married Charlotte Cooey on August 6, 1934 in Broadview, Saskatchewan
where they lived for 14 years before moving to Shaunavon, Saskatchewan.
Charlotte was born on December 7, 1914 in Souris, Manitoba. They operated the 6
Bar Ranch for 38 years residing in Shaunavon before moving to Irvine in 1986.

Charles and Charlotte had four sons, Laverne, Burton, Fergus and Ron.

In 1966 Mr. and Mrs. Ismond formed a Centennial project for Expo '67. This was
a wagon train to go to Montreal and was to arrive there for the grand opening
to be led through the gates by the Centennial Band. The trek got as far as
Brandon, Manitoba when the R.C.M.P. stopped them for traveling on the Trans
Canada Highway. This caused a great delay and they were unable to get there in
time for the grand opening. Mr. Ismond then contacted the Attorney General
Department and the Centennial Commission and they in turn contacted the Board
of Transportation Commission who ordered the R.C.M.P. to give full cooperation
to the wagon train. They then received escorts through cities and towns. With
all the confusion and trouble Mrs. Ismond became ill and was hospitalized in
Treherne, Manitoba. Mr. Ismond traveled on to Winnipeg, Manitoba to store the
wagons there for the winter between the Seine and Red Rivers and to await the
recovery of Charlotte. They proceeded on to Montreal on May 9, 1967 with
Charlotte driving the lead wagon. However, they arrived too late to participate
in any Expo attractions.

Mr. and Mrs. Ismond were members of the Milk River Wagon Train Association
which was located out of Malta, Montana, U.S.A. from 1971 to 1979. They have
been on numerous wagon train journeys with Mrs. Ismond driving the lead wagon
on many occasions.

Charlotte died on September 25, 1988. Charlie is presently making his home in
Irvine.

Tony and Katie (Hausauer) Jacobson

Anthony (Tony) Jacobson came to Irvine, Alberta in 1912 at the age of 22. He
was born in Bowdle, South Dakota, in 1890. Tony's father died when he was seven
years old, and his mother remarried to Ole Solverson in 1898. In 1912 the
family immigrated to Canada: Tony, with his brothers, Harry and Pete, and five
sisters, Tillie, Alice, Emma, Bertie, and Alma, and half-brothers Solvie,
Marvin, Albert, and Edward. Pete died at an early age.

Katie Hausauer, Tony Jacobson - 1919 (pic)

In Canada, Tony worked for the Porter and McLeay ranches. He saved up money and
started to buy and sell horses. In addition he did carpentry, which included
working on the building of the Empress Theatre in Medicine Hat. Tony operated a
livery stable and dray business for Henry Cook in Irvine between 1920 and 1928,
until the stable burned down. After the livery stable burned down, Tony started
to buy farms in the Irvine area, and still did odd jobs.

He met Katie Hausauer, who worked in the Irvine Hotel for Lou Sing and Mah
Gongh. Katie was born in 1896 in Medicine Hat. Her parents, John and Margaret
Hausauer, had come to Irvine from Eureka, South Dakota, in 1896. John Hausauer
had the butcher shop in Irvine. Katie attended school in Irvine with brothers
and sister, Eva, Johnny and Eddie. Her sister Margaret worked on the land and
didn't attend school.

Katie and Tony Jacobson (pic)

Tony and Katie were married February 28, 1920. On June 21, 1921 Tony and Katie
had a son, Raymond (Bonny).

Back: Stag Jones, Tony Jacobson; Front: Agnes, Katie Jacobson, Sara Jane Jones
(pic)

In 1928 Tony bought a new tractor and threshing machine from Carl Beny, and did
threshing in the Irvine and Walsh area. When Bonny was 17 years old, in 1938,
Tony sold the farm and bought the Irvine Garage from Harry Crookes and went
into business. He also bought a new 1938 two-ton Dodge truck. He sold gas at
the pumps at the garage and also had the Imperial Oil bulk station and
delivered gas. Gas was delivered to the farms in the Irvine district in 45
gallon drums. Delivering gas, hauling wheat and coal, and the garage was a full
time job. Tony also had the John Deere agency.

In 1945 Tony bought a farm from Phillip Schneider. Later he bought the garage
next to the Irvine Garage from Lou Bischke in March 1947, and operated this
garage, which was B.A. Oil and Gas. He also had the Case Farm Machinery
dealership. In 1948 he sold the two garages to the Wilde family. The Case
dealership was sold to Mr. Wittke.

After that time the family built a new building in Medicine Hat for the John
Deere agency which they operated as Jacobson Farm Equipment Limited. In 1955
Tony bought an irrigation business from Henry Schneider, four miles south of
Medicine Hat. Since they always had used farm machinery from the agency they
never had to buy machinery.

In 1957 Tony and Bonny sold the farm equipment business to Bert Henwood and
Rudy Enns, and went into farming full time. Tony kept on farming, and in 1961
Bonny went back into the farm equipment building and started up in used farm
machinery, new short line machinery, and irrigation equipment, as Du-al Sales
Limited. Tony later sold the farm to John Renke and more or less retired,
although he would help Bonny in his used farm machinery business, until 1976
when Bonny sold out in Medicine Hat and moved to Edmonton.

While in Medicine Hat, Tony was a member of the I.O.O.F. (Oddfellows) Lodge,
and also served for quite a few years on the police commission. Both Tony and
Katie loved gardening as well as farming and horses. Katie loved cooking,
baking, and collecting recipes. Although her education was minimal, she loved
reading books and magazines.

Tony and Katie moved to Edmonton in 1979, where Katie died the following year
on July 16, 1980. Tony Jacobson lived to the age of 95 and died December 20,
1985.

Raymond and Agnes (Schneider) Jacobson

Raymond (Bonny) Jacobson was born on June 21, 1921 to Tony and Katie Jacobson.
In 1939 he married Agnes Schneider, daughter of Phillip Schneider Sr. They took
up residence in Irvine, and in 1945 had a daughter, Jerrilynn. In 1953 they had
a son, Keith.

Raymond (Bonnie) and Agnes Jacobson (pic)

Bonny worked with his father in his businesses in Irvine and later in Medicine
Hat. He was with the I.O.O.F. Lodge for a short while, and during World War II
spent some time in the reserve army which had drills in Medicine Hat. He,
however, did not go overseas.

In 1961 Bonny went into the farm machinery business on his own. In 1976 he sold
out in Medicine Hat and moved to Edmonton. In 1977, Bonny and his son Keith
went into the Host Rent-a-Car business in Edmonton, which they sold in 1981.
Agnes died May 1, 1983.

The Jacobsons kept four trucks from Rent-a-truck and trucked for Northern
Messenger until 1986 when Bonny retired from there. They sold all but one truck
and worked on their own till now.

Jerrilynn married Ib Froberg in February 1973 and had two children, Bo and
Karen.

Keith married Jane Erinvold in 1985 and they now have their first child in
December 1987.

Harry and Rosabella (Rose) Jacobson

Harry Jacobson came to the Irvine area with his mother and stepfather, Ole
Solverson, from Bowdle, South Dakota, about the year 1912. Rosabella (Rose)
Orilla Driscoll was the daughter of George and Hattie (Ferran) Driscoll. She
was born at Minot, North Dakota, July 21, 1888 and came to Canada as a young
girl. She taught school for a brief time at Long Valley.

Rose (Driscoll) and Harry Jacobson - Wedding about 1917 (pic)

Well drilling equipment at Harry Jacobson's place (pic)

Harry Jacobson married Rose Driscoll about 1917 and they farmed in the Clover
Hill district where Harry had applied for entry on a homestead on the
SW 12-12-2-W4. Rose was a great lover of animals and had cats and a dog for her
pets. Harry was an active trustee in the district, taking great interest in the
school activities. After farming for about 30 years they sold their farm to
Albert Pahl and moved to Irvine in 1946. They later moved on to Magrath,
Alberta, where they both worked for the woolen mills. In 1947 they came back
and retired in Medicine Hat.

Rose Jacobson with her cats and pet dog - Roy (pic)

Harry passed away in 1965 and Rose continued to reside in her home until 1976,
when she moved to the Riverview Nursing Home (Now Central Park Lodge). She was
an avid reader and possessed many books. She passed away on March 19, 1979.
Harry and Rose Jacobson did not have any family. Both are buried in Hillside
Cemetery in Medicine Hat.

August Jans

August Jans immigrated to Canada from Bessarabia, South Russia with his wife
and children in 1903. In 1905 he applied for entry to homestead on the NE
28-10-3-4. Two of his sons were August A. and John.

August A., born in 1876, married Regina Schlenker.

John, born in 1891, married Maria Sackman.

August A. and Regina Jans

August A. Jans, oldest son of August Jans, was born in 1876 in Bessarabia,
South Russia. He married Regina Schlenker. They immigrated to Canada with his
parents in 1903. In 1904, he applied for entry to homestead the NW 28-10-3-W4.
They had a family of seven children, five sons and two daughters: Fred, John,
Henry, Jacob, Sam, Lydia and Martha. The family all attended Concordia School.

August was a religious man, and he helped to build the Newburg Church of God.
He was on the church board, and took over the ministry when there was no other
minister available. He was loved and respected by all.

In 1928, August and his son Fred bought their first threshing machine. They did
the threshing for the farmers in the community. The children were always
excited to see the threshing crew move into Dad's field, because Grandpa Jans
was always sure to have his pockets full of candy treats for all the kids.

In 1945, August and Regina retired from farming and moved to Medicine Hat. They
enjoyed their retirement for only a few short years. Regina passed away in
1946, and August in May, 1949.

Fred, John, Henry and Jacob all farmed in the Irvine district.

Sam married Anne Herringer. They had two children. Sam was in the ministry for
a number of years. After he quit the ministry, he worked at the Medicine Hat
Provincial Building until his retirement.

Lydia married Otto Brown. They have two children, Gary and Elaine. They farmed
in the Swift Current area until they retired to Swift Current. Lydia passed
away in August, 1981. Otto and the family still make their home in Swift
Current.

Martha married Emil Sulz. They have four children, Harold, Joyce, Ronnie, and
Barry. They farmed south of Irvine until they sold their farm and moved to
Medicine Hat. Emil passed away in November of 1985. Martha still makes her home
in Medicine Hat.

August A. Jans Family: Back: Sam, John, Fred, Henry, Jacob; Front: Lydia,
August, Regina, Martha (pic)

Fred Jans

Fred Jans was born in 1903, son of August and Regina Jans. He lived on the farm
with his parents, and brothers and sisters. He received his schooling at
Concordia School. In 1924 Fred married Bertha Sulz, daughter of Jacob and
Minnie Sulz. Fred and Bertha had one son, Clarence, born June 24, 1927. Bertha
passed away in July, 1928. In January of 1929, Fred married Elizabeth (Lizzie)
Sulz, sister of the late Bertha. Fred and Lizzie had three sons, Leonard, Edgar
and Elmer.

Fred Jans Family: Back: Elmer, Leonard, Gertie, Florence, Clarence, Edgar;
Front: Janice, Fred, Lizzie, Loretta (pic)

Fred and Lizzie lived on the farm, which they rented from his father: N-32-10-3.

In 1935 they settled on the Hillenberg farm, which was the SE 19-10-3. The
field work was all done with horses until Fred bought his first tractor. Times
were hard in the thirties, and when the crops were poor, Fred and some fellow
neighbours went up west to help with the harvest to earn a little income.

Their main source of income was milking cows, raising chickens and pigs. Cream
was sold for about $4 for a five gallon can, eggs sold for 10 cents a dozen,
and butter for 10 cents a pound. Fred and his father operated a threshing
machine for many years, doing custom work for the area farmers.

In January, 1948, Fred and Lizzie moved to Medicine Hat to care for his ailing
father, August Jans, who passed away in May, 1949. In the spring of 1951, they
moved back to the farm, where they continued to farm until 1966, when they
retired to Medicine Hat.

Fred passed away on November 28, 1977. Lizzie still makes her home in Medicine
Hat and enjoys gardening and crocheting.

Three of their sons, Clarence, Leonard and Edgar remained in this area.

Their youngest son, Elmer, married Janice Feininger, and they make their home
in Calgary. They have four children, Bradley, Holly, Darcy and Dwayne.

Kitchen History
by Janet Kitchen

The Kitchen family, Tom, Janet, and Tom Jr., moved to Irvine on July 1, 1976
from Creemore, Ontario via Seven Persons. Both Tom and myself, having been
raised in the country, felt this would be a good place to raise Tom Jr. who was
entering grade three at that time. Also, as Tom was a plumber and Irvine had
just got their water and sewer, we felt we could start a business and make a
living here.

The Kitchen name goes way back, I'm sure to the Mayflower. Tom is of English
descent with a bit of Scottish. His ancestors settled in the Southern Ontario
area and are still there, the best known being "Pa Ewing", Tom's maternal
grandfather.

The Kusch name (my maiden name) is well known in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan where
my great grandparents, Karl and Anna (Welker) Kusch, were pioneers. Grandpa
Henry Kusch was the first white boy born in Saskatoon. In 1983 they celebrated
their one hundredth family reunion get together.

We've enjoyed living in Irvine and being part of the Community. Tom Jr.
graduated from the Irvine school and has many friends living in the area.

Kitchen's plumbing has somehow weathered the ups and downs of the economy. It
will never make us rich but has always provided for us, nevertheless. It has
created a job opportunity for Tom Jr. who is apprenticing under his father.

Irvine has grown and many improvements have been made in the 11 years we have
lived here. We have seen many faces come and go and made a lot of acquaintances
over the years. I'm sure Irvine, Alberta will never be forgotten.

Jacob and Christina (Seher) Klein

Jacob Klein was born in Lehr, North Dakota on July 7, 1900 to Johann Klein and
Anna Marie Hausauer. He moved to Irvine as a young boy with his parents, living
there until he married Christina Seher on December 15, 1918.

Christina was the daughter of Christian and Christina Seher and was born at

After their marriage they farmed eight miles northeast of Irvine in the Clover
Hill area. Jack and Christina and their family of four moved to Medicine Hat in

ill with Parkinson's disease which disabled him until the time of his death on
May 23, 1968.

Jacob and Christina had four children, Alice, Edna, Frieda, and Harry.

Christina remarried Leonard Halverson and passed away in Medicine Hat on June
3, 1972.

Matthias and Dorothea Knodel
by June Knodel

Matthias Knodel and Dorothea Weissenburger were born in Friedenstahl,
Bessarabia and were of German descent. Matthias was born on January 22, 1863
and Dorothea on January 14, 1864. They were united in marriage in the year 1884
in Friedenstahl. Shortly after marriage the young couple, along with a cousin,
John Knodel, and his wife Elizabeth (a sister to Dorothea), left their homeland
for a land of freedom across the seas. Traveling by ship, seasickness overtook
many and hardships had to be faced as many did not reach their destination.

Matthias and Dorothea Knodel - June 1939 (pic)

Arriving at the American port of Ellis Island, they were soon on their way by
train to the wide open plains, only to face more hardships. They settled at
Java, South Dakota. Having come from a family that spun threads to make cloth
for their livelihood, Dorothea had made many aprons which she brought along. It
was now necessary to use them to make shirts for Matthias so he would have them
to wear to work. He had to work far from home at times and, being alone a great
deal of the time, Dorothea would make blocks out of sod and grass so a shack
could be built, giving them a home to live in. It was in this area around
Eureka, South Dakota that their six children were born: Elizabeth, on January
14, 1886, Reggen, August 1, 1889, Rosina, June 10, 1892, Matthias, 1894,
Andrew, September 1, 1896, and Folton, February 12, 1900.

Matthias Knodel Family: Back: Reggen, Matthias, Rosina; Front: Folton, Matthias
Sr., Andrew, Dorothea (pic)

Having heard of good land to the northwest upon which you could set your claim
and set up "homesteading", several men left to see if it was so. They were
pleased with what they saw as there was lots of grass for their cows. Shacks
were quickly erected on a parcel of land and some of the men returned to get
their families. In late April of 1903, the women and children were sent on
ahead by train, bringing only bedding, food, and personal belongings. Upon
arrival at their destination of Irvine, Alberta, they were forced to find
shelter in the station's coal shed, as there was nothing else available. It was
very cold and they were happy to have their warm bedding. The men didn't arrive
until several days later because they were making the journey by freight train
which was slow going. The older boys traveled with the men and each of them
brought two horses, two cows, chickens and a few items of furniture.

Matthias Knodel, along with some of the other immigrants, set their claim on
land in the Newburg and Josephsburg districts southeast of Irvine. The grass
grew very high and Indians were close by, but the families were not afraid of
them because the Indians didn't bother them. The immigrants were more afraid of
the ranchers because the ranchers were not happy with homesteaders moving in,
settling, and building fences so the cattle could no longer run at large. When
the settlers ploughed their land they were disgusted because they found an
enormous number of rocks, which had been covered by the tall grass. In the
middle of May a big snow storm came, the type of storm that hasn't been
repeated since. It snowed steady for eight days, let up for one day, then began
storming again and snowed another two full days. Many ranchers were nearly
wiped out as cattle were found dead after the storm was over.

Matthias Knodel built a very simple shack which consisted of a large bedroom,
very small kitchen and small forehouse. The kitchen contained a cupboard built
into the wall, a coal stove and table. The bedroom was very crowded, supporting
three beds. The land was ploughed a few acres a day with a small hand plough
drawn by horses.

After 16 years of farming in this area Matthias, his wife, and their youngest
son moved to Trochu, Alberta. However, they found financial pressures too great
so they returned and settled in the town of Irvine. They lived the remainder of
their days there in retirement. They are both buried in St. George Cemetery at
Irvine. Dorothea died in 1940 and Matthias in 1943.

Elizabeth married Jacob Fisher in 1902 and had five children.

Reggen married Gottlieb Koenig in 1913 and had five children.

Rosina married Fred Schneider on March 28, 1911 and had five children.

Matthias married Katie Weishaar in 1918 and had two children.

Andrew married Elizabeth Freimark on October 8, 1920 and had 13 children; four
died in infancy.

Folton married Olga Vossler on June 1, 1922 and had two daughters.

Matthias Jr. and Katie (Weishaar) Knodel
by June Knodel

Matthias Knodel was born in 1894 at Eureka, South Dakota, U.S.A. and was the
first son of Matthias and Dorothea Knodel. At the age of nine years he
immigrated to Canada along with his parents, brothers and sisters. He grew up
on a homestead in the Newburg district southeast of Irvine. He was united in
marriage in 1918 to the former Katie Weishaar, daughter of Bernhardt and
Christina Weishaar. They lived on a parcel of land that belonged to his dad.
Their home was destroyed by fire in 1919 and they then moved to Trochu along
with his parents, his younger brother Folton, oldest sister Elizabeth and Jacob
Fischer. When they returned a few years later they lived on the John Knodel
farm. After farming for two years they moved to Medicine Hat and purchased a
grocery store and butcher shop, which they owned and operated for several
years. Several Weishaar families made a move to Lloydminster east of Edmonton,
along the Alberta Saskatchewan border. Matthias and Katie made the move as
well. It was here Matthias spent the rest of his life. He died October 10,
1959. Their family was blessed with two children, Albert and Edna.

Matthias and Katie (Weishaar) Knodel - 1918 (pic)

Andrew and Elizabeth (Freimark) Knodel
by June Knodel

Andrew Knodel was born at Eureka, South Dakota, U.S.A. on September 1, 1896. He
was the fifth child of -Matthias and Dorothea (Weissenburger) Knodel. In late
April 1903 his parents, brothers and sisters came to Irvine, Alberta and set
their claim on a homestead in the Newburg District. The family farmed here for
about 16 years. When his parents and his brother, Folton, left for Trochu,
Andrew stayed on the homestead by himself.

Elizabeth Freimark was born June 18, 1903 in the Newburg District southeast of
Irvine. She was the first child of Gottlieb and Mary (Fischer) Freimark. She
came from a family of 13 children, two of whom died in infancy. When Elizabeth
was five years old a church was built by the area residents and she was
baptized by Rev. J.S. Domm, who was pastoring the church at the time. A school
was also built and Elizabeth was nine years old by then. It was a three mile
walk to this school which was named Sentinel. Because education was not
compulsory at that time she received only a grade three education as she was
needed at home to help with the work and babysit the younger children. When she
was 13 years old she was left with the housework, such as baking bread, cooking
meals and looking after the other children because her mother had to help with
the outside work. During this period of time and by the time she was 15 years
old, a certain neighbor boy by the name of Andrew Knodel had his eye on this
very capable young lady and when Elizabeth was 17 years old Andrew convinced
her parents that she should become his wife.

On October 8, 1920 Andrew and Elizabeth were married in the Memorial
Evangelical Church in Medicine Hat with Rev. Carl Gretzenger officiating. After
the wedding Elizabeth's mother packed some food items for the newlyweds and
they left for Andrew's humble shack just a few miles, and over the hill, from
her parents' home. Elizabeth cried as she left her folks, thinking she was
still too young for marriage and knowing her mother could still use her at home
to help with the other children. Many more tears were shed in her new home as
homesickness took over.

Andrew and Elizabeth (Freimark) Knodel - October 8, 1920 (pic)

Elizabeth received, as a dowry, three milk cows and from the income from these
most of the groceries and other necessities were purchased. Andrew had a car
but it was soon traded in for something more necessary and their means of
travel was then a buggy with a top on it. They traveled this way, as far as the
town of Irvine, for a long time before another car was purchased. They didn't
have very much in the material realm but were very content with what they did
have.

One year after their marriage, an old building on the Freimark homestead was
torn down by Andrew and his father-in-law and, using this material, they built
a new home on a parcel of land which Andrew received from his father. They
moved into their new two room house the following spring. It was decorated with
mud walls and unpainted floors. Apple boxes were used for kitchen cupboards and
a table was bought from an aunt. Elizabeth was given a bed and three old yellow
chairs from home and this completed their furnishings. Andrew worked with his
father-in-law, borrowing equipment that he did not have.

In January of 1922 a great revival broke out in the little country church which
had been moved two miles from their farmsite. Under the ministry of Rev. J.S.
Domm 60 people had accepted salvation and would now be living for Jesus Christ.
Andrew and Elizabeth were among these converts and were enjoying their new life
and new faith.

After they were married about seven years, two bedrooms, a pantry and cellar
were added to the house. These were certainly welcomed and needed.

Andrew Knodel farm home (pic)

Andrew would travel to Medicine Hat with a team of horses and because of the
distance would have to stay the night. When he made these trips he would take
along butter and eggs which he sold at the market. These were very hard times
as the economic slump in the United States and Europe led to jobless millions
there, and in all other industrial countries. This was known as the "Great
Depression" of 1929 to 1939. People had very little money and their products
brought very little income. For example, Andrew sold a real nice pig for only 3
cents a pound. They had their own milk, eggs, chickens, pork and would take
wheat to Maple Creek and have it ground to flour. Many people had to go on
"Relief" from the Government. The 1930's were also known as the "Dirty
Thirties". There was very little rain and the crops were poor. Dust storms were
very common, therefore, the skies were red with dust, many times from early
morning until late at night, lasting at times for several days. Some men would
work for the government when roads were built, but received no money, only a
deduction on their taxes. The year 1937 was the worst, as there was absolutely
no rain for crops and grasslands. That fall Andrew didn't have a kernel of
wheat to sell and also had to seek "Relief" from the government for the winter
months. In order to receive this they were allowed to own only four cows and
had to sell the others at the cheap price of $10 or $15 per cow. Calves were
sold at $5 apiece. They were not allowed a license to operate a car during this
time. They received apples, cheese, and potatoes and $5 a month for each child
for about four or five months.

In the year 1937 Andrew and Elizabeth made a trip to Havre, Montana. Before
they left they had sold four calves for $20 and butter and eggs for $15. With
this they were able to buy clothing for the family, overalls at 39 cents a pair
and yard goods for 15 cents a yard, and lodging for $1 a night. Later trips to
Havre, Montana for clothing, yard goods and food items were an annual affair.

In the spring of 1938 it began to rain and that year they had a fair crop and
things began to look better. They were then able to buy more land and cattle
and would make trips to the Cypress Hills where trees would be cut down and
taken home whenever needed. More modern equipment was being used; electricity
and telephone were certainly appreciated.

When Andrew made the decision to retire from farming he had a home built, by
Emann Construction, at 238 - 8 St. S.W. in Medicine Hat. On September 15, 1953
Andrew, at the age of 57, and Elizabeth, at 50 years of age, along with their
three youngest children, moved to their new home 35 miles from their farm.

The family of Andrew Knodel had been through hard and difficult times, but
because of his faith and trust in God, Andrew was always able to provide for
their needs. He will always be remembered as an understanding, loving, patient,
and kind Dad. There were, however, times when discipline had to be administered
and his children had to be taught what was right and what was wrong. Before
going out to work Andrew would take the family bible, read from it, and spend
time in prayer. He knew this was very important. On the Lord's Day everything
was shut down and only the necessary chores were done. No matter how ripe the
crop or sunny the day, Sunday was a day for rest and worship. All the family
would pack into the car and go to church. When they retired to Medicine Hat
their church membership was transferred to the Memorial Evangelical Church
which at this time was pastored by Rev. F.E. Vorroth. This was the church where
Andrew and Elizabeth had been united in marriage.

Andrew and Elizabeth Knodel 50th Anniv. - October 8,1970 (pic)

In 1962 Andrew purchased a small parcel of irrigation land which he helped farm
for a few years and later sold to his son and retired for life. When Andrew
retired he put away the rubber boots and began to enjoy fishing, camping, and
trips to Creston, B.C. and Portland, Oregon. On October 8, 1970 Andrew and
Elizabeth were honored at a family dinner and "Open House" at the Memorial
Evangelical Church as they celebrated 50 years of marriage. Andrew had been
blessed with good health until the fall of 1974 when his health began to fail.
He passed away on September 22, 1976 after a couple of years of lingering
illness. He is buried at Hillside Cemetery. Elizabeth continued to reside in
her home until the fall of 1985 when she moved to Primrose Villa and is
enjoying her retirement years there.

The union of Andrew and Elizabeth was blessed with a family of 13 children.
Four of the children died in infancy. There are nine living children, seven
sons and two daughters.

Rose was born on November 21, 1921 and was married to Arthur Lehr who passed
away on January 26, 1963. They had one daughter, Marjorie Jean.

Fred was born on January 5, 1923 and is married to Gladys (Lehr). They have
four daughters, Beatrice Doreen, Beverley Ann, Bernice Irene and Betty Roberta.

William "Bill" was born on August 14, 1924 and is married to Mary (Matz). They
have two children, Arlene Helen and Ryan William.

Andrew Knodel Family: Back: Albert, Jimmie, Lawrence, Clarence, Bennie,
William, Fred; Front: Marion, Elizabeth, Andrew, Rose (pic)

Bennie's two children are Ray Benjamin and Fay Matilda, and Marjorie has two
daughters, Sherry Lynn and Vicki Anne.

Daniel and Mathilda (Meier) Koenig
by Anne (Koenig) Klaiber

Daniel Koenig was born in 1896 in Bessarabia, Russia and came to Woodward,
Oklahoma, U.S.A. in 1900, with his parents Justina and Gotlieb. In 1909 Gotlieb
died, and in that year Justina and the rest of the family moved to Calgary,
Alberta. The family at this time consisted of Daniel, Christian, and three
sisters, Nathalia (Ohlhousen), Dorothea (Litke), and Lydia (Mauch), all of whom
are now deceased.

Justina married Phillip Keim of Acme, Alberta, but she died shortly after in
1911.

Dan Koenig married Mathilda Meier at Acme on March 6, 1916. Mathilda was the
daughter of Christian and Katherina Meier from the Irvine (Ross Creek), Alberta
district. Mathilda had four brothers, Jacob, Daniel, Edward and Isaac.

After Daniel and Mathilda were married, they lived for a short time in Acme and
then moved to Norton, Alberta in 1917, where they purchased some farmland and
farmed for several years. While living in the Norton community they had two
children, Anne, born August 20, 1917, and Elmore, born April 17, 1921. Anne
attended school part time at Concordia School and part time in Medicine Hat
during the winter months while Elmore got his schooling entirely at Concordia
School.

Dan Koenig Family: Matilda, Dan, Anne and Elmore - 1931 (pic)

My last year of schooling was taken exclusively at Concordia School. I recall
an incident during my last year of school at Concordia. As [previously
mentioned, all the previous years I attended school during the winter in
Medicine Hat at Elm Street School. This one winter morning, Elmore and I were
on our way to school with the single buggy, and as usual we stopped to pick up
our cousin Minnie Meier (Wooley). She wasn't quite ready so we were invited to
come into the house to warm up a bit. When we got ready to go, the horse and
buggy were gone. Our uncle Dan hooked up a team to a bobsled and followed the
buggy tracks. The horse had safely gone through a creek bed, through a gate and
then turned onto the road allowance to go east, went down a fairly steep hill
and arrived at the school completely intact. The children unhitched and put the
horse in the barn, wondering what had happened to us. We were thankful he
didn't decide to run away and wreck the buggy and harness!

The Koenig family suffered the hardships of the Great Depression along with
their neighbors, and hauled the grain harvested from their farm to the
elevators at Pashley and Irvine by team of horses and wagon. I recall my father
telling me that he went into one winter during the depression with only $60. As
if things weren't difficult enough during the depression, on May 11, 1936,
Daniel lost his wife Mathilda due to complications from surgery. He continued
to farm with the help of his children, until his own death on March 15, 1955.

Anne married Archie E. Klaiber in October 1943 and lived for a short while on
the Klaiber ranch at Little Plume, Alberta. They moved to Strathmore in April
of 1947. Anne and Archie had three sons, Bruce Baxter, now living in Brooks,
Grant Archie, of Strathmore, and Dean Daniel, living in Medicine Hat. Archie
passed away August 21, 1981.

Elmore married Dorothy McNeill of Strathmore, and farmed the home place for a
short time after which they moved to Youngstown where they farmed as well. They
presently live in Camrose, Alberta.

Gottlieb and Reggen (Knodel) Koenig
by June Knodel

Reggen Knodel, second child of Matthias and Dorothea Knodel, was born August 1,
1889 at Eureka, South Dakota, U.S.A. At age 14 years she immigrated to Canada
along with her parents, sisters and brothers arriving at Irvine, Alberta. On
April 14, 1913 she married Gottlieb Koenig, born November 1, 1889. They worked

on his parents' homestead. It was here four of their five children were born.
Their children are William, Rosie, Elizabeth (Lizzie), Esther and Nona.

Years later they moved to Medicine Hat and operated a grocery store. After
selling the store they moved to Indian Head, Saskatchewan. They farmed while
living at Indian Head. When they returned to Alberta they again settled in
Medicine Hat and Gottlieb was employed by the city until the time of his death.

Christof and Mary (Fandrick) Krahn
by Mrs. Elma Gast

Christof and Mary (Fandrick) Krahn came to Canada in 1910 with four children,
Ottilia (Klaudt), Mary (Makus), Katie (Langlands) and Gust Krahn. They raised
five more in Canada, John, Henry, Dave, Ida, and myself, Elma. They took up
farming 12 miles southeast of Irvine. They farmed all their lives with horses.
They drove to Graburn United Church and to town with horse and buggy.

The five children born in Canada went to Schneider School two and a half miles
away, which they walked every morning.

Christof Krahn died in 1933. Mary Krahn retired from the farm in 1936, moved to
Irvine and attended the Irvine Baptist Church until her death. Christof and
Mary Krahn were good Christians and honest, hard working people. Mary Krahn
died October 21, 1951 at the age of 75 years.

Christ and Mary (Fandrick) Krahn (pic)

Four of their children are still living. 1, Elma, am living in Kelowna B.C. and
married to Albert Gast. Katie is living in Medicine Hat and married to Peter
Langlands. Henry is living in Calgary and married to Margret, who was a war
bride. Gust, living in Prince Albert, a widower, was married to Mary
Rienhiller. Ottilia Klaudt was in a nursing home in Medicine Hat until she
passed away at 90 years of age.

J.B. and Bertha (Scheffelmeier) Krauss
by Jakob Krauss

I, Jacob Krauss, married Bertha Scheffelmeier on January 9, 1934 and started
farming with four horses. In October of the same year, we moved a house with
twelve horses from the Dan Meier place to the, then known, Beny place which I
had rented. We lived there until 1942. Crops were poor, but we made a living
milking cows, raising pigs and chickens. Our only means of travel were horse
and buggy or sleigh until 1938 when I bought my first car. I bought a tractor
in 1942 and then a combine in 1943. In 1942 we moved to Bertha's mother's place
(Rose Scheffelmeier) which we bought in 1947. In time we got more cattle, brand
right hip. We moved onto the John Kundert place in 1961. Our last move was to
Medicine Hat in 1974. Our family consisted of Kenneth, Shirley, Lorne and
Laverne.

Wilhelm and Katrina (Dick) Krausz
by Lorraine Steel

Wilhelm Krausz, son of Phillip Krausz and Katherine Bauff, was born July 14,
1855 in Padorstal, Russia.

Katrina Dick, daughter of Ludwig Dick, was born October 25, 1859 in Padorstal,
Russia.

Wilhelm and Katrina were married in Padorstal about 1879 and while living there
had three daughters: Amalia, 1880; Katherine, 1881; and Barbara, 1883. In 1886,
Wilhelm and Katrina and their three daughters immigrated to America coming to
Campbell County, South Dakota in the Eureka area. They took out a homestead at
Sutley, South Dakota and farmed there while they had an additional ten
children: Rosina, born 1885; William, January 18, 1887; Wilhalmina, 1888;
Elizabeth, 1890; Pauline, born December 19, 1891, passed away January 18, 1988;
Adolf, born 1893, died as a child in 1894; Julina, born 1895, died as a child
in 1902; Emil born 1897, died as a child in 1898; Johans, born 1900; and
Rudolf, born 1902.

In 1903 Wilhelm and Katrina Krausz sold their farm and belongings moving their
family to Irvine, Alberta. On April 1, 1903, they took out a homestead and
farmed at Irvine until 1910 when they sold their farm to John Schlaht. The
Krauszes left for Lodi, California, U.S.A. They worked in the Libby food
cannery and other places until their passing. Wilhelm died in Lodi on January
19, 1920, and Katrina died May 10, 1926.

William and Pauline Krausz
by Lorraine Steel

William Krausz was born January 18, 1887, at Sutley, Campbell County, South
Dakota, and had his schooling in this same area until he moved with his family
to a farm southeast of Irvine, Alberta. In 1904 William took out a homestead 11
miles southeast of Irvine which he got from the government as long as he could
prove he worked the land and farmed it right. It cost him $11 for a quarter
section of land. He built a log house 22 feet by 16 feet, plus he built a slab
barn and an outhouse made of slabs.

In January 1910 he married Pauline Rosenfelder who was born July 12, 1888 in
Bessarabia, Russia and was raised and educated there.

On this farm William and Pauline had five children: Victor, born November 1910;
Irna, February 1912; Frank, March 1914; Pauline, November 1915, who died two
days later; and Lillian, born September 1916. They were happy and did very well
on the farm. When they first had Victor the grass grew two feet tall those
years and Pauline put a red coat on him to spot him more easily. It was also
lonely, as there were no close neighbors, and the only means of travel was an
old wagon pulled by a horse.

In 1917, after some good crops, a large two-story home for the family and a new
barn were built.

In 1925 they rented the farm to Jack Stotz for three years while William and
Pauline with their family, Victor, Irna, Frank, and Lillian, moved to Lodi,
California to try their luck there. They worked in the fruit canneries and the
grape vineyards. William told of many good times and some bad times while in
California. Often he worked 16 hours a day at 40 cents an hour. In August 1928,
they were ready to move back to Irvine to get in full swing with farming again.
Farm prices were good at this time ($1.21 a bushel for hard red wheat) so
William had enough money to pay for a new International tractor for $2000, a
four-bottom International plow for $300, and a ten-foot International tandem
disc. He sold his work horses and broke up a lot of new ground. During the
depression, wheat prices were low (17 cents a bushel) and many farmers joined
the Wheat Pool, which meant the farmer got one third of the money for his grain
and the other two thirds of the money for his grain went to build elevators.

In 1936-37 there was no rain or snow and you could not raise a kernel of wheat
because it was too dry. By 1944 the farm was rented to the youngest son, Frank
Krausz, while William and Pauline moved to a new home built by their son Victor
at 777-9th Street in Medicine Hat, Alberta where they lived in their last
years. They loved to travel and went on many trips in the U.S.A. Pauline had
very poor health for nine years before she passed away. They had hoped a trip
to Mesa, Arizona would help her health but while en route to Mesa on Highway 89
North, she got very sick and died July 5, 1953. She is buried in Flagstaff,
Arizona. William lived in his home in Medicine Hat until his death March 11,
1968.

Victor Krausz

Victor married Nora Irene Sturm on December 12, 1936. In March 1937, after
staying the winter months with his parents, Victor and Nora moved to a farm
south of Walsh that he had bought in 1933. The farm had a little shack that

In 1939 Vic got a job from Mr. Oswald for 25 cents an hour for eight hours a

In March 1947, after hopeless tries at farming, they moved to Walsh, built a

Ed and Clara (Deering) Larson, Larson Cattle Company Limited
by Clara Larson

Ed was born December 1932 at Manyberries. He was raised and educated there. As
a young man he went out working for various ranchers in the area for several
years. Since 1957 he worked in partnership with his brothers. In 1957 the
Larson Brothers bought the feedlot at Irvine, which was owned by Earl Ligget.

In 1959 they bought the Walsh Ranch from Bob Lindsay. The Ranch was known as
the Sarnia Ranching Company at one time. The Larson Brothers then formed a
company, and it became Larson Cattle Company Limited.

I, Clara (Deering), was born and raised in the Robinson district, and went to
Robinson School. One winter we were bussed to Irvine. Mr. Chris Wirsch was our
bus driver. He had a pickup truck with a camper on it and that was the bus.
This was back in about 44-45. The winter was cold with a lot of snow those
years. Highways weren't like they are now. We got up in the dark and got back
in the dark. Dad took us with the horse and sleigh as far as the Robinson
School in order to get on the bus. We were happy to see spring come. We then
had a teacher for the rest of the term. The next few years we had the janitor
job at the school, which was no picnic in the winter time. In the early 50's
the school was closed down. The children then had to go to Cypress View School
which was located ten miles south of Irvine, and about three miles east of the
Robinson School.

Ed and Clara Jane Larson -1972 (pic)

I wasn't going to school anymore by then. I went to Medicine Hat to earn some
money. I worked at different jobs (restaurants and the potteries). The pay was
not what it is now-a-days. I got $200 or less a month and I thought I was rich,
but I didn't have to starve anyway. Life wasn't that bad, it was only how you
made it.

Ed and I met in 1963. We got married in September 1964. In 1966 we built our
new house at the feedlot. We are still residing here today and looking after
the business.

Henry and Hilda Lehr Family

Henry Lehr was born and raised in the Newburg district where his parents, John
and Lizzie Lehr, farmed and raised the rest of their family. Henry went to the
Newburg School. At the age of 20, in 1928, he moved a few miles north of his
father's farm to a small farm of his own. This farm consisted of three quarters
of land and had originally been owned by Jacob Hauck. The land was purchased by
Henry's father and was paid back with yearly crop payments from Henry. Henry
owned six horses but no cattle or even a dog. The buildings consisted mainly of
two log barns and one fairly large log house. The log house had a living room
and a bedroom downstairs and two bedrooms upstairs. There was also a lean-to
kitchen, pantry and porch on one side of the home which was very cold in the
winter. The kitchen was always moved into the living room area for winter. This
lean-to area was not only cold in the winter, but during rainy days in the
summer, it rained almost as much inside as it did outside. The inside of the
lean-to also seemed to have almost as many flies as the outside did. Henry met
his future bride, Hilda Schattle at Irvine.

Hilda Schattle was born in Wittenburg, South Russia in 1907. She came to Canada
in 1910 at the age of three. Her parents took up a homestead in the Little
Plume district. She and her brothers and sisters went to the Goose Lake School.
They had to walk several miles to school. Because it was too far for them to
walk in the cold winter, they missed a lot school.

At the age of 18, Hilda went to work in the Medicine Hat area for about a year,
for an Eagle Butte rancher and his wife, as a maid. Her chores included
cleaning the house, doing dishes, milking one cow and feeding orphaned lambs.
With her wages of $20 per month, she bought herself nice dresses. She had
learned to sew from her mother and was active in the Evangelical Church choir.

Henry and Hilda got married in Medicine Hat on March 27, 1930. The church
wedding was followed by a reception at the home of her parents, who were
residents of Medicine Hat at the time. Hilda received some cows and calves, six
of which were milked, one small pig and 20 chickens.

Henry Lehr Family: Back: Hilda, Henry; Front: Ruth, Phyllis, Frieda - 1946 (pic)

Two years later, their first daughter, Frieda, was born. They were blessed with
two more daughters, Phyllis, in 1937 and Ruth, in 1941. A few years later they
built a new home. They enjoyed having a big garden which included fruit trees
and melons. Besides the farming they raised chickens and sometimes turkeys and
pigs. Hilda did a lot of sewing and baking and helped with all of the outside
work, especially during haying time. When a binder was used to cut the crops
the bundles were put up in stooks. A lot of improvements were made on the farm
including a new barn and garage.

Henry and Hilda retired in Medicine Hat in the fall of 1960. They enjoyed their
new home and beautiful yard. Henry passed away in June of 1963. Hilda now
resides in the Haven of Rest Senior Citizens' Lodge in Medicine Hat.

In 1948, Frieda married Wallace Sauter. They farmed in the Irvine area until
1980, when they moved to Medicine Hat. They had two daughters, Gloria and Gail.

Phyllis married Norman Schneider in 1955, and they farmed in the Schneider
School area until 1981 when they moved to Medicine Hat. They had two children,
Douglas and Debbie.

In 1960, Ruth married Marvin Rath and they are still farming in the Robinson
district. They had five children, Beverly, Bonnie, Cheryl (died as an infant),
Randy and Cory.

John S. and Christina Lehr
by Gideon Lehr

John S. Lehr was born June 7, 1865 in the Colony of Kassel, South Russia, son
of Andrew and Rosina (Brandt) Lehr. Christina Weist was born March 25, 1868 in
the Colony of Rohrbach, South Russia. John and Christina were married November
6, 1887 at Eureka, South Dakota. In 1890 they homesteaded in North Dakota.

In 1896 the Zoo Railroad came in to start a little town. The Lehr brothers,
John and Andrew, each donated 40 acres, along with the Logan county and
McIntosh County each donating 40 acres. The town was built on these 160 acres,
the town being named Lehr, North Dakota.

In 1901, an epidemic of diphtheria spread into the area wiping out the children
of many families; my older brothers and sisters are all buried on that
homestead. My sister Lydia, being six months old and a nursing baby, never got
diphtheria. In 1902, sister Annie was born in North Dakota.

John S. Lehr Family: Back: Emil, Gideon, Bertha; Front: John, Christina (pic)

The family moved to a farm in Alberta, SE 11-10-3. I was born March 5 1906
while living on this place. In May 1908, our house was destroyed by fire.

The family then moved to Irvine. There my father was in partnership with Mr.
Schaller, having a store and Cockshutt machinery agency. They bought grain,
storing the grain in sort of an elevator which was beside the stores south of
the railroad. With horses and a high wagon, they'd drive under the elevator to
fill the wagon and then haul it over across the tracks and onto the platform.
With a chute from the high wagon they loaded the grain into the box car.

About 1913, we moved to Medicine Hat where we built a new house at 767 - 8
Street S.E. My father was retired and sort of waiting for us to grow up. In
1916 he traded this house and $4000 cash to R.C. Becker, a passenger train
conductor, for a ranch south of Irvine known as the A.T. Ranch. This place was
badly rundown with everybody's cattle and horses running on it. We built a new
house.

1918 was very dry and the Spanish Influenza was very bad. It didn't hit our
family so my parents went out with team and buggy every day to help the sick
while we children stayed home.

The winter of 1919 was very cold with so much snow the trail was four feet of
snow piled up and packed down. Hemorragic Septicemia got amongst our cattle. We
lost 29 head, having only 24 left in the spring. The price of hides was quite
high, so the dead ones had to be skinned. With the weather being so cold, I'd
open up the bottom and the legs, and all around the neck and ears. Then the
next day, I'd tie the head to a post and with a team of horses I would pull the
hide off.

The following years were quite good. By 1926 we had about 300 acres broken.
Crops in 1926 and 1927 were heavy.

In 1925 we bought land at Cardston that my brothers-in-law farmed for a time.
In the spring of 1928 the A.T. Ranch was sold to Fred Bollinger and we moved to
Cardston.

Mother passed away in my home at Cardston, August 20, 1929 and Father passed
away April 12, 1949. Both are buried in Hillside Cemetery in Medicine Hat.

Lydia, born October 3, 1900, married John Heinz March 18, 1919 and was living
at Hilda, Alberta. She passed away January 28, 1928. She had five children:
Elroy, Bill, Harry, Edna, and Ella.

Annie, born 1902, was married to John Diebert, remarried to Neil McNivan and
lives in Creston B.C.

Bertha married Chris Diebert and passed away April 12, 1975.

Gideon, born March 15, 1906, married Katie Will of Irvine. and is now married
to Emily Orman. Gideon and Katie had three boys. Katie passed away July 10,
1977.

Emil, born March 11, 1908, passed away September 19, 1988.

Ed. Note: Gideon Lehr passed away February 12, 1989.

Gideon and Katharine (Will) Lehr
by Gideon Lehr

I was born March 15, 1906 at Irvine, Alberta, son of John and Christina (Weist)
Lehr. While living in Irvine I started school, then in 1913 my family moved to
Medicine Hat, so attended Elizabeth Street, Toronto Street, Alexandra, and Elm
Street Schools in the city. In 1916, Dad bought the A.T. Ranch south of Irvine
from R.C. Becker so then I attended Berry Centre School to grade seven. The
spring of 1920 brought me a serious mishap. A neighbor boy, two years older and
two inches taller, had a, habit of wrangling; he got me down to my knees,
pushed me over backwards and broke my leg. This was my last day of school.

I remember 1927; there was a tremendous crop. We couldn't get a threshing
machine and crew in, so we bought a 22 inch Red River Special threshing
machine. Sam, Joseph, and Jack Patzer were on our crew. We threshed our crop,
the Patzer's crop, and Gottfried Schorr's crop until freeze up. We finished 500
bushels of wheat in the snow. A share of this crop was for me so I bought a
1925 Chevrolet Coach. I was the only one with a car. With grain prices down to
32 cents per bushel of wheat, most cars were made into Bennett Buggies, and I
still have one standing around. Also in 1927, I broke up 50 acres in what in
German we called "Aiste Valt and Zwiety Valt".

We slaughtered all our lambs. I did all the butchering. I would start at 2 p.m.
and would get them all hung up to cool off during the night. The next morning
we delivered them to the different butcher shops that had ordered them. We
usually had five or six a week to put in the back seat of the car to take to
Medicine Hat.

Gideon and Kate Lehr - 1972 (pic)

Water tower (pic)

On March 19, 1928 I married Katharine Will. She was born April 7, 1907 in
Odessa, South Russia, daughter of John and Magdelina (Kirschenman) Will.

Gideon Lehr's imported stallion (pic)

The same spring the A.T. Ranch was sold to Fred Bollinger and we moved to
Cardston. That year we were hailed out, but we milked four cows and sold cream.
I did some weasel trapping and fortunately caught a badger which brought $16;
while that new breaking, back at the A.T. Ranch, yielded over 60 bushels an
acre of number one wheat for the Bollingers.

Katharine passed away July 10, 1977.

I am now married a third time to Emily Edith Orman, a retired school teacher.
Emily is also a music teacher.

Katharine and I had three sons. Harold married Joan, lives in Boston, and has
two children. Lester married Eileen, lives in Calgary, and has two boys. Bob
married Jerrylin, lives in Cardston on the family farm, and has three children.

Lawrence and Rosa Lehr

Lawrence Lehr was born and raised in the Irvine area by his parents Reinhold
and Olga Lehr. His grandparents, Gustav and Regina Pahl, lived in the area. He
started school at Schneider School and his grade one teacher was Hubert
McLaughlin. In his teens his parents moved to the Duchess and Brooks area and
later they moved to the Feldman Lake School area south of Dunmore, where he
lived until he started on his own.

Lawrence and Rosa Lehr (pic)

Lawrence married Rosa M. Deering, daughter of Otto and Karoline Deering, and
rented land owned by Carl Beny of Medicine Hat (NW 31-10-1-4). They moved to
this place on February 2, 1944. They started farming with six horses, six cows,
two pigs and 15 chickens. They did their farming at this time with horses. They
fed their cows in the winter with one horse and a stone boat. In the summer of
1946 they bought their car, a 1928 Ford, for $200 and this car hated hills; the
only way up a hill was backward. In 1947 they bought a new John Deere tractor;
then farming became easier and busier. Lawrence did a lot of custom work with
his tractor.

In 1945 their daughter Carolyn was born. Carolyn started school at Schneider
School. She rode to school on a horse named Tiny. The school was closed the
next year. Then she went to Coal Centre School, and boarded with her Uncle Jim
and Aunt Mary Deering. In grade three she started at the Irvine School. Carolyn
now lives in Medicine Hat with her sons, Drew, Hugh, and Kyle.

Carolyn, Gary, Larry Lehr (pic)

Carolyn Lehr, Kyle; Back: Drew, Hugh(pic)

In 1948 their eldest son Larry Leroy was born. He attended Irvine School. After
graduation he worked at home for a year and then moved to Edmonton. There he
met his wife Shirley Bartko. They now live west of his parents (NE 5-11-2-4) on
the Art and Dave Schorr place. They have two children, Ryan and Lisa.

Gary Lawrence arrived in 1951. He also attended Irvine School, and after
graduating worked at home. In 1972 he married Elaine Schorr. They live east of
his parents on the old Frank Krausz place (SW 6-11-1-4). They have three
children, Reanne, Jarrette, and Rosanna.

In 1957 Lawrence and Rosa bought the land from Carl Beny's daughter, Helen Beny
Gibson. At this time Calgary Power arrived and because of their water they
moved one mile west and built up their farm of today (NE 36-10-2-4).

In 1975 the family started a new project, raising registered horned Herefords
(Lawrence Lehr and Sons) Lehrs Herefords, and are still raising them today and
still farming.

Larry and Shirley Lehr
by Larry Lehr

I was born Larry Leroy Lehr, March 5, 1948, to Lawrence and Rosa Lehr. I was
raised on the family farm (NE 36-10-2-4) and attended Irvine School from
1954-1966. After graduating I worked at home for a year then decided to try
city life. I moved to Edmonton and worked at McCoy Steel Works. I met Shirley
there in the fall of 1967 and we were married September 28, 1968. We had two
ministers and two wedding receptions, one in Edmonton and one in Medicine Hat,
so I guess you could say we're good and married.

We lived on the old Frank Krausz place (now owned by Gary and Elaine Lehr) the
first year, but times were tough and you couldn't sell any wheat so we moved
back to Edmonton for three years. I worked as a laborer for a construction
company and Shirley was a secretary for the Government. In the fall of 1972 we
bought the Art and Dave Schorr place (our present residence) and lived in the
old house without plumbing or central heating. I would get up in the middle of
the night and try to start the coal and wood stove with barbecue fluid starter,
otherwise we would have frozen to death during the night. I almost blew up the
house with the oil burner one night; I forgot to turn it down. We certainly
Appreciated our new home when it was finished in the spring of 1973.

Larry Lehr Family: Shirley, Lisa, Ryan, Larry (pic)

Shirley and I have two great kids: Ryan, born May 7, 1973, and Lisa, born
December 3, 1974. They have certainly kept us busy over the years. Between
music lessons, sports and 4-H Club activities we have put on a lot of miles.
They like motor biking and Lisa was the first to break her collar bone several
years ago. Ryan broke his arm this year motor biking and also his other arm
while playing hockey.

I played hockey for the first time last winter and really enjoyed it. Shirley
and I also enjoy skiing when we can find the time. Shirley enjoys many hobbies,
such as playing the organ, various arts and crafts and playing on the computer.
She started working part-time as a secretary/receptionist for the Medicine Hat
Credit Union in January, 1987.

Ryan and Lisa are a big help to me. Ryan can drive most of the machinery and
Lisa is becoming a pretty good cook. Lisa is also learning to drive the truck.
Pretty scary! We enjoy our life on the farm and hope to continue for many years.

Frederick and Fredricka Leicht
by Jack Stadel and Freda Scheffelmeier

Fredricka (Smith) Leicht was born in Gerson, Russia on December 31, 1860. In
1880 she was united in Holy Matrimony to Frederick Leicht. They immigrated to
South Dakota, U.S.A. in 1883, and in 1912 came to Irvine, Alberta.

They had three sons and two daughters: John, Fred, Jack, Emma, and Pauline.

They farmed in the Irvine district until 1920 when Frederick passed away.
Fredricka remained living in Irvine with her son John, who was a sectionman
working on the Canadian Pacific Railway there.

In 1943 John and his mother moved to Medicine Hat where he kept working as a
sectionman on the C.P.R. She lived with him until her passing. John met with an
accidental death on the C.P.R. April 9, 1952.
