(pic)

Fred (dec.) married Anne Martz (dec.) and had four children.

Jack (dec.) married Hilda Fischer and had one daughter.

Pauline (dec.) married Henry Arnold (dec.) and had six children.

Emma (dec.) married Gottlieb Stadel (dec.) and had nine children.

Gottlieb and Rosina (Lust) Lentz

Gottlieb Lentz, the patriarch of the Lentz families in southern Alberta was
born August 24, 1849 in Russia. He married Rosina Lust in their native Russia
on December 26, 1872.

Rosina was born January 7, 1852 in Russia. She had a brother, Jacob Lust, who
was married to Eva Miller. Jacob and his family lived in southern Alberta.
Jacob and Rosina also had a sister Louise, Mrs. Matthew Walter, who died about
1918 in the Caucasus in Russia. Mrs. Walter's children, however, did immigrate
to Canada. There were possibly two more brothers who never left Bessarabia.

Gottlieb was a stone mason in Russia. When he came to Canada he became a
homesteader. He applied for an entry for his homestead, SE 24-10-4-W4, in the
Josephsburg area on July 30, 1902. The homestead application stated that his
nationality was German but he came from South Russia. His family, including
himself, numbered nine. The two older daughters were married and consequently
would not have been included in that number. Gottlieb moved onto his homestead
in August and built his home in September of 1902. The house, built of logs,
measured 18 by 22 feet.

Gottlieb and Rosina Lentz (pic)

Gottlieb Lentz became a naturalized citizen on November 8, 1905. When he made
application for the title to his homestead in July of 1907 he owned six horses
and 19 head of cattle. His cultivated acreage was 40 acres. The title to the
homestead was issued by the Department of the Interior August 20, 1907.
Sometime between 1903 and 1906 he purchased an adjacent C.P.R. quarter, the
NE 13-10-4-W4.

While Gottlieb and Rosina lived on their homestead they were near some of their
children and Rosina's niece, Christina, Mrs. Fred Schwabe. Christ, their son,
lived on the C.P.R. quarter from 1905 to 1907. In August of 1903, their
daughter Dora Herman moved onto the Herman homestead which was east of the
C.P.R. quarter. Schwabes moved on to the quarter east of Hermans in July 1904
and another daughter Maria Jesse lived on the quarter against the south side of
Schwabes. The Jesse couple moved onto their homestead in 1904.

Gottlieb and Rosina Lentz lived on their homestead until the spring of 1914
when the Medicine Hat city directory lists their address as 624 Victoria
Avenue, present day 8th St. S.E.

Rosina was an accomplished tailoress and a midwife for 32 years. Gottlieb was a
basket maker and a fisherman. After retiring he spent many hours weaving
baskets. They celebrated their Golden Wedding Anniversary at the Swanson home
in Medicine Hat in 1922. Their last home was at 1132 Steel Street.

Gottlieb and Rosina both died November 30, 1928. Rosina, who lived with their
daughter Maria Jesse, died first and Gottlieb died only a few hours later at
the home of their youngest daughter, Bertha Swanson. They both died of heart
failure.

Gottlieb and Rosina had nine children.

Dora (Herman), born June 11, 1878, died June 1, 1951.

Maria (Jesse), born November 8, 1879, died October 13, 1957.

Christian, born August 23, 1881, died January 14, 1948.

Ida (Schlaht), born November 28, 1882, died March 8, 1975.

Gottlieb, born August 20, 1883, died June 14, 1946.

Christine, born October 8, 1888, died May 6, 1960.

Jacob was born December 9, 1890.

Samuel, born July 5, 1892, died in 1966.

Bertha (Swanson), born June 15, 1895, died July 12, 1958.

Dora, Christian, Gottlieb and Bertha remained living in Alberta. Maria had
lived in Alberta and Saskatchewan, Samuel in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario,
and Ida in Oregon, U.S.A. and Alberta, while Christine and Jacob spent most of
their lives in the United States.

Gottlieb and Rosina's descendants at the fourth and fifth generation level live
in the United States, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Ontario and Australia
with the largest concentration in Alberta.

Cattle brand registered to Gottlieb Lentz December 1, 1902 was -7R left rib.

Christian and Christine (Pahl) Lentz

Christian Lentz, the oldest son of Gottlieb and Rosina (Lust) Lentz, was born
in Bessarabia at either Plotz or Neu-Sarata. The year was 1881 and the month
was August. According to his confirmation certificate he was born August 23. He
was confirmed on May 11, 1897 in Neu-Sarata, Bessarabia by Pastor T. Paetsch.
Chris Lentz came to Canada with his parents and younger brothers and sisters.
He received the entry for his homestead on the SW 24-10-4-W4, on August 2,
1902. He worked for some time in the Rutherford sawmill at Elkwater.

Christian Lentz Family: Back: Ottilia, John, Sam, Fred, Bill, Bertha; Front:
Martha, Christian, Christine, Ida, Eva (pic)

Christine Pahl, the daughter of Johan and Eva (Neuman) Pahl, was born December
25, 1885 in Bessarabia. The place of her birth was probably Brienne, the same
town where her oldest brother, Christian Pahl was born. She was confirmed in
1901 by Pastor F. Schlarb.

Christine came to Canada with her widowed mother, and three younger brothers in
1902. It is believed that the Lentzes and Pahls traveled on the same ship.
Christine worked in both Walsh and Medicine Hat before her marriage to Chris
Lentz.

Christian and Christine were married July 17, 1904 in the St. Peter's Church at
Josephsburg, by the Evangelical Lutheran Pastor, Johannes Sillak. The young
married couple lived with Gottlieb and Rosina Lentz until June of 1905 at which
time they took up residence on the C.P.R. quarter of land purchased by Gottlieb
Sr. (SE 13-10-4-W4).

Their first child, Ottilia, was born January 14, 1905 at Josephsburg. Bertha
was born April 6, 1906, also at Josephsburg.

Chris became a naturalized citizen on November 8, 1905. The title or patent for
his homestead was applied for on July 23, 1907 and granted on November 20, 1907.

In 1902 Chris owned one horse and four head of cattle. By 1905, his livestock
included four horses and ten cattle but was reduced by 1907 to four horses and
five head of cattle. It was sometime after the summer of 1907 that Chris moved
with his wife and two daughters into the city of Medicine Hat, a distance of
about 25 miles from their homestead. After they moved to the city, a son, John,
was born and died at about six weeks of age in 1907. Samuel was born December
21, 1908.

The city directory for Medicine Hat for 1909 lists Chris Lentz as a "hide and
fur dealer near baseball grounds." The address for Chris Lentz Hide, Fur and
Junk Co. was 500 South Railway Street.

St. Peter Evangelical Lutheran Church was organized November 10, 1910 by Rev.
John Oberhammer. The founders were Frederick Sailer, Gottlieb Hehr, Michael
Entzminger, Samuel Zerbach and Christian Lentz. The congregation worshipped in
private homes until the first chapel was finished and dedicated on May 19,
1912. The church was built on a lot believed to be donated by Chris Lentz.

Fred was born February 21, 1911 and William was born December 10, 1912. It was
during this time that the "Chris Lentz Groceries and Dry Goods" store was built
at 867 Columbia Avenue. Columbia Avenue became 7th Avenue and is now Kingsway.

The Medicine Hat City Directory for the year 1913 lists Christian Lentz as
being in real estate. Their address at that date was 1408 Columbia Avenue.

While the family lived in the city, Tillie and Bertha became school age. They
went to Elizabeth Street School, not many blocks from their home.

In April of 1914 the Chris Lentz family moved out to the Gottlieb Lentz Sr.
homestead and Gottlieb and Rosina moved into Medicine Hat. The children
attended Concordia School.

For the first few years the family attended St. Peters Lutheran Church where
Pastor Sillak conducted morning services in German. The pastor provided the
music on his own organ which he carried with him. Later the family attended the
Gros Ventre Evangelical Church where Tillie and Bertha were taught to read and
write in German.

Chris not only farmed but also ran a tanning business. The hides were soaked in
a solution in a 45 gallon drum until the hair was ready to come off. Next the
hides were hung over a long round wooden object for scraping. The object that
the hide was hung over had no sharp edges so there would be no damage done to
the hide while being scraped. It was hung until partly dried, oiled and then
folded. More oil was worked into the hide by using a horse hitched to a wooden
tongue allowing more pressure to be added to the process of winding the leather
around a sort of centre post. Bertha drove the horse and then helped her father
remove the wrinkles from the leather using a semi-mechanical wooden block
press. The end product was known as rawhide and was used for making harness and
other leather goods.

Chris liked to fish during those early years. However, something that he really
enjoyed was driving around buying and selling. Christine did a fair amount of
knitting for her children.

The family had grown in number with the addition of one more son and three
daughters, all born at Gros Ventre. John was born April 9, 1917, Ida, May 31,
1920, Martha, February 5, 1923, and Eva, July 22, 1925.

Tillie and Bertha both got married and started families of their own.

Tillie and her husband bought land south of Dunmore in the fall of 1925. Then
Chris bought the Webber land, east of Tillie's place, in the fall of 1928, and
Fred and Sam farmed this in 1929. Chris and Christine, with their five youngest
children, moved down there in 1930. John and the three girls then attended
Feldman Lake School.

The children were all married except Eva, when Chris and Christine retired to
the city of Medicine Hat in the fall of 1944 to 869B 2nd Street S.E. Bill took
over the farm south of Dunmore and Fred had purchased the original homestead
several years earlier.

After retiring Chris enjoyed gardening. He died on January 11, 1948 in Medicine
Hat.

Christine remained in Medicine Hat until 1962 when she moved to Calgary to live
with Eva and Ed Muegge. She liked flowers. She also spent many hours making
rugs from cotton rags. She died in Calgary on March 20, 1964.

Christian and Christine Lentz were the progenitors of 187 descendants and up to
the end of May 1982 there are 176 direct line living descendants.

Fred and Martha Lentz
by Fred Lentz

Hi! I, Fred Lentz, was born February 21, 1911 in Medicine Hat while the family
was living in the city. My parents were Christian and Christine Lentz. My
brothers and sisters were Tillie (Meier), Bertha (Frisch), Sam Lentz, (myself),
Bill Lentz, John Lentz, Ida (Schumka), Martha (Lentz) and Eva (Muegge).

In April of 1914 we moved to the family farm which belonged to my grandparents.
My grandparents moved onto this homestead on August 2, 1902. When my parents
moved onto this homestead their parents moved to Medicine Hat. I attended the
Concordia School and after quitting school I worked with the family on the farm.

During the winter of 1927 my brother Sam and I with brother Bill's help skinned
over three thousand rabbits. With the proceeds from these rabbits we purchased
a touring car in 1928. Later we sold the touring car and bought a Model T Coupe.

Rabbits skinned by Fred, Sam and Bill Lentz (pic)

My dad bought the Webber place in 1928. Brother Sam and I batched there in
1929. We even tried to bake our own bread.

While visiting the neighbors place one night I met Martha Schorr. I thought to
myself "Martha is the girl for me."

Fred and Martha (Schorr) Lentz, March 1, 1930 (pic)

On March 1, 1930 I married Martha, the daughter of Christian and Dorothy (Rath)
Schorr. Martha was born April 15, 1910. Her brothers and sisters were Christina
(Gwinner), Olga (Schattle, Tschritter), Christ Schorr, (herself), John Schorr,
Jack Schorr, and Gottfried Schorr. She was raised in the Newburg area. Her
parents owned their homestead. In later years it belonged to her second eldest
brother John and now it belongs to Kenneth Krauss, who is John's son-in-law.

Martha and I needed a place to live so my parents moved to the Webber place.
Our first child, Esther (Anhorn, Tisnic), was born March 7, 1931. In the spring
of 1932 we moved to the Woolchester district near the Little Plume Church and
the Woolchester post office.

Violet (Otto), our second child, was born August 13, 1934. We rented land until
the fall of 1935 when we moved back and purchased my parents, home place.

Those early years were dry and hard years. We were grain farmers with only a
few range cows and a few milk cows. Martha had received four cows and other
barnyard animals from home. This is how our cattle herd got started.

The year of 1938 had its sad moments but it was also the beginning of good
years. We lost an infant daughter, Bernice Beatrice, born May 6, 1938. She only
lived to be about six weeks old. We bought a second hand truck and started
custom hauling for other farmers. I also bought my first tractor, a
Wallace-Massey Harris model. To use horses for farming was just taking too
long. We had our first good crop in 1938.

Leonard, our first son, was born September 10, 1939. He now owns the homestead
which belonged to me, my parents and my grandparents.

I continued to farm and did custom hauling until 1945 when I traded my truck as
part payment for another quarter of land. Our buildings were old and when we
had a hail storm that summer we lost all the shingles off the roof of the
house. We just replaced the shingles with heavy tar paper. That same year we
built a new barn.

James, our second son, was born February 16, 1946.

During the spring run off in 1947 there was so much water that it ran through
the house. The bedroom floors were about eight inches lower than the front room
so the water ran from the front room into the bedrooms. I dug a hole in the
side of the house so the water could run out. What a night we had listening to
the water roaring through the house. Needless to say we built a new house that
year. We had nothing but work and no time for holidays or traveling.

Another two quarters of land was purchased in 1948. Marlene (Moreton), our
youngest child, was born February 1, 1949.

We purchased the Schwabe place in 1953 which now belongs to my youngest son
James. This farm was the homestead of Christian Lentz's sister Dora (Herman,
Kallenberger). Dora remarried John Kallenberger after her husband Ed Herman
died in 1906. Also that same year we purchased the Yanke place.

We moved to the Schwabe place in the spring of 1954. Our old farm remained
empty until our eldest son Leonard got married in August of 1960. We purchased
the Wutzke place in 1956 and the Elmer Koenig place in 1959. The Schwabe place
stayed empty until the spring of 1970 when our youngest son James got married.

Fred Lentz Family: Back: Marlene, Leonard, Esther, James, Violet; Front:
Martha, Fred (pic)

Fred and Martha Lentz 50th Anniv., March 1, 1980 (pic)

Original Lentz homestead (pic)

December, 1967 we moved into 2099 Dunmore Road, SE, Medicine Hat. We still
reside at the same address.

We are members of the Southview Church of God. Martha's hands have to be busy
at all times so she likes to do all kinds of crafts. We have enjoyed traveling
to such places as Arizona, Las Vegas, Disneyland, Peace River and many other
points in Alberta. Martha and I celebrated our Golden Wedding Anniversary in
1980. My health has not been too good at present so we spend more time at home.
Martha, however, is as busy as ever.

Ed. Note: Fred Lentz died October 8, 1988.

Mollie (Lentz) Wilson
by Mollie Wilson

Mollie Lentz was born in Medicine Hat in 1917 and moved with her parents,
Gottlieb and Mary Lentz, to a farm eight miles north of Irvine in 1926. She was
educated at Long Valley School.

Mollie and William (Buck) Wilson (pic)

Mollie went to work in Medicine Hat in 1938. There she met William (Buck)
Wilson and they were wed in 1939. They had two children, Larry in 1947 and
Doreen in 1957.

Buck was overseas from 1940 to 1945, serving with the artillery. Mollie
remained in Medicine Hat and worked during the war.

Since 1961, Mollie and her family have lived in Edmonton.

Earl and Mary (Patzer) Ligget

Earl Ligget was born in Hendrum, Minnesota on November 7, 1900, son of William
Thorton and Anna Rebecca (Dawson) Ligget, coming to Medicine Hat with his
parents in 1902. Mary was born in Harvey, North Dakota on June 17, 1900,
daughter of Gottlieb and Elizabeth (Weiss) Patzer, coming with her parents to
Irvine to live on the homestead in 1906. What little education she got was at
Berry Centre School.

Earl and Mary Ligget, Yuma, Arizona - 1977 (pic)

Earl and Mary were married on November 2, 1923. They farmed and ranched in the
Elkwater district. Mary was a very active, hard working, outdoor girl. Plowing
and discing with six horses, that she'd brought in from pasture, harnessed, and
hitched up by herself, was no great effort. In 1928 she hauled 900 bushels of
wheat from Elkwater to Irvine with wagon and horses, bringing loads of coal,
gas and other supplies on her return trips. She did a lot of horseback riding
on the ranch, a very brave lady not scared of anything or anybody.

In 1939 they bought the Hausauers' place and operated a feedlot. In 1949 Earl
and Mary moved into their home in Medicine Hat. Earl bought the Great West
Hotel in Irvine in 1950, owned it until 1956 when he sold to Roy Ayling.

For many years Earl was a very well known cattle buyer. At first he drove to
farms and ranches in all of southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan,
buying their cattle. Then as the cattle auction sale companies developed, he
bought the cattle at these cattle sales. Through the years Earl owned several
feedlots.

In her retired years, Mary rode her horse Molly many times in the Medicine Hat
Stampede Parade, sometimes dressed as a clown, once dressed half as a bride and
half as a groom. Earl and Mary had no children but were very fond of their
nieces and nephews.

Earl passed away May 4, 1978 at the age of 77 years.

Mary has since remarried to Ron Ferges of Yuma, Arizona. They spend the winter
months at Yuma and the summer months in Mary's home in Medicine Hat.

Frederick and Charlotte Linderman

In 1904 Frederick and Charlotte (Wahl) Linderman and their children, Dora,
Fred, Charlotte, Katherine, Adam, John, Jacob, and Rosie, came to the Irvine
district from Eureka, South Dakota. A daughter, Maria, was born in 1905 and
passed away at two years of age.

The Lindermans took up a homestead about six miles south of Irvine and built a
log house on it. In 1910 they built a new two-story frame house north of their
first dwelling place and moved the log house to the new location. The frame
house was destroyed in 1983.

The Linderman children went to the Berry Centre School about four miles away.
They walked it many, many times, when no horses were available. One afternoon
after school wild cattle chased them. They climbed into the trees on the creek
flats, and stayed up in the trees until their parents came looking for them
late in the evening, with the team and buggy.

Mr. Linderman also raised horses besides farming. It is said he had the first
pinto stallion in the area brought in from the U.S.

In 1917 they built a new cottage house on the east side of the town of Irvine
to retire in. The house is still used. They left the farm and moved into their
new house in Irvine.

Mr. Linderman still kept active after moving to town. He supervised bridge
building in the area, and was foreman of the fire guard plowing along the CPR
tracks on down to Saskatchewan.

They lived in their house until their passing, Mr. Linderman in September of
1929, Mrs Linderman in December of 1931.

Dora, the eldest, married Archibald Flynn of Medicine Hat. She died
accidentally from a fall at the age of 21.

Fred had no survivors.

Charlotte (Lotty) married a widower, David Fode, of Hatton, Saskatchewan.

Katherine (Katie) married Carl Meier, son of Frederick and Dorothy (Sept) Meier
of Fox Creek, Alberta. They raised five children and lived south of Pashley.

Adam married in the 'States and had two children. He served in the army during
the First World War.

John married Pauline Arnold. They lived on the original Linderman homestead.
They had one son, George, and daughters, Lillian, Esther, and Bernice. A
daughter, Marjorie died at a young age.

Jacob (Jake) married Alice Sturm. They raised their family of four, Archie,
Bertie, Blanche, and Eileen, on a farm three and a half miles south of Irvine.

Rosie married Dudley Driscoll, son of George and Harriot Driscoll. They had six
children: Robert (Bob), Richard (Dick), James, Marion, William (Bill), and
Gordon. They farmed north of Pashley in the Clearwater District.

John and Pauline (Arnold) Linderman
by George Linderman

Fred Linderman was born 1865 in Eureka, South Dakota. Fred and Charlotte moved
to Canada in 1904 and settled in the Irvine district, six miles south of
Irvine. In 1917 they moved to the town of Irvine. They had nine children, four
boys and five girls.

John Linderman was born in 1899 and married Pauline Arnold in 1918. Pauline was
the daughter of John and Albina Arnold. John and Pauline lived three miles
south of Irvine and in 1920 moved to the home place, five miles south and one
mile east. They had five children: Lillian, Esther, George, Bernice and Margory.

We attended Berry Centre School - one classroom for grades one to eight, one
teacher for all grades. Once a year we had a visit from the school inspector
which was a bad day for all.

The winters were cold from October 1st to March 31st, with drifts of snow as
high as 15 feet. There were no cars all winter, as roads were all blocked
through the winter, so it was horses and bob sleighs. We survived through the
blizzards in the winter, and the dust storms in the summer.

Saturday night was always a great night in Irvine. We had a dime to spend - 5
cents for a cone of ice cream and 5 cents for a bottle of pop. The only
entertainment was sleigh riding in the winter and playing ball in the summer.
For spending money we trapped or shot rabbits and in summer we robbed magpie
nests and sold gopher tails at 2 cents apiece.

Jacob C. and Alice (Sturm) Linderman
by Archie Linderman

Jake Linderman was the second youngest child of Frederick and Charlotte (Wahl)
Linderman. They came from Odessa, Russia to Eureka, South Dakota, U.S.A., and
moved to the Irvine, Alberta district in 1904. Jake was born in Eureka in the
year 1900.

He received his education at Berry Centre School and as a young man settled on
the farm which was his father's second homestead. It was located three miles
south of Irvine on the Bull Trail, and just one and a half miles from the Sturm
farm. A rugged terrain known as the badlands separated the fence lines and the
road distance to Irvine was seven miles.

Alice Sturm was the oldest of seven girls whose parents were Emmanuel and
Margaret (Schlaht) Sturm. They also came from Odessa, Russia and settled in the
Thelma, Alberta district. Alice was born here in 1909, and when she was seven
years old the family moved to the farm four miles southwest of Irvine, now
owned by the Richard Resch family. Alice attended school in Irvine and later in
Medicine Hat.

J.C. Linderman Family: Blanche, Alice, Archie, Eileen, Jake, Bertie (pic)

Jake Linderman and Alice Sturm were married in 1926 and they had a family of
four: Archie, Bertie, Blanche and Eileen. Now there was constant travel over
the "badlands" to visit Goga and Gogi, as Archie nicknamed Grampa and Gramma
Sturm. These nicknames remained and were used by our family until the
grandparents passed on. And with Goga and Gogi lived Alice's younger sisters
the Sturm girls, Freda, Helen, Nora, Dena and Pearl, who were a constant
delight and much help to this growing family.

The family attended the Irvine School where Jake served some time on the Irvine
School District #892 Board. In 1936 the farm was rented to Henry and Lil
Trekofski while the family moved into the Linderman Estate home in Irvine. This
house was later purchased by Fred Nitschke. Jake worked for Harry Crookes'
Service Station for a few years before moving back to the farm. The family grew
up and left home and in the early 1950's the farm was sold to Carl Vossler. The
house was moved to Medicine Hat and the farmstead has been vacant ever since
that time.

Alice and Jake moved to Medicine Hat, then purchased and operated the Redcliff
Pool Hall for three years. They sold the pool hall, moved back to Irvine and
bought farm land east of Walsh. Jake drove the Bull Trail school bus, and
served on the Irvine Town Council, retiring due to ill health in 1960. He
passed away early in 1963 and is remembered as a quiet, sincere gentleman.

Alice married Wilfred Brandt in 1965 and continued to live in her home at
Irvine. She loved gardening and enjoyed her beautiful flowers. In her retiring
years the enjoyment of her family and friends were a part of every day. Alice
passed away in 1978 at age 70.

Archie married Margery Scheutzle of Schuler, Bertie married Anders Anderson of
the Clearwater district, Blanche became the wife of Robert Heinrich of Graburn,
and Eileen married Fred Entzminger of Medicine Hat. Blanche died in Medicine
Hat in 1980.

Jake and Alice were blessed with ten grandchildren, five boys and five girls,
which they enjoyed to the fullest. The grandchildren in turn were blessed with
many happy, fun-loving and very special memories of their grandparents.

Herb and Clara (Herman) Lust
by Herb and Clara Lust

After being married a couple of years, we moved from the Robinson District to
the Irvine District. It was tough starting to farm with no horses or tractor.
We even had to borrow a kitchen stove from my parents' summer kitchen. We had
only a saw and we borrowed a hammer from Uncle Fred Lust to put windows in the
house. At the time we had three children, Henry, Joanne, and Don. Within a few
years Jim, Florence, Alberta and Lloyd were born. Florence passed away with
polio in 1949. They all went to Schneider School from first to eighth grade.

Herb Lust children: Back: Jimmy, Joanne, Henry; Front: Lloyd, Alberta,
Florence, Don (pic)

Herb and Clara Lust (pic)

We milked cows in summer to sell cream to buy food and clothes. When Don got
the cows from the field he used to ride a cow back by the name of Lily. We also
raised a big garden. Most of our pastime in summer was visiting. One highlight
was butchering chickens on Saturday to take to Elkwater on Sunday. We also made
a lot of good ice cream.

Sometimes in winter Herb would clean snow off the dam before the children came
home from school. Then they would play hockey, children on skates and Herb on
shoes; they'd say he wasn't playing fair but they had lots of fun. They also
did pranks in school. Don threw a firecracker in school then ran outside right
into barbwire. He had a bad cut on his knee and had to be taken to Medicine Hat
to have it stitched. In summer all the schools in the district got together at
Elkwater and played baseball. What a good time they all had!

In 1953 we moved to Medicine Hat so the children could get more education.

Henry was a bank manager for 31 years.

Herb Lust Family: Back: Joanne, Clara, Herb, Henry; Middle: Alberta, Don,
Florence, Jim; Front: Lloyd (pic)

Joanne went in as a psychologist.

Don liked experimenting so he took bacteriology.

James has his own business in Medicine Hat.

Alberta works in the General Hospital as a supervisor.

Lloyd is a millwright with Chevron in Lamont.

George Mackie

George Mackie came up from Montana with a large band of sheep and settled in
the Pashley area, where he built a log house and then later moved it to the
center of section 33-12-2-4. The house was situated on the northeast corner of
the southwest quarter and the barn was built in the southwest corner of the
northeast quarter. He had many sheep camps in the area, a night camp in the
flat of section 29 and another by the spring on section 21.

The big summer camp was on the north side of the slough on section 33. The
herder happened to be there with the sheep during the heat of the day, when the
Benwell fire started on section 30-12-2-4. It burned out of control to the
northeast as far as the South Saskatchewan River. When the wind switched from
the southwest to the northeast, the fire burned itself out. The sheep and
herder survived the fire, being protected in the curve of the slough, but a
good portion of the flock was lost from inhaling the soot while moving them
across the burnt out area out to grass for grazing.

NE 23 was the site of George's big winter camp. He owned the S-3-12-2-4 and in
the summertime grazed the sheep along the C.P.R. tracks, right up to where the
Complex is now located.

In time he sold the sheep, went to Scotland and purchased purebred Clydesdale
horses, returning with them to section 33-12-2-4 where he had moved the log
house and built a 14 stall hip roofed barn.

In the days when Irvine held Summer Fairs, George would take in a string of
horses a quarter mile long, four- and six-horse tandem hitch teams, for the
draft pulling contests. There wasn't a time they would return home without any
ribbons. Each one of the 14 stalls had prize tickets on them, first, second,
and third, but most were first place tickets. He moved to Nanton in spring of
1925 because of the shortage of water.

Harry and Gloria (Freimark) Marren

Gloria Faith Freimark was born on December 1, 1946 in Medicine Hat. During the
16 years she lived with her parents, William and Edna Freimark, in the Irvine

winning athletic and academic awards. After graduation, she was enrolled in a

In 1974 the family moved to Medicine Hat where Harry and Gloria remained
working for Shur-Gain feeds and A.G.T. In 1975 they moved to their recently
purchased farm just west of Irvine, where they raised registered hogs and
Hereford cattle. Their daughter Jennifer Ann was born in Medicine Hat on May 3,

Gloria was employed at the Emergency Ward and Admitting Office at the Medicine
Hat Hospital until her passing on May 9, 1987. Presently, Harry and his

Christian Jr. and Lydia (Banek) Maser
by Edna (Maser) Schau

Christian Maser, son of Christian Sr. and Kathrina Maser, came to Canada in
1904 from Mound City, South Dakota with his parents. They took land about 20
miles south of Irvine, in the Josephsburg district, where they farmed and
raised cattle.

Lydia's parents, the Gottlieb Baneks, came to Canada from Campbell County,
South Dakota in 1905 and settled on a homestead about 15 miles south of Irvine.

The church was the social center of the community and that is where Christian
and Lydia met. They were married in the same church on April 7, 1916. After the
ceremony they went by horse and buggy to Christian's farm eight miles south of
Walsh, Alberta. They lived there and farmed for 11 years.

Christ and Lydia Maser - 1942 (pic)

Laura, Ben, Edna, Ida Maser - 1928 (pic)

During that time four children were born with the help of Mrs. Walker, the
district midwife.

When the three oldest children were of school age the nearest school was
Graburn Gap a distance of three and a half miles. It proved too great a task to
take the children to school in the morning and pick them up again at the end of
the school day. In the fall of 1926 the young couple decided to move to Irvine
for the winter. They rented a house on the south side of the livery barn. In
the spring they moved back to their farm again. A building was moved in about
one half mile south of their home to serve as the school. By fall no teacher
had been hired for the school. It appeared that school was still a long ways
away. They decided to sell their farm and move to Irvine to stay in 1927.

The children got all their schooling at the greystone, two room school. During
those school years, Ben played the part of "Felix the Cat" in a Christmas
concert and was known as "Kutz" thereafter.

Christian worked for Andrew Rieger in the dray and livery barn business in his
early years in Irvine. When Mr. Rieger retired, Dad bought his business.
Christian lived out his life here and died June 19, 1949, at age 56. Lydia sold
their home and stayed with her sister in Redcliff, Alberta for awhile. After
that she went to Grande Prairie, Alberta and lived out her time there. She died
on April 19, 1980 at age 84 in Grande Prairie and is buried there.

Ida was born March 11, 1917. She married Allister Fergusson on September 28,
1939. They had no children. Ida died on February 24, 1947 in Calgary and is
buried there.

Edna was born May 9, 1918. She married Paul Schau on August 12, 1938 in
Medicine Hat, Alberta. She is living in the Peace River Country at RR 2,
Sexsmith, Alberta at the present time. They have four children, Donald, Edith,
Judy and Norman.

Benjamin was born August 15, 1919. He married Jean Forrester on September 18,
1947 in Calgary. They had one daughter, Melanie Ann. Ben died March 6, 1980 in
Calgary and is buried there.

Loretta (Laura) was born March 31, 1921. Laura died July 4, 1933 and is buried
in Irvine.

Theodore and Louisa (Roll) Maser

Theodore (Ted) Maser was born December 17, 1893 in Eureka, South Dakota. He
immigrated to the Irvine area with his family at a very young age. They settled
in the Josephsburg area where his father ranched and farmed. Ted Maser had two
sisters, Magdalina and Ella, and six brothers, Jacob, Christ, Edward, John,
Phillip and Bill Maser.

Theodore Maser Family: Back: Louisa, O'Linda, Theodore; Front: Lloyd, Harvey,
George, Gladys (pic)

Louisa Roll was born December 8, 1900 in Odessa, South Russia. The family
immigrated to Canada in 1910. They settled in the Clover Hill area, where they
built a sod house. Part of the house was built of dirt logs, which is still
there and can be seen. In the early years Louisa Roll had to work very hard on
her dad's homestead, breaking land the old way with plough and horses, and
picking rocks by hand. Louisa had two sisters, Kay and Elizabeth, and five
brothers, Adam, John, Ted, George and Jack.

Theodore Maser and Louisa Roll were married in Irvine, November 10, 1923. They
lived in Irvine for a short time, then moved to the family farm three and a
half miles northeast of Irvine, SW 3-12-2-4. They ran cattle and farmed in this
area.

In the early years, before Ted Maser was married, he would travel by freight
all over Canada and the U.S.A. He would talk for hours on end of the fun and
adventures he had while on these freight train trips. One story I remember
quite well was when he met Jack Dempsey while riding the freight in
Walla-Walla, U.S.A. Later this man became one of the more famous heavy-weight
boxing champions of the world.

Mrs. Ted Maser was probably one of the best cooks in the country. She could
make a tasty meal out of next to nothing (this was back in the dirty thirties).
Threshing crews loved the freshly baked buns and coffee bread and those
appetizing home cooked meals. She always had a big garden and, in those days,
she won prizes for the best garden in the district. She loved flowers and
always had a beautiful flower garden.

Both Ted and Louisa were very active in all community affairs in and around
Irvine. Louisa belonged to the Lutheran Church W.I. women's club and also was a
member of the U.F.A. farmer's organization. Ted loved those Sunday afternoon
baseball games. He was a Charter Member of the Chinook Club of Irvine, which is
still a very active organization in Irvine today. He was a very strong member
of the United Farmers of Alberta, attending many meetings at the Provincial
level in Edmonton.

Mr. and Mrs. Ted Maser were blessed with five beautiful children.

Olinda went to Yellowknife and taught school for several years and later she
married Garnet Spencer at Yellowknife. They moved to Medicine Hat and managed
the Satellite Motel of which they were also owners. The had two daughters,
Katherine and Debra. After battling cancer for several years, Linda passed away
on the 28th of November 1987.

George and Harvey started a lumber yard in Irvine in 1949. They trucked lumber
from British Columbia and Alberta mills. There was a farm building boom in
those days and you couldn't truck lumber down fast enough. People would come
from as far away as Leader, Saskatchewan and Swift Current to buy lumber. In
1953 they moved their lumber business to Medicine Hat and are still operating
it today.

Harvey married Barbara Clapper and their children are Linda, David, Roxanne,
and Heather.

George and Ethel's children are Kelly, Darrell, and Brent.

Lloyd and Shirley live in Red Deer. Shirley is nursing and Lloyd is selling
Real Estate. They have four children, Kim, Kevin, Kammy, and Karen.

Gladys married Henry Haag. The moved to the Two Hills area where they are
ranching. Henry is also the Administrator of the Vegreville Hospital. Their
family consists of Jamie, Natalie, and Lindsay.

Irvine and district has many fond and joyful memories which will never be
forgotten by all the Maser Family.

Ed. note: Harvey died 15 December 1988 at the age of 62.

Konstantin Sr. and Bertha (Aman) Maser
by Clara Klaudt

Konstantin Maser, commonly known as Gust, was born March 29, 1894 in South
Russia. His wife Bertha (Aman) Maser was born in South Dakota, U.S.A. They were
married December 21, 1916 and settled on the home quarter in the Clover Hill
School District, northeast of Irvine.

Konstantin and Bertha (Aman) Maser, December 21, 1916 (pic)

The Masers raised a large family of six children, all of whom attended the
Clover Hill School. The oldest was Howard, then Clara, Konstantin (Kayo),
Elsie, Esther, and Victoria.

The family worked hard to earn a living, milking cows and raising chickens in
order to sell butter, cream and eggs to customers in Medicine Hat. They hauled
their drinking water and melted snow to wash clothes, and even had to pick cow
chips to burn in the cook stove.

The most exciting thing, which most of the family will never forget, is the
time a skunk got into the cellar. The smell was something else! Dad had checked
the whole cellar but couldn't find a trace of a skunk. Next morning after Dad
had left Mother offered Kayo 5 cents to go down into the cellar to get the
yeast to bake bread. Kayo got as far as the bottom of the stairs when he
spotted the glaring eyes of the skunk. He took off like a scared jack rabbit
over to the neighbors, the Glocks. Edwin Glock came over and shot the skunk in
the cellar. It took months to get rid of that smell.

The Masers attended the United Church in Irvine and hauled their grain to
Walsh. Their means of transportation was horse and buggy or sleigh. They heated
rocks in the winter to put their feet on to keep warm while they traveled.
Later they purchased a Model T Ford.

Dad Maser passed away December 21, 1945. Mother remarried to Reinhold Sauter
before passing away on May 18, 1948.

Howard joined the Army from 1941 to 1946 attached to the 40th Anti-Aircraft
Battery and the Halifax Coast Artillery as a cook. He married Molly Wahler May
12, 1943. They had two boys. Molly passed away February 18, 1972. Howard
remarried in May of 1975 to Kay Holden.

Clara married John Klaudt in August of 1943. They farmed in the Seven Persons
District before retiring to Medicine Hat in 1973. They have three boys and
three girls.

Konstantin married Martha Veil in September of 1945. He farmed the home farm,
drove school bus and worked at Medicine Hat College before retiring in Medicine
Hat. They have ten children, four boys and six girls.

Elsie married Bill Ebel in September of 1944. Bill was in the army for some
time before they moved to Schuler, where they owned Schuler Farm Supply. They
are now retired and living in Medicine Hat. They have three boys and two girls.

Esther married Elmer Sauter in October of 1948 and passed away suddenly on
January 31, 1949.

Victoria married Joe Cissell in February of 1949. They farmed in the Crossfield
district where they still reside. They have five children, four girls and one
boy.

Samuel and Eva (Holz) Mayer

from information supplied by Clarence Mayer, Manda Archer and Adolph Mayer
family

Samuel Mayer, born April 19, 1851, and Eva (Holz) Mayer, born July 27, 1854,
were originally from Germany, near the Black Forest area.

The first German settlements in the Black Sea district began in the years
1787-1790 while the Empress Catherine II was still reigning.

Also known as Catherine the Great, this German-born Empress issued a manifest
on July 22, 1763. The manifest hoped to stimulate the settlement of many
foreigners in Russia. Russia's vast uninhabited virgin steppe land was to be
brought into civilization. To do this, extraordinary inducements were necessary
in order to influence people to migrate and settle in these unknown wilds.

This manifest of 1763 included several provisions with a forever guarantee to
the colonists and their descendants: free land, tax exemption, local
self-government, mother tongue preference and above all, exemption from
military service. The manifest found ready response from thousands of war-weary
Germans following the end of the Seven Years War in 1763.

In 1804 another manifest was issued, this time by Catherine's grandson, Czar
Alexander I. Napoleon Bonaparte was ravaging Europe with his conquests,
consequently thousands more Germans left their war-torn country to settle in
the Ukraine, the Crimea and Bessarabia. The colonists remained culturally pure
German.

In 1871 an Imperial Decree abrogated the special privileges the colonists had
and in 1874 military conscription was instituted. As a result many fled to the
U.S. and Canada.

In 1899 Samuel and Eva Mayer sailed from Bessarabia on the Kaiser Friedrich
with their family of four daughters and seven sons, one of whom was married
with children. They landed in New York in April 1899 and traveled through South
Dakota, making their way to Irvine. Two sisters of Mrs. Mayer and their
families came with them.

Eva and Samuel Mayer (pic)

Samuel and Eva homesteaded the SE 22-10-3-W4, ten miles southwest of Irvine in
the Newburg district. Their first home was dug into the side of a hill and
enlarged with a sod addition. They had one more son in 1900.

Their farming consisted of grain, cattle, poultry, and horses to do the farm
work. They built a home on that quarter on the east side of the creek in Spring
Coulee. Later they moved across the creek to the west side into the house that
was built by their eldest son, Ludwig.

Samuel and Eva Mayer were very active in the Church of God in the Newburg
district. Many church services were held in a shed on their farm before the
Church of God was built in the Newburg area.

Samuel and Eva retired to 947 Yuill Street in Medicine Hat in about 1916 until
their passing, Samuel on October 11, 1925, and Eva on April 16, 1934. They are
buried in the Newburg Church of God cemetery.

Samuel and Eva had 12 children, eight sons and four daughters.

Ludwig (September 2, 1873 - October 4, 1949) married Maria Bischel and they had
nine children: Matilda, Karl, Helen, Samuel, Herbert, Adeline, Martha, Alfred,
and Emil. Maria died in 1926 and Ludwig married Emelia (February 2, 1888 -
December 9, 1982).

John, born July 17, 1875, married Emelia Weiss in 1904. Their family members
were David, Benjamin, Annie, Henry, Herbert, William, Clarence, Evelyn, Elsie,
and Wallace.

Magdalina (Lena), born October 31, 1880, married Adam Sturm (May 24, 1880 -
February 14, 1950) in 1902. Their family members were

Mayer Family Bible pages (pic)

Atfred, Frank, William (Bill), John, Harry, Samuel (Sam), James, Eva, Norma,
Rosie, and Emma.

Anna, born January 9, 1883, married John Weiss. Their family members were
Emanuel, Johnny (died very young), Wallace, Katie, Norma; Irene, Edith, and
Adeline.

Jacob James (Jack), born December 20, 1884 in Wittenburg, Bessarabia married
Fannie Rust. They had one son, James Gordon.

Rosa (May 20, 1888 - March 13, 1971) married Jacob (Jack) Dais (February 2,
1883 - ??)in 1906. Their family members were Roy, Wilfred (Bill), Minnie, Emma,
Alice, Daisy, and Anna.

Katherine (Kate), born January 23, 1890, married Fred Rabb (November 23, 1881 -
November 17, 1970). Their family members were Emil, Ruth and their half brother
Emanuel.

August, born December 29, 1891 in Bessarabia, Russia, married Katherine Kusler
(February 18, 1898 - October 28, 1964) on December 31, 1916. Their family
members were Melwin and Manda.

Henry (July 23, 1893 - October 1, 1977) married Emma Stroh. Their family
members were Viola, deceased in 1947; Daisy, deceased in 1926; and Esther.

Benjamin (Ben), born February 10, 1895, and his wife Emma, have four children
and reside in Sexsmith, Alberta.

Adolph, born April 18, 1897, married Magdalena (Maggie) Bischke in 1923. Their
family members were Harvey, Florence, Gladys, and Elmer.

Emil, born February 26, 1900 in Canada, and his wife Emma reside in Cherhill,
Alberta and have four children: Arthur, Marvin, Vernon, and Beverly.

Mayer Family Bible pages (pic)

Ludwig and Maria (Bischel) Mayer

Ludwig Mayer, born September 2, 1873 to Samuel and Eva Mayer in South Russia,
was married to Maria Bischel (1875-1926). They immigrated to Canada in 1899
along with his parents and three children: Mathilda (Olhausen), 1895-1981; Karl
(Charlie), 1897- 1976; and Helen (Gill), 1898-1958.

On arrival in Alberta they settled south of Irvine in Spring Coulee (a
tributary of Ross Creek) with Samuel and Eva Mayer on one side and Ludwig and
Maria on the other side of the creek. Word has it that they lived in a hole dug
in the side of a hill with a blanket hung over the entrance until some houses
were erected.

Their future home was some two miles farther down the valley where the rest of
the family was born: Sam, in 1900; Herbert, 1903 (deceased); Adeline (Meier),
1904; Martha (Meier), 1908-1979; Alfred, 1911; Emil, 1913-1987.

Memories of our grandmother Maria are vague as she died in 1926 but we do
remember that she loved us very much. She would leave a space on a slice of
bread smeared with jam so we could hold it without getting our fingers sticky.
An evening visit at Grandfather's farm in the summer would always include a
tour of the garden which had a wooden gate secured with a hook at the entrance
and was out of bounds unless escorted by adults. Any step outside the garden
paths would be considered to be on sacred ground.

Close to the summit of the hill leading down to the homestead was a clay pit
which was the source of many a dirt-plastered home in the area. This clay mixed
with straw and sometimes fresh cow manure filled many a crack in log barns and
chicken coops to keep the cold winter winds out. This clay pit also served as a
playground for the smaller boys who constructed an arterial of roads in the
banks that would be enviable to today's construction industry. They must have
had quite an imagination as they constructed their own miniature wagons drawn
by conformed bones as horses collected from skeletons of animals and
domesticated birds.

As the boys grew older time spent in the clay pit was absorbed with farming.
Alfred, the second youngest son, relates about the terrible dust storms from
blowing summer fallow fields that blew in on prairie grass. This native grass
was directly seeded into oats without pre-working; later on when the rains came
it yielded 90 bushels an acre. He also recalls a big snow storm in May of 1927
when the snow was waist deep. After the snow stopped it started to rain
continuously for a whole week thus melting the snow. This caused concern to the
settlers that they might have to evacuate as the swollen waters in the creek
rose. Cows with calves on the other sides of the small rivers were washed down
stream as they tried to cross.

Ludwig retired to Medicine Hat with his second wife Emelia (Olhausen) in 1936
where they lived until his passing in 1949 and Emelia in 1982.

Emil and Dorothy (Schultz) Mayer

Emil Mayer, son of Ludwig and Maria Mayer, was born in 1913 in the farm house
his father built. He got his education at Concordia School, three and a half
miles west of home. In 1934 Emil married Dorothy Schultz from Bruderheim,
Alberta. He bought the farm from his father. They farmed grain crops, and
raised cattle, sheep and chickens.

Ludwig Mayer Family: Back: Karl, Adeline, Sam, Martha, Helen, Herbert; Sitting:
Ludwig and Maria; Front: Alfred, Emil; Inset: Mathilda (pic)

Emil Mayer farm home (pic)

The Depression Years were tough. Crops were poor and cattle feed was scarce.
Thistles were cut and fed to cattle in winter. Farming was done by horses until
conditions improved in later years. Money for necessities was made from milk
cows and chickens. Cream sold in five gallon cans for $2.50, butter was made
and sold for 25 cents a pound, eggs sold at 15 cents a dozen. In the fall,
calves brought $4 each, and a cow bearing a calf sold for $17.

Emil's uncle was a sheep rancher at Pashley. When a ewe had twins, one had to
be taken away because there wasn't enough milk for both. Emil and Dorothy took
the extra ones home and raised them from a milk bottle.

Emil Mayer Family: Lionel, Emil, Dorothy (pic)

Entertainment and fun times were at picnics at Grayburn Gap on July 1st where
relatives and neighbors gathered. Emil built a wooden boat from a mail order
blueprint. They went fishing a lot at Elkwater Lake on weekends and days too
wet to work the farm. In winter it was curling and bonspiels at Irvine and
Medicine Hat.

Emil and Dorothy had one son Lionel, born in 1936 at Medicine Hat. He was
educated in Concordia School and Irvine High School. After graduating he got a
job in Medicine Hat and later learned a trade in welding. In 1957 Lionel
married Shirley Sulz. They had three children, one girl and two boys: Dean, Tim
and Julie.

Ed. Note: Emil died February 5, 1987.

John and Emelia (Weiss) Mayer
by Clarence Mayer

John Mayer, born July 17, 1875, came to Canada in 1899. Emelia Weiss, born
February 13, 1884, came to Canada in 1903. John Mayer and Emelia Weiss were
married May 28, 1904. They resided in the Newburg area. Three children were
born in that area: David on February 9, 1905; Benjamin on December 30, 1906;
and Annie on August 30, 1908.

John and Emelia Mayer 50th Anniv., 1954 (pic)

In about 1909, they moved to the Cypress Hills to the Fox area and took up
ranching. The ranch consisted of raising cattle, horses, sheep, pigs, poultry
and grain. They were successful at ranching. The cattle brand was 5M right
ribs, horse brand J/3 - left thigh. Their farming was done with horses. The
children attended school at Fox and Reserve Schools. They also made many
friends in the area. Seven children were born in the Cypress Hills: Henry on
August 27, 1910; Herbert on May 25, 1912; William on April 29, 1914; Clarence
on February 6, 1916; Evelyn on December 11, 1917; Elsie on January 4, 1920; and
Wallace on October 21, 1921.

David and Benjamin took over the ranch in the Cypress Hills. John and Emelia
and the rest of the family moved to Newburg in 1929, to the same farm where
Samuel and Eva Mayer had lived and to the house that was built by Ludwig Mayer
on SE 22-10-3-W4. They farmed there with horses. John Mayer loved his many fine
horses. They were successful at farming. John Mayer was also a gardener,
raising many vegetables.

Henry, Herbert, and William left the farm to seek employment elsewhere as there
was not enough work on the farm for all the family. To survive in the "dirty
thirties" was not easy, but the people in those days were hard workers, and
knew how to survive. When somebody needed help there was always someone there
to help. The vegetables and meat were raised on the farm. You could also trade
wheat at Dederer's Mill in Medicine Hat for flour and puffed wheat. The wheat
price in the "dirty thirties" hit a low 19 cents a bushel and John Mayer sold
some cattle at $6 a head.

Most of the grain was threshed by threshing machine and the grain was hauled to
Irvine and Medicine Hat elevators with horses and a 60 bushel wagon. In the
spring John used to take a wagon load of seed potatoes to Medicine Hat by team
and wagon.

The children got their education at Concordia School. They drove to school by
team and buggy, except when the horses were needed for farm work. Then the
children had to walk the three and a half miles, besides doing the farm chores
before and after school.

John and Emelia Mayer were supporters of the Church of God at Newburg. They had
many friends in the area. The girls, Annie, Evelyn and Elsie, played the organ
in the church: Annie until 1931 when she married Victor Ehret and moved to the
Ehret ranch south of the Cypress Hills; Evelyn until going to Camrose Bible
School.

John and Emelia retired to Balmoral Street in Medicine Hat in the fall of 1941.
Elsie and Wallace moved to Medicine Hat with them. John and Emelia are both
buried in Hillside Cemetery in Medicine Hat.

I think we should not forget our soldiers. The Second World War broke out in
1939. Henry Mayer served in the army and returned after the war. Wallace Mayer
served in the army with the Paratroopers and was in action overseas. He came
back after the war and settled in Medicine Hat.

Clarence and Martha (Fuchs) Mayer

Clarence Mayer took over the farm, SE 22-10-3-W4, from John and Emelia Mayer
when they retired to Medicine Hat in the fall of 1941.

Clarence Mayer Farm - house built by Ludwig Mayer (pic)

Clarence Mayer and Martha Fuchs were married October 14, 1945 and made their
home on the farm. They also had a half section of pasture south of Walsh,
Alberta.

Their farming consisted of grain, cattle, poultry and pigs. Their cattle brand
was 45, left rib, horse brand was X, left shoulder. The farm work was done with
horses until 1948 when they bought a tractor. Clarence also did a lot of custom
work for neighbors in the area, such as field spraying, cutting hay, baling hay
and straw, swathing and combining.

Clarence and Martha supported the Church of God at Newburg while they lived in
the area. They gave up the farm and moved to Calgary, Alberta in May, 1966.
Clarence took up work in a plastic plant in Calgary and retired June 30, 1979.

Clarence and Martha had two daughters: Delores Marilyn, born October 13, 1946,
and Lucille June, born November 14, 1951. The girls helped a lot with the farm
work. They got their education in the Irvine School. They went four miles to
and from school on the bus.

Clarence Mayer Family: Clarence, Martha, Delores, Lucille - 1962 (pic)

Delores finished her grade 12 in Irvine in 1964 and moved to Calgary to finish
her education. She married Jim Bolin in 1966. They made their home in Calgary
and had two children.

Lucille finished her grade 11 in Irvine School in 1966 and joined us in Calgary
where she finished her grade 12 at Crescent Heights School with top honors. She
went into computers after finishing school. Lucille married Tony Schaffer in
1972, and they made their home in Calgary. They have one daughter.

Katharine (Katie) and August Mayer (pic)

Katherine Kusler and August Mayer were married in the Irvine district on
December 31, 1916. They lived on a farm adjacent to the Samuel Mayer farm in
the Newburg district which was some 12 miles south of Irvine. Their son Melwin
took over the farm in 1946 at which time they moved to Elkwater where August
worked for the Park and helped build many of the park conveniences there. In
1970 August retired in Medicine Hat. Katherine passed away on October 28, 1964
and August on January 1, 1981. They had two children, Melwin and Manda.

August enjoyed telling the story of the day of their arrival in Medicine Hat.
The traveling days had been long and as their journey brought them to the
promised land the children must all have been excited to have finally arrived.
The city of Medicine Hat was a village full of Indian tents. Things were so
different. There was the local trading post; they soon learned to mix with the
Indians and picked up some words so they could communicate in that strange
tongue.

Melwin was the eldest of the August Mayer family. He was born October 28, 1918
and passed away February 2, 1982. He was married to Belinda Mack in 1941 after
which he served in the army. In 1942 they took over the home farm. Later they
moved to a ranch south of Elkwater and lived there until 1964 when they moved
to Keremeos, British Columbia. They had seven children.

Sharon was born on September 28, 1944 and is married to Paul Albrecht. They
reside in the Edmonton area and have two children.

Garry was born on April 20, 1949 and is married to Karen Susan Harvey. They
reside in Summerland, British Columbia and have three children.

Duncan, British Columbia and have two children.

Geraldine was born on August 11, 1951 and is a banker. She lives in Prince
George.

Roger was born on April 21, 1955 and is married to Donna Duncan. They live on
the home farm in Keremeos and have one child.

Robert (Bob) was born on February 6, 1959 and is working in northern Alberta.

Peggy was born on June 2, 1960 and is married to Dave Mutch. They are working
in northern Alberta and have two children.

Melwin and Belinda (Mack) Mayer
by Belinda Mayer

Melwin Mayer was born to August and Katie (Kusler) Mayer on October 28, 1917 in
the Concordia District. He was raised on a farm situated in Ross Creek near
Highway 48, now #41. He spent his younger years going to school at Concordia,
often having to walk to get there. He helped his dad on the farm when he was
able to. He was interested in grain farming and won a trip to Edmonton in a
Wheat Growing Contest in 1935. He soon wanted to spread his wings and fly after
helping his dad in his teen years on the farm. He took a trip west, riding
boxcars on the railroad. One year he met some nice people, the Forresters, in
Creston, British Columbia. Melwin worked for the C.P.R. for a short time
between 1941 and 42.

Melwin Mayer late 1930's (pic)

In his younger days, Mel was always trying new things and was always interested
in people and had many friends. He talked much about his plights working in the
coal mine at Elkwater, and logging with Tony Schacker. Mel loved horse back
riding and even took a course in Criminology. He was a hard worker and always
tried to make do with old machinery. His health began to fail when he had a bad
fall off a bucking horse and broke his upper leg while trailing cattle to the
community pasture in Thelma, Alberta. His joy and pride was driving an old
Model A Ford in the years between 1938-1943.

He joined the army in January 1943 and served as a trooper at Camrose, Alberta
and Dundurn, Saskatchewan until his discharge in 1944 because of a physical
handicap.

Melwin and Belinda Mayer - 1979 (pic)

Melwin married Belinda Mack, daughter of Fred and Christina Mack of the
Robinson district, on March 23, 1943. After his discharge from the Army, Melwin
and Belinda lived in the Concordia district on his father's (August Mayer)
farm. There they had a daughter, Sharon, on September 28, 1944.

In the fall of 1949, they moved to a ranch south of Cypress Hills in the Thelma
district where they had six more children: Garry, Sandra, Geraldine, Roger,
Robert and Peggy.

In 1964 they moved to Keremeos, British Columbia because of Metwin's health.
Mel farmed in the Keremeos area until 1976 when he rented his farm to his son
Roger. He retired for six years until he passed away on February 2, 1982. His
widow, Belinda Mayer, still lives near the farm in Keremeos.

Ed. Note: See August Mayer story for more on the children of Melwin and Belinda.

Henry and Emma (Stroh) Mayer
by Esther Miller

Henry Mayer, son of Samuel and Eva Mayer, born 1893 in Polcagrot, Russia,
immigrated to Canada in 1899 and settled with his parents in the Josephsburg
area. Henry had seven brothers and four sisters.

Henry and Emma Mayer (pic)

In 1913 Henry homesteaded in Thelma. In November of 1919 he married Emma Stroh.

Emma Stroh, daughter of Phillip and Katherine Stroh, born in 1902 in Eureka,
South Dakota, U.S.A., immigrated with her parents to Canada the same year,
1902, and settled in the Thelma district. Emma had three sisters and two
brothers.

Henry and Emma farmed in the Thelma district until 1923, when they moved to the
Irvine district. They farmed in that area until 1947, when they retired to
Medicine Hat.

Emma, Esther, Henry Mayer on cultivator - 1939 (pic)

Henry and Emma had three children: Viola, Daisy and Esther.

During the 1930's depression, many families in the Irvine area received salted
fish and apples, handed out by the Federal Government. Wood and coal were the
only sources of fuel for heating and cooking, the wood obtained from Elkwater,
and the coal from Medicine Lodge and from George British, as well as Irvine.

Henry also helped build the Church of God which was located on Highway 48, now
the 41, to Elkwater.

Adolph and Magdalena (Bischke) Mayer

Adolph Mayer, second youngest son of Samuel and Eva Mayer, was born in
Bessarabia, Russia in 1897. At the age of two years he traveled the long
journey with his parents to the Newburg district. Dad attended Newburg School
until the Concordia School was built, where he continued his education. When
his parents moved to Medicine Hat in 1916, Dad stayed on the family farm. Dad
continued to farm there for the next seven years until his marriage to
Magdalena Bischke.

Adolph Mayer (pic)

Magdalena, daughter of Ludwig and Magdalena Bischke, was born in 1905 in
Irvine. She was raised in the Concordia district and attended Concordia School.
Her education was often interrupted to stay home and take care of her younger
brothers and sisters. Mom stayed in Irvine with her grandparents (Wilhelm and
Magdalena Bischke) while she attended confirmation classes at the Christ
Lutheran Church.

Adolph met Magdalena during their time spent at Concordia School. They were
married in November, 1923. Their first home was on the farm at Newburg. They
left the farm in the spring of 1929 and moved to Medicine Hat. One year later
they bought the Bill Stewart farm northwest of Pashley. In time they purchased
more land which included the McCaslin and Webb farms and part of Mrs. Drinnan's
land. The farm was situated along Ross Creek. In the spring the family often
experienced flooding and though it caused severe erosion, the water never rose
high enough to damage any buildings.

Mom and Dad were ardent sheep ranchers, shearing their own sheep, carding the
wool which was spun on Dad's homemade spinning wheel. The wool was used for
knitting socks, mitts, sweaters and also made many beautiful wool quilts. They
butchered and sold lambs at $5 apiece to Safeway, Graham Groceteria and also to
Eatons, when Eatons had a grocery and meat department. The remaining lambs were
trailed to the feed lot in Medicine Hat for marketing every fall.

Adolph and Magdalena (Bischke) Mayer, 1923 (pic)

Magdalena and Adolph Mayer (pic)

Magdalena and Adolph Mayer 50th Anniv., 1973 (pic)

Milk cows and white turkeys were also a source of income on the family farm.
Cream was sold at 25 cents a quart, processed butter at two pounds for 25 cents
and the turkeys sold for $2 apiece. Dad always had a large garden and grew
watermelon and cantaloupe by the truckload.

When Abelein school was relocated to Irvine in 1941, aside from all his farm
duties, Dad became the school bus driver from the Pashley district until 1946.

Dad was very musical, his favorite instrument being a violin which came from
the old country in 1899 and has remained in our family. Dad could also play the
harmonica, organ, piano, guitar and in his later years taught himself to play
the accordion. The family spent many evenings playing and singing while Mom
spun wool in time to our music.

In 1957, Mom and Dad semi-retired to Medicine Hat for a short while. During
this time their youngest son Elmer and his wife Gladys took over the farm. In
1963 after Elmer moved to Medicine Hat, Mom and Dad moved back to the farm and
continued to farm with Elmer's help until it was sold in 1965.

Adolph Mayer Family: Adolph, Florence, Gladys, Harvey, Magdalena; Front: Elmer
(pic)

During Dad's retirement, he enjoyed fishing and gardening until his passing in
July, 1978. Mom sold the house a few years later and moved to the Mayfair
Manor. She continued to enjoy her knitting, crocheting and needlework until her
passing in December, 1985.

Mom and Dad were blessed with four children.

Harvey, father of two children by a previous marriage, has four grandchildren
and one great-grandchild. Later he married Marjorie (Nittle) Meidinger who had
three children (one of whom is deceased) and three grandchildren. Harvey and
Marge reside in Medicine Hat.

Florence and her husband Leonard Nelsen reside on a farm north of Irvine and
had four children (one of whom passed away as an infant) and three
grandchildren.

Gladys and her husband Tom Quast reside in Medicine Hat and have three children
and three grandchildren.

Elmer and his wife Gladys (Yanke) reside in Medicine Hat and have three
children and four grandchildren.

Syd C. McCormick
by Syd McCormick

My wife and family moved from Assiniboia, Saskatchewan in August 1953 to
Medicine Hat. I followed in November after having taught school for 18 years in
Saskatchewan, with five years in the armed services. I spent the early part of
1954 in the building business.

September 1954, I commenced teaching Industrial Arts and some Mathematics and
Science at the Irvine School.

I spent the next 18 years in the Irvine School, although I lived in Medicine
Hat. I often said I had a real friendship with birds and gophers on the road to
school, having made over 3600 trips back and forth.

My first classroom for Industrial Arts was a rural school which had been moved
into town. The equipment consisted of a coal stove in the middle of the room. I
took what tools I had and we managed to purchase a number of metal working
tools, welder and so on. Boys and some girls took Industrial Arts.

During the years from 1954 to 1972, the school grew from four classrooms and a
small gym, to 24 classrooms, a number of auxiliary rooms, and a new big gym.
This growth has continued during the last 16 years, and we can now be proud of
one of the best schools of its size.

I have so many fond memories of Irvine and surrounding countryside and its fine
people. The staff of nine teachers has grown to over 20 teachers with helpers.
Opportunities for students have increased a great deal. There were four grade
12 grads in June 1954 consisting of four girls and this number has grown to 26
in some years since. I can think of the many friendships that I made at Irvine
with pleasure, and the passing of many of them since leaves a great loss.

There were a number of highlights, one of which was the journey to Expo '67 in
Montreal. 68 students, several parents, Mr. Lemire and I went.

So many events and wonderful people were a part of my 18 years I will never
forget.

My 16 years of retirement have been good except for the loss of my wife Edna,
in 1981. I still reside at 512 - 8th St. NE, Medicine Hat, much slower at 82
but still interested.

F.G. McLaughlin and Family

Fredrick George McLaughlin was born in Aldsworth, Gloustershire, England on
July 31, 1876. At the age of six weeks he and his mother sailed for India,
where his father was a judge. He returned to England when he was old enough to
enter school. At the age of 15 he and two of his brothers, Stanley and Percy,
sailed for Canada, arriving in June 1893. Percy and Fred worked on a farm in
Ontario. In his diary Fred mentions that the Missus (Lady of the house) made a
birthday cake to celebrate his 16th birthday. Stanley came to Medicine Hat
where he entered the army bound for South Africa. Fred and Percy attended
Guelph College and in the summer of 1895 Fred left for the west on a harvest
excursion. Percy stayed in Oak Lake, Ontario. Fred worked in Manitoba,
Saskatchewan and Alberta, arriving in Medicine Hat in August of 1895 and got a
job ploughing the first fire guard to Gleichen, Alberta for the C.P.R., four
furrows up and four furrows back. He received $1.50 a mile and "board yourself"
for work. Fred slept under a wagon as no tents were supplied, nor was a stove.

After helping with a harvest at Stair, Fred returned to Medicine Hat. Friends
as well as rooms were in short supply, so he spent part of the winter in a
dugout just below the old hospital. After Christmas Fred left to spend some
time on the Red Deer River about 40 miles west of Empress, Alberta. There he
got very sick with dysentery. A native woman made a tea from the inner bark of
a rose bush for him. The cure was very effective in a short time. Fred came
back to Medicine Hat in March and went to work for Bill Struthers of Graburn
until August for wages of $18 a month.  Later he bought some cattle and Sam
Faucett wintered them in exchange for two months of labour. Another month's
work bought him a bull from Bill Struthers. Now Fred had a herd of 18 heifers
and one bull. In 1897, Percy came from Oak Lake, Ontario and they both took up
homesteads on adjoining quarters. There they ran horses and cattle. In 1898, on
his 21st birthday Fred returned to England with a shipment of cattle bound for
Glasgow. They were shipped from Walsh, Alberta and sold for $35 per head. Percy
and Fred bought and sold cattle, as well as working for others, and thus built
up their resources. Fred also managed accounts and kept books for others.

On February 1, 1904 Fred and George Haycock bought the hotel in Irvine and
George Armstrong took over the Warwick Livery Stables in July of the same year.
Fred sold his share of the hotel in 1905 to Haycock, who traded the hotel for a
ranch in the Sweet Grass Hills. In December of 1905 Fred took a load of cattle
and horses east to Montreal and spent the winter in England with his parents.
On his return trip he was accompanied by his sister Eva, who stayed with Fred's
fiancee, Katherine Armstrong.

Katherine Armstrong was born on September 23, 1878 at Markham, Ontario. She
came to Battle Creek, Alberta in the spring of 1900 to keep house for her
brothers, Peter and Will. In 1905 she became engaged to Fred McLaughlin and
they were married on June 16, 1908. They lived on Fred's homestead until they
sold out in 1912 and moved to Irvine. They had three sons, Hubert, Robert and
Lynn, who were raised and took their schooling in Irvine. Their niece Eva
(Stanley's daughter) joined the McLaughlin household. Eva married Lionel Chell
in August 1930.

McLaughlin Family: Back: Lynn, Katherine McLaughlin, Grandad Armstrong, Hubert
and (inset) Fred; Front: Annie and Ian, Emma and Evelyn McLaughlin (centre baby
not identified) (pic)

McLaughlin and Western Hospitality are synonymous. It was a stopping off place
for all friends, no matter in which direction they were traveling. Mrs.
McLaughlin was never sure how many people she was feeding or supplying beds for
in one day.

Mr. and Mrs. McLaughlin were very active in all the activities at Irvine.
Katherine McLaughlin and her sister-in-law Eva McLaughlin took over the Magnet
Opera House in 1913. This was the hub of all social activities, such as
parties, dances, meetings of various clubs, movies, and boxing matches.
Katherine was a life member of both the Irvine Women's Institute and the Red
Cross Society. Fred McLaughlin was secretary-treasurer of the town of Irvine as
well as the Irvine School and many of the outlying schools in the area. He also
had the telephone office, was an agent for the C.P.R. and Hudson's Bay Lands
and an agent for the McCormick Farming and Harvesting Machinery, and also had a
billiard room in Irvine. From 1937, until his retirement, he was
secretary-treasurer for the Cypress School Division, which had its office in
Medicine Hat. This was later known as the Medicine Hat School Division #4 and
is now again known as the Cypress School Division.

The McLaughlins did not give up their home in Irvine during those years, and it
still stands today. Mrs. McLaughlin died in December of 1963 and Mr. McLaughlin
in June of 1964.

Hubert McLaughlin

Hubert McLaughlin attended high school in Medicine Hat and Normal School in
Calgary. After teaching a few years, in 1942 he joined the Alberta Wheat Pool
as an agent at Iddesleigh, Alberta. He married Annie Mack and they had three
sons, Ian, Mack and Rick.

Ian married the former Phyllis Rieger. They had two sons, Troy and Patrick.
Troy died in 1985. Ian is an engineer at I.X.L. Brick and Tile Industries in
Medicine Hat.

Mack and Rick are farming and ranching in the Jenner, Alberta area.

The Story about Hubert and Wagon

When he was about eight years old Hubert received a miniature farm wagon to
which he harnessed his shetland pony, Toby. He decided he would be like the
rest of the farmers and tie his horse and wagon in the livery yard. Everything
went fine until Toby spooked the larger horses.

Pandemonium broke out. There were horses and wagons going in all directions.
Toby, wagon and Hubert went straight home. "They hadn't been there".

Robert G. McLaughlin

Robert G. McLaughlin was born in Medicine Hat, Alberta, February 13, 1915, the
son of Frederick G. and Kathryn (Armstrong) McLaughlin of Irvine, Alberta.

Elizabeth (Betty) Ritchie, daughter of Robert G. and Grace (Giberson) Ritchie,
was born in a sod house on the homestead at Compeer, Alberta on January 20,
1916 and moved with the family to Edmonton, Alberta in 1926.

Robert (Bob) McLaughlin, then employed as forest ranger with the Alberta
Forestry Service, was drafted into the Game Branch office to assist with the
registration of traplines, and there met Betty, who was the secretary involved
with that work. They were married, April 3, 1943 and lived for five years in
the Ram River district in the Clearwater Forest Reserve, patrolling the pack
trails and living out of pack boxes. The forestry cabins were few and far
between and often infested with pack rats, so more often then not they camped
in their tent.

Their oldest son, Harold Walter, born May 30, 1945 in Edmonton, and their
daughter, Muriel Jean, born in Nordegg, February 3, 1947, shared their
wilderness life until May, 1948. Bob transferred to Holmes Crossing, near Fort
Assiniboine, and after a year left the Forestry Service, moving to Edmonton for
five years. Two children, Janet Belle, born May 21, 1950, and Lorne David, born
February 20, 1953, joined the family. In March 1954 the family moved to
Paradise Valley, Alberta. A fifth child, Elaine Anne was born in 1956, but
survived only eight days.

They settled on a farm nine miles west of Paradise Valley for nine years.
Coincidentally, they learned the town of McLaughlin, Alberta, about ten miles
east of Paradise Valley, was named after two of Bob's great uncles who came to
the area soon after the turn of the century. Their names were Tom and John
McLaughlin.

The children loved the farm, particularly the arrival of the lambs each spring.
Their favorite pastime in summer was swimming in the beaver dam, and in winter,
skiing down the slopes on the skis their dad had hewed from poplar. During the
stormy winter of 1955- 56 the skis served a very useful purpose. Because the
roads were so plugged with snow, Harold and Muriel often skied the mile to the
bus driver's farm to catch the school bus. The children were active in school
sports, particularly basketball and curling.

In July 1963, the farm was sold and the McLaughlins moved into the village of
Paradise Valley, where Bob did carpentry work and raised a beautiful garden. In
1965 Betty became secretary-treasurer of the local Seed Cleaning Coop, and
secretary-librarian of the school in 1966, filling both positions
simultaneously until her retirement in 1981. She was elected Village Councilor
in 1972, and was Mayor from 1974 to 1980 when she retired. During her tenure in
office she was instrumental in organizing the Public Library which operated in
conjunction with the school library, and was vice-president of the Board for a
time, as well as secretary-treasurer. She also served as vice-president of the
local Recreation Board for a time. Betty was also active in the P.V. Church of
God, serving in various capacities for a number of years, including S.S.
Superintendent, teaching, secretary-treasurer, and writing for and editing the
church publication. Currently she is working in the organization and operation
of the Church library.

Harold worked for a time on power line installation in Northern Alberta before
joining the R.C.M.P. in October 1966. He has enjoyed an interesting career,
having traveled to Expo '70 in Osaka, Japan, as well as the Eastern U.S. He and
three companions rode with the B.C. Float in the 1970 Pasadena Rose-Bowl
Parade. In 1973 he was a member of the Equestrian team and the pageant with the
R.C.M.P. Centennial Review which was presented trans Canada. He had the honor
of riding escort to H.M. the Queen on several occasions and received a letter
of recognition for same. As well he holds a number of marksman and riding
trophies. He was awarded the Queen's Silver Jubilee Medal for excellency of
service. Presently he is Sergeant in charge of the R.C.M.P. Detachment in
Pemberton, B.C. He is married to April Lyn Richards of Middleton,
Massachusetts, U.S.A., and they have two children, Gwen, 17 and Scott, 14. They
enjoy biking and swimming in summer and skiing in winter.

Muriel took the position of operator with A.G.T. in Wainwright in 1964, then
transferred to Edmonton as ticket investigator for a year prior to her marriage
to Lawrence S. Willey of Wainwright, in June 1969. She returned to A.G.T.
Wainwright until 1975. Recently she received her certificate in Early Childhood
Development at Lake College, Vermilion, and is currently employed at
Wainwright. On graduation she received two scholarships for top standing in two
categories. The Willeys have two adopted children, Wade, 13 and Kara, 11. They
live on the farm near Wainwright. Lawrence is a technician with Petrocan. The
children are active in the 4-H Calf Club. Wade's strong points are piano and
singing, while Kara is into synchronized swimming.

Janet worked for a time with the Worker's Compensation Board, Edmonton, then
after training with McKay Technical, became key-punch operator with Great
Canadian Oil Sands at Fort McMurray. It was there she met Ross M. Reid,
engineer with the company. They were married December 26, 1970 and moved to
Pinawa, Manitoba, a year later where Ross took employment with Atomic Energy of
Canada at Whiteshell Park. Their three boys, Marlon, 16, Dallas, 14, and
Darren, 10, were born in Pinawa. In 1980 they moved to near St. John, New
Brunswick, where Ross works as Systems Supervisor with new Brunswick Power
(Atomic Energy). Janet took training and worked as investment councilor, and as
an income tax technician during the intervening years. She also had top marks
in the exams. As a family they enjoy surf-sailing, boating, swimming, and
skiing in winter.

Lorne worked for a time with Alberta Wheat Pool of Edmonton, but is now
employed with La Farge Cement, formerly Canada Cement. During this time he
apprenticed at N.A.I.T. and took his Mill-Wright Certificate with high
academic standing. In 1975 he married Diane Twitchell of Daysland, Alberta.
They have three children, Candance, aged 12, Shaun, aged 11, and Shane, aged
10. They live on an acreage east of Fort Saskatchewan. The children enjoy their
4-H Horse Club. The family love riding and occasional pack-trips into the
wilderness areas.

Lynn and Emma (Schneider) McLaughlin

Lynn Crofton McLaughlin was born to Frederick and Katherine McLaughlin in
Medicine Hat, Alberta on October 17, 1916. He took his schooling in Irvine and
