Emma was born to Jacob Jr. and Christina Schneider, on March 18, 1913. She

and Mrs. Zelsnick.

Lynn worked for the Town of Irvine as secretary-treasurer for 36 years until

Emma enjoys music, and still plays for the United Church every Sunday. She was

Evelyn Lynne (McLaughlin) Woodward

On October 15, 1960 she married Leslie Woodward and they had three children,

Larry O'Neill McLaughlin

Larry was born on August 2, 1943 in Medicine Hat, Alberta. He attended and
graduated from the Irvine School, after which he went to the University of
Calgary.

Larry has always been interested in farming and ranching. He and his friend
Harvey Aman were playing farming in the backyard one day when they were about
six years old and they heard via the radio that they could buy cows for 171:.
After counting their money they figured they could buy about ten calves,
therefore starting a herd and building it up year after year. Harvey's dad
owned a farm so they were all set for pasture. Needless to say, they were a
mite disappointed when they discovered the calves sold for 170 a pound and not
apiece.

After university Larry worked on a chicken ranch in the Acme, Alberta area and
then at the University of Calgary. He is presently living in Irvine.

Marlene was born on September 8, 1945 in Medicine Hat, Alberta. She received

from the School of Nursing Aides in Calgary, then worked in that field for
several years.

On July 16, 1965 she married Clifford Roll in Medicine Hat, moved to Calgary
for one year then back to Medicine Hat, where she and her family are now
residing. Clifford and Marlene have two children, Michael-Dean and Cora Lynn.

Philip and Margarite (North) McLeay
by Mary McLeay

Philip (Phil) McLeay came west to Lethbridge, North West Territories from
Watford, Ontario in 1891. In 1893, he and two other Lethbridge men, formed the
Lethbridge Sheep Company, located on the SW 35-11-3-W4. On one of his trips
from Lethbridge to Irvine, he was riding his saddle horse. He rode as far as
Purple Springs, pulled the saddle off his horse, used it for a pillow, and
slept out under the stars. When he was taking the train from Irvine to Medicine
Hat or Lethbridge, he would walk from his homestead two miles west of Irvine,
to the Irvine station, early in the morning. Then the station agent would flag
a train down by waving a lantern.

Phil was manager of the ranch, but it wasn't long before he bought the other
men's shares and owned the ranch. The most sheep he ran was between 3000 and
4000 head. Lambs came along in May and shearing was done in June. The wool was
bated and shipped to the Canadian Cooperative Wool Growers, Toronto. The lambs
were sold in the fall and shipped to Calgary or Moose Jaw. A sheep herder was
employed the year round, with extra help for shearing.

Mary (McLeay) Glennie (pic)

Mary (McLeay) Glennie, Mynnie (McLeay) Sheidle (pic)

In 1897 Phil married Margarite Agnes North. She had come from Guelph, Ontario
to teach school in Medicine Hat. She taught at the Toronto Street School which
was the only school in Medicine Hat at that time. The O.K. Economy Food Store
is now on that lot.

There were three children, Sadie Mynonah (Mynnie), Franklin (Frank) North and
Mary Enid. They attended public school in Irvine. Mynnie attended what was then
the Alexandra High School (now Alexandra Junior High) in Medicine Hat, then
took a dietitians course at Guelph, Ontario. Frank took a mechanics course at
Saskatoon, and Mary took a business course and studied music at Mount Royal
College in Calgary.

Mr. and Mrs. McLeay were interested and active in many community projects.
Their home was always open to strangers, especially teachers and bank clerks
that came to Irvine to work. During the 1918 'flu epidemic a makeshift hospital
was set up in the Cypress Hotel in Irvine. They, along with others, spent hours
nursing the 'flu patients.

Mrs. McLeay was a charter member of the Irvine Women's Institute, and was the
Irvine branch's first president. She was a member until her passing. Her
daughters, Mynnie and Mary, were also W.I. members. In the mid-30's, Mary was
elected Director of District #4 of the Alberta Women's Institute. She held that
post until she got married and moved to Calgary.

Methodist (later United Church) student ministers held summer services at Walsh
and Pashley. The McLeays attended and supported them and the Anglican Church in
Irvine. When weather and roads were suitable, they attended St. John's
Presbyterian Church in Medicine Hat, where they were married and the children
had been christened. Mr. McLeay died in 1924. Mrs. McLeay, along with her son
Frank as manager, carried on the ranching business. Mrs. McLeay died in 1934.

Mynnie was dietitian at the Baker Sanitarium, Calgary, until she married Clare
Sheidel and moved to Vancouver. She passed away there in 1973.

Mary married William (Bill) Glennie of Hatton, Saskatchewan. They moved to
Calgary where Bill worked with the Canadian Pacific Railway until his passing.
Mary is still living in Calgary.

Franklin and Mary (Glock) McLeay
by Mary (Glock) McLeay

Franklin (Frank) North McLeay was born in Medicine Hat, and raised on his
father's (Phil's) ranch at Irvine. He got his education in Irvine and took a
mechanics course at Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. After his father's death, Frank
helped his mother with the ranching business until her passing in 1934. As
manager-owner he also raised some Clydesdale horses. He lost the herd sire
during the 1934 "sleeping sickness" epidemic. He didn't replace the herd sire,
and later sold all the horses. Some went to a fox farm.

Brands used by the Lethbridge Sheep Company down through the years were the
diamond five monogram <5>, 9NK, 3C, L3 horse brands and the 3L cattle brand.
The 3L brand was used on all the cattle through the years until the ranch and
all the cattle were sold.

Some time between 1930 and 1934 Frank took a flying course. He and George
Clarke, his flying instructor, flew a plane from Chicago to Medicine Hat. He
never tried for his pilots license.

He played the saxophone in Glock's orchestra for many years.

Frank and I, Mary Glock, were married in 1945. I had worked at the ranch before
we were married.

During the Second World War, hired help was hard to get due to so many men
being in the armed forces. Frank then sold the sheep and changed to cattle
ranching. Along with my help, we were able to handle the cattle business,
running about 100 head. The calves were usually sold in the fall.

Frank and Mary (Glock) McLeay wedding - June 15, 1945 (pic)

Frank was one of the first men on the Ross Creek Irrigation District's board of
directors. Henry Cavan of Dunmore was instrumental in getting the irrigation
scheme started.

Frank and Raymond Jacobson were also the first to introduce propane gas into
the Irvine and Medicine Hat areas. Frank made propane installations south of
Walsh, Irvine and Medicine Hat to the U.S. Border, east into Saskatchewan, west
to the Magrath area, and north to the Jenner, Bindloss, Empress, Hilda, Schuler
areas, and also around Tilley, Brooks and Bassano. They had their business in
Medicine Hat and sold it in 1957.

We sold the ranch at Irvine in 1956 and moved to Medicine Hat. In 1957 Frank
and two partners bought the Rush Lake Cattle ranch at Chappice Lake. There were
300 breeding cows plus some heifers and 12 bulls. We were in that business
until 1963, then Frank sold his share and we moved back to Medicine Hat. We
bought a travel trailer and for the next 17 years we spent several months of
each winter in Florida. In 1962 we took a three month world cruise. Frank
enjoyed his retirement until his passing in 1981.

As for me, Mary Glock McLeay, I also played the saxophone in Glock's orchestra
for a few years. Playing in an orchestra at the time wasn't too profitable.
Admission to the dance was 25 cents. Dancing started at nine p.m. Free lunch
was served at midnight, and the dancing continued until three or four a.m.
Those of us in the orchestra were usually paid $1 each, never more. With that
$1 we bought reeds for our saxophones. There was never enough money for music,
so Frank usually bought the music out of pocket money.

In 1944 I took a Physical Training course at Mount Royal College, and had
ladies and girls Phys. Ed. classes in Irvine for three years. I also had a
girl's Cadet class one year. I joined the Irvine Women's Institute in 1942 and
was a member for 42 years, until the branch disbanded in 1984. For 18 or 20
years I collected used clothing for the Irvine W.I., from W.I. members,
friends, family, other W.I. branches,, and any clothing left over from Church
rummage sales. I checked everything before packing, often washed and mended
garments that needed it, made over many worn out adult garments into children's
clothes. I also collected the small cakes of used soap from Medicine Hat hotels
and motels for six or seven years. The clothes and soap were packed separately.
Then Frank would help me haul everything to the Medicine Hat Transport Company
for shipment to Calgary, to be shipped to the Third World countries. For
several years the clothing shipments to Calgary amounted to a few pounds less
than one ton per year, and the used soap shipments were a little less than
that. It was hard, heavy work at times, but I enjoyed it.

I was one of the chaperones for Medicine Hat's first Stampede Queen (I think
Judy Titlansvik) from the Wild Horse area, and Frank was in charge of all the
horses.

I still make my home in Medicine Hat.

The McLeish Family

The McLeish family, Mrs. McLeish, Pete, Jim and two sisters, came to Canada
from Scotland about 1900. It is believed that the two sisters did not live in
the Irvine area.

The home was built on the NW 4-12-2-W4 just north of the creek. The remains of
the cellar can still be seen. A lone rhubarb plant still survives today as a
mute reminder of where the family garden once was. In addition to farming, the
McLeish brothers engaged in other activities. A lime burning kiln was built
into the creek bank about a quarter of a mile west of the buildings. Here
alternate layers of wood and lime stone were burnt to make slake lime for
mortar. Many of the brick buildings in Irvine were constructed using the lime
produced here, including the Cypress Hotel and the Great West Hotel. Burnt
stones can still be found on the creek bank where the kiln once was. They also
did some strip mining for coal in an area about one and a half or two miles
east of Irvine and a half mile south (in the badland hills). The coal was very
soft and not of good commercial grade.

About 1909 the family moved to section 36-11-2-W4, just north of the Larmour
siding on the C.P.R. line, where they carried on farming operations. They
engaged in the raising of heavy draft horses and sold some hay. They started an
irrigation project using the water from the Box Elder Creek. A dam was
constructed in the south west corner of the section and irrigation canals were
built. All work was done with horses and a scraper. At that time water rights
came under the control of the Irrigation Act (Federal Legislation). James
McLeish was granted one of the first licenses in this area, giving him water
rights on the Box Elder Creek. The license was approved April 24, 1914.

In the mid 20's Pete left the area and Mrs. McLeish passed away. The original
building built on the NW 4 was moved to SE 4 by Jerry Dunn. Jim McLeish
continued his farming operations on section 36 using water from the Box Elder
to flood hayland and to irrigate a garden area.

Jim developed and patented a device to be used as the anchor for a three legged
tripod. The unit consisted of a triangular casting to which poles could be
attached. In the centre of the triangle was a heavy eye hook to which a block
and tackle could be hung. The unit was manufactured by the Medicine Hat Foundry
and sold for about $5.

Jim passed away about 1953.

Christian C. and Katherine (Hotman) Meier

Christian C. Meier was born in Glueckstahl, South Russia in 1860 and immigrated
to South Dakota, U.S.A. in 1885 with his wife Katherine, who was also born in
Glueckstahl on October 10, 1860. They farmed for many years in North and South
Dakota where four of their children were born.

Jacob Karl was born on January 26, 1888, Mathilda, on June 2, 1897, Nathaniel
(Dan), in July 1899, and Edward, on July 19, 1901. They were all born in
Eureka, South Dakota. In 1902 the family moved to Alberta, Canada where a
fourth son, Isaac, was born on November 2, 1904.

In later years Christian invented and erected his own stone flour mill on his
farm and did custom milling of grain for farmers at 10 cents per 100 pound sack
of grain. This flour mill was powered by a large wooden water wheel and worked
very well.

Katherine busied herself raising her young family. She is remembered for her
excellent borscht. She became ill and suffered much with a broken hip and died
in 1937 at the age of 77 years.

Christian C. and Katherine Meier, Anne Koenig (pic)

Christian and his family lived in the Irvine area until 1917 when he retired to
Yuill St. in Medicine Hat where he raised a very large garden and delivered his
produce to his family and friends on the farm. He later built a house on
Allowance Avenue where he lived until he went to live at the Haven of Rest. He
was remarried in 1949. He died in 1952 at the age of 92 and is buried in
Hillside Cemetery.

Jacob (Jack) married Emma Schwartz in 1907 and they have five sons, Johnathon,
Emil, Harry, Johnny and Samuel, and one daughter, Tilley (Logan), who are all
living in British Columbia. Jack died on May 5, 1936.

Mathilda married Daniel Koenig on March 6, 1916 and their story is included
elsewhere. She passed away May 14, 1936 just days after her brother Jack.

Dan married Louisa Schwartz and they have two daughters, Minnie (Woolley) and
Mabel (Schwabe) who are both residing in Medicine Hat. They also have one
grandchild, Charlotte, and two great-grand-children.

Edward married Adeline Mayer. Their story follows.

Isaac married Martha Mayer. Their story follows.

Edward and Adeline (Mayer) Meier

Edward Meier was born in 1901 in Eureka, South Dakota, the third son of
Christian and Katherine Meier and came to Canada with his parents in 1902. They
homesteaded on the SW 30-10-2-4 where he grew up and farmed with the family and
also learned to do carpentry work. He attended Concordia School.

Adeline (Mayer) and Edward Meier - December 18, 1926 (pic)

On December 18, 1926 Edward married Adeline Mayer, daughter of Ludwig and Maria
Mayer, in Medicine Hat. They settled on a farm south of Pashley, N 25-10-3-4.
They also raised cattle and operated a dairy. For many years the milk was
shipped by truck to Medicine Hat. In 1947 they moved to Medicine Hat and the
farm was rented to Albert Houff who later purchased it. It is presently owned
by Edward's brother Dan. Later Edward purchased land near the #3 Highway and
also some west of Medicine Hat. He and his son farmed this from town in 1953
and 1954. When his son Ken took over the farm, he pursued his hobbies of
fishing, wood-working, camping and traveling.

Edward Meier Family: Edward, Ken, Helen, Adeline (pic)

Edward Meier Family: Back: Ken, Edward; Front: Helen, Adeline - 1954 (pic)

Edward and Adeline celebrated 49 years of marriage before his passing on
September 22, 1974. He is buried at Hillside Cemetery. Adeline continued to
reside in their home at 111-4 St. S.W. until June of 1987 when she moved to a
senior lodge where she resides at the present time.

The Edward Meiers had two children. Ken was born February 19, 1928 and Helen on
March 22, 1930. They both attended Concordia School. Helen furthered her
education at Alexandra High School and graduated in 1948. She did secretarial
work until she was married in 1955.

Ken married Marlene Weiss, daughter of Emma and Emanuel Weiss, on September 18,
1954. They operated an irrigation and mixed farm until moving to Medicine Hat
in 1975. They have two children, Brian of Calgary and Lori of Medicine Hat, and
one granddaughter. Brian married Cathy Sharp and they have a baby girl, Kelly
Anne.

Helen married Thomas Kanning of Galata, Montana on June 3, 1955. They farmed
and ranched in Montana until Tom's passing in October 1975 at the age of 47
years and Helen's passing on June 10, 1981 at the age of 51 years. They had
four children, David of Havre, Montana, Karla and Michael of Bozeman, Montana
and Lisa of Boston, Massachusetts and seven grandchildren. Both Helen and Tom
are buried in Montana.

Isaac and Martha (Mayer) Meier

Isaac Meier was born on November 2, 1904 at Irvine. He married Martha Mayer in
1927 and they farmed in the Norton district until they retired to Medicine Hat
in 1946.

Isaac Meier had a natural talent in both violin and carpentry. He built several
houses including his own in Medicine Hat. He was a faithful member of the
Seventh Day Adventist church.

Martha died July 22, 1979 and Isaac on November 15, 1988.

Isaac and Martha's only son, Gordon, was born in December 1928. He married
Frances Vockeroth in June 1949. They had two sons, Ron and Don, who live in
Medicine Hat, one daughter, Elaine Welk, who lives in Ontario, and eight
grandchildren. Gordon passed away in February 1963 at the age of 34.

Fredrick and Dorothea (Sept) Meier
by Olga Weiss

Fredrick Karl Meier, son of Karl Anton and Christina (Stephan) Meier, was born
July 24, 1863 at Karlsruhe, Russia.

Dorothea, daughter of Gottfried and Katherina (Klaiber) Sept, was born March 7,
1868 at Malojareslawetz, Russia.

Fredrick and Dorothea were married August 25, 1885 at Stavropol, Russia. They
had 11 boys and one girl when they immigrated to North Dakota in 1908.
September 17, 1909 a girl, Rachel, was born but died soon after birth.

In 1910, they settled on the southern slopes of the Cypress Hills. June 25,
1911, another girl, Paulina, was born but passed away November 30, 1911 and is
buried in the Lebonon-Thelma Cemetery.

About this time the family moved onto the Wunsch farm at Thelma. Here Fredrick
got the job of hauling mail from Irvine to Thelma twice a week, stopping at
three post offices along the 32 mile route. Needing a place to spend the night
at each end of the route prompted him to buy a house in Irvine where he,
Dorothea, and the younger boys lived. Here the boys went to school. The older
boys and daughter, Lea, lived on the farm. While in Irvine, they kept a couple
of good milk cows whose milk was bottled and delivered to residents in town.

In 1915 the family moved back to the Cypress Hills, to Fox, where Fredrick
bought a quarter from Mr. George Wilson. He also took up the adjoining quarter
as a homestead.

In spring of 1916, Fredrick lost his left hand in a grain roller mill accident.
The long trip to Irvine by horse and democrat was very painful. From Irvine
they were able to go on to Medicine Hat's hospital in Mr. Fred Crewe's car.
After six weeks in hospital he returned home where spring work was completed
and he supervised the building of a new house.

In 1924 Fredrick and Dorothea moved to Medicine Hat to retire. Dorothea passed
away February 5, 1928. Fredrick remarried September 3, 1929 to Rosina (Kuch)
Sturm. Fredrick passed away March 22, 1936. Rosina passed away September 27,
1951 at Meadowview, Alberta where she was living with her daughter Magdelena
Meier.

The family consisted of 12 children.

Jacob (born March 22, 1886) was listed missing in action in World War I.

Fredrick Jr. (November 18, 1887 - August 26, 1961) married Bertha Schwabe,
ranched at Fox, and had eight children.

John (August 29, 1889 - May 3, 1939) married Katherina Stroh, ranched at Fox
and Graburn, and had five children.

Carl (December 10, 1891 - November 26, 1964) married Katherina Linderman, and
lived in the Irvine area.

August (September 1, 1893 - November 12, 1968) married Alvina Lautermilch, and
lived in the Coal Centre district.

Theodore (September 10, 1895 - May 24, 1935) married Myrtle Martin, ranched at
Val Marie, Saskatchewan, and had one son, Ted Jr.

Lea (July 18, 1897 - March 31, 1982) married John Fandrick, ranched at Thelma,
and had five children.

Elias (September 28, 1900 - June 10, 1970) married Ottilia Lentz, farmed south
of Dunmore, and had three children.

Philipp (September 28, 1901 - October 7, 1968) lived at Whitecourt, Alberta.

Andrew (August 17, 1903 - deceased) left for the U.S.A.

Reinhold (August 22, 1905) married his stepmother's daughter Magdelena Sturm.
They farmed at Fox, Clearwater Lake, Feldman Lake, and Scandia. In 1947 they
moved to Meadowview, Alberta, farmed there until 1961 and are now living in
retirement at Barrhead, Alberta. They have four children, Olga, Andy, Alice and
Herbert.

Joseph (September 6, 1907 - August, 1988) married Myrtle (Martin) Meier (his
brother Ted's widow) and lived in retirement in Edmonton. They had one son
David. Joseph passed away August 26, 1988.

Carl and Katherine (Linderman) Meier
submitted by Charlie and Norman Meier, to the best of their knowledge

Carl Meier was born December 10, 1891 in Bessarabia, Russia, the fourth son of
Frederick and Dorothea (Sept) Meier. Frederick Meier and family came to Canada
in 1911.

Katherine Linderman was born December 12, 1892 in Eureka, South Dakota, U.S.A.,
daughter of Frederick and Charlotte (Wahl) Linderman. Frederick Linderman and
family came to Canada in 1902.

Carl Meier met Katherine Linderman in Irvine in 1913 and soon after they were
married on September 22, 1913 at Irvine, Alberta. They made their first home at
Fox, Alberta. Their first daughter, Annie, was born in January 1914. They
worked very hard; starting a home and family was hard in those days, but
somehow they always seemed to manage. In March, the following year, another
daughter, Mary, was born.

Mr. and Mrs. Carl Meier (pic)

In 1916 Carl and his family moved to Irvine where Carl worked in the livery
stables. Wages were not all that great in those days. On October 12, 1916 their
first son, Charlie, was born. That meant another mouth to feed.

In 1917 they moved to the Frederick Linderman farm just south of Irvine. Here
they had their own cows to milk and could sell butter and cream. They raised
chickens, which meant more eggs to sell and for their own use.

In 1918 the second son, Phillip, was born, lived with them only a short while,
and passed away in 1919. From the Linderman farm they moved to a farm which was
in the Ross Creek flats, near the Berry Centre School.

In 1923 they moved to the Gros Ventre district near the Coal Centre School. All
through his farming Carl loved and was involved in breaking horses, and for
many years helped their friends and neighbors. Being with farm animals was his
joy. Here he also was in charge of a coal mining strip.

On August 27, 1925 a red-haired daughter, Leah, was born.

In 1926 they decided to move farther west to the Norton District near Feldman
Lake School. There was also coal in that creek, which Carl was in charge of. He
had been strip mining for several years with horses. A walking plow, slip, and
frezno had to move a lot of dirt to get to the seam of coal which was about
four feet thick. He worked hard to get enough coal for relief families in the
dirty thirties. In the late thirties the coal was finished; the Government
wouldn't allow them to go underground. Thanks for the coal; if they would have
had to buy this coal, it would have meant less of something else.

Times were tough back in those days. They milked cows and sold cream and butter
to keep the family clothed and fed. They milked up to eight cows, morning and
night, churned enough butter to take into Irvine to sell or trade in exchange
for groceries. Fresh cream and eggs were brought into Medicine Hat as well.

In January 1928 Norman was born. Then came the thirties (everyone does remember
them) however they always seemed to manage. All through the thirties it meant
hard work to make ends meet. In 1932 another boy, Robert, was born but, sad to
say, he only lived with them several months.

In 1943 they moved to Redcliff, Alberta. Here Carl worked as a watchman from
eleven p.m. to seven a.m. six days a week. They made their home at 722 - 2nd
Street South.

In 1961 Carl retired from the company. After his retirement he enjoyed
gardening as well as going to afternoon matinees; he especially enjoyed Roy
Rogers and Gene Autry movies. He loved all western music shows as he loved
horses.

Mr. and Mrs. Carl Meier 50th Anniv. (pic)

On September 22, 1963 Carl and Katherine celebrated their Golden Wedding
Anniversary with Open House being held at the home of their son, Norman Meier.
After a lengthy illness Carl passed away November 26, 1964. A year later
Katherine moved to Medicine Hat. When illness struck she was confined to the
Sunnyside Nursing Home. On April 27, 1969 she passed away.

Carl Meier Family: Leah, Charlie, Annie, Norman, Mary (pic)

There were five surviving children.

Annie, Mrs. Alex Trekofski, now Mrs. Leonard Meckelbory of Sundre, Alberta, had
four children: Esther and Glen Rhind, Earl and Ruth Trekofski, Elmer and
Marlene Trekofski, Elaine and Leonard Grykne.

Mary, Mrs. Walter O'Connor of Redcliff, Alberta (deceased) had six children:
Edward (deceased) and Frances O'Conner, Alfred and Helen O'Connor, Robert
(deceased), Gloria and Doug Picken, Melvin and Carol O'Connor (separated),
Stanley and Sandra O'Connor.

Charlie of Medicine Hat, Alberta had four children: Harvey and Carol Meier,
Linda and Wilbert Langille, Almina Kath and Barrie Neitz, and Elliott Meier.

Leah (McInnes, Bohnet, Flanders) of Campbell River, British Columbia had nine
children: Carl and Cheryl McInnes, Jeanette and David Brown, a baby deceased,
Jerry and Cindy Bohnet, Doreen and Arnie Berg, Brenda Bohnet, Wanda, David, and
Robert Flanders.

Norman and Matilda Meier of Medicine Hat, Alberta had six children: Diana and
Paul Metz, Darlene and Dennis Rathwell, Douglas and Natalie Meier, Daniel and
Marlene Meier, David and Eva Meier, and Delbert Meier (at home).

August and Alvina Meier
by Olga Weiss

August Meier, son of Fredrick and Dorothea (Sept) Meier, was born September 1,
1893 at Stavropol, Russia.

Alvina, daughter of John and Alvina (Schlecht) Lautermilch, was born August 10,
1904.

August and Alvina were married July 24, 1922. They lived at Fox for some time,
then moved south of Irvine to the Karl Becker place and then to the Coles'
place south of Dunmore until 1930.

They then moved to Medicine Hat, where August worked for many years at the
Medicine Hat Potteries. They were very active members of the Salvation Army.
Many can remember August carrying the flag leading the Salvation Army band in
the Medicine Hat Parade in the 1950's and 1960's.

Dora and Herman Kuehn (pic)

They had one daughter, Dora, born December 10, 1925, who, on June 5, 1954,
married Herman Kuehn. They farmed at Lloydminster and now are living in
Lloydminster in retirement. They have two sons: Terrance and Donald.

Johannes and Dorthea (Titus) Mock

Johannes Mock was born February 20, 1864 in Bessarabia, South Russia and
Dorthea Titus was born December 11, 1870 in Russia. They were married in the
town of Burstall, Bessarabia, South Russia. Johannes Mock had a harness and
saddle business in Russia and Dorthea was a home maker. When they received
letters from Canada, they started to make plans and in the year of 1911, they
packed up the trunks and suitcases and ten children and immigrated to Canada on
a cargo ship.

How they landed in the Walsh area is a question, but that is where they
settled. They farmed in the Many Island area for a short time with the help of
neighbors and their machinery. When the government opened up land for
homesteaders, they took up Section 16-13-2-4. They built a sod house and barn
and lived there for three years.

While living there twin boys were born, Jacob and Johannes. They were the only
children born in Canada. Johannes later died. Dorthea Mock was her own midwife
for the twins, as Irvine, the closest town, had no doctor available. Dorthea
Mock was midwife to many children in the area.

As it was hard to raise a large family, the older children moved out to find
jobs in Medicine Hat. They moved to Section 17 where they built their new home,
and the farm took shape. Chickens, milk cows, and pigs all helped to pay for
things. Johannes turned the sod house into a shop where he made harness and
tanned hides for people. His son Theodore took over the farming. Butter was
churned and taken to Medicine Hat to be sold on the market square or traded at
the store for other food. Johannes also raised garden produce. I can remember a
barn full of watermelon. Only the good ones were eaten and the pigs got the
rest.

Johannes Mock died on June 14, 1931 and Dorthea ran the farm with her son,
Jack, to the year 1933.

Jacob and Dorthea Singer (Mock) (pic)

Dorthea met Jack Singer from the small town of Hatton. They got married and
lived there a short time. They then bought a house in Irvine and she lived
there until her death on July 10, 1949.

She was loved by everyone and kept busy spinning and knitting for people. Jacob
Singer made many willow baskets for people. He moved to Medicine Hat and I
believe he lived to 90 years of age.

Johannes and Dorthea Mock had 12 children.

Mary (March 16, 1892 - November 22, 1955) married William Klaudt.

Reinhold (January 16, 1894 - July 7, 1967) married Tillie Paul (deceased 1984).

Dorthea (October 25, 1898 - January 11, 1974) married Martin Vossler (-
December 7, 1966).

Olga (deceased) married a Mr. Kundert.

Gottlieb (March 3, 1904 - October 16, 1978) married Mary Zieffle.

Theodore (June 25, 1908) married Lena Mock.

Natalie (August 16, 1910) married Emmanuel Elhart.

Jacob (June 21, 1913 - July 2, 1984) married Edna Bauman.

Wayne and Marlene (Lentz) Moreton
by Marlene (Lentz) Moreton

Hi! I'm Marlene (Lentz) Moreton, the youngest daughter of Martha and Fred Lentz
of Medicine Hat, Alberta. I was born in Medicine Hat on February 1, 1949 and
was raised on a farm in the Norton area. I received all my education in Irvine,
Alberta. After graduation in 1967 I went to work at Medicine Hat Co-op Ltd. and
from there I went to the Bank of Nova Scotia.

It was in Medicine Hat that I met my husband Wayne Grant Moreton, the eldest
son of Julie and Fred Steele and Leonard Moreton. Since Wayne's father was in
the army he was born in Essex County, Windsor, Ontario on November 3, 1941. He
was a few weeks old when they returned to Medicine Hat where they were from
originally. He was raised in Medicine Hat and went to work for CP Rail.

Wayne and I were married on September 27, 1969. After our honeymoon in
California we rented a house on Crescent Heights at 52-10 St. N.E. which we
purchased - a couple of years later. On November 16, 1970 we were blessed with
a darling baby girl whom we name Nicole Marlene. I quit work to be at home with
our baby. In 1976 I went to work at Hat Livestock Auction which was sold to
Airport Livestock Auction in 1977. In 1977 Wayne and I bought a section of land
about 40 miles southeast of Medicine Hat which we farm from the city. This land
was purchased from the government originally by a Freimark. Since that time it
had gone through about seven different owners. This area in the old days was
called the Sentinel area which is now called the Cypress View area.

Nicole, Marlene, Wayne Moreton (pic)

Since Wayne was raised in the city he had lots of things to learn. Our land had
just been broken when we purchased it from the last owner, Albert Pederzolli.
We had many experiences which happened to us that I'm sure I could write a book
about. We laugh about them now but at the time they were no laughing matter.
Things were made a bit easier for us because we had great neighbors, such as my
sister, Violet and her husband Allister Otto, and also the Elkwater Colony who
helped us a great deal. Since times are tough to start farming we have to
continue farming from the city so Wayne can keep his job.

Our family enjoys traveling, curling, golfing and skiing. Nicole also enjoys
figure skating and water skiing. She had done very well in curling by winning a
few medals such as a gold and a silver. We still reside at 52-10 St. N.E. Wayne
is still with CP Rail as a conductor. Presently he is on VIA which he enjoys
very much. I am still with Airport Livestock Auction. We continue to work our
farm together but with much less difficulty than when we started.

Sergius and Mary Nesdoly and Sons
by Mary Nesdoly

Sergius (Serge) Nesdoly was born in Blaine Lake, Saskatchewan on October 8,
1925. The youngest of a family of six, his two sisters married and three
brothers away to war, he left school to help his father on the family farm. On
November 22, 1943 he married Mary Marciniak, and in September 1947 they moved
to Alberta. They have two sons.

Serge was a loyal Irvinite. After working on several short term jobs, he became
a grain buyer for Lake of the Woods. During his tenure here he obtained an
Insurance agents license, and during his spare time sold Auto and Fire policies
for Yorkshire, Western Union and Saskatchewan Mutual Insurance Company and hail
policies for the Great American Insurance Company.

In 1958, when Lake of the Woods elevator was bought by the Pool, Serge was laid
off, so he bought the old two-story building on main street from Wong King and
converted it into an Insurance office. Because this was a large building, he
obtained a Sporting Goods license, and sold fishing supplies, small sports
equipment, etc. as well.

Under Ken Stephenson's supervision Serge became a hail adjuster for Great
American Insurance Company so from the early sixties till 1974 he spent his
summer months adjusting hail damaged crops throughout most of Alberta and
Saskatchewan.

In 1967 the family moved to Medicine Hat, but Serge continued to run the
Insurance business from his Irvine Office.

In 1971 he had the old two-story building demolished and replaced with a
smaller more suitable one which he bought from the Engel estate and moved to
the site. This building still serves as the "S.F. Nesdoly Agency" office today.

Serge died an untimely death in a highway accident on his way home from the
Irvine office on March 5, 1975. He was an active member of the Royal Canadian
Legion and the Order of the Elks, and a Life Member of the Irvine Chinook Club.

He enjoyed curling, fishing, hunting and hobby farming, growing a little grain
and running a few head of cattle, on a farm he bought from Fred and Dixon Rath
in 1970.

Mary (Marciniak) Nesdoly was born in Poland in 1923. She came to Canada with
her parents in 1926. After graduating from the Saskatoon Normal School, she
accepted her first teaching position in Brook Hill School, in the Blaine Lake
school district. There she met Serge and married. After teaching for five years
in this school district, she accepted a teaching position in Irvine, so the
family moved to Alberta.

She came to Irvine alone the last weekend in August, signed a teaching
contract, rented a two-room upstairs suite in the Freimark home, and began
teaching grades three and four in September 1947. Serge stayed behind to help
with harvesting, arriving in Irvine with their two year old, Armond, about two
weeks later.

The Nesdolys; lived in Freimark's upstairs suite for about two years, then
moved to a larger home on the north side of the tracks. They bought that home
in the early fifties and lived there until they moved to Medicine Hat in April
1967.

Mary taught grades three and four for eight years, took a year's leave of
absence, then returned to teach junior and senior high, with grade nine and ten
Home Economics for ten years. Her greatest joy was watching the Home Ec. girls
walking down the ramp wearing their creations during their annual fashion
shows. There were many bright, beautiful and capable girls in these classes,
every year. To supplement their Home Ec. course and provide a little extra
practical experience, the Home Ec. room, under Mary's supervision, was used to
prepare and serve the graduation banquet to the grade 12 grads, their parents
and guests, and the teaching staff, those ten years.

In the fall of '66, Mary took another year's leave of absence, and in April '67
the family moved to Medicine Hat. That fall Mary commuted to Irvine School.
Finding it too cumbersome, she resigned from the Medicine Hat S.D. #4 and in
the fall of '68 joined the teaching staff at McCoy High School in Medicine Hat.
Here she taught for another ten years. When Serge passed away in 1975, she
continued teaching at McCoy School, handled the S.F. Nesdoly Ins. business and
looked after their small farm south of Irvine. In June of 1978 she resigned
from teaching and devoted all her time to insurance and farming.

Armond, their elder son, was born in Blaine Lake, Saskatchewan on June 30,
1945. He came to Irvine with his parents in 1947. After graduating from the
Irvine High School he moved to Edmonton, where he married Kathy Adams. They
have three children, Theresa, Bradley, and Jackie. Theresa is married to Gerald
Comeau and they have a little daughter, Robyn.

Their other son, Murray, was born in the Medicine Hat Hospital on August 25,
1954. He attended Irvine School from grade one to eight, then moved to Medicine
Hat. After graduating from McCoy High School and the U of A in Edmonton with a
B.A. degree, he accepted a position with Manpower in Brooks. In March of 1980
he resigned from this job and moved back to Medicine Hat to run the Nesdoly
Insurance business. In 1985 he returned to school, graduating from the
Lethbridge University with a B.Ed. degree. While at the U of L, Murray met
Brenda Zatylny, and the two were married on July 16, 1988. Both Murray and
Brenda are now teaching in Medicine Hat, and Murray also comes to Irvine on a
regular basis to continue working with the Nesdoly Insurance Agency.

Philip and Carolina (Stotz) Neubauer

Philip Neubauer (1874-1923) married Carolina Stotz (1880-1952) on October 7,
1899. They came to the Clover Hill District in April 1910 where they took up a
homestead and preemption on the N-24-12-2. It was here they built a house and
barn with the help of Otto Brandt. The buildings stand until this day.

Caroline and Philip Neubauer (pic)

They were blessed with eleven children, five of whom died in infancy: John,
born 1900; Fred, 1902; Jacob, 1903; Louise, 1905-1906; Henry, 1907, Emilia,
1908-1910; 2nd Emilia, 1911-1911; Albert, 1912-1912; Karl, 1914-1914; 2nd
Albert, 1915; Emil, 1917.

Clover Hill School was built in 1914 on the SW 24-12-2. It served as school,
church, and a gathering point for the community. It played a vital part, not
only for Philip and Carolina and their family but for all the farmers that had
settled in Clover Hill.

Grain was drawn to Irvine, ten miles away, with horses and supplies and mail
were brought back.

Philip died suddenly November 17, 1923 and is buried in the Irvine Cemetery.

Carolina re-married Peter Schneider November 26, 1924. She along with Albert
and Emil, moved to Peter's farm, south of Irvine, where she remained until
retirement to Medicine Hat. Carolina Schneider died March 4, 1952 and is buried
in Hillside Cemetery, Medicine Hat.

The farm remains with the family at the time of writing. Fred Neubauer took
over after the untimely death of his father, Philip, and Roy, the present
owner, took over from his father, Fred.

John moved to Chicago where he made his permanent home.

Fred married Eva Stroh. They lived in the Irvine district and had two children,
Roy and Alice. Fred died in 1964. Fred and Roy's stories follow.

Jake went to Cardston where he owned and operated a Texaco Service Station. He
married Muriel Matkin. They had one daughter, Marilyn. Jake retired in Calgary,
where he died in 1964. Muriel lives with Marilyn and her husband Norman Tolk
and their family of five, in Brentwood, Tennessee.

When Henry left Clover Hill, he became a carpenter, and helped in the building
of elevators throughout the province, including the silver twin elevator at the
Pool in Irvine. He later managed elevators in Penhold, Beiseker and Balzac.
Henry served with the armed forces in World War II. He married Barbara Hagel in
Beiseker in 1947. They were blessed with a daughter, Lois, and a son, Neil
(1951-1952). Lois lives in Calgary and works with an Oil Company. Barbara died
in 1972. Henry is retired, along with friend Lucille, in Calgary.

Albert married Clara Kundert who died in 1957. He later married Ella Kundert.
He has one son, Barry.

Emil married Eleanor MacKinlay. They have two sons, George and Douglas.

Albert and Emil's stories follow.

Fred and Eva (Stroh) Neubauer

Fred Neubauer, born 1902, married Eva Stroh on November 25, 1928. After living
in Irvine a short time, they moved to the farm in Clover Hill

Eva (Stroh) and Fred Neubauer, November 25 1928 (pic)

Fred, as a young man, enjoyed playing baseball. He, along with Chuck Glock,
played the violin and entertained at dances and parties. Fred enjoyed life,
loved to tell jokes and then laughed so hard everyone would laugh along with
him. He liked entertainment and would go to the theatre to watch a movie or to
a hockey game whenever he could. Fred had one of the first cars in the Clover
Hill district and bounced over the country trails, a big improvement over a
team of horses.

When radios were invented, Fred and Eva had one of the first. It had earphones
with which you could listen. provided you got a hold of one. One day someone
got the idea of putting the earphones under a bread-dough mixing pan. It
worked! You could hear the radio throughout the room. Needless to say many
neighbors came to listen to the new magic - the Brandts, the Thomes, Harry
Hamilton, the Rolls, the Glocks, and the Woods. Cards and lunch usually
followed.

Fred and Eva moved to Irvine in 1953 and in 1961, they retired to Medicine Hat.
Fred died in 1963 and is buried in the Chapel Lawn Memorial Gardens. Eva is
still living in their home in Medicine Hat.

Fred Neubauer Family: Fred, Alice, Roy, Eva (pic)

Fred and Eva had two children, Roy and Alice.

Roy and his wife Leona live in Irvine along with their two sons, Bradley and
Mark.

Alice (Baker) lives in Calgary and is a nurse at the N.I.C.U. at the General
Hospital. Her two sons, Gary and Kelly, and Kelly's wife Sheri, live in Calgary
as well. Her daughter, Cindy and her husband, Dave Gowens, live in Ottawa.

Roy and Leona Neubauer

Roy Neubauer (1929) married Leona English (1935) on July 8, 1960.

Roy Neubauer (pic)

Roy was raised and educated in the Clover Hill and Irvine areas. After
graduating from Irvine High School, he worked for the RER.A. for five years as
an instrument man and draftsman on the Saint Mary's Milk River Project in
Southern Alberta. In 1953 he bought a school bus and drove for 12 years from
Medicine Hat to Irvine and nine years from Graburn to Irvine, and then as a
relief driver for six years.

Roy Neubauer Family: Roy, Bradley, Mark, Leona (pic)

Roy and Leona have two sons: Bradley, born in Medicine Hat in 1962, and Mark,
born in Medicine Hat in 1965. Brad has an Arts degree in Political Science from
the University of Calgary and Mark received a diploma from S.A.I.T. in
Electrical Engineering Technology. They both enjoy farming.

Leona has taught school in Irvine for 25 years. She taught C.G.I.T. for several
years, was the first president of the newly formed Irvine U.C.W., and later
held position of secretary, and has served on the church board. Roy and Leona
also held United Church Hi-C classes for young adults.

Roy has represented Irvine and Ward 2 of the M.D. of Cypress, 1971 to the
present date, on the Medicine Hat Regional Hospital Board. He has served on all
committees, chaired most committees, including the Executive committee. He
served on the planning committee from the time of the conception of the new
hospital until its completion. He is serving on the projects committee for the
renovation of the General Hospital, and is presently vice-chairman of the
Regional Hospital board.

Roy served on the building committee of the Peace United Church along with Stan
Wilde, Victor Wiedemann, and Ted Aman. Roy served on the Peace United board for
many years, some as chairman.

Roy held the position of mayor of Irvine 1967-71. During that time, natural gas
was brought to town. A new council chamber and fire hall were built. The first
fire engine for the town was purchased. The picnic grounds down in the creek
was established, and commissioned by the Honourable Harry Strom, the Minister
of Agriculture. The hardwood in the old Wiedemann store was laid, the posts
were taken from the middle, and some of the wall between it and the old Post
Office was removed. The Irvine and District Hall was established - now the New
Horizons. The Irvine and District Recreation Board was formed and grants from
the government based on a per capita basis were put into place; the board still
exists as the Ag Society. A street-light network was established, and a 40-60
split with the government of the province permitted the building and
maintenance of the dump ground. A road and drainage program was set up and
built. The Alberta Wheat Pool Elevator was also built. The Council commissioned
a study into water and sewer which was brought into town in later years. The
work done on many of the projects at that time was done on a voluntary basis by
the councilors and concerned people of the area for no pay.

The Roy Neubauers live in the town of Irvine and carry on their farm operations
from there.

Albert Neubauer

Albert Neubauer was born on October 30, 1915 at the family farm located nine
miles northeast of Irvine, in the Clover Hill district. He weighed a little
under two pounds at birth and survived. He attended school at Clover Hill for
grade one.

The family moved south, to the Cypress Hills, when his mother married Peter
Schneider on November 26, 1924. He then attended Sentinel School #1516 and
received his grade eight diploma.

Albert stayed home and worked on the family farm and milked cows during the
1930's.

Albert and his younger brother Emil started to play music and at one time had a
five piece orchestra, playing within a 100 mile radius of Irvine. Everybody
enjoyed their music and they played almost every weekend.

In 1946, Albert and Emil bought their own place in the Cypress Hills. After
batching for three years Albert married Clara Kundert, on December 31, 1949.
Barry Lee was born on July 17, 1951.

Beverly Ann was born on February 20, 1953 and died on November 24, 1953. On
February 21, 1957, Clara and her infant daughter died at childbirth.

On April 4, 1959, Albert married Ella Kundert.

In 1966 Albert and Emil decided to split their place and in 1969 Albert bought
a place one and a half mile south of Medicine Hat on the Black and White Trail.
Albert and Barry continue to farm and ranch together at the home place north of
the Cypress Hills and at the place south of Medicine Hat.

Albert retired as a director of the Walsh Cattle Marketing Association, in
1980, after 30 years of service.

Albert and Ella moved to Medicine Hat in 1982.

Emil Neubauer

Emil Neubauer, born in 1917, was the youngest of 11 children born to Philip and
Caroline Neubauer. Emil was six years old when his father died.

When Mrs. Neubauer married Peter Schneider, Emil and his brother Albert moved
with their mother to the Schneider farm south of Irvine. They remained there
until they started their farm in 1947 just east of the Schneider farm.

Emil married Eleanor MacKinlay in 1951 and they were blessed with two sons,
George and Douglas. George makes his home in Medicine Hat and Douglas runs the
home place.

Emil and Eleanor (Peggy) moved to Medicine Hat in 1983 and make their home
there.

Fred Nitschke Family

Fred Nitschke was born on January 2, 1892 in Kataloi, Romania. In 1906 he
immigrated with his family to the Yorkton, Saskatchewan area and then on to
Leader, Saskatchewan in 1909. In Leader, Fred established a homestead with his
wife, the former Kate Schissler, where they raised their three children: Edwin,
Florence and Jimmy. Fred was also an elevator agent in Leader for many years,
however, in 1933 during the depression when elevators were closing, he moved
with his family to Glaslyn, Saskatchewan where he again farmed. In 1937 the
Nitschke family moved to Irvine where Fred became an elevator agent until his
retirement. Fred's wife, Kate, was an Irvine Women's Institute member for many
years, as well as an active member of the Irvine United Church. Kate died in
January 1953.

The Nitschke family will be well remembered for their fantastic gardening
skills. Many people will remember Fred, an avid fisherman, traveling to Cavan
Lake in his Volkswagon to go fishing which was one of his favorite pastimes.

Fred and Kate Nitschke - 1948 (pic)

Fred later married Mrs. Hilda Pfeifer and continued to reside in Irvine until
his death in September, 1974. After Fred's death, Hilda moved to Maple Creek,
Saskatchewan to be near her daughter, Mrs. Alice Schaffer. Hilda died in
January 1985.

Florence trained to become a registered nurse, married, and had one daughter,
Kathleen, who also had a daughter of her own. Florence died in August 1972.

Jimmy died at the young age of 15 years.

Edwin (Ed) enlisted in the army in March 1942 and served in Canada, the central
Mediterranean and continental Europe. In 1945 while in England, Ed married the
former Margaret Gormely who was nursing in London at the time. When Ed and
Margaret returned to Canada they made their home in Walsh where Ed became the
Alberta Wheat Pool Elevator agent. Ed and Margaret had four children: Patricia,
Catherine, Joan and David who all attended Irvine School. Ed and Margaret also
operated the Post Office in Walsh for seven years until December 1977. Ed died
in January 1978. Margaret now lives in Medicine Hat close to her children and
grandchildren.

Patricia, married to Francis Eiserman, lives in Medicine Hat with their two
sons, Guy and Lee. Catherine, married to Cave Starling, lives in Strathmore,
Alberta and they have one son, Cave Jr. Joan, married to Gary Grimm, lives in
Medicine Hat with their two children, Garth and Marni. David, married to Jean
Miller, also resides in Medicine Hat with sons, Kevin and Brett.

Adam Nitz Family

Adam Nitz was born in Austria-Hungary in the mid-nineteenth century. He had a
large family as he was married three times. His first two wives died in
Austria. In 1910 he emigrated from Croatia, Austria with his third wife
Kathrina (Brod) and ten of twelve children.

The family came to the Many Island district in 1912. They detrained at Walsh,
Alberta and the older boys walked to the Many Island Lake district, some 12 or
15 miles northwest, to claim their homestead.

The children from his first wife were Adam, who stayed in the United States;
Mike; John, who stayed in Austria; and Martin. Karl was born to his second wife.

Mike married Katherine Bauder, had two sons and six daughters.

Martin farmed in the Many Island Lake area. (story follows)

Karl married Johanna Dietelback and they had no children.

Adam's third wife, Lena Brod, had three children of her own, one son and two
daughters: Phillip, Johanna, and Magdelena.

Phillip went North to Thorsby and farmed there.

Johanna married Rube Hunt of Lethbridge.

Magdelena married Alois Wiedemann of Irvine on September 24, 1920. They had
four sons and three daughters. Magdelena died in 1977.

Together Adam and Lena had three sons and one daughter:

Jacob married Kathrine Bauman and they had one daughter and two sons.

Elizabeth married George Lynch of Fernie, B.C. and presently they reside in
Lethbridge. She is the only living member of this generation. She has one
daughter and one son.

Philip Nitz had no family.

Peter was born in Canada and with his wife Mary, his son and his daughter,
settled in Lethbridge. Pete became a jeweler and had his own shop there for
many years.

Adam, with his sons, Mike Sr., Martin Sr., Karl and Jacob, all settled in the
Many Island District. Adam died in 1925 and son Jake took over the farm,
staying there until the late fifties.

Kathrina (Adam's wife) remarried Adam Staudt of Portland, Oregon. After his
death in 1928 she moved back to Irvine and lived with the Alois Wiedemann
family until her death in 1939.

Martin and Elizabeth (Deutchmann) Nitz

Martin Nitz Sr. married Elizabeth Deutchmann, who also immigrated from Austria,
and had four sons and two daughters.

They had three sons and one son-in-law serving in the Armed Services during the
second world war. John went into service in June 1941, and was discharged
January 1946. Adam went into services in June 1942 and was discharged March
1946. John and Adam were in war action. Martin Jr. entered service in May 1942
and was discharged January 1946. Son-in-law Edwin Feil was in the Air Force in
Canada.

Martin and Elizabeth Nitz lived in the Town of Irvine from about 1958 till 1963
when Martin died. Elizabeth lived on in Irvine till 1984, when she moved to
live with her daughter in Medicine Hat. At the age of 90 she went to live in
Central Park Lodge, where she is at present, July 1987.

Her daughter Annie and her husband Jim Pfeifer also lived in Irvine from 1976
to 1983. Jim built two homes in Heather Court while living in Irvine. Annie's
first husband, Hugo Feil, died in September 1964. They had two children.
Shirley married Norman Freimark and they have a daughter Ruth. Rodney Feil
married Debra Good and they have a son, Jason, and a daughter Jaime.

Carl and Amelia Olson
by Eva (Olson) Schmidek

Carl and Amelia Olson and family came to Canada in 1910 by covered wagon and
homesteaded on the NW 2-12-2-W4 in the Clover Hill District. Carl was
originally a bank manager in Chicago but, for health reasons he decided to
leave the city and the United States to live on a farm with fresh air. Carl was
killed on the 18th of May 1920 in an accident with four horses and a disc. He
is buried in the St. George Cemetery at Irvine. Mrs. Olson was left to care for
her family of five children, Pearl, Eva, Carl Jr., Cora and Bejorn (Byron).

Carl Olson Family: Back: Amelia, Carl holding Carl Jr.; Front: Pearl, Eva, Cora
in front of their sod house (pic)

Carl Olson Family: Back: Amelia; Front: Eva holding her dolls Buster and
Margaretta, Pearl, Cora holding doll Louise, Carl holding Carl Jr. (pic)

After her husband's death Amelia moved to Irvine and stayed a couple of years.
While in Irvine she took care of Florence Sing while Florence's mother was in a
sanitarium. Amelia then moved to Medicine Hat and the three older children
found work away from home. The two younger children were still attending
school. When the children were grown and on their own Mrs. Olson remarried and
left Medicine Hat. She moved to Great Falls, Montana. She eventually moved to
Everett, Washington and lived there until her death in 1957.

Pearl married Bill Brenton and lived at Kimberly B.C. They had four children.
After her husband died she moved to Nelson, B.C. and resided there the
remainder of her years.

Eva recalls going to the Clover Hill School and relates an incident when she,
Henry Neubauer, Johnny and Millie Glock tied up the shafts of their school
buggy and headed it down the hill close to Adam Roll Sr.'s place. The buggy
jumped the ruts at the bottom of the hill and went through a gate wrecking it
and the turn-table on the buggy. They were afraid what would happen when Mr.
Roll came down to investigate but apparently he just smiled and helped them
patch up the buggy and fix the gate. During the Spanish Flu outbreak, in 1918,
the Olsons were spared getting it and Pearl and Eva, with a team of horses and
democrat, went to the sick neighbors with food. They also fed and cared for
livestock where families were too ill to do their chores. Eva also remembers,
during this time, removing the dead from the beds and putting them on trucks
that came into the area to transport the bodies to Irvine where they were kept
until graves were dug. This sometimes took several days as it was during the
winter months and the ground was frozen so it was a slow process preparing
graves.

Eva married Paul Schmidek and they moved to the Norton district where they
farmed until they retired to Medicine Hat. They had two children, Gloria and
Ronald, who are both married. They also have four grandchildren and two great
grandchildren. Paul Schmidek died on November 26, 1988 and is buried in
Hillside Cemetery. Eva continues to reside in Medicine Hat.

Carl Jr. is married and he and his wife Bea live on the Olympic Penninsula, off
the coast of Seattle, Washington. They did not have any children.

Cora was accidentally killed when she was 17 years old.

Bejorn (Byron) was also married and had two children. He lives in California
just out of Los Angeles.

Karl and Katherine Otto

Karl Otto was born and raised in Neuburg, Russia. Katherine Praegitzer was born
in Romania, but later moved to Neuburg, Russia. They were married April 15,
1892. In 1893, they immigrated to Suttle, South Dakota, but they weren't too
happy there so they moved to Bowden, North Dakota. Still unhappy with this
area, in 1905 they moved to the Irvine district. They purchased the land, but
there were no buildings on it. The A T Ranch had an extra house and a few
buildings so they lived there. Buildings were built in the valley southeast of
the present location where there was shelter and ample water. They purchased a
car in 1915, but found it hard to go in and out of the valley, so buildings
were built at the present location.

Karl, Emma, Katherine Otto (pic)

In 1905, the Berry Centre School District was formed and the school house was
built. It could accommodate up to 36 pupils at one time. Mr. Daykin was the
first teacher.

Karl and Katherine had 12 children: Bertha, Katie, Rosie, Henry, Emil, Lydia,
Ben, Martha, and Emma, and three who died of diphtheria: August at 14, Alma at
eight, and Solomon at two years old. One of these children was laid to rest
down in the valley near the old house. Our neighbors the Eifforts also lost a
girl who is still buried about half a mile west of our home place.

Bertha married Sam Reiswig, lived in Lodi, California, and had two boys.

Katie married Christ Hagel. They had four girls and two boys and lived in
Sykton, North Dakota.

Rose married John Rub, had one boy and one girl, and lived in the Robinson area
and in Medicine Hat.

Henry married Vera Ansley and lived on the farm.

Emil married Maggie Hauck and had four girls.

Lydia married Dr. Breckinridge and lives in Lodi, California.

Ben married Martha Ricker, and had three boys and one girl.

Martha married Bill Ganz.

Emma married Albert Mattheis, had two boys, and lived in Hilda and Medicine Hat.

Tribute to Mother
by Ben Otto Sr.

When we were young we were so bold,
And we only thought our parents get old.
Fun and Frolic were our only thought,
Only our life would not come to naught.

Many a night our mother did spend,
Hoping our life would not come to an end.
She sat by the cradle and prayed many nights,
Hoping her baby would see the daylight.

Mothers have visions their children to be,
An honest example for others to see.
Time after time our mothers did pray,
Never to let someone lead them astray.

She mended our clothes with her two little hands,
Those that we tore when we played in the sand.
Her food was so lovely, so good to the taste,
But never, she let any food go to waste.

I remember my mother when she was so old,
The hardships she suffered had never been told.
Her cheeks were so wrinkled, her hair was so gray,
But always she smiled as she passed by the way.

By now our dear mother has gone to her rest,
I know she did those things she knew best.
Only her picture now hangs on the wall,
She doesn't seem to look so old at all.

I know there are mothers I'd like to compare,
But mothers like ours are very very rare.
Sometimes I weep and sometimes I pray,
To grant me permission to see her just one more day.

Oh, if I only could turn back the years,
I'd save my mommy many a tear.
We'd be more loving, more gentle and kind,
Not to be led as though we were blind.

Allister and Violet (Lentz) Otto
by Allister and Violet Otto

I, Allister Otto, the eldest son of Ben and Martha Otto, was born May 5, 1930
in Medicine Hat and raised on a farm about five miles south of Irvine,
presently owned and farmed by Ron Sauter. I received my education at the Berry
Centre School. It was located about three and one-half miles southeast from our
farm which I traveled to mainly on foot and sometimes by horse. Due to the
country schools being centralized in one locale, I was bussed to Irvine for the
last years of my schooling. In 1945 my father purchased my grandfather, Karl
Otto's farm which was located about three and a half miles farther south. I
moved there that fall with my parents and two brothers. I helped my father farm
until I was able to go and make my own living.

Being raised on a farm gave me a great interest in farm life. 1, therefore,
made farming my livelihood and in the early spring of 1951 I purchased my first
parcel of property from Fred Lentz, which was located five miles south of the
Trans Canada Highway, off the 41 Highway. Later that fall I married Violet
Lentz, daughter of Fred and Martha Lentz, of the Norton District southwest of
Irvine.

Allister and Violet Otto (pic)

Allister Otto Family: Back: Gerald, Marilyn, Harlow, Violet, Clifford, Front:
Dolores, Allister, Sheila (pic)

I, Violet, am the second eldest daughter of Fred and Martha Lentz. I was born
August 13, 1934 in Medicine Hat and raised on a farm which is now operated by
my brother Leonard. I received my education at the Concordia School. We were
three miles from school so we'd walk or travel by horseback. Sometimes we'd
take short cuts by cutting across the neighbours' fields. After I quit school,
I helped out on the family farm. I worked outside with my father many times. My
brothers were younger than 1, so it meant I had to take their place.

In 1949 I met Allister. We were engaged in April 1951 and were married on
November 26 that same year.

We were blessed with our first child, Gerald Wayne, September 3, 1952. We were
living on a half section of land and milking about five cows, so there wasn't
very much of an income, but we made a living.

In 1953, I, Allister, traded this farm back to my father-in-law in return for
property he had owned farther southwest of our location. This land was formerly
owned by Jacob Janke. The Krauss School was situated on this piece of property.
It was there that two more wonderful children came into our family: Dolores
Elaine, born February 8, 1954, and Harlow Donovan, born April 11, 1955. We
lived on this property until 1956, at which time we purchased a different farm,
from Fred and Helen Vossler, about 13 miles southeast of Irvine. We moved there
with our three children but our family was not complete until three more were
added: Marilyn Gwen, born February 17, 1957; Clifford Allister, born July 10,
1958; and Sheila May, born November 23, 1959. Our family of six was raised on
this farm which is still our present residence.

Otto children: Back: Harlow, Gerald; Middle: Marilyn, Dolores; Front: Sheila,
Clifford (pic)

Our children worked very hard in the years that they were growing up. Our farm
wasn't very large so we grew some cereal crops and increased our milking herd.
We bought dairy calves from Anders Anderson's dairy and raised them with our
own on the milk bucket, as many as 35 at one time.

Allister Otto family farm (pic)

Otto children and Violet: Back: Harlow, Gerald, Sheila, Violet; Front: Marilyn,
Clifford, Dolores (pic)

When our children came home from school each one had chores. The cows were to
be brought home, chop needed to be put in the manger, and the cream separator
had to be set together, etc. We milked up to 16 cows by hand but purchased
milking machines when we increased our herd to 29 head. We were in the dairy
business for 23 years. We were teased with our magpies (referring to the
Holstein cattle) but over the years the dairy is what furthered our success in
agriculture.

We decided to give up the dairy after our family grew up and some were starting
to leave home. We decided to go more into farming, which would be easier than
milking cows, so we added more property and replaced the dairy herd with a
cow-calf herd. One parcel that we purchased of a sentimental value was the
homestead of Violet's great grandmother, Eva Pahl. Violet's great grandmother
helped break some of this land in the early 1900's.

Despite the ups and downs in agriculture we are still making farming our
livelihood and intend to do so for a few years yet, health permitting.

Our children received their education at Irvine.

Gerald is living in Medicine Hat and is presently working for Oil Check Labs
Inc. as a Sales Representative. When the need arises he also helps out on the
farm. He has two children, Melanie and Sheldon, and is married to Sharon
Cameron.

Dolores is living in Colton, California, near Loma Linda, about 50 miles east
of Los Angeles. She received her Bachelor of Science Degree in Sociology at
Union College, Lincoln, Nebraska and graduated in 1982 at Loma Linda University
with a Masters Degree in Public Health and is currently working as an Assistant
Administrator in one of the State Hospitals. She is married to Balt Moreno and
has two children, Janelle and Jason.

Harlow and his wife Janice (Anderst) reside in Medicine Hat. He is owner and
operator of the H H Custom Seed and Feed plant in Bow Island. He has also taken
up farming in the Elkwater area.

Marilyn has taken up residence in Medicine Hat with her husband John Dunn. She
is a housewife and has two children, Amanda and Ryan.

Clifford and his wife Joanne (Anderst) are living in the Elkwater area with
their two children, Jeremy and Stephanie. He has taken up farming as his
livelihood.

Sheila resides in Medicine Hat and is employed at Bill Thompson Chev Olds
Cadillac Ltd. as assistant service manager.

Ben Jr. and Doreen (Yanke) Otto
by Doreen Otto

Ben Otto was born in Irvine and lived south of Irvine with his parents, Ben and

Garnett, Ben Jr., Doreen Otto (pic)

I, Doreen, was born in Medicine Hat and lived in the Norton district, Robinson
district and Irvine area with my parents, William and Martha Yanke. I received

Ben and I met and got married in 1952. We moved to Medicine Hat and we both

In the spring of 1955, we moved to Coronation to a farm, which we had purchased

team.

In the fall of 1960, we purchased the farm from Ben's parents. The farm was
originally built by Ben's grandfather, Karl Otto. While farming, Ben also drove
the school bus for seven years and I helped with the field work.

In the spring of 1973, we moved to Medicine Hat. We continued farming and Ben
drove truck for Medalta Transport for a number of years. At present, he is
semi-retired, but still farming. He enjoys doing woodwork. I enjoy working in
my garden and flower beds in the summer. In my leisure time, I like doing
various kinds of crafts. We both enjoy traveling and have spent some winters in
Arizona.

Garnett started and completed her education at the Irvine school (1961 - 1973).
While going to school, she took piano lessons in Medicine Hat and started
teaching piano. She started working as a bookkeeper in a chartered accountants
office in 1973 and is still employed there. She is also teaching piano in the
evenings. In her spare time, she likes to do crafts, travel, and play her
musical instruments.

Eva Pahl

Eva (Neuman) Pahl was born in 1851 in South Russia and immigrated as a widow to
Canada in 1902. Her husband Johan Pahl (1846-1902) had died that same year.

When Eva Pahl immigrated in 1902 she was accompanied by four children. At the
time she applied for an entry for a homestead, September 19, 1902, she stated
that she had two children, ages eight and ten, at home with her. She applied
for the NW 10-11-2-W4 in the Josephsburg area.

Eva Pahl (pic)

Mrs. Pahl homesteaded on the quarter adjacent to her son Christian Pahl and his
wife Justina. At the age of 56 years she applied for the title for her
homestead on August 28, 1907. Eva Pahl became a naturalized citizen on May 29,
1906. Sometime after August 1907 she married a Mr. Seitz.

Eva (Pahl) Seitz died October 24, 1918 in

Christian and Justina (Schlenker) Pahl
by Albert Pahl

Christian and Justina (Schlenker) Pahl immigrated to Canada from Bessarabia,
Russia in 1902 with Christian's mother and their two young children, Lydia and
Edward.

Gustina and Christian Pahl (pic)

While staying with and working for a family, they took out and improved a
homestead 21 kilometers southeast of Irvine, Alberta on the NE 10-10-2-W4 and
later obtained more land to make it a worthwhile operation. The first years
were spent in a sod shack enduring many hardships. Later they moved to a log
house and finally to a two story frame house and a full set of buildings.

By this time the rest of the nine children were born, and getting an education
at Sentinel School was a lot better than it used to be. As time went by some of
the older children went out on their own.

Edward, being handy with a saw and hammer, built a farm for himself and his
wife, the former Bertha Mogck, near the home place.

Lydia married Gustav Herman, Bertha married John Weiss, and both families
engaged in mixed farming in the district. No doubt, both daughters were looking
forward to their future endeavors.

The promise of going to the yearly picnic and sports day at Irvine always made
rock picking a little easier. One of the highlights was the relay race where
you had to circle the track, change horses, but keep the same saddle. Sometimes
in haste to beat the other team, the cinches weren't fastened too securely so
the outcome was always exciting.

Christian Pahl Family 1914-15: Back: Lydia, John; Front: Ed, Bertha, Christian,
Gilf, Lizzie, Justina, Hilda; Missing: Mary and Albert (pic)

There used to be a church approximately two kilometers west where people would
congregate and do a bit of visiting after the sermon.

John married Kate Weiss and they continued to operate the original farm. He had
a way with horses so that helped when he had to train some broncs for
replacement.

Following this, the remaining family moved to Medicine Hat, the youngest
members getting their education there.

Albert Pahl Family: Back: Ruth, Albert. Front: Sandra, Marjorie - 1950 (pic)

Christian Pahl Family: Back: Elizabeth, Edward, Bertha, John, Albert, Hilda,
Gotthelf (Gilf), Mary; Front: Christian, Lydia, Justina - 1942 (pic)

Elizabeth worked for an apple canning plant until Leonard Bauer came along and
chose her for his bride. They made their home in the Turner Valley area where
he was employed by an oil company.

Gotthelf (Gilf) had various jobs but decided that raising cattle and tilling
the soil were what he and his wife Edith (Maier) wanted to do, primarily in the
Medicine Hat area.

Hilda married Jonathan Meier. Thinking that a change from farming might be
better, they chose to go to the west coast for a change in climate plus job
opportunities. They and their families live in Maple Ridge, B.C.

Shortly after their marriage Mary, youngest daughter, and her husband Jack
Nittel went north to Goldfields, Saskatchewan. Life there was rugged, but with
nice scenery the time spent there will always be a pleasant memory. Later on he
had a business in construction at Calgary, Alberta where they now reside.

With the free style of life but some anxious moments at times, Albert, youngest
son, and his wife Ruth (Schultz) remained in the agricultural field.

Albert and Ruth (Schultz) Pahl
by Albert Pahl

Albert and Ruth (Schultz) Pahl and young daughter Marjorie moved to the Harry
Jacobsen farm SW 12-12-2-W4 north of Irvine, in the spring of 1945, from the
home place 19 kilometers south. Sandra, the other daughter, was born in
Medicine Hat June 1948.

We did not receive much moisture during the growing season in those six years
until the wet fall of 1951 which made it difficult to finish combining.

Having friendly neighbors and "fence line" telephones made it more enjoyable,
more so in the winter with blocked roads at times. The prospects of irrigation
looked more rewarding, so with that in mind we moved to Medicine Hat in 1952
and farmed in the Seven Persons area.

Gottlieb Patzer was born December 25, 1849 in Seimany, Bessarabia, South

Elizabeth Patzer (pic)

with Elizabeth's children, John and Christina Hoff, from her previous marriage

Gottlieb and Elizabeth farmed about four and a half miles south of Irvine. One

Samuel and Kathleen (Adel) Patzer
submitted by Remona J. Schmidt

The father of Samuel Patzer, Gottlieb Patzer was born on the 25th of December
1849 at Seneine, Bessarabia, South Russia. He was a young man when he moved to
Harvey, North Dakota, U.S.A. There he was married a second time to Elizabeth
Weisz. They had five children, Mary, Samuel, Joseph, Elizabeth and Jacob. About
1907 the family moved to Canada and took up a homestead four miles south of
Irvine, Alberta.

Samuel was born August 17, 1902 and was raised in the Irvine district. When he
was 19 years old his dad passed away. Being the oldest son, he had a lot of the
farming responsibilities. On May 14, 1927 he married Kathleen Adel. They made
their home on a farm south of Irvine, just a mile west of his mother's place,
milking, and raising poultry. The grain farming was done with horses.

The 1930's were very hot, dry and windy. The soil on the fields drifted away
and they had many crop failures. Because of the drought they had a loss of
horses, cows, calves and poultry. Sam found work, such as making water
cisterns, breaking horses, road work, building and working at the Irvine grain
elevator, and also trapping coyotes, rabbits, etc. in winter. He did the best
he knew how to keep his family going. Sundays a lot of the men neighbours would
gather at our house to have their hair cut. Sometimes they would bring along
their wives and families and visit. So food had to be prepared for dinner,
supper and lunch at about 11 p.m. As there was no refrigeration, chickens were
usually butchered just before the meal. Butter, milk, cream and homemade cheese
were hung down in a cistern in a pail, to the water level, to keep cool. The
water for washing dishes, bathing, laundry, etc. was carried from the dam by
pail and in winter snow was melted. We used a lot of cow-chips as fuel in the
cook-stove for cooking and baking in the summer-time.

They had two children at the time, Floyd and me, Remona. Gathering cow-chips
went along with our other farm chores such as milking, gathering eggs, and
helping clean the poultry house. Floyd and I gathered wood from the creek and
stored it for winter use. We also gathered rocks to line the dam bridge, and
buffalo bones which Dad would haul to Irvine and sell, receiving $3 per wagon
load. I guess they were bought to make bone-meal. Floyd and I attended Berry
Centre school. In 1939 Lynn was born and two years later Bud was born. We moved
to Medicine Hat in 1943, stayed four years, then moved to a farm in the Norton
district. In March 1957, Sam and Kathleen moved back to Medicine Hat with Lynn
and Bud. Floyd had bought a farm and lived there.

Sam worked until his retirement in 1972. One of his jobs was landscaping and
care-taking of the Chapel Lawn Memorial Gardens at Medicine Hat, Alberta. On
June 9, 1986 he passed away, and is now resting at the same Chapel Lawn
Memorial Gardens. Kathleen still lives in her home in the city.

I, Remona, married Harry Schmidt of the Sandy Point area June 12, 1949. We have
two sons.

Floyd married Ursalla Gouth December 26, 1956. They had a son and a daughter.
Floyd passed away April 8, 1962.

Lynn married Charlotte Newman May 2, 1959. They have three sons. They live on
an acreage near Sherwood Park, Alberta.

Bud married Deanne Brandel May 30, 1968. They have two daughters and live close
to Athabasca, Alberta.

The Reg Phaff Family

Reg Phaff, born and raised in Hatton, Saskatchewan, married Lorna Pender, a
Medicine Hat girl, in 1952.

We are relative newcomers to the Irvine District having purchased land on the
south side of the #1 Highway from Otto Tschritter in 1967. At that time Reg
worked in the 'Hat and operated the ranch with hired help.

Reg Phaff Family: Steve, Debbie, Colin, Lorna, Reg (pic)

In 1969 we leveled 82 acres of land along the highway and planted corn for
silage. Over the years we continued our land leveling program and now also grow
alfalfa. This flat land is well suited to the growing of these two crops under
irrigation.

In 1971 we built a new ranch house and became full-time ranchers specializing
in purebred Charolais cattle and calling our operation P Bar 3 Ranch. Our
fiberglass bull and sign at the highway has become a landmark in the area. As
our herd increased we developed the ranch adding a sale barn, sheds, corrals,
etc.

As well as selling cattle privately, every spring we hold our Annual Bull Sale
and 1989 was our 20th consecutive sale.

We have two sons, Ken and Steve. Ken and his wife Cindy (Stripling) live in
Calgary with their two children, Bryce and Brianne. Ken is a Civil Engineer
with Canuck Engineering Ltd. Steve and his wife Deb (Schneider) live on the
ranch with their two sons, Colin and Wyatt. Steve and Reg work closely together
when selecting bulls for sale and heifer replacements. Steve is building up a
Charolais herd of his own.

Our present hired man and Jack-of-all-trades is Ronald Young. His wife,
Barbara, works at the Treasury Branch in the 'Hat and they have a son, Jordan.

Reg's parents, John and Florence Phaff, live in the 'Hat and recently
celebrated their 65th Wedding Anniversary.

We moved to Irvine in 1979 and enjoy living here. It is a quiet and friendly
community. We have some horses and enjoy riding them in the summer.
