Porter Family History

James Porter

James Porter, his wife and four sons, left County of Tyrone, Northern Ireland
in 1834, where they lived a stones throw from the Londonderry Wall. They set
out for Canada in a sailing ship, a trip that lasted just over four weeks. They
landed in Montreal and then went to Kingston from there by packet steamer
across Lake Ontario to Burlington. They checked their holdings with the Canada
Company Office and proceeded along the Huron Road which had been completed in
1832. They carried their possessions and arrived at Goderich, the only
established settlement on the Huron road.

"Attorneys of the Canada Company did in consideration of the sum of thirty
pounds, lawful money of the Province of Canada, grant and release to James
Porter township of Goderich, County of Huron, and Province aforesaid, yeoman,
all that certain parcel or pact of land situate as follows composing Lot 18 in
the third concession containing 80 acres and all the rights, title, and
interest of the said Canada Company unto James Porter, his heirs and assigns
forever."

The eldest of the family was Samuel Porter. His three sons Bob, Dick and Jim
Porter arrived in Medicine Hat on September 1, 1883 after working their way
west on the CPR from Brandon, Manitoba. The family had lived at Wingham,
Ontario prior to coming west.

Arriving in Medicine Hat, the three brothers, along with their father Samuel,
worked on the steel railway bridge crossing the South Saskatchewan River. The
boys carried nuts, bolts, and hot rivets during the construction, while their
father had the contract to haul the sand and gravel for the bridge pilings.

The homestead was taken out in the area now known as Porter's Hill. The family
ranched there and on the Gros Ventre Creek near Pashley. In those days the
range was open and the cattle drifted into the sheltered valleys south of
Irvine. In 1900, the Porter brothers established their ranch on the Stoney
Creek.

The RP brand was registered in the 1880's with Bob using it on the right rib,
and Richard using it on the left rib. The two brands have been used continually
since that time by four generations of the Porter family. The Porter brothers
operated a horse ranch at Irvine where they had a livery stable, as well as the
Orangeville Ranch at Bingville, now part of the British Block. Horses were sold
to settlers and U.S. Cavalry buyers would come into Canada to purchase remounts.

Bob Porter married Florence Cook of Orangeville, Ontario in 1901. Emerson
Porter was born in 1902 and was the oldest of their four children. Mary died at
the age of seven of scarlet fever and Robert Dundas was killed playing lacrosse
in 1931. The only surviving member of the family, Clara Sereni still resides in
Lethbridge. While Emerson was enrolled in his first year of Medicine at the
University of Alberta in 1921, his father was killed in a gas explosion at the
family home in Medicine Hat. He returned home to take over the operation of the
RP Ranch.

Emerson Porter

In 1932, Emerson married Thelma Sodero, a Medicine Hat nurse. The Porters were
active in the community of Irvine. During the 1920's Emerson helped organize
the Irvine Stampede. He supplied bucking horses, two of which were later sold
to the Calgary Exhibition and Stampede Co. The two work horses, which were
known as Bud and Dude, became Nightmare and Coffee-grinder. The late Pete
Knight won the 1927 Calgary Saddle Bronc Championship on Coffee-grinder.

Thelma Porter was active in the Irvine Women's Institute and was District
Convener (1958-60). Because of the bad roads and weather conditions many of the
husbands accompanied their wives to Irvine to attend their monthly W.I.
meetings. Feeling that they could contribute something to the community, a
men's organization was formed in 1951. It became known as the Chinook Club of
Irvine and is still an active service club today.

Following a lifetime of dedication to family, ranching and community service,
James Emerson Porter died in 1965.

The Porters had one son Bob who married Donna-Lee Harstead, a teacher from
Brooks, in 1957. They have three children, Robert Lee, Richard William and
Marni-Lynn. Lee and Cindy Litton attended Medicine Hat College and were married
in 1981. They have one daughter, Jordan Brynn (1987). Cindy is a nurse at the
Medicine Hat Regional Hospital. Rick and Janet MacPhail received their degrees
in Agriculture and Education, respectively, at the University of Alberta in
1981. They were married in 1984. They have a son Richard Kalan (1985) and a
daughter Kelsey Blair (1987). Marni is presently attending Medicine Hat College.

In 1983, the 100th anniversary of the RP Ranch was celebrated. Since 1984, when
Bob became the Member of Parliament for the constituency of Medicine Hat, Lee
and Rick have been operating the RP Ranch.

They have one daughter, Audra Lynn. They live at Scandia, Alberta.

Fredrick Jr. and Tillie (Tetz) Rath

Fredrick and Christina Rath immigrated to Canada from Russia in 1903. They
purchased the original homestead land of E 30-10-2-4, E 29-10-2-4 and another
quarter from Mr. Gainer.

In 1929 Fredrick Jr. purchased all of section 30 and the west half of 29 from
Fredrick Sr. He married Tillie Tetz in 1937. In 1953 he purchased the Bill Sulz
land, half section of NW 32, and E 29, and in 1959 Fredrick Jr. and Tillie sold
the original homestead to Dixon and retired to the Medicine Hat area where they
still reside today.

They had three children, James, Dixon, and Winnie. We all attended the Berry
Centre School until it was sold to the Town of Bow Island. I remember those
long, cold, winter, three-and-a-half-mile walks and horseback rides to school.
At that time there was a story that it was so cold that when you lit a match it
would instantly freeze and you would have to wait till spring to light your
smoke. We continued our schooling at the Irvine High School.

Emmanuel and Pauline (Remfert) Retelback

Emmanuel Retelback arrived in Canada in 1914 at the age of 19 years. He worked
for a rancher for a time and also in the construction of a railroad bed north
of Redcliff. He then took up a homestead in the Bowmanton area. After a valiant
effort at clearing rocks from the land he was forced into giving it up as a
useless task.

Pauline Refert came to North America with her parents Mathew and Julia Remfert
in 1899. After a short stay in South Dakota they came to Irvine. Upon arrival,
they stayed in Irvine for a few days until they took up a homestead in the
vicinity of the Concordia School. Mathew took employment with a survey crew
until he saved enough money to begin farming. Julia and little Pauline were
left at home. "Home" incidentally was a sod shanty.

In 1917 Emmanuel and Pauline were married and for six years farmed on rented
properties in the Concordia and Norton districts, at which time they bought the
farm that son George still farms.

The couple had seven children: Albert married Augusta Hoffman; Martha married
Oscar Mauch; Addy married David Brost; Clara married Daniel Brost; Sam; George;
and Harry.

Louis and Katherine (Weiss) Rhodes
by George Rhodes

Louis Rhodes of Alsace, France/Germany and Katherine Weiss of Irvine were
married at Medicine Hat in 1912.

They were blessed by the stork four times as follows, Fred 1914, Mary 1916,
George 1918, Elizabeth 1920.

As best I can recall, times, occupations, and residences changed frequently,
but usually in that order. If this was disturbing to adults, it went unnoticed
by the children, who found adventure and fun in frequent moves.

In the spring of 1928, after three years in and near Prince George, B.C., we
returned to Irvine just in time to actively participate in the dusty thirties
depression.

These were the formative years for us four children and form we did, both good
and bad habits. We found humorous sides to most things on most days and we did
enjoy many good times, like sleigh riding parties and skating parties and huge
bon fires of railroad ties. The building of the skating rink fence in 1931 was
an enthusiastic endeavor as were many pleasure filled days of hockey and
skating.

As the thirties expired and the war came on, the family migrated as follows -
Mary and Betty to Vancouver Island where they opened a coffee shop near the
Tofino Airbase. Both married local boys and became mothers. Mary had a son and
daughter and Betty had one daughter. Mary passed away in 1958 and Betty lives
in Nanaimo, B.C.

Fred spent 12 years on the C.P.R. then went into the hotel business at the
coast where he married and retired. There were no children. He died in 1981.

George married Hilda Schneider in Medicine Hat in 1939 and moved to the Niagara
Frontier where he was discharged from the R.C.A.F. in December, 1945.
Subsequently they had one son, moved to Buffalo, New York and in 1954 to
Seattle, Washington where they are happily retired. Semi annual visits are
still made to Medicine Hat and sometimes to Irvine for some pleasant greetings
and happy reminiscing.

P.S. Since a second grade spelling match at Irvine I have learned to spell this
word SHIP. With volume, speed and clarity (and subsequent years of
embarrassment) I substituted a "T" for the "P".

Andrew and Katharina (Becker) Rieger
by Lea (Rieger) Weiss

Both my father, Andrew Rieger, and my mother, Katharina Becker, were born near
Hosmer, South Dakota. The Rieger family and the Becker family came to Canada in
1902 and settled south of Irvine.

My parents were married in a little country church south of Irvine in 1907.
They started their home on a farm and lived there until 1917. They had three
children, Lea, Eva, Edward; I was the oldest. Both Eva and Edward died in
infancy.

In 1917 we moved to Irvine and bought the S. Wiedeman house and lived in it
until moving to Medicine Hat in 1929. My father worked at different jobs until
he started draying.

I went to the old two room school, and after quitting school worked for Mr. A.
Wiedemann in his store. The Wiedemanns bought our house when we left Irvine,
and Herman still lives in it.

In 1918 the Congregational Church was built and my father and Mr. Jacob Aman
were the first trustees. It was later called the United Church and was
demolished several years ago and the new church was built.

Andrew Rieger, Clarence Weiss, Lea (Rieger) Weiss, Katharina Rieger (pic)

Clarence Weiss and I were married in Medicine Hat in 1933. In 1953 he drowned
at Lake Newell. My mother died in 1963, after a lengthy illness. My father
passed away suddenly in 1968.

I have many fond memories of Irvine and always enjoy going to see the
improvements being made. There are only a few familiar faces left. Some moved
away and some passed away. In the earlier days there were several more stores
but I think the Irvine people have reason to be proud of the one store that is
left.

Adam Sr. and Louise Roll
by Ida L. (Roll) Gill, Granddaughter

Adam Roll Sr. was born in 1864 at Wilhelmsdal (or Wasilevska - Russian
spelling) a village approximately 60 miles north east of Odessa, Russia near
the Black Sea. Louise (Becker) Roll was born on August 26, 1873, at Odessa and
was married to Adam in 1893. They carried on farming operations and Adam was
also a wine merchant, buying his grapes for wine from Bessarabia.

On April 4, 1910 they, along with their family of six children (three sons and
three daughters), left Odessa and sailed from Rotterdam on April 23, 1910, on
the S. S. New Amsterdam, immigrating to Canada. They arrived at New York port
of entry staying for a brief period at Ellis Island. On May 2nd of the same
year they traveled to Eureka, South Dakota to the home of Gustav Bitz. They
then came to Canada, to Irvine, Alberta, and filed for a homestead on the
SE 23-12-2-W4 in the district now known as Clover Hill.

Adam Roll Sr. and family passport (in Russian) - 1910 - Page 1 (pic)

Adam Roll Sr. and family passport (in Russian) - 1910 - Page 2 (pic)

Adam Roll Sr. (pic)

Louise Roll (pic)

Adam Roll Jr. and Louise Roll (pic)

Adam Roll Sr. homestead (pic)

Adam, Louise and their family built their home of logs and sod with barn and
all other outbuildings attached in one long row. This was a custom they brought
with them from Russia. A portion of the house is still standing on the
homestead. As the years went by they bought up more land in this immediate area
and engaged in farming and related operations as did many pioneers in those
early years. In 1911 and 1913 two more sons were born to this family. In 1917,
due to Adam's failing health, they purchased a home in Irvine and semi-retired
there until 1927 when Adam passed away at age 63. Between the period of 1917 to
about 1927 sons Adam and John farmed the home place. When the two younger sons,
Theodore and Jacob were old enough to do the farming, they and Louise again
moved out to the homestead and resided between there and the home in Irvine
until Theodore was married in 1935 and took charge of the farm. Louise Roll
once again took up residence in Irvine and resided there until 1947. In March
of 1947 she moved to the Haven of Rest at Medicine Hat and passed away in
August of the same year, age 74 years. Both Adam and Louise Roll are buried in
St. George Cemetery at Irvine. The original Adam Roll Sr. homestead is
currently owned by Darrell Maser (great grandson and fourth generation of the
Roll family.)

Their family was as follows:

Adam Jr. (deceased 1980) married Bertha Rauser.

Johann (deceased 1964) married Wilhelmina Trekofski (deceased 1985).

Elizabeth (deceased 1935) married Simon Dewalt (deceased 1960).

Louise (deceased 1956) married Theodore Maser (deceased 1970).

George (deceased 1987) married Emma Trekofski (deceased 1984).

Katherin married Stanley Vickers (deceased).

Theodore (deceased 1968) married Freda Paul (deceased 1983).

Jacob (deceased 1986) married Kathleen Kennedy (deceased 1975).

Adam Jr. and Bertha (Rauser) Roll
by Ida L. Gill, daughter

Adam Roll Jr., oldest child of Adam and Louise (Becker) Roll Sr., born on
August 26, 1894, his mother's 21st birthday, emigrated from Odessa Russia on
April 4, 1910 along with his parents, two brothers and three sisters, coming to
Canada to Irvine, Alberta. They settled on a farm homestead north of Irvine.

Many other settlers were also coming into this area at the same time and in
1912 application was made to organize a school district. Approval was not
granted until 1913 because of some opposition from the ranchers. After the
approval was granted a school was constructed on the SW 24-12-2-W4 and thus
came into being the Clover Hill School District. I don't know about the clover
but there certainly are many hills in the area. Mr. Jacob Zwick was the main
carpenter and Adam, along with many of the other neighbors, helped with the
construction. Teachers, coming into the area, offered evening classes for the
new residents and Adam was one of the students who would attend two evenings a
week, during the winter months, thus assisting him to learn the English
language.

Adam and Bertha (Rauser) Roll, March 11, 1917 (pic)

In 1916 or 1917 Adam obtained a homestead entry and filed on the NW 19-12-1-W4.
He built a small house here and, close by, a log and sod barn, and this he
called "Home".

Bertha Rauser, born February 2, 1899, daughter of Jacob and Anna Maria
(Duelker) Rauser, had also emigrated from Bessarabia, Russia in 1911 with her
parents and they settled on "The Bench" at Thelma, Alberta. As she grew up she
would go out and work for other homesteaders in the area. One family she
remembers in particular was Mr. and Mrs. Jim English.

When Adam's thoughts turned to finding himself a wife, he had to travel
considerably south for his bride. Adam and Bertha were married in Irvine, at
Christ Lutheran Church, on March 11, 1917, by Pastor J. Oberhammer.

In April of 1918 Adam and Bertha bought the S-30-12-1-W4, from a bachelor by
the name of Harold S. Tveten. They moved north onto the SW quarter where Mr.
Tveten had built a little home. The early and mid 20's were very dry years and
the wells were too shallow to provide sufficient water for the cattle so water
was hauled from some of the neighbors that had stronger flowing wells. This
took many hours out of every day and Bertha was the one delegated to do this
chore while Adam attended to the farming. In 1926 they moved to the Adam Roll
Sr. homestead and in 1927 they rented the Andreas Glock Sr. place and farmed
this along with their own to the north. During the summer of 1928 George Roll,
Adam's brother, purchased a well drilling rig and began drilling for water on
the original home place. Water was struck in abundance and again Adam and his
family moved back to their homestead.

Adam Roll Jr. Family: Rubin, Bertha, Oscar, Adam, Ida (pic)

Adam Roll Jr. Family -1937: Back: Ida, Rubin; Front: Adam, Bertha (pic)

During the lifetime of farming in the Clover Hill District Adam and Bertha
encountered some dry and lean years, the worst of which came during the "dirty
thirties", which proved a real struggle and struggle they did. They however
were not alone in this struggle. At times they had trouble making ends meet but
they did the best they could. Later they would reminisce on those years and
would admit they were still happy years in spite of all the hardships. During
the winter months it was not unusual to have several of the neighbors arrive at
another neighbor's home for a surprise card party followed by a midnight lunch,
supplied by the ladies. The next week would be some other neighbor's turn to be
surprised and so they made the rounds. I also recall attending, with my
parents, the one room rural school Christmas Concerts followed by a dance with
music supplied by local talent. These times of entertainment, though primitive,
were none the less well attended and enjoyed by all. This goes to prove that
money was not always necessary to create pleasure.

Dad and Mom, Adam and Bertha, along with their son, Rubin, continued to farm
until 1950. They then bought the former Lutheran Parsonage and moved to Irvine.
After the Clover Hill School closed Adam drove the school bus into Irvine. In
1962, due to ill health, he had to retire. They still had an interest in the
farm but in the fall of 1962, when their son was killed at a railroad crossing
at Walsh, they, along with Rubin's widow, disposed of the place.

In 1963 Adam and Bertha bought a house in Medicine Hat, on 9th St. S.E. and
resided there until Adam passed away on March 5, 1980 at age 85 years. He is
buried in Hillside Cemetery.

Bertha and Adam Roll 60th Anniv., March 11, 1977 (pic)

During Adam's lifetime he took great interest in politics and community
affairs. He was a trustee of the Clover Hill School District, a staunch
supporter and helped organize a Social Credit Local. He was also instrumental
in helping organize the Many Island Grazing Association. Mother, Bertha, being
of German descent and not having any formal schooling of the English language,
had to learn by "trial and error". She boarded many of the teachers while
living at Clover Hill, thus she was able to grasp the English language. She was
very much a home-maker and was "a mother away from home" to many of the female
homesick school teachers. Never did we have to want at a meal as there were
always the necessary staples in the home. She was able to cook plenty for every
one with whatever she had on hand in the kitchen. Many people will also
remember her for her home made noodles and kucha. When she invited anyone to
stay for lunch, you could be sure it usually ended up being a full course meal.
She also enjoyed her garden, crocheting and embroidery. Mom moved to Maranatha
Villa in 1981 and in September of 1983 she moved to the Haven of Rest where she
still resides. She is 90 years old and is in reasonably good health.

Bertha and Adam's family consisted of five children, two of whom died in
infancy.

Oscar Adam was born on July 17, 1918. He was not a very strong child. In late
1928 he developed diphtheria and passed away on January 14, 1929 at age ten
years. He is buried in Hillside Cemetery.

Rubin Jacob was born on April 6, 1920 and received all his education at the
Clover Hill School. More information is related elsewhere under "Rubin Roll".

Ida Louise (Gill) was born on May 26, 1921. She too received her education at
Clover Hill then attended Irvine School for her Grade 11 and one year at
Medicine Hat where she took a business course. She worked for School Division
No. 4, with the late Mr. F. G. McLaughlin, from 1940 to 1944. That same year
she married Harry Gill. More information on her and Harry's family is related
elsewhere under "Harry Gill".

Rubin Jacob Roll
By Ida L. Gill (Sister)

Rubin Jacob Roll, born April 6, 1920, was the second son of Bertha and Adam
Roll. He grew up and spent his entire life on the farm in the Clover Hill
District, where he also received his education, grades one to nine inclusive.
Rubin was a bit of a mischievous little fellow and in his first year of school
he decided, one day while he was in the school house alone, that it might be
fun to lock the door so no one could get in. When the teacher, Mr. Ralph Grant,
asked Rubin to open the door, he just laughed and thought it was a great joke.
Mr. Grant had to scale the wall and climb in the window to get into the school.
You can be sure this incident did not go unattended and, when Rubin came home
that evening and his parents were advised of his prank, he got his just reward
once more. Rubin had learned his lesson and decided no more "hanky panky".

Rubin Roll (pic)

Evelyn (McShane) Roll (pic)

After Rubin's school years he took up farming along with his parents. During
the depression years he would go elsewhere, in the fall of the year, and help
with harvesting at Vauxhall and logging at Wildwood, Alberta. When his parents
moved to Irvine he took over the farming and ranching operations.

On December 20, 1960 Rubin married a Scottish lass by name of Evelyn McShane.
Evelyn is the daughter of John and Anna (Dolan) McShane of Uddingston, Scotland
and came to Canada on January 25, 1960. Their son, Gerard Adam, was born on
December 17, 1961. Exactly one day after Gerard's first birthday Rubin was
killed crossing the railway at Walsh - December 18, 1962. He is buried at
Hillside Cemetery.

In the spring of 1963 Evelyn bought a house and moved to Medicine Hat with her
son. She worked at the Medicine Hat Hospital, in the dietary section, for a
number of years.

On October 14, 1967 Evelyn married George Bonagofsky and they built a new home
in the Crestwood area in Medicine Hat where they still live. George operates a
farm at Fox Valley, Saskatchewan and spends many hours out there during the
spring and summer. Evelyn looks after the home in the 'Hat and Gerard (still
single) has been working for the C.P.R. for several years.

Wilhelmina (Trekofski) and John Roll, February 1920 (pic)

John and Wilhelmina (Trekofski) Roll

John Roll, second son of Adam Roll Sr. and Louise, born January 15, 1896,
immigrated with his parents from Russia in 1910 at the age of 14 years. They
settled in Irvine, Alberta in 1911. During the years 1911 to 1918 John worked
as a labourer at various jobs including the C.P.R. in Manitoba, building
railway grade, being teamster driving teams of horses or oxen. In 1918, John
homesteaded the SE 10-12-2-W4 for two years. In February, 1920 he married
Wilhelmina Barbara Trekofski, who was born June 16, 1910. The newlyweds took up
residence and farmed the SE 23-12-2-W4 which was his parents' homestead. From
here they moved to the Norton area south of Dunmore where they farmed for five
or six years. In 1929 John and Minnie moved back north of Irvine to a farm they
purchased from Mr. Gutterud which was situated on the NE 18-12-1-W4. They
remained on this farm till 1953 in spring when Edwin, the youngest son, took
over the farm. John and Minnie bought a house in Irvine and lived there till
August 1964 when John passed away due to ill health. Wilhelmina, in 1966, sold
and moved to Medicine Hat and lived there till 1985, when she also passed away,
at the age of 84 years. They are both buried in the family plot in Hillside
Cemetery.

John Roll Farm (pic)

John Roll Family: John, Emil, Minnie, Rudolph, Helena, Edwin (pic)

During the period from 1920 to the time of John and Minnie's passing they
reared four children.

The first was a daughter, Helena, who married Fred Boettcher of Schuler,
Alberta. They have one daughter and two grandsons.

Next was Rudolph A. and he married the former Mary Miller of Rockyford. They
have two sons and two daughters and three grandchildren.

The third was Emil A. who joined the navy and while on the way overseas peace
was declared and he returned home. Upon his discharge from the navy he went to
work as a mechanic. At this time Emil decided to marry Mary Gaetz of Bow
Island. They have two sons and one daughter and four grandchildren.

Last was Edwin A. who was married and has two children and three grandchildren.
Edwin took over the farm in 1953 till 1979, at which time the farm that John
and Minnie purchased in 1929 and sold to the youngest son passed into other
hands, namely the Pasciel family.

George and Emma (Trekofski) Roll
by Gertrude (Roll) Engel

George Roll, the third son of Adam Sr. and Louise, immigrated to the Clover
Hill district with his parents in the year 1910. Dad attended school at Clover
Hill and Irvine and during his youth he worked on various ranches as far west
as the foothills, being quite adept at "breaking horses".

My parents were married on October 3, 1930. Their first home was north of Walsh
on a farmstead which they left to move into the hamlet of Walsh in the fall of
1938. Dad drove the first school bus from Walsh to Irvine from 1940 until he
retired.

Dad was somewhat of an inventor, operating a water well drilling rig throughout
the area. The first machine was powered by horses which were moved from one
location to another by elder son, Allan, until later a gasoline engine was
employed. Dad also made his own well casing using cinders and cement.

Emma (Trekofski) and George Roll, 1930 (pic)

George Roll Family: Back: Gertrude, Lily, Clifford, Agnes, Audrey, Marjorie;
Front: Allan, Emma, George, Glen (pic)

Upon retiring from school bus driving, Mom and Dad moved to Irvine, during
which time Dad painted apartments in Medicine Hat. Their last move took them to
Calgary, where they managed a number of apartment buildings, with Dad using his
painting talents to keep the buildings maintained. They enjoyed bowling with
the Calgary Seniors, as well as cribbage, horse shoes and shuffleboard. Mom,
Emma, succumbed to brain cancer in August 1984, after which Dad, George,
resided in a seniors' lodge and nursing home until his death in June 1987.

Their family consisted of three sons and five daughters: Gertrude married Allan
Engel; Lillian became Mrs. Ed Baumbach; Allan married Irene Beadle; Agnes
married Abdul Zeer; Glen; Audrey; Clifford married Marlene McLaughlin; and
Marjorie married Alex Prediger.

Theodor (Ted) Roll (most commonly used spelling of "Theodor")
by Shirley Jean (Roll) Tucker (additional information from Loretta (Roll)
Genert)

Except for a brief period when he attended college in Chicago, Ted Roll spent
his life in Irvine, Alberta, where he was born, attended school, and farmed.
Ted had a keen sense of community; and spent most of his adult life fighting
energetically to improve the quality of education in the Medicine Hat Rural
School District. As an aggressive and determined member and Chairman of School
Division #4, he championed the consolidation of rural schools in the division,
into the major area towns, but later, just as strongly opposed the compulsory
bussing of high school students to Medicine Hat. Ted believed passionately that
the school was the heart of the community, and that over centralization of the
school system would contribute irrevocably to the decline and decay of
small-town Alberta.

Ted was a fine leader, an extremely principled individual whose ideals and
concerns about community living are reflected in many modern concepts of urban
planning.

Ted was happiest when involved in social and political causes. He spent much
time and energy working for The Farmers' Union, Irvine Town Council, School
Divison #4 (for over 25 years!), the Liberal Party, the Cancer Society, the
Medicine Hat Hospital Board, the Board of Medicine Hat College (Charter Member).

Although the community of Irvine has never acknowledged the role Ted played in
attempting to strengthen and vitalize community life, his family and friends
were keenly aware that his life was sacrificed in those pursuits. Ted suffered
his first heart attack when he was 52, and died at 56.

We adored our father, were touched by his firm, but generous, supportive
nature, awed by his incredible vitality, and sometimes a little overwhelmed by
his stubborn commitment to his social and political ideals.

Sharon, born 1940, married Emery Fortin and has no children. Emery is a

Marilyn, born 1945, married Bryan Heibert and has two sons, Theodor (Ted) and

The Rub Family
submitted by Edwin Rub

Grandfather, Mr. Jacob Rub, was born in Germany. In the middle of the 1870's
his parents and their family, and many other families, moved to South Russia,
by invitation of the Russian government, to settle the land. They were given a
parcel of land, equal to about 160 acres, on condition that they develop it
agriculturally. The families lived in colonies located near Odessa on the north
west shore of the Black Sea.

After a score or so of years, the land for settlement was becoming increasingly
difficult to obtain. Also a change in government policy plus compulsory
military service persuaded the settlers to look elsewhere for a livelihood for
their growing family.

About 1894 or 95 they, along with many other families, immigrated to the United
States, landing at New York. They traveled inland and obtained land in South
Dakota. This was dry country and not suitable for agriculture. They looked to
the north and made their home at Jamestown, North Dakota, the government again
helping them to settle the area.

In 1905 they removed from North Dakota and came to Alberta, making their home
on a farm south of Irvine near Elkwater on Section 3-10-3-4. There they raised
their family of four sons and six daughters.

In 1920 the parents with their family, except the oldest son John, moved to
California where they resided until their passing. Surviving to date is the
youngest daughter, Rachel (White) of St. Helena, California.

John and Adeline (Trekofski) Sackman

John Sackman was born January 24, 1899 in Russia. He immigrated to Canada in
1914 with his parents, settling in the Newburg district. At the age of 24, John
married Adeline Trekofski on January 28, 1923. She was born August 23, 1902 in
the United States, moving to Canada at an early age.

John and Adeline farmed several places before settling on a mixed farm three
miles south of Irvine, just off what is referred to as the Bull Trail. They
have one son George, who was born January 18, 1925. On their farm they had milk
cows, chickens and other livestock. In those days, there was no running water
or electrical appliances. However, when radios first came about, they would
walk about one mile to Jake and Alice Linderman's to listen to their favorite
series of "Amos and Andy". John and Adeline were also great crokinole and card
players.

Adeline and John Sackman, 1958 (pic)

In 1955 due to John's ill health, they sold their farm and bought a house in
the town of Irvine. In May of 1961 John passed away. Adeline remained in
Irvine, extending her hospitality to anyone who came to visit. She was an avid
church-goer to the Peace United Church and a member of the U.C.W. group. She
also served as a church elder and the church janitor.

In 1978 she sold her home in Irvine and moved into Parkside Manor in Medicine
Hat. Adeline attends the many functions available at the Manor and the Veiner
Centre, such as playing various card games, bingo, and countless number of
teas. She also attends Memorial Salem United Church on a regular basis.

John Sackman Family: Adeline, George, John - 1946 (pic)

Adeline celebrated her 85th birthday in 1987. She is still very active and is
enjoying her retirement years to the fullest.

Her family includes her son George, a retired school teacher who married Ruth
Leinwebber and presently resides in Victoria, B.C., two grandsons, David and
Paul (married to Judy Anderson), who reside in Calgary, and three
great-grandchildren, Mark, Ryan, and Clare.

Clarence and Ida (Rieger) Sailer
submitted by Gene Sailer and Doris Murschel

Clarence and Ida (Reiger) Sailer moved to the farm (SW 17-11-4-W4) on the Gros
Ventre Creek in the spring of 1927 as a young couple with their first son,
Wallace. They raised beef cattle and grain (mostly wheat).

This was just prior to the "Hungry 30's". Dad (Clarence) did a lot of
veterinary work, riding on horseback over a large area trying to earn a few
dollars a week. Mom (Ida) milked cows and looked after the pigs and chickens
and raised a growing family.

Ida and Clarence Sailer (pic)

We all remember the stories of how Dad mined coal from the edge of his property
to keep the house heated over the winter months. Mom bailed water for a number
of cattle that were being boarded on the farm, even though the CV brand graced
only a few right ribs. They faced the same hardships during this time that
everyone else experienced. This period of time was seldom referred to as Mom
and Dad were both hard working individuals who looked forward to making the
best life for their family that they could.

By 1944, the whole set of children had arrived. There were six sons, Wallace,
Leonard, Allan, Melvin, Eugene, and Alfred, and three daughters, Doris, Vivian
and Marjorie. All of the children attended Coal Centre School which was located
on the edge of the Sailer farm. One of the boys was always the "janitor" and
was responsible for carrying water to the school from the farm house and
lighting the fire in the big pot bellied stove to heat the school all day
during the winter. Other family members swept floors, washed windows, cleaned
blackboards and brushes, and generally kept everything neat and tidy. Dad was a
member, and chairman, of this local school board for over 20 years. Often the
school teacher would board at the Sailer place. The last couple of years a
teacherage was built in the yard with Lena Wilson and Mr. Burkett as the last
two teachers before the school was closed at the end of the 1953-54 term.
Thereafter, all children in the area were bussed to Irvine School.

Allan, Wallace, Eugene, Clarence, Alfred, Len, Mel Sailer (pic)

The Glen Wooley dairy herd was purchased in June of 1951, and the family farm
became primarily a milk producing unit until 1957. Of course, every family
member had a set of chores to do, getting up each morning at 6:00 a.m. After
chores, milking and breakfast, it was off to school on the Pete Schaffer bus
while the older children worked on the farm.

Clarence was injured in a tractor accident in 1958, and overcame million-to-one
odds to keep his leg and walk again. His arterial transplant was only the third
ever done in Calgary, where surgeons operated while receiving instructions and
suggestions over the phone from Toronto. This slowed Dad down a bit, but didn't
come close to stopping him!

Clarence Sailer farm (pic)

The family farm was sold in 1960 and Clarence and Ida moved to Medicine Hat and
retirement. Dad passed away in March of 1979. Mom was an active member of the
Evangelical United Brethern Church and an avid gardener until her passing in
June of 1985. The oldest son Wallace died in November of 1984. They will long
be remembered by their family and all of their friends.

Len lives in Vernon, B.C. and is a foreman at Consumer Glass.

Doris (Mrs. Ernest Murschel) resides in Medicine Hat and is a homemaker.

Allan lives in Didsbury and is an identification officer with the Calgary City
Police.

Viv (Mrs. Oscar Schwab) lives in Calgary and is employed at Eatons as a payroll
clerk.

Mel lives in Calgary and is an accountant with an oil firm.

Gene lives in Medicine Hat and is a principal in the public school system.

Alfred lives in Coaldale and is a correctional officer with the Attorney
General's Department.

Marjorie (Mrs. David Loranger) lives in Medicine Hat and is employed by
Pattison Funeral Home.

Doris, Marg, Vivian Sailer (pic)

Gottfred and Dorothy (Rauser) Sauter

Gottfred Sauter was born in Kherson in the province of Bessarabia in Russia. In
1905, at the age of 20, he immigrated to Canada with his parents, Fredrick and
Emielia Sauter, along with one brother Carl and one sister Katie. The family
arrived by boat in New York and journeyed to Jamestown, North Dakota. In 1906,
they came to Canada by wagon. When they arrived at Swift Current, Saskatchewan
all of their belongings including their wagon, horses and a few cows were
loaded on a train and they traveled to Irvine, Alberta. Many German people had
settled in this area. Homesteads were available in an area called "the bench"
which was the Thelma area. After filing for a homestead, the family moved 40
miles south to start farming.

Gottfred and his brother had been educated in Russia, but his brother, Carl,
took more schooling in the city of Medicine Hat, enough to read English and
understand Mathematics. The brothers worked on ranches within the area. In
1907, their father passed away after being sick with pneumonia. Years later,
their mother remarried and moved to Odessa, Washington.

Gottfred worked as a ranchhand at the Mitchell Ranch. He later took up a
homestead of his own consisting of two quarters. On this land, he built a log
house to where he later brought his bride Dorothy Rauser. Dorothy Rauser was
born in Katsabach, in the province of Bessarabia, Russia. In 1911, at the age
of 22, she immigrated to Canada with her parents, Jacob and Anne Marie Rauser,
along with two sisters, Ida and Bertha. After coming to Montreal by boat, they
continued west on the train as far as Irvine. They joined two of Dorothy's
sisters, Mary and Christina (Mrs. John Fandrick) in the Thelma area. They had
arrived a year earlier. The parents also started a homestead with which Dorothy
and her sisters helped. She met Gottfred one day as he was passing by, taking
some horses to the Mitchell Ranch (about 14 miles south).

Gottfred, Dorothy and Alfred Sauter - 1915 (pic)

They were married in June of 1912, and farmed and raised cattle. They were
blessed with five children, Alfred, Hilda, Erna, Fred and Wallace. In 1924, a
new four room house was built with a living room. This was a great improvement
compared to the log house. The three oldest children attended the Lebanon
School, a distance of four miles away. Alfred also went to school in Irvine and
Vauxhall.

In 1929, the parents decided to buy some land south of Irvine, to be closer to
a school. Two quarters and 96 acres were bought, originally known as "the
Schubert place". This farm was located a quarter of a mile from the Berry
Centre School and teachers often boarded in their home. Later, two more
quarters of land were purchased from their closest neighbor, Phillip Schneider.

Their first gas powered vehicle was bought in 1938 and was a Chev half-ton
truck. The cultivated land was worked with horses until 1939. It was then that
a new Case tractor and a six-foot tiller were bought, which Gottfred was very
proud to own. Crops were often headered so the straw could be saved. In the
summertime, cows were always milked and cream and butter were sold for extra
money. Extra work included raising chickens and pigs. Dorothy did a lot of
canning with the produce from her big garden. Apple, crabapple and plum trees
were planted. There were usually lots of fruit and jams and jellies canned
including saskatoon and chokecherry.

Gottfred Sauter and 1939 Case tractor (pic)

In 1925, they suffered the loss of their oldest daughter, Hilda, who passed
away after a lengthy illness of diphtheria.

In the fall of 1943, Gottfred passed away. He suffered a heart attack after a
short stay in the Medicine Hat Hospital. Dorothy Sauter passed away in January
of 1979 at the age of 89 years.

Alfred married Susan Fandrick in 1932 and they farmed his farm in the Thelma
area until 1951, first moving to Medicine Hat and a few years later to
Claresholm, Alberta. They had three children, Vern, Audrey, and Barry who died
as an infant.

Erna married Art Boschee in 1934 and farmed in the Robinson and Irvine
districts until they moved to Medicine Hat. They had two children, Shirley and
Gerald.

Shortly after his father's death, Fred married Hilda Seitz. They lived with
Fred's mother until the spring of 1944, moving first to the "Ligget Ranch" near
Elkwater and a few years later to the Art Boschee farm. Their children are
Ronald, Sharon, Larry and Caroline. 1957 brought with it another move to the
Trekofski farm. Hilda and Fred moved to Medicine Hat in 1980.

Wallace married Frieda Lehr in 1948. They had taken over the family farm and
had two daughters, Gloria and Gail. They moved off the farm in 1980 to live in
Medicine Hat and later sold it in 1985.

Fred and Hilda Sauter

Fred Sauter was born January 5, 1922, the third child of Gottfred and Dorothy
Sauter, brother to Alfred, Erna (Boschee) and Wallace. As a child Fred attended
Berry Centre and Irvine School. In 1943 his father passed away. His mother
continued to live on the family farm for many years after. Fred met Hilda
Seitz, daughter of Christian and Rosina (Schlenker) Seitz of the Little Plume
District, and in October 1943 they were married.

For a short time Fred and his new wife lived on the family farm with his mother
and brother Wallace. In 1944 Fred and Hilda moved to the Earl Ligget Ranch near
Elkwater. In the same year their first son was born, Ronald Charles. In June
1946 their second child Sharon June was born. In this year (1946) they also
purchased and moved to the Art Boschee farm in the Robinson District. In 1949
Larry Wilfred was born. The three children traveled on horseback to attend
Cypress School. In 1955 their fourth child Caroline Ann was born. In 1957
Sauters moved to the present family farm, five miles south of Irvine,
previously owned by John Trekofski. The children completed their education at
the Irvine School.

Fred and Hilda semi-retired to Medicine Hat in 1980. Fred still does some
farming. They are both enjoying good health and are able to do some traveling.

Fred Sauter Family: Back: Carol, Larry, Sharon, Ron; Front: Fred, Hilda - 40th

Ronald married Betty Aman and they farm near Irvine.

Sharon completed a computer education in Calgary and later married Vern Fauth.
They presently reside in Calgary.

Ronald Charles and Betty (Aman) Sauter

In 1944 I was born in Medicine Hat General Hospital to Fred and Hilda (Seitz)
Sauter. At that time we lived on the Earl Ligget place near Elkwater and later
in the fall of 1946 moved to the Art Boschee place. I later attended Cypress
School which still stands high on a hill beside the 41 highway which in earlier
years was the 48 highway. We went to school everyday two miles on horseback and
sometimes did our visiting with the team and sleigh when the snow was so deep
that nothing else could get around.

On April 1st of 1957 we moved down closer to Irvine and bought the Johnny
Trekofski place which is in the Gros Ventre Creek Coulee, five miles south
along the 41 highway. I attended school in Irvine until 1962 at which time I
farmed with my dad as well as worked out on different jobs, Hycroft China, Robb
Construction, Irvine Texaco, tractor on road when #48 highway was reconstructed
in 1967, Ludwig and Sons as bus driver.

Ron Sauter Family: Conway, Ron, Craig, Betty, Troy (pic)

On October 21st, 1967, I married Betty (Aman) (our centennial project) and
settled down just a mile further east of Dad's farm on the Henry Trekofski
place which is situated where the Gros Ventre and Ross Creeks meet. At that
time I was still driving school bus.

As the farm started to grow and the cattle herd increased, we also started a
family. Our first son was born on December 26, 1969 whom we named Craig Ronald.
Our second son was born June 11, 1972 whom we named Troy Curtis. Our family was
not complete until our third son was born on April 16, 1982 whom we named
Conway Steven.

I have been active in our community serving as president of the Irvine
Recreation Board for many years. I was an original member when it was formed in
1971. I was an original member of the Ag Society and served a term as
president. I was the Irvine 4-H Beef Club leader for four years as well as
district Council Vice-president for three years, Stoney Hill Grazing Director,
Chinook Club member, executive on curling club, etc.

Betty, who was born and raised in the Irvine community, taught Sunday school
and Bible school for many years, was a U.C.W. member and president many years,
a graduate Explorer and C.G.I.T. member, junior choir member, Hi-C's, secretary
of Girl Guides, secretary-treasurer of Boy Scouts, active in 4-H work, and is
serving on Parent Council, etc.

Since I moved to the Irvine community in 1957 I have seen many changes, not
only in school expansion but also in recreation expansion. After taking part in
the construction of the Complex, Betty and I are happy that it is not only for
our present, but also for our future generations to enjoy. It is a community
project.

Wallace and Frieda (Lehr) Sauter

Wallace Sauter was born on October 20th, 1926. He was the youngest in his
family. His parents, Gottfred and Dorothy Sauter, had homesteaded in the Thelma
area. When Wallace was two years old his parents bought land and moved south of
Irvine in the Ross Creek. This farm was about a quarter of a mile from the
Berry Centre School. One of the reasons for the move was that the older
children had had a long distance to travel to the Lebanon School and the
parents wanted a school closer for the younger children to attend. Wallace's
oldest brother, Alfred, stayed on the farm at Thelma. His other brother, Fred,
and sister, Erna, also took their education at the Berry Centre School.

The house at the time of the move needed some renovations; later on a new
garage and barn were built. The family bought two more quarters of land from
their neighbor, Phillip Schneider. The children always helped with the farming
besides milking cows and other chores.

In 1943, Gottfred Sauter passed away after a short illness. At the young age of
16, Wallace took over the farm. His mother, Dorothy, moved to Medicine Hat in
1946. In 1948, Wallace married Frieda Lehr.

Frieda Lehr was born on January 14th, 1932 and was the oldest daughter of Henry
and Hilda Lehr. This family, along with sisters Phyllis and Ruth, lived on a
farm in the Spring Coulee which was about two miles south of the Berry Centre
School. Frieda and her sisters usually rode on horseback to school, except for
one year. That year they boarded in Irvine part time or caught a school bus at
the Elkwater road to Irvine School. Ruth finished her education in Irvine. The
children helped their parents with the chores and gardening.

During the first year Wallace and Frieda were married a new home was built.
This meant that the old home had to be torn down. Some of the furniture was
moved into the nearby garage and granaries. A basement was dug with a hand
scraper and horses. The contractors came out and stayed a few days at a time.
This meant a lot of meals had to be cooked. The house was finished in the fall
of 1949, just in time for the birth of their first daughter, Gloria. Three
years later, in 1953, their second addition, another daughter, Gail, was born.

Albert and Gloria (Sauter) Billey, Frieda and Wallace Sauter, Gail (Sauter) and
Bob Boschee (pic)

Jolene, Kevin Boschee, Quinton, Quadelle Billey, Michelle Boschee (pic)

In 1957, electricity was installed which brought with it many conveniences like
running water and television. Wallace did his farming with a 44 Massey tractor
for many years. He bought his first Ford one-ton truck in 1949. Besides
farming, there was always lots of extra work, such as putting up much needed
new buildings like a new barn and granaries and also new corrals. The family
milked cows and raised chickens for many years. Gardening and canning were also
done annually. Gloria and Gail helped with chores and housework.

The family were members of Christ Lutheran Church in Irvine where the girls
attended Sunday School. The girls took their elementary and high school
education at Irvine, traveling in with the school bus.

Gloria graduated from high school in 1967 and continued her education in the
Medicine Hat College and also the University of Alberta in Edmonton. She
married Albert Billey in 1968. They both taught school at Schuler for two years
and then moved to Ponoka. They still live in Ponoka with their children,
Quinton and Quadelle.

Gail graduated in 1971 from high school and continued her education at SAIT in
Calgary, graduating from the Health Record Technician program. She married Bob
Boschee in 1971 and has worked both at the Foothills and Grace Hospital in
Calgary. They still live in Calgary and have three children, Jolene, Kevin and
Michelle.

Wallace and Frieda farmed until 1980 and then moved to Medicine Hat. They sold
their farm in 1985.

Karl (Charlie) and Mary (Rauser) Sauter
submitted by Fred Sauter (Vauxhall)

Karl (Charlie) Sauter, brother of Gottfred Sauter, was born August 13, 1892 and
came to Canada with his parents as a very young man, from Kherson near Odessa,
Russia. His parents, Mr. and Mrs. Frederick Sauter and a sister and brother
first arrived in North Dakota, U.S.A. and then came on to Canada in 1907. They
settled in the Thelma District. Eventually Charlie met and married Mary Rauser
and moved into the town of Irvine where he first worked for Sam Kalmbach. While
living in Irvine two daughters, Edith and Elsie, were born to them.

Charlie and his family left Irvine in 1918 to live in Vauxhall and here they
stayed until 1949. While in Vauxhall three more children, Fred, Charlie Jr.,
and Marion, were born. Charlie Sr. operated a lumber yard until they moved to
Calgary to retire.

Charlie passed away on August 4, 1969 at age 77. His wife Mary passed away on
February 3, 1978 at age 83. They are both buried in Hillside Cemetery in
Medicine Hat.

Gottlieb and Caroline (Hausauer) Schaffer
by Rosina Braun

Gottlieb Schaffer was born on July 24, 1854 at Glueckstal, South Russia while
Caroline Hausauer was born at Klein Neudorf, South Russia on February 17, 1860.
Following their marriage on October 10, 1877 at Klein Neudorf, they resided in
Glueckstal for a period and later in Odessa, Russia. Eight children were born
to them in Russia. At that time it was the custom to draft boys of 15 and 16
years of age into the Russian army. As their eldest sons were nearing draft
age, they decided to go to America. They traveled to Liverpool, England where
they boarded the S.S. Vancouver, arriving at Halifax on April 10, 1893. They
proceeded by train to Winnipeg where they were quarantined before crossing the
border at Neche, settling near Eureka, South Dakota. They later took up a
homestead near Ashley, North Dakota where they farmed for several years.
Several more children were born to them while they were living in the United
States. In all, 23 children came to bless their union, some dying at birth and
in infancy.

In 1908 Gottlieb came to Canada to look for a homestead. By this time some of
their family had already married and settled in the Dakotas. In the spring of
1909 the Schaffer family sold their property and some of their belongings,
loaded their remaining possessions and livestock into freight cars and headed
for Canada. Some of the boys rode in the eight cars to feed and water the
livestock while the rest of the family traveled in passenger cars. They settled
at Irvine, Alberta, homesteading on the SE 9-13-3-W4.

Gottlieb Schaffer Family: Back: Phillip, Christoph. Middle: Christina, Martha,
Katherine. Front: Gottlieb, Peter, Caroline (pic)

All but two sons of their large family eventually came to Canada. Their son
Peter took over the homestead when they retired to Irvine in 1928. In 1930 they
moved to Medicine Hat where they remained until their passing, Caroline on
January 24, 1932 at the age of 72 and Gottlieb on March 24, 1936 at the age of
82.

The family consisted of the following members:

1. John C. (born March 4, 1878 at Glueckstal) married Frederika Schock (born
March 19, 1879 at Glueckstal) on December 29, 1900. John was the founder of the
town of Long Lake, South Dakota, having the first house, store and machinery
agency there. In June of 1979 the town celebrated its 50th anniversary. John
and Frederika had four children, one dying in infancy. Ferdinand resides in
Long Lake. Arthur passed away on February 24, 1962 and Anna Adefine Rath on
April 9, 1981. Frederika passed away in April 1909. John then married Christina
Mair in December 1909. John passed away in July 1935 and Christina in July 1953.

2. Gottlieb (born February 24, 1880 at Glueckstal) married Sarah Herman (born
July 8, 1883 at Glueckstal) on January 1, 1904 at Ashley, North Dakota. They
farmed near Ashley until retiring to the town of Ashley. They had eight
children, one dying as a child. Emilia Nitschke and Viola Gohl reside in
Ashley, Maggie Bendewald in Leola, South Dakota and Lydia Schilling in
Aberdeen, South Dakota. Edwin passed away on January 7, 1963, Emil on September
19, 1972 and Enoch on August 1, 1984. Gottlieb passed away on November 30,
1956, and Sarah on April 20, 1958.

3. Karoline (born February 21, 1883 at Glueckstal) married Philip George in
1902 at Ashley, North Dakota. He passed away in 1903. In 1904 she married Karl
Helm at Ashley. They adopted a son, John Albin, who passed away in 1976, and
had a daughter Martha, who resides in Calgary. Karl Helm passed away in 1909.
Karoline then moved to Irvine to be near her parents. In 1910 she married Otto
Deering, born on March 26, 1887 at Albota, Russia. They lived in and around
Irvine and the Clearwater district until retiring to Medicine Hat in 1945. Otto
passed away on March 24, 1947 and Karoline on October 29, 1963. They had ten
children, one died in infancy. Emil (Jim), Edwin, John and Herbert reside in
Medicine Hat, Ruben and Freda Yanke in Calgary, Gordon in Mayerthorpe, Esther
Foulston in San Francisco, California and Rosa Lehr near Irvine.

4. Margaret (born September 16, 1884 at Glueckstal) married August March (born
November 9, 1881 at Friedenstahl, Russia) on June 3, 1903 at Ashley, North
Dakota. In 1913 they went to Clearwater and stayed with the Schaffers for a
year before homesteading in the Hilda district. They farmed there until
August's passing on April 28, 1946. Margaret retired to Medicine Hat, passing
away on August 28, 1956. They had a large family of 24 children, some dying in
infancy. Alice Frisch and Willie reside in Medicine Hat and August Junior in
Edmonton. Caroline Becker Joyce passed away on May 11, 1961, Rosina Levie on
May 9, 1968, Ludwig on September 20, 1971, Martha Derheim on May 15, 1974,
Gottlieb on December 14, 1975 and Mary Reuer on September 10, 1985.

5. Jacob (born June 16, 1886 at Glueckstal) married Lydia Mueller (born October
8, 1887 at Tripp, South Dakota) on January 25, 1905 at Ashley, North Dakota.
They lived in the Ashley district until 1911 when they took up a homestead in
the Schuler district. They moved to Bassano in 1922, where Jacob passed away on
January 29, 1931 and Lydia on December 18, 1962. They had 14 children, some
dying in infancy. Rosina Meidinger, Katerine Rutscke and Henry reside in
Bassano, Johnnie in Medicine Hat, Ruben in Airdrie and William in Brooks. Edwin
passed away on February 5, 1955, Lenora Pietz on June 29, 1968, Jacob on
February 9, 1977 and Ella Cowan on April 6, 1986.

6. Christdoff was born in November, 1889 at Odessa. He went with his parents to
the Clearwater district where he passed away in March, 1914.

7. Philip was born on October 2, 1893 at Eureka. He went with his parents to
the Clearwater district and took up a homestead nearby. He returned to Ashley
where he married Christina Herman (born June 21, 1890) on December 4, 1914. He
returned to Canada with his bride, farming there until his sudden death in June
1924, after being struck by lightning. They had six children. Frieda Kaiser
resides in Hussar and Olga MacKenzie in Calgary. Walter passed away on July 18,
1942, John on August 28, 1976, Maggie Haberer Hewko on August 6, 1986 and
Albert on February 14, 1987. Following Philip's death, the family sold their
farm and moved to Hussar, Alberta where Christina married John Oster. John had
some children from a previous marriage and together they also had a son,
Benjamin, who resides in Hussar. Christina passed away on August 28, 1942.

8. Katherine (born January 16, 1897 at Ashley) married George Kaiser (born
September 20, 1880 at Hoffensdal, Russia) on December 24, 1913 at Irvine. They
homesteaded in the Schuler district, farming there until 1924 when they moved
to the Hussar district. They retired to Calgary in 1949 where Katherine passed
away on November 24, 1971 and George on February 23, 1974. They had 12
children. Katie Taubert Reinhardt resides in Calgary, George, Herbert, Albert
and Caroline Sayer in Hussar, Willie in Caroline, Martha Schrenk in Lind,
Washington and Rosie and Margaret in Vancouver, B.C.

9. Christina (born September 20, 1898 at Ashley) married Gottfried Ruch (born
January 6, 1891 at Matildendorf, Bessarabia, Russia) on January 20, 1916 at
Irvine. They homesteaded in the Horsham district. In 1923 and 1924 they farmed
the Schaffer farm, returning to Horsham until retiring to Medicine Hat in 1947.
Gottfried passed away on May 23, 1948 and Christina on September 8, 1976. They
had seven children, five dying in infancy and Albert on August 28, 1970. Rosina
Braun resides in Medicine Hat.

10. Martha (born May 7, 1900 at Ashley) married Edward Weishaar (born in 1894
near Bessarabia, Russia) on November 25, 1916 at Irvine. They had one son,
Emil, who passed away in August, 1985. Martha passed away in 1918. Edward then
married Katie Mutschler in 1919 and moved to Lloydminster, farming there until
retiring to Medicine Hat. Edward passed away on October 18, 1969.

11. Peter (born June 7, 1903 at Ashley) married Helen Weishaar (born July 10,
1906 at Irvine) on October 13, 1921 at Irvine. They resided in the Clearwater
district and in Irvine until Peter's passing on December 21, 1961. Helen moved
to Redcliff in 1962 and retired to Medicine Hat in 1964. She passed away on
December 3, 1975. They had eight children, two dying as infants and Emil on
October 24, 1975. Edwin, Roy and Lorine Mock reside in Medicine Hat, Harvey in
Redcliff, and Clarence in Maple Creek.

In 1980, descendants of Gottlieb and Caroline Schaffer included 56
grandchildren, 171 great-grandchildren, 197 great-great-grandchildren and 5
great-great-great-grandchildren.

George Kaiser Junior sent this little story about Grandma and
Grandpa Schaffer:

I do not remember much about my grandparents, but my mother told us that while
they still lived in Irvine, Grandpa had to go to Medicine Hat on business and
Grandma wanted to go along. He said she could not accompany him, but she always
had a few tricks up her sleeve. When Grandpa left for the station to purchase
his ticket and board the train, she followed far enough behind him so that he
could not see her. Once he was aboard, she also got on, hiding in the bathroom
until the train arrived in Medicine Hat. She then quickly disembarked and was
waiting for her husband on the platform when he got off. When he saw her there,
they say he turned pale with shock for he could not feature her being there
ahead of him or even if it really was her.

Karoline Schaffer
by Martha Salway

Karoline Schaffer, daughter of Carolina (Hausauer) and Gottlieb Schaffer of
Ashley, North Dakota, was united in marriage to Karl Helm, son of Barbara
(Hochhalter) and Jakob Helm of Lehr, North Dakota, on January 12, 1904 in
Ashley, North Dakota.

Karl Helm passed away in 1909 and Karoline (Schaffer) Helm came to Canada to be
with her parents who now resided at Clearwater, bringing with her all of her
possessions and her two young children, John Albin Helm and Martha Magdelena
Helm.

While at Clearwater, she met Otto Deering of Josephsburg. The following is an
excerpt taken from the Medicine Hat News dated January 20, 1910.

"The marriage of Otto Deering, of Josephburg and Karoline Schaffer Helm, of
Irvine was performed by the Rev. J S. Datun, at the groom's home, on January
11, 1910. A large circle of friends and acquaintances were present to witness
the pleasing affairs and many good wishes were heartily extended."

The couple lived on a farm in the Clearwater district. In 1910, they moved to
the town of Irvine. Otto owned a pool hall and was also in the dray delivery
business. Otto Deering passed away on March 23, 1947. Karoline passed away
October 29, 1963.

John Albin Helm married Carolina Stotz at Irvine, in December 1923. This
marriage was blessed with six children; Odella Jean, Edwin Albin, Allan Harold,
Hilma Rose, Dorothy Iris, and Edith.

Martha Helm Deering was united in marriage on January 26, 1928 to John Barlow
Salway at Cardston, Alberta. In 1941, they moved to Medicine Hat, and in 1964,
moved to Calgary. John Barlow Salway passed away on November 13, 1983. Martha
Salway resides in Calgary. The couple were blessed with three children.
Millicent Alfreda and Glynn Redford of Eugene, Oregon have five children,
Rodney, Derek, Randall, Robbie, and Lori Ann married to Garry Rainsdons. They
all reside in U.S.A. Affred Barlow Helm Salway married Mary Alice Panchot. They
reside at Ronan, Montana and have four children, Sandra Ann Kastella of Denver,
Colorado, John Miyne and Dora of St. Ignatius, Montana, and Kasey Barlow
attending college at Missoula, Montana. John Edward Salway married Katherine
Knesh. They have two children, Lee Edward and Tracy. They all reside at
Kelowna, B.C.

Karoline and Otto Deering had ten children.

Jim Otto married Mary McLeod. They lived in the Irvine district and now live in
Medicine Hat.

Gordon Walter, residing at Mayerthorpe, married Nellie Wilkinson.

Edwin Emmanuel married Evelyn Richardson and resides at Medicine Hat.

John Samuel married Joyce Cannings and resides at Medicine Hat.

Ruben Daniel married Luella Peters and lives in Calgary.

Herbert Peter married Melba Yanke and lives in Medicine Hat.

Esther Edna married Lance Rogers and resides at San Diego, California.

Freda Katharine of Calgary married George Yankee.

Benjamin passed away in infancy.

Rosa Marie married Lawrence Lehr. They reside in the Irvine district.

Peter and Helen (Weishaar) Schaffer

Peter Schaffer was born in Ashley, North Dakota on June 7, 1903, and moved to
the Irvine district in 1908. Helen (Weishaar) Schaffer was born south of Irvine
in 1906. They were married October 13, 1921 in Irvine and had eight children,
of whom two died at birth.

Peter Schaffer Family: Back: Clarence, Edwin, Emil; Front: Harvey, Peter,
Helen, Lorine, Roy - 1940 (pic)

Peter Schaffer Family: Back: Roy, Clarence, Emil, Florence and Edwin Schaffer,
Howard Mock, Harvey Schaffer; Front: Mary, Alice, Irene, Helen, Peter, Lorine
(Mock), Audrey Schaffer (pic)

Throughout their lifetime, Pete and Helen partook in numerous ventures. After
farming from 1921 to 1941 they moved into town. Peter worked for the Imperial
Garage as a mechanic. Later, Peter and two of his sons, Harvey and Roy, built a
new garage and service station on the Trans Canada Highway in Irvine. They sold
the garage in 1954. Pete and Helen also had a coffee shop in the hotel for a
time.

In 1955, Pete started work for the Medicine Hat School Division #4, driving a
school bus to Irvine. He was also the maintenance supervisor of the Irvine
School until his passing on December 21, 1961. Helen moved to Medicine Hat
after Pete passed away and lived there until her passing on December 3, 1975.

Edwin and Florence (Otto) Schaffer

Edwin was the oldest son of Pete and Helen Schaffer, born December 7, 1922 in
Irvine. Florence Otto was born in Irvine, March 2, 1927.

Edwin and Florence were married in Irvine July 3, 1943. They did some farming
and Ed also worked for Harry Crookes, hauling grain and coal and doing custom
work for farmers. Florence worked in the cafe in Irvine for a while. They had
three children, Leverne, Leroy, and Lenora, all born in Irvine.

In 1949, they moved to Redcliff. Edwin worked for Dominion Glass from 1949 to
1956, as a machinist and mechanic. In 1956, he and his brother Harvey started a
garage business. In 1969 Edwin sold his share to his son, Leverne and Harvey.
In 1973, he bought an appliance and sporting goods store and sold it in 1975.

Florence worked for Dominion Glass from 1952 to 1965.

Ed and Florence moved to Medicine Hat in 1981. In 1984 they moved into the
Mayfair Manor which they looked after for two years. Florence passed away
November 2, 1986.

In 1987, Ed moved back to Redcliff where he is living now.

Leverne married Hughene Fraser in 1965. They have three children: Laura Leah,
David Russell, and Tara Lynn. They moved to Calgary in 1979 where they still
reside.

Leroy married Gloria Hurlbert in 1967. They have two children: Natalie and
Jason. They live in Fort Assinaboine, Alberta.

Lenora married Dale Stein in 1968. They have two children: Vincent and Kristin.
They live in Medicine Hat.

Clarence and Alice (Pfeifer) Schaffer

Clarence Schaffer, second eldest son of Pete and Helen Schaffer, married Alice
Pfeifer, only daughter of Otto and Hilda Pfeifer, April 28, 1948.

They lived in Irvine and worked at various jobs in the community and district
until April 16, 1950 when he began working with CP Rail. They remained in
Irvine until 1959 when Clarence's job with the CPR took them to Portreeve,
Saskatchewan. In 1965 they moved to Maple Creek, Saskatchewan. In September
1986, Clarence retired from the CPR and they still reside in Maple Creek. Their
two daughters Sharlaine and Elaine who were born in Irvine also live in Maple
Creek.

Sharlaine married Donald Dean and has a daughter Leea and a son Derek.

Elaine married Harland Pollock and has two daughters, Kelly and Sandi.

Emil and Irene (Schneider) Schaffer

married Irene Schneider September 1949. They had four children: Ron, Robert,
Valerie, and Debra.

Ron is single and lives in Windermere, B.C.

Robert married Gitte Bjerrisgaard in 1975. They have two boys, Mark and Dereck.
Robert has a sheet metal business in Redcliff and his wife has a dress making
shop.

George and Louise (Scherbinske) Schaller

George Schaller was born on March 18, 1864 in Mitskchdorf, Canton Worth at the
Sauer in lower Alsace-Lorraine, a province in northeast France. He was a young
man when he and brother Henry immigrated to the United States to Ellendale,
North Dakota. There he met and married Louise Scherbinske (born 1872). She was
the daughter of John and Caroline Scherbinske who had emigrated from Posthul,
South Russia to the U.S. in the 1880's.

Following the marriage of Louise to George Schaller on January 17, 1892, they
continued to farm in Ellendale and also Kulm, North Dakota until 1902 when they
immigrated to Canada settling on a farm south of Irvine, N.W.T., Canada.

Schaller - Becker house and George Schaller Sr. family: Back: George Sr.,
Louise holding George Jr., Emma, Edith; Front: Linda, Hilda, Alyce (pic)

Louise Schaller managed the family farm for a number of years while husband
George pursued business enterprises in the town of Irvine with Weiss & Co. and
later as a grain buyer. Later they sold the farm and moved into the town
permanently. Their family home is still in existence in the town of Irvine. The
Weiss & Co. store of which George Schaller was associated included such members
as Henry Vockeroth, Mr. Brandt, Carl Beny, John Weiss Sr., Chris Weiss Sr., and
Chris Weiss Jr. At that time the store sold general merchandise as well as all
types of farm implements.

The store was later sold to Carl Beny and then to Schneider brothers and is now
known as Wiedemann's General Store.

After selling his interest in the Weiss & Co. store, George Schaller bought the
managing share of an elevator grain buying business which is still operating as
the Alberta Wheat Pool elevator in Irvine.

While in the implement business in Irvine, George would often take horses in
trade for machinery and when the herd grew large enough he arranged to trail
them to Northern Saskatchewan locations. Land was being opened up to
homesteaders at the time and horses were in demand for farming. On one occasion
in 1919, Mr. Mike Klaibert, Jack Klaibert, Edward Hiles and Chris Jorgenson
were hired to move 100 head to Turtleford, Saskatchewan. The trip took ten days
to move them the 350 miles and Mike Klaibert stayed with them to do the selling.

George Schaller Sr. passed away in 1920 at the age of 56. Louise later married
K. P. (Karl) Becker of Irvine, and she died in 1927. George and Louise are both
buried in the family plot in the Irvine Cemetery beside Louise's parents,
Caroline and John Scherbinske.

Alyce, Emma, Linda, Edith, Hilda, Esther (front) Schaller - 1920's (pic)

George and Louise Schaller had a family of nine daughters, Magdalena, Emma,
Edith, Linda, Hilda, Alyce, Clara, Stella, Esther and one son George Jr.

Magdalena died in infancy (September 15, 1892-September 29, 1892).

Emma (1893-1970) married Emanuel Weiss in the Irvine Baptist Church in 1914.
They had six children: Elmer (1916-1985), Ralph (1917) of Medicine Hat; Ella
(1925), now Mrs. W. Starling, Edmonton; Mildred (1920-1926); Marlene (1931),
now Mrs. Ken Meier, Medicine Hat; Donald (1933) of Medicine Hat.

Edith (1896-1970) married Christian Jorgensen June 14, 1920 and they had two
children, Earl of Nelson, B.C. and Marjorie MacBain of Castlegar, B.C.

Linda (1899-1963) married Rev. Gus Rutsch and they had three children, Alvin,
Liz Harnish and Darlene Hoover, all of the U.S.

Hilda (1902-1970) married Russel Minier and they had two children, Isabelle and
Benny Frank.

Alyce (1904) married Walter Willicke on November 10, 1928. They lived in Salem,
Oregon where Alyce still resides.

Clara Lilia (1905) died at age nine months.

Stella Maria (1909) died at age three months.

George Jr. (1911-1965) married Corrine Newman in January, 1946 and lived in New
York for many years until his passing.

Esther (1916-1968) married Les Norris and later L. Bogenreif (1946). They had
two children, Sharon and Cliff of the U.S.

Andreas (Andrew) and Rosina (Rosie) (Hehr) Scheffelmeier

Andreas Scheffelmeier was born December 1, 1874 in Torutino, Bessarabia, South
Russia. Rosina Hehr was born May 1, 1876 at Wittenberg, Bessarabia. Her parents
were Johann George Hehr and Friedrika Gunther and her grandparents were
Matthias Hehr and Christina Gackle, and Jacob Gunther and Rosina Goldman.

Rosina and Andrew Scheffelmeier (pic)

Andrew Scheffelmeier and Rosie Hehr were married in South Russia. As a young
married couple, 24 and 22, they immigrated to Canada, arriving May 17, 1899 at
Halifax, Nova Scotia on the S.S. Carthaginean which sailed from Liverpool,
England. On the passenger list they were listed as Andress and Rosine
Schaffelmetz.

They eventually settled south of Medicine Hat, Alberta, where they farmed and
raised their children.

Robert Scheffelmeier (pic)

Andrew died November 6, 1936 and is buried in the Newburg Church cemetery south
of Irvine.

In 1942 Jack and Bertha Krauss moved to the Scheffelmeier farm with Rosie
Scheffelmeier, and in 1947, when the farm was sold to Jack Krauss, Rosie moved
to Medicine Hat, Alberta. She died there on May 11, 1963.

Emil, Albert, Alfred Scheffelmeier (pic)

Robert, born October 31, 1900 (dec), married Maggie (Lena) Gaub (dec) and had
two children.

Emanuel, born in 1902, died in infancy.

Albert, born March 11, 1903 (dec), married Eva Frisch and had two children.

Alfred, born November 19, 1906 was not married.

Edith (Ida), born December 17, 1907, married Oscar Widmer (dec) and had one son.

Lydia, born December 24, 1909 (dec), married Emil Derheim (dec) and had three
children.

Bertha, born June 3, 1913, married Jacob Krauss and had four children.

Emil, born September 15, 1915, married Freda Stadel and had two children.

Martha, born April 15, 1917, married Neal Stadel (dec) and had three children.
Later she married Arthur Hallin.

Annie, born March 27, 1919, married Jacob Schorr (dec) and had two children.

Andrew Scheffelmeier Family: Martha, Bertha, Andreas, Rosina holding Annie,
Lydia, Ida(pic)

Emil and Freda (Stadel) Scheffelmeier

Emil was born September 15, 1915 and attended Concordia School. He lived with
his mother and helped on the farm until 1941 when the farm was sold. He moved
to Medicine Hat and worked in different places, mainly for the Medicine Hat
Feeding Company. In the wintertime he helped to feed livestock and when they
started their cattle sales he also worked at the sales. Then Emil purchased his
first truck from the Medicine Hat Feeding Company in 1942 and started general
trucking.

In 1943, Emil married Freda Stadel. They had two children, Gwen and Lyle. The
children both attended schools in Medicine Hat. Gwen is married, lives in
Edmonton, and has two girls. Lyle is not married.

Emil Scheffelmeier Family: Lyle, Emil, Gwen, Freda (pic)

Emil Scheffelmeier truck (pic)

As years went by Emil increased his fleet of trucks and in 1951 started working
for oil companies hauling pipes, fracking sands, and drilling mud. He also
hauled water when the Trans Canada Highway was first rebuilt from the
Saskatchewan border to Suffield, Alberta.

Fleet of trucks belonging to Emil Scheffelmeier (pic)

In 1963 Emil sold out to Joyline Transport, Ron Draudson and Lorne Bohnet. From
that time on he has been semi-retired in Medicine Hat.

John and Carolina Scherbinske

John Scherbinske and Carolina Heier were both born in 1831. They were married
in Posthul, South Russia, and had three sons and three daughters: Konrad, John,
and Frederick, Christina, Louise, and Carolina.

They immigrated to North Dakota in May, 1886 and farmed there for many years.
Their daughter Louise had married George Schaller in North Dakota and had moved
to Irvine, N.W.T. After Scherbinskes had retired for a number of years they
moved to Irvine, as well, to live with their daughter Louise Schaller. They had
already lived to a good age and it was unusual for such elderly people to move
West.

Both John and Carolina passed away in the year of the great flu epidemic in
1918 at age 87 and are buried in the Irvine Cemetery.

Christian and Ida (Lentz) Schlaht
by Robert L. Moro

Christian Schlaht was born December 21, 1879 in South Russia. He came to Canada
about the turn of the century and took up a homestead five miles east of
Irvine. In 1902 he married Ida Lentz on December 26th in her home in Irvine.
Ida was born in Vetterburg, Russia on November 28, 1882 and also came to Canada
at the turn of the century.

Christian and Ida Schlaht (pic)

To them five children were born: Ida, Albert and three of whom passed away in
their early childhood.

In 1920 the family moved to Walla Walla, Washington, for a period of six years
and then returned to Alberta where they farmed in the Galahad district until
1930. They then returned to their homestead at Irvine where they farmed until
1945 when they retired and settled in Alliance, Alberta. In 1949 they moved to
Medicine Hat. Christian Schlaht passed away October 20, 1955, aged 75 years.

Albert Schlaht, Gottlieb Lentz, Ida and Christian Schlaht (pic)

In 1956, after her husband's death, Ida Schlaht moved to Alliance where she
resided with her grandson, Robert Moro and his wife Ruby, until her death on
March 8, 1975, aged 92 years.

Their daughter Ida was born at Josephsburg, Alberta on March 3, 1905. She
married Louis Moro in 1926 at Walla Walla, Washington. To them one son, Robert
Moro, was born on December 6, 1926. They also moved to Galahad, Alberta. On
March 22, 1932, Ida was again married to Anton Thalman. They had three
daughters, Delores, Doreen and Audrey. Ida Thalman passed away on February 9,
1962.

Albert was born at Irvine on December 24, 1908. He married Alma Blumhagen of
Galahad on October 26, 1930. They farmed at Coleridge, Alberta from 1930 to
1936, then returned to the Galahad area where they farmed until their
retirement, and now reside in Galahad. They have three children, Violet, Sharon
and Gordon.

The Christian Schlahts also raised their grandson Robert Moro (sometimes called
Bobby Schlaht). Robert attended Schlaht School and Irvine High School. In 1945
he moved to Alliance, Alberta where he still farms. He married Ruby Rombough of
Alliance on June 23, 1950.

The Christian Schlaht brand was T^P

George and Laura (Jans) Schlaht

George Schlaht was born in Walsh, the youngest child of Phillip and Dorothy
Schlaht. He was raised and educated in Walsh.

Laura was the eldest daughter of Johannes (John) and Natalia Jans, also of
Walsh. She also grew up in Walsh and attended public school there and later
went to high school in Irvine.

George and Laura were married in Medicine Hat on July 3, 1948 and resided in
Walsh until the following year when they took up residence in Irvine. George
worked for Buster Crewe in the farm implement business for a short time prior
to a move to Calgary where he was employed in the construction industry.

In 1950 George and Laura returned to Irvine. They went into the garage business
when they purchased a half share in the business from George's brother Bill.
His brother August (Gus) was also a partner in the business for a time before
George became sole owner and manager. George had the North Star dealership at
the service station and handled bulk farm fuel as well. He remained in the
business when it was purchased by Shell Oil. He bought the building and has
continued to sell Shell products for over 35 years. He has received plaques
throughout the years from Shell Oil for continuous service to the public.

In 1960 George purchased a tractor and excavating equipment and with his
brother Bill, installed the first water and sewer systems in Irvine and
surrounding area. Most were in use until the town put in public water works.
Many area farms and ranches are still getting their water supply from the
original systems.

George served the Town of Irvine as councilor for some years and as mayor for
several terms between 1961 and 1977. He was also instrumental in the planning
and construction of Irvine's first artificial ice curling facility in the late
1950's.

George and Laura have supported numerous organizations and clubs in the town
and district and continue to sponsor many by supplying trophies annually to 4H,
curling and other area activities.

They still reside in Irvine at time of writing in 1987.

George and Laura have two children.

Blaine was born in 1954 and married Sandy Maser, daughter of Kayo and Martha
Maser. They have two children: Melonie was born in 1976, and Sheldon in 1982.
They reside in Medicine Hat where Blaine is employed as a glazier.

Their daughter Jo Ann was born in 1961 and married Warren Schneider in 1981.
Warren is the son of Laura and the late Gordon Schneider. Jo Ann and Warren
lived in Irvine for a short time before moving to the Schneider farm where they
