Ernst and Bertha Schmidt

Ernst Schmidt settled on the E 13-13-2-W4 in the Irvine district in April 1910.
Ernst and his wife Bertha, along with four of their children, Anna (b. 1891),
August (b. 1894), Minna (b. 1899), and Wilhelm (b. 1901), came to Alberta from
Becker County, Minnesota where they had farmed since 1889. Their oldest son
Albert (b. 1888) remained in Minnesota until 1917 when he came to Alberta and
joined the family at their Many Island Lakes farm.

Ernst Friedrich Henry Schmidt was born in Greifenburg, Pomerania, Germany on
July 26 1860 and baptized in the Lutheran faith on Augusi 5, 1860. He spent the
next 24 years in Germany where he was educated and also served as a
noncommissioned officer in the Prussian Army. His two older brothers died from
scarlet fever within a day of each other on June 13 and 14, 1869 and his father
Wilhelm also died in Germany c. 1880.

Ernst immigrated to United States in August 1884. His mother Fredrikka Louise
(b. 1836), along with her younger son Johannes (b. 1871) and daughter Elizabeth
(b. 1874) followed Ernst to America in March 1886 and all eventually settled in
Becker County, Minnesota.

Ernst Schmidt married Bertha Johanna Wilhelmina Grunke (b. 1859) at the St.
Johanne's Lutheran Church in Fort Ridgely, Minnesota on November 4, 1887. The
Grunke family were also from Pomerania and had immigrated to America in 1879.
They settled near Fairfax, Minnesota where many descendants still live. Ernst
became a naturalized American citizen in 1897 and later a Canadian citizen at
the Medicine Hat court house in January 1914.

Daughter Anna married Frank Cowan in 1916 and they had eight children.

Minna married Alvin Tohm and they had one son. Minna's second marriage was to
Everett Brandt.

Albert married Mildred Dennis in 1919 and they had two children.

August married Nellie Josephine Johnson in 1921 and they had three children.

Wilhelm married Lydia Knechtel in 1928 and they had two children.

In 1924 the Ernst Schmidt family left their Many Island Lakes farm due to the
continuing dry years and farmed once again in the Violet Grove, Drayton Valley
district west of Edmonton. Bertha died on July 12, 1937 at age 77 and Ernst on
January 29, 1945 at age 84. Ernst and Bertha are buried side-by-side in the
Drayton Valley cemetery.

Johannes Schmidt

Johannes Schmidt settled on the SE 23 and the SW 24-13-2-W4 in the Irvine
district in 1910 adjacent to his brother Ernst and brother-in-law William
Trieglaff.

Johannes was born in Greifenburg, Pomerania, Germany on August 7, 1871. He
immigrated to United States along with his widowed mother and younger sister
Elizabeth in March 1886. They joined Ernst in Minnesota and eventually settled
in Becker County. Johannes became a naturalized American citizen in 1897 and
later a Canadian citizen on April 8, 1913.

Johannes Schmidt married Augusta Uecker in Minnesota on December 17, 1896. Five
children were born of this union. Elizabeth (b. 1897), Anton (b. 1899), Martha
(b. 1900), Augusta (b. 1903) and Lawrence (b. 1904). Augusta (Uecker) Schmidt
(b. 1878) died from tuberculosis on April 4, 1906 at age 27 leaving her young
family without a mother. The children grew up with the Ernst Schmidt and
William and Elizabeth Trieglaff families. Anton died in Minnesota in 1909 at
age ten and Augusta Emilie remained with her Uecker grandparents in Minnesota
when the Schmidt and Trieglaff families moved to southern Alberta.

Johannes married his second wife Mathilda (Mueller) Rohloff on December 13,
1917 at Medicine Hat, Alberta. Johannes and Mathilda had seven children: Otto
(b. 1918), Edith, Emma, Maria (b. 1921), Elsa, Emil (b. 1923) and Arthur (b.
1928).

The Johannes Schmidt family left their Many Island Lakes farm in 1924 and
settled on another farm near Fallis, Alberta west of Edmonton. They remained at
Fallis for some time but then moved again to another farm eight miles west and
three miles north of Olds, Alberta. Otto remained on the family farm at Olds
after his father died. Two of his sisters married ranchers in the Sundre area
and Emil and Arthur along with their families have farms near Peace River,
Alberta.

Johannes Schmidt died at his farm near Olds on January 7, 1956 at age 84.
Mathilda Schmidt died in Olds on January 9, 1965 at age 83. Johannes and his
wife Mathilda are buried side-by-side in the pioneer Hainstock cemetery near
Olds, Alberta.

Frederick and Martha (Lautermilch) Schmidt

Frederick Schmidt and Martha Lautermilch were married in November 1904 in
Odessa, Russia. They farmed there until 1906 when they immigrated to Argentina
where they farmed for six years, and then moved back to Russia. In 1912 Fred
and Martha immigrated to Canada and established their new home in the town of
Irvine. After five years in town they moved to the farm north of Irvine, where
they farmed until December 1947 at which time they retired to Irvine.

Fred Schmidt passed away August 22, 1950 at the age of 69. Martha Schmidt
passed away May 13, 1964.

Fred and Martha had one son Henry, born October 8, 1917, and a daughter Ida,
born in 1919. Three other sons were born to Frederick and Martha, but died in
infancy. Ida, Mrs. Logan, passed away in 1979.

Henry and Matilda Schmidt

Henry Schmidt married Matilda Kersch at Hussar, Alberta on December 14, 1946
and settled on the family farm at Irvine. They had one daughter, Margaret. Mrs.
Schmidt passed away on January 30, 1952 at the age of 27. Mr. Schmidt continued
to farm until illness forced his retirement to Medicine Hat in 1968.

He married Martha Schneider in 1970 and resided in Medicine Hat until his
passing on March 13, 1976.

Margaret Schmidt was born in Drumheller, Alberta where her parents worked for a
short time before settling on the Schmidt homestead eight miles north of
Irvine. She attended grade school and high school in Irvine graduating in 1966.
She then took a one year business course in Medicine Hat.

Keith and Margaret (Schmidt) Elhart; Inset: Bobbie Dee Elhart; Inset: Jordon
Elhart (pic)

In 1970 she was married to Keith Elhart. Since that time they have lived in
Medicine Hat, Calgary, and Winnipeg and in 1979 returned to settle in Medicine
Hat. Keith is manager of Central Guaranty Trust and has been with Trust
Companies for the past 15 years.

Margaret and Keith have one daughter named Bobbie Dee, age 15, and one son
Jordon, age eight.

John and Rosina (Leicht) Schmidt
by Ted Aman

John Schmidt was born in Germany and at the age of 14 immigrated to Russia
where they were offering free land.

A large group came from Germany and settled in villages where they had German
schools and churches. Later he married Rosina Leicht, immigrated to South
Dakota and settled on a farm near Eureka, South Dakota.

In 1902 he took up a homestead south of Irvine and, in coming to Canada in
1903, he canceled the first and took up another.

There were nine children born to John and Rosina Schmidt. The oldest one, John,
never married and stayed with his parents while they were still alive, and
later with his brothers and sisters.

Christ married Rosina Aman and farmed near Eureka, South Dakota.

Rosina married John Wolfe, who was a car dealer in Java, South Dakota.

Margaret married George Wolfe, who farmed near Eureka, South Dakota.

Philip married Sophia Bertch and settled near Carbon, Alberta.

Rosina and John Schmidt (pic)

Elizabeth married Jacob Aman and settled near Irvine, Alberta.

Peter married Katie Maier and settled in the Clearwater district.

David married Lydia Zaiser and took up a homestead south of Irvine, later moved
to a farm at Rockyford, and still later to Innisfail.

Jack married Rachel Reele and lived in Medicine Hat where he worked for Todd's
Grocery. He later moved to Kansas City, Kansas where he managed a store.

Grandma Rosina Schmidt passed away in 1909. In 1911 Grandpa John Schmidt moved
to Medicine Hat and built a new home on Elm Street. He remarried Christina
Meyer and he lived in this home until his passing.

Ludwig and Christina Schmidt

Ludwig and Christina Schmidt emigrated from Bessarabia, Russia in 1886 to
Eureka, South Dakota and from there in 1912 to Irvine, Alberta, where they
lived for several months, storing their furniture and farm equipment there
until they moved to their homestead near Schuler, Alberta.

Their daughter, Theresa, was employed at the hotel in Irvine as a cook until
her marriage to Emanuel Zaiser in 1912.

Edwin and Annie (Vossler) Schneider

Edwin Schneider was born in 1908 south of Irvine to Pauline and Peter
Schneider. He had two sisters and three brothers. He went to Sentinel School.
In 1930 he took up farming four miles north of Irvine. He farmed his land with
horses. In later years he farmed with a tractor. He lived in a sod house built
in 1910, which is still standing in 1988.

He moved to an apartment in Irvine in 1937. His income was supplemented by
barbering there from 1932 to 1973.

Edwin served in the army from 1942 to 1946, serving in England and Germany in
the Calgary Highlanders.

Annie (Vossler) and Edwin Schneider (pic)

He married Annie Vossler and they farmed until 1973 when they retired. They
were caretakers at the curling rink for years. Their hobbies were curling,
skating, and bowling. Annie kept busy with gardening, knitting, crocheting and
volunteer work. She was team captain for the Canadian Cancer Society for 21
years, served as treasurer for the Irvine Ladies' Curling Club for eight years,
and is presently a volunteer for the Medicine Hat Regional Hospital and a
member of the Auxiliary.

George and Louise (Bachman) Schneider
by Phyllis and Norman Schneider

George Schneider and his wife Louise (Bachman) emigrated from Odessa, Russia in
June, 1903 with seven of their children: Bertha, John, Louise, Sam, Gottlieb
and Albert. Emma, Rosa and Rosalia had died in Russia.

George Schneider Family: Back: Frieda, Emmanuel, Ernest, William, Katie; Front:
George, Louise (pic)

Certificate of Naturalization - George Schneider - 1906 (pic)

They homesteaded on the SE 2-11-2-W4 south of Irvine. They built their sod
house on the preemption quarter NW 34-10-4-W4 and farmed there until 1914. Born
in Canada were Edward, August, Ernest, William, Katharina, Emanuel and Frieda.

George then bought his brother Jacob's farm on the SW 23-10-2-W4 and moved his
family there. George was also a blacksmith and did all his own repairs. They
farmed until they retired to Medicine Hat in 1928 with Ernest, Katie and

George and Louise lived in Medicine Hat until their passing. George died at the
age of 79, March 12, 1948. Louise was a very avid gardener until she passed
away November 20, 1950 at the age of 81.

George Phillip and Elizabeth (Schmidt) Schneider

George Phillip Schneider was born in Neudorf, South Russia on March 14, 1863.
At the age of 20 he married Elizabeth Schmidt. They came to North Dakota in
1891, lived there 14 years then came to Canada. They farmed in the Ross Creek
area, seven miles south of Irvine.

They had ten children: August, Phillip, Elizabeth, George, Christina, Adam,
Jacob, John, Marie, and Magdalina.

George and Elizabeth moved to Medicine Hat in 1927. He passed away March 14,
1948 at 84 years.

August Sr. and Kathrine (Rinke) Schneider

August Schneider migrated by horse and buggy with his family, the George
Phillip Schneiders, from South Dakota, U.S.A. in the year 1905. August married
Kathrine Rinke in 1906 and settled on a homestead six miles south of Irvine,
section 6-11-2. This was close to the Bull Trail.

The years were very hard, working with horses to break up the lands. Mother
Schneider was truly a pioneer woman, working beside her husband and also
raising nine children.

In their earlier years on the farm, they also had a language barrier. The few
farmers who lived around were of German descent. Before the children went to
school the English language was spoken very little. Knowing of this language
barrier, I have to mention this incident which was laughed about for years. Dad
Schneider was plowing a field with his horses when he saw a lone man walking
toward him. The two men exchanged friendly greetings. (The man had trouble with
his Model A on a prairie road which, of course, Dad didn't know.) The fellow
asked very nicely, "Do you have a monkey wrench?" Dad, not understanding
English very well, thought the man said, "Do you have a monkey ranch?" Dad
thought, "My gosh, this man thinks I raise monkeys on my farm," so Dad replied
in broken English, "No. No. I am a straight farmer. I do not raise monkeys."
The man broke out with laughter and it took a bit of explaining to Dad
Schneider that he had car trouble down on the Bull Trail and he needed a monkey
wrench to handle his car problems.

August Sr. and Kathrine Schneider (pic)

Mr. and Mrs. August Schneider retired from the farm in 1951 to the town of
Irvine. August and Kathrine Schneider had nine children.

Leah was married to Bill Maser in 1932.

August Jr. married Annie Ulrich in 1934.

Lydia married Emanuel Schlenker in 1933.

Alma married Ruben Derheim in 1934.

Ida married Tom Fritz in 1946.

Edwin married Mary Adel in 1937.

Gordon married Laura Schrieber in 1948.

Esther married Gordon Hurlbert in 1946.

Archie married Gladys Schmidt in 1948.

The Schneider girls left the farm and the area after they were married and went
their separate ways.

The boys tried their hand at farming and eventually drifted away to various
jobs in Medicine Hat, where they now live with their own families. Their
stories follow.

Gordon and Laura Schneider

Gordon and Laura did stay on the homestead farm until the year 1981. They had

Warren and his wife, Jo-Ann (Schlaht), now live on the homestead farm, doing

August and Annie (Ulrich) Schneider

Annie and August Schneider Jr. were married in 1933. Annie was the daughter of
Emanuel and Lydia Ulrich.

They farmed on a half section farm which was called the Crawford place. This
farm was on the west side of the Bull Trail, five miles south of Irvine.

The first two years of marriage were very hard and their home was a basement
under a wheat granary. Eventually an old two room house was moved onto this
piece of land. They fixed it up the best they could for a home in which they
lived from 1934 to 1943. Our only son Glen was born on this farm.

Annie, Glen and August Schneider (pic)

In 1943 they moved to the town of Irvine. August then got into the buying and
selling of cattle. The house in Irvine was sold in 1946 and they built a feed
lot a half mile west of Irvine. After a few years in the feed lot business it
was sold and they then retired to Medicine Hat.

Edwin and Mary (Adel) Schneider
by Mary Schneider

Edwin "Ace" Schneider met and married Mary Adel of Medicine Hat in 1937.

Our home was a half section north of Edwin's parents' farm. I was a girl from
the city and pretty dumb when it came to farm life. I had to learn how to make
a fire in a wood and coal stove. While learning how to cook and bake bread,
there were many burnt fingers and elbows reaching into the hot oven. Mother
Schneider was a wonderful teacher and I soon learned to be a farmer's wife.
While on this farm, we had our two children. Ronald was born in 1942 and Sharon
in 1945.

Mary and Edwin Schneider (pic)

In 1946 the Berry Centre School was moved from the Ross Creek District to
within a half mile of the August Schneider Sr. farm on the Bull Trail. This
Berry Centre School is where all of the Schneider children got their education.
Edwin and I had the country teachers live with us for a number of years: Paul
Shaw, Margret Miller, Walter Balyck, Edith Volk, Rose Metz, Elaine Smith, and
Vera Kronberg. These people all spent a school term at our home. Our son Ron
started his first year of school at Berry Centre.

In 1952 we had had enough of the poor years on the farm and we then moved to
Medicine Hat. Edwin worked for the Ogilvie Flour Mills for 16 years, then
worked for the Medicine Hat School Division until he retired in 1981. I worked
at the Medicine Hat Hospital from 1953 to 1960, then changed jobs and worked as
a Central Supply Clerk at the Medical Arts Clinic until my retirement in 1980.

Ron and Sharon were both educated in Medicine Hat. Ron married Leone Butler
from B.C. and now lives in Whitby, Ontario. They have two children.

Sharon married Alan Penner from Grassy Lake. They live on an acreage south of
Medicine Hat. They also have two children.

Archie and Gladys (Schmidt) Schneider

I was born March 3, 1925 in the town of Irvine, educated in Berry Centre School
District in the Irvine area, and lived with my parents, August P. and Katherine
Schneider, on their farm. At the age of 19 I was called into the Army Service
of the Second World War where I took basic training for one year. When
discharged from the Army, I went back to my parents' farm for two years.

In 1948 I got married to Gladys Schmidt on October 22.

In the fall of 1950 I left the farm and moved to Medicine Hat, Alberta where I
worked for the Alberta Government, in the Transportation Department, until
retiring in the spring of 1985.

We have four children: Laverne A., born December 9, 1949, Marlene G., born
November 18, 1951, and, twins, Pamela and Peggy, born July 9, 1961. Laverne,
Marlene, and Peggy are all married with families. Pamela, who is at home with
us, unfortunately was diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis at the young age of 16
years.

George Gordon and Lydia (Heather) Schneider

George Gordon Schneider was born in 1892 at Harvey, North Dakota, U.S.A. He

Centre district, south of Irvine in 1905.

In 1914, he homesteaded in the Fox Valley district. Three years later, he

George G. Schneider Family: George, Reuben, Edna, Lydia (pic)

there until their passing, George in 1975 and Lydia in 1976.

Ben and Maria (Rath) Schneider
by Wesley Schneider

Ben, son of Jacob and Christina Schneider, was the second child in a family of
four, born February 28, 1911. His brother and sisters were Theodore Emma
(McLaughlin) and Martha (Kundert).

Ben, or as nicknamed Ike, was raised and educated in Irvine. He married Maria
Rath, November 14. 1932.

Maria Rath was also born, raised and educated in the Irvine District. She was
the youngest daughter in a family of eight. Her parents were Fredrick and
Christina Rath. Her brothers and sisters were Jack, John, Frederick, Lydia,
Pauline, Olga, and Emma. Her parents farmed south of Irvine.

Ben and Maria farmed south of Irvine. They had one son, Wesley Jacob, born
September 23, 1938.

In 1951, they sold their farm to Ralph Wutzke, and moved into Irvine. In 1958,
they retired to Medicine Hat where they resided until their deaths. Ben passed
away December 7, 1965: Maria passed away October 14, 1985.

I, Wesley, was raised and educated in Irvine. In 1955, I started working on
road construction, and in 1960, started working for the city of Medicine Hat,
which is where I'm still employed as a machine operator. On November 4, 1961 I
married Irene Vossler of Brooks, daughter of Martin and Dorothea Vossler who, I
might add, also farmed north of Irvine in their earlier years.

Irene and I have two children, David Earl, born October 3, 1963 and Mavis
Marie, born September 1, 1968. They both graduated from Medicine Hat High
School, and are presently employed.

My fond memories of Irvine are playing baseball and skating. One year there was
so much water lying around that, when it froze, we skated from the Irvine
School to the C.P.R. station a Walsh. There was only one stretch in between
where we had to take our skates off and walk over a hill then nut them on again
to skate the rest of The way.

Frederick and Rosina (Knodel) Schneider
By Mrs Pal (Rosie) Hunsicker (additions by Esther Manske)

Frederick Schneider was born March 6, 1890 at Suttle, South Dakota, U.S.A., to
Jacob and Elizabeth (Graff) Schneider and came to Irvine in 1903 with his
parents. They homesteaded south of Irvine in the Josephsburg District.

Fred and Rosina (Knodel) Schneider - 1911 (pic)

Rosina, the third daughter of Matthias and Dorothea (Weissenburger) Knodel, was
born on June 10, 1892, at Eureka, South Dakota, U.S.A. and in 1903 she also
immigrated to Canada with her parents. They arrived at Irvine and lived on a
family homestead in the Newburg district.

Fred and Rosie were married on March 28, 1911, in the little Schneider
schoolhouse. They moved to Hilda where they farmed until 1917 at which time
they moved into Irvine and built a home which is still there.

My dad (Fred) and his brother Jake had the Schneider Brothers Store in Irvine
from 1922 to 1949 until my folks retired to Medicine Hat.

Fred died on May 13, 1970 and Rosie on August 7, 1980.

Fred Schneider residence - 1930's (pic)

Fred Schneider Family: Back: Rosie, Emil; Front: Irene, Fred, Freddie, Rosie,
Esther (pic)

Five children were born to Fred and Rosie Schneider.

Emil was born in 1912. He taught school in the area for a few years and then
ran the Citizen's Lumber Yard for a time. He also served as Mayor of Irvine. He
married Blanche Barger who was also a school teacher. She taught in Irvine and
surrounding area for several years. They had no children. Blanche died November
22, 1965 and Emil in April of 1969.

I, Rosie, was born in 1916 at Hilda and was one year old when we moved back to
Irvine. I served as postmistress from 1937 to 1939 at which time I left for
Minneapolis, Minnesota. I married Paul Hunsicker and we have four children.

Emil and Blanche (Barger) Schneider (pic)

Esther was born in 1924 and married Reinhold (Ray) Manske. They lived in
Medicine Hat until 1949 and then moved to Winnipeg. In 1956 they moved to
Hayward, California and they feel this was a good move. Ray and Esther are both
retired. They had a family of five children but one son drowned. Their children
and eight grandchildren live near by.

Irene was born in 1927 and is married to Harry Morris. They have four children
and live in Medicine Hat.

Both Esther and Irene had their turn working in the Post Office of which our
dad was postmaster from 1937 to 1949.

Fred was born in 1928 and became a dentist. He married Marjorie Brown. They
live in Vulcan and had five children but one died.

We children grew up in Irvine and had our schooling in the two-roomed
building. Irvine was quite a prosperous and busy town during the time I lived
there and I have many fond memories of the people and the times. They were good
years and Irvine helped to shape our lives.

Fred and Rosie Schneider 50th Anniv., March 29, 1961 (pic)

Christian Sr. and Dora (Rath) Schorr
by Hertha (Gwinner) Sulz

Christian Schorr was born on February 20, 1874 in South Russia, the son of
Ludwig Schorr Sr.

Dora Rath was born on September 15, 1874, the daughter of Johannes Rath.

Christian and Dora Schorr (pic)

Christian and Dora were married on August 15, 1896 in Wittenburg, Russia. They
came to Canada in 1898 to the Newburg district. They had no house so they dug a
cave down by the creek, on the farm where Ken and Diane Krauss now live. They
made a stove out of mud and rocks. They cooked their meals on it and baked
their bread in the oven. It kept hot for a long time. It was also used for
heat. Their main meals were kneffles, strudels, sauerkraut, dumplings,
potatoes, rabbits and pork. Their door was a blanket hung across the doorway.
Their lights were candles.

The first winter was awfully cold. They had made sauerkraut in a wooden barrel,
but it froze so hard they had to chop it out with an ax. The potatoes froze so
they had to eat frozen potatoes all winter. They slept on a mattress made of
straw or dried corn leaves stuffed into a big bag.

Their first child, a daughter Maria, was born on March 21, 1898. She passed
away in infancy. The second child also passed away in infancy.

They moved to the Gros Ventre area close to where Grandmother Schorr's sister
Justina Flaig and her husband Christian lived. Christina was born November 2,
1902. Mrs. Flaig (her aunt) took care of her, bathed her, and breast fed her.
She also had a baby daughter, Lydia, to care for so she took care of both
babies at the same time. Christina's aunt always said if she would not have fed
her and took care of her, she would have died too, as her mother, Dora, was
always out helping Christian.

Olga was born on October 13, 1905 and Christian Jr. on November 18, 1907 at
Gros Ventre.

They then moved on to the Stickel quarter, where they built a house and a barn.
This is now owned by John and Darlene Burgevitz. Martha was born April 15, 1910
and John was born August 15, 1911.

Grandfather's brother Gottfried, his wife Anna Maria and son Arnold came to
Canada to Gros Ventre in March, 1911. A four room house was built for them half
a mile from Grandfather's place. The house and a barn were built of logs and a
mixture of mud and straw. These buildings are still in the yard of the
Burgevitz farm.

Grandfather then got a piece of land from Johannes Weiss and they moved on it.
They built another house, barn and sheds. This farm is now owned by Fred Geigle.

The children went to Gros Ventre school. Tothills lived on the place now owned
by Don Boschee. Mrs. Tothill was the school teacher. The Tothill post office
was named after them, as they operated it for many years.

The Schorrs moved back to the Newburg district where they lived at first, but
this time they built on the other side of the creek where Ken and Diane Krauss
now live.

Jacob was born on March 15, 1913 and Gottfried on September 19, 1914 in Newburg.

The children went to Newburg school, a one-room school with one teacher. Up to
50 students went to this school at one time.

Christina, my mother, was the oldest so she had to help Grandfather break the
horses so they could work the fields. Times were tough when they started out
and they were poor, but they worked hard and soon had themselves established.
My mother was taught how to sew with a sewing machine, by her aunt, so she had
to sew all the clothes for the other children. She married Jacob Gwinner in
1921. They moved to the Newburg district from Schuler and worked with
Grandfather.

My dad and my grandfather headered together for a number of years. My dad would
drive the header and cut the wheat. There was an elevator on the left side of
the header. My uncle Gottfried Schorr would drive the header box along side of
the header, so the wheat that was lifted on the elevator would go into the
header box. Uncle Jacob Schorr would spread it in the header box. When I,
Hertha, was 11 years old I had to drive the header box all the time. Uncle
Jacob had one header box and when it was full he would take it to stack it up.
Grandfather made the stacks when Uncle Jacob unloaded the crop. Uncle Gottfried
had another header box empty, so I had to jump from the full box to the empty
one and take it to be filled up. We would header for a whole week, depending on
how much crop was ripe to cut. We would then move to our farm and header our
crop. Sometimes it took three weeks in one stretch. Grandfather, Uncle Jacob
and Uncle Gottfried would come along to help us.

Grandfather and Grandmother lived three and a half miles north of our place. We
loved being at our Grandmother's house as she always had some treats for us.

The farm is now owned by the fourth generation: Christian Schorr, John Schorr,
Diane (Schorr) Krauss, Keith Krauss.

My grandparents farmed for many years, working hard to establish their farm.
Grandfather bought many more farms for their sons and their families. They
moved to Medicine Hat in 1939 and bought a house on Elm Street where they lived
for 12 years. Ill health set in and Grandfather Christian Schorr passed away
March 15, 1951 at the age of 77 years. Grandmother Dora Schorr passed away on
September 19, 1957 at the age of 83 years.

Jacob Schorr passed away May 23, 1974 at the age of 61 years, Gottfried Schorr
on July 26, 1975 at the age of 62 years, and Christina (Schorr) Gwinner on
December 6, 1979 at the age of 77 years.

My grandparents and my mother, Christina, were true believers in God and the
Bible, which was read and studied every day. Their children were taught to
believe in the Bible for their guidance and daily blessings. They are sadly
missed by all of the families.

Jacob and Annie (Scheffelmeier) Schorr

Jacob Schorr, known as Jack by family and friends, was born March 15, 1913. He
was the son of Christian and Dorothy Schorr who emigrated from Bessarabia in
Southern Russia in the late 1800's. Jack and his three brothers and three
sisters were raised in the Newburg district which was about 12 miles south of
Irvine. They attended Newburg School.

When Jack was 25 years old he married Annie Scheffelmeier who was 19. Annie was
born March 26, 1919 in the Tothill district. She was the daughter of Rosie and
Andrew Scheffelmeier who also emigrated from Bessarabia, Russia. When Annie's
parents were in their early 20's they left from Liverpool, England on the Ship
S.S. Carthaginian and arrived in Canada on May 17, 1899 at Halifax, Nova
Scotia. Annie had five brothers and four sisters who grew up in the Concordia
district which is about 12 miles south and two miles west of Irvine. They
attended Concordia School.

Annie (Scheffelmeier) and Jack Schorr - 1938 (pic)

Jack and Annie were married November 19, 1938 in Medicine Hat. They settled
down on a farm ten miles south of Irvine, along the 41 Highway. They spent the
next 25 years farming in this area and raising their two daughters, Sandra and
Glenda. Their children attended Irvine School until 1964 when the family moved
to Medicine Hat. The farm was sold a couple of years later.

Annie remembers in the early 1950's they had a huge fire on their farm which
lasted for days. Jack and she had been shopping in Medicine Hat and when they
arrived home their barn was in flames. There was a strong wind, so they were
worried it might spread to the house, etc. Neighbors and friends from all over
the surrounding area came to help put it out. They tried to contain the fire by
using the tractor to plow a fire guard. The barn, which had cattle feed in it,
and a shed were completely burned down.

Jack passed away May 23, 1974 at the age of 61. His wife Annie still resides in
Medicine Hat.

Jack Schorr Family: Glenda, Jack, Annie, Sandra (pic)

Their oldest daughter Sandra and her husband Larry Stach and their two
daughters, Misty and Amber, live in Redcliff.

Their youngest daughter Glenda and her husband Don Schaufele and their two
children, Brandon and Tara, live in Medicine Hat.

Gottfried and Anna Maria Schorr

Our parents, Gottfried Schorr and Anna Maria Seitz, were married in
Ober-Altboten, Wittenberg, Bessarabia, Russia in 1906. Soon after their
marriage Father was drafted to serve in the Russian Army.

After serving a period of three years in the army in Siberia our parents
decided to immigrate to Canada. Father's sister Leana and her husband Gottlieb
Rath decided to come at the same time. Two brothers, Christian and Ludwig
Schorr, had previously immigrated to Canada in 1889 and 1903. Our mother's
family immigrated to Germany and from there most of them went on to Argentina.

The impending revolution in Russia and their young adventurous spirit led our
parents to search for better opportunities and a more secure life. They had to
leave behind family and friends, the coziness of village life and a mild fruit
growing climate for the unknown wide open spaces of Canada.

Gottfried Schorr Family: Back: Albert, Arnold, Mike, Emil, Ben. Front:
Gottfried, Elsie, Anna Marie (pic)

In 1911 they arrived in Canada and homesteaded in the Tothill area, south of
Medicine Hat. They lived with relatives until a shack was fixed up. Later a
clay house and barn were built which are still in existence today. Although
they settled in the same area as relatives and friends it took an hour or more
of driving by horse and buggy to get a helping hand when needed or to pay a
visit.

In 1917 they purchased the Stelter homestead in the Newburg district and moved
there in 1918. The land price was $25 an acre. On this farm there was a log
house and barn which had been built by the Stelter family. Logs for the
buildings were brought from the Cypress Hills. The barn which was in excellent
condition is still in use today and will be for decades to come. The town of
Irvine, ten miles away, was the nearest centre they could go to for supplies.

Father and the boys broke up more land for farming with a one-bottom plough to
add to what had previously been broken by the Stelters. Father, who never rode
a horse and being a good walker, a practice learned in the army, walked most
everywhere he went. He often told the story of how on one such occasion a herd
of wild cattle took after him. In his excitement he pitched a rock at them,
luckily hitting one on the head which dropped it unconscious and this stopped
the herd long enough to let him make his getaway.

The grain grown on the farm was hauled to Irvine by horse and wagon and needed
supplies were then brought back on their return. Eggs, butter and cream were
also sold to supplement the income. In the fall staples such as flour, sugar,
and dried fruit were bought in large quantities to last the winter. In 1928
father purchased his first car. Then, in 1929 he bought a 1030 McCormick
tractor and threshing machine with which he threshed our own crop and also
those of some of our neighbors. It took a lot of organizing in those days of no
freezers, to keep a food supply of meat and such on hand to feed a threshing
crew. Even though the crew put in long tiring hours, they still had enough
energy left at the end of the day to pull jokes and pranks on each other.

The farmers were hard hit by the depression and drought of the thirties. In
1937 the wind and dust never stopped blowing and rain was nonexistent. Feed for
the horses and cattle was scarce and many did not make it through the winter.
To keep vegetables growing we had to water them by hand. Living in a deep
coulee by the Ross Creek was a bonus for us as we had lots of trees and bushes
and protection from the wind. Most years we could pick wild berries such as
chokecherries, saskatoons, mullberries bullberries and gooseberries for
preserving.

We kept one garden just for watermelon, muskmelon and pumpkin. In this sunny
sandy location the melons grew prolifically. It was a daily morning chore for
us to bring in the ripening melons with our little wagon. For some of our melon
loving friends it was a regular habit every year to pay us a visit on a Sunday
for a melon feed, which we enjoyed sharing with them.

Wash day was certainly Blue Monday in those days, some scrubbing on the
washboard, finer things by hand and the rest in the messy rocker type washer,
which took all day. Mother sewed most of the children's clothes, even little
suits for church. We milked cows, made butter, cottage cheese and buttermilk,
did our own baking, raised chickens for eggs and meat, and ducks and geese for
meat and feathers which we used for quilts and pillows.

Social life revolved around church, school, visits with neighbors and
occasional overnight visits to relatives who lived farther away. We kids
enjoyed trips to Irvine and really looked forward to the occasional trip to
Medicine Hat.

Since all the children were interested in farming, our parents worked hard to
help each one start out on their own farm. Mother and Father retired to
Medicine Hat in 1947 leaving their youngest son, Ben, to mind the home place.
They enjoyed the conveniences of the city. They grew a prolific garden, enough
for themselves, family and friends. Father loved the farm and was often out
there to lend a helping hand.

Our mother, Anna Maria, passed away in 1959. Later Father remarried, to Mrs.
Christina Stern. In 1970 our father passed away.

Arnold, born in Russia, married Hilda Rath.

Gottfried and Anna Marie Schorr 50th Anniversary (pic)

Emil, born in Tothill, married Hilda Vossler and they have one son, David.

Olga died at seven years of age during a diphtheria epidemic.

Mike married Rachel Redelback and they have three children, Stanley, Sharon and
Brian. Mike died in a car accident in 1978.

Elsie married Bill Heller and they have two sons, Lloyd and Wayne.

Albert married Irene Seitz and they have three daughters, Elaine, Carmen, and
Melanie.

Ben married Erna Oswald and they have a son, Barry, and a daughter, Marian.

Emil and Hilda (Vossler) Schorr

Emil Schorr was born in the Gros Ventre district approximately 25 miles south
of Medicine Hat, to Gottfried and Anna Maria Schorr in the year 1915. Two years
later, the Gottfried Schorr family moved to the Irvine district to a farm
approximately ten miles south of Irvine. It was there that Emil grew up and was
educated at the Newburg School.

Emil Schorr Family: Back: Tony, Bruce Schorr, Eugene Stehr, Donna Schorr;
Middle: Stephanie, Stacy, Emil, Hilda, Phylis, Rhonda, Dave, Patsy; Front:
Sandy, Mandy, Mikie, Becky Schorr (pic)

In 1935, Emil married Hilda Vossler. Hilda was born in the same district in
1914 to Christoph and Martha Vossler. Hilda was also educated in the Newburg
School and both Emil and Hilda attended the Newburg Church of God.

After they were married in 1935, the couple moved to a farm in the Elkwater
area. These were the depression years and money was very scarce. The couple had
no car for the first few years and had to drive to town to do their shopping
with horse and buggy. They started out by milking six cows and doing grain
farming. Wheat was approximately 50 cents a bushel.

Their only son, David, was born in July 1936. Hilda and Emil continued to farm
in the same area until 1959 when they sold their home farm to their son and
moved to Medicine Hat. Emil kept active for many years after that by farming
and ranching from town on some land that he kept in the Irvine and Elkwater
district.

The couple are now retired and continue to reside in Medicine Hat. They have 12
grandchildren (nine girls and three boys) and two great-grandsons.

Mike and Rachel Schorr
by Sharon (Schorr) Keeler

Mike Schorr was the third son of Gottfried and Anna Maria Schorr, born on June
19th, 1920. Mike was raised on his father's farm in the Newburg district.

Mike was called to the Canadian Army in 1940, but was discharged due to health
reasons. Shortly after, Mike went to Calgary and enrolled in a Barber School.
He completed the course, received his Barber's Certificate and then worked for
some time in Calgary.

In 1942 Mike returned to Newburg to his father's farm at which time he
purchased the Dan Wirsch farm in the Robinson district. In 1944 Mike married
Rachel, the only daughter of Christ and Katherina Redelback of the Miller
district in Saskatchewan. Mike and Rachel continued farming on the Wirsch
farmstead. In 1945 and 1946 the crops looked good and promising, but both years
the crops were completely hailed out. Dad, Mike, worked the land with horses
for the first couple of years. At that time the crops were cut with binders,
stooked and threshed. Family and neighbors would work together when it was
threshing time. Mom, Rachel, would often have to cook for a threshing crew of
approximately 12 men. In 1951 Dad purchased his first combine.

Rachel (Redleback) and Mike Schorr (pic)

In the fall, Dad and Ed Derheim would haul timber by horse and wagon from the
Cypress Hills. The timber would have to be cut and stacked ready for the
winter. Coal, which was also a primary source of fuel, was obtained from the
mine at Elkwater.

In March 1955, a gas well was drilled on the homestead, which meant we could
have a gas cooking stove and gas heaters, we wouldn't have to haul coal and
wood, and we wouldn't have to read by kerosene mantle and coal oil lights.

In 1959 we received Calgary Power which led to the installation of indoor
plumbing, television and other electrical conveniences.

Mike and Rachel had three children, Stanley, born in December 1945, Sharon,
born in October 1948, and Brian, born in April 1952. Stan attended the primary
grades at Robinson School, until it closed, and then Stan and Sharon attended
the Newburg School for a short while until the Cypress View School was
completed. Stan and Sharon attended Cypress View School until 1959 and then
attended Irvine School.

Almost everything was grown or raised on the farm. We milked cows, made our own
butter, had a large garden, raised our own beef, pork and poultry and did all
the baking. You can bet there were no "soaps" in the afternoon!

We remember the winters (early 50's) when we would get so much snow it would
almost cover the tallest trees. We would have to dig our way down to the door
to get into the coal and wood shed. It was a thrill for us kids to get a sleigh
ride when the roads were impassable for vehicles.

Sharon, Rachel, Stan Schorr - 1951 snowstorm (pic)

We recall the time Dad and Harry Gill went to a horse auction in Redcliff and
came home with a so called "tame horse" until Dad tried to ride him in the
corral at home, only to find himself on the ground. Dad tried his utmost to
break that horse, but the horse won and Dad had to sell him.

Besides farming, Dad loved horses and cattle. As the years went by and things
became more financially secure, advancements were made in both the farming and
cattle business. Dad raised Registered Polled Herefords for many years, was a
member of the Medicine Hat Hereford Association and American Breeders Service.
Dad and Mom attended many cattle shows and visited many fellow Hereford
breeders.

As the children became of age they each had their share of work to do on the
farm to help out. Life revolved around our home, school, church, family and
friends. Saturdays we went to Medicine Hat for shopping and music lessons. Our
family loved music and many evenings were spent around the piano singing. Many
Friday, Saturday and Sunday evenings were spent visiting or having friends,
family or neighbors in, usually for supper and then playing games after. On
Sundays we went to the Newburg Church which was only a mile from our house;
services were held every second Sunday.

Mike and Rachel Schorr (pic)

Dad and Mom retired from the farm in the Robinson District in the fall of 1967
and moved to an acreage just outside of the City of Medicine Hat where they
lived until the fall of 1969. They later decided to buy an irrigation farm near
Seven Persons, along with Sharon and her husband Clive. In 1974 they moved back
to Medicine Hat taking up residence in the Crestwood area. Having two sons
living on the farm, Dad enjoyed giving them a hand when they needed help. Being
semi-retired at this point, Mom and Dad were able to take winter vacations to
warmer climates. Their special times together were cut short when Dad was
killed suddenly in an auto accident in July 1978. Mom is still residing in the
same home in Medicine Hat, and spends her days taking care of her home,
gardening, visiting with neighbors, knitting, and baby-sitting grandchildren,
etc.

Stan married Mavis McKnight, daughter of Dean and Lora McKnight of Bow Island,
in June 1967. They lived and farmed on the home place until October 1975 when
they moved to Medicine Hat and took up residence in Crescent Heights. Stan
worked for Goodyear Tire that winter and for the Department of Highways the
following spring. In 1976 he started working for the City of Medicine Hat and
is presently foreman of Sweeping, Public Works Department. Mavis has worked as
a Unit Clerk for the Medicine Hat Regional Hospital since 1984, on Pediatrics,
Labor Delivery, and Neonatal Nursery. Stan and Mavis have three girls, Dana,
Lori and Lisa. Dana is presently taking Secretarial Science at the Medicine Hat
college and graduates in April, 1988. She is engaged to Bruce Kapcala with the
fall of 1989 as their tentative wedding date. Lori graduates from Grade twelve
at CHHS in June, 1988, and intends to pursue a career in Law Enforcement. Lisa
is in grade eight at CHHS and will graduate in 1992.

Mike Schorr Family: Back: Sonya, Mike Keeler, Lori, Dana, Lisa, Stan, Mavis,
Andrea, Erin Schorr; Front: Clive, Sharon (Schorr) Keeler, Rachel, Lori, Cole,
Brian, Randi Schorr (pic)

Sharon married Clive Keeler, son of Alfred and Daphne Keeler, of Medicine Hat,
in October, 1965. Clive and Sharon took up residence in Medicine Hat. Clive had
already started work with Fischer's Plumbing and Heating, apprenticing as a
sheet metal mechanic. Sharon worked part time at the City Bakery and later at
Woolworth's and also continued studying piano and taught piano lessons for many
years. In 1971 Sharon and Clive moved onto an irrigation farm with Dad and Mom
and farmed while Clive also continued working in Medicine Hat. In 1974 they
moved back into Medicine Hat. Sharon obtained her Secretarial Science
Certificate at the Medicine Hat College in 1976 and later that year obtained
employment with the law firm of Niblock and Company where she presently works
as a Paralegal. After having worked for other sheet metal shops for 20 years,
in 1985 Clive opened his own sheet metal business, operating as C.K. Sheet
Metal Ltd., installing furnaces, air-conditioners and fire places. Clive and
Sharon have two children, Mike and Sonya, who both attended and graduated from
Crescent Heights High School. After graduating Mike started apprenticing as a
sheet metal mechanic and worked for two years. He attended the Medicine Hat
College this year while also working for his dad. Sonya is presently attending
John Casablancas Career College in Calgary with hopes of establishing a career
in the fashion industry.

Brian attended Irvine School until grade nine. He then attended Medicine Hat
High School and graduated in 1970. Brian married Arlene Crews, daughter of Bob
and Clara Crews of Medicine Hat, in July 1972. During the first three years of
marriage, Brian worked part time at Black's Hardware and helped his Dad and
Clive on the farm at Seven Persons. Arlene worked as a secretary at Dom Glass
in Redcliff. They started farming in 1975 in the Wisdom area. They had two
girls, Andrea (1975) and Erin (1978). Arlene passed away in April 1983 after a
two year battle with cancer. In May 1985 Brian married Lori Breum, daughter of
Jack and Iris Breum of Stavely, Alberta. Lori was employed at that time with
the accounting firm of Johnston Morrison and Associates. Brian and Lori have
two more children, a daughter, Randi (1985) and a son, Cole (1987). Andrea in
grade six, and Erin in grade four, attend Herald School in Medicine Hat. They
are both taking piano lessons. Brian and Lori and their family reside in the
Wisdom area and continue to farm.

We have many fond memories of our farm in the Robinson district and are proud
to be part of its history.

Elsie (Schorr) Heller
by Elsie Heller

The fondest memories I have as a child are those of playing in the hills
surrounding our farm. Whatever the season there was always lots to see and do.

Bill Heller Family: Back: Bill, Lloyd, Wayne; Middle: Elsie, Paulette, Kathy;
Front: Stephanie, Mathew, Rosalyn, Anne (pic)

In the spring, melting snow banks on the hillsides sent streams of water to the
swelling Ross Creek below, after which the wild flowers such as crocus and
shooting stars sprouted all over. With spring also came young geese, ducks,
chickens and calves and sometimes a foal or two. Wild geese and ducks had their
young along the creek.

We covered every corner of our coulee searching for the milk cows which at
times became a real chore.

In early summer the wild strawberries appeared in the pastures and on our way
home from school we could spot them from a distance. The tiny berries packed
with flavor were delicious on homemade ice cream. The windup school picnic was
always fun. Erna Herman's mother would often send an iced cake decorated with
wild strawberries, the flavor of which permeated this delicious cake.

Fall meant off to school again. I loved school, also recess to share with the
other kids. I remember the highlight of school was practicing for the Christmas
concert and the big night of the concert. In winter we had some hair raising
sleigh rides down the hills.

During the depression and drought we had little spending money. We did our
visiting on horseback and dreamed the unlikely dream of living like our
favorite movie star. Most of us were in the same boat and in spite of it all
enjoyed the little we had.

After getting married, Bill and I moved onto a farm nine miles south of Walsh.
The only building on this farm was a straw topped shed. We built a small house,
chicken house and hip roofed barn with logs that Bill and his brother John
hauled from the Cypress Hills. We stayed here for five years then moved to a
ranch twelve miles north of Walsh and retired from there in 1980. Our two sons
and their families reside there now and operate the ranch.

Lloyd and Paulette have two children Mathew and Stephanie.

Wayne and Kathy who have two girls Anne and Rosalyn.

Albert and Irene (Seitz) Schorr

I, Albert Schorr, started farming on the NW 7-10-2-W4 in 1945 at 21 years of
age. This land was originally owned by the C.P.R., and then by Gottlieb Zaiser.
Later Jacob Gast farmed the land until my father, Gottfried Schorr, bought it
from Gasts in 1928.

My father's farm was situated one mile north along the Ross Creek which is
where I grew up. In my family there were my parents, Gottfried and Mary, and in
order of age, my brothers, Arnold, Emil, Mike, and my sister Elsie (Mrs. Bill
Heller), myself, and my youngest brother Ben. As a young child, I remember
playing with my sister and brothers among the trees and land marks of the
Indian teepees and campsites. I remember looking forward to the excitement of
the threshing crew arriving at our farm.

Albert Schorr Farm (pic)

Newburg School was two miles to the south where we walked, rain or shine,
except when there was deep snow, we used horse and sleigh. We helped with
milking cows plus other farm chores. At a young age we helped with the
headering when there were poor crops and later on pitched bundles with the
threshing crew. At the age of 18, I operated my Dad's threshing machine. In
winter Mike, Ben, and I broke and trained draft and saddle horses. Trapping and
shooting rabbits, skunks, coyotes was a way of earning spending money.

At 22, I bought my first car (second hand) for $900. I didn't keep it, since
the axle broke on my first trip to visit my girlfriend, Irene. Henry Ford's
invention didn't get me very far with my first car. I went back to the more
reliable source - my horse. Irene lived on a farm which was ten miles away,
near Elkwater, and I always said that was as far as my horse would take me. The
following year, 1947, I bought another car, a maroon Chevrolet, which lasted
for a number of years after I was married.

I got married to Irene Seitz, daughter of Jacob and Christna Seitz, on November
22, 1947 at the Washington Avenue Church of God, Medicine Hat, Alberta.

Irene (Seitz) and Albert Schorr, November 22, 1947 (pic)

We settled on our farm, farming with horses, plus a tractor (steel wheels) and
other machinery jointly owned with my brother Ben. Along with milking cows and
shipping cream and grain farming, cattle were another source of income.
Hereford cattle were the main attraction, starting with some cattle from my
father's herd and a few head from my father-in-law, Jacob Seitz. To improve our
herd we always bought registered purebred bulls.

Making loose hay stacks for winter feed was a long hard process. The hay was
cut with a mower, which was horse drawn, later to become tractor drawn. At
times there was great disappointment when fresh cut hay was blown away by a
windstorm. The hay was raked and pitchforked onto a horsedrawn rack, and from
there it was unloaded by hand and stacked. The cattle were fed this loosely
stacked hay with horses, sleigh and rack, for a number of years.

We would visit the neighbors with horses and sleigh, which was very pleasant on
a moonlight night except when a storm came up. For the first ten years after
marriage we had bad roads to travel by car and in winter sometimes we went
through fields dodging deep snow to get to the better roads.

CanAm Tour: Back on horses: Rosanna and Gary Lehr, Charmaine Clark, Reanne
Lehr, Camile Clark, Melanie (S.A. Hereford Princess 1987-88) and Albert Schorr;
Front: Elaine Lehr, Carmen Clark, Sherry Toweson (Alberta Hereford Queen
1987-88), Geoffrey Watson, Jarrett Lehr, Irene Schorr (pic)

The summer pasture, just below Elkwater Provincial Park, along the Cypress
Hills, was bought from the Sauter family in 1946, formerly owned by Earl and
Mary Ligget. The cattle have always been trailed 15 miles to the summer pasture
after branding in spring and back home in October.

We had threshing crews up until 1951. Our crop was combined by brother Mike for
two years. We then bought our own combine in 1953 and did our own harvesting.

In 1959 we built our new home with electricity (Calgary Power), indoor
plumbing, lights, water heaters, etc.; it was a great advancement.

We bought land in 1970 from Jim and Vila Boschee, the homestead of Jacob and
Emma Boschee. This land is used for winter pasture because of shelter, springs,
and feed supply.

The Purebred Hereford Association CanAm Tour was traveling through parts of
United States and Canada in 1988. By invitation, some of our commercial cows
were included for viewing, along the highway by the summer pastures just below
Elkwater. This was one of the highlights in our lifetime.

Our area has always had a high level of cold spells in winter and usually a lot
of snow. Welcomed early March chinooks create spring runoffs. The hot summer
days are usually cooled quickly with cool evening breezes from the Cypress
Hills.

We have three daughters. They all helped along with the family farm and love
the country lifestyle.

Elaine Marie, born April 2, 1953, attended a centralized Cypress View School
for five years traveling with the bus. They were transferred to Irvine and she
graduated from high school in 1972. She was a 4-H Beef Club member for seven
years, plays the piano, and enjoys sewing. Elaine Marie married Gary Lawrence,
son of Lawrence and Rosa Lehr, October 27, 1972. They have three children:
Reanne Sheri, Jarrett Jarmin and Rosanna Marie. They reside in the Irvine area.

Carmen Faye, born January 29, 1959, graduated from Irvine High School in 1977.
She was a 4-H member, in competition for stampede queen, studied four years of
music, and enjoys crafts. Carmen Faye married Timothy James, son of Hattie and
the late John Clark, June 16, 1978. They have three daughters: Charmaine Tessa
and Camile Eileen (twins), and Adrianne Christine. They are residing at Eagle
Butte, Alberta.

Albert Schorr Family: Back: Irene, Melanie; Front: Carmen, Albert, Elaine (pic)

Melanie Ann, born September 29, 1968, graduated from Irvine High School in 1986
and attended Medicine Hat College, 1986 to 1988. She is working for her ARCT in
piano. She was a 4-H member, Southern Alberta Hereford princess, 1987-88. Her
favorite hobbies are painting and curling. She is to be married November 4,
1989 to Geoffory Edric Watson of Maple Creek, Saskatchewan.

We celebrated our fortieth anniversary November 22, 1987.

We have enjoyed this area of country living.

Ben and Erna (Oswald) Schorr
submitted by Ben Schorr

I, Benjamin, youngest son of Gottfried and Anna Maria (Seitz) Schorr, was born
and raised on the farm south of Irvine, in the Newburg district.

During the summer, school days meant hurrying in the morning to help with
morning chores, such as milking cows, feeding pigs and milk cow's calves, wash
up, grab the syrup pail lunch pail and head off on a two mile trek to Newburg
School.

During the winter I set a trap line and again I had a morning chore of checking
traps before setting off for school. These trap lines would net a little
"pocket money". Prices for a coyote fur would vary from $3 to $8, weasels and
skunks $2 to $3, and rabbits 25 cents. A bounty was paid by the government on
gopher tails, magpie and crow eggs and legs. Gophers were snared and magpie and
crow's nests were raided for eggs and the young birds. These catches were
brought to school and recorded by the teacher who paid us accordingly. I
believe the prices were 1 cent per gopher tail, 1 to 2 cents per egg and 5
cents for a set of birds legs.

In the fall of 1947, my parents moved to Medicine Hat and I took over the farm.
My bachelor days ended March, 1952 when I married Erna Oswald, a teacher at
Concordia School. We bought our marriage license from Mr. Steve Wiedeman of
Irvine and were married in the old Memorial Evangelical Church in Medicine Hat.
Two children were born to this union, a son Barry Benjamin, born December 3,
1952, and a daughter, Marian Louise, born April 23, 1957. They attended Cypress
View and Irvine Schools. Barry graduated in 1971 and Marian in 1975.

In 1958 a new house was built and because the logs of the old house were still
very sound it was converted into a machine shed.

Ben Schorr Family: Barry, Erna, Ben, Marian (pic)

With the introduction of Calgary Power in the spring of 1959, we now could
enjoy the luxuries of indoor plumbing and central heating. Coal and wood
stoves, high test lights and irons were replaced with electrical appliances.

Needless to say farming became more mechanized. I bought my first combine in
1957 and for the first time we did our own combining. Over the years the method
of handling bales changed from loading and stacking by hand to the more modern
automatic bale-wagon.

In 1972 we bought the original Fred Rath farm from his son Jim. The house was
sold to Mr. A. Hauck and moved to Redcliff.

In 1973, after graduating from Olds College, Barry joined me in the farming
operation. Our greatest pride and joy has always been our herd of commercial
Hereford cattle, therefore it is understandable that over the years our herd
has gradually increased and the greater portion of cultivated land has been
seeded back into grass. We are conservationists believing we have to keep the
land in as good or better condition for future generations.

Erna and I moved to Medicine Hat in January 1983. For the next five years, most
of the spring and summer months were spent out at the farm, helping Barry.

On June 24, 1988 Barry married Sandra Jean, daughter of Bill and Jean Smith, of
Calgary. Their family consists of Mathew, 9, Christy, 6, Jackie, 5 and Benjamin
William, born May 3, 1989.

Marian attended Medicine Hat College, University of Calgary and Wilfrid Laurier
University of Kitchener-Waterloo, Ontario, receiving her B.S.W. and M.S.W.
degrees. She is presently residing in Hamilton, Ontario and working for the
cities of Hamilton and Wentworth's Department of Social Work as a family
counselor.

Bert and Mary Simmons

Bert Simmons, born in Medicine Hat March 14, 1917, was perhaps destined to be a
railroader. His father, George Simmons, born in Walkerton, Ontario February 23,
1875, was employed by Grand Trunk Railway. He came west in 1899 and did a
little prospecting for gold in the Caribou Country before joining the C.P.R. in
Medicine Hat in 1901. He started as a brakeman and later worked as a conductor
until he retired in 1940.

Bert's grandfather, John Simmons, born in Tonbridge, Kent, England in 1844,
worked as an operator-agent for C.N.R. at Palmerston, Ontario for many years.

Bert grew up in Medicine Hat at 399 Belfast Street. He attended Connaught
Public School and Alexander High School. After school hours he delivered the
Albertan, ushered in the Monarch Theatre and worked in the White Spot. During
the summer holidays he worked on his uncle Jack Scott's farm at Benyon or
worked with uncles Ed and Andy Moore on a farm near Beaverlodge in the Peace
River Country. Bert was never idle and had a great desire to homestead in the
Peace River. However his father advised him to go operating on the C.P.R. Jobs
were scarce and Bert worked only a few months a year during his training period
between 1937-40. He had no car and bus and train service were not good so he
often traveled by freight in the engine or caboose. He worked at Dunmore, Maple
Creek, Rocky Mountain House, Raymond, Leduc, East Coulee, and Golden Prairie as
a relief operator.

Mary (Starling) and Bert Simmons - 1941 (PIC)

I, Mary Starling, was born in Medicine Hat September 15, 1918 to Catherine and
Cave Starling. My mother, Catherine (Boswell) Starling, was born in Chester,
England. Her father, Richard Boswell, was born in England in 1868. He taught
school in Chester, England until 1910 when he came to Canada and settled in the
Red Deer district. He was the first teacher from Britain to attend the Calgary
Normal School to obtain his Alberta teaching certificate.

His first school was at Wildhorse and he walked there from Medicine Hat.
Inspector Sweet knew him and later, when he inspected Cypress School near
Elkwater where I was teaching (my first school), he told me he had never known
anyone who walked the long distances my grandfather did.

Later Grandpa taught at a Hutterite Colony and at Clover Hill School near
Irvine. Ted Roll was one of his students. He taught at numerous schools in
Alberta. His wife died in 1928 and he remarried and returned to England where
he taught for several years. He returned to Canada and taught in Northern
Alberta until he was 80 years old. He died in 1952. He wrote a poetic novel,
"Nora", a romance of the Great War, World War One.

I, Mary Simmons, was honored by the Irvine United Church Women on their 25th
Anniversary. I had been the first president (1962). It was a real surprise as I
received an invitation to a luncheon not knowing I was to be the guest of
honour. It was a lovely afternoon and I received my 25th year pin and a lovely
bouquet of flowers. Betty Sauter, president, Betty Frisch, secretary, and
Shirley Hagel, treasurer of Irvine U.C.W. planned such an enjoyable afternoon.
We had a lovely luncheon at noon in the beautiful basement hall. The mothers of
the E.C.S. catered to this and it was delicious. Laura Schlaht decorated a huge
cake made to commemorate the 25th Anniversary of the Irvine U.C.W. Emma
McLaughlin played the piano and we sang some favorite hymns in the sanctuary.

My memories of Irvine are very happy ones. It was a friendly community and we
spent 11 of our happiest years there. Victor hated to move to Nanton but the
Irvine station was being closed so Bert bid on Nanton and we had five happy
years there. Then we went to Leduc and then Coalhurst and Bert retired in 1971.
We made our home in Medicine Hat.

Bert died of cancer on February 15, 1987. It was wonderful support for the
family to have such a big turnout of old friends at the funeral held at
Riverside Presbyterian Church. They came from Edmonton, Calgary, Wrentham,
Irvine, Claydon, Stettler, Red Deer and Lethbridge.

We had a family of three boys: George was born while we were at Suffield, Clint
arrived between moves and Vic was born at Irvine in 1952. They received most of
their education in the Irvine School.

Bert Simmons Family: Clinton, Bert, Mary, George; Front: Victor (pic)

George lives in Edmonton and works for Edmonton telephones.

Clint lives in Stirling and works as an electrician in Coalhurst.

Vic lives in Medicine Hat. He married Deb Gehring and they have a son, Brock,
and a daughter, Heather.

George Smith
by George Smith

My parents emigrated from Scotland in 1910 and homesteaded nine miles north of
Irvine, NE 13-13-3-W4, where I was born October 7th, 1911, followed by five
brothers, all living.

One brother and his family live near me and the other four are all on farms
west of Red Deer, Alberta.

I made many trips to Long Valley School barefoot, as well as going to Irvine by
saddle horse for mail and groceries.

We moved west of Red Deer in early December 1924 along with the Pete Andersons,
their two girls and three boys, and the Arthur Cattons, their one girl and
three boys. There were seven car loads of stuff and 15 kids.

I remember neighbors going through our yard with barrels of water on
stone-boats to fight a prairie fire. The water was hauled by a team of horses.

The land my father sold was on a crop payment plan. My Uncle James Johnston was
killed in France in 1915. His half section which cornered father's to the north
west, S 23-13-3-W4, was sold February 20, 1928 for the equivalent of 3799
bushels of wheat to be paid as a crop share. With 1930 in the offing no doubt
it was quite cheap land.

Oscar Soderquist
by Elmer Allan Soderquist

In 1909, or 1910 my father, Oscar Soderquist, who was living in Washburn, North
Dakota, filed on land up in Alberta. He was allotted a quarter section listed
as NE 12-12-2-W4, 60 acres between the town of Irvine and Walsh.

He came up in the year of 1910 to start improving land. Being a carpenter, he
got a job in Medicine Hat working in the Ogilvie Flour Mill. He married and
lived in Medicine Hat for a year or more, then moved back to the homestead, in
a two room shack. This is where my memories start.

When we lived in our shack, my Dad would go to work with his tools on the back
of his bicycle. His work took him away from home for a week or more at a time,
which left only my mother and myself at home.

We used to have some pretty scary moments at times, especially during the
spring and summer. Often my mother would wake me up late at night or early in
the morning. We could hear the sounds of singing, laughter, loud talking, the
clinking of tug chains, and the creaking of wagons coming down the road about
two hundred feet away. These were the Gypsies traveling through, and it was
days like those, when it was said that they preferred white children and would
kidnap them if they could. Because of this, my mother was a pretty good shot
with a .22 caliber gun which was always beside her bed. She woke me up so I
wouldn't make a noise to attract any attention.

When I was around four or five years old, my dad moved a larger house onto the
property. In about 1916, we moved into our big house which was, or seemed a lot
safer, so we thought! During the summer days in 1916, one of those big thunder
storms came up, and the next thing we knew, there were hailstones the size of
hens-eggs. Mother grabbed some blankets and pillows and held them up to the
windows, but to no avail; they were all broken. The hailstones were still
around three days later and we were able to make some ice-cream (a real treat
in those days). However, our flax field and our wheat field were pulverized
into the ground.

It was from here I started my school days. How well I remember the first
morning. My mother took me up to the Clover Hill School to meet my first
teacher, Miss Crawford. It was approximately a mile, which took me across the
prairie and around a large slough or "Duck Soup Lake" as it was known then, and
then up a hill to the school house. In the cloak room to hang up coats etc.
were three pound Burns lard pails of sandwiches and "Rawleighs" liniment
bottles of milk. It was a one room school with grades from one to eight, and
one teacher whose desk was at the rear on a raised up platform. The platform
was also used as a stage during our concerts. It was next to a large
ornamental, tin, wood and coal furnace. My, how it felt nice to get close to it
during the winter months.

My first book was a soft cover "Alexander" reader. After that we graduated to
the hard cover primer and so it went until the change to Canadian readers at
"book 4".

It is here that I will endeavor to list the pupils, names as remembered. Edwin
and Mary Glock, Millie Glock, Thorvald, Helga, Ole and Olga (twins) Gutterud,
George Hamilton, Tom Wood, Henry and Fred Neubauer, Douglas Black and sister,
Paul Zwick, Carl, Ben, and Claudia Brandt.

Sorry if I have since forgotten some of the pupils names. Now for the teachers.
There was Miss Crawford, Reidar Torjussen, and who could forget Mr. Shoemaker?
(The checker player?)

Then in 1920 I was blessed with an arrival of a brother, Ernest, who has since
passed away in the year 1955.

Oscar S. Soderquist Family: Mrs. Soderquist, Oscar, Elmer; Front: Ernest - 1927
(pic)

In the year 1918, my Father purchased another quarter section of land from
Michael Essar, who resided in the city of Trail, British Columbia. It was the
SE 12-12-2-W4.

The following years the drought, grasshoppers, and dust-storms set in and
forced us to give up and move into Central Alberta, west of Red Deer. This
ended my contacts in the Clover Hill District.

Christmas Card, 1922 (pic)

Gottlieb and Emma (Uicht) Stadel
by Jack Stadel and Freda Scheffelmeier

Emma Leicht was born in North Dakota February 25, 1896. She immigrated with her
parents to Canada in 1912 and in 1915 was united in marriage to Gottlieb Stadel.

Gottlieb Stadel was born in Romania, October 6, 1893. He immigrated to the
U.S.A. in 1909 to Streeter, North Dakota. In 1913 he immigrated to Irvine,
Alberta, working as a labourer on the C.P.R. In 1918 he became a section
foreman with the C.P.R. starting at Larmour and in 1931, was transferred to
Mackid, Saskatchewan.

In the spring of 1933, he was transferred to Pashley, Alberta and resided in
Pashley until his retirement in October, 1953. They retired and made their home
in Medicine Hat after 35 years of work on the C.P.R.

They had nine children, six boys and three girls. Gottlieb died in infancy.

Neal, born April 23, 1917, married to Martha Scheffelmeier, had two girls and
one boy, and lived in Medicine Hat. Neal died June 10, 1943 in an accident on
the C.P.R. yards in Medicine Hat where he worked as a switchman.

Jack worked as a B and B Foreman on the C.P.R. for 43 years. He is retired and
living in Medicine Hat. He married Minnie Moore and had two boys and two girls.

Freda married Emil Scheffelmeier, had one son and one daughter, and is living
in Medicine Hat.

Flora married Vic Longacre, had one daughter, and is living in Okotoks.

Howard met with a fatal accident at the Pashley Elevator when he was eight
years old.

Esther died in infancy.

Edwin (deceased) was single and lived in Medicine Hat.

Clarence is living in Okotoks.

While we were living in Larmour, Neal, Jack, Freda, and Flora went to the
Schlaht School. When we were transferred to Mackid, Saskatchewan, Neal, Jack,
Flora, Freda and Howard attended Somerset School. When we were transferred back
to Pashley, Jack, Freda, Flora, and Howard attended the Abelein School. Edwin
and Clarence also started there.

Ed. Note: Jack Stadel died on September 18, 1988.

Doug Staniforth

Doug Staniforth was born in Belper, Derbyshire, England. He came to Canada with
his brother in 1897 and on to Medicine Hat in about 1900. He took out a
homestead on the NW 10-12-2-W4 about 1910 and later acquired the NE quarter as
well. His shack was located near the NE corner of the section. The flat stones
used as a foundation are still visible.

With the outbreak of war in 1914 Doug enlisted in the 31st Battalion, Winnipeg
Rifles and served overseas as a machine gunner until his discharge in 1918 with
the rank of sergeant.

He returned to his homestead and farmed until about 1924. He then moved to
Calgary to become the bookkeeper for Burns Packing Co. in their newly opened
meat cannery section.

He was married in 1937, retired in 1960 and passed away February 1982.

Ludwig and Amalia Stelter
by E. Stelter

Ludwig Stelter, the second of three children born to Martin and Marrianna
(Riechert) Stelter, was born in Poland in 1855. When he was 12, the family
moved to the Ukraine, where they farmed. In 1880 he married Amalia Demm.

Amalia Demm, the youngest of four children, was born on Christmas day, 1863 in
Poland. Her father was a government official who was killed by guerrillas only
eight days after she was born. After her mother remarried the family moved to
the Ukraine. This is where she met Ludwig.

After his marriage, Ludwig worked as a tenant farmer in Russia, but seeing no
future in this, he was encouraged to immigrate to Canada. He and three of his
friends, none of whom spoke English, arrived in Winnipeg in 1887. In a year he
managed to send for his wife and two young daughters, Matilda and Lydia.

Until 1891 he worked in Winnipeg and two sons, Albert and Frederick were born.
When work became available in Edmonton, he worked on the railway line to
Calgary. He then secured a permanent position with the C.P.R. at Dunmore. This
is where Charles and Mary were born.

Tragedy struck the Stelter family in 1895, when Matilda, the oldest daughter,
became lost while rounding up the cows one evening. Even though the N.W.M.P.
and people from all the surrounding areas helped in the search no trace of her
was ever found. For many years after, rumors of what could have happened to her
were spread throughout Alberta.

In 1896, the family obtained a homestead at Josephsburg, which was 20 miles
from Dunmore. Five more children were born, Everett, Arthur, Emma, Edwin and
Elsie. For many years Amalia ran the post office from her home. The post office
was known as "Newburg".

Amalia and Ludwig were Lutheran, but they were impressed with the Moravian form
of worship, and after writing to Bethlehem about their convictions, the Rev.
Clement Hoyler visited them, and in 1898 they joined the Moravian Church. Until
they moved to Bruderheim they ran their own church services and prayer meetings.

In the spring of 1918, they sold the farm at Josephsburg to the Schorr Brothers
(Chris and Gottfried) and moved to Bruderheim. The grandson of Gottfried is
presently farming that homestead.

Ludwig and Amalia, who were married for 66 years, both died in 1946.

Emelia, their first child born in Russia in 1881 died one year later.

Matilda, born in 1883 in Russia, was lost and presumed dead in Dunmore in 1895.

Lydia, who was born in 1886, married Emil Henkleman. Emil died in 1959, Lydia
in 1970.

Albert, who was born in Winnipeg in 1889, married Katherine Hillenburg. After
Albert's retirement from the Baptist ministry they lived in Edmonton and then
Medicine Hat. He died in 1957, Katherine in 1972.

Frederick, who was born in Winnipeg, married Emma Henkleman in 1916. He died in
1956. Emma died in 1966.

Charles, born in Dunmore in 1893, married Martha Schwanke. Martha died in 1968,
Charles in 1983.

Mary was born in Dunmore in 1895. She married Gus Schwanke and they farmed west
of Bruderheim. Gus died in 1957, Mary in 1982.

Everett was born in 1897 in Josephsburg. He married Elizabeth Schultz of
Bruderheim in 1922. They are living in Taber at the present time, where they
have been for the past 52 years.

Arthur was born at Josephsburg in 1901. He married Elsie Driesner in 1932. They

Johann and Rosina (Bieber) Stotz

Johann Stotz was born in Glueckstahl, South Russia in August 1866. Rosina
Bieber was born April 7, 1870 in Glueckstahl, the daughter of Johann and Rosina
(Hausauer) Bieber. Johann Stotz and Rosina Bieber were married in 1889. They
left Russia and arrived in Eureka, South Dakota in 1899 with four children,
Jacob, Johann, Eva and Rosina. They traveled to Eureka via Canada, landing at
Montreal and then going by train to Winnipeg and on to the United States. They
farmed in McPherson County, South Dakota until 1907 when they moved to Canada,
to Irvine, Alberta. While living in South Dakota they had three more children,
Charlotte, Martha and Caroline. The family was farming south of Irvine at the
time of Johann's death on December 23, 1908 at the age of 42 years. In 1909
Rosina Stotz and her six children took up a homestead north of the town of
Irvine.

Johann Stotz relatives: Back: Louise Bieber, John and Gottlieb Bieber, Johann
and Rosina (Bieber) Stotz; Front: Johannes and Rosina (Hausauer) Bieber, Peter
and Christina Hausauer (pic)

In 1910 Rosina Stotz married a neighboring farmer, Peter Herth, a widower with
five children. One son Peter Herth Jr. was born to them. Peter Herth died in
September 1941 and Rosina moved to Medicine Hat shortly after, making her home
with her daughter Charlotte Kozmyk. She passed away on January 23, 1942 and is
buried beside her husband, Peter Herth, in St. George's Cemetery in Irvine.

Rosina Herth lived a very hard life bearing 13 children but only the surviving
children are known. Besides raising her own seven children, she helped to raise
the five Herth children, Edward, Christina Sophia, Amelia and Henry. Besides
these she helped raise five grandchildren.

Rosina Herth was a very good cook and she could feed her large household on
very little. Her big apron pockets always held some treasure.

She loved her garden and had the best and biggest gooseberries in the country,
but her flowers were her pride and joy. The hollyhocks, cosmos, larkspurs, and
poppies were always bright and cheerful.

Jacob Stotz, (March 22, 1891-October 1944) married Christina Herth (b. July 9,
1894). They had four children.

Johann, born June 1894, died 1901.

Eva (May 3, 1896-October 18, 1918) married Christian Oswald and had two
children.

Rosina (May 9, 1898-October 28, 1918) married Edward Herth (October 2,
1895-January 30, 1971) and had one daughter.

Charlotte (January 23, 1902-June 20, 1968) married Adam Kozmyk (April 21,
1896-November 19, 1969) and had four children.

Martha (June 3, 1904-January 16, 1961) had four children.

Caroline (April 24, 1906-June 11, 1982) married Alvin Helm and had two sons.
She married a second time to Claude Lockwood (April 24, 1906-September 23,
1956) and they had five children.

Peter Herth was born November 19, 1910 and died April 10, 1966.
