Fred and Emelie (Krauss) Stuber

Fred Stuber was born in Russia in 1901. He immigrated to Canada with his
parents in 1912 at the age of 11 years. He attended Schneider School and worked
with his father on a farm south of Irvine.

On January 8, 1925, he married Emelie Krauss in Medicine Hat. They farmed about
one mile north of his parents' farm. In 1928, they moved to a farm,
NE 5-11-3-W4, in the Coal Centre School district, where they raised their family
of eight children. The children all attended school at Coal Centre which was
three miles north of the home place. Their transportation to and from school
was horse and buggy or sleigh and a lot of times they would walk. They boarded
the school teacher, Gladys Longhurst, from 1933-1935.

Fred did the janitorial work for the school, such as fixing fences, cleaning
the stables and hauling coal in the winter for heating, for a large sum of $4 a
month. I remember one Saturday morning, Dad and the boys, Walter and Jim, were
hauling some coal to the school. After unloading the coal, they left the horses
and wagon unattended in the school yard while they were cleaning the stables,
and finding by surprise no horses there when they were done. The horses had
made their way home with no driver. When the horses got to the yard, they were
spooked by the dogs and they took off around in circles through the yard
leaving mother with no clothes line. They finally stopped at the barn. By that
time, Dad and the boys had walked home.

Times were hard so they milked quite a few cows and made their own butter which
they sold, along with eggs, to customers in Medicine Hat. A lot of meals were
made from dough, which cut down on the grocery bill. I remember Mom used to buy
used clothing at the Market Place which she would take apart and make clothing
for the kids. She would wash and bleach flour sacks which were also used for
bedding or clothing. They farmed and worked their land using horses until 1941,
when Dad bought his first tractor. In 1954, they moved to Irvine and Walter
took over the farm. In 1965, they moved to Medicine Hat where they still
reside. They are still both in good health and enjoy their garden and flowers.

Their family consists of eight children:

Alice married Herb Flaig. Herb worked at the Foundry and at the Five Roses
Flour Mill. Alice worked at various places but had worked for many years at the
Medicine Hat Co-op when she retired in 1987. They have two sons, Lyle and
Bruce. Herb passed away suddenly in 1978.

Walter married Lily Rath. They have one daughter Cheryl. Walter took over the
family farm, where he still farms.

Florence married Clarence Jans. They have three children, Linda, Carol and
Steven.

Jim married Loretta Ginther. Jim left the Irvine area in his younger years and
went to work for a farmer in the Carbon district where he met Loretta. They
were married in 1953 and make their home at Drumheller where he is now retired.
For many years, Jim worked for the Department of Highways and then for the City
of Drumheller, on the towns water and sewer. Jim and Loretta have three
children, Stanley, Debbie and Ken.

Irene married Richard Jans. They have four sons, Leslie, Randy, Darwin and
Dwayne. They are residing in Medicine Hat.

Beatrice married Freddie Bollinger in 1952. They have four children, Dennis,
Rodney, Darrell and Sherry.

Doreen married Eddie Rath. They have three sons, Gregory, Keith and Kelvin.
They farm south of Irvine.

Rose married Eugene Kraemer. Eugene worked on the C.P.R. for several years,
then for Alberta Wheat Pool. They are now residing in Grassy Lake where they
run Country Food Store. They have three children, Reginald, Cindy and Kevin.

Through the years there have been many ups and downs and, I'm sure with a
family of eight, there were a lot of exciting moments.

Fred and Emelie now have 23 grandchildren and 21 great-grandchildren.

Peter and Friederika (Mack) Sturm

Peter Sturm, son of Peter and Christina (Sinkbeil) Sturm, was born February,
1844 in Katzbach, Bessarabia, Russia.

Friederika Mack, daughter of Johann and Regina (Schmied) Mack, was born May 27,
1851 in Wittenberg, Bessarabia.

Peter and Friederika were married November 21, 1868. Four sons and one daughter
died of a plague while the family lived in Russia. The Sturms were anxious to
emigrate because they did not want their sons to be drafted into the Russian
army. Also there was no land available to them and no future in working for
large landowners. Peter and Friederika Sturm immigrated to Canada in 1898 along
with their nine children: Christian, born September 24, 1875; Maria Justina,
born January 2, 1879; Adam, born May 24, 1880; Charles, born April 1, 1882;
Frederick, born August 30, 1883; Emanual, born December 27, 1885; John, born
November 26, 1887; David, born June 9, 1890; and Juliann Christine, born August
30, 1892.

Their unforgettable ocean voyage began in Germany aboard a cattle freighter
which had several partitions. The Sturms were in the portion of the ship where
the anchor chain was located. During turbulence the anchor chain would slide
across the floor and the rats would follow its movement. During one terrible
storm young Julia was thrown out of her mother's arms and under the bunk. The
passengers became violently ill partially from motion sickness and more likely
from the putrid sauerkraut and sowbelly they were fed. Fortunately Mother Sturm
had packed some homemade bread in trunks which she doled out secretly to her
children to comfort them. The crew spoke fluent German and called the seasick
passengers "Russische schweine" (Russian pigs), among other names. This
experience prepared the family for what was ahead.

The ship docked in Halifax, Nova Scotia some 28 or 29 days later and the Sturms
boarded a C.P.R. train which took them to the station at Coleridge (Dunmore).
The Sturms, who understood no English, needed an interpreter to notify their
contacts, the Bohnets, of their arrival. They stopped wagon after wagon until a
German speaking traveler finally came along who knew where the Bohnet family
lived and went to tell them.

Meanwhile the Sturm family remained at the train station for four or five days
with little or no food. The starving children wandered away to the Ross Creek
north of the station where they caught and ate a few small fish. One of the
Bohnets arrived and brought the Sturms to the Bohnet farm in the Josephsburg
area where they fed and lodged them temporarily. When they fed their starving
guests the first time, they were surprised at the amount of food such a large
family could eat.

Peter Sturm immediately took out a homestead in the Josephsburg area. He
borrowed horses and equipment from Adam Sackman to bring his land into
production. The youngest children received schooling in the Josephsburg area
but the older ones were required for farm work. One by one the Sturm children
left home to seek their own fortunes and establish families.

Peter Sturm died in February 1909 and was buried in the Josephsburg cemetery.
Later Friederika retired to Irvine where she lived across the street from her
daughter Justina and her husband Christian Weiss. Even in her older years
Friederika possessed great physical strength and a feisty disposition. What she
did not possess was a liking for dogs that bit people. Once, when grandson
Alfred was nipped by Justina's dog at the Weiss house in Irvine, Friederika
hurled the offending dog against the side of the house with such a force that
the dog lost consciousness. Justina came running out of the house to see what
happened and was told (by her mother) to keep quiet or the same would happen to
her.

Eventually Friederika's house in Irvine was torn down and the lumber salvaged
to become part of John Sturm's house in the Thelma district. Friederika lived
temporarily with her son John, then stayed briefly with each of her children in
turn. She died at Adam Sturm's farm on September 11, 1934 and was buried in the
Josephsburg cemetery

Back: Amelia (Stelter) Sturm, David, Emanuel Sturm; Front: Justina (Sturm)
Weiss, Christian Weiss, Juliana (Sturm) Connolly?, Bertine (Helgeson) Sturm,
Fred Sturm Sr. (pic)

Fred Sr. and Bertine Sturm

Fred Sturm, Sr., son of Peter and Friederika (Mack) Sturm, was born August 30,
1883 in Bessarabia, Russia and came to Canada in 1898 at age 15. He was able to
read German and Russian but never received any English schooling.

As a young single man Fred rode to Montana on horseback to work as a hired hand
on a ranch in the Havre area. Because he was a newcomer he was often ordered to
cook for the rest of the hired hands. One day Fred was tired of trying to cook
in a camp that had little in the way of provisions. He left his raking to
prepare the noon meal and 15 minutes later the men sat down to eat the hard
beans that had never even reached simmering point. He was never asked to cook
again.

Fred got into a scrap with the wrong cowhand and was run off the ranch with
gunfire. Unnerved, he returned to Alberta without belongings or food. Hunger
forced him to raid a garden near the Canada-U.S. border where he ate raw
kohlrabi.

By the next year he was bold enough to head for Montana again. The Milk River
that ran through Havre swelled its banks to a threatening width due to the
spring thaw. Fred forded the river on horseback as there were no bridges or
ferries. This time he met an amiable Norwegian girl who was employed as a maid
on the Buckley ranch where he worked.

Fred and Bertine (Helgeson) Sturm Sr. Wedding - February 5, 1905 (pic)

Bertine Helgeson Tjorn, daughter of Tonnes Helgeson Tjorn and Kari (1varsdotter
Vassbo) Tjorn, was born November 16, 1880 at Stavanger, Norway. On February 5,
1905 Fred Sturm and Bertine Helgeson were married at Sweetgrass, Montana. They
packed their belongings and left for Alberta. Fred took his new bride to Irvine
where they lived with Justina and Christian Weiss. Justina and the new Mrs.
Sturm got along well.

Fred took a job at a livery barn for over two years. He cleaned the barn, fed
and watered the horses and even chauffeured people by horse and buggy. One
winter day he was hired to drive a lady with a small son to the Thelma district
to visit relatives. The gentle snowfall at Irvine became heavier and the wind
gathered speed as the travelers proceeded south. By late afternoon they reached
the bench. The approaching nightfall and whipping snow confused them as they
drove in circles. Fred realized that they would freeze to death unless they
found shelter. He allowed the horses to drift with the wind until they reached
a haystack. Despite the woman's apprehension, the travelers burrowed deep into
the stack and stayed there all night. The storm subsided and the next morning
they continued their journey, thankful to be alive.

About 1908 the Sturms and their daughters, Gladys and Julia, moved to the
Thelma district. In the spring of 1910 little Julia died following a brief
illness. Three children were born to them while they lived on the bench: Agnes,
Peter and Gertrude. It is believed that Fred delivered Gertrude, and that a
neighbor lady was called afterwards to bathe the infant.

Farming on the bench did not prove to be very successful. Waist-high crops
were destroyed by killing frosts. Discouraged by low income, Fred sold the land
after 1916 and moved north.

In the Newburg district he attempted to buy a farm, the NE 33-9-2-W4, owned by
Gottlieb Freimark. Fred built a barn, house, corrals and a small dam. The three
youngest Sturm children, Esther, Fred Jr., and Jean, were born at Newburg. The
harvests of 1918 and 1920 yielded barely enough grain for chicken feed. With no
cattle or grain to sell it was impossible to make land payments while
supporting a large family. In frustration he sought to sell the land back to
the Freimarks.

A new opportunity came when Fred's son-in-law, William Good, wished to sell his
farm in the Sentinel district. In 1927 Gladys and William moved to a ranch in
Saskatchewan and the Sturms moved to the Good farm, SW 12-10-2-W4. Fred Sr.
used the profit from the bumper crops of 1927 and 1928 to pay for the farm. In
1929 Agnes married John Flaig.

The large Sturm family was cramped in their two bedroom house. Fred Sr. bought
the former Bischke house in Irvine and had it moved out to the farm with a team
of 24 horses. With the help of relatives and neighbors, the Sturms built on an
addition using the lumber from the old house. The children provided most of the
labor in salvaging the lumber while the family lived in a granary over the
summer.

The Sturm children were brought up in a strict home where work, not leisure,
was the order of the day. Fred Sr. was religious in his own way though he
seldom participated in the organized church. The children were not allowed to
play cards or attend dances but these rules were broken a few times. One night
Gertie and Esther crawled out of an upstairs bedroom window and lowered
themselves to the ground by a ladder. The girls stole away in the darkness,
carrying their silk stockings and dress shoes with them, to attend a dance at
the Charlie Good farm. The farmhouse was so crowded that the revelers moved the
dancing to Sentinel School. Gertie and Esther were a little nervous because
their father served on the school board so they made certain they were home
before daylight.

The mid-thirties brought soil erosion, swarms of grasshoppers and desperate
times. The crop was cut for grain feed to sustain work horses while cows were
sold at $5 per head. Cows that were too weak to stand after calving were fed
gruel made from chopped grain and water or they were destroyed. There was no
hay so Russian thistles were cut for feed. Many people left the area including
Peter and Ida Sturm who moved to the Tofield area in 1936. The government
provided aid to the drought stricken area by sending oats and hay as well as
food: apples, carrots, cheese, potatoes and turnips.

Many of the men hopped freight trains and traveled to other parts of the
country to earn a living. In 1937, Fred Sturm Jr., John Flaig and Hugo Widmer
rode a freight to Calgary where they nearly landed in the river trying to avoid
the authorities. They hid in some brush until the train was out of sight and
spent the night at the Calgary train station where hobos ate raw cabbage. The
next day they jumped another train which took them to the Olds area. They were
hired by local farmers and paid $1 per day plus board for preparing granaries.
Stooking was worth $2 per day while threshing paid $2.50 per day.

The forties brought a return to better times with improved crops and adequate
feed for livestock. The Sturm children were grown up and leaving home. Esther
and Gertrude left home in the early 1940's to obtain work and marry. Jean
married in 1944.

In early 1948 Fred and Bertha Sturm retired to 963 Dominion Street in Medicine
Hat while Fred Jr. operated the family farm. Fred Sr. died October 29, 1952.
Bertha remained in her own home helping to care for her granddaughter Florence
following Gertrude Sundstrom's death. Bertha Sturm died January 24, 1963 at 82
years of age.

Back: Agnes and Pete Sturm, Gladys and William Good; Front: Rachel Good, Jean
Sturm, Florence Good, Fred Sturm Jr., Esther, Gertie, Bertha, Fred Sturm Sr.;
Seated: Earl Good (pic)

(4) Peter Alexander Sturm

Peter Sturm was born October 14, 1911 in the Thelma district. Following his
schooling at Newburg he worked on the farm.

On March 18, 1934 he married Ida Heller at Graburn Church of God. The couple
lived with Peter's parents until October 1936 when they moved to the Tofield
area. After ten years in the Tofield area Peter and Ida moved to Mission, B.C.

Peter and Ida are semi-retired at Ponoka, Alberta.

They have three children: Norman, Shirley, and Garry. Shirley and Ed Kossowan
have a son, Sheldon. Garry and Mary Anne (Estelle) have a son, Harold.

(5) Gertrude (Sturm) Sundstrom

Gertrude Sturm was born in the Thelma district on May 27, 1915. She received
her schooling in the Newburg and Sentinel district. After leaving home she was
employed in Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan before coming to the Claresholm area where
she worked as a domestic helper.

In 1939 Gertrude married Gus Sundstrom. They lived at Wainwright and Claresholm
before moving to an acreage near Shepard, Alberta. Gertrude and Gus had two
children, Marvin and Florence.

Gertrude died March 13, 1951 at 35 years of age. Gus and Marvin moved to
Calgary. Florence was raised by her aunt Esther and grandmother in Medicine
Hat. Gus died in 1967.

Marvin married Elke Zimmer. Florence and Doug Scott have two children, Pamela
and Graham.

(6) Esther (Sturm) Sundstrom

Esther Sturm was born in the Newburg district on September 22, 1918. She
attended school in the Newburg and Sentinel district after which she worked at
home. Later she was employed as a domestic helper near Claresholm.

In 1942 Esther married Maurice Sundstrom. They lived briefly at Rimbey, Calgary
and then Claresholm. In the fall of 1951 Esther, Maurice and their son Vernon
settled in Medicine Hat where Maurice worked for the city. Esther became
responsible for the care of her young niece Florence following Gertrude
Sundstrom's death. She also took part time employment at Eaton's for about two
years.

Esther and Maurice are retired in Medicine Hat. Vernon and Donna (Henchelwood)
Sundstrom have three sons, Devin, Perry and Kyle.

(7) Fredrick Burtle Sturm

Fred Sturm Jr. was born in the Newburg district on April 14, 1921. He was
raised and educated in the Sentinel district after which he worked on the farm.

In 1937, at 16 years of age, Fred rode the boxcars along with John Flaig and
Hugo Widmer to the Olds area where he worked for a month during the harvest. He
became an avid outdoorsman and hunter who delighted in bringing wild game home
to his mother.

Following his parents' retirement, Fred operated the family farm. In January
1952 Fred married Ida Bittner in Medicine Hat. They had one daughter Betty Ann.
Fred Sturm was one of the original members of the Stony Hill Grazing
Association.

Fred died November 5, 1973. The farm was sold the following year and Ida
retired to Medicine Hat. Betty and Leonard Janke have four children, Stephanie,
Christine, Ryan and Catherine.

(8) Genava "Jean" (Sturm) Zieffle

Jean Sturm was born in the Newburg district on August 17, 1923 and received her
schooling at Sentinel School. She completed the eighth grade by age 13 when she
left school to work at home.

In 1944 she married Charlie Zieffle. For about one year Charlie and Jean rented
a farm located northeast of the Sturm farm. When their daughter Fay was four
weeks old they moved to the Piapot area where they farmed until their
retirement in 1972.

Charlie died in 1979. Jean continues to reside in Medicine Hat. Fay and Frank
Godec have three children, Maria, Mark and Michelle.

Emanuel and Margaret (Schlaht) Sturm

Peter Sturm was Emanuel Sturm's father. Emanuel was 11 years old when they
immigrated to Canada. Emanuel had to go to work at the age of 11 and got a job
as a range rider. In the fall the range riders would go on a cattle round-up.
They always took Emanuel along on the long journey of the round-up to help
along. They would have a trail wagon along for a kitchen with their food and a
cook. There weren't any fences in those days; it was wide open prairie. I
remember Dad (Emanuel) saying the round-up could take them into the U.S.A. Each
owner had his own brand to identify his cattle and horses. When Emanuel was old
enough to take up a homestead, it was in the Thelma district. When Emanuel
married Margaret Schlaht they lived on the homestead until their eldest
daughter, Alice, was old enough to go to school. They moved to Irvine in the
fall, and in the spring they moved four miles southwest of Irvine. Emanuel
traded his homestead in Thelma for Mr. McNaught's homestead.

Margaret was a baby when the Schlaht family immigrated to California, U.S.A. In
1903, when Margaret was 12 years old, the Schlaht family came to Canada and
took up residence eight miles southeast of Irvine. The Schlaht family had nine
children, four boys and five girls. Margaret and her younger sister had to herd
cattle from morning to evening to keep them from wandering away. The people got
together and built a school on Schlaht land. It was named "Schlaht School".
Margaret got two years of education. Margaret worked for a ranger's wife before
she got married to Emanuel. Margaret was the one that taught Emanuel to read
and in later years he loved reading.

Emanuel and Margaret had six girls: Alice, Frieda, Helen, Nora, Christina and
Pearl. The girls all got their education in the town of Irvine. We drove four
miles to school with horse and buggy until the snow came in the fall. We
couldn't go back to school until spring after the snow was gone. We didn't have
any warm clothes to wear like they do now.

Margaret, Emanuel and Alice Sturm 1908 (pic)

Alice married Jake Linderman. They lived three miles south of Irvine. They had
four children: Archie, Bertie, Blanche and Eileen. They got their education in
Irvine. They also traveled to school with horse and buggy.

Frieda married John Trekofski. They lived eight miles south of Irvine. They had
two children, twins, Clairie and Larry. They were bussed to Irvine for their
education.

Helen married John Sulz. They had one child, Shirley.

Nora married Victor Krause. They lived in Walsh. They had two children,
Lorraine and Peggy. The girls got part of their education in Walsh and later
were bussed to Irvine for their high school education.

Christina married Dave Sulz. They lived north of Irvine. They had three
children: Jeanette, Jim, and Grace. They got part of their education in Irvine
until the family moved to Hanna, Alberta where the children finished their
education.

George and Barbara (Genert) Sulz

George Sulz was born in 1848, son of John (b. 1805) and Caroline (Hoffman) (b.
1812). He married Barbara Genert (born December 28, 1849). They came to Canada
from Bessarabia in 1903 with his family. He and several of his sons and his
son-in-law took up homesteads south of Irvine. His children included Jacob,
Rosina, Wilhelm (William), Karl, Chris, and Fred.

Jacob (July 11, 1875-July 1960) married Wilhemina Deering (September 24,
1878-October 15, 1941) and had four sons and four daughters.

Rosina (July 10, 1877-December 23, 1949) married Michael Hehr and had three
sons and two daughters.

Wilhelm (May 2, 1881-June 3, 1966) married Christina Yanke on October 23, 1904.
They had four children. Martha, born in 1905, married Emil Freimark; Bertha
married Paul Ammann; William married Erna Krausz and died in 1983; Fred married
Marjorie Nittle. Marj passed away on January 2, 1989 at age 70 and their
daughter, Marlene, predeceased her mother on August 18, 1988. Fred lives in
Medicine Hat.

Karl (May 2, 1884-April 8, 1947) married Martha Vossler. They had six children.
Emil married Martha Jans and died November 11, 1980; John married Helen Sturm
and died July 25, 1981; Karl (Charlie) married Hertha Gwinner; Dave married
Christina (Tina) Sturm; Viola married Albert Christman; Annie married Walter
Becker.

Chris (June 2, 1888-August 31, 1920) married Christina Wahl. Their children
included Josephine (Jo) and Anne (Cherry).

Fred (December 11, 1890-February 5, 1954) married Lydia Rath. They had seven
children, two of whom died in infancy. Leah (Lily) married Art Deering; Rose
married Walter Flemmer; Edward married Jean Flemmer; Marion married William
Kerner; James married Rose Weimer.

Jacob and Wilhemina (Deering) Sulz

Jacob Sulz was born July 11, 1875 in Bessarabia, where he married Wilhemina
Deering in 1901. Their first child, Mary, was born in 1902, prior to their
immigrating to Canada in 1903 * Jacob and Wilhemina homesteaded in the
Josephsburg area six miles south of Irvine and their family increased: Otto was
born in 1904, Bertha in 1907, Fred in 1909, and Emmanuel in 1910. In March
1911, they bought a farm in the Robinson area and here Lizzie was born in 1912,
Martha in 1915, and Ben in 1918.

Mary married William Bischke and they farmed in the same area for many years.
They had four children: Leah, Alice, Edna, and Reuben.

Otto married Emma Kelm and had two children, Wallace and Howard. When Otto died
in 1936, Emma moved to Hanna.

Bertha (Jans) died in 1928.

Fred married Hilda Mack and farmed in the area until they moved to Medicine Hat
in 1957 with their four children: Ken, Florence, Norman and Betty Ann.

Emmanuel married Esther Franz and with their three children, Edward, Doris and
Patty, farmed north of Irvine. Emmanuel also worked for the C.P.R. for many
years.

Lizzie and her husband Fred Jans and four sons, Clarence, Leonard, Edgar and
Elmer, farmed next to the Bischke's until 1966 when they moved to Medicine Hat.

Martha, married to Ed Walker, farmed in Hilda and later operated a dairy six
miles east of Medicine Hat along with their two daughters, Gloria and Ruby.

Ben married Esther Walker and farmed the home farm until 1947 when they moved
to Medicine Hat where Ben worked for Crystal Dairies. They had three children:
Rosemarie, Sharon and Daryl.

When the Sulzes moved to the area, there was no school district until 1921 when
the Robinson School was built. During those first years the Cypress and Gros
Ventre Schools were in operation but were full, as well as being quite a
distance from the farm. Schooling for the older children was limited to two or
three months in the Gros Ventre E.U.B. church. The younger children were
educated in the Robinson School.

The main trading centre was Irvine and many hours were spent hauling grain and
livestock there by horse and wagon and picking up groceries, coal, and other
staples.

Besides farming, Jacob was a blacksmith, sharpening plough shears for many a
neighbor. He tanned leather and was a harness maker, both for his own use and
for sale to neighboring farms.

Wilhemina, like many pioneer women, carded and spun her own wool for the
knitting of countless socks and mitts.

Wilhemina died in 1941 and Jacob continued to farm until 1947 when he retired
to Medicine Hat where he died in 1960. He was a healthy robust man and died two
days short of his 85th birthday, still weighing close to his normal 250 pounds.

The home farm was sold in 1957 and the only descendants farming in the area are
grandsons, Clarence and Edgar Jans and Reuben Bischke.

Fred and Hilda Sulz

In 1940, Fred Sulz, son of Jacob and Wilhemina, married Hilda Mack, daughter of
Fred and Christina Mack, and farmed with his parents. Farm buildings were moved
to a part of the family farm that had been purchased from the Hudson Bay
Company in 1916. They farmed there until 1947 when this part of the farm was
sold and they then moved to the home place when Jacob retired.

Fred Sulz Family: Back: Fred, Kenneth, Hilda; Front: Norman, Betty Ann,
Florence (pic)

Fred and Hilda had four children: Kenneth, who with his wife, Marilyn and three
children, David, Dan and Leanne, live in Duncan, B.C.; Florence Mock and her
three children, Marlin, Debora and Robert who all reside in Medicine Hat;
Norman and his wife Shirley who live in Okotoks; and Betty Ann and Bill Harder
who live in Estevan, Saskatchewan and have three children, Sheila, Steven and
Dean.

All of the children attended the Robinson School until it closed in 1954 and
then were bussed to Cypress View School. The Sulz family boarded the school
teachers from 1947 to 1952 and all had the dubious duty of getting the children
to school by horse and buggy. Ken's first teacher, Mrs. Langel, decided she did
not need his "expert" six year old guidance to get home and sent him on ahead.
She stayed on at school working until it was nearly dark and decided to take a
short cut home. Well after dark, she ended up at the Henry Wutzke farm some
three miles in the opposite direction.

In 1957, the Sulzes moved to Medicine Hat where Fred worked in construction and
with City Parks. Fred passed away March 25, 1987 at the age of 78.

William Jr. and Erna (Krausz) Sulz

William Sulz Jr. farmed on the old homestead that his grandfather George Sulz
had taken up, NE 29-10-2-W4. He was married to Erna Krausz. They had four girls
born into this family. Gwen, married to Norm Picke, has two children and
resides in Edmonton. Arleen, married to Bob Pfingsttag, has one child and
resides in Osoyoos, B.C. Janice, married to Tony Quaife, has one child and
resides at Armstrong, B.C. Daphenee passed away in July 1960 in an accident.

William sold his farm in 1949 and the family moved to Kamloops, B.C. and went
into the motel business, returning to Medicine Hat in the late fifties to work
for Klemm Electric and Propane Outlet. He delivered propane in the Medicine Hat
area for a number of years. He moved back to Osoyoos, B.C. in the late
seventies, went into the motel business again, and retired there.

He passed away on January 17, 1983 in Osoyoos. His wife Erna resides at Osoyoos.

John and Helen (Sturm) Sulz

John Sulz, son of Karl and Martha (Vossler) Sulz, married Helen Sturm. They
lived nine miles south of Irvine. They had one child, Shirley.

Shirley received her education from grade one to seven in Medicine Hat at Elm
Street School. She then went to Berry Centre School either on horseback or
walked one and a half miles until they lost their home in a fire caused by
lightning. After this they moved in with Helen's dad, Emanuel Sturm, in Irvine
and Shirley finished her education in Irvine.

John drove the school bus from 1957 to 1973. He drove the bus route up to Pete
Armstrong's for many years. There wasn't any gravel on the road from the
correction line up to Armstrongs' for the first year. John also drove the bus
out on the Stony Hill Route; he drove as far south as Harvey Good's.

John Sulz Family: Helen, Shirley, John (pic)

It was tough going at times when the snow would blow and bank up on the road.
They would send a snow plow out to plow the snow into the ditches and when the
wind started blowing, the road blew in as high as what the snow plow had pushed
out. John was driving a four wheel drive, but it wasn't good enough to get
through the snow banks. What else could he do but shovel his way through? John
did a lot of shoveling. He got paid for driving but not the shoveling. In 1974
John and Helen moved to Medicine Hat and retired.

Karl (Charlie) and Hertha (Gwinner) Sulz

I, Hertha, was born unto Jacob and Christina (Schorr) Gwinner on March 27, 1922
in Schuler, Alberta., I went to Newburg School District #346 and spent my youth
on my parents' farm helping them.

Karl (Charlie) Sulz was born unto Karl and Martha (Vossler) Sulz on April 28,
1919 in Irvine, Alberta. He went to Berry Centre School, Schneider School, and
also went to Medicine Hat. The family moved to the Strong place, W 14-11-3-W4.

In 1939 Charlie was called into the army for one month in October. Then in 1940
he was drafted into the army as Pte. Charlie Sulz 600900, stationed in various
camps in Canada. In March 1944 he got leave to come home to do the seeding and
summer-fallow.

Karl and I got married on April 18, 1944 and lived on his parents' farm. His
parents moved off in October 1943. The summer was hot and very dry and the
crops were poor. In 1945 we had no water for our milk cows. My parents repaired
the house on the John Weiss place, then moved us onto it. We lived on the
NW 18-9-3-W4. (W 1/2NE 18-9-3-W4, N 1/2 SE 18-9-3-W4) The SW 18-9-3-W4 was mine.
Our first crop was a real good crop, and we had plenty of water and hay for our
cattle.

Karl Sulz home - 1947 (John Weiss place) (pic)

In 1949 we bought our first tractor, a Minneapolis, from Albert Crewe in
Irvine. In 1950 my dad built a new house for us and we moved in, in January
1951. In 1951 we bought another farm, the farm of Andrew and Katherine Seitz,
the NE, NW, and SW 17-9-3-W4. We bought a new Dodge car in 1952. Before the use
of combines, we bindered our grain and had to put the bundles in stooks before
they could be threshed. We sold our calves in the fall to pay expenses until we
had our cattle established. Our cattle brand was"\CH/ - right rib. We milked
from eight to twelve cows in the summer and one or two cows in the winter for
milk, and raised chickens, ducks, geese and turkeys. Pigs we raised for our own
use to butcher in the fall. We sold our farm and ranch in 1966 and moved to
Medicine Hat on the 29th of June.

Karl, Loretta, Hertha, Darlene Sulz; Front: Clinton (pic)

We were blessed with three children: Darlene Gloria, born August 28, 1945;
Loretta Florence, born August 27, 1946; and Clinton Charles, born December 14,
1963.

Darlene went one year to Cypress School, then both daughters went to Gros
Ventre School. In 1953 they attended the Cypress View School, which was Newburg
School District before. In 1957 they were bussed to Irvine. Mr. Christian
Wirsch was the bus driver for many years. Karl bought a school bus and bussed
for two terms, 1962 to 1964. Loretta graduated in 1964, and then went on to
College in Calgary. Darlene took a hair styling course and was working when we
moved to Medicine Hat.

Karl worked over the summer months for Arthur Boschee for the Massey-Harris
Company. In the fall he helped combine and worked for Taurus Janitorial
Service. In October 1969 he started to work for School District #76. He retired
May 3, 1983.

I was busy cleaning, gardening, canning, painting inside and out, and raising
our son and sending him off to school. I did a lot of baking: bread, kuchen,
cinnamon rolls, buns, pies and cakes and the cookies the boys loved to eat.

Now Karl is active in pool playing and bowling for pastime. I have lots to do
in my house for now. I had great pleasure in baking, but now everyone has to
cut down on baked things.

Fredrick and Lydia (Rath) Sulz
submitted by Larry and Joan Deering

Fred and Lydia came to Canada in 1902 and 1903 from Bessarabia. Bessarabia is
an area in Southwest Russia bordered by the Dnestr River on the north and east,
the Danube River and the Black Sea on the south, and the Prut River on the
west. The entire area lies along the eastern border of Romania. Bessarabia is
an agricultural area that produces cereal crops, tobacco, grapes, etc. It was
during the communist oppression that people of the region fled to other parts
of the world. It appears their families came to Canada settling in the Irvine
area to take up homesteads continuing on with their agricultural backgrounds.

Fredrick Sulz was born on December 11, 1890 in Bessarabia, the youngest of the
family of George and Barbara (Genert) Sulz, and came to Irvine at the age of 12
with the rest of his family.

Lydia Rath was born November 10, 1898 in Bessarabia, the oldest of the family
of Fredrick and Christina (Stuber) Rath, and came to Irvine at the age of five
with her parents and one brother. The rest of her brothers and sisters were
born here.

Fred and Lydia married January 16, 1916. They rented a farm for a short while
and then moved to Irvine only to move back to farming in 1930. The farm they
purchased from Mr. Banek in 1930 is still today a family farm. Fred and Lydia
had seven children, five daughters and two sons. Two daughters, Annie, at the
age of four, and Alice, at the age of two, passed away in childhood. Fred and
Lydia continued to farm during the hardships of the 1930s and up to retiring in
1948, leaving the family farm operation to son Ed. Upon retiring to Medicine
Hat, they built a home at 901-7th Avenue S.E., at which location today is a
Shell self-serve service station on Kingsway. Shortly after celebrating 38
years of marriage Fred passed away February 5, 1954 at the age of 63. Lydia
continued to live in the family home and raise the youngest family member, Jim,
who was nine years old when his father passed on. Lydia passed away March 31,
1967 at the age of 68 after a lengthy bout with cancer.

The family history continues with the eldest daughter, Lily, born January 16,
1917. She went to Irvine, Schlaht, and Schneider Schools and remained at home
until marrying Arthur Deering (born October 20, 1921) on November 6, 1943. Lily
and Art rented a farm in the Gros Ventre Creek area from her uncle William
Sulz, until taking over her family farm from brother Ed in December of 1951.
They added a half section to the family farm, buying from William Sulz Jr. Lily
and Art have three sons, Larry, Glen, and Ray. Lily passed away June 23, 1989.

Larry, born October 23, 1944, married Joan Feil (born September 21, 1945) on
July 2, 1965. Larry spent ten years away from the family farm pursuing a
post-secondary education and accounting career with his wife Joan who taught
school in Calgary. In 1973 they bought cousin Emil Sulz's farm and moved back
to the family farm. Three children were born: Mark, November 8, 1971; Coreen,
October 25, 1973; and Paul, January 16, 1979. Paul was a good birthday
surprise, being born on grandma's birthday, who herself was born on her
parents' first wedding anniversary. Larry, actively involved in community
recreation since 1976, is currently the secretary/treasurer of the Irvine and
District Agriculture Society. He was councilor for Improvement District #1
beginning with the municipal elections in October 1983. The Improvement
District incorporated to become the Municipal District of Cypress #1 January 1,
1985 of which Larry is presently serving as a councilor. Larry and Joan remain
on the home quarter of the family farm, the rest being farmed by brother Glenn.

Glenn, born on September 7, 1947, was delivered by Grandma Deering (midwife)
and went to Irvine School. He married Louise Telke (born June 16, 1951) of
Medicine Hat on April 3, 1971. Glenn and Louise purchased a neighbouring farm,
which was Lydia's sister Olga's family farm, to continue farming to the
present. Glenn and Louise have two children, Denise, born January 24, 1976, and
Derek, born March 15, 1981.

Ray was also delivered by Grandma Deering, on October 17, 1952. Ray graduated
from Irvine School and pursued two years of post-secondary Police Science
education at Mount Royal College in Calgary. After serving a short time on the
Medicine Hat Police Force, Ray switched occupations and is presently a
journeyman carpenter in Medicine Hat. Ray met Gloria Bryant (born November 16,
1953) while in Calgary. They married on November 24, 1973. Ray and Gloria have
two sons, Daniel, born March 31, 1980, and Sandon, born May 16, 1983.

Rose, born July 2, 1924, went to Schlaht and Schneider Schools. Rose married
Walter Flemmer (June 19, 1917-December 25, 1963) on October 10, 1945. Rose and
Walter (from south of Walsh) moved to Medicine Hat shortly after being married,
where Walter worked for a construction company for a short time before going to
work for Canada Post Corporation until his passing. Rose and Walter had two
sons and one daughter. Floyd, born September 15, 1947, married Peggy Peterson
(born October 25, 1948) on October 25, 1969. Floyd has pursued a career as a
journeyman parts-man beginning in Medicine Hat, going to Kindersley, Vancouver,
and back to Medicine Hat where he works for Zelmor Automotive. Floyd and Peggy
have three daughters, Dana, born June 12, 1971; Katherine, born August 30,
1973; and Christine, born January 1, 1977. Stanley, born June 5, 1949, married
Brenda Heffley (born October 29, 1950) on August 10, 1968. Stan is a journeyman
in autobody. His career began in Medicine Hat, took him to Calgary and back to
Medicine Hat, where he has his own business, DAS Custom & Collision. Stan and
Brenda have two children, Lorne, born April 30, 1970, and Patricia, born June
14, 1972. Shirley was born December 22, 1951. She married Rick Chalifoux (born
April 10, 1949) on October 28, 1972. Shirley and Rick (an electrician) have
three daughters, Damara, born October 5, 1977, Myra, born June 11, 1979, and
Lisa, born April 9, 1981. Shirley is presently living in Calgary and raising
their three daughters.

Ed, born February 1, 1927, married Jean Flemmer (born November 16, 1926),
sister to Rose's husband, Walter, on October 19, 1946. Ed took over the family
farm from his dad in 1948 and moved to Medicine Hat shortly after he left the
farm in 1951. Ed was employed by Dempster Farm Equipment, Steiner Petroleum and
as a school custodian. Ed and Jean are living in Medicine Hat. They have two
sons. Barry, born March 16, 1951, married Marlene Hirshkorn (born September 29,
1954) on December 4, 1971. Barry is currently employed as a millwright for the
City of Medicine Hat. Barry and Marlene have two children, Anjela Leah, born
March 30, 1972, and Jerry, born October 24, 1973. Lorne, born June 10, 1952,
married Robin Toker (born September 12, 1956) on July 9, 1977. Lorne is
currently living in Redcliff and has worked for the C.P.R. for 17 years.

Marion, born January 12, 1929, went to Schneider School. Marion moved to
Medicine Hat with her parents when they retired from the farm in 1948. She
married Bill Kerner (born February 25, 1925) on November 8, 1952. Bill worked
for Dempster Farm Equipment before being employed by Canada Post Corporation to
present day. They have two children, Rodney, born October 8, 1964, and Laurie,
born April 29, 1966.

Jim, the youngest of the family, was born April 9, 1944. He was nine when his
father passed away. Jim stayed at home with his mother during her illness until
her passing in 1967. Some years later, Jim married Rose Weimer (born October 2,
1948) on January 19, 1981. He worked for a few years as a journeyman
auto-bodyman for Gardiner Motors before becoming an owner operator of Deluxe
Central Cabs. Jim and Rose have two daughters, Joanne, born January 11, 1971,
and Darlene, born February 4, 1972.

Edward and Jean (Flemmer) Sulz

Edward Sulz was born February 1, 1927 at Irvine, son of Fred and Lydia (Rath)
Sulz. He was raised on the family farm south of Irvine and attended Schneider
School.

I, Jean, was born November 16, 1926 at Graburn, daughter of Christian and
Magdelina (Weishaar) Flemmer of Graburn but in the Saskatchewan portion of the
district. I was raised on this family farm and attended Miller School. Ed and I
were married October 19, 1946 in the Graburn United Church.

We lived with Ed's parents until September 1947 when we moved to Medicine Hat.
In February 1948 Ed's father had a stroke so we moved back to the farm. Ed's
parents moved to Medicine Hat that summer and built a new house. We were on the
family farm until December 1951, then moved to the Fred Vossler farm for a
season. In September 1952 we moved to Medicine Hat where Ed worked at the
Dempster Farm Equipment.

We had two sons:

Barry was born March 16, 1951. He is married to Marlene Hirsekorn. They had one
daughter and one son.

Lorne Edward was born June 10, 1952. He married Robin Toker and has one
daughter.

Michael and Maria (Oljar) Svihura
by Mary Ann (Mrs. Pete) Weigel

Michael Svihura was born January 27, 1902 and Maria (Oljar) Svihura was born
December 21, 1903. They were both born in Czechoslovakia, raised, educated and
married there before they came to Canada in 1929.

They settled in the Clover Hill District and farmed there until 1940. That year
they moved to Medicine Hat and Michael worked at several jobs at the Maple Leaf
Mills until he retired. He died in 1969.

Maria continued to reside in Medicine Hat. She was a member of the Senior
Citizens and Friendship Society. Maria passed away on December 5, 1976.

Both Michael and Maria Svihura are buried at Hillside Cemetery.

Michael, Jean, Edward Svihura 1939 (pic)

Edward, Maria, Jean Svihura - 1939 (pic)

Their family consisted of one son, Edward, living in Calgary, and two
daughters, Jean (Mrs. Al Dirk) and Mary Ann (Mrs. Pete Weigel), who both reside
in Medicine Hat.

Sophia Thiede

Sophia was born on July 28, 1902 in Odessa, Russia. She immigrated to Campbell
County, Herried, South Dakota, U.S.A. with her parents Jacob and Dorothea
Thiede. On February 14, 1914 they moved to Irvine. Jacob was a farmer and a
school janitor. Dorothea was an avid gardener and had a beautiful yard and
garden when most other yards were dry and bare. Sophia was the only child.

Her father, born January 6, 1877, died December 23, 1938 and her mother, born
on November 5, 1877, died April 9, 1962.

Jacob, Sophia, Dorothea Thiede (pic)

Sophie feeding chickens (pic)

Sophia worked in what was known as Silver's General Store which became the
Schneider Bros' General Store and finally Wiedemann's General Store. Sophia
retired after 50 years of employment on February 28, 1971. After her retirement
she served as Town Councilor, the first lady councilor, for a short period of
time prior to moving to Medicine Hat where she resided in the Luther Manor
until she was hospitalized.

Sophia had a keen interest in sports, she was a superb baseball player and she
loved skating and curling. She took a great interest in children and gardening.
She taught Sunday school for a number of years at the Baptist Church. Her
friends in the community were her family; she lived for them and they accepted
her as one of their own.

Sophia Thiede in 1926 car (pic)

On several holidays she traveled to Coeur d'Alene, Idaho, U.S.A. to visit her
cousin, Linda Mattis.

Sophia passed away on January 1, 1989 at the age of 86 years.

Joseph McNae Thomson
by Ian Thomson

Joseph McNae Thomson was born in Scotland, October 27, 1883. Following his
education of only grade four and later employment in Wolverhampton, England, he
sailed by steamer in the spring of 1909 to meet a cousin at Tierra Del Fuego,
Chile, and to work for Duncan, Fox and Company. This English based firm owned
four large sheep ranches in Patagonia, and in 1912 they sheared over one
million sheep.

Joseph returned to Scotland in April of 1913 and following a holiday he came to
Irvine to work for Phil McLeay. In October 1914 he and about a hundred men from
the Medicine Hat area enlisted in the 31st Battalion in Calgary. Following the
war he returned to the McLeay ranch.

Mary Thomson, born 1890, arrived from Scotland in March of 1922 and they were
married at the McLeay ranch (in the present Kevin Freimark home) on the last
day of the same month.

Joseph M. Thomson - in uniform (pic)

Joseph M. and Mary Thomson - 1922 (pic)

Thomson Store - 1925 Irvine (burned down in June 1925) (pic)

Dad later purchased a General Store in Irvine which he operated until it was
lost by fire in June of 1925. A grocery salesman told him about a similar store
that was for sale in Milo. He came to Milo and negotiated a deal for the
business, arriving here with his wife and young son Jim, on the last day of
September. He continued in the grocery business until his retirement in 1950.

Mary and Jim Thomson in Irvine (pic)

Jim Thomson - in uniform (1923-1943) (pic)

Dad passed away in April of 1971 and Mother in April of 1984.

Jim, born in 1923, died in England during a training exercise with the R.C.A.F.
in 1943. There were four other children in the family.

Joe, born in 1926, served in the navy during W.W. II, took over the store from
his father in 1951, and operated it until his retirement in 1981. He married
Bernice Anderson of Milo and they have one son, Jim, now a lawyer in Calgary.

Jean was born in 1928 and following her education she received her R.N. from
the Royal Alexandra in Edmonton. She retired in July of 1987 and is presently
living in Milo.

Ian, born in 1932, has lived in the Milo area all his life and farms.

Robbie, born in 1935, received his B.Sc. in Civil Engineering from U. of A. and
later added his Masters, specializing in soil and cement. He is presently
project manager for the construction of Canada Olympic Park in Calgary. He
married Sharon Phillips of Milo and they have three sons, David, at U. of A. in
Dentistry, Blair in U. of C., and Douglas in high school.

Albert Tohm

Albert Tohm came to Irvine from North Dakota to homestead in the Irvine area in
1911 on the NE 20-12-2-W4, returning to North Dakota for the winter months. He
moved here permanently in 1913 with his wife Elizabeth (Lizzie) and seven
children and started to build a house. They brought with them a full line of
farm machinery and livestock and also the lumber from their dismantled
buildings on C.P. Rail. They broke the land with a team of oxen. They ran a
small flock of sheep purchased from George Mackie when he sold his sheep.
Albert grew his own tobacco and cured it and also spun the wool that he needed
for the knitting that he did for his family.

His place was a place for friends and neighbors to gather on Sundays, winter or
summer: in the summer for ball games held down in the flat or to practice new
numbers for the orchestra; in the winter for house parties and impromptu dances
when the orchestra was practicing. Albert was a warmhearted person who loved
children and would baby-sit for mothers with small and young babies, so that
they would be able to enjoy themselves for a portion of the day or evening. In
the winter, if there wasn't a dance at one of the school houses in the area,
Wilkinson, Long Valley, Clover Hill or Many Island, they gathered for a visit
and there would be an impromptu party or dance held in the parlor. They had an
organ and piano, and most of the family were able to play an instrument or were
able to chord on the piano or organ, along with anyone else who was there that
could play.

Lizzie passed away in 1918 during the Flu Epidemic when the youngest child was
six months old. They had 12 children: Alvin (Al), Clarence, Leo, Art, Lillian,
Clara and Willard, born in the States; Anne, Verna, Minnie, Esther and Herman,
born on the farm here.

Because of the drought in the 30's Albert, Clarence and Esther moved to
Wildwood in 1936. Esther passed away up there. Clarence stayed and continued to
farm there. Albert returned home and passed away in 1939.

Al married Minnie Schmidt and homesteaded in the Many Island Lake area,
divorced and moved to Seattle, Washington and eventually remarried. There was a
son Edwin from the first marriage.

Clarence stayed single and farmed in the Wildwood, Alberta area until the time
of his passing.

Leo also stayed single, moved to the Didsbury, Alberta area working for various
farmers in the area, retired and moved to Didsbury where he lived until the
time of his passing.

Art moved back to North Dakota, married and then eventually moved to Seattle,
Washington. They had three children, Sandra, Mary Jo, and Ken.

Lillian went to work at Gull Lake, Saskatchewan, married Mike Moritz and
operated a farm north of Gull Lake. They had four boys Ronald, Gordon, Harold
and Arnold.

Clara also went to work at Gull Lake and married Karl Kirk. Later they moved to
Spruce Grove, Alberta. She has two step children, Betty and Vera.

Willard married Violet Engel, lived on the home place for a short time and then
moved to Didsbury, where they farmed until his passing. They had three
children, Lyla, Jean and Ken.

Anne married William (Bill) Trekofski, lived on a farm south of Irvine, just on
the west side of 41, moved to the Wildwood, Alberta area for a period of time
and then moved back to Medicine Hat. She still lives in Medicine Hat. They had
three children, Evangeline, Melvin and Lyla.

Verna married Edwin Engel.

Minnie married Carl Brandt and moved to the Wildwood area where they farmed,
later moving into Edmonton, where she worked at University Hospital and still
resides. They had one son, Bryant.

Esther passed away as a young lady.

Herman married Ruth and farmed in the Carstairs, Alberta district until his
retirement, when they moved into Didsbury, Alberta. They had three children,
Donna, Kenneth and Allan.

Michael and Wilhelmina Trekofski

Michael and Wilhelmina Trekofski came from Bowdle, South Dakota in 1903 to the
Irvine area. With them came their three sons and their wives: Fred and Amelia
(Petzke), Joseph and Elizabeth (Doerr), and John and Christine (Pietzke).

They all took up homesteads southwest of Irvine. Michael and his wife moved to
Irvine and lived in a shack until they had their house built in 1918. Joe took
his dad's homestead and farmed it with his own as their farms were next to each
other.

Michael Trekofski and some of his family (pic)

Michael and Wilhelmina Trekofski with Doerr children: Back: Sam, Rudy, Gotlieb;
Front: Molly, Oscar, Martha (pic)

When Michael and Wilhelmina died years later their son Joe and Elizabeth moved
into their house in Irvine. It is still in use at this time. John and Adeline
Sackman lived in it, after which it was sold to Brian and Karen Waldbauer, and
later bought by Kim and Karen Kramer.

Michael Trekofski, besides three sons also had a daughter, Pauline. She didn't
come to Canada when the rest of the family did. She was married to Carl Doerr
and they had four sons and two daughters. After their family was grown up, they
moved to the Irvine district for a few years. Carl Doerr died while they were
living in Irvine and Pauline moved back to the States to be with her family.

Fred and Amelia (Petzke) Trekofski

Fred Trekofski and Amelia (Molly) Petzke were married on February 17, 1898 in
South Dakota.

Fred and a friend came to Canada by train a few years after he was married, to
see what opportunities there were. Fred liked the Irvine District, while his
friend went on to Olds. Fred went back to get his family. In 1903 Fred, his
wife, and two sons, Bill and Sam, Fred's father Michael, and Fred's brothers,
came by train to homestead south of Irvine. When they came to Canada, they
loaded all their belongings into a box car and brought them with them. Fred had
numerous farms, finally settling on the Crooks place in the Gros Ventre Creek
in 1925, farming there until 1944 when his son John took over the farm.

Fred and Amelia (Molly) Trekofski 50th Anniv. - 1948 (pic)

Fred and Amelia (Molly) Trekofski 50th Anniv. Cake (pic)

Fred was busy farming and Molly did the housework and cooking. She did very
nice embroidery. They raised seven children.

Bill married Ann Tohm. They farmed a short time in the Gros Ventre Creek area
then moved to Medicine Hat. Bill worked for many years with the Dept. of
Highways until his retirement. They raised three children. Bill is deceased.

Ann (Tohm) and Bill Trekofski - October 14, 1930 (pic)

Sam married Frieda Oberhammer. Sam worked on the C.P.R. as a section man in
various locations and retired as a section foreman, making their home in
Calgary after his retirement. They raised two children. Sam and Frieda are both
deceased.

Lydia married Harold Oberhammer. They farmed north of Pashley for many years
prior to moving to Medicine Hat. Lydia was a good cook and did some crocheting.
They raised nine children. Harold and Lydia are both deceased.

Eva married Henry Christensen in Tilley, Alberta, later moving to Langley B.C.
where Henry worked as a logger until retirement. You will always see Eva with a
crochet hook in her hand. They raised five children. Henry is deceased.

Hilda followed her sister to the coast, where she met Vince Palkowski and
married him. He was a welder in the shipyards then. Hilda was a seamstress.
They started building single dwelling homes while still working their other
jobs. They gave up their jobs and went into building apartments and managing
them. They have retired to an acreage in Richmond, B.C.

Martha married Bill Heather. Bill was in the Canadian Armed Forces. They lived
in Medicine Hat until they moved to Langley, B.C. where they presently reside.
Bill worked mostly as a maintenance person. Martha did a lot of sewing,
knitting and crocheting and was a good cook and baker. They raised two children.

John married Frieda Sturm on December 27, 1935. Twins were born to them on May
25, 1938: Clairie and Larry. John took over the family farm in 1944. They
farmed there until 1957 when they moved to Medicine Hat. In 1958 they purchased
the Emil Freimark ranch, selling to the Tschritter family in 1959, and once
again returning to Medicine Hat. John was seasonally employed with the Parks
Department until his retirement in 1978. Frieda passed away in September of
1974. John now resides in White Rock, B.C.

Del and Clairie Jane (Trekofski) Leitch
by Clairie Jane Leitch

Hi, I am Clairie Jane (Trekofski) Leitch born May 25, 1938, twin daughter of
John and Frieda Trekofski. My twin brother, Larry, and I were raised on a farm
along the Gros Ventre Creek located seven miles southwest of Irvine. We
received our education from grades one to twelve at the Irvine School.

Completing grade 12 in 1957, I started working for James Richardson and Sons
Securities Limited in Medicine Hat, working there until 1964. I was married on
September 16, 1961 to Harland Delmar (Del) Leitch. Del was employed at Alberta
Western Beef at the time. In the spring of 1964 the company started to go bad,
so we had to do something different. In the same year we put our name on the
list for an adoption, and were fortunate to receive a baby girl in March 1964.
Her name is Gaye Jewel. She was born February 22 and was only three weeks old
when we picked her up in Calgary. She attended schools in Lethbridge, Calgary,
Okotoks, back to Lethbridge, and graduated from high school in Okotoks when she
was 16. She attended the University in Lethbridge on a Volleyball Scholarship
and graduated from the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon in May 1987,
with a Psychology and Sociology degree. She is presently working at Hull Homes
in Calgary.

In September 1964 we moved to Lethbridge where Del was employed with Oliver
Industrial. In 1968 we adopted another baby girl, Crystal Jane, who was six
weeks old and was born on May 22, 1968. She attended schools in Okotoks,
Lethbridge, back to Okotoks, and Saskatoon, where she is now residing. Crystal
completed her grade 12 in June 1987 when she graduated from Walter Murray Comp.
High School. Crystal plans to get married in August, 1988.

Fred Trekofski Family: Back: Bill, Eva, Lydia, Hilda, Sam; Front: John, Molly,
Fred, Martha (pic)

We lived in Lethbridge until December, 1969 when we were transferred to
Calgary. In 1975 we were transferred back to Lethbridge. In 1976 we were
blessed with a baby boy, Jamie John, born on October 8. He attended school
beginning in Okotoks and taking part of grades two and all of three in
Saskatoon, where we lived a short time as Del was employed with HyPower. Jamie
is 11 now and attending school in Okotoks.

We moved back to Okotoks from Saskatoon in May of 1986. Del is employed with
City Machinery in Calgary, a very progressing company. I am busy at home on our
acreage at Okotoks, where I am involved with quilting, stained glass, design
knitting (sweaters), tole-painting, rose-maulling, and sewing.

Larry and Noreen Trekofski

Larry was born May 25, 1938 in Medicine Hat General Hospital to John and Frieda
Trekofski. He was raised south of Irvine and attended school at Irvine.

The family moved from the farm to Medicine Hat in 1957, returning to farm in
1958, once again moving to Medicine Hat in 1959.

Larry married Noreen Ford in Elgin, Manitoba on July 9, 1960.

After completing high school, Larry worked for Imperial Oil, Dominion Glass,
Northwest Nitro Chemicals and sold cars for Beny Motors, until 1961, when he
commenced employment with Beneficial Finance in Edmonton. He was transferred to
Kamloops in 1963, back to Edmonton in 1964 and to Medicine Hat in July of 1965,
residing there for ten years. Larry was transferred again to Edmonton in 1975
as supervisor.

He left Beneficial in 1976 to join Province of Alberta Treasury Branches. He
was transferred to Calgary in 1980 and back to Edmonton in 1982. Larry
presently works at Treasury Branches Head Office as Assistant Superintendent of
Credit.

He still runs cattle during the summer on the family farm west of Medicine Hat
and has revenue property in Medicine Hat.

Joseph and Elizabeth (Doerr) Trekofski

Joseph Trekofski was born on September 1, 1877 in Arzies, Russia. Elizabeth
Doerr was born in Rosenthal, Russia. They immigrated to the Dakotas as small
children with their respective parents. They were married on April 15, 1900 in
Bowdle, South Dakota and moved to Canada in 1903 and took up a homestead
southwest of the town of Irvine along with Uncle Fred, Uncle John, and their
dad, Michael Trekofski. There were 13 children born to Joe and Elizabeth but
only nine grew to be adults. Joe took over his dad's homestead in 1916 or 17
and farmed it with his own. He sold the homestead to Isaac Meier after which he
rented farms until he retired into Irvine in 1933 where they lived until his
passing on September 2, 1951.

He worked for the Irvine School a number of years as custodian.

Beatta, Reinhardt Fredrick, Helmuth Henry, Alexander, Herbert (died in
infancy), Freda (died in infancy), Gottlieb (died in infancy), Emma, Linda,
George, Elizabeth (died as a child), and Benjamin.

Nine grew to be adults, married and moved to their own places and raised
families of their own. There is only Linda left of the offspring of Joe and
Elizabeth.

Helmuth Henry and Lydia Trekofski

Henry, as he was known, was born in the district of Irvine in the year 1905,
and there spent his growing years.

In 1928 he went to Scottsburg, Saskatchewan to work, helping out with the
harvesting. There he met Lydia Siebel.

Lydia was born in the year 1912 and lived her early years around Scottsburg,
Saskatchewan.

After their meeting at some neighbors, it seems that love had started to bloom.
Henry returned home after harvest and the following year he returned to
Scottsburg.

Henry and Lydia were married March 31, 1930. Returning to Alberta, they made
their living working for a number of farmers around Irvine and district. They
also spent a short sojourn in the village of Irvine.

Through the years they were blessed with four children, Ruby, Evelyn, Joseph,
and Patricia.

Henry Trekofski Family: Back: Ruby, Joe, Evelyn; Front: Henry, Pat, Lydia (pic)

progressed their children left for lives of their own.

deteriorated and they sold the farm and moved to Irvine in the fall of 1965.
Lydia went to work for Stan and Eileen Wilde as cook and waitress in their

Lydia worked in a number of jobs such as cook, waitress, janitor for the

Alex and Annie Trekofski
by Annie (Trekofski) Mickelborg

Alex (Alexander) Trekofski was born January 20, 1907, son of Joseph and
Elizabeth (Doerr) Trekofski, and was raised and educated in the Irvine area.

I, Annie, was born January 10, 1914, daughter of Carl and Katherine (Linderman)
Meier, also raised and educated in the Irvine area.

Alex and I were married November 2, 1931.

We farmed in the Pashley area for the next five years. Times were hard in those
depression years. In July 1932, a very bad hail storm hit us, which broke
windows on our house, and all our crop hailed out. In August 1932, our first
baby, Esther, was born. That fall we moved into a house in Pashley for a year
as we had no water on our land. At the time there was a post office, section
house, three other houses, a grain elevator and a small depot there. Our house
was near the railway and Trans Canada Highway. We saw many, many men riding the
C.P.R. boxcars going west and back, day after day, looking for work but little
could be found. We had many men coming to the door asking for food or a place
to sleep. Many times I felt very uneasy about it but we never came to any harm.
Most men were gentlemen. There were one or two that scared us. They banged on
the door late at night when we were asleep, and wanted to get in. Their
language certainly wasn't very nice. We'd send them over to the depot where
they could be warm and sleep as a fire was always kept going in the depot when
it was cold. We felt very sorry for these fellows. Many had wives and children
at home with hardly anything to eat or wear.

Times were hard on the farmers, too. Wheat sold for 19 cents a bushel; eggs 5
cents a dozen; butter 8 cents a pound and so on. In 1934 we moved back on our
land. One year the wire worms took the crop; another year grasshoppers were
very bad; another we were dried out.

In 1934, our first son, Earl, was born. That summer we had to carry the water
for the house a quarter of a mile. That kept you slim, especially when it came
to wash day and the baby's wash.

In the fall of 1936, we bought the Heather place about six miles north of
Irvine, and moved there. Our second son, Elmer, was born here.

In the winter of 1936 and '37, we tossed the idea around in our minds to leave
the drought area, so in the spring of 1937, we sold the place again and made
preparations to move northwest to Central Alberta. Alex went up there by bus to
see what he could do for a place. While he was gone a real misfortune hit us.
It was so dry the grass didn't green up that spring. Instead, a weed came up
nice and green. It was very poisonous and they called it Wild Onion. The cows
went after this weed and one by one all our cattle and all our milk cows died.
A cow would be fine in the evening and be dead the next morning. Our hearts
were heavy with all this loss. These cows were our livelihood. However, in
spite of losing all our cattle we went ahead with our plans to leave the
drought area.

Alex prepared a covered wagon for us to travel in and take whatever possessions
we could. On a bright sunny morning, July 10, 1937, Alex and I, with our three
children, boarded our covered wagon and left Irvine. We moved northwest to
Central Alberta and settled in the beautiful Knee Hill Valley area. We had
another little girl, Elaine, three years later.

Due to ill health, we sold the farm and moved into Innisfail. Alex passed away
January 5, 1966. I have since married Leonard Mickelborg and we live in
retirement in Sundre.

Esther is now a pastor's wife, married to Glen Rhind. They live in Kelowna, B.C.

Earl and his wife, Ruth Schalm, are missionaries in South America.

Elmer, his wife Marlene Martin, and family live in Richmond, B.C. and he has
his own business.

Elaine and her husband, Leonard Grynki, and two children have a nice big farm
northeast of Barrhead, Alberta.

Memories of my early childhood include an incident occurring in the spring of
1919 on a sunny Sunday morning. The family was going to visit the Emanuel
Sturms who lived in the creek flats. When we got to the creek, which was close
to the Sturm farm yard, it was flooding. Driving into the creek to cross we
discovered it was deeper and the current stronger than it appeared. When we
were part way across, the churning water upset the buggy, dumping the family of
five into the muddy turbulent water, and taking the buggy and team downstream.
Dad was the only one who could swim. He managed to rescue us, three children,
two and a half years to five years old and Mom. Dad worked speedily lest
someone would drown, as we floundered around in the deep dirty water. He set us
at the edge of the water one by one and quickly went in after another, until we
were all rescued. What a close call! Then we made our way up to the Sturm
house. After everyone was looked after, Dad and Mr. Sturm went to see about the
horses. But sad to say, both horses had drowned due to being hitched to the
buggy. I remember being sick in bed all day.

Another incident I recall when we lived in the Coal Center School District
happened when Mom and I were coming home from the hamlet of Pashley with the
team and buggy. The single tree came off on the evener and hit the horse in the
hind legs causing a runaway buggy. The buggy upset into a bunch of tangled up
barb wire. We had to have a doctor sew up my badly cut scalp. It also caused me
to miss three weeks of school.

Carl and Katie Meier, Annie (Meier) Trekofski, Alice Ryks, Alex Trekofski (pic)

John and Christine Trekofski

Dad, John Trekofski, was born in Bessarabia, Russia on October 1, around 1877.
At a very young age his family immigrated to Bowdle, South Dakota, U.S.A.

In 1900 he married Christine Pietzke. Their first daughter, Adeline was born in
August 1902. In the spring of 1903 they came to Canada, settling in the town of
Irvine for a short period of time.

While in Irvine, Dad worked in a machine shop. However because he was still a
farmer at heart, they decided to take up a homestead nine miles southwest of
Irvine. Two more daughters were born, Emma and Rosie. In the very early spring
in 1908 Christine died suddenly, leaving Dad with three small children. In the
fall of the same year he met and married Christine Wilson, who was born May 1,
1889 at Odessa, South Russia. Mom not only became a wife, but a mother too, all
on the same day. She was very devoted to the three little girls. However in
late 1909 to early 1910, a diphtheria epidemic struck, claiming the lives of
Emma and Rosie.

Marie Trekofski, Johnnie Doering, Christine, Emil (Al) Trekofski; Seated: John
Trekofski (pic)

Earning a living was very tough in those days, making it difficult to carry on
in one place. Consequently, the family was forced to leave this homestead. They
moved around to various places, but finally settled on a farm north of Irvine.
Because of the economic conditions, the older children had to work away from
home while still going to school.

Our family was very musical, played various instruments, and loved to sing. We
spent a lot of our spare time entertaining that way.

A total of 11 children were born through the years, with some passing away in
infancy, leaving seven. They were Ida, Sophie, Elsie, Victoria, Marie, Al
(Emil), Paul. However serious illness claimed the lives of Ida, Elsie, and Paul
in their early ages. Then in 1940 tragedy struck again, with Marie, age 18,
passing away in March of purpura, and in September Dad's life was claimed as a
result of a car accident. This left Mom to run the farm with Al's help. In 1942
she sold the farm and moved to Calgary.

Through the years Mom had married three times and was widowed three times. In
1975 she moved into the George Boyak Nursing Home in Calgary, and in 1987 was
transferred to the Cross Bow Auxiliary Hospital. On January 23, 1988 she passed
away at the age of 98 years young.

The four remaining children and their families include the following:

Adeline married John Sackman (deceased) and resides in the Parkside Manor in
Medicine Hat, Alberta. They have one son George.

Sophie married Albert (Bert) Schneidmiller (deceased) and lives in Calgary,
Alberta. They have two sons, Bruce and Vernon.

Victoria married John Doering and resides in Medicine Hat, Alberta. They have
three children: Leona, Janet, and Garry.

Al married Estelle Geraud and lives in Coquitlam, B.C. Al has two daughters,
Holly and Joy, from a previous marriage.

Victoria (Trekofski) Doering, Al, Sophie (Trekofski) Schneidmiller, Adeline
(Trekofski) Sackman; Seated: Christine Trekofski (pic)

William Trieglaff

The William Trieglaff family came to the Irvine district in 1910 from Becker
County, Minnesota where William had farmed since 1887. They settled on the NE
23 and the NW 24-13-2-W4 near the Many Island Lake post office. William's land
joined that of his brother-in-law Johannes Schmidt on the south side.

William's twin sons, John and Fred, had land bordering that of their father.
John settled on the E 24 and Fred on the E 25-13-2-W4. John and Fred also owned
the S-26. The Trieglaff and Schmidt relatives had 12 adjoining quarter sections
between them.

William Trieglaff was born March 20, 1866 in Falkenburg, Germany. He came to
America with his parents, August and Fredericka (Hentel) Trieglaff, in the
spring of 1868. They lived in Chicago for about a year and briefly in Duluth
before moving to Minnesota in 1871.

William married Elizabeth Schmidt, sister of Ernst and Johannes Schmidt, on
April 13, 1890. William and Elizabeth had six children: Mary (b. 1891), twins
John and Fred (b. 1893), Anna (b. 1897), Elizabeth (b. 1900) and Wilhelm (b.
1903). Mary Trieglaff married Edward Kruger. Fred married Lydia Koenig and
Wilhelm married Lydia's sister Emma Koenig. Anna married Michael Robanske and
Elizabeth married Frank Prunkle. John never married.

The Trieglaff farms in southern Alberta produced some good crops but the
continuing years without rainfall in the 1920's forced many of the farmers in
this area to look for land elsewhere while others abandoned their farms and
changed their occupations in order to support their families.

William and Elizabeth left their Many Island Lake farm about 1924 and moved
north to a more promising farming area near Rossington, Alberta, northwest of
Edmonton. Elizabeth died on November 22, 1928 and William on February 3, 1942.
They are buried at Westlock, Alberta.

Jacob and Justina Tschritter

Jacob Tschritter was born July 22, 1867 in Alt-Elf Bessarabia, Russia. His
wife, Justina Wanke Rath (adopted by the Ferdinand Raths), was born June 26,
1870. The political atmosphere in Russia was getting very bad. The Russian
people hated the Germans that had migrated there and been given homesteads in
the hope that they would farm the land better and provide more food for the
country.

Jacob took his wife and four children, his in-laws, the Ferdinand Raths, and
his brother Johannes and family (13 people), aboard the Kaiser Wilhelm der
Grosse (ship) and came to Canada in 1898. They homesteaded the farm 12 miles
south of Irvine on the Bull Trail in the Ross Creek. They built a large log
house, 20 x 52, and veranda, full length of the house, broke land and had some
cattle. They helped build the Newburg School, which was used for church
services, funerals, weddings, as a meeting place, and as a school.

Jacob and Justina had 14 children: Wilhelmina, 1893, Maria, 1894, Jacob, 1895,
August, 1897, Emanual, 1898 (died at 18 months), Jacob Jr., 1899, Alvina, 1900,
James, 1901, Albert, 1903 (died three months), David, 1904, Rachel, 1905,
Benjamin, 1906, Hulda, 1908, and Victor, 1909.

In 1912 Jacob returned to Russia for a three month visit. He told of the good
country and tried to persuade more of his family to migrate here. When he
returned he brought his nephew Wilhelm, and convinced his sister Maria and her
husband August Tschritter to bring their family here. After the August
Tschritters arrived Jacob sold his land to them and moved to Irvine for three
and a half years, then moved eight miles north and three west of Irvine. The
children attended the Clearwater School.

After all their children left home Jacob and Justina moved to Medicine Hat.
Justina passed away at the age of 65.

Ten years later Jacob married Emelia Salmeier. Some years later she also passed
away. Later his eyesight failed and he moved in with his son and
daughter-in-law David and Maggie Tschritter in Taber, Alberta. Jacob passed
away November 18, 1966, eight months short of his one hundredth birthday. Jacob
and Justina are buried in Hillside Cemetery in Medicine Hat.

August Sr. and Maria Tschritter

Maria (Tschritter) Tschritter was born March 1863, and her husband August
Tschritter Sr. was born August 8, 1862. They had eight children.

Maria and August Tschritter came to Canada from the Caucasus, Russia in 1913.
They came to the Robinson place where their son William was, and bought the
place for $10,000 cash. Thereafter they bought the farm from Jacob Tschritter
and moved there. They farmed with horses. August Jr. attended Newburg School
when he was 11 years old. Both August Sr. and Jr. were hard working, honest and
compassionate, always willing to lend a helping hand to people in need. They
were Lutheran and attended church regularly.

Maria was ill the last years of her life and died January 23, 1935. August Sr.
died June 5, 1940. They are buried in the Robinson cemetery. Until their deaths
they lived on the farm with August Jr., his wife Katherine, and family.

Frederick and Augustina (Lehr) Tschritter
by Edward Tschritter

Frederick Tschritter was born August 24, 1896 in Bessarabia, Russia. As a child
he lived in a village in North Caucasus near the Sea of Azov. He had taken shoe
making and harness making as a trade. He learned to read and write in German
and could speak some Russian. As a lad of 17 in late summer of 1913, he came to
Canada with his father and mother, August and Maria, and his brothers and
sisters. He stayed on the farm to help his parents ranch and farm south of
Irvine. He bought the Schaller homestead of N 6-10-2-W4 in the spring of 1916.

On June 24 of the same year he married Augustina Lehr. She was born October 17,
1899 in North Dakota, came to Canada as a girt of three years old with her
parents, Mr. and Mrs. John Lehr. They homesteaded on SE 31-9-2-W4.

Later on Fred bought the S 6-10-2-W4 from Chris Schorr. It was the Sommer
homestead. He sold his land to us boys and moved to Medicine Hat in October of
1949.

Most of the teachers boarded at our house, as the Newburg School was so close.

Dad passed away in March of 1975. Mother lived in her house in the 'Hat until
her passing on August 7, 1988. She loved to garden and look after her flowers.

Frederick and Augustina had six sons and one girl. David died in 1917 in
infancy. Edith, born December 26, 1918, married Emanuel Weiland of Manyberries
and had three children. They now live in the 'Hat. Emil, born April 1920, farms
in Manyberries. Edward, born December 24, 1922, farms the homestead. He married
Emma Klaudt October 8, 1949 and they have two children. Arthur, born March 8,
1925, married Bernice Hammer on October 23, 1948 and lives in Chilliwack, B.C.
He runs a motel, is a plumber by trade, and has four children. Otto, born June
23, 1926, married Adeline Wutzke in June 1949. They have four children and farm
south of the 'Hat. Edmund, born March 28, 1933, married Violet Roth on May 10,
1958. He has two children and lives in Medicine Hat.

One of the stories Dad used to tell us is about how a lot of the people had
taken sick on the boat on the voyage over, and how he helped to take care of
them and never got sick. Mother recalls that on her wedding day they went by
horse and buggy to Irvine, took the train to the 'Hat, got married and came
back the next day.
