Fred, Edith; Front: Edmund - 1938 (pic)

Augustina and Fred Tschritter 50th Anniv. - 1966 (pic)

Edith (Ida) Tschritter Weiland

I, Edith, was the first child born to Augustine and Fred Tschritter, on
December 26, 1918. I received my education in the Newburg District, along with
music lessons. In the Newburg Evangelical Church I played the piano for three
years for church services.

Being the oldest child and only daughter, and also having five younger
brothers, Emil, Edward, Arthur, Otto, and Edmund, a lot was expected from me.
Baby-sitting and cooking meals were some of my chores.

My mother helped with the outside work. Everything was done with horses. At
seeding time they would work all day. The horses would have to be changed to
six fresh ones by noon. At harvest time, Mother would also haul wheat to
Irvine, which was 12 miles away. The wheat was hauled with two wagons; Mother
drove one team and Dad another. This was an exhausting all day trip.

We lived about ten miles from Elkwater Lake and I recall once when Dad took us
to the lake to fish, which we always enjoyed, but that day we were in for a
surprise. We were in the middle of the lake fishing when a terrible storm came
up so quickly. The wind was frightening but I remember Dad told us to sit still
and not move. Finally, we were washed up on shore. That day we were all sorry
we didn't catch any fish, but happy everyone was all right.

I loved the outdoor life. We had a garden and grew our vegetables, milked cows,
and had chickens and turkeys, which meant plenty of work.

In the winter, Dad was a great entertainer and loved to play checkers, and on
Sundays we'd all go to church. He made a sleigh and closed in three sides. I
remember going down a hill when the sleigh fell over and we all ended up on top
of each other, but no one fell out. Winters were cold and we were all really
bundled up with big blankets covering our heads. There were many days when it
was 30 below.

I remember, Dad and I used to trail the cows a mile from home for water, which
I enjoyed. Everyone had a horse to ride so on weekends we all used to meet at
someone's home for entertainment. It was nothing to ride ten miles; it seemed
easy. There were no cars to drive.

Edith and Emanuel Weiland - 1938 (pic)

In 1938, I married Emanuel Weiland and moved to the Manyberries district, along
with six cows and some home furnishings my parents gave me. Emanuel took over
his parents farm and plenty of things were needed. With what we had and with
lots of hard work we made a good living. We later had three children.

Jean Bernice was born September 23, 1942 and was educated in the New Home
School and in Medicine Hat. She is married to George Hall and they reside in
Okotoks. They have a son, Shane, and Jean has two children from a previous
marriage, Heather Kim and Braden Dean Gracey.

Marlene Inas was born April 17, 1947 and was educated in Manyberries and
Medicine Hat. She graduated from the Galt School of Nursing in 1968 and married
Lynn Hirsche. They reside in Coaldale and have three children, Tanya, Tyler and
Tera. Marlene has remained active in nursing and Lynn owns Lynn's Transport
which serves the Lethbridge and Manyberries area.

Wayne Edward was born September 23, 1955 and was educated in Manyberries and in
Lethbridge. He married Rita Welzel in 1976 and has two children, Ryan David and
Matthew Adam. Wayne took over the farm in 1976 at which time we moved into
Medicine Hat. Later, in 1983, Wayne and his family sold out and moved to a
ranch in the Buffalo area, about 100 miles north of Medicine Hat.

Back: Wayne, Edith, Emanuel; Front: Marlene, Jean Weiland (pic)

of 22, I started farming in the Irvine district. In 1963 I sold my farm, moved
to Manyberries and bought a farm from Emanuel Weiland, on which I still reside.

Edward Tschritter
by Emma Tschritter

Edward Tschritter was born on the 24th day of December 1922, in the Newburg
area where he went to school. He started school at the age of five. That winter
he fell and froze his hands so he stayed home until spring. Guess he didn't
dress too warm as he did not have far to go - just across the road. At the age
of 19 he went into the army. It was fun at times, with all the traveling, but
he had some hard training in the B.C. mountains. Many a night they had to sleep
out in the open or on cement floors. He enjoyed the time spent along the west
coast and liked the time they spent on the water. Someday he'd like to take a
cruise for a month or so when he's retired and has the time. After the war was
over in 1945, he went to work in Medicine Hat. He did not like city life so he
went to work on his sister's ranch.

On October 8, 1948 we, Edward and Emma Klaudt of Golden Prairie, were married.
We had no money or time for a honeymoon as the teacher was already boarding at
the homestead.

We bought the homestead of N 6-10-2-W4 in the fall of 1949, along with some
cows from Ed's Dad, for which we paid $1000 a head. The price was so high
because of foot and mouth disease.

The first year we had no way to travel but to go along with Otto and his wife.
In 1950 we bought our first truck from Ed's brother, Emil. In October 1953 we
bought more land, S 6-10-2-W4, so we could run more cattle.

I gave room and board to the Newburg teachers until the Cypress View School was
built in 1954. All of our grandchildren go to Irvine School.

Our children never attended the Newburg School, but Ron sure went over a lot.
As a young boy, whenever he disappeared, he was sure to be at the school house.

Being born and raised in Saskatchewan where it snowed and stayed all winter, it
was hard to get used to all the wind and blizzards we had out south. There was
the one in the spring of 1951. The teacher at the time was Frank Friesen. His
car and our truck were blown over so you could just see the front end. They
used a horse and scraper to get them out. I'll never forget the day on March
31, 1954 when I came home with our baby girl. My brother, Leonard, drove us
out. It was a nice day in the 'Hat with water everywhere. When we got out south
it was blowing snow and we got stuck, so Leonard had to walk two miles to get
Ed and a team of horses to pull us home. The car stalled and it was getting
pretty cold with a little baby.

Ron Tschritter, 2 years - 1952 (pic)

In July of 1971 we bought the Lehr homestead of 31-9-2-W4, the same place where
Ed's mother grew up as a young girl. She told us how she had to carry many a
pail of water from the Ross Creek. We moved in and did a lot of remodeling that
winter. It was nice to have running water. We lived on the place until 1983
when we had a house built in Medicine Hat.

We still enjoy working out at the farm. Ed may not be breaking any more horses,
but he still loves to ride his horses and work with cattle. He can't wait for
spring to come. He spends many a day on his tractor farming his land.

Ronald Wayne was born June 25, 1950. He married Lavinia Faichuk on June 28,
1975. They have two children, Christine Lyne, born February 23, 1978, and
Conrad Wayne, born November 27, 1980. They live in the Newburg area. Ron farms
both the Tschritter and Lehr homesteads and drives school bus.

Edward Tschritter Family: Ronald, Carol, Emma, Ed - 1974 (pic)

Caroline Dale, born March 20, 1954, married Barry Schlenker on March 23, 1974.
They have two girls, Carla Lee, born February 7, 1978, and Candace Sherre, born
June 23, 1982. They live on a ranch near Elkwater.

Otto and Adeline (Wutzke) Tschritter
submitted by Mrs. and Mrs. Otto Tschritter

On June 26, 1949, Otto Tschritter and 1, Adeline Wutzke, were married at the
E.U.B. Church on Braemer Street in Medicine Hat, Alberta.

After a short honeymoon at Banff and Lake Louise we lived with Otto's parents,
Fred and Augustina Tschritter, for about four months. It was an extremely dry
summer and the crops were not good enough to combine or thresh so we used the
header for feed for the cattle.

In about October we moved to an old farm house, which was bought from Chris
Schorr, about one and a half miles from Otto's parents' place. Two years later
we built a house and barn on some hayland we had bought between Walsh and
Irvine. There we lived and made hay for about three years. Then we moved to the
Woolchester area (where I had gone to school) for about one and a half years,
and then to a large ranch 30 miles south of Maple Creek in the Murrydale area.
From there we moved to Pashley. We lived there, half a mile off the Trans
Canada Highway, for about seven years.

In 1967 we built a home in Medicine Hat after selling the ranch in Pashley to
Reg Phaff, who still resides there. We bought my mother's home place in the
Woolchester area and some more land around the area, and that's where our two
sons and Otto are straight-grain farming.

Otto Tschritter Family: Back: Terry, Glen; Front: Linda, Otto, Adeline, Donna
(pic)

We had four children, two girls and two boys. The eldest was Donna Pearl, who
married David Lloyd Green. Linda May married Leigh Elmer Dickout. Glenn Otto
married Debbie Lucelle Wolfer. Terry Malcom married Morena Lynn Rarick.

August Jr. and Katherine Tschritter

August Tschritter was born November 24, 1901 in the Caucasus, South Russia and
came to Canada in 1913 with his parents, August and Maria Tschritter, and some
brothers and sisters. He attended Newburg School when he was 11 years old.

Katherine (Reiser Rath) Dabler was born December 28, 1898 in South Russia. She
came to Canada in 1926 from Odessa, Russia, after the revolution. The Russians
had killed her husband, father and some brothers. She left behind her
stepmother, two sisters and some brothers. One sister, Maggie (Gast), came with
her. The Russians hated all Germans because the government had given them
homesteads to persuade them to come to Russia to improve the land and grow more
food. Being hard workers and good managers, they prospered and soon bought more
land and cattle.

August and Katherine were married on December 29, 1928 and had three children,
Irma, Edna, and Dena, who attended Newburg School.

Katherine and August Tschritter Jr. - December 29, 1928 (pic)

The dirty thirties are well remembered; dust a quarter inch thick had to be
cleaned off the window sills, furniture, etc. daily.

We picked gallons of gooseberries that grew along the creek on the farm and
made jam for our school lunch. Many others were not so fortunate. Some had
potato sandwiches, others lard sandwiches. We drove to the Cypress Hills with
team and buggy and picked cream cans full of saskatoon berries, so we had over
100 quarts of fruit.

August Jr. bought his first car in 1926, and his first big tractor in 1929, a
McCormick Deering. We had no money to run the car during the thirties, so for
nine years it was jacked up in the garage to save the tires. We hauled many
loads of firewood and coal from the Cypress Hills. Then the snows came and
times got better in 1938. The first combine was bought in 1941. The second
World War was on and the German language was forbidden. We bought a radio to
hear the news of the war.

Katherine died January 13, 1959. August now lives in Medicine Hat. August Jr.
(Dad) was a very strict father. However he always did his best for his
children. Sometimes he went about it in a wrong way, but his intentions were
always good and he spent his life working for us. His philosophy was, "Each
generation must work for the next". He also believed in setting a good example.

1. Irma, born November 30, 1929, married Albert Ulrich on June 26, 1948. Albert
was born November 4, 1926. Albert and Irma and family lived in the Cypress
Hills on the Ulrich place for 31 years. They had three children. Linnette Ann,
born July 3, 1953, married Leslie Waldbauer and they have two children,
Clinton, 16, Christina, 13.  They farm in the Graburn area. Stanley, born June
20, 1957, married Shannon Saville. They have two children, Tyson Cole, four,
and Kayleen Desi Rae, two, and are expecting another in June. They farm and
ranch at Manyberries (Pakowki ranch). Dennis, born October 16, 1959, married
Kim Daffy. They have two children: Sylvia Dawn, four, Curtis James, two, and
are also ranching and farming (Pakowki ranch) at Manyberries.

Bill Ulrich

Bill Ulrich is the son of Alexander and Rosie Ulrich. Bill was born in Stony
Plain, Alberta, September 10, 1924. He was the fifth of six children.

Alice Ulrich is the daughter of Theodore and Matilda Wutzke. Alice was born
January 2, 1927. She was the second of seven children.

Bill and Alice were married November 10, 1945 at the Grace United Church in
Medicine Hat. They resided in the Woolchester area from 1945 to 1949. In the
fall of 1949 Bill and Alice purchased a farm from John Vossler south of Irvine.
The first year the crops were very poor due to a very dry year. Bill and Alice
lived at Fred Vossler's place while they renovated their whole house. When they
did move into their house there were days when they had to leave due to severe
dust storms. After a few very dry years and poor crops things improved and
crops improved. Bill and Alice had about 20 cattle of which ten were milk cows.
They also raised ducks, geese, and some chickens.

Bill and Alice resided in the Irvine area until 1956 when they sold their farm
to Bill Lastuka and moved to a farm south of Elkwater. They presently reside at
2313 - 20th Avenue S.E., Medicine Hat.

Bill and Alice have three children.

area. Gerald married Patricia Meier, daughter of Bill and Ellie Meier of Maple
Creek, Saskatchewan, on August 14, 1970. They have two sons, Garrett and
Corbett. Gerald and Pat now reside on an acreage at Stony Plain and Gerald is
working for the Government of Alberta.

Donna Mae was born August 6, 1952 while Bill and Alice resided in the Irvine
area. Donna married John Langill, son of Mack and Lucy Langill of Brantford,
Ontario, June 25, 1971. They have two daughters, Pamela and Renaye. John and
Donna presently reside in Medicine Hat.

Paul and Clara Vaessen

My roots developed on a farm at Leipzig, Saskatchewan. I attended a rural
school until grade ten. My high school was completed at boarding school, St.
Thomas College in 1944. I attended Saskatoon Normal School and received my
teaching certificate there. I taught in small hamlets in Saskatchewan for three
years before deciding the pastures were "greener" across the border in Alberta.

My first position was at Schuler where I met and married Clara Haas. Clara and
I spent the next seven years between Schuler and Suffield. During this period
our horizons broadened and so did our family. Deborah Ann was born December 23,
1950 and Paula Marie January 28, 1955.

In 1957 I accepted the Vice Principalship of Irvine school along with teaching
duties in Mathematics and Social Studies in the senior high school grades.

My tenure at Irvine was very rewarding both from a professional viewpoint and
friendship bonding. My involvement with education, curling club, Irvine Mercury
Ball Club and other social activities allowed both myself and Clara to develop
lasting bonds with people of Irvine and district. During this period we also
found time to add two more new members to our family: Carla Joan born July 8,
1958 and Neil Paul (first boy) on January 29, 1962.

This "golden era" came to an end at the end of June 1962. Personal aspirations
motivated me to migrate to the city of Medicine Hat and in particular to McCoy
High School where I taught high school Mathematics. I became vice principal one
year later and one year after, the principal, which position I held until my
retirement in June, 1978. During this period we added our final addition to our
family, Mark Alan born May 28, 1965.

During my final year at McCoy, thoughts of what to do during retirement passed
though my mind. A sixth sense assured me that Clara would prefer not having me
under foot all the time.

Hat Farm Supply, a farm equipment dealership, was for sale. Along with two
partners this was purchased. A new challenge was born. Many customers were
former students, an enjoyable challenge which continues today.

Clara and I are now back where we started in 1950 without family at home. Clara
developed many hobbies over the years and enjoys them immensely today,
knitting, crocheting, needle point and ceramics.

Our daughter, Debbie, is married to Gordon Wiebe who is an accountant with
Johnson Morrison and Company. They have two children, Nicole, age eleven and
Kari, age six.

Paula and Brian Pancoast also have two children, Angela, age 16 and Drew, age
14. They live in Okotoks where Brian is employed with Canadian Northern
Exploration.

Our youngest daughter, Carla, married Craig Babcock who is employed in coal
research by Luscar Mining at Edson, Alberta. They have three children: Jason,
age ten; Jamie, age nine; and Amanda, age three.

Neil, our older son, owns Master Farm Supply at Lethbridge. Two years ago, he
married Connie Rasmussen and they have one boy, Jordon Paul, age ten months.

Mark married Vicki Johnsen of Medicine Hat on July 9, 1988. Mark is in the
final stages of entering the air corps of the armed forces as a flight
controller. His wife Vicki is Manageress of Mariposa in Medicine Hat. At the
present time their family consists of a German Shepherd dog who recently gave
birth to eight offspring, most of which had new homes before they were born.

A soft spot lingers in our hearts for Irvine and District residents.
Reminiscing about events from 1957 to 1962 is not uncommon to our household.

Clara and I want to thank you for the opportunity to contribute to your history
book. Our sincere appreciation goes out to the history book staff who took on
this task. Your reward will come, I am certain, when the book is published.

Jacob and Eva Veil
by Frieda Will

Jacob Veil, son of Theobald and Christina (Dockter) Veil, was born September
19, 1899 in Neudorf, South Russia. He was one of a family of six. Eva Hieb,
daughter of Baldazar and Carolina (Schaffer) Hieb was born February 23, 1900,
also in Neudorf, South Russia. This family had eight girls and one boy.

Jacob and Eva were married April 27, 1923 in Neudorf.

They left Neudorf on November 20, 1928, with their two daughters, Eva aged
five, and Martha aged three, heading for America, the land of plenty. They
could take along only a few of their personal belongings. After a short stay in
Germany, to clear all papers, they got on the ship which left for America. The
ship was the Minadosa, which was one of the oldest ships to have made the most
journeys across the ocean. On February 26, 1929 they came to Canada, and were
met by relatives and friends in Irvine, Alberta.

Paul Vaessen Family: Back: Neil, Paul, Mark; Front: Paula, Deborah, Clara,
Carla (pic)

Two more daughters were born to them in Canada, Frieda in 1931, and Ella in
1935.

Jacob Veil Family: Back: Jacob, Eva, Martha; Front: Frieda, Eva holding Ella
(pic)

They worked for different farmers in the surrounding areas, such as Gus Herman
and Fredrick Sulz. They then rented land from August Jans for several years. At
this time Father helped supplement the farm income by tanning hides in the
winter, and also mending harness for neighbors. I well remember having to lead
the horse to turn the hides, so many times this way, then so many times the
other way. I guess that was one way of learning to count.

Jacob Veil Family: Martha, Eva, Eva and Jacob, Frieda, Ella (pic)

They also grew a lot of feed corn in those years, which was sold as grain corn.

In 1943, they bought the Andrew and Charles Glock land north of Irvine. As time
went on and prices got better, more land was added to this holding. In 1955
they bought a house in Medicine Hat, and farmed from the city. In 1965 they
sold the farm to Lawrence Knodel and retired. They enjoyed their garden, did a
lot of fishing, and also did some traveling.

Father was in failing health for some time before he passed away on March 10,
1986 at age 87. Mother still lives in her house and enjoys fairly good health.

Henry John Vockeroth
by Frances (Vockeroth) Miller

Henry John Vockeroth emigrated from Essen, Germany in 1897 and applied for a
homestead at Irvine, SE 2-11-3-W4. In 1903 he was cropping 30 acres, had 145
cattle, 24 horses, and eight pigs. He had a 26' x 32' home, built of stone and
lumber, stables, corrals, and a granary.

From his first marriage he had one son, John Henry.

In 1896 he married a second time to Juliana Tesch and five children were born
in this marriage. Four of these children were born on the Ross Creek Ranch at
Josephsburg, Northwest Territories: Louise, March 1898; Bill, July 1899; Bob,
October 1901; and Otto, April 1903. Their fifth child, Carl was born in Irvine
in January 1905 and passed away January 1906. that same year on May 18, Juliana
died.

In January 1907 Henry went to Winnipeg for a much-needed wife and mother. He
married Frances Zimmerman who had just come to Canada from Russia. To this
marriage two sons were born: Andrew, October 1907; and Theodore, June 1909.

From the Ross Creek Ranch the family moved to Irvine where Henry assumed a
partnership in a general store. After a time he sold his share and moved to
Walsh where he bought Grant's store and went into a partnership with George
Sept. The business was called the Walsh Trading Co. and the store sold
everything from binder twine to International machinery. After the Company
dissolved, Henry went into business by himself. The sign outside the store
described it: "CASH STORE -SELLS FOR LESS".

In 1914 Fred Mund rafted lumber down the river and a store was built at
Westerham, where Henry ran the store and Louise was the bookkeeper. They were
there only one year and then moved back to the Walsh district where they farmed
north of the C.P.R. tracks. Henry died at Walsh in 1932.

John Henry, at age 23 in 1902, a single farmer, applied for a homestead in the
Irvine district, SE 4-11-3-W4. By 1905 he had built a 15' x 16' house, a small
barn, and fenced all of the homestead. When not on the homestead he was in the
U.S.A. studying agriculture. In 1906 his house was somewhat demolished and he
went back to the United States to finish his course. He canceled the homestead
in 1907 and went to Germany where he married. He moved to Outlook, Saskatchewan
where he was a jeweler. During the Second World War the government moved him to
Fort William, Ontario where he was recruited to make sights for guns used in
airplanes. After the war he resumed his jewelry work and stayed in Fort William
until his death in 1969.

Louise worked as a bookkeeper in Hatton, Saskatchewan where she met Herman
Schneider and they married in 1917. They farmed at Surprise, Saskatchewan until
1953 when they retired to Redcliff, Alberta. Louise moved to Medicine Hat in
1962 where she remained until her passing in 1975.

Bill did not move back to Walsh with the family when they left Westerham. He
went to the Schuler area and worked on farms for $30 a month! There he met
Charlotte Schlaht and they were married in 1922. They farmed in Alberta on a
rented farm eight miles from Schuler until 1934 when they moved to Surprise,
Saskatchewan. In 1955 they retired to Medicine Hat where they are still living
in their own residence.

Bob worked at odd jobs and finally married a Drumheller girl, where they lived
until the 1960's, when they retired to Victoria, B.C. Bob passed away in
December 1982.

Otto worked for Jack McDonald, north of Walsh. He married a Winnipeg girl and
lived there until his death in April 1980.

Vockeroth children: Louise, Otto (front), Bob, Bill (pic)

Frances and John Henry Vockeroth - 1921 (pic)

Andrew completed his schooling (to grade eight) in Walsh. He remembers his
first teacher was Miss Inkster. At the age of 11, he left school for a month to
help on his sister Louise's farm in Saskatchewan. There he drove the header
box, as well as doing other needed jobs. After he finished school he worked at
Schroeder's Farm and Ranch Store for seven and a half years. Andrew became
"Speed" and the name has stayed with him through the years. (He remembers
selling eggs at U per dozen and butter at 100 per pound.) He also recalls a
three-story barn that was built in Walsh. The bottom floor held cattle, the
second floor sheep and the top held the hay. When the barn was completed an
orchestra was hired and a big party was held ... for about 1000 people! In 1928
he married Ivy Flood, from Walsh, and they lived there until their move to
Medicine Hat, where he worked at odd jobs and construction until his employment
with the C.P.R. He has remained in Medicine Hat since his retirement.

Theodore (Ted) took some schooling in Walsh and completed his education at
Concordia College in Edmonton. He married a Drumheller girl and lived at
Drumheller until his retirement. He passed away in March 1985.

Andrew and Ted were the battery for many a ball game! Andrew was the catcher,
and Ted the "southpaw" pitcher in games played at Irvine, Maple Creek, Hatton,
and always at Graburn Gap on "Sports Day!"

Martin Voss Family
by Bertha Neumann

My Parents, Rev. and Mrs. Martin Voss and their four children, Henry, Helen,
Bertha, and Marie, moved to Irvine in October 1935. We lived in the manse, as
my father was serving Christ Lutheran Church at Irvine, and parishes in Thelma
and Walsh, Alberta and Neuheim, Saskatchewan. It was quite a change in our
lives from the lush green fields and forests of Manitoba, to the drought-ridden
burnt-brown treeless hills of Irvine. The first dust storm was frightening. I
remember racing home from a country visit trying to beat the storm. There were
nights when my mother placed damp cloths over our noses and mouth so we were
able to breathe. Next morning we were able to write our names in the dust on
all the surfaces, even the walls.

We all continued our education in Alberta. Henry furthered his by taking a
diesel mechanics course in the States. When the war began, he joined the
R.C.A.F. and trained as an aeroengineer mechanic. After the war, he volunteered
(through the Lutheran Church) for a two year term to serve as a missionary
worker in New Guinea. Here he met and married Ruth Heber, who was there as a
nurse volunteer. Their two year stint turned into a service of 25 years. Their
four sons were all born in New Guinea. After moving back to Canada they worked
for some years in Winnipeg, then moved to Calgary, where they have since
retired.

Martin Voss Children: Marie, Bertha, Helen, Henry (pic)

Helen completed her high school in Medicine Hat, then took nurse's training in
Winnipeg. She worked in several provinces and when she married Morris Gulliver
they settled permanently in Blenheim, Ontario. They have three daughters.
Morris died in 1979.

I, Bertha, completed my high school in Irvine, then attended Normal School in
Calgary. After teaching one year each in Longfellow, Concordia and Irvine, I
moved to Winnipeg. There I took Kindergarten courses and taught it for two
years. I married Heinz Neumann of Waldersee and moved out to the farm. We have
two sons and one daughter. Our younger son took over the family farm when we
retired to Neepawa in the fall of 1981.

Marie completed her high school in Medicine Hat then took nurse's training in
Winnipeg. She worked in several hospitals in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Since
her marriage to George Phoenix, they have lived in Preeceville, Saskatchewan.
They have one daughter.

My parents continued working in the Irvine parish until June 1947 when my
father retired. They moved to Winnipeg and enjoyed 20 years of retirement.
Father died in 1967, three months after celebrating their 50th wedding
anniversary. Mother died in 1969.

Martin Voss Family: Back: Helen, Marie, Bertha (Henry missing); Front: Mrs.
Voss and Rev. Martin Voss 50th Anniv. - 1967 (pic)

Johannes (John) Sr. and Katharine Vossler

John Vossler Sr. immigrated to Canada from Albota, Bessarabia in 1903 with his
wife Katharine and five sons and two daughters, two daughters-in-law and five
grandchildren. Seasickness at sea, a little excitement on land when Grandma
thought the train was going to run into the river, and disappointment when they
saw all the dead cattle along the railroad track as they came closer to their
destination - "Oh, what did we get ourselves into," remarked Grandfather.
However, that did not discourage them. Grandfather applied for his homestead
that spring, the SE 20. He farmed and raised cattle. The older boys, too, took
up homesteads.

John and Katherine Vossler (pic)

Johannes, John Jr., married Louise Hehr and Christian married Margaret Sackman
in the old country. Fred married Mary Miller and settled in the Walsh area.
Christopher married Martha Fode and they settled in the Newburg district.
Martin married Dora Mock and they went to the U.S.A. and later settled north of
Irvine. Mary married Gottlieb Lentz and settled north of Irvine. Martha married
Karl Sulz and settled south of Irvine.

Grandfather and Grandmother were hard working people. Grandfather helped to
make basements with rocks and cement in Irvine which are still in use. They
retired to Medicine Hat in 1916 or 1917 after Christopher took over the farm.
They kept busy with their garden. I still remember Grandmother's pepper
pickles. She knitted and spun wool for the family. She used to weave in the old
country for clothing and blankets. Grandmother fell from the attic and broke
her arm and later died; Grandfather was run over by the train because his
hearing was poor. They died in 1928 and 1929.

They left their home in Bessarabia later in life .to make a better home for
themselves, their children and grandchildren. It took a lot of courage to start
all over at their age. Grandfather went back once more for a visit.

John Jr. and Louisa (Hehr) Vossler

John Vossler Jr. was born April 5, 1874 in Albota, Bessarabia to Johann and
Katharine Vossler. He married Louisa Hehr. They arrived in Irvine June 18, 1903
with his parents, brothers and sister and three children, John III, Rebecca and
Martha.

They were met by Jack Sailer who lived north of Irvine where they stayed until
they had homes built for themselves. They lived in a barn. It was in this barn
that Olga, their fourth child was born. Seven more children were born.

John III married Emma Wutzke. Rebecca married Bonosky, and later was married to
Gust Schneider. Martha married Valentine Knodel. Olga married Folton Knodel.
Fred married Helen Olhausen. Jack married Mary Olhausen. Another was Emma.
Matilda drowned at the age of seven. Emil married Clara Degg. Otto married
Mabel Degg. Elsie married Rick Dysa.

John Jr. was a hard working man. He ran a threshing outfit for years. He was
remembered for his singing and devotion to his church.

John B. and Emma (Wutzke) Vossler

John B. Vossler, the oldest of 11 children, was born October 22, 1896 in
Albota, Bessarabia and immigrated to Canada in May 1903 with his parents,
Johannes and Louise Vossler. They homesteaded 11 miles south of Irvine, Alberta.

On November 14, 1920 he married Emma Wutzke at Robinson, Alberta. Emma was born
May 10, 1901. They farmed in the Gros Ventre area until 1922 when they
purchased a farm of two quarters one mile north of his parents homestead in the
Irvine district. They continued farming here until 1937. During this time they
had three children: Alice, who was born June 18, 1922 at Gros Ventre; Esther,
who was born June 29, 1924 at Irvine; and Roy, who was born August 16, 1927 at
Irvine. In 1937 the family moved to Duchess, Alberta until 1939 when they
returned to their farm in Irvine for another four years. They purchased a farm
at Tilley, Alberta in 1943 and farmed there until 1948 when they purchased a
house in Medicine Hat, Alberta. They continued living in Medicine Hat but went
back to farming in 1950 when a farm 12 miles south of Medicine Hat was
purchased. It was at this farm that John was accidentally killed in a tractor
accident on April 13, 1955. Roy still farms this same land today. Emma
continues to live at 459-11 Street SE in Medicine Hat with her daughter and
son-in-law, Anton and Alice Urlacher.

Alice married Anton Urlacher February 8, 1943 in Medicine Hat. After serving in
the army, Anton was employed at Dominion Glass for 37 years until he retired.

Christopher and Martha (Fode) Vossler

Christopher Vossler was born in Albota, Bessarabia and immigrated to Canada in
1903 with his parents and brothers and sisters and settled in the Irvine
district. He worked on the railroad at Kincord, the Brick and Tile in Medicine
Hat, and for some ranchers in the Cypress Hills. He applied for his homestead
in 1904 and he married Martha Fode in 1911. Martha immigrated to Canada from
Postal, Romania with her sister and brother-in-law. She lost her parents at an
early age. She worked as a domestic in Irvine until she got married.

They had eight children three of whom died in infancy. Hilda married Emil
Schorr and they lived in the Elkwater area. Annie married Edwin Schneider and
they live in Irvine. Christoph married Edna Ziegenhagel and they live in the
Elkwater area. Carl married Eva Veil and lived near Irvine. Leo took over the
family farm.

Dad broke his land with a hand plow. They had to break about ten acres of land,
put up some fences and buildings each year. This was required to hold the land.
They built a sod barn and a log house. The logs were hauled from the Cypress
Hills. The walls were plastered with a clayish soil which was mixed with straw
and water. A horse was used to mix it. The horse was led around and around and
the mud was shoveled to the center until it was well mixed and then used to
plaster the walls. The finish coat was mixed with sand and clay. The walls were
then white washed, calcimined or papered. If they needed a little bit of mud,
the children got in the act with their bare feet; this was usually fun.

For light, a coal oil lamp was placed in the center of the table and the family
usually sat around it. Dad would read his bible, newspaper, or Sunday school
paper. Mother would knit, us girls would do fancy work while the younger ones
would do homework. Later we had high-test lamps which hung from the ceiling in
the middle of the room.

Dad and Mother lived on the homestead until 1916 or 1917 when they took over
Grandfather's farm. There was still open prairie; Mother would hurry to get the
cows home before it got too late, as the cows would wander far from home. On
the way home Mother would gather cow chips for the kitchen stove. Cow manure
from the cow shed was cut with a spade into 16 inch blocks and stacked in a T
pattern, leaving space for drying. This was used for fuel, as well as coal
which was mined on the Bench. For fire wood, logs were hauled home from the
hills and sawed with a hand saw which had a handle on each end and was pulled
back and forth by two people.

All field work was done with horses. Repairing the harnesses was the first
chore to be done in the spring. It took Dad weeks of hard work. It was done
with two needles and an awl. Then the harnesses were hammered smooth with a
hammer and oiled. Wheat was cleaned with a fanning mill turned by hand.

Harvesting was done with a binder, sometimes shared by two brothers or
neighbors. The bundles were stacked in stooks, and when dry, hauled on round
stacks that came to a peak at the top, and later threshed. In later years more
people owned threshing machines. They formed crews, each farmer using his own
team to haul the bundles directly to the machine. From six to eight teams were
needed. Wheat was hauled with horses and wagon from the machine and unloaded by
hand. The ladies usually helped unloading and shoveling in the granaries. Three
big meals and two lunches had to be prepared each day. Bread and kuchen were
made every day. Sometimes the threshers stayed for a week at one place.

In the late twenties or early thirties the headers came into existence. The
crop was cut and elevated into a headerbox, then unloaded onto a stack, and
later threshed. Usually six to eight men were needed. This eliminated a lot of
hard work.

Mother used to make butter and sell it in the stores in Irvine. When the men
were busy, she and some neighbor lady would drive with horse and buggy to
Irvine with their cream, butter, and eggs. Some years later when we had a car
and there were fewer stores in Irvine, we took the cream to the creamery and
butter and eggs to the Medicine Hat Trading Company in exchange for groceries
and other necessities. Butter was made in a butter churn. The butter churn had
a five-gallon barrel with a handle attached on both sides that was pushed back
and forth to make the barrel go round and round, and presto - butter. But
beware if the stopper gets caught on some clothing, z-o-o-m, there goes your
cream! Although it was hard work a little humour made it much easier.

We had a big garden every year: a corn patch watermelon patch, and potato
patch. Carrots were stored in sand for winter use. Sauerkraut was made in a 20
gallon crock. Watermelon, cucumbers green tomatoes, and carrots were pickled in
a barrel. Wild berries were picked and canned for fruit. Jam was made from
berries, watermelon and muskmelons. However, some years the watermelon and
muskmelons were smashed by vandals.

For spending money the young boys would sell gopher tails and magpie and crow
eggs, and trap rabbits, skunks and weasels. When it came to skunks they needed
a little help, so they convinced their younger sister to help to skin one -
good pay, 10 cents each - and to top it, the wind happened to come from all
directions!

Mother had a terrible accident in 1942 when a bull attacked her while they were
sorting cattle. She was in the hospital for some time and suffered the rest of
her life from it. They moved to Medicine Hat in 1945. Dad worked at the
greenhouse for some time and kept busy with his garden and yard. Mother busied
herself with fancy work and making quilts.

Christoph and Martha (Fode) Vossler (pic)

Dad died in 1969 at the age of 85 and Mother died in 1972 at the age of 79.
They had ten grandchildren.

Annie (Vossler) Schneider

I, Annie K. (Vossler) Schneider, was born in 1916 in Irvine to Christopher and
Martha Vossler. I attended Newburg School, graduated from Gardner College, and
attended Knifle private secretarial school in Camrose. I worked in Edmonton
during the summer holidays, and spent one year at Yorkton, Saskatchewan after
graduation. I then returned home to finish some correspondence courses, but for
some unforeseen circumstances had to give it up and took up mixed farming.

I farmed the W 8-10-2-W4 and NE 19. Farming was done with horses and I was the
last in that area to use horses. Change to tractor farming made the work easier
but more hours were put in. There was little under cultivation, so I broke more
land with a plow and this land had to be disced a number of times to make a
good seed bed. Broken ribs and discing did not go together! Spring time was
usually a busy time with land work and young animals to look after. Medicine
bottle and pill box were often needed and one time a sewing needle and size ten
thread to sew up a little pigs tummy after its mother stepped on it. My luck -
it made it!

I sold out in 1959 and built a home in Irvine.

Martin and Dorthea (Mock) Vossler
by Katharina Ziegler

Vossler Family Farm - 1972 (pic)

My grandfather, Johannes Vossler, and his wife Katharina and family immigrated
to Canada from Russia in May 1903. They homesteaded south of Irvine, in the
Newburg district. They bought a house in Medicine Hat after their youngest son
got married. My grandfather did odd jobs and he loved to garden. They also kept
chickens in town and neighbors would pick up the eggs. He often went down to
the mill and cleaned up the spilled grain and hauled it home on a little wagon.
When the single plane came to town, my grandfather took his first plane ride
for $5 which made my grandmother very nervous, for fear that they may crash. My
grandmother was a little woman and a wonderful cook. I remember her feather
bed, about four feet high and kept straight as the table top. She had many
friends to visit her every day.

Martin Vossler, one of Johannes Vossler's younger boys, looked for work away
from home as the older boys helped on the farm. He found a job in Medicine Hat,
building the Five Roses Mill. In those days there were no cranes; it was wheel
barrow, ropes, pails and shovels. This mill is still in use today for grain.

Here in Medicine Hat, he met his bride to be, Dorthea Mock, the youngest in her
family who had also found a job in the city.

They started to make wedding plans and were married April 11, 1915, Martin, at
the age of 22 and Dorthea, 18. They moved to his father's homestead and later
he took up his own, 14 miles northeast of Irvine. They started to build their
dream home with help from brothers and neighbors. After the house was built,
they needed a barn. Logs were hauled from Cypress Hills, and a log barn for two
horses and two cows came into the picture. The chicken barn was built of logs
and plastered with clay and straw.

House built in 1915 (pic)

Martin Vossler Barn (pic)

Machinery was borrowed to break the land and seed the crops. Acreage was small
and crops got poorer and poorer. As they could not see any future staying on
the farm any longer, they pulled up stakes, and moved to Portland, Oregon. They
could not find any work there so they moved to Olympia, Washington. They bought
a five acre lot which was to the back of the ocean arm, and built a new home.
While clearing some of the timber to build a wood shed, Martin decided to burn
some of the brush, not knowing the fire creeps along the under brush. This
started a big fire which was stopped by the big clearing on the other acreages.

Martin got a job at the Olympia sawmill and worked there until a fruit farmer
gave him a job running the fruit farm in Yakima, Washington; so another move
was made. Here they lived for two years and then the news came from Canada,
about how the crops were yielding from 40 to 45 bushels per acre, and straw
piles were like mountains.

Another move began back to Canada and the homestead. They stayed on the
homestead for four years, and then the same story began, no rain, no crops,
just dust storms. In those days there were no handouts but sometimes there was
a box car of apples from British Columbia or fish from the east. To make ends
meet, Martin took on the job building roads with horses and scrapers. Some of
these roads are improved now and are highways for school busses. The wagon
trails were closed by the people taking up leases for cattle, and fences were
built.

The closest school was Many Island. The teacher was given some wages and room
and board by the people. Irvine was the closest town and those were horse and
buggy days. The crops were poor and the people would work together, helping
each other.

Mr. Walstrom had a threshing machine and my father ran it. The men would pitch
from what they called header stacks. The work was very hard for man and horses.
One year the grasshoppers were so bad that when the men stopped for dinner they
would push the pitch fork handles in the stack, because the hoppers would chew
the wooden handles.

Threshing day was a busy day for the women folk, with a six o'clock breakfast,
nine o'clock lunch, twelve o'clock dinner, four o'clock lunch and then supper.

After four years Martin Vossler pulled up stakes again. He made a sale, got
very little, and moved on again. He found a farm that he liked at Duchess,
Alberta and started again.

Martin and Dorothea Vossler - 1961 (pic)

Here he farmed with his son John until John was called into the army. John was
stationed in Jamaica until the end of the war.

Martin Vossler sold his farm in 1946 when they moved to Brooks and here they
built their last home, where they lived until their deaths, Martin's in 1966
and Dorthea's, in 1974.

Our Mother and Dad enjoyed their family even through hard times. They
celebrated their 25th and 50th Anniversary with all their children, 17
grandchildren and ten great-grandchildren.

One son and one daughter died at young age.

Katharina and Charles Ziegler live in Medicine Hat and had three children,
Sharion, Stan (deceased), and Leslie.

John and Rosalie live in Vancouver, B.C.

Mary Jane and Bob Master live in Mesa, Arizona and have three children, Sherry,
Robert, and Mary.

Theodore and Bernice live in North Surrey, B.C. and have two children, Gregory
and Dean.

Lorine and Wilbert Mulbueir live in Brooks and have five children, Rodney,
Cindy, Lynn, Darren, and Darcy.

Irene and Wes Schneider live in Medicine Hat and have two children, David and
Mavis.

Joanne and Jim Holmes live in Calgary and have two children, Leanne and Lee
Martin.

Martin Vossler Family (pic)

Simon and Lydia Wahler
by Lydia (Wahler) Klaudt

My parents, Simon and Lydia Wahler, who after arriving in Canada in 1928 from
Russia, first lived on the Ed Glock farm northeast of Irvine. We lived there
one year or more, a family of six, Dad, Simon, Mom, Lydia, and children, Amelia
(Molly), Frieda, Lydia Jr., Reinhold, and Helen, who was born while we lived
there. We attended the Lutheran Church in Irvine. The Konstantin Masers were
our neighbors. In the fall of 1930 we moved east to four miles north of Walsh
on the H. Fromm place. John was born here.

Molly and Frieda and sometimes Lydia drove a two wheel buggy drawn by one horse
to Walsh School. We kept the horse in Jack Flemmer's barn during school hours.
Miss Phyllis Dunn was the teacher.

Lydia and Simon Wahler (pic)

Simon and Lydia Wahler children: Back: Reinhold, Reuben, Helen, Violet, John.
Front: Freda, Phyllis, Lydia; Inset: Mollie (pic)

Because Dad and Mom had such bad luck on this farm, they rented a farm in
spring of 1931 from A. Brost just northwest of Irvine, to which we moved. We
attended the Congregational United Church, a few miles north of our place.
Strikes were our closest neighbors, also Franzes and Roths. We kids went to
Pashley School where Charlie Allen was teaching. It was at this school we got
our first vaccination and inoculation and were our arms sore!

In the spring of 1933 we moved to Woolchester and purchased a farm from John
and Anna Rath. Here Phyllis, Reuben, and Violet were born. Dad passed away
November 1937. We were here two more years, then moved to Medicine Hat,
Alberta. We kids got jobs so Mother could make a go in life.

As the years progressed we married as follows: Molly married Howard Maser and
lived in Medicine Hat. Frieda married Emil Derheim, and later Frank McKenzie,
and lives in Calgary. Lydia married Albert Klaudt and lives at North Pender
Island, B.C. Reinhold married Eilleen Patton and lives at Calgary. Helen
married Elmer Sauter and lives at Calgary. John married Betty Durkin and later
Christina Davidson, and lives in Sidney, B.C. Phyllis married Elmer Frisch and
later Carl Chichenko and they live in Maple Ridge, B.C. Reuben married Linda
Junk and lives in Kelowna, B.C. Violet married Alfred Pratt and lives in
Calgary.

Everyone has made a success in life when all is said and done. Mother passed
away in December 1980 and Molly in February 1972.

The rest of us still pay taxes, and enjoy being around.

Winton and Jean (Schmidt) Wangsness

Jean and I were married November 7, 1949 at her parents' home in the Talbot

After we were married I was employed by Central Alberta Dairy Pool in

milking cows.

In the spring of 1960 I started work as battery operator for Petcal Co. Ltd.,
who contracted for Canadian Homestead. In 1969 I was transferred to Duchess and
operated their oil plant at Princess. In 1971 I was transferred to the plant at
Hatton and moved into Irvine, where we are at the present time. Canadian
Homestead amalgamated with Inter City Gas and I am now employed by them.

Reinhold and Margaret Weishaar
by Adeline (Weishaar) Bexson

I have fond memories of attending Robinson School, riding to school, three and
a half miles, on a grey horse named Bob who would never let anyone pass him.
Consequently, we hit the dirt a few times. I remember making rubber ice on a
ditch by the school at lunch hour, the ice breaking and all of us getting wet.
Our poor teacher tried to get our clothes dry before it was time to go home.
Surprising how we survived it all!
