John and Barbara Weiss
submitted by Don Weiss

John and Barbara Weiss came to Canada in 1892, they brought their whole family
and took up a homestead in the Josephsburg district part of which is now known
as Tothill. The family also included two daughters of John's previous marriage,
Catherine and Rose, as well as two of the mother's daughters, also by a
previous marriage, Christina and Regina. Together they had six more children,
John Jr., Mary, Dora, David, Ferdinand and Emmanuel, who was less than six
months old when they arrived here. They came from Bessarabia, a region touching
the Black Sea, now part of Russia.

John Weiss Sr. (pic)

John Weiss later became a prosperous farmer, rancher and merchant in the town
of Irvine, Alberta in 1903. He was instrumental in helping many others who came
in with the great rush of settlers 1910-1912. It was rather sad that this good
man was rendered speechless the last two years of his life by a stroke but he
walked to church every Sunday.

Destiny was not too kind to the six daughters of this combined family.
Christina and Regina died as teenagers of diphtheria.

Catherine married Andrew Wendland and she died in 1905 leaving six young
children: Justina, Christina, Rose, Dora, John and Emma. Andrew Wendland died
in 1911 so some of the younger children were raised by other relatives.

Rose married Christian Jensen and lived on a ranch near Lundbreck, Alberta.
They both died within a few hours of each other, he of cancer and she of
pneumonia, June 5th and June 6th, 1911, leaving eight young children ranging
from sixteen to nine months of age: Henry, Jack, Anne, Christian Jr., Arthur,
Fred, Edward and Mary. All these children except Henry were placed in foster
homes or adopted. Henry was killed in action in France in 1918 and the rest are
scattered from northern Alberta to Ontario and Anne is living in Reno, Nevada.

John Jr. married Annie Mayer and their children were Emmanuel, Katie, John,
Wallace, Adeline, Edith, Norma and Irene.

David married Dora Heidinger. Their eight children were Martha, Emma, Harris,
Alice, Lance, Lillian, Irene and Vera.

Ferdinand married Lena Flaig and their children were Martha, Arthur, Hilda and
Elizabeth.

Dora married Jack McKean and also lived on a ranch near Lundbreck, Alberta; and
his death in 1913 left her a widow with three young children: Dorothy, Wallace
and John. She married John Hillenberg in 1916 and in 1933 was again widowed
leaving her with two small children, Estelle and Marjorie. Estelle was a school
librarian in Irvine in later years. Marjorie's son David Mack owns an acreage
in Irvine where his great grandfather started.

Mary, at the age of four, lost her hearing and the power of speech but not long
after developed a sort of language of her own and made herself understood
amazingly well for the rest of her life, living to the ripe old age of 93.

Emmanuel was the youngest and was born in 1892. He married Emma Schaller of
Irvine and their children were Elmer, Ralph, Mildred, Ella, Marlene and Donald.

The four sons, John, David, Ferdinand and Emmanuel, all became successful in
agriculture and raised fine families.

Fred Sr. and Justina Weiss

In 1881 Fred Weiss, his wife Justina, and their three sons, Henry, Christian,
and Gottlieb, left Bessarabia, Russia to immigrate to the U.S.A. They settled
on a homestead near Scotland, South Dakota. There three more sons were born,
John, Fred Jr. and David.

Fred Weiss Sr. (pic)

Fred Weiss Sr. was a very ambitious man and disposed to seek adventure. So in
1889 he immigrated once more, this time to Canada, settling on a homestead
south of Irvine. He was the first of the Weisses to come to Canada. Four more
sons were born here, Robert, Emil, Emanuel and Alfred, to complete a family of
ten sons.

After his homestead was well established Fred Weiss Sr. moved into the town of
Irvine and formed several businesses called Fred Weiss and Sons Enterprises
with his brothers John and Christian along with three Ziaser brothers. He had
his own money or tokens that could only be used in his store. They started a
sawmill in the Cypress Hills, and stores in Irvine selling groceries, clothing,
hardware, furniture, lumber, farm machinery, cattle and horses to the many
settlers who came after the turn of the century.

Fred Weiss Sr. was called upon many times during those pioneer days to set
broken bones and give other medical help because doctors were few and far away.
How and where he acquired these medical skills we really don't know but we
heard a lot about his good work setting bones.

He retired in 1920 and moved with two of his sons to Lodi, California. He lived
the rest of his life there and passed away in 1929. His wife passed away soon
after him. The two sons Emanuel and Dave died in California also. Three sons
remained in the Irvine area, Christian, John, and Fred Jr., the other five sons
moved to various points in Alberta and British Columbia.

Christian and Justina (Sturm) Weiss

Christian Weiss, son of Fred Weiss Sr., was born September 15, 1878 in
Alt-Postal, Bessarabia, Russia and came to the Irvine district about 1888.

Justina Maria Sturm, daughter of Peter and Friedericka Sturm, was born January
2, 1879 in Teplitz, Bessarabia. In 1898 she came to Canada with her parents to
the Josephsburg district where they farmed.

Christian and Justina were married on January 11, 1900. They had three
children, Hugo, Olinda, and Clarence.

They farmed in the Josephsburg district for awhile then moved to Irvine where
Christian worked in one or another of his father's many enterprises. They had
been residents of Irvine for nearly 60 years at the time of their passing,
Justina on January 16, 1957, and Christian on September 4, 1957.

Hugo was born September 11, 1902. He was married to Blanche Ethel Bailey. They
had two children, Lloyd and Marjorie, and were living in Cincinnati, Ohio at
the time of his passing on July 2, 1967.

Olinda was born at Irvine on December 12, 1904. She received her education at
Irvine and later was employed in Wiedemann's Store. She spent a few years at
Kansas City, Missouri, where her brother resided at that time. Later she worked
at Claresholm for several seasons, and from then on devoted her entire life to
the care of her father, and later of her mother, until her own health failed
and she was confined to hospital. Olinda died April 5, 1957, just three months
after her mother's death.

Clarence Henry was born on December 5, 1907 at Irvine, where he lived until
1933 when he moved to Medicine Hat. On November 10, 1933, he married Lea
Rieger. Lea was born September 4, 1908 in the Gros Ventre area, the daughter of
Mr. and Mrs. Andrew Rieger. Clarence was employed by Hutton's Electric at the
time of his accidental drowning in Lake Newell on October 11, 1953.

Fred Jr. and Christina (Schlaht) Weiss

Fred Weiss Jr. married Christina Schlaht. Fred and Christian ran the store in
Irvine until a terrible misfortune hit them by fire in l908. Then Fred Jr. took
up a homestead seven miles east of Irvine. That same year a daughter, Alice,
was born but died at birth. She was buried in the Schlaht cemetery, on NW
12-11-2-4, one mile south of the homestead.

They moved back to Irvine and started a harness shop. In 1910 a daughter,
Irene, was born and in 1912 a son, George. In 1915 they moved back to the farm
again after the harness shop was burned to the ground. This time they traded an
organ for a cow and stayed on the farm. In 1918 there was a terrible world flu
epidemic. In 1919 a daughter, Kathleen, was born. It was a long cold winter
that year and hundreds of cattle and horses lost their lives in the snow
storms. The winters were very cold and the summers were very dry and hot.

In 1923 another daughter, Esther, was born, and in 1924 another son, Harry.

Christina and Fred Weiss Jr. (pic)

Roy was born in 1926 but passed away in Irvine three years later, and was
buried in the Irvine cemetery.

Things were very poor, never any crops and prices of cattle were low. Back in
the early 1920's we did a lot of custom land breaking for our neighbors. In
1927 and 1928 things were looking better. There were bumper crops in 1928 and
the price of wheat was up to $2 a bushel. Our dad bought a new 15-30 IHC
tractor and also a new 36" threshing machine and went out threshing for the
neighbors. After harvest he bought a new 1929 Pontiac car. In 1930 things went
to hell! The economy collapsed, wheat was selling for 18 cents a bushel and
crops were very poor. We also had a big hail storm and no rain. Cattle went
down to 1 cent a pound, eggs were - 5 cents a dozen, butter 9 cents a pound,
and milk 20 quarts for $1. Many people removed the motors from their cars, put
hitches on them and called them Bennett Buggies. That was when Prime Minister
R.B. Bennett was in power.

In 1933 the Depression set in - very, very poor times; wages were 25 cents a
day. Food and clothing were cheap, but there was no money to buy them with.
Many people were on relief, receiving $5 a month. Food was brought in such as
frozen fish, apples, cheese and beans. In order to qualify you had to have less
than eight cows per person. We had our own milk, butter, eggs and meat, so we
didn't qualify.

As years went by things got better. In 1938 we had a bumper crop and in 1939
another good crop. We bought our first combine, a Massey Harris, ten-foot with
power take off. It was bought in Irvine from Bischke and Huddlestone, and for
years we did custom combining for 75 cents to $1 an acre.

In 1939 our parents bought a new Pontiac and they were pretty proud of it; it
had a big six motor in it.

Our uncle Alfred bought the first tractor called Happy Farmer, which was
manufactured in Medicine Hat.

Fred Weiss (our dad) farmed until 1945 when they moved to Medicine Hat to
retire, but for the next few years they moved to the farm in the summer time to
help with the farming. Then Harry got married in 1950 and he took over the farm.

Our dad passed away in 1952 at the age of 65 and our mother in 1975 at the age
of 86.

In 1977, Harry moved to Medicine Hat and farmed from the city. He later sold
most of the farm land to the Elkwater Hutterite Colony.

Harry and Doris (Jans) Weiss

I, Harry, am the youngest of five children born to Fred and Christina Weiss. I
grew up in the Irvine district and went to Schlaht School. I took over my dad's
farm when they retired and moved to Medicine Hat. In 1950 I got married to
Doris Jans from the Graburn area south of Walsh.

Doris and Harry Weiss (pic)

Jerry and Harlan Weiss (pic)

We have two boys, Jerry of Winnipeg, Manitoba and Harlan of Grande Prairie,
Alberta. Both had their education at Irvine School. We also have two
grandchildren, Mark and Denise Weiss.

We farmed in the Irvine area for 26 years. In 1976 we semi-retired to Medicine
Hat.

I have been a Chinook Club member since 1951, also a past president, a life
member of the Elks Club for 25 years, and a 14 year member of the Moose Lodge.

Christian and Christina (Heller) Weiss by Becky Weiss

Christian Weiss was born in Postal, Bessarabia, South Russia, on February 17,
1863. His family were farmers so his youth was spent on the farm. As a young
man he served in the Russian Army for seven years during which time he saw
action in the Russo-Turkish War and was made an officer of quite high rank.

On February 7, 1892, he married Christina Heller, who was also born in Postal,
Bessarabia, on September 9, 1870. Upon leaving the army he again took up
farming. Four children were born to them while still in Russia: Christina
(January 1893), who died at a few weeks of age; Frederich Henry (December
1893); Martha (1895); and Justina (Gusta) (1897).

Christian's brother Fred came to Canada in 1888, followed by his oldest brother
John in 1892 and their letters home told of the opportunity for free land in
Canada. He took up the challenge and in March 1898 he left Postal with his wife
Christina and their three children for Bremen, Germany, their first stop on
their long journey to Canada. There were ten other families who were going to
Canada at the same time, and Christian was made caretaker of them all. Before
leaving Postal, Christina made him a strong money belt for his gold pieces and
these gold pieces were exchanged for paper money in Bremen. While in Bremen,
pink eye broke out in one of the families and they were all quarantined for
eight days before they were allowed to board ship. Finally on April 7, 1898,
they sailed from Bremen aboard the Kaiser Wilhelm the Great, the largest ship
afloat at that time. They docked in New York City, U.S.A. on May 10, 1898. In
New York they boarded a train heading for Winnipeg, their first stop to change
to a Canadian Pacific Railway train going to Western Canada, arriving at
Coleridge (now Dunmore), Territory of Assiniboia, on May 17, 1898.

The first night was spent in the railroad station while they waited for Fred
and John Weiss to come and get them and take them to their new home, a
homestead at Josephsberg (now Tothill). A house had been built for them and
they moved in with the few belongings they brought with them. When Christina
started unpacking her trunks and boxes she found everything solid with mold.
Their clothing, bedding, papers, books and pictures were all ruined. When they
boarded ship in Germany their belongings were put through a steam bath to
disinfect them and of course they didn't have a chance to dry out in the hold
of the ship, therefore, everything got moldy.

They were awed at the vast expanse of prairie and the barren hills, so
different from the homeland they had left. It was no strange thing for them to
see hundreds of Indians roaming the prairie. Most of the Indians were friendly
and Christian became a very good friend to one of the Indian Chiefs.

Their home was always open to friend, neighbor, Indian, and the North West
Mounted Police when they were on patrol. There was many a meal cooked and a bed
provided for the unexpected visitor. In later years Mother Weiss used to say
that at times she thought she was running a hotel and restaurant.

However, farming did not go too well, and in 1901 he moved his family to
Irvine, where he went into business with his brother, Fred. They built many of
the homes in Irvine, some of which are still being lived in. He was one of the
many volunteers who helped to build the first school in Irvine, and this
building is still in use today as a museum.

Christian Weiss Family - 1909: John, Mrs. Christian Weiss, Mary, Gusta,
Christian Herbert, (baby) Rueben (pic)

The first big store in Irvine was opened in 1901 by Fred and Christian Weiss.
They later formed a company with Mr. G. Schaller, Mr. Brandt, Mr. H. Vockeroth
and Chris Weiss (Fred's son) and they hired Mr. Carl Beny as their bookkeeper.
It became known as the Weiss and Co. Store and they sold food, clothing, shoes,
candy, material, hardware, machinery, guns, traps, furs and lumber. It was the
forerunner of the one stop supermarket of today. At this time the town of
Irvine was growing and prospering and the opportunity for new enterprises was
very good, so Mr. Schaller, Mr. Brandt and Mr. Vockeroth each went into
business for themselves, leaving Fred, his son Chris and Christian with the
store. In 1908 tragedy struck, the store burned down and they lost everything.

After the fire, he decided to go farming again buying a farm south of Irvine,
which was later owned by Charlie Good. He farmed for about a year and then
decided to move his family to Winnipeg, where he went into real estate. The big
city and apartment living were not to their liking, so again they sold what
they had and moved back to Irvine. He bought a farm about 16 miles south of the
town. The family stayed in Irvine so the children would be close to school, and
he farmed from town, with the family going there in the summer. They continued
farming until 1924.

Those pioneer days were filled with many trials and hardships, but also many
blessings and progress. He was called upon so often to care for the sick and
bury the dead, as he served as a lay minister of the Baptist Church for many
years. During the 1918 flu epidemic he nursed many of the sick, but did not get
the flu himself and his was one of the very few families who did not lose a
member to the flu.

Seven more children were born to them after their arrival in Canada: Johan
(1899-1903), who died at the age of three years; Mary (1901), John Christian
(1903); Herbert Emanuel (1905); Rueben Benjamin (1909); Freda Johanna (1912);
and Emma Christina (Sally) (1915).

In 1924 they moved to Medicine Hat to make their home. They both remained
active in the Grace Baptist Church. He served almost continually as a Sunday
School teacher and Deacon, and she was a life member of the Ladies Aid of the
Church. His family and religion were the first and foremost things in his life
and he was happiest when he was helping someone less fortunate than himself.

On February 7, 1942 they celebrated 50 years of a happy and fruitful marriage.
He died on May 30, 1944 after an operation, the only time he was ever sick in
his life. He lived 81 years of a very useful happy Christian life, loved and
respected by all how knew him.

Christian Weiss children - 1915: Back: John, Freda, Herbert, Rueben; Front:
Sally (pic)

Christina lived in the family home until 1949, doing her own work, raising a
huge garden with many flowers that were the envy of the neighbourhood. In 1949
she rented the house and went into the Baptist Haven of Rest. She stayed there
until May 1950 when she moved in with her son Reuben and his family. In
November she sold the family house. In April 1951 she went to Calgary to live
with her daughter Martha Heine. She passed away peacefully in Calgary on June
29, 1951 at the age of 80 years. She lived a full life dedicated to her
husband, family and God.

The love and Christian principles of family carried on to their children in
their marriages and homes. Four of their children, Martha (married to Gust
Heine), Justina (married to Walter Good), Mary (married to Ingeman Erickson)
and John (married to Bertha Pahl), celebrated 50 or more years of marriage,
with Justina (Gusta) and Walter Good celebrating their 60th wedding anniversary
in June 1977.

Christian Weiss Family: Back: Martha, Gusta, Herbert, Reuben, Mary, Freda;
Front: Sally, Christian, Mrs. Christian Weiss, John; 50th Anniv. February 7,
1942 (pic)

Their children, as many families seem to do, scattered to many parts of the
country. Among the descendants of Christian Weiss are 15 who carry the Weiss
surname so I am sure the family will carry on for a few more generations.

In 1989, Rueben and Justina Good are the only survivors of this family. Rueben
is 80 years old and Justina is 91.

Histories follow of the four sons, Frederich, John, Herbert, and Rueben, and
the Martha and Gustav Heine history is included elsewhere.

Justina was born December 23, 1897 in Postal, Bessarabia. Gusta and Walter Good
were married in Medicine Hat on June 14, 1917. They had two children, Lawrence
and Beatrice, and lived on a ranch 17 miles south of Irvine, retiring to
Medicine Hat in 1945. They celebrated 70 years of marriage in 1987 and had been
married 71 years when Walter died on July 13, 1988.

Mary was born in Josephsburg on May 8, 1901. She married Engmund Erickson on
July 17, 1918 and they farmed in the Surprise, Saskatchewan and Olds, Alberta
districts. They retired to Calgary in 1955. In 1968 they celebrated 50 years of
marriage. Mary passed away on April 5, 1969 and Engmund, on August 22, 1974.
Engmund and Mary had eight children: four sons, Melvin (who died in 1925),
Vernon, Gilbert, and Elmer, and four daughters, Melva, Doreen, Delores, and
Joan.

Freda was born in Irvine on February 26, 1912. On May 11, 1928 she married
Ludwig Olhausen, son of Anton and Amelia (Dey) Olhausen. They had a daughter,
Doris. After Ludwig's death, Freda went to Olds, Alberta to work and on January
27, 1937 she married Luther Petersen. Luther was killed in an accident on
October 11, 1977 and Freda died on January 24, 1984.

Emma (Sally) was born in Irvine on August 31, 1915. She moved with her parents
to Medicine Hat in 1924 and took her schooling at Elm Street School. She went
to Olds to work in 1932. In 1939 she married Bill Walker of Crossfield. They
were divorced in 1946. In 1949 Sally married Samuel Thomas. They lived in
Canmore where Sam was employed with the C.P.R. as an express agent. He died in
1966 and Sally moved to Calgary. On June 8, 1969 she married Roy Noble of
Elkwater and they made their home there until 1975 when they moved to Irvine.
Sally passed away in Medicine Hat after a lengthy illness on February 17, 1976.
Although Sally never had any children of her own she was a "second mother" to
many of her nieces and nephews.

Frederich Henry and Ida (Ziffle) Weiss
by Becky Weiss

Frederich Henry Weiss was born in Postal, Bessarabia, South Russia on December
10, 1893. He came to Canada to Irvine, Alberta with his parents in 1898. In
1912 he joined the army serving in the Cavalry. One of the conditions in
joining the Cavalry at that time was that you had to supply your own horses, so
Fred took two of the horses from the farm and rode all the way to Edmonton to
"join up".

Fred and Ida Weiss - Wedding June 1917 (pic)

In June 1917 he married Ida Ziffle. They farmed south of Irvine until 1920 when
they moved to Minot, North Dakota. In 1922 they moved to Los Angeles,
California where Fred went into the cement contracting business. He died very
suddenly of spinal meningitis on May 26, 1929, a young man 36 years of age.

Fred and Ida had two sons, Gene and Warren.

Gene and Virgie (Dodson) now make their home at Fort Walton Beach, Florida.
Gene is retired from the U.S. Air Force.

Warren and Rose Weiss made their home in Los Angeles, California, where Warren
is also a cement contractor. Warren served in the U.S. Navy during World War II.

Gene, Ida (Mrs. Fred Weiss) holding Warren - 1921 (pic)

Ida continued to live in Los Angeles until she married Neil Unruh. They lived
in Lancaster, California where she remained until her death on June 3, 1973 at
the age of 72 years.

John and Bertha (Pahl) Weiss
by Bertha Weiss

John Weiss was born on April 1, 1903 at Irvine, Alberta. John is the son of
Christian and Christina (Heller) Weiss. Christian and Christina homesteaded 15
miles south of Irvine. This is where Levern and Olga Weiss live today.

Bertha Pahl, daughter of Christian and Gustina (Schlenker) Pahl, was born on
May 29, 1907 in the Newburg area. She lived with her parents on their
homestead, which was approximately 13 miles south of Irvine.

On July 24, 1924, Bertha Pahl and John Weiss were married by Reverend Gishler.
They lived with John's parents for ten months. In the spring of 1925 they moved
to their own place, which was one mile east of the Christian Weiss homestead.
This land is now owned by Lawrence Lehr. They moved a hip-roof barn onto their
place from Fred Weiss's place and lived in the lean-to of the barn till they
built their new house that summer. The house was 24' x 24'. Fred and Ida Weiss
and sons, Warren and Eugene, lived one mile north of the Christian Weiss
homestead.

John's father gave them one quarter of land and they bought one quarter. The
first year they threshed 600 bushels of wheat and the second year they threshed
300 bushels of wheat. That was barely enough to live on and pay the taxes. They
used a horse and wagon to get around and also hauled their wheat to Irvine in a
wagon. What they really enjoyed was the fence telephone, so they could
communicate with their neighbors.

Their first car was a model T Ford. Their first tractor was a Rumley which cost
$800. Later they bought a threshing machine. They got 30 a bushel for
threshing. John threshed for 12 years.

John and Bertha Weiss (pic)

They lived and farmed in Alberta for 28 years. John built a house in Medicine
Hat in 1951 on 7th Street S.E. and they lived there approximately one year.

They bought the Caswell ranch 15 miles cast of Maple Creek in 1952 and ranched
there for ten years. In 1959 they rented a house in Maple Creek and lived there
for one school year. In 1962 they built a new house in the Crestwood area of
Medicine Hat where Bertha still lives. They had five children.

John Weiss Family: Back: Kenneth, Frances, Johnny; Front: Gloria, Bertha, John,
Rose (pic)

Ken and Lorna Weiss ranch 18 miles south of Maple Creek, Saskatchewan. They
have four children, Warren, Lance, Bryce, and Loree.

Frances and Erik Neilson live at Kelowna, B.C. where Frances is a teacher. Erik
works at Brenda Mines. Frances has three children, Guy, John, and James.

Johnny and Vera Weiss ranch 15 miles east of Maple Creek, Saskatchewan. They
have three children, Brent, Peggy Ann, and Kevin.

Gloria and Morley Bowyer live 28 miles south of Swift Current, Saskatchewan.
Morley works for Saskatchewan Crop Insurance. Gloria has four children, Salene,
Sylvia, Anita and Alerin.

Rose and Rob Pender farm and ranch 13 miles south of Irvine, Alberta. Rob is
also a real estate salesman. They have two children, Lisa and Shane.

Rob Pender Family: Shane, Rob, Rose, Lisa (pic)

Ken Weiss Family
submitted by Ken and Lorna Weiss

I, Kenneth Gordon Weiss, was born in Medicine Hat on April 12, 1929 and raised
on our farm south of Irvine, Alberta in the Newburg District. My parents are
John and Bertha (Pahl) Weiss and I am the second eldest of a family of six
children.

As a young boy I attended Sentinel school and when I started in grade one I
could hardly speak a word of English. My first teacher, Miss Walker, was really
nice to me and would give me a star for good work, then give me some candy when
the rest of the kids left the room. Getting to and from school in those days
was an adventure in itself. Being the eldest, it was my job to drive the horse
and buggy and take Frances and Johnnie the two and a half miles to school.
Coming home would sometimes be a free for all horse race, with everyone hanging
on for dear life, while we tried to beat the Knodel and Freimark kids.

Life in our community centered around school and going to Newburg Church where,
it seemed to me, long sermons of fire and brimstone were preached while the
congregation sat on hard benches. If I remember right, my thoughts were mostly
on what Mom was making for Sunday dinner and not on the sermon.

One time when I was about eight years old, Dad brought three sharpened
plowshares home and told me to take them over to the shop. I had barely picked
them up and started off, when I dropped them on my toe. My first words were
"These forfluetee scharray" and Dad, who was listening, said he'd like to see
me later. After staying in the shop as long as I could, I faced up to my
strapping for swearing and made sure I never swore in front of Dad again.

As I grew older I helped farm with horses. One day I'll never forget was when I
was harrowing on the Schneider quarter, driving four horses and walking behind.
Dad told me, "Don't ever turn too short or the harrows will flip over." Sure
enough, I did just that and had a runaway.

The dirty thirties were hard times for everyone, but we always had enough to
eat and loving parents and all the family around, including grandparents,
aunts, uncles and cousins. Looking back things weren't so bad.

In the fall of 1949 my parents bought the Kealey Place (one section) nine miles
south of Piapot, Saskatchewan. After improving it some during the next few
years, I moved there in the spring of 1952 and built a bachelor shack, 12' x
16'. With Dad's help that same year we bought the John Schaal place in the
Kealey Springs district, on the Bench south of Piapot, consisting of four
sections. Things were looking pretty good I thought, first the land, then the
house and now the best part, finding a wife.

That fall my carefree bachelor life came to an end when I went to the Old
Timers' Dance in Maple Creek, October 1, 1952 and met the school marm, Lorna
Francis from Crossfell School. Lorna, the youngest daughter of Raymond and Alma
(Little) Francis, was born at Admiral, Saskatchewan. Her parents homesteaded
there in 1911 and raised a family of seven on the family farm. We were married
on June 29, 1953 in the Fifth Avenue United Church, Medicine Hat and our
attendants were Vern Koenig, Johnnie Weiss, Rose-Marie Weiss and Linda McCann.
Our ushers were two more carefree Irvine bachelors at that time, Norman
Schneider and Lawrence Knodel. We came home from our honeymoon to the Schaal
place and Lorna taught another term at Crossfell. We also added on four
quarters right beside the Schaal place (known as the Dyer land) that same year
with the help of Grace and Ray Snider of Eastend.

Lorna and Ken Weiss wedding (pic)

On July 27, 1954 our first son Warren was born and finding the Bench winters
too severe we moved back to our place at Piapot. Again with Ray's help we added
on three quarters of Mrs. Cumberland's land, situated right next to Dad's place
at Piapot.

In 1956 Lorna returned to school again, spending one term at Manville and the
next at Petain. We then sold all our holdings in 1958 at Piapot and on the
Bench and purchased the Harry Bette's ranch southwest of Maple Creek, which now
consists of 20 quarter sections having added two sections in 1984.

I became interested in Charolais cattle and we imported our first full French
heifer in 1967. We were the first ones to do so in this area. Lorna and I went
to France in 1969 to see these cattle being raised on the farms and eventually
imported a total of five head. Today we are still actively raising
Charolais-Hereford cross cattle with the help of our family.

Warren, born July 27, 1954 at Maple Creek, married Jeannie Everest on June 21,
1975. They have two boys, Jamie, nine and Mark, seven. Warren is greens-keeper
at the golf course in Maple Creek and Jeannie works at the Credit Union.

Lance was born September 18, 1958 at Maple Creek and married Jayne Hohne from
Medicine Hat on January 3, 1987. They have one son Cole Justin. Jayne worked
with E.C.S. They now live on the ranch.

Bryce, born September 22, 1963 at Maple Creek, married Dena Bircham from Piapot
June 30, 1984. They also live on the ranch, but Dena, who graduated from the
University of Saskatchewan, is an accountant, B.C., C.M.A., at Warlodge
Enterprizes in Maple Creek.

Loree Lynne, born November 18, 1964 at Maple Creek, married Laurent Couture on
September 26, 1986. They have one daughter, Chantel. After both graduating from
the University of Saskatchewan, Loree with her Bachelor of Education Degree and
Larry with a Physical Education Degree, they live and teach at Fort Qu'Appelle,
Saskatchewan.

The Nicol and Bowyer Family
by Gloria Weiss-Nicol-Bowyer 1988

I, Gloria Weiss, was born in Medicine Hat on December 18, 1940, and raised on
the homestead of my parents, John and Bertha Weiss, located in the Newburg area
16 miles southeast of Irvine, Alberta.

I recall our farm home having the modern convenience of electric power,
supplied by batteries and a wind charger, a cistern pump and a fence phone to
nearby neighbors, the Knodels.

Heat was a coal and wood fired cook stove in the kitchen and a potbellied
heater called "Boss" in the living area.

For the first six school years of my life I attended a one room country school,
Sentinel. I rode horseback or traveled by buggy, three miles each way daily,
for my education.

Being brought up in a religious, loving family home, we attended church
regularly. During the summer holidays I would ride to church to attend Bible
School.

We were a very close family and it just was natural to help Mom and Dad with
all the required chores.

The biggest annual event was the Medicine Hat Rodeo, a fun time for all, with
friends, neighbors and new kids to meet and play with.

In 1952 Mom and Dad bought the Caswell Ranch near Piapot, Saskatchewan. This
was a new adventure, meeting new friends, going to a new school and our own
farm was supplied with electricity by Saskatchewan Power. From Caswell School I
attended high school in Piapot. In 1957 I left home to begin a career of
cosmetology in Winnipeg, Manitoba, residing with my sister Fran and her husband
Rip and boys. I continued my career in hairdressing at Medicine Hat and later
in Maple Creek, until my marriage to Glen.

Glen Albert Nicol was born on January 13, 1938 and was the only son of Albert
and Marion (Sorboe) Nicol. He attended school at Sidewood, Tompkins and Maple
Creek. While going to school in Maple Creek he spent many hours around the
local garages, learning mechanic skills, which was a great benefit to a country
boy. Glen enjoyed all sorts of sports and was especially enthused with a good
game of cards.

Glen Nicol (Gloria Weiss) Family (pic)

Glen and I were married on February 25, 1960 and resided on the Nicol Ranch,
which was originated in 1888 by Frank Nicol, located in the Sidewood district.
We built a new home on the ranch in 1960, featuring modern conveniences such as
automatic dishwasher and washer and dryer. The telephone followed a short time
later.

On February 23, 1961 we became the proud parents of tiny twin girls, Sylvia and
Selene. On February 18, 1962 Anita was born, which made our family seem like
triplets. Our only son, Alerin was born on September 13, 1966. We were busy,
proud happy parents raising our family as well as attending to our farm and
ranching duties.

In August of 1974 Glen was taken from us in a tragic car accident. We missed
him so, but life continued on, with many things to do for my children, as well
as to continue as I could with the farming and ranching with the help of my
in-laws, Albert and Marion.

I met Morley Bowyer, the third of a family of four, son of Frank and Emma
(Sather) Bowyer formerly of the Maple Creek area.

Morley was an elevator manager at Hanley, Saskatchewan. With our relationship
continuing he started to buy grain in Tompkins for the Pioneer. Morley and
family, Carmen and Wade, moved to the ranch. His eldest daughter Rhonda was
married and living in Lethbridge.

Morley and I were married at Las Vegas, November 6, 1979. My sister Rosemarie
and her husband Rob Pender and friends Bill and Lorraine Torok were attendants.
In 1982 Morley had to take early retirement from the Tompkins Pioneer Grain
Elevator because of grain dust. He took the postmaster's job in Piapot, but
being a very active person, this was a short lived job. Morley started to work
with Crop Insurance and became the supervisor of Crop Insurance for Southwest
Saskatchewan in 1984. This employment resulted in the move to Swift Current
where the regional office is located. By this time our four girls had finished
high school and we only had our boys: Alerin taking his grade eleven and twelve
and Wade taking grade eight and nine.

After two years of city living, we were prompt to want country living again, so
we bought an acreage at Neville, Saskatchewan 25 miles southeast of Swift
Current. Wade, our only son at home now, is being bussed to Swift Current High
School.

Morley is still with Crop Insurance and we're both enjoying the tranquillity of
the country and raising the usual farm animals.

As of now we see this as our heaven of retirement. Morley and I are now blessed
with three grandchildren: Rhonda's son Dustin Bowyer, Selene's daughter
Kirstine Nicol, and Walt and Anita's daughter Alyssa Bilych.

Herbert Emanuel and Olinda (Boschee) Weiss

Marvilla Josephine (Weiss) and Victor Opp

I, Marvilla Josephine, was born September 25, 1927 at Irvine, Alberta. I was
raised and educated on the family farm 13 miles south of Irvine, attending
Sentinel School until the age of 15. At the age of 17, I left home to work at
the Medalta Potteries in Medicine Hat. A year later, on March 8, 1945 in
Medicine Hat, I married Victor Opp. Victor, son of Christian and Elizabeth
(Schneider) Opp, was born on November 14, 1919 at Eve, Alberta. He was raised
and educated at Burstall, Saskatchewan. At the age of 21, he was called to
serve in the army, and six years later received his discharge.

During the first years of our married life we did a lot of moving in the city
as housing at that time was hard to find. I can still remember the first suite
we rented. It was a basement suite where the table was hinged to the wall when
not in use. As the suite was not ready yet, the kitchen and bedroom were all in
one. About six months later we finally found a place a bit bigger.

After his discharge from the army, Victor worked at Beny Motors for eight
years. For the next 23 years he was employed by the Texaco Gas Company,
delivering bulk gas to customers on farms and filling stations until, due to
ill health, he was unable to drive the bulk gas truck. Then he worked for a
time as a security guard at Dominion Glass Company in Redcliff.

I worked at K-Mart store from 1972 to 1979. In 1964, we bought our first house.
Victor passed away July 14, 1978.

I have since sold the house and live in an apartment. Our family is as follows:

Sharon was born December 31, 1947, and is married to Eldon Blanchard, son of
George and Jean (Fortney) Blanchard. Eldon is employed with the C.P.R. and
Sharon is a secretary at St. Mary's Church. They have a daughter and a son.
Cheryl was married to Jamie Smithson on May 9, 1987. They reside at Lethbridge,
Alberta. Murray is attending school in Medicine Hat.

Brian was born May 19, 1952 and was married to Cathy, daughter of Anton and
Barbara (Scherger) Hilsendeger on March 8, 1976. They have a son, Dwayne, born
in 1977, and twins, a boy and a girl, James and Jamie, born in 1981. Brian is
employed with Crane Canada Inc.

Bonnie, our youngest daughter was born April 1, 1965. She had been married to
Andrew Sykes. Bonnie and her young son live in Redcliff. Bonnie works as a
cashier.

Bernice (Weiss) Lehr

I, Bernice Lehr, am the daughter of Herbert and Olinda (Boschee) Weiss of
Irvine and was born December 20,1930 in Medicine Hat. I grew up on the farm
southeast of Irvine, attending the one-roomed Sentinel School, with one teacher
for all of us kids. There were times in winter when getting to school was tough
as there was lots of snow. Sometimes the horses barely made it and we were
nearly frozen by the time we got there. We had a lot of fun in the spring and
summer playing ball and we won lots of tournaments, even if we got there by
horse and buggy. It was fun!

We had lots of chores to do when we got home from school, such as milking cows
and feeding pigs, so our homework was always last. Going to school ended and I
grew up and got married in 1948 to Ernie Lehr.

The Rueben Weiss Family
by Rueben B. Weiss

I, Rueben Benjamin Weiss, was born in Irvine, Alberta on January 20, 1909, the
youngest son of Christian and Christina (Heller) Weiss. I attended school in
Irvine and after my parents moved to the farm south of Irvine I went to school
there. I was going to school in Irvine when the school burnt down and if it had
not been for Sophie Thiede taking me by the hand and leading me out I might not
have been around to tell my story. Sophie and I have remained friends to this
day.

My sister and brother-in-law, Martha and Gust Heine, moved to California in
1922 and shortly after I moved down there to live with them. I stayed in
California until 1929 when I came back to Canada and bought a farm south of
Irvine. On March 11, 1932 I married Christina Stuber, daughter of John and Anna
Marie (Schuler) Stuber. In 1938 I sold the farm to Fred Vossler and moved to
Tilley to an irrigation farm. Christina passed away on April 17, 1940 after a
lengthy illness, at the age of 27 years. Christina and I had two sons, Franklin
and Allan. I also had a stepdaughter Vivian, who is now married to Lawrence
Waldbauer and lives in Walsh.

After Christina's death I moved to Medicine Hat where I worked on construction
for a few years. I ran the paver for F. R. Gibbs and I paved many of the
streets in Medicine Hat and the tarmac at Medicine Hat Airport. I also paved
many auxiliary airports in the district.

Becky and Rueben Weiss (pic)

On July 28, 1942 I married Rebecca (Becky) Kozmyk, the daughter of Adam and
Charlotte (Stotz) Kozmyk. We have three children, Thomas, Jerald and Betty.

For many years I worked as a mechanic at Beny Motors, Park Garage and Karl
Kramer's Garage. In 1951 we moved to Brooks where I worked as service manager
for Pheasant Motors. In 1956 I bought Crestwood Service in Medicine Hat and we
moved again.

At the same time Becky ran Stan's of Crestwood so we were both very busy, with
both businesses being open seven days a week. III health forced Becky to give
up the store in 1959. I sold the garage in 1967 and went selling cars for five
years. In 1975 Becky's brother Stan died and we again found ourselves in the
grocery business. However the long hours seven days a week proved to be too
much and we sold in 1976.

Since that time we have done a lot of traveling and for a few years enjoyed the
hobby of carpentry. However, a severe case of emphysema has put a stop to that
because of the dust. We still enjoy camping and fishing and spend most of the
summer at different "fishing holes".

Our five children are as follows:

Rueben Weiss Family: Back: Frank, Betty, Jerry, Tom; Front: Rueben and Becky
(pic)

Franklin married Phyllis Western and lives in Burnaby, B.C. He has one son,
Kelly, and two grandsons, Paul and Mark. He also has two stepsons, Glen and
James Western, and two step-grand-children.

Allan (Weiss) Stuber married Marlene Sulz and lives in Medicine Hat. Allan
divides his time between Medicine Hat and Elkwater where he works for the

Thomas married Pat Gammon and they had two daughters, Laura and Nicolette. They

children, Lorne and Arlette, and one granddaughter, Evelyn.

We have ten grandchildren and three great grandchildren and we are proud of
them all.

We still live in Medicine Hat and probably will for the rest of our lives.

Stephen and Maria Wiedeman

Stephen Weideman was born in Germany in 1881, and after five years in Paris and
England immigrated to Canada in 1908. He joined the Royal North West Mounted
Police in Regina. After training he was posted to Irvine, where a large number
of German speaking people were taking up homesteads and settling the
surrounding area.

Stephen was stationed at Irvine from 1908 to 1913 and was promoted to Corporal
in charge of the three man detachment. Travel was by horseback and Stephen was
a welcome visitor at the farms and ranches from the U.S.A. and Saskatchewan
borders to Hilda and Schuler.

After leaving the force in 1913 he set up a real estate and insurance business
in Irvine and also as a Notary Public did a lot of legal work for the settlers,
and in later years was an official auditor, also doing a lot of Income Tax
returns.

Maria (Bechtold) Wiedeman was born in 1881 in Germany. She left home at 17 for
Paris where she was a governess for nine years. In 1908 she immigrated to the
U.S.A. and worked as a governess in Chicago and Seattle for a Mayers family.

Stephen and Maria Wiedeman (pic)

Maria and Stephen, who became acquainted through friends in Germany, were
married in Medicine Hat June 1st, 1916 by Father Reibel. They took up residence
in Irvine, except for a few years when they farmed south east of town. When
Hans, Richard and Gertrude became of school age, they moved back to Irvine.

From 1927-1948 Maria and Stephen operated the Golden Rule Store, just east of
the hotel. Stephen had his office at the back of the store, having been
appointed Justice of Peace in the 1930's, and to Magistrate from 1945 to 1961.

Maria Wiedeman and Bob Davidson, the C.P.R. Agent, as members of the School
Board were instrumental in setting up Irvine's first high school in the 1930's.
Maria's name has been placed on the Alberta Honor Roll for her years of service
with the Irvine Women's Institute.

Stephen's Mounted Police uniform is on display at the Medicine Hat Museum as a
tribute to his service.

Hans (Slim), born 1917, was employed with the Alberta Wheat Pool in the 1930's.
During World War II he served in the Canadian Postal Corps as a Corporal in
Ottawa. He married Joyce Hodgins who was also in the service. After their
discharges, Hans worked for Alberta Wheat Pool at Irvine and Joyce supervised
at Berry Centre School. In 1948 Hans was transferred to Schuler to operate the
Pool elevator there and Joyce taught school. Hans passed away in 1979 and
Joyce, now retired, lives in Medicine Hat. They had one son, Allen Stephen, who
married Maria Schafer of Schuler. They reside in St. Albert where he is
employed with Alberta Energy.

Richard Wiedeman and Morley Geiger (pic)

Richard, born in 1918, now retired in Medicine Hat after 40 years with C.P.
Rail as a trainman and conductor, married Rose Oriold R.N. of Empress in 1947.
They have three children, Dale of Montreal, Joanne of Vancouver, and Lois
Kokoski of Calgary.

Gertrude, born 1920, was one of Irvine's first high school graduating class.
She attended Normal School in Calgary, after which she taught at Newburg School
south of Irvine and also at the Irvine School from 1939-45. In 1945 she married
Captain Jim Oliphant newly returned from the Second World War. They lived in
various places in Alberta, but mostly in St. Albert, where Gert taught school
and Jim operated a General Insurance business. In 1980 they retired and live in
Clearbrook B.C. They have three children: Carol Fischer, Denver, Colorado;
Janet Gates, Fort Smith, N.W.T.; and John, Vancouver.

Josephine, born 1923, passed away in infancy.

Alois and Magdelina (Brod) Wiedemann

Alois Wiedemann was born in Dilingen, Germany on June 18, 1891. He received his
education there and in February, 1914 he immigrated to Canada to join his
brother Stephen, who had previously settled in Irvine. Alois worked in the
greenhouses in Medicine Hat for several years and in 1917 he started a business
as a Rawleigh man selling medicines, spices, etc. door to door and farm to
farm, traveling far and wide about the district with his team and wagon. He
endured many hardships during the cold winters, often being caught in below
zero weather and blinding snow storms.

It was while on these rounds of the countryside that he met Magdelena Brod
(step daughter of Adam Nitz) and they were married on September 24, 1920.

Alois continued as a Rawleigh man until February 24, 1923 when he opened his
own General Store in Irvine, in the building now occupied by the Post Office.

A few years later he purchased the Sam Kalmbach building on the corner (now the
Seniors Recreation Centre and Town Office) and moved his store into the larger
premises. In 1938 he integrated the Treasury Branch Agency with his store. In
1949 he purchased the larger Beny building down the street, taking sons Herman
and Victor into the store business with him. Sixty-five years after opening his
first store, Wiedemann's General Store continues to serve the town and district
with dedication and the personal touch.

Alois passed away in 1961 and Magdelena in 1977. Seven children were born to
Mr. and Mrs. Wiedemann:

Herman still resides in Irvine and continues to run the store and Treasury
Branch.

Anna (Mrs. Roy Gale) lives in Dunmore where she and her husband operated a
store and service station for many years.

Victor now resides in Medicine Hat, and for the last number of years has been
employed as a hail adjuster for the Provincial Government. His wife Betty still
teaches at Irvine.

Alois Wiedemann Family: Back: Herman, Anna, Otto, Wally, Victor. Front:
Lillian, Alois, Magdelena, Roy (pic)

Wally (Mrs. Francis O'Hara) lives in Edmonton where she and her husband have
been teachers for many years.

Otto and his wife Joan own a greenhouse in Redcliff.

Roy is a lawyer and he and his wife, Elaine, live in Medicine Hat.

Lillian and her husband Joe Machacek operate a farm near Taber.

From these families there are now 31 grandchildren and 15 great-grandchildren.

Victor and Betty (Clarke) Wiedemann

In August of 1949, Victor Wiedemann, son of Alois and Magdelina Wiedemann,
married Betty Clarke, daughter of Francis and Susan Clarke. The couple took up
residence in Irvine.

Victor became a partner in the Wiedemann General Store, and continued to work
there until 1973. He became interested in the cattle business and raised
Charolais cattle for several years, importing some of his stock from France.

In recent years Victor has been working with the Alberta Hail and Crop
Insurance, both as salesman, and in the adjusting area.

He and his son Barry have also developed an interest in raising bees, to
produce queen bees, as well as honey.

Victor Wiedemann children (pic)

Betty taught school for a few years during their first years of marriage, then
returned to it after their children were in school.

Victor and Betty had five children, all of whom were raised and received their
schooling in Irvine.

Judy went on to become a teacher. She married Wayne Knight, who is in Real
Estate. She and her husband live in Medicine Hat and she teaches at Crescent
Heights school.

Roger also became a teacher and is living in Medicine Hat. He and his wife
Judy, also a teacher, have two sons, Sandon and Jayde.

Joan went into nursing. She married Bill Glockner, a fireman, and they are
living in Medicine Hat. Joan and Bill have two children, Beth and Steven.

Gregory took his training in Business Management, and is presently employed at
the Goodyear plant. His wife, Naida, is a teacher. They reside in Medicine Hat.

Barry took some training in Power Engineering. He is presently employed at
Fifth Avenue Church, and he and Victor are building up a small business in
raising queen bees and honey production. His wife Loreen is in production at
CHAT-TV. They have one daughter Jennifer.

The Wildes
by Joyce (Wilde) Scott

In 1949, Harry and Mabel Wilde and sons, Stan and Harold, moved to Irvine to
take over the business formerly owned by Jacobson and Son which included the
John Deere Agency, Imperial Oil and B.A. Stations.

It was to be a brief venture for Harry and Harold, but Stan continued to live
in Irvine for several years, eventually operating the Texaco Service Station.
In 1952 he married Eileen Harding and their chosen daughter Merilee became part
of the family in 1956.

Victor Wiedemann Family: Back: Barry Wiedemann, Bill Glockner, Wayne and Judy
Knight, Gregory, Naida and Roger Wiedemann; Middle: Loreen Wiedemann, Joan
Glockner, Betty and Victor Wiedemann, Judy Wiedemann; Front: (children) Beth
Glockner, Jennifer Wiedemann, Steven Glockner, Jade and Sandon Wiedemann (pic)

Harold married Rosemarie Metz of Richmound and in 1950 they returned to that
town to operate the Esso Bulk Station. They later moved to Gull Lake,
Saskatchewan to run a similar operation. They had a family of four.

Edna Bryden, a daughter of Harry and Mabel, also lived in Irvine briefly when
she came to help when the business was purchased.

The Harry Wildes returned to Maple Creek, although Harry had business interests
in Richmound for a few years.

Although not all of the Wilde family actually lived in the community, we
remember some of the friendly residents we became acquainted with while
spending holidays with our parents. These include the Clarkes, Jess Joneses,
Wiedemanns, Sophie Thiede and Mrs. Wheatley.

Harry passed away in 1956, Stan in 1967, and Mabel in 1979.

The bell tower in front of the Irvine Peace United Church was erected by the
Wilde family in memory of Harry and Stan.

John and Magdalena (Kirschenmann) Will
by Frieda Will

John Will was born December 9, 1882 in Bessarabia, Russia in the village of
Neudorf. He served in the First World War for three years, plus a number of
years in the Home Revolution.

Magdalena Kirschenmann was born in Neudorf, Russia on April 27, 1884. They were
married there in 1906.

To this marriage there were born seven children, four of these died in early
childhood.

They immigrated to Canada, arriving in Irvine by train on September 26, 1926,
with their three children, Katherine, Louise and William. After staying with
friends in Irvine for a few days, they went with Mr. Stroh, the mail driver, to
Thelma, Alberta, where they stayed for some time. When they immigrated, the
idea was to come to Canada first, then immigrate to the U.S.A. as there were
two brothers living there. As fate would have it, this could not be done.

They worked for several different farmers in the area, then rented land in the
Schuler area, then moved back south of Irvine, renting land from Mr. John S.
Lehr.

In 1932 they purchased the K.P. Becker place, NW 28-11-3-W4. There was not much
of a house there so a two story house was moved out from Irvine. As years went
by they added more land to this holding and operated as a father and son
operation.

John, William, Magdalena Will (pic)

John Will Family: Back: Katherine, William, Louise; Front: John and Magdalena
(pic)

In 1950 Mr. and Mrs. Will purchased a home in Medicine Hat and moved to the
city in November. Mr. Will had been in ill health for some time and passed away
on April 18, 1951, at the age of 68 years.

Magdalena enjoyed gardening on the farm and in town, and always had lots of
vegetables for everyone. She lived in her house until the spring of 1964 when
she had a stroke and spent the next six years in a nursing home in Medicine
Hat. She passed away November 29, 1970 at age 86 years.

Katherine married Gideon Lehr in 1928. Shortly after, they moved to the
Cardston area where they farmed and ranched. They have three boys, Harold,
Lester and Bob. Harold and Joan live in Boston, Lester and Eileen live in
Calgary. Bob and Jerrylin live on the family farm at Cardston.

Certificate of Naturalization - Johan Will - 1935, side 2 (pic)

Louise married Jacob Bechtold in 1936. They farmed south of Irvine for a while,
then purchased a blacksmith shop in Irvine. Now retired, they live in Medicine
Hat. They have four children. Christ and Shirley, Wilbert and Anita, Louise
Lorraine and Con all reside in Calgary. Clarence and Terry live in Medicine Hat.

William married Frieda Veil in December 1950. They carried on the operation of
the family farm.
