William and Frieda (Veil) Will
by Frieda Will

In 1950 William purchased the family farm from his father and began farming on
his own. In December of 1950 he and I, Frieda Veil, were married.

There was no electricity in those days, but in the fall of 1951 we purchased a
power plant from Frank McLeay, consisting of a motor and a dozen or more
batteries. What an improvement over the coal-oil lamps! We also bought a
propane fridge the same year and could keep things really well then.

Roads were poor, and many a time we would be snowed in for several weeks.
William would ride to Irvine to pick up the mail and get some groceries.

The year 1951 was a wet year, crops sprouted in the stand, in the stooks and in
the swaths. We had lots of grain, but of poor quality. Cattle prices were not
too bad until foot and mouth disease broke out. The bottom fell out of the
cattle market overnight, and took several years to recover. The early 60's were
very dry years, no snow in the winter and no rain in the summer.

Johan Will passport (in Russian) - 1926 (pic)

Certificate of Naturalization - Magdalena Will - 1935, side 1 (pic)

Frieda (Veil) and William Will - December 9, 1950 (pic

In 1973 we sold the home place, and built a new place along the #1 Highway on
the north side of the C.P.R. tracks. This was our hay land and we thought it
would be a good place to semi-retire. We raised hay and cattle. This property
had irrigation on it, therefore it was easier to manage while living there.

We did a fair bit of traveling over the years, and enjoyed the more relaxed way
of life.

William was active in farm organizations, was secretary of the Irvine Farmers
Union from the mid 50's until they disbanded. He was on the Unifarm board as
District Chairman, then Alternate Region Director and then became Region 13
Director, which position he held until 1984. William was one of the original
water users of the Ross Creek Irrigation District which was formed in 1949, and
was the chairman of this at the time of his passing. He was also acting
chairman when Pashley Mutual Telephone was formed in 1959.

Will Farm - 1986 (pic)

Frieda and William Will, 25th Anniv., December 9, 1975 (pic)

Frieda and William Will (pic)

William belonged to Toastmaster Club from 1986-87, and did a fair bit of
judging at Medicine Hat school speak-offs, which he enjoyed. He was active in
the Lutheran Church in Irvine and held various positions from time to time.

I, Frieda, was active in the Women's Institute, receiving my 30 years of
service pin before they disbanded in 1984. I was also involved in church
activities and in Unifarm.

William passed away suddenly on May 24, 1987 while visiting with friends in the
Manyberries area, at age 61.

I sold the farm to John and Faye Beierbach, and now reside in the Southridge
area in Medicine Hat.

August and Agatha Wirsch

August and Agatha Wirsch immigrated to Canada in 1899 from Albota, Bessarabia,
South Russia. With them they brought their two oldest children, Lynda and John.
August took up his homestead in 1901 in the Josephsburg district of the
Northwest Territories. This later became the Robinson district of Southern
Alberta. The Wirsch family increased with the birth of two more sons, Christian
and Fred, and also two more daughters, Elizabeth and Olga. There were several
children that died at an early age.

August Wirsch Family: Lydia, Agatha, Fred, Christian, August, John. Front:
Olga, Elizabeth (pic)

In 1910 the family moved to Medicine Hat so that the children could go to
school in the winter time. August continued to farm; his sons would join him in
the summer.

August and Agatha continued this arrangement until their second son Christian
took over the family homestead.

During the early years in Medicine Hat, Fred was looking after some horses when
one kicked him and he was killed.

The two youngest daughters are still living. Elizabeth (Mrs. John Klassen)
lives in Nanaimo, B.C. and Olga (Mrs. Charlie Pudwell) lives in Medicine Hat.

Christian and Mathilda (Jans) Wirsch

Christian Wirsch took over the family homestead after his marriage to Mathilda
Jans of the Walsh district in 1920. They farmed until the later 1940's when
they moved into Irvine. Christ started to drive a school bus in 1944 from the
Robinson district to Irvine. He was one of the first bus drivers in the Irvine
area. He drove until 1963 when he retired.

Christ was also the town's shoemaker for many years. First he rented a small
room from Alois Wiedemann, then later he moved his shoe repair shop to the back
porch of his house on Walsh Street.

Christ and Mathilda were active members of the Irvine Church of God until it
closed down in the 1950's.

Christian Wirsch Family: Back: Walter, Edwin. Front: Lawrence, Christian,
Marlene, Mathilda, Roy (pic)

They continued to live in Irvine until Christ's death in 1977. Mathilda stayed
on in her home until August of 1985 when she moved to the Cypress View Lodge.
She entered the hospital in May of 1988 where she remained, returning only
briefly to Cypress View Lodge, until she passed away on July 24, 1988.

Christ and Mathilda had five children: Walter married Irene Nittel and died in
1970; Edwin married Gladys Kirby Long and lives in Trail, B.C.; Roy married
Rachel Roth and lives in Medicine Hat; Lawrence married Valerie Erickson and
lives in Calgary; and Marlene married Clarence Roth and lives in the Irvine
district. There are 11 grand-children and six great-grandchildren to complete
this family.

Daniel and Anna (Hollstein) Wirsch
by Elma Koenig

Daniel Wirsch arrived with his father August Sr. at Irvine, N.W.T. in March of
1899, at the age of 16, from Bessarabia.

He worked for the various ranchers in the district, also for the C.P.R. when
the roundhouse was being constructed in Medicine Hat. The going wage was $1 per
day for carrying bricks to the masons.

In the year 1904 he took up a homestead adjacent to his father's in what was
then the Josephsburg district, eventually adding three more quarters to it,
4-10-3-W4. His cattle brand was and horse brand, Double D and bar. He often
spoke of the big blizzard of 1903 in late May.

In 1906 he married Anna K. Hollstein, who had arrived with her family from
Leige, Belgium, in 1903.

Three daughters were born to them, Anna Bertha (Mrs. John Jans), Dorothea (Mrs.
Henry Jans), both of Medicine Hat, and Elma (Mrs. Manny Koenig) of Coaldale.

There being no school in the district, the two oldest girls were enrolled in a
private school run by the Seventh Day Adventist Church until Robinson School
was built. The first teacher was a Mrs. Banks.

Daniel and Anna sold their farm to Mike Schorr and retired to Chilliwack in
1943. They returned to Medicine Hat in 1955, where they resided until their
passing, Anna in 1963 and Daniel in 1972.

Otto and Hulda (Schulz) Wittke
by Art Wittke

Otto and Hulda (Schulz) Wittke, their two sons Emil and Arthur, immigrated to
Canada in 1928. They settled in the Clearwater area where Otto thought he would
try farming. He purchased a section of farm land from the Hudson Bay Company on
crop payments, but the next few years were tough; he could not make the
payments and a living at farming. He then decided to move to Irvine and try
black-smithing, the trade he learned in the old country. One daughter, Elsie,
was born while on the farm.

Wittke blacksmith, barn and house - 1933 (pic)

In 1932 he purchased a piece of property from the town of Irvine for $300. It
included a small house and barn and was located on the west side of town. He
converted a granary into his first blacksmith shop and, with all hand made
tools, started a general repair and blacksmith shop. The next few years were
better; customers appreciated his skill and workmanship. They supported the
business to the point where the shop became too small, so it was expanded to
twice its size. An addition and renovation was also made to the house.

Otto was very inventive. He built tools and equipment which were used to
manufacture agricultural tools and attachments. By 1941 the business had again
outgrown the old shop which was then torn down and a complete new shop was
built on the same location. This was now the Irvine Machine Shop. This shop was
equipped with more power tools, welders, shapers, cutters, etc. Goods such as
duck foot seeder attachments, grain augers, and scrapers were manufactured on a
larger scale. These goods were marketed as far as Swift Current and Lethbridge.
At this time Emil and Art were working in the business.

In 1944 Otto Wittke purchased a section of farm land at Pashley from Ed
McCorvie for $3500. Two years later he purchased a quarter section from Frank
McLeay for $700, and a quarter section from G. Stadel for $900. This quarter
included the Pashley townsite. Along with the business he operated this farm
until 1951 when he retired from the business and moved to Medicine Hat. He
continued farming from there until 1967 when the farm was sold to Emil and Art.

In 1948 Emil and Art purchased the Case inventory from Tony Jacobson, and
became dealers in farm machinery for the J. I. Case Company. They operated this
business along with the machine shop. As the sales in farm machinery increased,
the manufacturing of goods stopped.

Wittke house newly renovated - 1938 (pic)

In 1950 a new brick building was built across the street from the machine shop,
it housed the dealership along with Texaco gas pumps. This building was built
of used materials purchased in Medicine Hat from the salvage depot of the WW II
concentration camp.

In 1954 the Trans Canada Highway was built through Irvine and was located south
of the home place and shop. A parcel of land was purchased from the town
next-to the new highway and a service station that also housed the dealership
was built. Business was carried on from this location until it was sold in 1957.

Art and Emit purchased the Nichols' Farm Equipment business in Medicine Hat, to
where both families relocated. The lots in Irvine were sold, and both houses
were moved to Medicine Hat.

The Wittke family was very active in church work, also took part in various
singing and musical playing activities, one of which was a singing quartet,
with Emil, Art, Elsie, and Clara, on CHAT Radio McMullen Bible Hour. All the
members of the family attended the Irvine School; Ben and Esther continued
their education in Medicine Hat.

Otto Wittke Family: Back: Elsie, Art, Emil, Clara; Front: Freda, Hulda, Esther,
Otto, Ben (pic)

Emil took his basic training in the army at Petawawa, Ontario. In 1946 he
married Ruth Herringer from Medicine Hat. They built a house just east of the
home place in Irvine, then in 1953, sold this house and built a larger home.
Emil served on the town council, and as fire chief. While in Irvine they had
four children. Janice married Clare Rattai. They have two children and now live
in Winnipeg. Gerald married Arlis Baker. They have three children and now live
in Medicine Hat. Ken married Marlyn Crawford. They have four children and now
live in Medicine Hat. Carolyn married Mel Snyder. They have two children, and
live in Medicine Hat. Kevin was born in Medicine Hat, and is living at home.

The Otto Wittkes: Back: Harvey Johnson, Emil, Ben and Art Wittke, Gabe Adams,
Harold Flemmer; Front: Esther Davis, Elsie Johnson, Ruth, Donnis, Otto, Hulda
and Sophie Wittke, Clara Adams, Freda Flemmer (pic)

Art married Sophie Hausauer of Irvine in 1951 and for a short time they lived
in a suite above the old post office. After his parents moved to Medicine Hat
they moved into the old house, which was later torn down and rebuilt. Art and
Sophie were active in the curling club; Art helped build the old curling rink.
He also played baseball for many years for teams at Irvine, Elkwater, Walsh and
Redcliff. He also served on the town council. They had two children while in
Irvine. Susan married Robin Rollefstad. They have three boys and live in
Medicine Hat. Wade married Donna Shabatka. They have two children and live in
Medicine Hat.

Elsie married Harvey Johnson. They have three children and live in Vancouver.

Clara married Gabe Adams. They have three children and live in Vancouver.

Freda married Harold Flemmer. They have two children and live in Calgary.

Ben married Donnis Johnson. They have two children and live in Surnmerland, B.C.

Esther married David Davis. They have two children and live in Vancouver.

Tom and Ida (Bechtold) Wood
by Thomas N. Wood

Mom and Dad (Thomas Wood Sr. and his wife Ann) with their three children, Ethel
ten years old, Horace eight years, and Tom (me) two and a half years old,
emigrated from England arriving in Medicine Hat, Alberta on March 27th, 1907.

Dad worked for the city for about four years, most of that time as engineer in
the old powerhouse.

Ann and Thomas Wood Sr. - 1940's (pic)

Some of my vivid memories of our days in Medicine Hat are of our horse Prince,
affectionately called "old bones" because he was always so fat and chubby,
Jack, a big hound that followed my brother Horace home one day and our cat
Tabby. Tabby was one of the household, but Prince and Jack were going concerns.
Every Sunday morning, without fail, when we stepped out into the backyard after
breakfast, there was Prince standing between the buggy shafts ready to take off
for the day and Jack lying beneath the buggy all set to go along as body guard.

In 1910, Dad had filed on a homestead, the NW 18-12-1-W4 and a pre-empetion SW
19-12-1-W4. So in May 1911, we loaded into a box car in Medicine Hat what
farming equipment we had acquired and shipped it to Walsh, Alberta. Then we
moved out to a bachelor's shack that was near the homestead and lived there
until we had a shack built and a tent set up, and then, we were in business.
Because of the availability of water we later changed things around and had SW
19-12-1-W4 designated the homestead.

We three children grew up on the farm and received part of our education at
Clover Hill School #2584.

We finally worked the farm into a ranch and of course went through the dirty
thirties, but all in all we had a happy life.

Ethel Wood - 1940's (pic)

Lillian and Horace Wood -1968 (pic)

Ethel never married. In June 1929, Horace married Lillian Rowley of Coaldale
and Turin. They had six children, Alvin, Kenneth, Audry, Wayne, Gerald, and
Patricia.

In July 1938, I (Tom) married Ida Bechtold of the Irvine area. We had two
children, Charmaine and Carol.

Ida and Tom Wood - 1958

Tom and Ida Wood 50th Anniv. - July 1988 (pic)

Dad (Thomas Wood Sr.) passed away in June 1954. After Dad's death, the rest of
the family carried on with the ranch. Over the years it grew to be quite a
profitable operation. In 1963 Ethel, Ida and I retired to live in Irvine,
Alberta and Wayne (Horace's son) took over the ranch as a renter. Then in 1965,
Wayne bought the ranch, and later in March 1967, sold it to Harvey Freimark.
Horace and Lillian lived on the ranch until it was sold. Horace and Lillian
then retired and lived in Redcliff.

We had lost Mom in 1958. Then on December 22, 1970, Ethel went to join Mom and
Dad in Hillside Cemetery, Medicine Hat, Alberta.

Horace and Lillian lived in Redcliff for several years, then after spending
some time in the River-view Nursing Home, Horace passed away on November 15,
1978, and is buried in the Redcliff Cemetery. Lillian now lives in the Lutheran
Manor, Medicine Hat, and Ida and I still live in our home in Irvine, Alberta.

Albert and Agnes Woodward

Albert C. Woodward was born in 1891 in England and came to Canada (Ontario) in
1906. He moved to Alberta about 1908 and worked on a farm in the Retlaw area
and in Medicine Hat until filing on his homestead about 1910. His shack was
located close to the south side of the quarter where he constructed a small
dugout for stock water.

He enlisted in the Calgary Light Horse (Cavalry Unit), later transferred to the
13th Battalion Winnipeg Rifles and served overseas with the Canadian
Expeditionary Force. He was wounded at the battle of Vimy Ridge in France in
1917.

He married Agnes Huckle on December 6, 1917 and returned to Canada in January
1918 to be discharged from the army.

A. Woodward family not identified (pic)

He returned to his homestead and was joined by his bride in the spring of 1918.
They moved their home from the SE 16-12-2-W4 to the SW 4-12-2-W4 in 1920 and
then to the SE 17-12-2-W4 in 1934. He constructed a dam to capture the spring
run off and developed a small irrigation project. In cooperation with the
Brooks Horticultural station he developed an experimental orchard. He was
successful in growing apples, plums, cherries, and a variety of small fruit.
Thanks to the water, he and his wife were able to grow a good garden even
during the worst drought years of the 1930's. The vegetables were canned or
dried, while potatoes and turnips were stored in the root cellar for the
winter. With the help of relief supplies of dried cod and salt herring from the
Maritimes they were able to keep their family of six children fed during the
depression.

After 1938, crop conditions improved as did the economy of the country and life
became a little easier. The dam was enlarged and the irrigation project
improved. He built a large poultry house for over 1000 laying hens. Hatching
eggs were shipped to the Fox Hatcheries in Calgary.

The war and the difficult depression years took their toll on his health and he
was forced to leave the farm in the late 40's. They made their home in Medicine
Hat but continued to be very active in the affairs of the farm. The farm was
operated first by his oldest son Gordon and then by his youngest son Leslie.

In 1967 they celebrated their 50th Wedding Anniversary.

Agnes and Albert Woodward 50th Anniv. - 1967 (pic)

Albert Woodward passed away in December 1971 and his wife Agnes, in October
1976.

They had seven children (one died as an infant) and had 15 grandchildren at the
time of their passing. Their children were Gordon, Winifred, Elsie, Dorothy,
Roy, and Leslie.

Gordon Albert Woodward

I, Gordon Albert Woodward, the oldest son of Albert and Agnes Woodward, was
born in Medicine Hat and lived there for a year, then lived on the homestead
north of Irvine. About 1920 I moved to the George Dunn farm now owned by Herb
Frisch. As with most families I had to find work at an early age because of
hard times.

My work was various, from repairman with #4 School Division to digging water
wells and making cement well tile for 30 years. I had the dray outfit in
Irvine, made water troughs, and spray painted farm buildings.

I am on the church board, was on town council, and was fire chief in Irvine.

I have three children.

Tom married to Diane Schuh. They have two children, Shannyn and Trevor.

Sandra married Gerald Andres. They have two children, Ryan and Randi.

Wayne is single.

Winifred (Woodward) Schlichenmayer

I am Winifred Agnes Schlichenmayer (Winnie Woodward), born in Medicine Hat,
Alberta on March 27, 1920, the second child of Albert and Agnes Woodward of
Irvine. I attended school in Irvine, receiving a grade eight School Leaving
Diploma in June 1934.

In 1936-1937 I was a member of the Irvine Peppy Pals, a girls' club under the
wing of the Women's Institute of Alberta. Mrs. Lionel Chell was our leader. We
went for a week's holiday to Elkwater Lake in 1936. We were taken there in the
box of Buster Crewe's big delivery truck. Mrs. Henry Cook and Mrs. Stephen
Wiedeman were our guides, cooks and care takers.

I attended the Institute of Technology and Art in Calgary, Alberta, taking a
course in dressmaking and received a diploma May 31, 1941. In June 19411 worked
at Caldwell's Knitting Factory and in February 1942, worked in the drapery
department in Hudson's Bay in Calgary. October 1942 I worked at Mitchell's
Tailor Shop in Calgary, altering and repairing Air Force uniforms. June 1945 I
was put on Mitchell's staff for making men's tailored suits. 1947 saw me in
Weiner's Men's Store, Charlie's Tailor Shop, and Jack's Suit Store doing the
alterations.

March 13, 1948 I married Albert Schlichenmayer of Torrington, Alberta moving
onto his 320 acre farm of prairie wool, brush and trees, with 16 acres
cultivated, and into a 16 x 20 unfinished shack with a coal and wood stove and
kerosene lights, a decided change from the bright lights and conveniences of
Calgary.

In the summer of 1948 we built a 16 x 20 slab barn with a four-foot open loft
on top where we put feed for the cattle. It also helped for warmth in the
winter.

To our home were born three children: Julia Agnes, on March 23, 1949; William
Albert, September 11, 1952; and Jocelyn Katherine, November 4, 1954.

Over the years we cleared brush by hand and pulled trees with tractor and
chains. With the power of a faithful John Deere D tractor and a breaker plow we
broke the land to grow grain.

In 1961, a 28 x 40 house was built, with 10 x 12 entry and a full basement.
From June 1966 through January 1986, this was a foster home for four babies and
16 teenagers. For some of the teenagers, grown up now, it is still home.

1969 through 1979 we raised and butchered broiler chickens year round. We had a
few pigs from 1981 to 1985. The following year we made a heavy wire hog lot
with divided pens and runways. Now we have a 25 sow operation, some weaners,
and some finished hogs. The hog lot is equipped with waterers, self feeders,
two wooden farrowing barns, and slab and straw shelters for weaners, feeders
and dry sows.

In 1984 the farm land was rented to William and we kept a few cows. Albert
retired due to ill health in 1985 and passed away on April 28, 1988. I continue
to live on the farm raising my hogs and enjoying the country life.

Elsie Violet (Woodward) Mackey

Born July 13, 1922, I grew up on a farm east and north of Irvine, Alberta, with
my parents Albert and Agnes Woodward and my two sisters and three brothers. I
attended Irvine School from 1928 to 1941. I joined the girls' club, The Irvine
Peppy Pals in 1936-37. It was associated with the Irvine Women's Institute.

In 1941-42, I successfully completed a Dressmaking Course at the Academy of
Useful Arts in Calgary followed by a six months apprenticeship in Medicine Hat,
Alberta. I have continued my interest in craft courses throughout the years
including Ceramics at the University of Calgary and at Universal Ceramics
eventually qualifying as an instructor. Sewing and crafts have become an
intricate part of my life.

I was employed at the Dominion Glass Co. at Redcliff for about six years as a
packer. I helped load many boxcars with loose beer bottles for shipment to
Lethbridge and Calgary.

For 28 years I was employed at the Calgary General Hospital, working in various
departments, mainly as a hospital assistant with the recreational therapists in
the Rehabilitation Department with the geriatric group. I later qualified as a
recreational therapist graduating with honors from Mount Royal College in
Calgary.

I became a swimming instructor in 1965 and swam 100 miles during the year at
the Kilarney Swimming Pool in 1967 for Calgary's Centennial. I completed the
feat again in 1968 and 1987.

I married Bob Mackey of Nanton, Alberta in 1964, a heavy duty mechanic and
aircraft mechanic for Canadian Pacific Airlines (repairs).

We moved to Cochrane, Alberta in 1979 where he was employed as the first
manager of the Cochrane Ranche Historic Site. He passed away July 2, 1982 at
the age of 64.

Bob and Elsie (Woodward) Mackey Wedding - 1964 (pic)

Since my retirement in 19811 am involved with the Big Hill Senior Citizens'
Lodge in Cochrane teaching ceramics and other crafts. I am a member of the Big
Hill Senior Citizens' Activity Society which was instrumental in acquiring a
bus for the pleasure of the seniors of Cochrane through the Transportation
Grant System. I am now in charge of organizing and coordinating bus tours for
the seniors of Cochrane. Our trips include day trips, overnights, two or three
days, and up to one-week outings.

I belong to the Big Hill Artisans Guild which is involved with the Bethany Care
Centre (Nursing Home and Lodge) in Cochrane with different types of crafts. I
also continue my hobby at home of decorated china of all sorts, including
souvenir plates of historic events such as Irvine's 75th Anniversary, Water
Valley's Oldest Church, Cochrane Ranche Historic Site "Men of Vision", and hand
painted scenery on vases using a special technique, and many other crafts.

I have also enjoyed some extensive traveling to such places as Alaska and the
Yukon, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, the Hawaiian Islands, Vancouver to Ontario
with many points between, Florida, New Orleans, Washington, D.C., the Bahamas,
and hopefully, more to follow.

My dad's motto, which he lived by and taught his children, was as follows:

  Many a man faileth
  Because his 'wishbone'
  Is where his 'backbone'
  Ought to be.

He never wished for anything that he didn't work to accomplish. He wasn't
always successful - but he tried. It is a wonderful motto to follow!

Dorothy Maud Woodward

I was born Dorothy Maud Woodward on 29 March 1925, fourth living child of Agnes
and Albert Woodward. I attended grades one to nine in the old two-room school
in Irvine, grades ten and eleven in the old city hall across the tracks. The
first year of grade 12 we went to Medicine Hat High School. Because of the war,
there was no teacher in Irvine. My last year of grade 12 was spent in Irvine in
1944.

I attended U. of A. 1944-45 then returned to Medicine Hat where I worked at
Crystal Dairy as tab technician, then at the Suffield Exp. Station in the same
capacity. There I met Ernest Edward Amero, a divorced man with three little
girls, Edith, Esther, and Edna. We married 25 March 1950 and lived in Medicine
Hat. Ralph was born 10 December 1950.

The section where Ernest worked was disbanded in 1953. In June that year Edith
ran away and we were never able to find her.

In December 1953 we moved to Long Beach, California where Ernie found work in
the aircraft industry. We leased a motel in 1954 for a year. In 1955 we started
our own jewelry store in Lomita where we had bought our first home. Eldon was
born that fall, I December 1955. Heidi was born 5 December 1957 and Lynol, 24
November 1959. We sold our Lomita home and moved to Torrance in 1962. In 1968
we sold out everything and moved to Buhl, Idaho where we had bought a jewelry
store. Buhl is a small city of some 3500 people near Twin Falls. It is an
irrigated desert farming and dairy area, growing corn for the Green Giant plant
in Buhl, sugar beets for Amalgamated Sugar Plant in Twin Falls, famous Idaho
potatoes, alfalfa hay for the dairy farms, and boasting the largest rainbow
trout farms in the world.

We operated the jewelry store until the fall of 1982 when we closed out because
of Ernie's poor health. He had diabetes, a heart condition and, in 1984, was
operated on for lung cancer. We spent the winter of 1984-85 in warm Arizona so
his lung could heal but on the way home, in Las Vegas on 23 March 1985, he died
of a massive heart attack.

I continue to live on my five acre farm growing fruits and vegetables. My
hobbies started with knitting, crocheting and embroidery as a child, Over the
years I have added macrame, leather tooling, ceramics, miniature houses, and
sculpture. I also like to write poetry. While Ernie was alive our chief
recreation was motorcycling.

My children are all married and gone their own ways.

Esther married Richard Cirks 7 June 1957, has one girl and one granddaughter,
and lives in Oyama, B.C.

Ralph married Elsie Hennessey 3 March 1968, has one boy and one girl, and lives
in Redding, California.

Edna married Dan Edwards 29 January 1970, has no children, and lives in Long
Beach, California.

Heidi married Michael Hadley 26 June 1974, has four girls and one boy, and
lives in Lompoc, California.

Eldon married Bonnie Pinkston 4 July 1976, has two boys and one girl, and lives
in Redding, California.

Lynol married Holly Hallstrom 13 November 1982, has one boy and lives in
Pacific, Washington, a suburb of Seattle.

Roy Woodward

I attended Irvine School and graduated from there in 1947. Following this, I
attended and graduated from Olds Agricultural College.

I worked for one year at the Lethbridge Research Station. I was then employed
as assistant chemist for the Alberta Linseed Oil Company in Medicine Hat.

In July of 1954, I was hired by the Provincial Government, Improvement District
Branch, to carry out the general reassessment of farm land in ID #1 and #22
(now MDI). A transfer to Calgary in 1958 followed. Here I was employed as
assessor for the Department of Municipal Affairs.

I returned to Medicine Hat in 1968 as District Assessment Supervisor to open an
assessment office. I was promoted to Regional Assessment Manager, responsible
for all assessments in the southeast region of the province. I retired from
Government service in May of 1987.

In June of 1953, I married Reita Odenbach and we raised two girls, Deborah and
Roxanne.

Gordon and Edna Wunsch

Gordon and Edna Wunsch were married at Medicine Hat May 2, 1965. Gordon's
father emigrated from Russia and his mother from  North Dakota. They
homesteaded south of Elkwater and raised eight children there.

Gordon was born south of Elkwater in 1927 and took his schooling at Lebanon
School. He ranched and ran a sawmill until 1963 when he came to work for the
Park at Elkwater. In 1968 he became mail contractor from Elkwater to Irvine
(which he still is) and owned and operated Elkwater Express to Medicine Hat,
Irvine and Walsh until 1978.

In 1965 he took charge of Elkwater Alliance Church (which Edna had led for
seven years) and he has been lay pastor there for 24 years.

Edna was born in Regina in 1921 and took all her schooling there including five
years of Bible College before coming to Medicine Hat to help in the church and
work at Eatons for 15 years (1950- 1965). In 1965 she married Gordon and came
to live at Elkwater. Edna operated the Elkwater Post Office as Postmaster for
11 years until they moved to the Irvine District in 1979. She then was
Postmaster at Walsh for seven years until she retired in December 1986.

Gordon ran a school bus to Irvine (1979-1988) from Walsh and later to Irvine
from Dunmore. He is presently a seed specialist and salesman for Prairie Seeds
of Nisku, Alberta.

Gordon and Edna are far more interested in the future than the past. Life gets
better as it goes along.

At 16 years of age Edna decided to follow God and let him plan her life. Gordon
found God at age 33 and has followed him ever since. Now in their 60's they can
say that it was the wisest decision they ever made. They have enjoyed
everything that they have ever done together but the ministry has been their
greatest joy and life has been very good with God.

Christof and Pauline (Krauss) Yanke

The Christof Yanke family moved into the Irvine district from the Norton
district in March 1952. They had purchased a section of land along with a
section of leased land from Gilf Pahl who had acquired it from Harry Jacobsen.
During the first year some improvements were made to the house, such as a
kitchen, which his wife Pauline thought might prove useful, and two bedrooms
for their children, Ray and Linda. An older daughter, Melba, had already
married and lived in Medicine Hat.

Chris, as he was commonly called, experienced ten years of relatively good
crops as did most farmers near him during the fifties. This relative prosperity
allowed him and his family to retire from farming in 1961. Chris bought a house
in Irvine directly across from the school and moved his family into their new
home in the fall. He and Pauline lived at this residence until the spring of
1965, when they moved to the village of Elkwater.

William and Martha (Herman) Yanke
by Doreen Otto

My dad, William Yanke, was born in October 1910 in Gros Ventre, Alberta. He was
one of nine children born to Christoph and Katherine Yanke.

My mom, Martha Yanke, was born in January 1909 in the Newburg district. She is
the eldest of five children born to Samuel and Bertha Herman.

Martha and William Yanke - 1978 (pic)

Dad lived with his parents and helped with the farming. Then he met Mom and
they were married on March 18, 1932. They farmed with Dad's parents for awhile.
They had one child, Doreen, who was born in 1933. They then lived on several
rented farms for approximately fourteen years. In 1948, they purchased and
lived on the Emanuel Sturm farm.

In August 1958, a team of scientists from the natural history branch of the
National Museum of Canada, Ottawa discovered an almost intact skeleton of a
Chasmosaurus dinosaur on a hillside in the Ross Creek area. It took nine days
to remove the skeleton which measured about 15 feet in length.

Dinosaur found in the hills, William Yanke farm (pic)

They continued to farm there until the spring of 1963, at which time they sold
the farm and retired in Medicine Hat.

Dad became ill in 1979 and passed away on August 15th. Mom still resides in her
home in Medicine Hat.

Gottlieb and Christina (Broneske) Zaiser

Gottlieb Zaiser and his wife, Christina (Broneske), were one of the many
families who immigrated to Canada from Bessarabia, Russia in the early part of
the 1890's. They landed in Winnipeg, Manitoba where they lived for a number of
years before moving across the Prairies to homestead near Josephsburg, and from
there to Irvine.

Gottlieb and Christina Zaiser (pic)

Gottlieb and Christina had 13 children, seven of whom survived and grew up at
Irvine. They were Rosalee, Lydia, Emanuel, Albert, John, Dave and Emma (Joyce).
Joyce, who was born in 1900, is now in 1988, the only survivor. There are
approximately 20 grandchildren and many great-grandchildren.

Gottlieb was a Baptist, and besides being a farmer at Josephsburg, he traveled
the country preaching the Gospel and later turned his hand to business
enterprises in Irvine.

In March 1904, he opened a Land Office and became a Justice of the Peace and an
agent for one of the Medicine Hat flour mills. In April of that year he opened
a farm implement office.

Zaiser's Farm Machinery, Gottlieb and Emanuel 3rd and 4th from left (pic)

Zaiser brothers, Emanuel 3rd from top and John below and left (pic)

In May 1904, he was allowed to sell marriage licenses. He must have also
continued his farm connections as the Medicine Hat News of May 1906 reports
that he made the first sale at the new Farmers Market, selling a pig for 100 a
pound.

In April 1908, the first meeting of the Agricultural Society was held in Irvine
and Gottlieb was appointed agent for the Society.

Zaiser Implement Business - 2nd Gottlieb, 5th Emanuel Zaiser (pic)

On January 1, 1913, together with his son Emanuel, he was licensed to sell real
estate. The cost of the license was $25.

He was always very interested in all community affairs and took an active part
until 1917 when they left Irvine.

Their oldest son Emanuel married Emma Roloff in 1911 and worked in the store
operated by her father. Emma died on March 15, 1912.

On September 18, 1912, Emanuel married Theresa Schmidt.

Medicine Hat News items of March 1914 show John Zaiser as a member of the local
Fire Brigade in Irvine and his younger brother, Albert, as a young boxer.

In 1916 the family moved to Leader, Saskatchewan.

Henry and Katherine (Schultz) Zeller

Henry and Katherine (Schultz) Zeller were both born in Bessarabia, Russia. The
family originally consisted of 11 children, seven of whom were born in "the old
country". Of these seven, twin boys died in infancy and three other boys died
during a flu epidemic in 1911. Therefore when Henry and Katherine came to
Canada in December of 1912, they brought only two children with them, Ida and
John. Four more children were born in Canada: Mary, Arthur, Martha and Olga.
The youngest daughter, Olga, died of measles in 1924, at two years of age. The
surviving five children lived in the Irvine area between the years of 1921 to
the mid 1930's.

Zeller brothers and sisters: Back: Art, John Zeller; Front: Mary Herter, Ida
Krause, Martha Carruth (pic)

Originally, when the Zeller family arrived in Canada, they settled in the
Kingcourth, Saskatchewan area. In 1921, Henry Zeller purchased a farm located
three and a half miles north of Irvine. The purchase was made from Sam
Kalmbach, but the farm was better known as the Baumbach homestead. While living
here, all five children either walked or rode horses to attend Wilkinson
School. Henry Zeller remained here with his family until retiring to Medicine
Hat in 1930. For six years after their father's retirement, John and Art farmed
the land together and then Art took over as sole operator.

Ida married Henry Frey in 1928 and had two daughters; their second daughter,
Esther, died in 1944. Now widowed, Ida lives in Chilliwack, British Columbia.

John married Mary Bollinger in 1930 and had two sons and two daughters. One of
their sons, Richard, died in 1966. They presently are living in Medicine Hat.

Mary married Dan Herter in 1931. They were blessed with five boys, and live in
Medicine Hat.

Martha married Alex Mann in 1932 and had one son. In 1943 she was remarried to
John Carruth. Now widowed, she lives in Medicine Hat.

Arthur married Rachel Doering in 1941 and had two sons and five daughters. The
older son, Kenneth, died in 1965.

Art and Rachel (Doering) Zeller

Arthur Zeller is a long-time resident of the Irvine district, coming here at
the age of five, and remaining to the present day. He is the son of the late
Henry and Katherine (Schultz) Zeller.

Rachel Doering was the youngest daughter of Nathaniel and Justina Doering, the
only Doering child who stayed in Irvine all her life.

Rachel Doering and Arthur Zeller were married in February of 1941. In those
years, the area was just starting to recuperate from The Dirty Thirties and the
farmers had to put in a lot of long, hard hours to try to get ahead. For Art
and Rachel this meant raising chickens, milking many cows (without the aid of
milking machines), putting crops in every year, and threshing and harvesting,
without the big equipment that is so commonly in use today. In addition to
this, Art and Rachel were devoted to building a second generation of "Zellers"
to live in the Irvine community. Their family consisted of two boys, Kenneth
and James and five daughters, Shirley, Betty, Olivia, Judy, and Joan.

Donald "Kenneth" married Donna Herman in 1963. They purchased a farm six miles
north of Irvine and had two boys. When Kenneth passed away in 1965, Donna moved
her young family to Medicine Hat. She was later remarried to Harvey Jacober,
and added a daughter to her family.

Art and Rachel (Doering) Zeller, February 11, 1941 (pic)

Zeller Family - 1946: Back: Rachel, Art holding Betty; Front: Shirley, Kenneth
(pic)

Shirley married Elmer Hagel in 1961. They have three sons and two daughters and
have settled in Irvine.

Art Zeller Family: Back: Shirley, Kenneth, Betty, Olivia; Front: Joan, Art,
James, Rachel, Judy (pic)

Betty married Mel Boschee in 1964. They presently live in Foremost, and have
one son and one daughter.

Olivia married Bill Lucas in 1970. They have lived in Irvine since that time,
and have one son and one daughter.

Joan married Gary Bruce in 1972. They lived in Thompson, Manitoba and had one
son. In 1987, Joan was remarried to Gordon Collard. They have one daughter and
are making Redcliff their home.

Judy married Ed Stock in 1974. They have two daughters and one son, and live on
a farm east of Medicine Hat.

James married Janet Ziebart in 1984. They now have two sons and live on the
same farm that Henry Zeller purchased when he came to Alberta.

Art and Rachel retired to the town of Irvine in 1983. They treated themselves
to many trips, not only in Canada and the United States, but also to Europe.
However, they were never too busy to have time for their family and friends.
They also became involved in numerous community clubs and events. To mention a
few, the United Church Choir, the 4-H Club, the Chinook Club, and the New
Horizons Organization. Art has also been very active in the past, being the
Cypress School Board Trustee for 18 years and mayor of Irvine for one term.

In August of 1987, Rachel passed away. Art continues to live in Irvine, leading
a healthy and full life. He continues to travel, be involved in community
events, and help on his son's farm. In his spare time, he enjoys spending time
with his family and friends.

Rachel and Art Zeller 40th Anniv. - February 11, 1981 (pic)

The second generation of Zellers to be raised in the Irvine community has grown
and moved on to their own life styles, and to building a third generation.
Unfortunately though, out of these Zellers, there have been only four boys born
to carry on the Zeller name. Only two, Nicholas James and Mitchel Alan Zeller,
are presently living here. Being only three years old right now, Nicholas is
not even thinking about taking over the family farm. But eventually, if he does
decide to stay, he will feel the same pride that Art Zeller feels whenever he
sees his grandsons playing in the yard - the pride in knowing that the great
grandfather, the grandfather, and the father have worked together, almost as a
team, to make the Zeller farm a successful operation, with the great
grandmother, the grandmother, and the mother making it a comfortable place to
call home. May the tradition continue!

Theodore and Hanna (Ulrich) Ziegler

Theodore Ziegler was born in Russia on November 1, 1883, son of Jacob and
Magdelina Ziegler, to a family of seven brothers and four sisters. His father
worked for the city as county clerk and his mother was a homemaker. All the
boys had to have army training.

At the age of 26 Theodore Ziegler decided he would like to come to America. He
had a brother living in North Dakota so that's where he immigrated. He did not
like it there as the winters were very cold and the snow was deep. They had to
shovel tunnels from the house to the barn. Theodore had a brother living in
Thelma, Alberta so in 1910 he came to Canada, and got a job working for Jim
English.

In the year 1911 he moved to Irvine where he worked at carpentry, his trade in
Russia. That same year he took up a homestead in the SE 30-12-2-4.

Hanna Ulrich immigrated to Canada with her parents, John and Fedricka Ulrich.
They took up a homestead about 20 miles north of Irvine. There they built a
house of rock and sod. The same material was used for other buildings.

Theodore Ziegler house on homestead (pic)

Irvine was the closest town for people living in the Hilda and Schuler areas,
therefore, the Ulrichs had to do all their shopping in Irvine. It was here in
Irvine that Hanna got a job working for Mrs. Carl Beny.

Theodore and Hanna Ziegler (pic)

Hanna Ulrich met Theodore Ziegler in Irvine and wedding plans were made for
June 25, 1911. After the wedding Theodore Ziegler started to build their home
on the homestead, plus doing other jobs. They lived in Irvine until 1915 when
they moved to the farm with their two children, Edith and Charles. Four more
children were born on the farm, Helen, Bill, Edna and Margret.

Times were hard, so Theodore took on jobs building for people in the districts
north and south of Irvine. If these buildings were ever torn down, the initials
T.Z. might be found somewhere.

The Ziegler homestead was a handy stopover for homesteaders traveling from the
Hilda and Schuler areas to Irvine. Since there were no roads and fences were
few they would travel across country creating many wagon trails. Some of these
trails can still be found across the hills. Sometimes a storm would come up or
the horses played out due to the deep snow or long trips.

One favorite story often told was of one couple in particular. "Mamma" not
wanting to miss a trip to Irvine, which wasn't often, took the foot warmer,
quilts and all the warm things she could find and along she would go. On their
way home, a snow storm came up. They got lost and ended up at the Zieglers'.
Mamma's husband, "Papa", asked if they could stay until the storm let up. The
men put the horses in the barn, got warmed up, and had supper. About ten
o'clock, it was still blowing hard. Papa let out a gasp and said, "Oh, no! I
forgot all about Mamma!" Running to the sleigh, they found her still wrapped up
and sound asleep. Waking up, she looked up and said, "Are we home now?"

The Ziegler children went to Wilkinson School, which was built on the quarter
next to their homestead. When the snow was deep, they would drive to school
with the team and sleigh, then turn the team around to go home on their own.
Later Wilkinson School was moved to Irvine and the children from the area were
bussed to school. The Theodore Ziegler family continued to farm with their sons
and daughters until 1938, when they moved back to Irvine with their younger
daughters, Edna and Margret, who finished their school years there.

Charles took over the farm, the girls left home and found jobs to help along
through the hard times, and Bill joined the Army. From 1940 to 1950, Theodore
Ziegler drove a school bus from Dunmore to Irvine. The first bus was a half-ton
truck with a wooden shell, the entrance was at the rear, and the outside of the
windows was covered with chicken wire. The next van was a more modern type. He
always had his passengers under control with no hanky-panky. He had nice treats
for the children at Christmas and Easter. All the children loved Grandpa.

When Theodore retired from school bus driving, he and the other old gentlemen
of Irvine had a social hour at Wiedemann's Store, where many tall tales were
told.

In 1948 Mrs. Hanna Ziegler became ill and had to live in a nursing home in
Medicine Hat. Theodore then sold the big house and bought a smaller one.

He would come to the farm as he loved the harvest. One day while driving the
big grain truck, the hot exhaust pipe started a fire in the high stubble. He
was saved by the hired man's quick thinking.

Theodore Ziegler lived in Irvine until his passing in 1957, and eight days
later his wife, Hanna, passed away.

Charles and Katharina Ziegler have three children, Sharion, Stan (deceased),
and Leslie.

Edith and Walter Tate (deceased) of B.C. had three children, Harold, Barbara,
and Janice.

Bill (William), and his wife Phyllis had three children, William, Katherine,
and Jim. They live in Calgary. After the war ended in 1944, Bill went to Banff
and worked as a butcher. From there he went to Calgary and had his own butcher
business. When he got married he moved to Edmonton where he had a store and
butcher shop. He died at the young age of 44.

Helen and Niel (deceased) Tomalison of Edmonton had two children, Tommy and
Robert.

Edna and Stafford (deceased September 13, 1988) Leflar of Medicine Hat had
three children, Marion, David, and Carol.

Margret Olesen lives in Claresholm.

Charles and Kay (Katherina Vossler) Ziegler

Charles Ziegler, son of Theodore and Hanna Ziegler, was born August 4, 1914,
the day World War I was declared. They lived on a homestead four and a half
miles north of Irvine. Charles had one brother and four sisters, Bill, Edith,
Helen, Edna, and Margret. They all went to Wilkinson School. Charles said all
the fun he had after school was working on the farm helping Dad.

Charles took over the farm in 1938 and farmed and batched for three years. He
hit the poor years when there were no crops, so he took on a job with a survey
crew around Waterton and Pincher Creek. He also did census taking north and
south of Irvine.

Katherina Vossler is the daughter of Martin and Dorthea Vossler, who
homesteaded north of Irvine in 1915. Kay has two brothers and four sisters. She
started school in Olympia and Yakima, Washington and finished at the Many
Island School.

Charles met Katherina Vossler who came to visit relatives. Kay had a job at the
Hotel as a chef. They were married November 14, 1941 in Calgary. The minister
who married them had served in Irvine at one time. They spent their honeymoon
in Edmonton. They moved to the farm and started farming. Their first year was
very good, some cattle and a tractor were bought. From there things got better
and no hand outs were needed.

Charles Ziegler Family: Back: Stan, Sharon, Leslie; Front: Charles and Kay (pic)

They started their little family, Sharion was born in 1942, Stanley, in 1944,
and Leslie, in 1946.

Sharion went to Irvine School. After graduation she went to Nursing School and
then took Nursing Aide. She married Barney Heather in 1964. They have three
children, Shield, Wayne, and Brian, and they live in Calgary.

Stanley finished his schooling, went working and then came back to the farm. He
married Lexy Lane in 1968 and they had four children, Stacey, Justin, Garth,
and Dixie. They farmed for some time, then sold and moved to Pine Lake where
they bought a tourist camp. Lexy and the children still live there, as our
Stanley (deceased) left us in 1986.

Leslie went to grade nine and quit school to help his dad on the farm. He
married Nadine Papove in 1969. They have one son, Russell, and live in Irvine.
Leslie went into the contracting business and Nadine is a substitute teacher.

When the children were old enough they went to Sunday School. They were in the
Beef and Grain Clubs and won some prizes. They tried hard to keep up with the
clubs. They enjoyed their trips and camps.

4-H Beef Club: Stan, Sharon, Les Ziegler and their calves (pic)

Charles and Kay were members of the church, Home and School, and United
Farmers. They had a Birthday Club where once a month they either went to the
neighbors or their own home for card parties. They had some very good times on
the farm.

They also had some disasters. One day a heavy cloud came into the sky and in a
few minutes a sheet of ice came down. It destroyed a lot of the poultry and
broke all the windows on the west side of all the buildings. Another time a
hurricane came and took a building and blew it all over the place. It turned
the bobsled upside down.

Four Generations: Back: Kay Ziegler (grandmother), Sharon Heather (mother);
Front: Dorothea Vossler (great grandmother), Shiela Heather (baby) (pic)

In 1957 they planted a shelter belt. The trees did very well in spite of poor
conditions and very little rain. Charles bought a three-ton truck and went
trucking, hauling coal from the mine out by Echo Dale Park.

In 1969 they bought a house in Medicine Hat where they still live. They still
have the farm and some cattle, which Charles looks after for his pastime. He
loves the cattle sales and belongs to the Cypress Club. Kay has been very
active in Medicine Hat. She worked for the Auxiliary Hospital, curled, golfed,
did art and pottery, and still loves the garden.

Give Thanks Wild Rose Country

It matters not how far I roam,
My thoughts go back to my country home.
In the land of the rockies and the rose,
With all the beauty of nature's clothes.
I'm happy when I'm in the west,
Because it's where I feel the best.
There's summer rains and winter snows,
And through an arch the chinook blows.
From my home upon a hill,
When the night is dark, and the air is still,
I look up into the sky,
To the home of Him on high.
A coyote yodels to a northern light,
And a great owl talks sometimes at night.
When a crocus comes, I know it's spring,
And the birds that can, begin to sing.
Warmed by the sun and kissed by the rain,
The wild rose grows on our western plain.
There's nothing pleases my eyes and nose,
As much as does our Prairie Rose.
On the morning air rings a stallion's call,
And colts and calves run around 'till fall.
When on my horse or in my car,
I keep on course by the great North Star.
After a summer of sun and rain,
My fields are covered with grass and grain,
When I start to harvest I never stop,
I stack my hay and store my crop.
I came with two hands from my Mother,
One for myself and one for another.
I use them both when I am able,
And help with food for every table.
I know not when the call may come,
To answer for the things I've done.
But when my work is ended and I'm laid beneath the sod,
I hope to go where my friends have gone, to be with them and God.
